text:
Senators write: “…The definitions proposed by the SNPRM [Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking] would remove federal protections for 80 percent of streams in the United States and 95 percent of individual wetlands, which makes a mockery of the congressional intent behind the Clean Water Act.”

November 7, 2026 - Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works’ Fisheries, Water, and Wildlife Subcommittee, and Ed Markey (D-Mass.) are calling on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to abandon their new proposal that threatens to harm public health and leave communities vulnerable to flooding and loss of access to clean drinking water.

The EPA’s new proposal to revise the definition of the Waters of the United States (WOTUS) rule replaces the proposed November 2025 standard with an even more extreme one, defining “relatively permanent” to mean “perennial” waters, stripping federal protections for hundreds of bodies of waters. Previously, in January 2026, the Senators urged the agencies to reverse this proposal.

“As we explained then, excluding these waters from federal protection threatens drinking water, increases downstream pollution and flood risk, and shifts substantial costs onto states, communities, and ratepayers. We are disappointed that your agencies have not only chosen to disregard all of these concerns, but have put out a second, more extreme proposal that does even more harm. We urge you to abandon this effort altogether and remember your statutory responsibilities to protect drinking water, public health, and the environment,” the Senators wrote in a letter to the EPA.

EPA’s latest proposal goes further to eliminate safeguards on bodies of waters that were already reduced by the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Sackett v. EPA. Additionally, the Senators raise concern with the subsequent harms this proposal will have on state and tribes’ capacity to manage waters, as well as on American households, who will bear the financial costs.

“…Pollution does not respect the arbitrary boundaries laid out in these proposals. When upstream waters lose federal protection, downstream communities do not cease experiencing their effects of that loss…the costs of additional pollution, degraded drinking water sources and the associated health risks, diminished flood protection, and lost aquatic habitat are shifted to states, Tribes, municipalities, water utilities, and ultimately the American taxpayer,” the Senators wrote.

“The Clean Water Act was enacted to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” Proposing to systematically exclude waters known to be critical to that integrity ignores science and defeats the purpose of the Act…We urge you to abandon this disastrous SNPRM as well as the 2025 proposal and leave the 2023 conforming rule in place,” the Senators concluded.

The EPW Committee’s Ranking Member, U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), also signed the letter.

The full text of the letter can be found here and below.

Dear Administrator Zeldin and Mr. Forsgren:

We write to express our serious concern regarding the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ September 9, 2026 Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) that proposes to further narrow which waters would receive federal protections under the Clean Water Act. On January 28, 2026, we urged the agencies to abandon the proposed 2025 waters of the United States (WOTUS) rule. As we explained then, excluding these waters from federal protection threatens drinking water, increases downstream pollution and flood risk, and shifts substantial costs onto states, communities, and ratepayers. We are disappointed that your agencies have not only chosen to disregard all of these concerns, but have put out a second, more extreme proposal that does even more harm. We urge you to abandon this effort altogether and remember your statutory responsibilities to protect drinking water, public health, and the environment.

The core proposal of the SNPRM is to define “relatively permanent” waters to include only perennial waters, which the proposal suggests defining as “having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions.” The SNPRM includes limited exceptions for drought, dry spells, and low tides, and allows only a single interruption of no more than 30 consecutive days annually. The SNPRM also considers a definition of “continuous surface connection” that would require even perennial surface water within a wetland to be continuously connected to a jurisdictional water in order to merit protection as WOTUS.

Limiting “relatively permanent” waters to perennial and interconnected waters would be scientifically indefensible and would put downstream water quality at risk. EPA’s own scientific record demonstrates why. EPA’s review of more than 1,200 peer-reviewed studies concluded that streams are connected to downstream waters regardless of their size or frequency of flow and strongly influence downstream physical, chemical, and biological conditions. That review, and numerous other independent scientific studies, found that perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral tributaries transport water, sediment, nutrients, contaminants, organic material, and organisms through river networks and collectively affect larger downstream waters. Further, the definitions proposed by the SNPRM would remove federal protections for 80 percent of streams in the United States and 95 percent of individual wetlands, which makes a mockery of the congressional intent behind the Clean Water Act.

Your agencies acknowledge these concerns in the SNPRM and recognize the functions served by ephemeral streams. The agencies also acknowledge that the majority of wetlands would not satisfy the supplemental definition of “continuous surface connection,” because most wetlands do not contain perennial surface water. Even more, your agencies concede that the 30-day threshold is not “scientifically-grounded” and is proposed only because it is “easy to administer.” Given these acknowledgements, it appears the entirety of the SNPRM is contradictory— proposing changes that go against the very scientific findings cited in the notice. “Easy to administer” does not justify the neglect of waterways that contribute on average 55% of the water found in larger rivers – the protection of which is the mission of your agencies and the Clean Water Act.

The SNPRM also includes an arbitrary five-year cutoff for waters impacted by drought conditions, a policy that would cause particular harm to more arid regions like the West. After five years of dry conditions, such drought conditions would be treated as the new baseline. As American Rivers explains in its public comment, this would “convert a growing share of currently ‘relatively permanent’ waters to non-jurisdictional status over time, particularly in the West, as droughts lengthen and recur more frequently.”

The agencies justify these contradictions and known harms in part by claiming that the proposal allegedly provides regulatory clarity, giving landowners clearer notice of Clean Water Act obligations. But administrative simplicity cannot provide cover for a scientifically and legally indefensible interpretation of the Clean Water Act, as its primary purpose is to protect waters from pollution. Moreover, this SNPRM would not provide clarity, as it would inevitably lead to litigation and overwhelm state and tribal capacity to manage waters. The agencies acknowledge in the supplemental proposal that “Tribes may disproportionately rely on the Federal Government for water program implementation and enforcement of water quality violations” and “many Tribes are still building capacity and may lack resources to create a Tribal water program.” This SNPRM will remove federal protections for many waters Tribes may care about, thus pulling the rug out from under them.

As we emphasized in January, pollution does not respect the arbitrary boundaries laid out in these proposals. When upstream waters lose federal protection, downstream communities do not cease experiencing their effects of that loss. And states are not going to be able to fill the gaps left by the SNPRM. One state’s hypothetical capacity to regulate their own waters, absent federal law, does not mean as much when an under-resourced, upstream state exports the cost of their water quality remediation downstream. Instead, the costs of additional pollution, degraded drinking water sources and the associated health risks, diminished flood protection, and lost aquatic habitat are shifted to states, Tribes, municipalities, water utilities, and ultimately the American taxpayer. Our previous letter warned that narrowing WOTUS in this manner would transfer responsibility and costs downstream rather than eliminate them. The recent supplemental proposal fails to heed that warning and would multiply these costs to the American people.

text:
This is the fourth and final post in our four-part “BAAJA Blast” series covering the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, released on September 30, 2026. Check out our earlier posts on the bill’s provisions on transmission, offshore wind, and data centers and large loads.

A note on timing. We close out this series in a very different political climate than the one in which we began it. This week’s midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of both congressional chambers starting in January 2027, have called this legislation’s future into question. Will BAAJA disappear into the ether during the lame-duck session? We can’t say for sure. Some House Democrats, including the member in line to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, argue that Democrats could write a better bill next Congress; the bill’s sponsors and major industry groups, on the other hand, are pushing to finish the job this year, and the November 9 Senate cloture vote should be the first real test of whether they can. Come what may, we close out our BAAJA Blast series today with our observations on the bill’s treatment of DERs and VPPs.

On September 30, 2026, Senate negotiators released the text of the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (“BAAJA”). For distributed energy resources (“DERs”) and virtual power plants (“VPPs”), the bill comes at a critical moment. Aggregators (which we call “VPP providers” here) increasingly bundle behind-the-meter resources—which continue to proliferate year-over-year—into VPPs that sell services back to the grid. Yet six years after the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) issued Order No. 2222, several grid operators have yet to fully comply, and VPPs have begun striking deals directly with buyers.

As we have written before, AI-driven load growth is creating immense pressure to activate the demand side of the grid, and deploying VPPs is among the fastest ways to unlock new capacity. If enacted, BAAJA would replace the tariff-by-tariff process under Order No. 2222 with a statutory deadline: Section 2108 would require grid operators to admit qualifying aggregations into their wholesale markets within 18 months, limit utility interference, bar double payment, and fund a voluntary program to streamline local permitting for rooftop solar, batteries, and EV chargers. In our view, Section 2108 would likely get aggregations through the market door faster than Order No. 2222 has; whether it makes operating VPPs in the wholesale markets a durable business, however, would depend on questions the bill leaves to grid operators and states.

Our data center post previewed Section 2108’s basic market-access rule. In this post, we take a closer look at the provision as a whole, even as we note that the bill itself still faces significant hurdles. A Senate cloture vote on the motion to proceed is expected as early as November 9; passage would require 60 votes, and any Senate bill would have to be reconciled with the House’s permitting legislation before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. A promised manager’s amendment could change the text. And again, with this week’s midterm elections turning control over Congress to the Democrats come January 2027, the fate of the bill is even less certain.

What Counts as a DER Under BAAJA

DERs are small generation, storage, or load-management assets on the distribution system, such as rooftop solar, batteries, EV chargers, and smart thermostats. A VPP is a group of DERs that a VPP provider controls through software to act like a single power plant.

Industry observers will be familiar with both these concepts; BAAJA, however, uses neither term. Section 2108, titled “Dispatchable energy systems market access,” instead defines a “qualifying behind-the-meter distributed energy system facility” (a “qualifying BTM DES facility”). The facility must be an energy storage system, fuel cell, generator, or “other resource” that can be brought online within 15 minutes and whose output the grid operator can dispatch on signal. It must sit behind a retail customer’s meter, have a rated capacity of at least 5 kilowatts, and have metering and telemetry sufficient to dispatch and settle it. That equipment need not be owned or installed by the utility and may include device-level equipment such as inverters. A “qualifying BTM DES aggregation” is two or more such facilities with a combined capacity of at least 100 kilowatts.

Points to Watch: The dispatchability test is a question many VPP businesses already grapple with in assembling their aggregations. Standalone rooftop solar would not appear to qualify unless paired with storage. Less clear is whether controllable load, such as a network of smart thermostats, counts as an “other resource” whose “output” can be dispatched. In our view, the better reading is that flexible load able to respond within 15 minutes would qualify, but the text does not say so expressly, and the question could surface in the first round of compliance filings. Separately, the definition includes generators with no emissions condition, so on-site gas units could qualify. This language is worth watching in the promised manager’s amendment.

Wholesale Market Access (New FPA Section 229)

Section 2108 would add a new Section 229 to the Federal Power Act, the foundational statute establishing federal jurisdiction over interstate transmission and wholesale power sales. Beginning 18 months after enactment, it would not be “just and reasonable” (the legal standard FERC uses to evaluate the legality of jurisdictional rates) for any Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”) or Independent System Operator (“ISO”) to maintain rules that prevent a qualifying aggregation from participating in its energy, capacity, or ancillary services markets.

The bill would also declare three specific practices unjust and unreasonable: imposing metering, telemetry, or equipment requirements beyond the statutory definitions; requiring participation in the energy market as a precondition to participation in the capacity market; and requiring a facility to participate jointly with a co-located resource in order to join an aggregation. Each RTO and ISO would have to file compliant market rules within 180 days of enactment, and FERC would have 180 days to approve them or impose changes. FERC would also have to act on complaints alleging noncompliance within 180 days.

Section 2108 is best understood as a legislative fix for Order No. 2222, under which three barriers have persisted: costly metering requirements, unclear rules for resources earning revenue in both state programs and wholesale markets, and distribution utilities’ control over interconnection. Section 2108 would address each directly, though it reaches only behind-the-meter resources, and its fixed deadline would leave far less room for grid operator stakeholder-process delay.

Point to Watch: Compliance filings would be due at 180 days, but the market-access standard would not take effect until 18 months, and it does not depend on a new FERC rulemaking, making it less exposed to the missed-deadline risk that hangs over other provisions. But access is not the same as value. The economics of market participation would turn on details the bill leaves to grid operators, especially how much capacity credit aggregations receive. If accreditation methods discount aggregated resources heavily, aggregations could win market entry and still find margins too thin to justify participating. We expect capacity accreditation to become the main battleground once the access question is settled.

Dual Participation, Not Double Payment

Many DERs already earn money from state programs, such as net metering or a utility demand response program. Section 2108 would let them keep doing so: participation in a state program would not disqualify a facility from wholesale markets, and nothing would require a facility to enter wholesale markets at all. What the bill would bar is “double compensation,” meaning payment from both a wholesale market and a state program for the same service in the same time interval.

Within 180 days, each RTO and ISO would have to file settlement rules that exclude, service by service, any quantity already compensated under a state program. The bill’s own example illustrates the approach: a battery that earns retail credit for energy, but not for capacity or ancillary services, could still earn wholesale capacity and ancillary services revenue, just not wholesale energy revenue. Distribution utilities would have to supply the interval metering and program-participation data needed to make this work, subject to state customer-privacy protections.

VPP providers would carry much of the compliance burden. Each would have to certify which state programs paid each facility and that no double compensation was retained, and those certifications would be treated as statements to FERC for enforcement purposes. FERC would have to order disgorgement of any double compensation and, if it was knowingly retained, could impose penalties of up to three times the amount per day and suspend or terminate participation. Participants would also file public annual reports, due each March 30.

Point to Watch: The enforcement framework cuts both ways for VPP providers. A complainant would bear the burden of proving double compensation occurred or is imminent and could not be avoided through reasonable billing adjustments, and complaints would be limited to five years. But VPP providers should expect to invest in settlement tracking and data systems well before market access takes effect. On balance, we think the framework is workable, but compliance costs and treble-penalty exposure could weigh more heavily on smaller providers.

Distribution Utility Obligations (New FPA Section 230)

Section 2108 would also add a new Section 230 targeting distribution-level obstacles that have kept DERs out of wholesale markets. Within an RTO or ISO footprint, distribution utilities would have to interconnect wholesale-eligible behind-the-meter resources in a timely way, allow them to export, accept the same metering and telemetry data the wholesale market uses, and not use their control of the distribution system or retail sales to block or unreasonably condition market participation. Actions reasonably necessary for safety and reliability would remain permitted. FERC would enforce these obligations and would have to act on complaints within 180 days.

The provision includes significant limits. The interconnection obligation would yield to state law, and FERC would gain no authority over distribution-level interconnection rates or terms. State regulators would decide how wholesale metering data adjusts retail bills. For public power utilities and certain cooperatives, the requirements would be voluntary unless state law requires them. And qualifying a facility would not, by itself, bring it or its retail or distribution service under FERC jurisdiction. In practice, the utility obligations would operate more as a federal default than a guarantee.

Points to Watch:

State regulators would be in the driver’s seat. Because the utility obligations yield to state law, state commissions, such as the New York Public Service Commission for NYISO-area resources, would largely determine how much of the distribution-side benefit reaches aggregations. We expect the provision to work best in states already pushing VPP policy, where the federal default would reinforce existing direction, and least in states whose utilities have resisted aggregation. Developers should track state proceedings as closely as FERC compliance filings.

Data access. VPPs depend on utility distribution data to verify performance and get paid in full. The bill’s data-sharing requirement would help, but it is among the provisions most likely to be honored in form and slow-walked in practice, and its effectiveness would depend on grid operator formats and schedules, state privacy rules, and how quickly FERC acts on complaints.

Beyond Market Access: Local Permitting and Storage

Most rooftop solar, building batteries, and campus microgrids need only local permits, so the bill’s federal environmental review reforms would largely bypass them. Section 2108(e) instead would have the Department of Energy (“DOE”) stand up, within 180 days, a program supporting voluntary, streamlined local permitting and inspection for solar, batteries of at least 2 kilowatt-hours, EV chargers of at least 2 kilowatts, and hydrogen refueling, including an expanded online platform, technical assistance, and possible certification and prizes for participating jurisdictions. The bill would authorize $20 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2031.

Other provisions would ease siting for storage. Adding energy storage at or near an existing transmission or distribution facility would be categorically excluded from review under the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”) and Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, as would reconductoring, which we discussed in our transmission post. The Departments of the Interior and Agriculture would also have to adopt categorical exclusions for batteries on previously disturbed land and for small solar installations on federal property.

Point to Watch: The DOE program would be voluntary for local governments, and its funding would be authorized, not appropriated. At $20 million a year, it is modest relative to the number of permitting jurisdictions nationwide. We see it as a useful nudge toward standardized, faster local permitting rather than a fix, and its impact would depend on whether Congress funds it and how many jurisdictions sign on.

Looking Ahead

For VPP providers and device makers, Section 2108 would offer guaranteed RTO and ISO market access, fewer utility equipment requirements, and a firm deadline, along with real compliance obligations. Building owners could gain a new revenue stream from dispatchable equipment. Utilities would take on new interconnection and data-sharing duties, tempered by state authority. Customers outside RTO and ISO regions, including much of the Southeast and West, would see less direct benefit. An open question is whether the provision ultimately favors storage paired with clean generation or opens a new path for behind-the-meter gas.

So, would it work? We think that, if enacted, Section 2108 would deliver on market access: the deadline would be firm, the standard would be self-executing, and the prohibited practices target the barriers that have stalled Order No. 2222.

It is less likely, on its own, to make VPPs a mainstream grid resource. That outcome would depend on capacity accreditation, on how states use their room to displace the utility obligations, and on whether the dispatchability test is read to include flexible load. Aggregators, device makers, and building owners should expect compliance filings, accreditation proceedings, and state dockets to be where the practical value of Section 2108 is decided, and should plan their engagement accordingly.

This concludes our BAAJA Blast series; thank you for following along. We will continue to track the bill’s progress and its implications for developers, investors, and other market participants.

text:
Australia has been urged to set aside support for its near US$100bn fossil fuel export industries and fight for a global agreement to move away from coal, gas and oil as its climate change minister, Chris Bowen, leads negotiations between nearly 200 countries at UN talks this week.

Delegates will gather in the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Monday for Cop31, two weeks of climate talks held amid geopolitical turmoil, with conflict in the Middle East driving an oil price crisis that has raised living costs across the globe.

The talks – which open two months after climate scientists confirmed global heating would reach at least 1.8C – will seek support for a new 2035 electrification goal, backed by Turkey and Australia, to have 35% of final energy use around the world coming from electricity instead of fossil fuels.

Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. About one fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas exports also come from its shores – on par with Qatar, but behind the world’s biggest exporter, the United States. The government expects the export value of the three fuels to be $141bn (US$98bn) this financial year.

Turkey and Australia vied for hosting rights and came to a compromise with Turkey as president of the conference and Australia president of the negotiations themselves.

Bowen, the Cop31 president of negotiations, will try to somehow find consensus across rich fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia and emerging economic giants – including the world’s biggest emitter, China – and poorer vulnerable countries for whom climate change is seen as an existential threat.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter

Speaking to the Guardian on Thursday, Bowen highlighted three areas of focus: minimising overshoot past the 1.5C Paris agreement temperature goal; helping poorer countries to access enough finance to deal with the climate crisis; and the new electrification goal. Ocean protection is likely to be another major theme.

Climate advocates have questioned if, as a major fossil fuel producer, Australia can keep the world moving away from fossil fuels.

Bowen dismissed that notion, saying all countries were dealing with the transition and Australia’s domestic moves away from coal in electricity had been recognised internationally.

Not on the official Cop31 agenda is any mention of countries developing detailed plans to transition away from fossil fuels – a step seen by climate experts as central to limiting the crisis.

The Australian scientist Bill Hare, the chief executive of Climate Analytics and veteran Cop attender, said countries agreed at the 2023 summit that a transition was needed and the president of last year’s climate summit, Brazil, had progressed calls for countries to develop plans to leave fossil fuels behind, even when it couldn’t find consensus at the talks.

“Australia could pitch this up – to continue this process of developing a fossil fuel roadmap. Australia could do that,” said Hare.

“Why should this process stop? That’s a hard political question for Australia to answer. I think [Bowen] needs to be brave at this Cop.”

Brazil published the first global fossil fuel roadmap this week but experts pointed to a lack of benchmarks or timelines.

Hare said a “critical issue” at Cop31 was to address the 1.5C overshoot.

“Fossil fuels are critical to that because they are about 75% of global emissions. We can’t limit overshoot without a very rapid transition away from fossil fuels. Whatever the theatre of the talks is, this has to be the central point.”

Climate and energy policy is divisive in Australia with the conservative Coalition, in opposition, pledging to scrap the 2050 net zero emissions target, and the rightwing populist party One Nation rejecting the science of climate change entirely. Both are vocal in their objections to renewable energy projects.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will need to thread this political needle when he speaks during a two-day leaders summit at the talks.

Cover decision

Turkey and Australia want the talks to end with an overarching agreement from all countries – known as a cover decision. The UN talks work by consensus, meaning every country must agree before resolutions are passed.

Prof Frank Jotzo, an economist and climate policy expert at the Australian National University, said he doubted all participants would agree on mapping a route away from fossil fuels because “those countries that want to keep that out of the process will simply prevail in having that struck off the agenda”.

“The Australian government will want to play this very safe,” he said. “I think the Australian presidency will have a strong focus on an orderly procedure with no surprises.”

More than 500 mostly Australian scientists and academics wrote to Albanese this week pleading for an end to coal and gas approvals and asking for a legislated plan to phase out fossil fuel production that protects workers and communities.

“Australia cannot credibly lead on climate abroad nor ensure national nor regional security while it expands coal and gas at home,” the letter said. “We ask you to be brave, to be bold, and to act with the urgency that the evidence demands.”

They wrote that championing access to climate finance while approving new coal and gas projects “invites the charge of hypocrisy”.

Kathryn McCallum, the director of strategy at the Climate Action Network Australia, said the Albanese government had approved 38 coal, oil and gas projects since it was elected in 2022. Those developments include extending the life of one of the biggest gas projects on the planet – Woodside’s giant North West Shelf processing facility in Western Australia – until 2070.

“Australia has the opportunity to play a climate leadership role, but as one of the biggest producers and exporters that’s expanding coal and gas production at an enormous scale, it doesn’t pass the pub test to talk about limiting overshoot while approving corporate proposals for new coal and gas,” McCallum said.

“A lot of people are asking if Australia is serious [about climate action] because of these approvals.

“Australia will be right in the spotlight. The Australian government needs to stand up to the corporations that want to export this coal and gas, and act in the global interest.”

text: Democrats swept in the U.S. midterm elections this week, and that could be a boon for several groups of stocks, according to Wall Street analysts. On Tuesday, Democrats flipped seven Senate and more than 40 House seats, giving the left-leaning party majority representation in Congress. That means Democrats will have greater say over legislative priorities on Capitol Hill — a power that has big implications for companies and their stocks. Stocks were volatile in the trading sessions following Election Day. The S & P 500 finished the week down 2.7%. Tech stocks got hit particularly hard, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 3.4% during the same period. The 30-stock Dow Jones Industrial Average fared better, only sliding 0.9% during the week. However, Wall Street has identified some potential winners amid the churn. A blue tsunami could bolster U.S. solar, airline and healthcare stocks, among others, several analysts said in notes to clients. Here are a few stocks they highlighted. Drone-related stocks With more Democrats soon to be in power, drone makers and drone battery manufacturers are likely to see their shares trade higher, according to William Blair. The investment firm noted that Democrats have stated their intention to lend more support to Ukraine in its war against Russia, which could lead to more money flowing to companies that make drones and the parts that power them. AMPX 3M mountain Amprius Technologies stock over the past three months One such firm that stands to benefit is drone battery manufacturer, Amprius Technologies , per William Blair. Roughly 50% of the company’s revenue has been directly tied to Ukraine or to allies supporting the effort in 2026, according to the investment firm. “We view Amprius as a midterm winner as the ‘blue wave’ brings more support for Ukraine, a large driver of Amprius’s demand,” analyst Mark Shooter said Friday. “The midterm outcome could reverse the U.S. position from decreasing to increasing Ukraine funding, de-risk demand from this conflict, and offer expansion to Amprius revenues in 2027.” Shooter has an outperform rating on Amprius. The stock has pulled back more than 22% over the past three months, but added 1.5% this week. Clean energy stocks Renewable energy firms, which generate energy via solar, wind or hydro power, could get a boost following the midterm elections, according to several industry analysts. “Some smaller policy tailwinds are possible: Congress is still considering a permitting reform bill ... [which has been] flagged as benefiting clean energy and geothermal,” Wolfe Research analyst Tobin Marcus said Thursday. “And some incoming governors are proposing renewable mandates for data center power.” FSLR 3M mountain First Solar performance over the past three months One stock that stands out is First Solar , according to William Blair. “Democrats swept the midterms, winning both chambers of Congress and flipping five governorships in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada, as of the time of writing,” analyst Jed Dorsheimer wrote in a Thursday note to clients. “Ultimately, we believe this will unlock support at a local level for more utility-scale solar procurement and siting.” The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act , which aims to expedite federal permit issuances to solar projects and expand grid development, is likely to become law with Democrats in power, the analyst added. Dorsheimer upgraded First Solar to outperform from market perform. Shares of the solar panel maker were up 15% over the past week, though the stock is down 23% so far in 2026. Healthcare Healthcare stocks are also poised to benefit from Democrats’ congressional gains. Making medical care accessible is a major aim of the political party’s agenda, which bodes well for some healthcare stocks, according to Wolfe Research. “Presumptive Speaker Jeffries has explicitly indicated that [lawmakers’] ‘first 100 hours’ agenda will include fully repealing the Medicaid cuts … and restoring the expanded [Affordable Care Act] premium tax credits that expired at the end of 2025,” Wolfe’s Marcus wrote Thursday. “So it makes perfect sense for investors to be focused on healthcare after the blue wave.” The analyst noted that the potential tailwinds could be greatest for hospitals, although it could take “quite a while” for those to materialize. Shares of hospital operators HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services have popped 4.6% and 11.1%, respectively, since the beginning of this week. More broadly, healthcare stocks have surged as of late. The Vanguard Health Care Index Fund ETF (VHT) has climbed more than 10% over the past three months as investors have rotated out of technology stocks and embraced more defensive plays due to credit risks tied to the ongoing artificial intelligence buildout. Airline stocks Airline stocks could rally following a big blue sweep this election season, according to Citigroup. “Investors … may be missing the effect that a dramatic increase in consumer sentiment among Democrats in the wake of the midterms could have on consumer discretionary demand, such as air travel,” Citigroup analyst John Godyn said Wednesday in a note to clients. “As long as Republican consumer sentiment does not collapse 1:1 with any improvement in Democrat consumer sentiment (and implicitly assuming that Democrats and Republicans travel roughly a similar amount per capita), one could argue that the midterms may give airlines a boost in demand.” The U.S. Global Jets ETF (JETS) , which invests in U.S. and international airlines, has risen about 2% since Election Day. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines led gains among airlines this past week, jumping 8.8% and 8.2%, respectively. Specialty REITs A few specialty Real Estate Investment Trusts are likely to rally, according to Barclays. “Voters largely favored candidates and ballot measures that oppose data center development … [which] could slow the pace of industry-wide construction,” analyst Brendan Lynch said Wednesday in a note to clients. “We view our coverage as net beneficiaries from the pricing power that limitations on construction will create.” Lynch pointed to Equinix , Iron Mountain and Digital Realty Trust as three potential beneficiaries of that shift. “Our sense is that EQIX and IRM’s pipelines are essentially fully approved, and DLR faces only limited permitting risk for projects that would commence years from now,” the analyst wrote. Those three REITs have fallen between 4% and 13% over the past three months, largely due to rising interest rates that have diminished the appeal of some dividends and lowered property valuations. However, the pullback offers a good opportunity to scoop up shares, according to Barclays.

text:
Autoblog and Yahoo may earn commission from links in this article.

As the American market gears up for a shift in zero-emission mobility, BMW is sweetening the deal for its upcoming lineup. The German luxury automaker officially launched a new public charging promotion designed specifically for eligible 2027 electric vehicles, including the all-new iX3, the midsize i5, and the flagship i7 sedan. The program is designed to alleviate range anxiety and provide immediate value to buyers and lessees transitioning to electric drivetrains.

The new BMW ChargingNetwork package provides exactly $500 in total public charging credits, but the funds are strategically divided. Buyers receive a $300 credit that is universally accepted across more than 15 major public charging providers, including heavy hitters like ChargePoint, EVgo, and Shell Recharge. The remaining $200 is dedicated exclusively to the rapidly expanding IONNA network. Furthermore, the promotion includes a complimentary one-year BMW Membership at IONNA, which guarantees a 25 percent discount on all charging sessions during the 12-month trial period.

Infrastructure and Fast Charging

This targeted incentive program arrives at a crucial moment for the industry. While the US is adding EV chargers at a record pace, navigating multiple payment apps and networks remains a significant pain point for new owners. By integrating this $500 credit directly into the My BMW digital wallet, the automaker streamlines the entire process. Once enrolled through the proprietary app, the credits are automatically applied to eligible charging sessions without requiring the driver to swipe a physical credit card.

Beyond the financial incentives, the 2027 model year represents a massive technical leap for BMW. The upcoming Neue Klasse architecture, underpinning vehicles like the i3 sedan and iX3, utilizes an advanced 800-volt electrical system capable of incredibly fast 400 kW charging speeds. Additionally, BMW has confirmed that all 2027 electric models will feature a native NACS (North American Charging Standard) port, officially solidifying BMW's choice of Tesla's Supercharger network while still including a CCS adapter for legacy stations.

Timing is Everything

While the $500 package is a fantastic perk, prospective buyers must pay close attention to the fine print. According to the official terms, both the charging credits and the discounted IONNA membership expire exactly one year from the date the vehicle is sold or leased. The countdown clock starts ticking the moment you take delivery of the car, not when you finally get around to enrolling in the app.

The promotion demonstrates BMW's commitment to supporting the rapid growth of electric vehicle infrastructure. By subsidizing the first year of public charging and equipping its 2027 lineup with native NACS hardware, the automaker is working hard to eliminate the common technical hurdles that currently prevent mass EV adoption in the luxury segment.

text:
You might think of BAAJA as the sound that comes out of your mouth when someone tells a good joke. Or, you might think of it as a place you could vacation when it gets cold. But, I want to introduce you to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a new piece of legislation that was recently introduced in the Senate and which will be voted on early this month. If passed, it will then move to the House.

This piece of legislation is a long awaited bipartisan permitting reform and transmission enhancing act that is much needed to eventually increase electrification (i.e. transportation and heating), decrease fossil fuel usage, and increase renewable energy to do it.

Reports from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that in 2021, 85% of new energy capacity was clean energy. More than 97% of new energy projects currently awaiting permits are clean energy, and just 3% are natural gas . In each of the past three years, 84% of new energy capacity built in the United States was clean energy.

Currently, however, it takes 5-10 years for permitting and development of new energy projects to occur in our country due to overlapping requirements between regulatory agencies and extended periods for judicial reviews, forming a bottleneck in the permitting of all energy projects, and delays in getting clean energy online in the urgent manner in which we need it.

One of the four co-sponsors of this bill, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) has been a champion for climate action in the Senate for years. In fact, if you go to YouTube, and search Sheldon Whitehouse Climate Change, you will come up with many recordings of him advocating/pleading for action amongst his fellow legislators.

For instance, one is entitled, “The Simple Truth: Climate Change Portends a Cascade of Destabilizing Financial Market Collapses.” And there are many others. So, it is telling that he added his name as a co-sponsor to the BAAJA Act (S. 5653) crafted by Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and they were also joined by Martin Heinrich (D-NM), and Mike Lee (R-UT).

This bill will need to pass in both chambers and get presidential signature, but if passed, this legislation would streamline the procedures needed to review energy projects, improve agency coordination, add to America’s transmission capacity, and provide the certainty that clean energy developers need to plan and move forward on their projects with confidence. Specifically, it offers strong protections for projects that have already been permitted. No presidential administration or federal agency would be able to interrupt an already-permitting project on a whim.

If you want to learn more about this bill and/or tell your legislators about it, go to cclusa.org/baaja , where you will find more information and links and a quick and easy way to make your voice heard.

In this season of Thanksgiving, many thanks to these legislators and their staff who have put much time and effort into constructing this much needed legislation.

title: Tribal Leaders Oppose Senate Permitting Bill Despite Changes in Substitute Amendment
authors: Levi Rickert, Elyse Wild, Mark Trahant, Levi Rickert Publisher
description:
A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has released a substitute amendment to legislation intended to streamline federal permitting, lower energy costs and create jobs.
“First, the premise that Tribes, Tribal sovereignty, and Tribal decision-making are impediments to federal permitting is a fallacy.
Tribal Nations, when at the table early in the planning and design process, are key to successful project outcomes.
But the process of 5653 in this lame duck session is a rush job and insulting to sovereign Tribal Nations.
It is about whether Tribal Nations will have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lands, resources and communities.
text:
A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has released a substitute amendment to legislation intended to streamline federal permitting, lower energy costs and create jobs.

However, the proposed changes have done little to ease concerns among tribal leaders who say the legislation threatens tribal sovereignty and diminishes the role of Tribal Nations in federal decision-making.

U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), chairwoman of the EPW Committee; and Mike Lee (R-Utah), chairman of the ENR Committee, released the substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on Saturday.

The amendment includes clarifying, conforming and technical changes intended to reflect feedback received since the legislation’s introduction in September. The legislation is designated S. 5653.

The bill’s amendment comes on the heels of a virtual press conference Friday, during which tribal leaders voiced their opposition to the passage of BAAJA.

Despite the revisions, National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) President Mark Macarro told Native News Online that the changes do not adequately address Tribal Nations’ concerns.

Macarro strongly criticized both the substance of the legislation and the process being used to advance it during the lame-duck session of Congress.

“First, the premise that Tribes, Tribal sovereignty, and Tribal decision-making are impediments to federal permitting is a fallacy. Tribal Nations, when at the table early in the planning and design process, are key to successful project outcomes.

“Any amendments to S. 5653 merely puts lipstick on a pig. This bill is rotten from the inside and there is no fixing the rot. Tribal sovereignty continues to be diminished in this bill.

“An amendment of this magnitude demands regular order, which would allow deliberation and meaningful consultation with Tribes. But the process of 5653 in this lame duck session is a rush job and insulting to sovereign Tribal Nations. They are selling out the Tribal Nations for green energy,” Macarro said in an email to Native News Online on Saturday.

Heinrich defended the revised legislation, saying the substitute amendment incorporates feedback from Tribal Nations and New Mexicans while addressing energy affordability.

“I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment, and I’m proud to join my colleagues in releasing it today. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help lower energy costs, strengthen Tribal consultation, and create more good-paying jobs,” Heinrich said.

He added that the legislation would require data centers to pay for the electricity they consume and the grid upgrades needed to support their operations, rather than shifting those expenses to households.

“It also makes sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause, instead of passing those costs on to New Mexico families. Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse also emphasized the bipartisan effort behind the legislation and the feedback received from lawmakers, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves BAAJA and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Whitehouse said.

“Now’s it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs,” he added.

The disagreement highlights a fundamental divide over federal permitting reform: while the legislation’s supporters argue that changes are needed to accelerate energy development, lower costs and expand infrastructure, tribal leaders continue to question whether the proposed approach adequately protects Tribal Nations’ sovereign authority.

For Macarro and NCAI, the issue extends beyond technical changes to permitting requirements. It is about whether Tribal Nations will have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lands, resources and communities.

NCAI maintains that Tribal Nations must be engaged early in the planning and development of projects, with their sovereignty and decision-making authority respected throughout the federal permitting process.

description:
If there’s any incoming congressional freshman who understands how voter anger about data centers supercharged this week’s election, it’s Will Lawrence.

Safety here also means making sure that we're not sacrificing people and the planet to build data centers.

He told her that the movement against data centers gives him “a real sense of hope.” Read more from Katie and the mayor here.
text:
Welcome back to Power Play! Senior writer Molly Taft has been tackling topics around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. With the elections over, Power Play will be going on hiatus. But if you’ve got a question or thought for a story, feel free to shoot Molly an email at molly_taft@wired.com or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.

If there’s any incoming congressional freshman who understands how voter anger about data centers supercharged this week’s election, it’s Will Lawrence.

A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America who helped found the Sunrise Movement, Lawrence centered his campaign on opposition to data centers from the beginning, months before many other candidates had caught on. It helped him win a challenging primary in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District against much-better-funded opponents, and this week, he defeated incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive House races in the country. (Elon Musk’s America PAC chipped in $340,000 against Lawrence.)

For this last edition of Power Play, I caught up with Lawrence about what the future holds for data center developers and for voters concerned about them, and what his plans are when he gets to Washington, DC, next year.

MOLLY TAFT: I’ve seen some post-election takes that data centers weren’t as big of a factor for voters as media coverage may suggest. I’m curious as to what you heard from voters in the last weeks of the campaign about how data centers may be competing with other big issues in this election.

WILL LAWRENCE: What are the two headlines on the election? It's been about costs, and it’s about corruption. Data centers speak directly to costs and to the legalized corruption that's become ordinary business in our rigged economy. They’re taking tax breaks, they’re sucking up water, they’re proposing to use double or triple the total capacity of the grid in Michigan, they’re threatening people’s home values.

Advertisement

All of this is being done because the playing field is fundamentally slanted away from local communities and towards these mega corporations. People have attempted to exert community control and local oversight, and they've been challenged in court by these Silicon Valley companies.

You see an economy and a political order that is favoring the wealthy few over the many. It really makes a mockery of democracy itself. Why is it that we keep having to play whack-a-mole against these individual projects? It shows that people in Silicon Valley and Wall Street and DC have made these decisions for us, and it speaks of the lack of economic democracy.

There have been a lot of announcements from big tech companies in recent weeks, making promises to be more transparent, to use less water, to not use NDAs—OpenAI released a bunch of commitments the day after the election. Do you think these compromises are enough to sway people?

I haven’t seen any of the specific proposals. But if they’re feeling the heat, that’s good. What they've offered so far has been completely inadequate, and it's going to take a lot to win back trust.

There was just a new hyperscale data center proposed in the last week before the election in Delhi Township, south of Lansing, close to Mason. There was an announcement made by a local economic development agency and a would-be developer. They said, “This is going to be different. We're going to do a six-month community engagement process before we even decide if we are going to build a data center, but if we do, it's going to have all these protections. And we want to hear from you.”

The township board scrambled [to put together] an emergency meeting. Two hundred fifty people showed up, probably more than that—it was overflowing. And people said, OK, the answer is still no. It’s going to take a lot of work [from the companies] to convince anybody that anything has actually changed.

Have any tech companies reached out to you?

I haven’t spoken to any of these companies.

When you go to Washington in January, what are some of the first policies you’re going to try and work on around data centers?

I'm going to fight for a federal data center moratorium, and along with it, a pause on advanced AI development. The risks simply do not match up to the benefits at this time. We've got to have a conversation across all of the different stakeholders to determine what an appropriate regulatory agenda looks like.

Would that be a pause similar to what Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed, where it's contingent on AI safety regulations?

Yes. Safety here also means making sure that we're not sacrificing people and the planet to build data centers. We need to have appropriate regulations on both of those aspects.

What about using oversight or investigatory levers?

Certainly—it makes sense. We build cars here in Michigan. If GM put a car on the market that had a 1 percent chance of exploding on the highway and killing everybody inside, it would never go to market. If it did, they would be sued out of existence.

But these Silicon Valley companies, they tell us that they're actively developing a product that has a 10 percent chance of killing everybody on planet Earth. I mean, what are we talking about? This is obviously reckless endangerment, according to any existing standard of consumer protection law. There should be investigations into that, and there should be suits filed to provide a sanction against companies for engaging in unacceptable risks that are a public hazard.

What We’re Writing

It’s been a busy week for the WIRED newsroom! My colleague Tori Elliott and I tackled how data centers factored into the blue tsunami that swept the country on Tuesday. (Spoiler alert: Voters really, really want regulations on data centers.) Over on the Business desk, Caroline Haskins looked at how the election results are sending tech bros scrambling to find other locations to build data centers—including in space.

And earlier this week, WIRED’s global editorial director, Katie Drummond, sat down with New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani to talk about his first year in office. He told her that the movement against data centers gives him “a real sense of hope.” Read more from Katie and the mayor here.

What We’re Reading

The Hill got a scoop that some environmental groups have begun to talk with tech companies about setting standards for data centers on everything from emissions to community engagement.

ProPublica reports on how interior secretary Doug Burgum stands to gain from a possible data center build-out on public lands.

Anti-data-center activists broke into a Microsoft data center construction site in Amsterdam on Friday as part of a wave of planned protests across Europe. Reuters has more.

text:
Ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and stubbornly high gas prices have pushed buyers towards more efficient cars in recent months, and some automakers have seen sales boosts as a result. Hybrid vehicles in particular have seen a spike in popularity, since unlike battery EVs (BEVs), hybrids can offer significant fuel savings without needing to rely on the public charging network. Toyota remains the biggest player in the U.S. hybrid car market according to Q3 data from Cox, but it isn't the fastest growing.

That title instead goes to Kia, which sold 36,000 more hybrid vehicles in the last quarter compared to the same time last year. Its sister brand Hyundai wasn't far behind, selling 30,000 more hybrids than it did the previous year. Still, it's not like Toyota had a bad quarter — it still shifted 32,000 more hybrid vehicles than it did in a year ago. That gave it a 44 percent share in the overall hybrid market, a slightly smaller share in percentage terms than last year, despite selling more hybrid vehicles than before.

As well as Hyundai, Kia, and Toyota all benefitting from the hybrid vehicle boom, several other Asian manufacturers are also cashing in. Both Honda and Subaru recorded higher hybrid sales than Q3 2025, although their sales gains were not as significant as their Korean rivals. Honda is said to be planning to focus its future plans around hybrid cars, with recent reports suggesting that its best-selling models like the CR-V might be ditching gas-only engines altogether.

Hybrid vehicles are proving increasingly popular with buyers, but the same can't be said for EVs. According to Cox, EVs made up around 6 percent of the market in Q3 2026, a significant drop compared to their market share in the same period in 2025. However, there's a good reason for that: Federal EV tax credits were axed in late 2025, which led to a spike in EV demand in Q3 as buyers rushed to take advantage of the scheme before it ended.

As such, EV demand in Q3 2025 was unusually high, and Q3 2026 is more representative of the ongoing demand, according to Cox's analysts. Buyers looking for a used EV in the last quarter would have found that more inventory was available compared to the same time the previous year, although average used prices have increased even as the average price for a new EV has dropped.

Although market trends continue to change, the broader picture is that electrified vehicles are still becoming increasingly popular with American buyers. Demand for BEVs remains, albeit at a smaller level than last year, and some buyers still think PHEVs are the smartest choice, but the convenience of fuel-sipping hybrids (HEV) has proven to be the biggest draw for buyers in recent months.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

EV sales in the US are beginning to tick up again, and BMW is determined to grab a slice of the action. The German automaker has begun offering a free EV charging package to anyone who purchases a 2027 BMW i5, BMW i7, or BMW iX3. The package includes $500 in charging credits, which seems like small potatoes compared to the cost of a BMW. Still, it’s better than nothing, and it positions the company to compete in a rapidly evolving landscape that includes free charging hours.

Free Hours And EV Charging

The “free hours” trend has already emerged in the US, where Texas (of course!) is an epicenter of activity. The idea is to smooth out peak weekday demand spikes and take advantage of spare capacity on the grid by offering ratepayers an incentive to use more electricity during nighttime hours, with the leading utility Constellation being a representative example.

“When you sign up for a free night electricity plan, a smart meter monitors your energy usage by time of day,” Constellation explains. The company offers a “Free Power Hours” plan between midnight and 4 a.m. every night.

“Constellation also offers Discounted Nights & Fair Days, with discounted electricity supply rates from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.,” the company adds.

Constellation notes that standard service charges and other fees apply. They also advise that the free plan is not a good fit for households with heavy electricity use during the day, when higher rates apply.

Still, access to EV charging at a minimal cost is a tantalizing incentive for some households. Constellation currently offers its “FreeCharge” plan between midnight and 4 a.m. to ratepayers in Pennsylvania as well as Texas.

A $500 EV Charging Credit From BMW

Against this backdrop, a mere $500 EV charging credit for a BMW is not much of an incentive, at least not in states where free hours are available. The monthly lease for the 2027 BMW i5, for example, clocks in at almost $750. Purchasing the car outright will set you back almost $70,000, including the destination fee.

Still, any incentive is better than no incentive, and the new offer provides BMW an opportunity to hitch its star to the free hours trend. “The new offer, available beginning November 5, 2026, is designed to make public charging simpler, more convenient and more affordable for BMW customers,” explains BMW.

“The package includes a $300 BMW Charging Network credit that can be used at participating charging providers1, as well as a separate $200 credit for charging at IONNA locations,” the company elaborates, with IONNA referring to a consortium of EV makers (including BMW) focused on improving the driver experience at charging stations.

In addition to the $200 IONNA credit, BMW is also offering a one-year IONNA membership plan that provides for a 25% charging discount.

For the record, the BMW Charging Network includes more than 180,000 charging stations compatible with the company’s My BMW app.

BMW: You Gotta Belieeeeeeeve…

Over and above the EV charging package, BMW is also among the electrification stakeholders that did not throw in the towel after last year’s EV sales crash. Despite the premature demise of the federal EV tax credit on September 30 of 2025, the number of public EV charging stations in the US has continued to increase, and charging networks have become more sophisticated and convenient.

In addition to the hookup with IONNA, for example, the BMW Charging Network includes Shell Recharge, Electrify America, ChargePoint, and EVgo among others.

“The company also has invested in Plug & Charge, which simplifies the charging experience; and ChargeScape, a collaborative effort to help manage the flow of energy between EVs and the power grid,” BMW added in a press statement last week.

Next Steps For EV Charging In The US

ChargeScape represents another indication that Trump’s war against EVs was over before it started, tax credits or not.

ChargeScape launched three years ago as a joint venture between BMW, Ford, and the US branch of Honda. “Benefiting both EV customers and the electric utility industry in the U.S. and Canada, ChargeScape will unlock entirely new value that EVs can provide to the electric grid, while enabling EV customers to earn financial benefits through a variety of managed charging and energy-sharing services never before possible with traditional gasoline-powered vehicles,” the three automakers enthused in a press statement dated December 29, 2023.

“ChargeScape’s platform will give electric utilities access to EV battery energy across a wide pool of EVs. Participating EV customers will have the potential to earn financial benefits by charging at ‘grid-friendly’ times through flexible and managed schedules,” the partners elaborated.

“The development of this project comes at a time when electric vehicle sales and infrastructure growth are ramping up quickly,” the partners added.

That was certainly an optimistic take on the future of EV sales in the US, but that was December of 2023. Just about one year later, then-candidate Donald Trump sailed to victory on Election Day 2024, winning a second turn around the Oval Office with a plan to stop the vehicle electrification trend in its tracks.

Still, ChargeScape soldiered on. By September of 2024 the alliance was ready for launch, to be joined by Nissan just one month later. ChargeScape also added the startup Rivian to its rolls in June of this year, with an option to add bidirectional EV charging. Other automakers, including Tesla, also use the platform.

The bidirectional charging element is where things get particularly interesting. The technology emerged in the early 2000’s, enabling EV drivers to power their home from their car battery, or send electricity to the grid. Unlocking the mass market potential of bidirectional charging is a next-level challenge, and the free hours trend could help accelerate uptake. With free hours EV charging, drivers can store electricity at minimal cost during those periods, and discharge it to trim the cost of electricity for their homes during periods when higher electricity rates apply.

Ford is particularly excited about the potential for bidirectional charging to scale up. The company’s forthcoming Ford Fathom electric pickup truck comes with an internal inverter that converts the DC charge from the battery into an AC current for home use. The built-in inverter eliminates the cost of the external, wall mounted inverter otherwise needed for bidirectional charging at home.

title: National Trust votes to seek banking partner more in tune with its environmental policies
description:
“Meanwhile our bank, Barclays, undermines our conservation mission by channelling billions of dollars into fossil fuel expansion,” James said.
However, the National Trust has made clear that the tender will not be restricted to specialist ethical banks.
Barclays has defended its relationship with the National Trust and its wider approach to financing the energy sector.
A spokesperson said: “It is our privilege to support and bank the National Trust and we value their engagement on these important topics.
Restore Trust, a group of National Trust members, has said the vote shows the organisation is straying from its core purpose.
text:
The National Trust has voted overwhelmingly to seek a new banking partner in a significant victory for members who have long argued that its relationship with Barclays was at odds with its commitment to protecting the natural world.

The resolution, passed at the charity’s annual general meeting on Saturday with the backing of its board of trustees, instructs the organisation to begin a competitive tendering process for its banking arrangements.

That process will, for the first time, centre on the condition that the new bank demonstrates a positive commitment to protecting biodiversity and reducing the human-induced climate crisis.

Campaigners said the result, 53,256 votes for and 4,094 against, sent a message that charities should apply the same environmental standards to their financial relationships as they do to their investments and suppliers.

Others questioned the significance of the success, with insiders suggesting that the tendering process will not take place for at least a year.

Despite supporting the vote the National Trust sounded a qualifying note, with Sandy Nairne, deputy chair of the board of trustees, warning: “The outcome of the ballot provides the board with an important indication of members’ views, but it is not binding on the trustees.

“The trustees will carefully consider the result alongside the discussion we have heard today as part of their future decision making,” he added.

“This result highlights a profound shift in NGO accountability,” said Drew James, a proposer of the resolution and a member of Christian Climate Action.

“Civil society looks to charities, universities and faith groups to sever ties with financial institutions failing to match their ethical standards.”

The move follows years of pressure from members concerned about Barclays’ financing of the fossil fuel industry. The bank has been criticised for its support for oil and gas expansion, including fracking and methane gas infrastructure, while the National Trust has repeatedly identified the climate emergency and the decline of nature as the greatest threats to the landscapes, wildlife and historic properties in its care.

The vote came as the trust faces mounting consequences of extreme weather across its portfolio of countryside, coastline and historic buildings. A wildfire at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk in July destroyed 104 hectares (256 acres) of ancient heathland, with campaigners estimating that the damage would take 25 years to recover. Other trust properties have faced the effects of flash flooding, prolonged drought and increasingly severe weather.

James said the relationship with Barclays was particularly difficult to reconcile with the Trust’s public position on the climate crisis. “For years, our trustees have declared climate change and the decline in nature to be the biggest threat to the places in our care. Each is human-induced, and the pace is quickening,” he said.

He pointed to comments made by the trust’s chief executive at a seminar during the Labour party conference, in which the executive identified keeping fossil fuels in the ground as the most significant response to the climate breakdown.

“Meanwhile our bank, Barclays, undermines our conservation mission by channelling billions of dollars into fossil fuel expansion,” James said.

The resolution’s supporters argued that the trust’s association with the bank was inconsistent with its responsibilities under the National Trust Act 1907, which established its duty to preserve places of historic interest and natural beauty for the benefit of the nation.

They also pointed to the Trust’s previous advice to the public, encouraging them to bank ethically. “It is contradictory for the organisation to hold its own banking provider to a lower standard than its suppliers and investment portfolio,” said James.

However, the National Trust has made clear that the tender will not be restricted to specialist ethical banks. In its supporting statement for the vote, the board said the tender “must remain open to the major UK clearing banks”.

It added that “while some members may understandably aspire to the use of a specialist ethical bank, the evidence presented to the board of trustees indicates that no such provider currently has the combination of cash handling capability, lending capacity, payments infrastructure and operational scale required to support an organisation of the Trust’s size and complexity”.

Barclays has defended its relationship with the National Trust and its wider approach to financing the energy sector. A spokesperson said: “It is our privilege to support and bank the National Trust and we value their engagement on these important topics.

“As a leading energy financier, we recognise the interconnectedness of economic growth, energy security and affordability and decarbonisation to meet society’s needs. Over the past three years, we have facilitated more than $300bn (£225bn) of sustainable and transition finance, including billions for cleaner energy projects here in the UK, and invested millions into climate tech.”

Campaigners, however, dispute the significance of the $300bn fund, pointing to Barclays’ latest annual report which states that fossil fuel entities can access it, provided the money is not designated directly for oil and gas activity.

“This means that a reduction in carbon intensity, such as a switch from tar sands extraction to natural gas, could qualify for sustainability backing even if it results in a net increase in total carbon emissions,” said James.

Restore Trust, a group of National Trust members, has said the vote shows the organisation is straying from its core purpose.

Cornelia van der Poll, its chair, called the vote “a distraction from the National Trust’s charitable purpose of properly maintaining all the historic buildings and countryside in its care”.

title: IF TESLA Can't Make People Want An EV Pickup Then That Is PROOF There Was ... - AutoSpies
description:
Other electric pickups (F-150 Lightning, Rivian R1T, Silverado EV) have also remained niche compared with the millions of gas and diesel trucks sold annually.
Real-world figures of 90–160 miles between charges are common with substantial trailers, versus 400–600+ miles per tank in a comparable gas or diesel truck.
Current lithium-ion packs deliver roughly 170–230 Wh/kg at the pack level and still cost enough that a large truck battery adds thousands of dollars and hundreds of pounds.
That physics-and-economics gap is why EV pickups have not displaced traditional ones for the majority of truck buyers.
Today’s technology cannot yet deliver the towing range, refueling convenience, and cost profile that most pickup buyers require.
text:
Tesla planned the Cybertruck line for roughly 250,000 units a year. Real-world demand has landed far lower—around 20,000–40,000 in peak years and an annualized pace closer to 30,000 more recently, according to industry estimates. Elon Musk has said production will wind down at Giga Texas around mid-2027 to free space for the Cybercab. Other electric pickups (F-150 Lightning, Rivian R1T, Silverado EV) have also remained niche compared with the millions of gas and diesel trucks sold annually. When the company with the strongest brand, charging network, and vertical integration in the EV space cannot move volume, the underlying constraints apply industry-wide.

The core issue is how people actually use pickups. A large share of buyers tow boats, campers, equipment trailers, or work gear, often on longer trips. Independent tests consistently show EV trucks lose 40–60% or more of their range under heavy towing loads. Real-world figures of 90–160 miles between charges are common with substantial trailers, versus 400–600+ miles per tank in a comparable gas or diesel truck. A five-minute fuel stop becomes a multi-hour charging session (or a search for rare high-power chargers that can handle the load). Battery weight further cuts payload capacity. Buyers who need the truck to work as a truck—rather than a lifestyle or local-use vehicle—still choose gasoline or diesel for the combination of range, refueling speed, cost, and proven capability in heat, cold, and remote areas.

Current lithium-ion packs deliver roughly 170–230 Wh/kg at the pack level and still cost enough that a large truck battery adds thousands of dollars and hundreds of pounds. That physics-and-economics gap is why EV pickups have not displaced traditional ones for the majority of truck buyers.

The picture changes only when the technology moves decisively. Once energy density rises enough that a battery delivering 1,000-mile unladen range (and competitive towing range) is far smaller and lighter, and pack costs fall by an order of magnitude or more, the compromises shrink. At that point—whether through solid-state cells, denser chemistries, or other advances—an electric truck can match the practical utility of a gas truck while adding lower operating costs, quieter operation, and instant torque. Buyers who currently reject EVs for towing and range reasons will then have a genuine alternative.

Design choices and pricing played a role in the Cybertruck’s trajectory, but the fundamental barrier is the battery. Today’s technology cannot yet deliver the towing range, refueling convenience, and cost profile that most pickup buyers require. When it can, the market will shift. Until then, gas and diesel trucks will continue to dominate the segment for good, practical reasons.
