title: What midterm election blue wave rebuke of Trump means for renewable energy - CNBC
description:
But renewable energy investing remains alive and well, notably among public and private funders of infrastructure projects and clean technology innovation.
And following the midterm elections that gave climate-friendly Democrats control of the House and Senate, the prospects of reviving the clean energy agenda suddenly brightened.
Opportunities can be found through public equity investments like mutual funds and ETFs that are constructed to invest in clean energy companies.
She added that it’s challenging to break down the number of clients who are specifically focused on clean energy and clean tech.
The U.S. is on pace to add a record 89 GW of clean energy capacity by the end of 2026, with installations projected to exceed that level in 2027, according to BloombergNEF’s latest US Clean Energy Market Outlook.
text:
As recently as 2022, many leaders in corporate America and the investment community were singing the praises of ESG — environmental, social, governance — as the foundation of stakeholder capitalism. It didn’t take long for that tune to change, for understandable reasons.

President Trump didn’t just make “ESG”, “sustainability” and “climate change” dirty words in his “green new scam” rhetoric. The Trump administration’s rollback of environmental regulations, elimination of clean energy subsidies and tax credits, defunding and halting of wind and solar projects, and embrace of the fossil fuels industry accelerated the backlash.

But renewable energy investing remains alive and well, notably among public and private funders of infrastructure projects and clean technology innovation. And following the midterm elections that gave climate-friendly Democrats control of the House and Senate, the prospects of reviving the clean energy agenda suddenly brightened.

Clean energy and solar stocks rallied the day after the election results, which “potentially reduces the risk of further political interference with renewable energy incentives and provides greater protection for the long-term economics of U.S. wind, solar and battery storage investments,” Barclays analysts led by Peter Crampton wrote in a note.

While Trump can veto legislation to restore subsidies and credits and revive projects, and continue to issue executive orders on energy policy, some Republicans may be more inclined to help Democrats override the president in order to appeal to voters outraged over high energy prices — a sentiment expressed in the passage of multiple state initiatives to impede the build-out of electricity-hungry data centers.

The blue wave also shines a spotlight on a bipartisan permitting-reform bill awaiting Senate approval. Several progressive Democrats want to put off the vote until the new Congress convenes in January, giving them time to rewrite provisions favoring renewables projects over fossil fuel ventures.

Ultimately, the midterms could improve the outlook for investors focused on clean energy. That is likely to start with impact investors who specifically seek to generate a competitive financial rate of return alongside positive, proactive social and environmental impact. Opportunities can be found through public equity investments like mutual funds and ETFs that are constructed to invest in clean energy companies. But many investors also seek out pure-play clean energy positions offered through fixed income, private equity, private credit, venture capital, real assets and community-focused investments.

“There are many different approaches that could lead impact investors to be thinking about clean energy investments,” said Amit Bouri, who’s retiring as CEO of the Global Impact Investing Network at year’s end. GIIN’s 2026 survey of impact investors found that 56% have funds invested in clean energy and 25% plan to increase those investments over the next five years. The survey was conducted prior to the midterms.

“Clean energy infrastructure can be really compelling from an investment standpoint, because the financial thesis and impact thesis are mutually reinforcing,” said Justina Lai, chief impact officer at LNW, a wealth management advisory firm. LNW has about $3.5 billion of its total $12.1 billion assets under management invested in impact strategies. She added that it’s challenging to break down the number of clients who are specifically focused on clean energy and clean tech. “Climate change or climate action writ large is likely the most common impact priority that we encounter with our clients,” she said.

While it might be hard to focus on the potential in the renewable energy sector in 2026 with energy commodities leading all sectors of the market as crude oil prices surged, some of the factors Lai cites should be on the radar of investors beyond the impact investing space.

She pointed to the nation’s growing electricity demand — partly tied to data centers — its aging and constrained grid infrastructure, the increasing need for energy storage, the effects of geopolitics on energy security and rising energy costs as major factors driving clean energy investing. Simultaneously, though, because of declining costs and continuing maturity of many clean technologies, “we know that renewables are the lowest cost form of new-build generation, even on a fully unsubsidized basis,” she said.

The proof is in the gigawatts. The U.S. is on pace to add a record 89 GW of clean energy capacity by the end of 2026, with installations projected to exceed that level in 2027, according to BloombergNEF’s latest US Clean Energy Market Outlook. In just the first half of this year, the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy recently reported, 11.5 GW of solar, 8.3 GW of battery storage and 6.3 GW of wind power were installed.

U.S. investment in clean energy and transportation alone totaled $75 billion in the second quarter of 2026, the second-highest quarterly figure on record and up 22% from the previous quarter, according to the Clean Investment Monitor, a joint project of Rhodium Group and MIT’s Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research.

The supply chain has amped up, too. By the third quarter of this year, manufacturing capacity for solar modules, wind blades and nacelles had expanded by roughly 50% from the first quarter of 2025, reflecting new facilities that have come online, the CIM reported in October. And over the past four quarters, $277 billion was invested across the country in the manufacture and deployment of renewable energy, non-fossil fuel vehicles, building electrification and carbon-management technology.

“Investment has consistently been very strong in solar and storage at the utility scale,” said Hannah Hess, director, energy and climate at Rhodium. That makes sense from a bottom-line perspective, she said, “particularly when some of the deadlines for these projects have changed for them to be eligible for tax credits.”

Hess is referring to provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which significantly hastened the sunsets and deadlines for federal clean energy tax credits compared to the original timeline set by the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act. Solar and wind projects had to begin construction by July 4 of this year or be placed into service by December 31, 2027, to claim standard investment or production tax credits.

‘A rich time to be looking at this space’

Meanwhile, even with the Trump administration’s concerted efforts to rescind much of the $1.6 trillion set aside for clean energy under Biden’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and the IRA, nearly $600 billion remains available, according to a Politico analysis. Keeping that third of the funding pipeline open bodes well for clean energy developers and investors, especially considering the midterm results.

“Despite the gutting of the IRA, our long-term thesis and our clients’ long-term views on clean energy remain the same,” said Roraj Pradhananga, chief investment officer at Veris Wealth Partners, an advisory firm that specializes in impact investing. “If we look at the volatility and risk-adjusted returns of the traditional energy sector, in the long run, shifting to renewable energy makes the most [economic] sense,” even when taking the tax credits out of the equation, he said.

Veris manages $3 billion across asset classes, Pradhananga said, using various vehicles, including public markets, private debt and infrastructure funds. “Climate solutions tend to be the largest allocation for our clients. We recently allocated to strategies from GPs like Closed Loop Partners, Streetlife Ventures, SJF Ventures, New Energy Capital and Sunwealth.”

The proliferation of AI data centers was a hot-button issue in the midterms. Voters in 10 states weighed in on 41 local initiatives, which included complete bans on new construction, pausing ongoing and planned facilities and restrictions on energy consumption. All but one passed. And although newly elected governors in three states — Ohio, Texas and Georgia — ran on platforms critical of data centers, they’re not calling for permanent bans.

For instance, Gina Hinojosa, governor-elect of Texas, said during a CNN interview on November 5, “We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections.” She also emphasized giving local communities a meaningful say in whether and how facilities operate. That echoes Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro’s cautious approach to data center development in that state. In August, he issued an executive order that places a host of restrictions on developers.

The upshot for AI companies may be a slowdown in new data center construction, increased input from local residents and officials, and self-financing for electricity and water usage. Yet they are not expected to change their long-term expansion plans. A few days before the election, Goldman Sachs said, “While U.S. data center development faces increasing political and community opposition, project data and our updated capacity estimates suggest that the...growth outlook through 2027 remains largely unchanged.” The Wall Street firm forecast data center power demand to grow 38% or 12 GW in 2026 and 38% or 17 GW in 2027.

On Friday, OpenAI’s CFO told CNBC the company will not be changing its investment plans despite the election results. White House economic advisor Kevin Hassett expressed a similarly optimistic view of continued investing on CNBC on Friday. “We respect the localities that decide that’s what they want to do,” Hassett said. “But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren’t affected by these ballot initiatives.”

From another perspective, the risks associated with AI and data centers could be beneficial to renewable energy investments. “If anything, sustainability concerns around AI actually reinforce their interest in climate action,” Lai said. “The growth in AI and data centers could drive significant new fossil fuel generation, so our clients are motivated to ensure that more of that [electricity] demand is met by renewables.”

That’s true for many of Veris’ clients, too, Pradhananga said. But he also acknowledged that because natural gas is a prominent fuel source for large-scale utilities, as well as behind-the-meter LNG turbines that power many data centers, “there are some [of our] clients who view this as part of the transition” from fossil fuels to renewables, espousing the often-mentioned “all of the above” approach to the changeover. “This is where we do have exposure to utilities in [our] public markets portfolio.”

Public consternation over data centers, a Democratic-controlled Congress come January and, at least for now, a voting map across the country that has swung significantly towards the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential election, could create a trifecta of tailwinds for investors in renewable energy and clean-tech. And while any moratorium on data centers could impact renewable project development on a case-by-case basis, it might also promote investments in transmission grid upgrades that allow utility-scale solar and wind installations to tie into existing and proposed data centers.

It could also speed up research and development of emissions-free power generation, energy-efficiency and other technologies that climate-tech VCs are funding. Due to the AI boom, renewable energy companies have faced stiffer competition in recent years for venture capital dollars previously targeting climate change and decarbonization. But climate-tech VC hit $26 billion in the first half of 2026, a 55% increase year over year, according to market-intelligence firm Currence.

“There are very interesting infrastructure opportunities in [climate investing], including advanced fusion ventures, floating offshore wind turbines and solar plus storage operations,” said Adam Wolfensohn, a clean-energy investment advocate and advisor. “All of these technologies keep getting better and cheaper, unlocking so much more potential for renewables and new financial structures. It’s a rich time to be looking at this space.”

Among the guiding resources the GIIN offers to its 350 member organizations in 40-plus countries, including 126 in the U.S., is a recently launched climate solutions investing framework. “It’s designed to help investors make sense of the landscape of climate solutions and to ensure they have rigor around the actual climate impacts underpinning an investment strategy,” Bouri said. “A lot of things have green labels on them, but what we are really focused on is what drives real results for people and the planet.”

name: Detroit Environment
title: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer - ClickOnDetroit
description:
An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana.
Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.
When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part.
Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.
Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.
text:
BENGALURU – For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely.

Winter also brings severe smog to parts of Pakistan and China, where warmer air can act as a lid, trapping colder air and pollution near the ground. In eastern Europe, burning coal and wood to heat homes also adds to winter pollution. Western Hemisphere countries, meanwhile, face their own seasonal air-quality problems, as summer wildfires send smoke across vast areas of the United States and Canada.

Experts say no matter where you live or when you face pollution, simple steps such as checking the air quality index, wearing a well-fitting mask and using air purifiers can reduce exposure to harmful pollutants.

An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana. Fireworks traditionally set off during the holiday, which starts Sunday, can make polluted air more dangerous.

As Diwali approaches, here are ways to reduce exposure to polluted air.

Check the air before heading out

Fireworks add a sharp burst of pollution to a much bigger problem. Across India, Pakistan and other parts of South Asia, traffic, factories, dust from construction and burning of crop residues and waste foul the air. Weak winds and stagnant winter air allow that pollution to build up.

“Poor air quality is our all-year-round problem in our country,” said Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance. Narayan said firecrackers add to the problem.

India’s air quality index turns pollution measurements into a health warning. AQI readings of 201–300 mean “poor,” 301–400 “very poor” and 401–500 “severe.” Severe levels can harm even healthy people.

Check pollution levels on government or privately run websites before heading outdoors. Look for data from a nearby monitoring station and the time of its last update. A citywide average can conceal a polluted neighborhood.

The problem is especially bad in Delhi, where fine particle pollution averaged about 19 times the World Health Organization’s annual guideline last year. Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.

City authorities have responded with temporary construction, industrial and vehicle restrictions. Public health experts said such measures often fail to address the root causes. The city of more than 20 million people is also implementing a long-term plan to promote use of electric vehicles.

Make your mask fit

Dr. Arvind Kumar, a chest surgeon at Medanta hospital near Delhi and founder trustee of the Lung Care Foundation, recommends using properly fitted N95 or N99 masks outdoors during periods of heavy pollution. These masks are available at pharmacies, hardware stores and online retailers.

N95 filters are designed to capture at least 95% of airborne particles; N99 filters are made to capture at least 99%. The particle respirator masks do not filter harmful gases.

Cover your nose, mouth and chin. Shape the nose clip and check the seal every time. Facial hair can break that seal. The aim, Kumar said, is to ensure “all the breathing is through the mask and not around the mask.”

Replace disposable masks when dirty, damaged or hard to breathe through. Never put a mask on a child younger than 2. People with heart or lung disease should seek medical advice about mask use.

Loose surgical masks, cloth masks and scarves offer unreliable protection against fine particles.

Kumar said pollution can cause persistent coughing, inflame the airways and trigger asthma-like attacks. He also cited increased risks of pneumonia, heart attacks and strokes, while linking prolonged exposure to impaired lung development in children and lung cancer.

Kumar said people should avoid strenuous exercise outdoors during heavy pollution, including early mornings, when pollution levels can be high.

Match the purifier to the room

Using the right air purifiers indoors can help. The devices draw in air to filter out pollutants, then recirculate the cleaner air.

A purifier needs enough capacity to clean the air of the room where it runs. Look for a high-efficiency particulate air, or HEPA, filter. Then check its clean air delivery rate, which is the volume of filtered air it supplies.

Place the purifier where you spend the most time, such as the bedroom. Keep its airflow clear and run it consistently.

HEPA filters trap particles. Substantial activated-carbon filters can remove some gases. No purifier removes every pollutant. Avoid machines that deliberately produce ozone, which irritates the lungs.

Cleaner indoor air reduces exposure, but a purifier cannot eliminate pollution’s health risks, Kumar said.

Celebrate with less smoke

Kumar said it’s important to avoid incense, mosquito coils and candles. Their particles can linger indoors for hours, especially in poorly ventilated rooms, while fireworks pollution can persist overnight, depending on the weather. When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part. Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.

“If one wants to celebrate and really enjoy the festival of Diwali, avoid bursting firecrackers,” said Narayan, the public health expert.

India’s health ministry also recommends reducing smoky cooking and using a kitchen exhaust that vents outdoors. Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.

Personal precautions have limits. Narayan said people who earn their livelihoods outdoors cannot simply stay home. Many families also cannot afford air purifiers.

She called for sustained action on pollution sources and affordable health care for those already suffering. Masks and filters can reduce exposure, but lasting protection requires governments to clean the air.

“It’s our responsibility to hold our governments accountable,” Narayan said. “There’s no other way about it.”

name: American Energy
title: Democrats take control of Congress. Trump's energy policy faces two years under scrutiny
description:
The White House faces hearings and uncomfortable questions The most visible change after the Democratic majority takes office will be Congress’s strengthened oversight role.
The committees are expected to seek documents and communications between energy companies and the administration.
Democrats can launch investigations into production contracts, federal land leases or relationships between energy companies and the White House.
The Democratic majority can therefore change how Trump’s energy agenda is pursued, but it will find it much harder to change its direction.
The White House faces more frequent hearings, demands for the release of documents and greater pressure to explain its agreements with energy companies.
text:
A Democratic victory in both chambers of Congress will make it harder for Donald Trump to push through his agenda. The new majority may investigate agreements between the administration and energy companies, scrutinize the use of tariff powers or raise questions about oil and gas production. But a major shift in US energy policy is unlikely. A number of key powers remain in the hands of the president, and Democrats do not have the majority needed to override his veto, S&P Global reports in its analysis.

The White House faces hearings and uncomfortable questions

The most visible change after the Democratic majority takes office will be Congress’s strengthened oversight role. Democrats will be able to launch their own investigations, hold hearings and demand documents and communications related to the administration’s decisions from both the administration and private companies.

One of the first targets could be the White House’s relationship with the oil industry. According to S&P Global, congressional committees may focus, for example, on Trump’s executive order “Unleashing American Energy", which directed the Department of the Interior to expand leasing of federal land and waters for production. The committees are expected to seek documents and communications between energy companies and the administration.

Specific agreements with private companies may also come under scrutiny. Democrats are already seeking information about the terms of the US involvement in Venezuela’s oil sector, including an agreement with North America Blue Energy Partners. Under the deal, the US government received a 35% stake and priority access to 20 % of production at cost.

Such scrutiny will not, by itself, cancel the agreements. It could, however, raise their political and legal costs and deter investors, particularly smaller ones. Greater uncertainty around longer-term investments could be one practical consequence of the new balance of power. A more pronounced impact may be felt by projects approved in 2027 and 2028, while the immediate effect on US oil production is expected to be limited.

Source: Flickr / Lindsey G / CC BY 2.0

Trump’s tariffs may face greater pressure

Trade policy is another area where the balance of power will shift. Democrats criticize the scale of Trump’s tariffs and their impact on businesses and consumers. With oversight of Congress, they will have more scope to examine how the president uses his tariff powers and try to limit his latitude.

They can introduce proposals to tighten the rules, demand greater transparency and use hearings to put political pressure on the administration. Any change would be significant for parts of US industry. In 2025, for example, the Trump administration raised tariffs on steel and aluminum imports to 50 %.

A swift return to the pre-Trump tariff policy is unlikely, however. The president can veto new legislation, and Democrats do not have the majority needed to automatically override a veto. Nor is there complete agreement within the Democratic Party on the use of tariffs. Rather than abolishing tariffs, the more likely goal will be to limit presidential powers and subject individual measures to greater political scrutiny.

Oil and gas: more of a brake than a reversal

The same logic will apply to the extraction sector. Democrats can launch investigations into production contracts, federal land leases or relationships between energy companies and the White House. They can also use the budget process and block parts of the new legislative agenda.

Their ability to change policies already in place is limited, however, and the current federal leasing program cannot be significantly halted over the next two years. Legislation passed in 2025 also requires at least 30 lease sales in the Gulf of Mexico by 2040.

Similar limits apply to electric vehicles and renewable energy. Democrats will have a stronger platform for advancing these issues, but restoring federal incentives would still require Trump’s signature or a majority able to override his veto. The Democratic majority can therefore change how Trump’s energy agenda is pursued, but it will find it much harder to change its direction.

Offshore wind farm. Source: Unsplash

Markets have already reacted to the change

The election result was also immediately reflected in energy markets, although geopolitics played the leading role. Oil futures fell sharply on November 4, as investors viewed the Democratic victory as a factor reducing the risk of further US-Iranian escalation. S&P Global reports that the December WTI contract fell by $8.39 to $87.70 per barrel during the day, while January Brent fell by $9.58 to $94.02.

“The Democratic victory changes the political cost of continuing the war with Iran,”Rystad Energy chief economist Claudio Galimberti said.“With both chambers of Congress now able to pass resolutions, block funding for the war and delay the approval of nominations, the administration has less political room to continue on its current course and faces greater institutional pressure to reach an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz.”

Democrats make gains in oil-producing Texas

The election result affected more than the balance of power in Congress. In Texas, the largest oil producer in the United States, Democrats won a seat on the state’s oil and gas regulator, the Railroad Commission of Texas, for the first time since 1995. Democrat Jon Rosenthal was elected to the three-member regulatory body. The commission oversees, among other things, oil and gas production, pipeline safety and gas utilities.

Rosenthal wants to push for stricter oversight of gas companies’ costs and greater billing transparency. In the production sector, he is focused on curbing the flaring of excess gas, speeding up the closure of abandoned wells and tightening the financial requirements attached to new production permits.

His victory does not, by itself, signal a major shift in the regulation of Texas’s oil and gas sector. Republicans Christi Craddick and Wayne Christian hold the commission’s other two seats, so Rosenthal will need the support of at least one of them to advance his priorities.

Two years under greater scrutiny

The new balance of power does not necessarily mean conflict on every issue. There is broader bipartisan agreement on supporting domestic production and processing of rare earths. Disputes are more likely to concern specific projects, the terms of public support and how they are approved.

The main change in Washington, then, is not an immediate rewrite of Trump’s energy strategy. Democrats have gained tools to scrutinize its implementation, raise its political costs and, in some cases, slow it down. The White House faces more frequent hearings, demands for the release of documents and greater pressure to explain its agreements with energy companies.

The president, however, retains considerable latitude in areas such as foreign policy, regulation and trade measures. Trump is not losing control of his energy policy. But from January, he will be pursuing it before a Congress with a much greater incentive to keep a close eye on him.

title: EPA Air Standards and Public Health Risks - EarthTimes

Still, they show why these EPA Air Standards are treated as health rules as much as environmental rules.

What EPA Air Standards Can Still Do Air rules work through several mechanisms.
What Remains Unresolved In EPA Air Standards The public health impact of EPA Air Standards after the 2026 changes will depend on three factors: how courts treat the rollbacks, how EPA completes required PM2.5 designations, and how states respond in areas that fail to meet the annual particle standard.
text:
EPA Air Standards became a central public health issue in 2026 after the Environmental Protection Agency moved to unwind several climate and pollution rules while courts kept a stricter fine-particle standard in force. As of November 7, 2026, some actions were final, some remained subject to litigation or agency deadlines, and some health estimates came from independent modeling rather than measured outcomes.

The public health question is not limited to greenhouse gases. The supplied research connects the 2026 actions to fine particulate matter, ground-level ozone, mercury, sulfur dioxide and toxic metals. Those pollutants are regulated through different legal tools, but the health pathway is similar: weaker emissions limits can raise exposure, and higher exposure can increase risks for premature death, respiratory disease, cardiovascular harm, emergency care and hospital admissions.

EPA Air Standards And The Health Baseline

EPA Air Standards Under Court Deadlines

The clearest regulatory baseline in the record is the fine-particle National Ambient Air Quality Standard. On March 6, 2024, EPA issued a final rule lowering the primary annual standard for PM2.5 from 12 micrograms per cubic meter to 9 micrograms per cubic meter. According to the Harvard Environmental and Energy Law Program, the D.C. Circuit upheld the tighter standard in June 2026, and on July 17, 2026, a federal district court ordered EPA to make attainment designations by February 6, 2027 Harvard EELP tracker.

That standard matters because PM2.5 is small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The research notes report that estimated 2032 health benefits from the 2024 standard include reductions in adult and infant mortality, emergency department visits and hospital admissions. The same notes cite annual monetized health benefits of $20 billion to $46 billion, compared with estimated annual control costs of about $594 million.

Those figures are estimates, not confirmed future outcomes. They depend on emissions, compliance, monitoring, economic activity and population exposure. Still, they show why these EPA Air Standards are treated as health rules as much as environmental rules.

Why Fine Particles Change The Health Calculation

Fine particles are produced directly by combustion and can also form in the atmosphere from precursor pollutants. Public health agencies have long treated PM2.5 as one of the most consequential air pollutants because exposure is linked to heart and lung disease. The 2024 standard did not ban a source category; it required states and EPA to determine which areas met or failed to meet the revised annual limit and then use Clean Air Act tools to address nonattainment areas.

The July 17, 2026 court order did not decide how each area would comply. It required EPA to complete the next administrative step by February 6, 2027. That deadline is significant because designations can influence permitting, planning and state implementation obligations.

Rollbacks Already Finalized In 2026

Endangerment Finding And Power Rules

Separate from the PM2.5 standard, the research record says EPA formally repealed the 2009 endangerment finding in February 2026. That finding had been the legal basis for major greenhouse gas rules affecting vehicles and power plants. In or around September 2026, EPA finalized rollbacks of greenhouse gas emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants, according to analysis published by Resources for the Future Resources analysis.

Changes to EPA Air Standards in this area did not directly set a PM2.5 concentration limit. The health issue arises because greenhouse gas rules for power plants and vehicles can also reduce co-pollutants from combustion. If those rules are weakened, modeling suggests that emissions pathways can shift in ways that raise PM2.5 and ozone exposure.

An internal EarthTimes review of related agency actions reached a similar public-health framing in its coverage of the EPA emissions repeal, while policy communication around these decisions is also followed by related public-policy sites such as Comunicacao e Politica, which covers similar topics.

Modeled Deaths And Economic Losses

The Resources for the Future analysis cited in the research estimates that the combined effects of rollbacks to power plant and vehicle greenhouse gas standards would increase PM2.5 and ozone pollution and cause 95,000 premature deaths in the United States between 2032 and 2050. The same research reports that the modeled impacts would fall disproportionately in the Midwest and Eastern states.

The supplied research also reports that forgone health and climate benefits would exceed $3.4 trillion. That figure combines air-quality health effects with broader climate damages. It should be read as a modeled estimate, not as a measured cost already incurred. The result depends on assumptions about emissions, energy demand, technology adoption, valuation of mortality risk and climate damages.

Health Channels Affected By Regulatory Changes

Fine Particles, Ozone And Toxic Metals

The main health channels identified in the research are PM2.5 and ozone. PM2.5 is associated with mortality and cardiopulmonary harm. Ozone is associated with respiratory effects and can worsen asthma and other lung conditions. Rollbacks that increase fossil-fuel combustion or slow emissions reductions can affect both pollutants through direct emissions and atmospheric chemistry.

The research also describes a separate dispute over mercury and air toxics standards for power plants. It says that in March 2026, health and environmental groups sued after the repeal of the 2024 update to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standard. The research notes state that the repealed update would have cut mercury emissions by 70 percent and nickel, arsenic, lead and other toxic metals by two-thirds, with an estimated $420 million in health cost savings by 2037.

Those mercury-related figures are presented here as claims contained in the supplied research record. The legal outcome of the March 2026 challenge is not established in the material provided. For public health, the unresolved issue is whether the prior mercury and toxic metal limits, or some replacement standard, will determine future power-plant controls.

Heavy-Duty Vehicles And Unresolved Protections

The research notes also identify proposed changes affecting heavy-duty trucks and buses. EPA’s 2023 standards for those vehicles were estimated to prevent up to 2,900 early deaths and generate $200 billion in health benefits between 2027 and 2045. The research says proposed changes would reduce those protections.

The final legal status of those proposed changes is not fully documented in the supplied record. That distinction matters. A proposal can shape investment expectations and public debate, but health effects depend on whether the proposal becomes final, how it is written, when it takes effect and whether courts uphold it.

What EPA Air Standards Can Still Do

Air rules work through several mechanisms. Ambient standards set health-based concentration targets. Source standards limit emissions from specific sectors, such as vehicles or power plants. Benefit-cost analysis shapes how agencies compare compliance costs with avoided illness, death and environmental harm.

The research notes say EPA adopted a 2026 policy change to stop assigning a dollar value to health benefits from reductions in PM2.5 and ozone, citing uncertainty. Critics argue that such a change can make deregulation appear less costly to the public. The confirmed point is narrower: changing how health benefits are counted can affect the written justification for future rules, even if the underlying medical risk remains.

Final actions: the February 2026 repeal of the endangerment finding and the September 2026 power-plant greenhouse gas rollback are described as finalized in the research.

Court-backed standard: the 2024 PM2.5 standard remained in place after the D.C. Circuit ruling in June 2026.

Pending step: EPA must make PM2.5 attainment designations by February 6, 2027, under the July 17, 2026 district court order.

Unresolved areas: the final status and health impact of some vehicle and toxics-related changes depend on future agency action and litigation.

What Remains Unresolved In EPA Air Standards

The public health impact of EPA Air Standards after the 2026 changes will depend on three factors: how courts treat the rollbacks, how EPA completes required PM2.5 designations, and how states respond in areas that fail to meet the annual particle standard.

The strongest supported finding in the research is that weaker emissions rules can have health consequences beyond climate policy. Independent modeling links the 2026 rollback package to higher PM2.5 and ozone pollution and estimates large mortality and economic effects over the 2032 to 2050 period. Those estimates are not a substitute for future monitoring data, but they provide a warning signal for regulators and health agencies.

The PM2.5 standard points in the other direction. It remains a tighter health-based benchmark after the June 2026 appeals ruling, and the February 6, 2027 designation deadline gives EPA a specific obligation. Whether that standard offsets health risks from other rollbacks will depend on implementation, enforcement and the pollution mix in each region.

For communities near power plants, highways and industrial corridors, the issue is practical rather than abstract. Small changes in emission limits can affect exposure over years. The policy record through November 7, 2026 shows a split path: some national protections were weakened, while one major particle standard survived court review and moved toward implementation.

text:
BMW is making public charging more affordable for customers buying or leasing select 2027 electric vehicles in the United States. BMW of North America has announced a new charging benefits package worth $500, along with a complimentary one-year membership at IONNA, giving eligible EV owners additional savings and access to a growing public charging network.

Available now, the offer is designed to simplify public charging and reduce ownership costs for customers of eligible 2027 BMW electric vehicles.

The new BMW charging package combines two separate credits that can be used across participating public charging networks.

Eligible customers will receive:

– $300 BMW ChargingNetwork credit: Usable at participating public charging providers across the United States.

– $200 IONNA charging credit: Specifically designated for charging sessions at IONNA locations.

– One year of complimentary IONNA Membership: Includes a 25% discount on charging during the membership period.

The combined $500 in charging credits can help offset public charging expenses during the first year of ownership. Once the applicable credits have been exhausted, subsequent charging sessions will be billed to the customer’s payment method on file.

According to Alexander Schleicher, Head of E-Mobility at BMW of North America, making public charging more accessible is an important part of improving the overall electric vehicle ownership experience.

BMW also highlights the integration of its ChargingNetwork into the My BMW app, allowing drivers to locate charging stations, access compatible services and manage payments through a single platform.

The charging promotion is available to customers who purchase or lease eligible Model Year 2027 versions of three BMW electric vehicles: BMW i5, BMW i7 and BMW iX3.

Customers who purchased or leased an eligible 2027 model before the program’s November 5 launch date may also qualify for the benefits.

The charging credits and complimentary membership are valid for up to one year from the vehicle’s retail date.

To activate the offer, eligible owners must enroll through the My BMW app. The process involves navigating to Charging > Services > Charging Wallet > BMW ChargingNetwork, completing the required account setup and accepting the available charging package.

After enrollment, the credits and membership benefits will appear in the customer’s Digital Charging Wallet. Qualifying charging sessions will then automatically use the available credits.

Additional eligibility details and program terms are available through BMW USA.

Beyond the new financial incentives, BMW is continuing to expand its integrated public charging experience in the United States.

The BMW ChargingNetwork provides access to more than 180,000 compatible public charging stations through the My BMW app. The network brings together multiple charging providers, allowing BMW drivers to find and manage charging sessions without having to navigate several different platforms.

Participating providers include IONNA, Shell Recharge, Electrify America, ChargePoint and EVgo, among others.

BMW is also investing in technologies intended to make public charging more convenient. Its Plug & Charge integration is designed to simplify the charging process by reducing the need for manual authentication and payment steps at compatible stations.

Another initiative is ChargeScape, a collaborative project focused on managing energy flows between electric vehicles and the power grid. Such technology could play an increasingly important role as EV adoption grows and electricity demand changes.

The new charging incentives arrive as BMW prepares to expand its all-electric vehicle portfolio in the United States.

The automaker plans to introduce the BMW iX5 and BMW i3 to the U.S. market in the first quarter of 2027, adding more options to its growing electric vehicle lineup.

America's electricity system is undergoing a major transformation as solar power and battery storage capture an increasing share of new energy investment.

According to the Solar Energy Industries Association, solar and storage accounted for a reported 91% of new power capacity added to the US grid in the first quarter of 2026—the highest share described in its report.

Solar farms can add substantial generating capacity relatively quickly, while battery systems help shift electricity from periods of abundant generation to hours when demand is higher. Together, these technologies can help meet rising electricity needs from data centres, factories and homes.

However, installed capacity measured in megawatts is not the same as electricity generated over time. Solar output varies with weather and daylight, while batteries have finite storage capacity and require charging. A reliable electricity system still needs adequate transmission, flexible generation and other resources to meet demand during every hour.

The reported figure nevertheless highlights how central solar and batteries have become to America's power expansion.

Could solar and battery storage become the dominant source of new electricity capacity in the United States for years to come?

text:
Three-line summary

*Democrats, emboldened by a sweeping midterm win, are expected to push to reverse President Donald Trump's anti-renewable policies.

*The party is stressing lower electricity bills and supply reliability rather than climate action. Costs for transmission grids and storage are a variable.

*With liquefied natural gas now a core U.S. export, the strategic value of fossil fuels is drawing fresh attention to a dual-track approach that runs them alongside renewables.

With the U.S. midterm elections ending in a Democratic landslide — a "blue tsunami" — attention has turned to where American energy policy goes from here. The prevailing view is that Democrats will stick to their traditional pro-renewable stance. Yet even a renewable-centered policy, analysts say, is likely to look different from what came before. Above all, the Democrats too will find it hard to sideline fossil fuels, a core U.S. export resource that generates enormous economic benefits.

Democrats Set to Brake Trump's Anti-Renewable, Anti-Climate Agenda

Having captured both chambers of Congress, Democrats are likely to begin reversing Trump's agenda in earnest. That is a natural next step, given the public opposition to the president that the vote laid bare. Energy policy appears to be no exception, meaning the party will start targeting the Trump administration's anti-renewable and anti-climate measures. Trump, of course, remains in the White House, so Democrats are expected to concentrate on slowing his policies through legislation, budget leverage and oversight of the executive branch.

What anti-renewable and anti-climate measures have come out of Trump's second term? Broadly, they include an early termination of tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), cuts to clean-energy subsidies and budgets, tighter permitting for solar and wind projects, and orders halting offshore wind construction. It is no exaggeration to say that a fairly wide-ranging campaign against renewables has been under way over the past two years or so. Those steps have now become a prime Democratic target. Among them, efforts to restore the IRA — the party's signature green industrial policy, enacted under the Biden administration — began well before the election. In March, 164 House Democrats, including Rep. Sean Casten, jointly introduced the Energy Bills Relief Act. The bill would restore clean-energy tax credits and renewable support funds and bar discriminatory permitting for solar and wind projects.

Democrats Lead With Electricity Bills, Not Climate

Some analysts argue the party's aim is not simply to revive green policy. S&P Global Commodity Insights noted that during the midterm campaign Democrats presented solar and wind as the key alternative for holding down electricity rates. According to the investment bank Lazard, the levelized cost of energy for large-scale U.S. solar starts at $40 per megawatt-hour and onshore wind at $37, cheaper than combined-cycle gas at $51, coal at $72 and new nuclear at $175. Regional variation remains wide, but in the U.S. renewables are judged to be economically competitive.

That, the argument goes, is why Democrats have begun promoting renewables as energy that improves voters' finances rather than for their climate benefits. Inside Climate News, a U.S. nonprofit outlet covering climate, found that Democrats had dramatically reduced references to climate change in press releases and campaign messaging. That mood is reflected in the party's renewable strategy.

An economics-first strategy can cut both ways. If renewable generation costs stay low, there may be no stronger card for winning voters over. But a rising share of renewables does not translate directly into lower electricity bills. In particular, the more renewables are used, the more essential it becomes to expand infrastructure such as transmission networks and storage, including batteries — and those costs have to be counted too. If voters come to feel that renewables are not as cheap as advertised, would the economics argument not boomerang straight back? That would put the party's pro-renewable stance at risk. Come to think of it, even the IRA's name put reducing inflation front and center, rather than declaring a goal of expanding renewables to cut greenhouse gases.

Gas and Renewables on Two Tracks: The Obama Playbook Returns

Above all, the mood inside the party has shifted from an emphasis on renewables alone. James Talarico, who became the first Democratic senator from Texas — the heart of American conservatism — in 38 years, said on his campaign website that the state could "create new jobs in cutting-edge fields such as geothermal and hydrogen, and further expand jobs tied to oil, gas, wind, solar and batteries." The remark is read as support for renewables without ruling out fossil fuels.

That may partly reflect the fact that Texas is home to the Permian Basin, the heartland of U.S. shale gas. But the dual-track strategy of growing fossil fuels and renewables together is one Democrats have emphasized once before. The shale revolution spread in earnest in the U.S. during the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama. Obama's line in his 2012 State of the Union address — that the country needs an "all-of-the-above" strategy that develops every available American energy source — became the symbolic moment for that two-track approach.

Fourteen years on, LNG has become a core U.S. export. According to S&P Global Commodity Insights, U.S. LNG exports totaled $44 billion last year, roughly three times the export value of the film and television industry, a flagship U.S. service export and symbol of American soft power. LNG exports have caught up to more than 80% of passenger-car exports, a mainstay of U.S. manufacturing, and about 70% of semiconductor exports. LNG is also projected to contribute a cumulative $1.4 trillion to U.S. gross domestic product through 2040. It will be hard for Democrats to neglect such a performer.

So much for what these midterm elections, which ended in a blue tsunami, could mean for U.S. energy policy. In sum, Democratic energy policy will keep its renewable-centered direction, but the yardstick for judging that policy is widening beyond climate response to include energy prices and supply reliability. We will keep watching how U.S. energy policy evolves.

text:
Ann Arbor (Informed Comment) – The Netanyahu-Trump war on Iran has put global oil prices up to as much as $118 a barrel at some points. That spike translated into elevated gasoline and diesel prices, putting pressure not only on consumers but on governments, since many states subsidize fuel for their populations. As a result, many governments and consumers have come to feel that they simply cannot afford Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles, as Malaysia’s DS&F reports. Laos banned the import of gasoline cars for much of 2026. Other countries put in policies to favor EV sales, often reducing tariffs on their import. Kenya, France, Italy and other countries have seen unrest over high fuel prices.

In China, New Energy Vehicles are now 67% of new car sales, and ten percent of the vehicles on the road are EVs. These include battery electric, plug-in hybrid, and hybrid vehicles, though pure battery electric is the most popular in China.

Since gasoline car sales have plummeted in China, and many German and American automakers were mainly selling ICE vehicles to the Chinese market, this change means that, e.g., German auto exports to China have fallen off a cliff this year.

The Straits Times reports that “the big three German carmakers’ annual vehicle deliveries in China fell about a third between 2019 and 2025 to 3.87 million, according to AFP calculations based on company disclosures.”

At the same time, Chinese brands came to capture 65.3% of the domestic market, up from 37.8%, over the same period. The Chinese brands offer a variety of EVs, most of them increasingly inexpensive and chock full of fancy electronic features that make a lot of American and German autos look primitive, not to mention pricey and smelly. China’s government has also vastly expanded the number of public charging points.

Daniel Sherman Fernandez at DS&F writes, “Chinese automakers maintain vehicle development cycles of 18 to 24 months, compared to 36 to 48 months for traditional European and Japanese auto brands.” This faster development cycle allows Chinese firms to pivot quickly.

Chinese automakers also, he says, produce their powertrains and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) batteries in-house, avoiding the price rollercoaster of nickel and cobalt prices.

Chinese firm BYD’s lower-end Seagull hatchback goes for $8,000! BYDs can charge to 70% in as little as five minutes. The BYD Denza B-9 can go 663 miles on a charge.

The Straits Times says that German automakers were hobbled by their long experience in making well-engineered ICE cars and that executives could not imagine being out-engineered by the Chinese in a new technology the Germans were reluctant to adopt. There was a certain amount of hubris in their downfall, since Carl Benz had developed an internal combustion vehicle in the late 19th century.

AFP quoted Tu Le of Sino Auto Insights as saying that the Germans brought an analogue toy to a digital party.

Photo by Michael Förtsch on Unsplash

Benjamin Wehrmann writes for Clean Energy Wire, however, that German executives’ calculations were also driven by profit considerations. Luxury ICE cars have a bigger profit margin:

“The surge in demand for electric vehicles (EVs) is turning into a challenge for Germany’s carmakers because combustion models are more profitable and EV production cannot keep up with orders, causing them to lose customers to foreign competitors, the business daily Handelsblatt reported. “For many years, German manufacturers’ EVs were shunned by customers. Now sales of a new EV generation significantly exceed expectations. For their profitability, this is bad news,” the newspaper said.”

He concludes,

“The rapid shift in demand is partly driven by customers seeking alternatives to combustion engine cars as fuel prices have skyrocketed in the wake of the US-Israeli-led war on Iran. The accelerating uptake of electric cars has led to a rise of cheaper Chinese competitors, spurring concerns about a wave of job losses among carmakers and industry suppliers in Europe.

Changing attitudes towards EVs are posing a predicament for the carmakers: if they fail to satisfy demand, customers will switch to Chinese brands. If they sell more EVs themselves, their financial woes will deepen, the newspaper concluded.”

US automakers will face the same headwinds abroad as do the Germans, and for the same reasons. As someone who lives in the Detroit area, I’m petrified that the backwardness of the Big Three in the U.S. will lead to their decline, and with it the backbone of America’s industry. Trump’s idea that we can be successful with antiquated fossil fuels and gas guzzlers was never realistic. But when he let Netanyahu talk him into the Iran War, he accelerated the crisis.

USA – The Andersons has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Harvestone Low Carbon Partners (HLCP) from Energy Capital Partners (ECP) for US$915 million, strengthening its ethanol production capacity and expanding its low-carbon fuel manufacturing capabilities.

The acquisition will add approximately 215 million gallons of annual ethanol production capacity through three existing biorefineries operated by Harvestone in North Dakota and Indiana.

After completion, The Andersons’ combined ethanol production platform is expected to reach approximately 730 million gallons annually, representing more than a 40% expansion in its Renewables business.

Harvestone operates the Blue Flint and Dakota Spirit AgEnergy facilities in North Dakota and the Iroquois Bio-Energy Company plant in Indiana.

The facilities produce corn-based ethanol and are strategically located near geological formations suitable for carbon capture and sequestration (CCS).

The company has developed and commercialized integrated carbon capture infrastructure, enabling it to reduce the carbon intensity of its ethanol production and access premium low-carbon fuel markets.

The acquisition will strengthen The Andersons’ position in the renewable energy sector by combining Harvestone’s low-carbon production expertise with its existing grain origination, merchandising and logistics operations.

The integration is expected to improve corn procurement, optimize transportation and create additional value from ethanol co-products, including distillers dried grains with solubles (DDGS) and distillers corn oil.

Approximately half of the US$915 million purchase price is attributed to anticipated cash flows from the US 45Z Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit and 45Q Carbon Oxide Sequestration Tax Credit programmes. The remaining value relates to Harvestone’s underlying ethanol operations and additional low-carbon fuel opportunities.

The Andersons expects to finance the transaction through approximately US$300 million in borrowings under its existing revolving credit facility and US$615 million in additional long-term debt. US Bank National Association and Farm Credit Mid-America have provided committed financing.

The company expects the acquisition to immediately contribute to earnings per share and cash flows while keeping its long-term debt-to-EBITDA ratio below its target of 2.5 times.

Commenting on the acquisition, Bill Krueger, president and chief executive officer of The Andersons, said Harvestone’s established low-carbon ethanol capabilities, production economics and strategically positioned facilities complement the company’s existing operations and provide opportunities for profitable growth.

The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 or early in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

The acquisition reflects continued investment in renewable fuels as producers seek to improve production efficiency, reduce emissions and capture growing opportunities in lower-carbon energy markets.

text:
Government officials, scientists, climate organizations and business leaders from around the world are set to come together in Turkey this week for the annual international climate conference, COP31. And for the second year in a row, an official Trump administration delegation will not be present.

Short for the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the conference is part of a multinational treaty that was adopted in 1992. When the Paris Agreement was signed in 2015, COPs became a primary tool for working out the details on how to achieve the goals of the agreement.

The annual meetings are the forum for countries, non-governmental organizations, and other interested parties to discuss global efforts to combat human-induced climate change and negotiate agreements on topics such as mitigation, financing and adaptation.

This year's conference is being held in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 leadership says the conference presents an important opportunity for countries to strengthen cooperation and accelerate climate action, describing it as both an "implementation COP" and a "COP of the future," with a focus on translating commitments into clear, measurable progress.

Why is the U.S. not officially attending COP31?

Nearly 200 countries participate in the UNFCCC, and most attend the COP annually.

On the first day of his second term, President Donald Trump signed an executive order announcing that the U.S. would withdraw from the Paris Agreement for the second time.

The U.S. is also withdrawing from the UNFCCC, following an executive order signed by Trump on January 7. This withdrawal will become official next year.

While federal U.S. representation will be absent from COP31, state and local leaders, as well as scientists, advocates, community leaders and members of non-governmental organizations from across the country will be attending.

A U.S. delegation of more than 100 leaders will participate in COP31, including U.S. governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, organized by America Is All In, Climate Mayors and the U.S. Climate Alliance.

"America Is All In is showing up in force at COP31 to let the world know that millions of Americans are still in," said Gina McCarthy, America Is All In Chair, 13th U.S. EPA administrator, and former White House National Climate advisor. "Mayors, governors, and cross-sector leaders from all across our country will be in Türkiye to demonstrate the strength of U.S. subnational climate leadership and build partnerships and solutions that advance people's lives everywhere."

What's on the agenda for COP31?

COP31 leaders say turning collective ambition into concrete action has become increasingly urgent. This year, the conference will focus on several priority themes, including the clean energy transition and electrification, waste and methane reduction, climate-resilient cities, youth and education and advancing climate finance commitments, an issue that the body has struggled with in the past.

Recent reports from the U.N. and independent organizations reveal a substantial gap between countries' pledges on emissions reductions and what is required to limit additional global warming in the coming decades.

"Last year in Brazil, a focus was on adaptation and helping vulnerable countries and communities pay for and manage the consequences of climate change. I would like to see COP31 be a place where we focus on how to deliver," Dr. Alexis Abramson, Dean of Columbia Climate School, told ABC News.

Delegates will also work on several proposed global goals, including increasing the share of energy demand met by electricity from just over 20% in 2024 to 35% by 2035. The hope is that by electrifying more industries and communities, clean renewable power can replace fossil fuel generation and reduce those greenhouse gas emissions.

Climate groups tell ABC News that they would also like to see more attention paid to adapting to the dangers of climate change, including funding efforts to protect communities from the most severe impacts. And after the damage is done, they want to see more international funds available to cover the repairs and losses, especially for poorer countries.

"COP 31 really needs to be the moment when adaptation and loss and damage move from the margins to the center of climate action," said Adelle Thomas, Senior Director of Climate Adaptation at the National Resources Defense Council. "An overall framing for this COP in particular is that we need to stop treating mitigation, adaptation, and loss and damage as competing priorities."

The rapid growth of artificial intelligence and data centers is also a key part of the conference's agenda as rising demand for computing power raises concerns about energy resources and environmental impacts.

Ahead of the conference, leaders released the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, inviting countries and organizations to sign on voluntarily. The pledge aims to address mounting concerns, while also evaluating it as a potential new tool to drive climate action.

"We must openly discuss AI's growing energy ​consumption, and it is time for governments to start setting the terms. ​We expect companies to be transparent about their energy use and to power their operations with clean energy," Kurum said.

While the pledge signals a growing commitment to addressing the environmental impact, questions remain about accountability, transparency and how progress will be measured.

"Responsibly managing AI requires establishing strong guardrails: powering data centers with clean energy, mandating full disclosure, including of AI companies' energy and water use and system impacts, requiring companies to pay for their own grid upgrades, and giving local communities a genuine seat at the table from day one," said Evan Tachovsky, Chief Data and AI Officer at World Resources Institute.

Global efforts continue to fall short

COP31 comes at a time when many key indicators show the world is falling further behind on several climate goals.

According to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the planet is on track to officially breach the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold within the next few years, and is now encouraging countries to shift their focus to limiting further warming.

"Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible -- and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement.

Atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) levels surged to a new record high in 2025, surpassing 2024, according to the World Meteorological Organization.

Since the 1960s, the growth rate of atmospheric CO2 has tripled, accelerating from an annual average increase of 0.8 ppm per year to 2.4 ppm per year between 2011 to 2020. Concentrations of two other long-lived greenhouse gases linked to human activities, methane and nitrous oxide, also reached new record highs last year.

These greenhouse gases are the primary driver of human-induced climate change.

Despite these challenges, the report points to significant progress since the adoption of the Paris Agreement, with expanding opportunities to accelerate action. Renewable energy has grown rapidly, coal and oil use has increased more slowly than projected, and policies have helped lower emissions in many countries.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly. It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies," said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP.

Whether COP31 will result in agreements on these policies remains to be seen. But climate experts told ABC News that success in Turkey shouldn't be measured only by what happens in the negotiating sessions. Rather, they say that much of the work, known as the Action Agenda, gets done in smaller meetings and one-on-one discussions.

For many leaders working to prevent the worst impacts of climate change, COPs are a rare opportunity to get in-person time with the people who do have the power and knowledge to implement the vision of the original Paris Agreement and move the needle.

text:
Tesla’s decision to end Cybertruck production in Texas is only the loudest chapter in a bigger retreat. Business Insider reports that the full-size electric truck bet at Ford, General Motors, Stellantis and Tesla has largely fallen apart, and the company filings behind that claim put hard numbers on it. Ford took a $19.5 billion charge after dropping its electric pickup. GM has booked nearly $11 billion in write-downs since 2025. Stellantis recorded $26 billion in write-downs, and its Ram REV never reached production.

Elon Musk set the latest news cycle on November 6, when he said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck output at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year. The reason he gave was room for the Cybercab. That is a planned wind-down, not an overnight shutdown, and the difference matters for owners, suppliers and anyone tracking the electric truck bet as an investment story. We covered the first reaction in our earlier report on the Giga Texas wind-down. This piece zooms out to the whole segment.

Three automakers, three different electric pickups, and one shared outcome: demand fell short of what the factories were built to deliver. The sections below separate what the record confirms from what is interpretation. They also add up the write-downs, check the Cybertruck’s own sales trend, and lay out what could come next for hardware buyers, suppliers and investors.
