The Vigo County Area Plan Commission voted Wednesday evening, making a favorable recommendation to the county’s zoning ordinance.

That zoning amendment would allow Battery Energy Storage Systems — or BESS — as a special exception.

The recommendation goes to the Board of Commissioners, said Sydney Shahar, assistant director of the Area Planning Department, which serves both Vigo County and the city of Terre Haute.

The Board of Commissioners take up the matter at 9 a.m. Tuesday at the Vigo County Annex, and it could make a decision on the amendment at that time,

A BESS can be a strategic precursor or a fast-track bridge to a data center.

A BESS can integrate with a data center to provide extended backup power, manage heavy electricity demand spikes and smooth out power fluctuations caused by AI workloads, according to information available online, including AI-generated summaries.

Switzer expects healthy debate at Tuesday’s Commissioners meeting.

“I have heard from numerous members of our community regarding the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project, including those who support it and those who have expressed concerns,” he said.

“I respect those differing opinions and believe it’s important that we listen to the public and carefully consider the facts before making decisions that impact our community,” he said.

Switzer added, “I have been transparent about my support for this project. I believe responsible economic development and private investment are important to Vigo County’s future, provided projects meet appropriate safety, zoning, and regulatory requirements.”

Switzer said Area Planning’s BESS exemption doesn’t necessarily mean a data center looms on Vigo County’s horizon.

“There is no direct correlation between a BESS project and a data center,” Switzer said. “Battery energy storage facilities store electricity and help support the electrical grid, while data centers are facilities that consume electricity to operate computing equipment.

“Although both involve energy infrastructure, approving zoning provisions for battery storage does not automatically pave the way for a data center or establish any connection between the two.”

Commissioner Mark Clinkenbeard is a member of Area Plan Commission, but did not attend Wednesday’s meeting.

“I will be looking over the ordinance this weekend and going back and watching the last meeting (video on YouTube),” he said, adding, “We are having our legal counsel look over it.”

Commissioner Mike Morris was contacted a couple of times on Thursday and Friday but had no comment.

In a matter not directly tied to the zoning amendment, the Vigo County Council may be looking at a measure prohibiting it from providing any financial assistance to data centers at its Nov. 16 and 23 meetings.

Councilwoman Nancy Allsup is behind the resolution that initially was to have started its journey before the council this past Wednesday, but the scheduled council meetings were pushed back to the 16th and 23rd. There are, as of yet, no agendas published for those meetings.

The resolution before the council reads in part, “Data center developments may require substantial investments in electrical infrastructure, water and sewer systems, road improvements, emergency services and other public facilities.” It adds, “Discretionary public subsidies for privately operated data centers are not a fiscal priority of Vigo County.”

text:
Air Date: Week of November 6, 2026

The United States Capitol building in Washington, D.C. A new Democratic-majority Congress will convene in early January 2027. (Photo: Noclip, Wikimedia Commons public domain)

Hosts Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering continue our roundtable discussion with Vernon Loeb, Marianne Lavelle, and Dan Gearino of Inside Climate News about voters’ frustration with high fuel prices and the opportunity for a Democratic-led Congress to now focus on clean energy to reduce energy costs. We talk about what voters expect the Democratic party to deliver in the final two years of the Trump presidency and beyond.

Transcript

DOERING: It’s Living on Earth, I’m Jenni Doering

CURWOOD: And I’m Steve Curwood.

We’re here with colleagues from our media partner Inside Climate News, unpacking the blockbuster win for Democrats in the midterm elections and what it could mean for environmental protection during President Trump’s final 2 years in office. So, Marianne, let’s drill down on how energy played with voters, what did we see here?

LAVELLE: Right, some of the polling before the election showed that voters were much more worried about Republican energy policies than they were about Democratic climate policies being costly. And this is after the last two years the Trump administration has been ringing that bell that the Democrats want to give you the costly Green Deal, but voters just were not buying it. They know what they're paying for energy, and they know that that's related to this fossil fuel energy policy of the administration.

CURWOOD: With great profits for the fossil fuel industry through this campaign. I mean, underscored.

LAVELLE: It just so happened that they reported their profits last week, right before the election, and they're like triple what they were last year. And that's not because they're putting out a better product or anything. It's because purely the run-up in global prices.

LOEB: And Trump went on the campaign trail bragging about how great the oil industry profits were, and essentially saying, "I don't really care about people's concerns about pump prices. Isn't it great that all the money the oil industry is raking in?"

LAVELLE: What he said is this is money we're raking in as a country. But that's not how, how consumers experience it. It's really the oil companies that are raking in those profits, and their executives are the ones who have the most shares in those companies and who feel the benefits the most.

DOERING: So I mean, this is fascinating. Like, to what extent do you think Democrats now have the upper hand when it comes to issues like energy affordability, and what do they need to do to deliver on that in this Congress?

LAVELLE: Well, for the last 10 years at least, we've been in this incredibly polarized atmosphere where it's hard to imagine Democrats and Republicans working together on anything. But look at the way people voted, across the board in a bipartisan way, and the people they're sending to Washington know some of the voters were Republicans as well. They're all wanting the same thing, which is action on the out of control costs and the power that industries like the fossil fuel industry, like big tech, have over their lives. And so, I think what you're going to see is the Democrats trying to find some common ground with the Republicans who are now going to be there in the minority, on how they can address these issues that all of their voters said they cared about. I mean, one thing that comes to the top of the list is windfall profits taxes on the oil and gas industry as we were just talking about. What other industry has seen its profits, not its revenue, its profits, triple? And so there's so much that that money could be invested in to transition us away from this vulnerability that we have. The first ideas you're going to see are all going to be about affordability, and of course, the cheapest form of energy are the renewables, and that is the messaging we're going to see around what kind of legislation is going to be tried in the next Congress.

CURWOOD: So, in this tsunami for the Democrats, we've seen this huge switch from control away from the Republicans. But correct me if I'm wrong, but I think the electorate is mostly in the middle, mostly independent, and in many of these elections, the folks who really end up deciding what happens. I don't think there were a lot of defections from the hardcore Republicans this time around. What do the Democrats need to do now in this sector of protecting the environment and dealing with the climate emergency and and energy affordability? What do they need to do to keep that vast middle that, at the end of the day, elected them this time, and if they want to keep getting reelected, will need to show up next time?

LAVELLE: One of the interesting things is the moderate members of the Democratic Party up on the Hill already have gathered in this new Democrat coalition, and have organized, and talking about just these things, putting affordability front and center. And there also has been a lot of effort in the leadership to get the more centrist Democrats working with more left Democrats and seeing where their common ground is, so that the party doesn't have the inter-party fighting that has really made it hard for the Republicans to govern over the last few years. So I think it's a challenge, there's no question, but I think that people are going into this new Congress with a lot of positive vibes, so to speak. At least that's what the sense I'm getting from talking to people. They're not talking about what divides the Democrats, but what they can do together.

CURWOOD: Vernon, talk to me about this.

LOEB: The last time the Democrats did pretty well in the midterms in 2018, they came back to Washington talking about the Green New Deal, and it turned into very quickly a culture war slogan that they got clubbed with over the head for the next two years. Now, they're not talking about the Green New Deal. They're not even talking about climate change. They're talking about data centers and affordability, and those are populist slogans, if you will, that play across both sides of the aisle very effectively. And so they've learned a powerful lesson there, and it's easy now to make the case for solar and wind as cheaper alternatives. With Iran in, in charge of the Strait of Hormuz and gas still sitting at $4.50 a gallon and diesel sitting at $6.30 a gallon, and so the Democrats rhetorically, I think, are in a much smarter, stronger tactical position now than they were in 2018.

CURWOOD: So, looking ahead, you know, the next two years, Mr. Trump is still president of the United States. How does this win stack up against dealing with him in the White House?

LAVELLE: One of the models I've heard some of the Democratic lawmakers talk about is the housing affordability bill that Congress passed that Trump did not want to sign. He actually wanted to put his voter bill in it, and Congress wouldn't do it. But it was a bipartisan bill, and it had just such strong support across the board, and he let it pass without his signature. He let it go into law without his signature. That's kind of the model for what they're looking to do: bills that are just so popular that Trump will either deal with them or will just back away from a fight that just doesn't look good for him or his legacy. But of course, Trump is mercurial, if nothing else, so we'll have to see. One of the energy experts that I talked to today pointed out that a lot of the big environmental legislation of our era, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Air Act, passed with Democratic Congresses and a Republican president, and that divided government sometimes can work if both sides see a way to compromise.

DOERING: Yeah.

CURWOOD: Vernon, you're thinking. I can see.

LOEB: Well, Trump sounded a sort of conciliatory note last night, saying, "Yeah, we'll work with Democrats. We'll figure out a way to do it." How much interest and energy he has left for legislating, he's never had much of a legislative agenda. He's bypassed Congress almost completely. How much energy he has for governing, it remains to be seen. Who knows what we're going to get from Trump in his last two years. A lot of people feel his health is sort of failing. His mental acuity clearly is not what it once was, so I think it's an unknown at this point, and it's also in my mind an unknown how Republicans now will react to him. He kept them in line amazingly well. They were really afraid of crossing him and crossing MAGA, but now he's a lame duck. Everybody's a free agent, and I think you're going to see a lot of Republicans starting to chart a more independent path away from Trump, thinking about their next election in the House two years from now. One of the most interesting things I heard last night was somebody quoting Lindsey Graham from 2015 when Trump came down the golden escalator, and right around that time, Lindsey Graham said, "If we support this man for president, he will destroy us. He will destroy the party, and he will destroy us all." And fast forward a decade, with Lindsey Graham's sister on the ballot, and she loses to a neophyte Democrat pediatrician.

LAVELLE: Because she was handpicked by Trump, and South Carolina voters were very upset at his intervention, and yeah, the irony is unbelievable.

LOEB: Yeah, and if you look at Trump's influence on the Senate races, you can argue that both Democratic seats in Georgia were the result of Trump picks a cycle ago. You can say that Talarico's victory over Paxton was attributable to Trump's support for Paxton. You've got Lindsey Graham's sister, and so Trump clearly gets an assist for the Democrats in about four or five Senate seats.

CURWOOD: Hey Dan, before we go, how can the Democrats keep support of middle America? Take advantage of, of the wins that they've had now to build up something solid there.

GEARINO: Well, to try to kind of unpack that, when's the last time Democrats had a night as good as this? And it wasn't a lot of these wave elections we've seen just in the last couple decades. You have to go way back. You have to go back to post-Watergate. So, who was elected out of the post-Watergate era in Iowa? Tom Harkin was one of those elected. He was one of the Watergate babies as they called them, and you saw this generation of a lot of them were in the Midwest. A lot of them were everywhere. You were winning in conservative areas. Oh wow, a Democrat won there? There were some really politically talented people who may not have won except for the political climate of that very precise moment. But once they got there, they stayed. And I can look at a couple of these people who won in the House and the Senate, and it'd be hard to imagine them losing when they run for reelection in two years or in six years, they're just political talents who happen to be running at the right time. And a key part of that is just listening to your constituents, realizing who you represent, and delivering for them. It is really not that complicated. I think there are names that were part of this election cycle that we are going to have as part of our lives for a very long time because they're good at politics, and that's in Democrat-leaning states, Republican-leaning states, swing states. So yeah, that's, that's kind of how you do it, I think.

CURWOOD: All right, that then brings up the question: dare I ask about 2028?

LOEB: Well, like Dan was just saying, there's a lot of young talent out there in the Democratic field now. You've got Jon Ossoff, who's in his 40s. You've got Turek in Iowa. You've got Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania. You have Andy Beshear in Kentucky. Got Mark Kelly in Arizona. You've got Gavin Newsom in California. I think all of those guys would fare well against, who-knows-who will be the Republican candidates. But if the MAGA holdovers are still there, I guess it would either be J.D. Vance or Marco Rubio. But I think the Democratic candidates stack up pretty well. And remember, the Senate wins pretty much guarantee the Democrats the Senate through the next presidential election. So you're going to have the presidential election with a Democratic Congress, and you've got Texas in place suddenly that completely changes the whole electoral map that the country has sort of played by for 30 or 40 years. You know, you had that group of swing states that the Democrats had to win. Suddenly, they're not so important anymore if the Democrats win Texas and all those electoral votes. So '28 is going to be, like unbelievably interesting.

CURWOOD: All right, Dan, what do you think?

GEARINO: There's this fascinating inversion of the way this gets talked about, and it's just changed so much in the last year or so. There was a time not long ago when reasonable people would say the Democrats had no bench. You could probably go eight or nine deep with Democrats that would be plausible presidential candidates, and there are a few of them who won yesterday. And then you look at this rupturing of the kind of Trump base; it makes it so that all of a sudden they're the ones that don't have a very deep bench. It's like you've got J.D. Vance and who, you know who would be next Marco Rubio, and then okay, who's fifth or sixth up? And it's just wild, and it just kind of shows things change rapidly, you know. And if you fixate too much on the moment that you're in, you're gonna just go nuts, because things change quick. The piece I'm writing today, I'm trying to fit in this quote from, oh, the former Colorado Governor Bill Ritter, and he had this comment in an interview a couple weeks ago where he was talking about like the swinging screen door, and that the thing is the door hits you in the rear end. You know, basically there are ups and downs in political life, and that reversal can come quick. And I think that that's something on a day when Democrats are just celebrating, they can just see just in recent history how that can turn quick.

CURWOOD: Hey, before we go, of course we are objective journalists. We have views and responses, of course, but one of the dogs in this particular fight is our own profession: the ability to report the news and to function in a democracy with a free press that's enshrined in the Constitution. What does this win by the Democrats mean for press freedom in America, do you think?

LOEB: Well, I think it's important. You know, Trump has shown a willingness to go after the press, to file lawsuits, to intimidate, to throw reporters out of institutions that they have a right to cover, to decide who can come to the Pentagon, who can cover wars, who can go to the White House briefing room, and I think a democratic victory, taking the country back to the norms that we operated under in terms of government and the press for my entire career, which is like going on 50 years now, I think it's an important moment to kind of reestablish those norms, and I think it augurs well for press freedom going forward. The other big thing that, when you talk about press freedom, has really now become ownership of networks. You know, you've got Fox News, you've got CBS now in the hands of a billionaire family. You've got CNN, you know, in the hands of a conglomerate that's more friendly to Trump, and that's something that we really didn't have, you know, a generation ago. That kind of bifurcation, almost, of the mainstream media. So how that's going to play out really remains to be seen. But from my perspective, in terms of picking which reporters can go to the White House briefing room and which ones can't, I, I hope, you know, we're, we're moving to an era where that's not going to happen quite so easily.

DOERING: Well, we want to thank you, Vernon Loeb is Executive Editor of Inside Climate News. Thank you so much for being here.

LOEB: Sure, thanks for having me.

DOERING: And Marianne Lavelle, Washington Bureau Chief at ICN.

LAVELLE: Thanks, glad to be here.

DOERING: And Dan Gearino, clean energy reporter at ICN. Thank you all so much.

GEARINO: Yep, thank you.

LAVELLE: Thank you.

CURWOOD: And thanks to all three of you for coming and keeping the story going. And I'm looking forward to what's coming next.

text:
The Chamber of Progress is urging congressional Democrats to introduce legislation in 2027 to require data center operators to cover electricity costs, disclose water consumption, and provide economic benefits to surrounding communities.

In a Nov. 4 memo, the technology policy group outlined its legislative priorities for the next Congress, including three proposed measures designed to address the growing energy and infrastructure demands associated with data center development.

Three proposed bills target electricity, public benefits, and water use

One central recommendation, the Pay Your Own Way Act, would require data center campuses consuming 100 megawatts or more to cover the full incremental cost of supplying them with electricity. The legislation would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish a model electricity tariff for large power users. It would also condition federal grid funding on states adopting equivalent tariff structures.

According to the Chamber of Progress, the proposal would make the Ratepayer Protection Pledge binding on data center operators, aiming to prevent residential customers from absorbing electricity costs associated with large-scale data center demand.

A second proposal, the Public Dollars, Public Benefits Act, would connect expedited federal permitting and access to federal land with requirements that data centers operate without public subsidies. The measure would also establish public registries of financial incentives and direct federal cost-sharing toward shared electric grid infrastructure intended to reduce costs for ratepayers.

The third proposal, the Closed Loop Act, would establish state-level water-use disclosure requirements for large industrial facilities and introduce performance-based water consumption standards. The measure would coordinate water and electricity reviews while providing funding for research and conservation incentives.

Beyond infrastructure and resource requirements, the Chamber of Progress is recommending local hiring commitments, apprenticeship opportunities, and workforce training programs to ensure surrounding communities receive economic benefits from data center construction and operations.

Local opposition adds pressure for greater oversight

The recommendations come amid growing opposition to data center development in communities nationwide.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Democrats, has also called for restrictions on new facilities, citing local ballot measures voters approved in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Data center restrictions appeared on ballots in 40 jurisdictions across 10 states, with voters approving restrictions in virtually every contest, according to preliminary results. A few results remained pending, while Hardwood, N.D., was a notable exception, with voters rejecting restrictions on data center development.

NBC exit polling found that 76% of voters opposed construction of new data centers in their communities. The polling also found that 56% considered data centers a crucial or major factor in their choice of congressional candidates.

“National data center moratorium now,” Sanders wrote in a post on X. “Americans don’t want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity’s future.”

Janine Yorio, CEO of Community Digital Technologies, attributed the growing opposition to data centers to the physical visibility of data centers and the disconnect between the communities hosting them and the people benefiting financially from their development.

Data centers, she said, have become the most visible representation of the artificial intelligence industry. However, a moratorium, as Sanders has suggested, would not solve the overarching issue, she explained.

“People are going to expect to be brought along with the AI economy and not left behind by it,” she said.

Practical legislation to address data center concerns could provide that “people that live in data center communities actually own a piece of the data centers themselves. If data centers don’t create jobs, they should still help make local people more prosperous.”

“I do not fundamentally believe that AI will slow down or that data centers will never get built. But the economic framework under which all these things move forward, I believe, is going to change significantly,” she said.

Incoming Democrats outline data center proposals

Data center oversight is also emerging as a priority among incoming Democrats, several of whom have called for greater accountability for the industry’s effects on local communities and energy infrastructure.

Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, has proposed making data center operators responsible for the costs associated with their facilities. His plan includes ending tax incentives for large technology companies, requiring major energy users to finance infrastructure improvements, and establishing federal standards for new data center projects.

Talarico has also expressed support for closed-loop cooling systems to reduce water consumption and giving local communities greater authority over data center development decisions.

Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., has similarly called for federal requirements that ensure data centers pay their own electricity costs rather than shifting expenses to residential ratepayers.

Hamilton has also said that companies should earn the support of the communities where they establish operations.

title: COP31 and Climate Action's New Centers of Gravity | Council on Foreign Relations
description:

Although the multilateral process remains central to addressing climate change, one must also recognize that climate action is accelerating beyond the negotiating room.
The African Union’s Climate Action Innovation Hub illustrates how entrepreneurs across the continent are developing innovative solutions to Africa’s climate challenges.

text:
Consensus-based climate negotiations are slow, especially as countries disagree over finance, responsibility, and the pace of change. Multilateralism—climate multilateralism, in particular—is in a tough spot.

The blame cannot all be laid at the door of the Trump administration. In Europe, political parties critical of development assistance and the impact of climate action on domestic competitiveness are becoming more prominent, while budgets are shifting toward defense spending. Energy security is the new watchword, both in the Global North and the Global South—a concept that can be used to justify switching away from fossil fuel imports, but equally to call for continued exploitation of domestic fossil fuel resources.

In periods of threat and uncertainty, time horizons shorten and circles of concern narrow. The call for ambitious action against a global challenge like climate change, which will worsen for coming generations, is being drowned out and even actively shouted down. Yet climate impacts are crossing borders and escalating while the resources available to respond are deeply insufficient and unequally distributed.

The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and its Paris Agreement remain an essential shared decision-making forum. In this complex global environment, the forum allows countries to voice their concerns and hold others accountable. Countries can grapple with important questions that cannot be resolved by markets, such as how historical emissions should shape the responsibilities countries have in addressing climate change, how and by whom the immense costs of adaptation and the losses and damages of climate change are financed, and how to navigate a just energy transition at national and global levels. For vulnerable countries, those questions are central to realizing a more just world and maintaining trust in the multilateral system.

Although the multilateral process remains central to addressing climate change, one must also recognize that climate action is accelerating beyond the negotiating room.

Governments are revising energy and industrial priorities, while cities and communities are developing ground-level solutions to manage worsening heat, floods, and water stress. Businesses and financial institutions are developing innovative products, technologies, and financial instruments. Clean energy is being embraced as a pathway to affordable power, jobs, and industrial opportunities, as well as a way to contribute to greater energy security. Increasingly, altruism is not the main calculus in making the right climate decisions; it is simply the economically and strategically sensible thing to do.

The African Union’s Climate Action Innovation Hub illustrates how entrepreneurs across the continent are developing innovative solutions to Africa’s climate challenges. These innovators show how climate action can be linked to greater resilience, innovation, and job growth. However, such action must also be linked with capital to scale its impact.

The vital areas of dynamism and innovation in climate action can be found in cities, on farms, and in financial institutions, but the painstaking work of multilateral negotiation on shared responsibilities and collective action cannot be abandoned—it must be defended.

In Climate Action, Solar Leads the Way

Globally, climate action is shifting from pledges to deployment, with energy security and industrial policy emerging as new centers of gravity. Solar provides the evidence.

Total global solar capacity in 2025 was over ten times greater than it was in 2015 and has grown by more than four times what the International Energy Agency predicted in 2015. Prices have dropped dramatically, making solar the cheapest energy source in many places. Solar photovoltaic (PV) adoption is expected to account for almost 80 percent of growth in renewable electricity capacity worldwide and, in 2025, solar PVs accounted for over one-quarter of energy demand growth. Battery capacity additions also increased by about 40 percent.

Despite rising demand for electricity, including from artificial intelligence (AI) and increased use of air-conditioning, the climb in global energy-related carbon emissions remained slow last year—around 0.4 percent. And this year, as flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled, they are on course to drop by 0.5 percent.

Even as nations built out liquefied natural gas and restarted coal plants in response to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, they sought to reduce their dependence on imported fossil fuels. The support provided by China’s industrial policy for clean energy technology helped it to underwrite the global spread of solar.

Growth in solar allowed some nations to insulate themselves against fuel price volatility. But it also deepened dependence on Chinese industry and technology. China itself doubled down on solar and other low-emissions technology. The United States, however, took a different path, shifting federal policy to favor fossil fuels under President Donald Trump.

Meanwhile, communities are struggling to adapt to climate impacts like flooding and extreme heat. Meteorologists expect the 2026–27 El Niño to spread weather and temperature extremes across the globe. The world is unprepared for these record-breaking events that cut across boundaries and exceed prior experience. As the glacial collapse in Nepal and Tibet revealed, the gulf between adapting to climate change and its power to destroy is widening. Better monitoring and early-warning systems are urgently needed to reduce damage from future climate-fueled calamities.

As climate impacts mount and adaptation lags, entrepreneurs, nations, and scientists have increasingly embraced atmospheric interventions. No binding governance regime sets guardrails, meaning nations or private actors could deploy them with global effects. This issue can no longer remain in the shadows; it requires immediate multilateral action to oversee experimentation and manage any potential usage.

That solar energy is spreading widely is a welcome development in the fight against rising greenhouse gas emissions. But that spread alone will not meet the moment when it comes to sparing people from climate harm. As nations gather in Turkey for the thirty-first Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change in November, they can celebrate the emissions reduction achieved by the turn to solar and other renewables. However, this year’s record-setting high temperatures should serve as a prod to accelerate climate action. It is time to honor past promises to prevent the rise of temperatures to catastrophic levels.

The Real Climate Innovation is political, not technological

Climate change has been considered by many to be the greatest challenge of the twenty-first century. This led to the development of effective technological solutions that have begun to turn the tide in decreasing global greenhouse gas emissions. Policymakers have at their disposal the tools required to stave off the worst of the climate crisis and meet the Paris Agreement targets of 1.5°C (2.7°F) to 2°C (3.6°F) of warming.

However, it has become clear that the world will soon exceed the more ambitious of the two targets, and even the more problematic 2°C target seems likely to be surpassed. This ongoing failure is not the result of a lack of technological tools, know-how, and innovations required for success, as renewables have quickly become cheaper than fossil-fueled sources of energy, and various incentive structures exist that have been proven to encourage the adoption of less carbon-intensive modes of production. That governments continue to fall short of the required action is instead a political problem fanned by the flames of disinformation and polarization.

The good news is that those issues are already spurring significant action to address climate change today—namely through the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change (GIIICC) and similar governance agreements aimed at combating the scourge of climate disinformation. The initiative funds journalism, research, and public outreach campaigns, and serves an important coordinating role for like-minded actors to ensure greater access to accurate, reliable, and accessible data in countries around the world. Initiatives like the GIIICC are more important than ever, as they not only deal with the specific issue of the ever-worsening climate crisis, but also seek to promote healthier information ecosystems.

As information systems become increasingly disaggregated, polluted, and divided, the social fabric that enables societies and healthy functioning democracies is further strained. The GIIICC serves as a global convening function to provide funding and support for traditional journalists, researchers, and trusted community messengers in order to promote healthier information ecosystems.

Therefore, the GIIICC, along with the UN Global Principles for Information Integrity, the International Partnership for Information and Democracy, and similar ongoing efforts to maintain effective multilateral governance, are pivotal, not only for dealing with transborder problems, such as climate change, but also for the continuation of the weakening liberal international order.

text:
Introduction

The chairs and ranking members of the Senate Environment and Public Works and Energy and Natural Resources Committees introduced S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), on September 30, 2026. BAAJA is organized into seven titles across two divisions. This report provides an overview of the as-introduced version of BAAJA Division A, Title IV, which is titled "Project Certainty."

Title IV contains three sections. Section 1401 would restrict agencies' authority to alter or repeal existing permits or interfere with operation or construction of fully permitted projects. Section 1401 would also authorize suits to enforce those restrictions and would entitle prevailing plaintiffs to injunctive relief and damages, including 25% to 50% of total project costs. Section 1402 would allow developers of certain projects to challenge permitting delays or denials that were allegedly "due to a pattern of disparate treatment" against projects of the same type. As with Section 1401, Section 1402 would entitle prevailing plaintiffs to injunctive relief and damages, including 50% to 100% of total anticipated construction costs. Finally, Section 1403 would allow developers to sue to enforce agencies' compliance with a one-year deadline to approve or deny complete applications for authorizations or permits that do not require an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS) under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).1 Under Section 1403, prevailing plaintiffs would be entitled to certain injunctive relief, but not to damages.

This report summarizes Sections 1401, 1402, and 1403. It then identifies considerations for Congress, including the potential implications of damage awards under Sections 1401 and 1402, and uncertainties about the scope and potential impact of those sections.

BAAJA's "Project Certainty" Provisions

BAAJA Sections 1401, 1402, and 1403 concern "Federal authorization[s] or permit[s]," a term defined to include "an authorization, permit, record of decision, right-of-way," other specified agency actions, and "any other approval or order that is necessary" to construct a project or operate a project at full capacity.2 Each of those sections is discussed in turn below.

Section 1401

BAAJA Section 1401 would prohibit agencies from taking "any new action" that would (1) "revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, amend, or alter" a federal authorization or permit effective on or after September 16, 2026, or (2) "interfere with or prevent the construction or operation at full capacity of a project that has secured all necessary Federal authorizations and permits."3

These prohibitions would be subject to five exceptions. Under Section 1401, an agency would be able to take an otherwise prohibited action only if

1. a court orders it to do so;

2. the holder of a federal authorization or permit materially breached the terms of its authorization or permit "or otherwise violated applicable law";

3. the authorization or permit was obtained "through fraud, intentional concealment, or material misrepresentation";

4. the action is "necessary to prevent specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm or damage to life, property, national security, or defense that is based on new," previously unavailable information; or

5. the permit or authorization holder requests the action.4

Agencies invoking the fourth of those exceptions would be authorized to take only "reasonably limited" action "necessary to remedy the specific issue" giving rise to the asserted threat.5

Before acting under any of Section 1401's five exceptions, agencies would need to give written notification to the "project sponsor or holder of" the authorization or permit.6 That notice would need to provide "a detailed explanation of the action," identify "the statutory authority relied on for the action," and include "the evidence supporting the action."7

Section 1401 would authorize a project sponsor or holder of a permit or authorization to sue to enforce its terms. This cause of action would alter the status quo in several respects. First, under existing law, the party challenging agency action bears the burden of persuasion. By contrast, Section 1401 would "place the burden" on the government. Second, in suits challenging permitting actions, judicial review is currently governed by the statutes underlying the challenged actions or by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and reviewing courts typically defer to agencies' factual findings and policy judgments.8 Section 1401 would supersede these existing statutes and replace their deferential standards of review with a requirement that agencies establish "by clear and convincing evidence" that permit modifications, rescissions, or suspensions fell within one of Section 1401's five enumerated exceptions.9 Third, at present there exists no cross-statute authorization to challenge "any" agency "action" that interferes with construction or operation at full capacity of full permitted facilities.10 By creating such a cause of action,11 Section 1401 would potentially expand the scope of challengeable agency conduct.

Suits challenging agency action under Section 1401 could be brought in the federal courts of appeals, or, if no existing statute provides for direct circuit-court review of the challenged action, then in the district court where the affected project is located.12 Review in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims would be expressly precluded.13 Section 1401 also contains a "special rule" for projects that were recently subject to a "stop-work order." If that prior stop-work order was enjoined (barred) by a federal court in the year before BAAJA's enactment, then Section 1401 would grant jurisdiction to "the same judge" that enjoined the stop-work order to "hear a complaint or motion under this section," "assuming that judge continues to sit in the same district."14

Existing statutes generally authorize reviewing courts to vacate agency actions found to be unlawful.15 In some cases these laws also grant prevailing plaintiffs attorney fees and costs of litigation,16 but they do not provide for damage awards.

Section 1401 would expand the scope of available remedies by entitling prevailing plaintiffs to each of these five forms of relief:

1. reinstatement of its permit or authorization "and the termination of any action by the Federal agency preventing the construction or operation of the project";

2. "injunctive relief preventing a Federal agency from taking any new action that would revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, amend, or alter a previously granted Federal authorization or permit or take any other action to interfere with or prevent the construction or operation at full capacity of a project without first obtaining a court order to that effect from the same judge";

3. reasonable attorney fees and costs of litigation;

4. "any costs" associated with delay attributable to the challenged agency action; and

5. "not less than 25 percent and not more than 50 percent of the total of all costs incurred by" the plaintiff "in connection with the project as of the date of the action and not otherwise recovered."17

Courts would determine the recoverable amount of "total costs . . . incurred" by considering "the degree to which" the defendant agency acted in bad faith, the degree to which "there exists a pattern of similar Federal interference in other projects," and the "actual degree" of economic harm to the project sponsor or operator.18

Section 1401 would authorize the payment of awards from the appropriation codified at 31 U.S.C. § 1304, which is commonly known as the "Judgment Fund."19 Administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury), the Judgment Fund is a permanent and indefinite appropriation that provides unlimited funds to pay monetary settlements and court-ordered judgments, subject to certain requirements.20

Section 1402

BAAJA Section 1402 would state a sense of the Congress that federal agencies should "treat all applications for Federal authorizations or permits fairly and efficiently."21 To that end, the section would authorize those seeking permits for "specific type[s] of covered project[s]"—generally, projects related to energy production22—to sue in the federal district court in which their project is located and challenge an agency's allegedly unreasonable delay or improper denial of federal permits or authorizations.23

Section 1402 defines "delay" as "more than 60 days beyond" specified deadlines, which for completed environmental documents range from roughly one year for agency actions that do not require an EIS under NEPA, to two years for those that do, plus an additional 90–120 days to approve "all outstanding authorizations" after completing the review.24

To establish a claim of "unreasonabl[e]" delay or "improper[]" denial under Section 1402, a plaintiff would need to show that

1. its application for the delayed or denied government action "satisfies all applicable Federal law";

2. if granted, the requested permit or authorization would not be canceled for violating federal law, or for having been obtained through fraud, intentional concealment, or material misrepresentation; and

3. the government's delay or inaction reflected a "pattern of disparate treatment" against projects of the same type that "occurred after" BAAJA's enactment.25

Section 1402 would define a "pattern of disparate treatment" as a "substantial" increase in the rate of "unreasonably delayed" or "improperly denied" government action for energy projects of the same type, as compared with the rates of delayed or denied actions for projects of that type over the previous five calendar years.26 This "empirically demonstrated statistical pattern" would also need to be "the result of an intentional course" of government action "to create such a pattern."27

Section 1402 does not specify what would constitute a "substantial" increase in the relevant rates of permit denial or delay, but to support a claim, such an increase would need to persist for at least 180 days after BAAJA's enactment for actions that do not require an EIS and for at least 280 days after BAAJA's enactment for those that do.28

A plaintiff suing under Section 1402 would have to produce "prima facie evidence" of disparate treatment using "empirical evidence."29 Section 1402 does not define that term, but treats "empirical evidence" as something other than evidence "that demonstrates a bias in the permitting regime," such as executive branch statements or policies.30 Plaintiffs "may" provide such evidence of "bias" to "support" their "empirical evidence" but would not be required to do so.31

If a plaintiff produced prima facie evidence of disparate treatment, Section 1402 would shift the burden of evidence production to the government, which would have to "provide to the applicant and the court raw statistical data for the calendar year in which the action is brought and the preceding 5 calendar years showing, with respect to the specific type of covered project at issue," the number and percentage of federal permits or authorizations granted, delayed, and denied.32 The reviewing court would then need to base its decision only on the plaintiff's evidence, the government's "raw statistical data," and "the administrative record before the agency."33

Section 1402 would entitle prevailing plaintiffs to four forms of relief:

1. injunctive relief, "as provided by applicable Federal law";

2. "reasonable" attorney fees and costs of litigation;

3. "economic damages, including any costs associated with the applicable denial or delay, as the court determines appropriate"; and

4. "damages in an amount equal to not less than 50 percent and not more than 100 percent of the total reasonably expected cost of construction of the project."34

As in Section 1401, Section 1402 would direct courts to determine the recoverable amount of reasonably expected construction costs by considering "the degree to which" the defendant agency acted in bad faith, the degree to which "there exists a pattern of similar Federal interference" in other projects, and the "actual degree" of economic harm to the project sponsor or operator.35

To be eligible for a remedy under Section 1402, a plaintiff would need to "demonstrate" that it possesses the "technical and financial ability" to construct the type of project at issue.36 A plaintiff that received a remedy under Section 1402 would then need to "complete the applicable specific type of covered project," or, barring certain extenuating circumstances, would need to repay any money it received. Section 1402 does not provide a deadline for project completion.37

As with Section 1401, funds awarded under Section 1402 would be payable from the Judgment Fund.38

Section 1402 would prohibit the use of class actions by barring any "party with a claim under this section or any other person" from suing "as a representative party on behalf of any member of a specific type of covered project."39

For covered projects requiring one or more federal authorizations or permits that do not require an EA or EIS, Section 1402(c) would also establish a timeline for agencies to "render decisions on all applicable covered applications." Specifically, agencies would have one year to render decisions from the date on which "the latest of the covered applications is determined to be complete."40

Section 1403

BAAJA Section 1403 would provide applicants for federal authorizations or permits that do not require an EA or an EIS a "right to petition" for "judicial review of . . . compliance" with "the deadline established under section 1402(c) with respect to the covered application."41

Section 1403 would not require compliance with the deadline in 1402(c) if a federal agency could establish by clear and convincing evidence that its delay was caused by

1. "a natural disaster, act of God, or act of war that reasonably impaired" an agency's ability to comply;

2. "a national emergency" that necessitated delay;

3. "the covered application being based on fraud or material misrepresentations of fact";

4. the applicant withholding necessary information after the agency has made "a reasonable and timely" request for that information; or

5. a lapse in appropriations lasting more than 14 days that precluded compliance.42

Section 1403 would authorize suits in the federal district court in which the project is located and would direct reviewing courts to "establish an expedited schedule for briefing and disposition," and to issue a decision within 120 days of a suit's commencement, barring "extraordinary circumstances."43

A prevailing plaintiff would be entitled to a court "order requiring a decision on" its application within 60 days, and to other "injunctive relief, as appropriate, to give effect to this section."44 Courts would be authorized "to retain jurisdiction to ensure compliance" with terms of their orders.45

Considerations for Congress

Payments from the Judgment Fund

As noted above, Sections 1401 and 1402 would authorize payments from the Judgment Fund to satisfy awards of economic damages and project costs. Those sections refer only to court-ordered judgments, but unless "otherwise provided by law," if a given action could result in a court-ordered judgment payable from the Judgment Fund, then a settlement of that action will be payable from the Judgment Fund as well.46 This general rule extends to settlements entered by the Attorney General or his designee to resolve "imminent" litigation.47 Thus, a claimant seeking relief under Section 1401 or 1402 would not need to prevail in court (or even file suit) to recoup payment, and could instead resolve its claims by entering an out-of-court agreement with the Department of Justice (DOJ).48

Execution of those agreements would be difficult to prevent. Parties can generally resolve their disputes through out-of-court settlements without any court action.49 The Judgment Fund then provides for unlimited automatic payment—without further congressional intervention—of settlements (and judgments) that Treasury certifies as meeting statutory criteria.50

In the past, concerns about such payments have prompted some Members to propose bills that would have prohibited use of the Judgment Fund to satisfy certain settlements or judgments.51 If Congress wanted to restrict Judgment Fund payments under Sections 1401 and 1402 to court-ordered awards, it could consider adding similar limitations in those provisions.

Whether obtained through settlement or judgment, monetary awards under Sections 1401 or 1402 could increase Judgment Fund expenditures relative to historical baselines. Recent events may suggest the scale of that potential increase. Over the 17 fiscal years beginning in FY2009 and running through FY2025, the Judgment Fund paid an average of roughly $3.5 billion per year to resolve more than 6,000 claims annually.52 In fewer than seven months, between late April and mid-October 2026, DOJ and the Department of the Interior (DOI) drew roughly $3.8 billion from the Judgment Fund53 to pay 10 out-of-court settlements with developers of offshore wind projects.54 Those payments, which ranged from $3.6 million to $1.1 billion, corresponded to amounts that the developers had paid to secure offshore wind leases that DOI later decided to cancel.55 By providing for awards of 25% to 50% of "total" project costs,56 or 5% to 100% of "total reasonably expected" construction costs,57 Section 1401 could result in significantly larger awards.

Section 1401's Impacts on Other Statutory Provisions

Section 1401 would restrict federal agencies' ability to revise, rescind, or suspend "any . . . approval or order that is necessary" to construct or operate a project at full capacity.58 It would also prohibit, with certain exceptions, "any . . . action" by the federal government that "interfere[s] with . . . construction or operation at full capacity" of fully permitted projects.59 Given the breadth of these proscriptions, Section 1401 could potentially impact agencies' ability to exercise their authority under existing statutes.

To illustrate, some statutes direct the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to periodically review and, if necessary, revise pollution-control standards and guidelines for new and existing facilities.60 Other statutes and regulations authorize or require agencies to modify federal authorizations or permits upon certain triggering events, including the discovery of new information about the environmental impacts of permitted activities.61 Section 1401 could be read to conflict with these legal frameworks. For instance, a court might bar EPA from issuing new, more stringent regulations if those regulations interfered with "operation at full capacity" of projects that had secured all necessary federal authorizations or permits.62 Similarly, a court might construe Section 1401's prohibition on permit modifications to bar even those permit modifications that are expressly required under other laws.

While possible, such outcomes are not certain. When interpreting statutes, courts apply a presumption against implied repeals,63 and when specific statutory provisions appear to conflict with more general provisions, courts often presume that the specific controls the general.64 Thus, as commentators have noted,65 courts construing Section 1401 may conclude, in the absence of explicit statutory language to the contrary, that Congress did not mean for Section 1401's broad prohibitions to sweep away more particularized statutory directives.

It is also possible that courts would disagree about the proper interpretation of Section 1401, with some courts reading that provision to override provisions in existing statutes, such as the Clean Water Act or Clean Air Act,66 and other courts reaching the opposite conclusion. Such divergent interpretations could lead to inconsistent application of federal law.

If desired, Congress could provide express direction on whether Section 1401 would supersede or leave intact existing statutory provisions. For instance, Congress could disclaim intent to modify existing laws, or, conversely, provide that Section 1401 governs notwithstanding any other provision of law. Alternatively, Congress could define "federal authorization or permit" or agency "action" to exclude activities under certain statutes.

Section 1402's Intent Requirement of Lack Thereof

Section 1402 would create a cause of action to challenge certain permit delays or denials that are "due to a pattern of disparate treatment,"67 defined, in part, to mean an "empirically demonstrated" "substantial" statistical increase in rates of "unreasonably delayed" or "improperly denied" permits as compared to a five-year baseline.68 It is unclear, however, if the government could be held liable under Section 1402 whenever its actions create such a pattern, or, alternatively, only when it both creates a pattern of disparate treatment and intends to do so. Parts of Section 1402 could be read to support either interpretation.

Section 1402 defines "pattern of disparate treatment" to mean not just a "statistical pattern," but one that is "the result of an intentional course of action undertaken by the Federal Government to create such a pattern."69 The latter definitional phrase suggests that plaintiffs suing under Section 1402 would need to establish the government's subjective motivation to obtain relief.

Different provisions in Section 1402 suggest otherwise. For example, Section 1402(d)(1)(B)(i)–(ii) would allow plaintiffs to make a prima facie showing of disparate treatment based only on "empirical evidence," which plaintiffs could, but would not be required to, supplement with additional evidence "that demonstrates a bias." Section 1402(d)(1)(C) would then direct the reviewing court to consider the alleged pattern of disparate treatment based only on the plaintiffs' evidence, the "raw statistical data" submitted by the government, and an agency's administrative record. Given these evidentiary constraints, Section 1402 appears to contemplate a finding of liability without any direct evidence that the government intended to create a pattern of disparate treatment.

The presence or absence of a specific intent requirement in Section 1402 has implications for the scope of potential liability under that section. On the one hand, if a "pattern of disparate treatment" means nothing more than a statistical increase in rates of permit delay or denial for a given project type, then even lawful, good-faith permit denials could give rise to liability. On the other hand, if the government can be held liable only when it acts with specific intent, then agencies might evade liability by employing facially neutral policies that disproportionately impact disfavored project types.

description:

text:
OTTAWA — Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says she's confident billions of dollars in tax credits in the new federal budget will encourage private investment to build out Canada's electricity grid.

Thursday's federal budget committed $50 billion to help implement Ottawa's electricity strategy, which looks to double the size of the grid by 2050. More than $38 billion was committed to tax credits the government says will stay in place until 2042.

Speaking to The Canadian Press on Thursday, Dabrusin said the measures came from government consultations on the electricity strategy.

"These are the things that people have set out for us when we have done consultations," she said.

"We put out our electricity strategy earlier this year. This is what was told to us is what was needed, and I think that this is a huge step forward for how we build up clean energy for our country."

Thursday's budget included measures to extend the existing Clean Technology and Clean Electricity Investment tax credits to the end of 2040 — the former was supposed to be phased out in 2034. The budget also proposed to expand eligibility for the latter tax credit "for the highest-voltage intra-provincial electricity transmission lines in each province" for property acquired.

The budget also signalled Ottawa's intent to update the Clean Electricity Regulations. The government said the goal is to introduce flexibility into the current system.

That includes allowing power plants to operate for longer and laying the groundwork for the government's planned LNG buildout, as Ottawa indicated in its electricity strategy.

The strategy, released in May, placed a heavy emphasis on expanding the role of natural gas in powering the grid.

"Under some interpretations of the current electricity regulations, it would be difficult to build some additional natural gas that would complement much bigger builds," Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the time.

"We have some of the cheapest gas in the world in Canada," he said, citing natural gas as an affordability play in the strategy. Carney said at the time the strategy had a goal of lowering energy costs for 70 per cent of Canadian households.

The budget also promised $4 billion over 10 years for electricity infrastructure, including new funding for a Natural Resources program to expand renewable energy.

That program has paid out more than $1.3 billion for more than 100 projects dating back to 2021.

In a media statement, Clean Energy Canada, a think tank out of Simon Fraser University, welcomed the focus on building clean electricity supply but said the government must set clear goals.

"Today's federal budget provides significant investments in electrifying Canada's economy and households, but further work will be required to establish the concrete goals needed to fully realize a generational opportunity," executive director Rachel Doran said.

"While moving from plans to action is critical, without concrete goals, Canada risks trading a climate plan with an accountability metric to one that is a list of actions without a final destination."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

title: What Illinois Fleets Can Actually Get for a Class 5-8 Electric Replacement - ACT News
description:

text:
Illinois has opened two funding channels for fleets willing to take diesel trucks off the road and put battery-electric ones in their place.

The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency recently announced the launch of its Clean Trucks Program, pairing grant money for vehicle replacement with a contract effort to give fleets hands-on technical guidance. Both pieces sit under the agency’s broader Driving a Cleaner Illinois initiative.

Most fleets will look at the grant money first. Illinois EPA has posted a Notice of Funding Opportunity with roughly $935,000 behind it, covering up to 45% of the cost of swapping an eligible diesel Class 5-8 truck for a new battery-electric one. The source is the State Diesel Emissions Reduction Act program, which lets participating states run grants, rebates, and loans to cut diesel emissions.

The second piece, the Clean Fleet and Freight Concierge Service, carries an estimated $3 million in contracts. Illinois EPA will not staff it. The agency is seeking qualified firms to run the service and advise small and medium fleets statewide on electric trucks and the charging they require.

The program is meant to help fleet operators “lower emissions, reduce fuel costs, and strengthen Illinois’ clean transportation future,” according to Illinois EPA Director James Jennings, adding that the Concierge Service is aimed at operators interested in moving from diesel to electric who do not know where to start.

The $3 million traces back to the U.S. EPA Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program. Illinois EPA received CPRG funding in 2024 to support zero-emission commercial vehicle and infrastructure deployment across the state, including the Concierge Service.

Illinois EPA is seeking Concierge firms for a Northern Region and a Southern Region, and it defines those regions as the areas served primarily by the PJM and MISO utility grids. The state is organizing fleet electrification advice around grid territory rather than around county lines or metropolitan areas.

That choice sits close to where truck electrification projects actually stall. Vehicle selection is the tractable part. Available capacity at the service point, the scope and duration of an interconnection study, and the cost and schedule of any distribution upgrade are set by the utility and shaped by the regional transmission organization it operates within. ComEd territory in and around Chicago falls under PJM. Ameren Illinois territory downstate falls under MISO. Two fleets running comparable duty cycles on either side of that line can face different timelines to energize the same charger.

The Clean Trucks Program is not the only Illinois money available to fleets buying electric trucks. Round 9 of the state’s Volkswagen settlement funding remains open, offering up to $18 million for all-electric trucks. That opportunity covers Class 4-8 local freight trucks at 14,001 pounds GVWR and above, along with Class 8 port drayage trucks at 33,001 pounds and above. Class 4-7 port drayage trucks are not eligible.

The Round 9 cost share is larger than the DERA program’s and varies by applicant type. Government applicants receive 75% of eligible costs and contribute 25%. Non-government applicants receive 50% and contribute the other half. The minimum award is $100,000, in-kind contributions are not accepted, and applicants must own both the trucks and any requested charging infrastructure. Fleets that lease their trucks are not eligible. Illinois EPA posted the opportunity on September 10, 2025, and is taking applications on a first-come, first-served basis until the funding is depleted. Applicants must pre-qualify through the state’s Grant Accountability and Transparency Act portal before applying.

Fleets mapping out where chargers already exist can check the state’s interactive map of public charging stations, which covers more than 450 sites supported or funded by Illinois, including stations built under the Illinois Department of Transportation’s National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program. The map filters by Level 2 and Level 3 ports and by site type, and separates stations that have been awarded but are not yet online from those currently operating.

title: Vancouver gets a factory for floating wave-energy data centers - OPB
description:
Investors and scientists have touted ocean energy as a potential renewable energy source for years, but it’s yet to yield profits on any large scale.
Oregon State University operates an $80 million wave energy hub near Newport.
Panthalassa says its un-anchored deep ocean nodes, which use the power they generate instead of distributing it on the grid, set its model apart.
“Some people call it advanced wave energy.
Some people call it open ocean wave energy.
text:
An Oregon startup that’s raised more than $300 million this year to use wave power to generate energy for artificial intelligence hubs unveiled the Southwest Washington factory Friday, where it aims to build nodes to power this new kind of renewable energy.

Panthalassa — the company takes its name from the super ocean that took up most of the surface of the planet Earth 190 million years ago — hopes to seed deep oceans around the globe with self-driving buoys and then use that energy to power floating AI computation hubs. The hubs wouldn’t come with the same baggage — carbon emissions, fresh water contamination and neighborhood disruption — that have brought about a backlash against data centers on land.

The investment marks the Portland-based company’s first attempt at moving from custom manufacturing to an assembly line, but while a significant investment in the region, it’s also a test of its theory that it will eventually be able to make and deploy its “nodes” at additional factories around the globe.

Investors and scientists have touted ocean energy as a potential renewable energy source for years, but it’s yet to yield profits on any large scale. Oregon State University operates an $80 million wave energy hub near Newport. And at least a dozen businesses around the globe are racing Panthalassa to prove out the business case — each with a different approach. Some are anchored near the shore. Many want to connect directly to electrical grids. Panthalassa says its un-anchored deep ocean nodes, which use the power they generate instead of distributing it on the grid, set its model apart.

“It turns out that there’s a lot of energy in the middle of the ocean. So we said to ourselves, what would it take? What could we do to build a technology that captured that energy cheaply, reliably, that could transit out into the resource on its own?” said CEO Garth Sheldon-Coulson in an interview with OPB on Friday in Vancouver, where the company started fabricating prototypes in 2022.

Panthalassa’s nodes, which float hundreds of miles from shore, look like enormous white orbs, larger than a sailboat, covered in ladders and portals. But like icebergs, much more lies beneath the surface — each node sits atop a hollow tube that lifts seawater into its power-generating turbines. The full assembly can be six stories high, although most is below the water.

“The technology that we’ve created, you can call it different things,” Sheldon-Coulson said. “Some people call it advanced wave energy. Some people call it open ocean wave energy. Some people call it ocean hydro because it works like a hydroelectric dam. But whatever you call it, it will be the cheapest green electrons on the planet.”

It may sound like a bombastic promise, but tests of prototypes have been successful enough to woo big investors and political support in both Oregon and Washington.

Peter Thiel, a high-profile Republican billionaire venture capitalist and AI evangelist, recruited other tech industry leaders to help Panthalassa raise $140 million this spring. The company sought another $225 million from venture capital groups this summer. Now, according to industry press, the company is valued at close to $2 billion.

Now, some of that money is helping the company move from building one node at a time to manufacturing them on an assembly line in Vancouver.

On Friday, Panthalassa unveiled the factory it developed to do just that, a vast open warehouse near the Columbia River that was part of the Kaiser Shipyard, which built more than 140 ships to support the U.S. effort in World War II.

When fully staffed, about 50 people will work there, rolling plate steel into shape and using robotic welding technology to construct nodes that can be shipped down the Columbia and deployed deep in the ocean.

The ultimate goal is to develop a blueprint that Panthalassa can use to create factories for its nodes around the globe.

“The first step towards a fleet begins here,” said Dana Hartsig, Panthalassa’s vice president of manufacturing.

text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani met with nonprofits in Puerto Rico on Friday as officials announced a $280,000 partnership to help the U.S. territory confront emergencies.

The partnership between Hispanic Federation and the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York comes as Puerto Rico struggles with chronic power outages and intermittent water shortages while it tries to rebuild from Hurricane Maria and other disasters.

The nonprofit Hispanic Federation said the money would equip 10 community-run resiliency hubs across the island with increased water storage capacity; some also would receive rain-collection systems, kitchen infrastructure and solar power with battery storage.

"Puerto Rico’s families have lived through more disasters than anyone should have to,” said Frankie Miranda, president and CEO of Hispanic Federation.

The Federal Home Loan Bank of New York is contributing $210,000 to the effort while Hispanic Federation raised an additional $70,000, officials said.

“Conversations about climate change and environmental justice are essential to the wellbeing and future of our communities,” said New York Gov. Kathy Hochul.

She and Mamdani are among a group of New York government officials in Puerto Rico for a four-day, annual conference.

The announcement comes months after the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump canceled solar projects in Puerto Rico that were supposed to help thousands of low-income families. One project, worth $400 million, would have seen the installation of solar and battery storage systems in low-income homes and those with medical needs.

The U.S. Department of Energy has said the money initially slated for solar projects would instead be used to help maintain Puerto Rico’s crumbling power grid, which was razed by Hurricane Maria in September 2017. The grid, however, was already weakened given a lack of maintenance and investment.

The decisions prompted outrage on the island as federal support for solar projects fades.

Last week, six Puerto Rico residents sued the U.S. Energy Department and its secretary, Chris Wright, following the scrapping of a $1 billion federally funded program to provide solar power and battery storage to those who most needed it.

“The cost of such systems remains out of reach for the majority of Puerto Ricans,” the lawsuit stated.

Among those suing is 63-year-old Arecibo resident Ileana Ríos, who is diabetic and needs to refrigerate her insulin. Meanwhile, her son has asthma and needs to use a nebulizer, which requires electricity.

The lawsuit noted that Ríos “regularly loses power when the weather is stable and always loses power during storms, sometimes for several weeks at a time.”

The other residents who sued also have serious health conditions and need equipment or medications that rely on electricity.

The lawsuit requests that a judge order the U.S. Energy Department to reinstate the grant program, among other things.

The U.S. Department of Energy did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

The funding loss has been a blow to nonprofits and others who faced months of uncertainty and confusion as they awaited the Trump administration’s decision on whether and how it would continue the program.

“We had a lot of uncertainty. ... At some points it just felt like we were talking to no one," said Sybelle Rodriguez del Valle, director of operations at the energy resilience nonprofit Barrio Eléctrico, which was part of the U.S. Energy Department program.

Barrio Eléctrico provides electric service to more than 500 families across 12 municipalities in Puerto Rico and was poised to provide resilient energy for 1,200 families with funds from the federal program. It had only completed about one-third of its projects before the program ended, losing an estimated $16 million to $20 million in funding.

___

Associated Press reporter Gabriela Aoun Angueira contributed to this report.

title: The race is on to build the first fusion power plant — and Europe is looking to Japan for help - CNBC

Munich-based Proxima Fusion signed memoranda of understanding with two Japanese industrial partners, Fujikura and Kyoto Fusioneering, in Tokyo on Oct. 28.
“Fusion is a silver bullet because the promise is abundant, clean, limitless energy.” Fusion energy seeks to replicate the way the sun produces power, using super-heated plasma to fuse two light atomic nuclei into one heavier one, releasing vast amounts of energy in the process.

text:
Shulz | E+ | Getty Images

The race is on to build the world’s first commercial fusion power plant — and one of Europe’s leading contenders in the field has just received a boost.

Munich-based Proxima Fusion signed memoranda of understanding with two Japanese industrial partners, Fujikura and Kyoto Fusioneering, in Tokyo on Oct. 28. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who was visiting in a bid to deepen trade ties — were both in attendance.

Ann Mettler, president of Catalyse Europe, a Brussels-based clean-energy think tank, and a former vice president of Breakthrough Energy, said developing the technology should be a strategic imperative for Europe.

“Europe is a resource-poor geography and we are very dependent on China. The world is in competition for technological supremacy — this is a zero-sum game,” Mettler told CNBC, speaking in a personal capacity.

“Fusion is a silver bullet because the promise is abundant, clean, limitless energy.”

Fusion energy seeks to replicate the way the sun produces power, using super-heated plasma to fuse two light atomic nuclei into one heavier one, releasing vast amounts of energy in the process.

There are two main approaches: one uses high-powered lasers, while the other uses powerful magnets to confine the plasma. Proxima is developing a type of magnetic device called a stellarator, which is designed to hold the plasma in place for long periods.

The agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering will expand existing work on next-generation gyrotrons — devices that generate high-power microwaves used to heat the plasma.

Why HTS tape matters

Proxima’s agreement with 141-year-old Fujikura will explore plans for industrial-scale manufacturing in Germany of high-temperature superconducting, or HTS, tape, a specialized metallic tape that is superconducting at relatively high temperatures and can carry electrical current with virtually no resistive losses.

The tape is wound into coils to form powerful magnets that confine and control the heated plasma inside the stellarator.

Anadolu | Anadolu | Getty Images

Francesco Sciortino, CEO and co-founder of Proxima Fusion, told CNBC that Fujikura, which employs over 50,000 people worldwide, was a leader in manufacturing high-temperature superconductors, having built its reputation in optical fibers. “They think this tape has the potential to be the next optical fibre,” he said.

He said Proxima, which is studying plans to build a manufacturing facility in Lower Saxony, hoped to make around 5,000 kilometers, or 3,100 miles, of tape annually by 2030.

The 140 million euro ($160 million) facility would be financed partly by the proceeds of a $468 million funding round in July, which valued Proxima, whose backers include Alphabet -owned Google, at $2.7 billion.

Proxima expects to need around 20,000 kilometers (12,400 miles) of the tape for its “Alpha” fusion demonstrator and a further 40,000 kilometers (24,900 miles) for its planned “Stellaris” fusion power station.

Europe’s fusion supply chain

Sciortino said that establishing production of the tape in Germany was crucial as it would help Europe create the expertise and supply chains needed to turn its fusion research leadership into industrial capability.

This is where Europe has historically struggled, according to Catalyse Europe’s Mettler.

If Europe is first to develop this technology, it will give us a huge advantage, but key to that will be building the supply chain

Ann Mettler

Catalyse Europe

“Every geography wants to turn leadership in science into industrial leadership and this is where Europe has traditionally been not so good — turning that scientific leadership into euros,” she said.

While Europe had industrial giants to be proud of, disruptors tended to be more successful in frontier technologies, according to Mettler.

“If Europe is first to develop this technology, it will give us a huge advantage, but key to that will be building the supply chain,” she said.

Commercial fusion competitors

Sciortino said he remains confident Proxima will be the first company to turn on a pilot plant — but stressed the key to profitability would be making that plant as simple as possible to operate.

“You can have complexity in the design, manufacturing and operation of the plant,” he said. “We can take care of the complexity in the design and manufacturing, but our view is that there needs to be simplicity in the operation. We are aiming for net energy gain during the early 2030s.”

But Proxima has some well-heeled competitors. They include U.S.-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems, which is also backed by Google, and Helion Energy, as well as Canada’s General Fusion. China has a number of state-backed players, most notably China Fusion Energy Co., while Tokyo-based Helical Fusion leads Japan’s push.

“The supply chain in fusion energy needs to be built years before — people often think of frontier technologies as a switch that can be thrown,” Mettler said. “That is not the case here.”
