title: Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP, with 70 GWh covered by supply agreements
description:
BYD plans to reach 30 GWh of sodium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, while CATL aims to exceed 1 GWh in sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026.
Higher upfront costs, lower total cost of ownership Sodium-ion batteries currently have higher upfront costs than LFP batteries.
The global average stands at $229/kWh, compared with approximately $200/kWh for LFP batteries.
In July 2026, China reintroduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while exempting sodium-ion batteries until the end of 2028.
Wood Mackenzie expects the 2030–2035 period to be decisive for sodium-ion batteries to achieve economic competitiveness.
text:
Sodium-ion battery technology is entering the commercial production phase and emerging as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries, driven by supply chain diversification, strong low-temperature performance, and the potential for lower total cost of ownership. According to an analysis by Wood Mackenzie, supply agreements totaling more than 70 GWh are already in place.

The study, which examines markets in China, the United States, Germany, and India, identifies sodium-ion batteries as the most promising emerging alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Leading manufacturers are expected to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by late 2026, while parity at the module and system levels is not expected until after 2030.

China is leading the commercialization of the technology. BYD plans to reach 30 GWh of sodium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, while CATL aims to exceed 1 GWh in sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026.

Supply agreements for sodium-ion batteries are already in place in China, the United States, and Europe, while India remains in the early stages of commercial validation. For the 2026–2035 period, Wood Mackenzie estimates a learning rate of 18% to 20% in China, reflecting the greater maturity of its industrial supply chain.

Planned manufacturing capacity currently exceeds demand, although the growing number of supply agreements points to the technology’s gradual adoption in the market.

Higher upfront costs, lower total cost of ownership

Sodium-ion batteries currently have higher upfront costs than LFP batteries. The global average stands at $229/kWh, compared with approximately $200/kWh for LFP batteries. However, Wood Mackenzie estimates that sodium-ion batteries could achieve a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project lifetime.

The difference is primarily attributed to the elimination of capacity expansion cycles and lower operating costs. The economics of sodium-ion systems remain relatively stable across storage durations of two to four hours.

The study identifies raw material supply security, service life, and a wider operating temperature range as key technical advantages of sodium-ion batteries. The latter could make them particularly suitable for applications in cold climates, where lithium-ion batteries may require additional thermal management systems.

Regulation accelerates development

Industrial and trade policies are playing an increasingly important role in the competitiveness of different battery chemistries. In July 2026, China reintroduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while exempting sodium-ion batteries until the end of 2028. LFP batteries became subject to a 2% levy in September 2026, which is set to increase to 4% in September 2027.

In the United States, tariffs of approximately 58% on energy storage cells imported from China, combined with production tax credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), are encouraging domestic sodium-ion battery manufacturing.

In Europe, carbon footprint declaration requirements under the EU Battery Regulation could favor technologies with supply chains that are less dependent on certain critical raw materials. Meanwhile, India is supporting domestic manufacturing through a $1.25 billion incentive program and tariff exemptions for certain types of manufacturing equipment.

Wood Mackenzie expects the 2030–2035 period to be decisive for sodium-ion batteries to achieve economic competitiveness. For energy storage projects currently under development, LFP remains the most commercially mature option for storage durations of two to four hours.

description:
NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE | NEE Price Prediction) and AES (NYSE:AES) both build wind, solar and battery projects for power-hungry data centers.
Batteries Fill NextEra’s Backlog as AES Courts Hyperscalers NextEra posted adjusted EPS of $1.24 against a $1.18 consensus, its 6th consecutive beat.

text:
NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE | NEE Price Prediction) and AES (NYSE:AES) both build wind, solar and battery projects for power-hungry data centers. This week, Democrats won control of the Senate and House, and renewable stocks rallied on better odds that clean energy tax credits survive. NextEra’s October earnings report and AES’s pending buyout show two very different ways to profit from that demand.

Batteries Fill NextEra’s Backlog as AES Courts Hyperscalers

NextEra posted adjusted EPS of $1.24 against a $1.18 consensus, its 6th consecutive beat. Revenue of $8.09B missed expectations of $8.88B. That gap hurts less than it looks, because the earnings line is the steadier measure for a utility. Energy Resources added 3.7 gigawatts to its backlog, and 2.4 gigawatts of that was battery storage. Customers want capacity fast, and batteries are the fastest product NextEra can deliver.

Florida Power & Light also raised its large-load outlook from 6 gigawatts to 8 gigawatts by 2032, and management plans to serve the first of that load mostly with storage.

Back on its Q3 2025 call, AES reported an 11.1 GW backlog of signed contracts, including 4 GW with hyperscaler customers. Its chief executive said then that returns on data center projects sat “at the higher end of our expected range of 12% to 15%.” Those figures are now dated.

Business Driver NextEra AES Growth Engine Battery storage, federal hubs Hyperscaler contracts Regulated Base Florida Power & Light AES Indiana, AES Ohio Next Big Event Dominion Energy (NYSE:D) merger Take-private sale

NextEra Keeps Expanding While AES Sells Itself

NextEra continues adding new lines of business. It signed agreements for three federal hubs totaling ~16.5 GW in Texas and Pennsylvania. It collects fees on those hubs without putting in its own capital. It is also restarting the Duane Arnold nuclear plant and pursuing the Dominion merger. The chief executive put it plainly: “Our growth plan is not dependent on any single technology, customer market, or policy outcome.”

AES took the opposite route. It agreed to a cash buyout by GIP and EQT, so its stock now trades close to the deal price. Shares rose just 0.98% over the past month, while NextEra gained 13.23%. The election rally mostly passed AES by.

Both companies benefit from the tax credits. The clean electricity investment credit applies to “any energy storage technology”, and the production credit can be sold to an unrelated buyer under Section 6418. A Democratic Congress makes those credits more secure for NextEra’s battery backlog and AES’s solar-plus-storage projects.

Virginia Regulators and a Florida Data Center Deal Come Next

Final Dominion orders in Virginia and South Carolina are expected in January 2027. I will be watching for any concessions regulators demand. Investors can also continues an eye on FPL, where management said it was “confident about announcing a deal before the end of the year.” For AES, closing the buyout is what matters now.

Analyst Ratings and Valuation Set NextEra Apart From AES

AES now trades largely on the result of its pending buyout. All 9 covering analysts rate it a hold, with a $15 target. That leaves little upside unless the deal falls through. NextEra trades near 20x forward earnings, a premium multiple, and it is the company that continues adding storage capacity as the tax credits look safer. NextEra’s outlook would shift if Virginia regulators push the Dominion terms too far.

title: THIS WEEK IN CLIMATE ACTION - NOVEMBER 6, 2026 - League of Conservation Voters
description:
These wins highlight how voters rejected Trump’s energy agenda and policies that have driven up energy costs.
The days of commonsense clean energy bills and ratepayer protections passing the House only to be killed in the Senate are over.
Governor-Elect Dr. Amy Acton ran on a platform of lowering energy costs, holding data centers accountable, and building healthy communities.
GCV ACTION FUND TAKE: Georgia Conservation Voters Action Fund Executive Director Brionté McCorkle said, “Georgians didn’t flip this Commission by accident.
VALCV TAKE: Virginia LCV Director of Advocacy and Campaigns Blair St. Ledger-Olson said, “A healthy environment is impossible without a healthy democracy.
text:
Your weekly resource to learn what the environmental movement is saying about the news of the day and the political fight of our generation. This week, voters made their voices loud and clear. They rejected Trump and Republicans’ disastrous energy policies by overwhelmingly electing candidates that will work to lower utility bills, bring more affordable clean energy online, and hold Big Polluters, Big Tech, and monopoly utilities accountable.

Be sure to follow LCV on Facebook, Instagram, BlueSky, and TikTok.

QUOTES OF THE WEEK:

“This was a wave, and what that means is that where we went on offense, deep into Trump territory, and where the margins were razor thin, Energy Bill Voters who we targeted made the difference, and this movement played a really big role in making that happen.”

— Pete Maysmith, LCV president, on how the cost of energy mobilized voters to elect pro-clean energy champions in this week’s elections.

“We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now.”

– A spokesperson for Hakeem Jeffries on Democratic priorities in the new Congress.

“Candidates won up and down the ballot because they campaigned on an unapologetic affordability agenda: standing up to corporate utilities, making data centers pay for their own costs, expanding access to locally produced cheap clean energy and creating family-sustaining union jobs.”

– Molly Parzen, executive director of Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania, on the role of affordability in the midterm election.

TOP NEWS IN THE ENERGY ELECTION

NATIONAL NEWS

VOTERS ELECT PRO-CLEAN ENERGY CHAMPIONS NATIONWIDE: Voters elected pro-climate, pro-democracy majorities in the U.S. House and Senate, alongside climate champions in state and local races across the country. These wins highlight how voters rejected Trump’s energy agenda and policies that have driven up energy costs. LCV Action Fund endorsed candidates won elections in the following states: Alabama, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Hawai’i, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin. For more, check out LCV’s New Member Guide.

OUR TAKE: On Tuesday, LCV President Pete Maysmith said, “Energy Bill Voters showed up in unprecedented numbers, even in deep Republican territory, to reject Trump’s dirty energy agenda. Tonight’s election results show that Trump’s energy agenda was not only an economic disaster for voters, but also a political disaster for Republicans. Voters have had enough of Trump and Congressional Republicans who sided with Big Oil, Big Polluters, monopoly utilities, and Big Tech time and time again to raise our costs. The voters have spoken, Trump must end his disastrous energy policy now. Stop the attacks on clean energy, stop the special favors for Big Oil, end the war.

“LCV and our affiliated entities, along with the broader climate and clean energy movement, invested more than ever during the midterms and went on offense in Trump territory to reach voters. This election, Energy Bill Voters elected new leaders to take back the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives. We look forward to working with these new majorities to advance affordable clean energy solutions across the country and cannot wait to work with these pro-environment, pro-democracy champions to protect the health of our communities, push back against Trump’s corrupt giveaways to corporate interests and Big Polluters, and fight for free and fair elections.”

TAKE 2: At a press conference following the election, LCV President Pete Maysmith said, “Voters across the country told us at the ballot box what we have been hearing from them since last year: they are tired of paying more for energy, things are too expensive, the system is rigged against them, things aren’t working and they need help. I heard this myself from voters going door to door last week. So let’s get something out of the way right at the top. President Trump, the voters have spoken, you must end your disastrous energy policy NOW. Stop the attacks on clean energy, stop the special favors for Big Oil, end the war. All of this needs to stop immediately.”

TAKE 3: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “On Tuesday, we saw historic wins across the country as Energy Bill Voters decisively rejected Trump and Congressional Republicans’ agenda of corruption and skyrocketing costs, including utility costs. LCV Victory Fund and affiliated entities invested over $125 million this cycle to take back the Senate and the House in order to lower energy costs, stand up to Big Polluters, Big Tech, and monopoly utilities, protect and build out clean energy, and protect clean air and water.”

VOTERS DEFEAT ALL DIRTY DOZEN CANDIDATES FOR THE FIRST TIME: Voters defeated all 12 Dirty Dozen candidates on LCV’s 2026 Dirty Dozen list, holding them accountable for siding with corporate polluters over their communities. The candidates backed policies that raised energy costs and threatened clean air and water, and voters held them accountable.

OUR TAKE: LCV Victory Fund Senior Vice President of Campaigns Sara Schreiber said, “For the first time ever, LCV Victory Fund defeated all 12 candidates on the federal Dirty Dozen. This is a list of candidates who consistently side against the environment and are running in competitive races that have a serious chance to affect the outcome, includes villains like Jon Husted who has raised utility bills in Ohio, pushed for taxpayer dollars to bailout FirstEnergy, and has taken hundreds of thousands of dollars from data center interests, and Michael Whatley, who is a former lobbyist for Big Oil and Duke Energy.”

STATE NEWS

VOTERS REJECT BIG OIL/BIG TECH, WITH 6 (AS OF NOW) NEW CLEAN ENERGY TRIFECTAS: Arizona, Nevada, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Pennsylvania will now all have clean energy majorities in 2027. Alaska might be a seventh once all races are called. These elections were won by candidates for governor and state Legislature endorsed by LCV affiliates that promised action to set strong guardrails for data centers, lower energy costs, and build affordable clean energy.

CHISPA AZ TAKE: Chispa Arizona Executive Director Vianey Olivarria said: “For us at Chispa Arizona, the power of our people and our work is deeply personal. Corporations see our environment as disposable and people as a revenue stream but while it may feel that their influence and power is unyielding, this historic victory proves that when we organize, we are a force that they should not underestimate. I am honored and humbled to stand today shoulder to shoulder with our partners at Activate 48 – LUCHA, OVOV, Worker Power. For so long, we have worked together to defend our people and our communities, and now, today, we see every fight was worth it.”

MLCV TAKE: Michigan LCV Deputy Director Bob Allison said, “Michiganders are tired of skyrocketing energy bills and a system where DTE and Consumers money pollutes our politics – and they made their feelings on it crystal clear. For too long our state’s monopoly utilities, which have provided some of the worst service in the country, have swayed lawmakers with massive political donations, blocking common sense policies to lower our energy bills. Those days are coming to an end.”

NCL TAKE: Nevada Conservation League Executive Director Kristee Watson said, “Nevadans overwhelmingly voted for leaders who will lower their energy bills and protect the places that make Nevada home. We went all in for Aaron Ford because he committed to stopping the flawed demand charge, holding greedy utilities and data centers accountable, protecting our water resources and public lands, and accelerating the transition from polluting fossil fuels to local clean energy. NCL’s efforts helped carry him across the finish line, and now we look forward to working with him and the Legislature to deliver this conservation agenda.”

WCV TAKE: Wisconsin Conservation Voters Executive Director Kerry Schumann said, “Last night, Wisconsinites made history. By electing David Crowley as our next governor alongside full pro-conservation control of the State Legislature, voters sent an unmistakable message that we want bold action on climate, safe drinking water for every community, and a democracy that belongs to everyone.

“David Crowley has proven throughout his career that he knows how to tackle complex public health and environmental challenges while delivering real results for working families. With pro-conservation leadership guiding both the executive branch and the legislature, we finally have the mandate to make permanent, historic gains for Wisconsin and secure a brighter, cleaner future for ourselves and future generations.”

CVPA TAKE: Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania Executive Director Molly Parzen said, “This is a watershed moment for our commonwealth. For the first time in more than three decades, Pennsylvanians have elected a pro-environment majority in both the state House and the state Senate. This historic victory was driven by voters from every corner of Pennsylvania who demanded an end to corporate greed, skyrocketing utility bills and handouts to billionaire Big Tech CEOs.

“The legislative bottleneck that paralyzed Harrisburg for years is finally broken. The days of commonsense clean energy bills and ratepayer protections passing the House only to be killed in the Senate are over. We now have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to deliver transformational change and turn Pennsylvania into a national leader on energy affordability and environmental protection.”

TX, GA, OH, AND LIKELY AK FLIP GOVERNORS MANSIONS FROM CLIMATE VILLAINS: While not trifectas like the states listed above, new governors in Georgia, Ohio, Texas, and, pending final results, Alaska, flipped their seats from anti-climate, anti-clean energy opponents. These states will also have major opportunities for progress and a clear mandate from voters to lower energy costs and build affordable clean energy.

OEC ACTION FUND TAKE: Ohio Environmental Council Action Fund Chief Executive Officer Carol Kauffman said, “Ohioans voted for change on Tuesday night. Governor-Elect Dr. Amy Acton ran on a platform of lowering energy costs, holding data centers accountable, and building healthy communities. The OEC Action Fund and our members worked hard to elect Dr. Acton, and we are thrilled that our next Governor is a leader who will work to improve the quality of life for every Ohioan. We congratulate Dr. Acton on her victory and urge the Ohio legislature to listen to the voters by working with the Governor-Elect to find common ground. Ohioans demand results, not partisan political games. Let’s get to work.”

NEW CLIMATE CHAMPION GOVERNORS ARE READY TO SET A STANDARD FOR THE NATION: Hannah Pingree in Maine and Deb Haaland in New Mexico will come into governors mansions in 2027 and have run as unabashed champions for climate action, clean energy, and protecting public lands. Both LCV state affiliates supported the candidates early in primaries, endorsing them as leaders who have spent careers championing the environment.

MCV TAKE: Maine Conservation Voters Executive Director Maureen Drouin said, “We congratulate Hannah on a positive, future-focused campaign and a hard-earned victory. Today’s result shows that Mainers want leaders like Hannah who will stand up to polluters and ensure our air, land, and water are protected for future generations. We’re looking forward to working with the Governor-elect to build a future in Maine where people and nature thrive through a healthy environment, a strong democracy, and a sustainable economy.”

CVNM TAKE: Conservation Voters of New Mexico Chief Executive Officer Demis Foster said, “Here at home, New Mexican voters showed up in a record turn out to elect Deb Haaland, the first Native American woman governor in our nation. Along with her running mate, Stephanie Garcia Richard, two women will be at the helm of our state for the first time in our state’s history. Governor-Elect Haaland and Lt. Governor-Elect Richard are the proven environmental champions we need to lead our state into a chapter of ambitious action on climate and protection of water, public lands, and cultural heritage. We look forward to the roll out of their ambitious climate and conservation agenda, starting day one.”

GEORGIA VOTERS FLIP PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION: Georgia voters re-elected Commissioner Peter Hubbard to a full term and elected Shelia Edwards to the Public Service Commission’s open District 5 seat, giving Democrats a 3-2 majority on the commission for the first time since the 1990s. Edwards won despite more than $2.5 million in pro-industry spending supporting her opponent. The new majority will oversee utility rates, data center expansion, and decisions shaping Georgia’s energy future.

GCV ACTION FUND TAKE: Georgia Conservation Voters Action Fund Executive Director Brionté McCorkle said, “Georgians didn’t flip this Commission by accident. This has been years in the making. In communities across Georgia, people have organized around high power bills and demanded more accountability from the people and corporations making decisions about their energy future. Tonight, voters changed who has the power to make those decisions. Now the test is what happens next. We ran against the idea that Georgians should finance Big Tech’s electricity. That question reaches across party lines because people understand fairness. If a company needs enormous amounts of new infrastructure to make money, families and small businesses should not be left carrying the costs and risks.”

COLORADO VOTERS REJECT AMENDMENT 82: Colorado voters rejected Amendment 82, which would have established a constitutional right to buy and sell natural gas. Defeating this amendment protects Colorado’s ability to advance clean energy and public health safeguards.

CONSERVATION COLORADO TAKE: Conservation Colorado CEO Kelly Nordini said, “Advance Colorado and its anonymous donors spent millions trying to convince Coloradans to lock profits for polluters into our state constitution, but voters saw through it and rejected Amendment 82. As Coloradans face the consequences of a changing climate and energy costs keep rising, voters chose to keep moving forward with the clean energy solutions that protect our environment, safeguard public health and safety, and make energy more affordable for families and businesses.”

MICHIGAN VOTERS APPROVE MONEY OUT OF POLITICS BALLOT MEASURE: Michigan voters approved Proposal 2 with 84% support, banning monopoly electric utilities and major government contractors from making political campaign contributions. The measure also expands disclosure rules for political communications.

MLCV TAKE: Michigan LCV Deputy Director Bob Allison said, “Michiganders are tired of skyrocketing energy bills and a system where DTE and Consumers money pollutes our politics – and they made their feelings on it crystal clear. For too long our state’s monopoly utilities, which have provided some of the worst service in the country, have swayed lawmakers with massive political donations, blocking common sense policies to lower our energy bills. Those days are coming to an end.”

VIRGINIA VOTERS APPROVE HISTORIC VOTING RIGHTS MEASURE: Virginia voters approved Ballot Measure 3, a referendum to automatically restore voting rights to eligible citizens convicted of felonies upon their release from incarceration.

VALCV TAKE: Virginia LCV Director of Advocacy and Campaigns Blair St. Ledger-Olson said, “A healthy environment is impossible without a healthy democracy. Tonight’s outcome restores the right to vote for hundreds of thousands of disenfranchised Virginians and enshrines in our constitution a fair and just standard to ensure that all eligible Virginians have a fundamental right to vote. After years of hard work to get this measure across the finish line, we are finally rid of one of the last vestiges of Jim Crow in Virginia. We are committed to continuing to fight for voting rights, to reach and engage more Virginians across the Commonwealth in our democracy, and to help secure solutions that empower communities and protect them from environmental harms.”

EUGENE, OR VOTERS APPROVE CLEAN ENERGY FUND: Voters in Eugene, Oregon approved Measure 20-388, the Eugene Clean Energy Fund, which establishes a fee on billion-dollar corporations and is expected to generate at least $15 million annually for local climate projects, clean energy jobs, and energy efficiency.

OLCV TAKE: Oregon LCV Political & Organizing Director and Energy Fund Steering Committee Member Britney VanCitters said, “Passage of Measure 20-388 is a resounding statement that Eugene is ready to lead in creating a cleaner and greener future for our communities. Eugenians raised their voices loud and clear because they know we can’t count on the state or federal government to deliver cleaner, local and more affordable energy. Establishing the Eugene Clean Energy Fund means we are ready to take action at the local level, an example we hope other cities will follow.”

ICYMI: NATIONAL NEWS

REVOLUTION WIND, VINEYARD WIND NOW FULLY OPERATIONAL: Two major offshore wind projects have completed construction and are delivering much needed cost-saving and reliable clean energy to New England’s electrical grid as energy demand grows. The 800-megawatt Vineyard Wind project off the coast of Massachusetts and the 704-megawatt Revolution Wind project off the coast of Rhode Island have both reached full commercial operation. These projects faced pushback from the Trump administration through illegal stop-work orders before federal judges allowed construction to resume. Vineyard Wind can power roughly 400,000 homes at full capacity and is expected to save customers $1.4 billion over 20 years. Revolution Wind can power roughly 350,000 homes at full capacity and is expected to save customers $500 million annually.

ELM TAKE: Environmental League of Massachusetts Senior Director of Offshore Wind Katie Segal said, “New England is better off now that we have not one but TWO fully commercially operational projects. We are in for a difficult winter and wind will help with costs and reliability.”

NEW ON THE POWER SOURCE BLOG AND SOCIALS:

ON THE BLOG: Stay tuned for exciting new content, coming soon to The Power Source blog!

ON OUR SOCIALS: Election Day came and Energy Bill Voters understood the assignment. This week, we celebrated climate and clean energy champions winning up and down the ballot, thanked the organizers and voters who made it happen, and broke down what the results mean for energy bills, Big Polluters, Big Tech, and the fight for affordable clean energy. The election may be over, but the work is just getting started.

text:
HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is promising to pause construction of new data centers to "protect Texans." Still, a political expert says the ban will apply only to new projects, not those already operating or under construction.

Hinojosa said she wants rules and guidelines for data centers, which are powering the artificial intelligence boom. In a new interview, she said data centers and community protections can go hand in hand.

"We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans," Hinojosa said. "Right now what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of."

Nancy Sims, a political science lecturer at the University of Houston, said Hinojosa can really only take action on future data centers.

"You can't really freeze mid-construction," Sims said. "They've been granted their permits. They've been granted their tax abatements. And you can't, as governor, go in and repeal those right away. What she can do is put a moratorium on new data centers."

SEE ALSO: University of Houston poll shows likely Texas voters' concerns on data centers

Sims also noted the broader landscape Hinojosa is stepping into.

"Greg Abbott gave the richest taxpayer handouts to data centers of any state in the country, invited them all into Texas; there is now this gold rush into Texas, and there are no rules," Sims said.

Investors reacted negatively to Tuesday's election results nationwide. Stocks tumbled Thursday but began bouncing back Friday.

Hinojosa has outlined goals for the next legislative session on data centers, including requiring American union jobs, creating full transparency, lowering costs for Texans, making data centers pay for themselves, and putting water and power for Texans first.

Sims said Hinojosa will also be able to appoint leaders overseeing permit processes, even with a Republican-controlled Senate.

RELATED: Democrat Gina Hinojosa elected Texas' first Latina governor, ousts Republican incumbent Greg Abbott

"I think that you will see Gina Hinojosa make changes at the Public Utility Commission, at the Texas Council on Environmental Quality," Sims said. "These areas that have been issuing the data center permits will change."

In a campaign video before she won, Hinojosa symbolically burned the law allowing tax breaks for data centers.

"It's time to burn it to the ground and elect a governor who will work for the people of Texas," she said in the video.

text:
NICE VIEW 👌 You’re looking straight down the core of our nation’s oldest nuclear power plant – Nine Mile Point in Oswego, NY. This was taken during a previous refueling outage that typically happens every 18-to-24 months at plants across the country. You can tell straight away that this is a boiling water reactor due to the number of assemblies and their checkerboard loading pattern. The shiny squares are the tops of fresh fuel assemblies that are being loaded into the core for the first time. The darker ones are irradiated fuel bundles that have already been through at least one fuel cycle and typically remain in the core for 3-to-5 years. The blue glow you see is coming from the irradiated fuel assemblies and is caused by a phenomenon known as Cherenkov radiation. It happens when electrically charged particles travel faster than the speed of light in that same medium, which in this case is water. The refueling bridge above the core travels back and forth between the fuel pool and the core to swap out old fuel and reposition the existing assemblies to maximize the efficiency of the reactor. 🎥: Constellation

NUCLEAR 101 (Nuclear Science Week Edition!) ⚛️: The sodium-cooled fast reactor uses liquid metal (sodium) as a coolant instead of water that is typically used in U.S. commercial power plants. This allows the coolant to operate at higher temperatures and lower pressures than current reactors—improving the efficiency of the system. Fast reactors use fast-moving neutrons that could allow them to operate on both fissile material and used fuel from current reactors to produce electricity.

On the night of the midterm elections, I saw Pete Buttigieg speak on NBC, highli…

Voters just delivered a resounding message across the nation: They will hold peo…



Spiritus exists to make abundant, affordable low-carbon energy. Getting there will take every kind of energy the country can produce: wind, solar, geothermal, nuclear and the oil and gas that still supply most of America’s energy.

That is why our company proudly supports Sen. Martin Heinrich’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, and why we believe New Mexico can lead the energy transition by showing that low-carbon energy production delivers on both economic and climate ambitions.

In August, the senator toured our facility at the Nambé Pueblo Development Corporation complex, where a direct air capture system we designed and built in New Mexico pulls carbon dioxide from the air. He listened to how we are partnering with oil and gas producers to take the technology into the field to produce low-carbon energy. That move, from the lab to the oil patch, is where permitting starts to decide whether a company like ours succeeds.

The bill, which Heinrich introduced last month with Republican and Democratic committee leaders, aims to deliver cheaper, more reliable energy of all kinds as well as the jobs that come with it while keeping the safeguards that make projects worth building.

For a young company, time is the scarcest resource. Our next step is a larger system in an operating oil field. If permits arrive on schedule and stay in place once issued, we can deliver on budget and keep raising the capital to grow. If they stall for years, a technology born in New Mexico gets built somewhere else or not at all.

The federal clock matters more here than almost anywhere else. About two-thirds of New Mexico’s Permian oil comes from federal land. The bill gives environmental reviews firm deadlines, two years for a full impact statement and one for an assessment and protects permits from reversal once granted. Carbon capture and storage are covered, alongside solar, wind, transmission and geothermal.

Speed still comes with scrutiny. Environmental review still happens, tribal consultation is written into law and projects can still be challenged in court. Tribal nations have raised serious concerns, and those concerns fully deserve consideration as the bill moves forward.

New Mexico has already shown what clear rules can do. Its 2021 methane rules banned routine venting and flaring. Today the state’s methane intensity is 1.2%, less than half the 3.1% in neighboring Texas, even though production on the New Mexico side of the Permian has more than doubled since 2020.

Producers adapted and kept investing because a business can plan around rules that are clear and consistent. The bill would bring that same certainty to federal permitting.

Carbon management is a next step in the energy transition. Producers already inject large volumes of carbon dioxide into mature fields to recover oil that conventional methods leave behind, but much of that CO2 comes from distant natural deposits.

Spiritus is building systems that capture CO2 from the air at the oil field itself, so no pipeline is needed. That CO2 goes underground and stays there, measured to federal standards. The result is a lower-carbon barrel from fields New Mexico has already proven, with less pressure to drill in new and more sensitive places.

The same technology can clean up industrial emissions of all kinds — including from data centers. Faster, more predictable permitting decisions mean we can build more carbon management projects sooner and at lower cost.

The Senate is scheduled to take its first vote Monday. New Mexico has the oil, the workforce and a record of smart rules that make production cleaner. With this bill, it can show the world what low-carbon energy looks like. Heinrich is right to lead the way.

Charles Cadieu is CEO and co-founder of Spiritus, a New Mexico-based energy technology company developing a new source of CO2 to increase production from existing U.S. oil fields.

text:
OTTAWA — Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says she’s confident billions of dollars in tax credits in the new federal budget will encourage private investment to build out Canada’s electricity grid.

Thursday’s federal budget committed $50 billion to help implement Ottawa’s electricity strategy, which looks to double the size of the grid by 2050. More than $38 billion was committed to tax credits the government says will stay in place until 2042.

Speaking to The Canadian Press on Thursday, Dabrusin said the measures came from government consultations on the electricity strategy.

“These are the things that people have set out for us when we have done consultations,” she said.

“We put out our electricity strategy earlier this year. This is what was told to us is what was needed, and I think that this is a huge step forward for how we build up clean energy for our country.”

Thursday’s budget included measures to extend the existing Clean Technology and Clean Electricity Investment tax credits to the end of 2040 — the former was supposed to be phased out in 2034. The budget also proposed to expand eligibility for the latter tax credit “for the highest-voltage intra-provincial electricity transmission lines in each province” for property acquired.

The budget also signalled Ottawa’s intent to update the Clean Electricity Regulations. The government said the goal is to introduce flexibility into the current system.

That includes allowing power plants to operate for longer and laying the groundwork for the government’s planned LNG buildout, as Ottawa indicated in its electricity strategy.

The strategy, released in May, placed a heavy emphasis on expanding the role of natural gas in powering the grid.

“Under some interpretations of the current electricity regulations, it would be difficult to build some additional natural gas that would complement much bigger builds,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the time.

“We have some of the cheapest gas in the world in Canada,” he said, citing natural gas as an affordability play in the strategy. Carney said at the time the strategy had a goal of lowering energy costs for 70 per cent of Canadian households.

The budget also promised $4 billion over 10 years for electricity infrastructure, including new funding for a Natural Resources program to expand renewable energy.

That program has paid out more than $1.3 billion for more than 100 projects dating back to 2021.

In a media statement, Clean Energy Canada, a think tank out of Simon Fraser University, welcomed the focus on building clean electricity supply but said the government must set clear goals.

“Today’s federal budget provides significant investments in electrifying Canada’s economy and households, but further work will be required to establish the concrete goals needed to fully realize a generational opportunity,” executive director Rachel Doran said.

“While moving from plans to action is critical, without concrete goals, Canada risks trading a climate plan with an accountability metric to one that is a list of actions without a final destination.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026.

text:
Share and Download

Tuesday’s decisive Democratic wave reached deep into down-ballot races, including those for critical state attorney general (AG) offices. Democrats won nearly all of the closely contested AG races and gained five offices, bringing them to 29 AGs to Republicans’ 22. The flips include Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas, states where Republicans had held the office for years and, in Texas, for decades. The results reflected an electorate voting largely along party lines, with very little ticket splitting, and powerful coattail effects from top-of-the-ballot US Senate races. In Georgia, for example, the Democratic AG candidate’s vote share ran within a few points of the party’s candidates for governor, lieutenant governor, and secretary of state.

These results will reshape the state AG landscape. Texas and Georgia, with their current Republican AGs, had been among the most active Republican offices challenging federal policy under the Biden Administration, and, more recently, supporting the Trump Administration’s agenda. Now, both states’ Democratic AGs-elect have made clear they will push back on the Trump Administration where they see federal overreach.

Many of the incoming AGs have signaled a degree of AI skepticism, and virtually all of them have focused on the issues of affordability (especially with respect to utility costs), consumer protection, antitrust and competition, and corporate accountability. This likely means even more scrutiny of pricing, market concentration, scams, and AI-related consumer harms.

Below, we briefly profile each of the new AGs and assess what their arrival portends for companies within their reach.

Flipped Seats and Surprise Outcomes

Georgia

Democratic State Representative Tanya Miller was elected as Georgia AG, defeating Republican State Senator Brian Strickland by roughly 11 points. She replaces Republican Chris Carr and will be the first woman to serve as Georgia’s AG and the first Democrat to hold the office since 2010. Miller, a former federal prosecutor, ran on a platform of public safety, consumer protection, and government accountability. She pledged to make the office Georgians’ “law firm.”

Consumer protection and competition. AG-elect Miller has vowed to use the state’s consumer protection tools and the office’s “full anti-trust authority.” Miller’s focus on grocery prices, utilities, and antitrust suggests heightened scrutiny of pricing and market concentration, along with enforcement against scams, robocalls, and predatory lending.

Public safety. In addition to her top priorities related to crime, her pledge to pursue businesses that enable human trafficking could expand scrutiny of companies in affected industries.

Federal and multistate litigation. Miller has said she would potentially but not reflexively join Democratic AGs in multistate litigation against Trump Administration policies, depending on whether doing so would help Georgians.

AG-elect Miller has spent more than two decades as a courtroom litigator, including as a federal prosecutor in New York and as Chief Senior District Attorney in the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office. She has served in the Georgia House since 2023, and her colleagues elected her House Democratic Caucus Chair in November 2024.

Iowa

Iowa voters elected Democrat Nate Willems as AG, defeating Republican incumbent Brenna Bird 51–49. Prior to Bird’s election in 2022, the seat was long held by Democrat Tom Miller. Willems campaigned on workers’ rights, affordability, consumer protection, corporate accountability, public safety, protection for Iowa seniors, and environmental protection.

Labor and employment. Similar to a number of other Democratic AGs, Willems promised to create a dedicated Wage Theft Recovery Unit to investigate employers not only for alleged wage theft but also for worker misclassification and other labor law violations; such units often receive referrals from local organized labor chapters regarding nonunion shops.

Environment. Willems also emphasized holding corporations accountable for pollution and has pledged not to accept campaign contributions from corporate actors that are under investigation or have been found responsible for pollution. His plans additionally call for notifying nearby residents when settlements involving pollution incidents are reached.

Federal and multistate litigation. Willems has pledged to focus on issues directly affecting Iowans rather than national political litigation.

AG-elect Willems is a workers’ compensation and labor attorney at a private law firm. He has longstanding ties to organized labor, serving on the executive board of the Hawkeye Area Labor Council, American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations. Willems was elected to the Iowa House of Representatives in 2008 and served from 2009 to 2013, including on the Labor, Education, and Ways and Means Committees. He served as vice chair of the Labor Committee during his first term and ranking member of the Education Committee during his second.

Kansas

In a rematch of their 2022 race, Democrat Chris Mann is expected to narrowly defeat incumbent Republican AG Kris Kobach (as of publication, Kobach has not conceded). Kobach had won that earlier race by fewer than 16,000 votes. Mann successfully ran as a nonpartisan, law enforcement-first candidate under the line “not Team Red or Team Blue, but Team Kansas.” His campaign drew support across party lines, as well as the endorsement of the Kansas State Lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police, its first for a Democratic AG candidate since 2002. Several of AG-elect Mann’s priorities bear directly on business.

AI, technology, and privacy. Mann has said he will work with the legislature on guardrails against the unauthorized use of consumer data. He has also called for protecting children from unregulated AI chatbots.

Consumer protection and competition. Mann has made consumer fraud and scams a centerpiece, citing more than $30 million in Kansas scam losses in the first half of 2026. He has also pledged to go after deceptive pricing, including surge pricing and individualized pricing based on a consumer’s purchase history. Expect the office to expand its consumer protection enforcement, especially with respect to data privacy, algorithmic and dynamic pricing, and AI products aimed at minors.

Agriculture and natural resources. He has also proposed a new Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources in the AG’s office.

Public safety. Mann has also emphasized traditional public safety work, including fentanyl and drug trafficking, elder abuse, and domestic violence.

Federal and multistate litigation. Mann criticized Kobach for spending state resources on culture-war litigation at the expense of supporting local prosecutors. Mann’s victory likely means the end of Kansas’s role as a high-profile conservative litigant in cases involving federal policy, a role it played prominently under Kobach. His law enforcement background and nonpartisan positioning point to a pragmatic office rather than a reflexively progressive one, particularly on federal issues. Expect Mann to look for opportunities to participate in bipartisan coalitions, including ones that are state-interest-based rather than politically oriented.

AG-elect Mann is a former police officer and later served as prosecutor in Wyandotte County and as a senior staff attorney at the Kansas Securities Commission, where he handled fraud and scams. Since 2016, he has run his own law firm, focusing on representing victims of drunk driving. He previously served on the national board of Mothers Against Drunk Driving and helped pass Kansas’s ignition-interlock law for DUI offenders.

Ohio

Democrat John J. Kulewicz defeated Republican State Auditor Keith Faber in a close race. Kulewicz will be the first Democrat to lead the Ohio AG’s Office since Richard Cordray, later Consumer Financial Protection Bureau director, left the office in 2011. Kulewicz ran on getting “back to the basic issues that Ohioans care about,” which means “taking on corrupt politicians,” “price-fixing monopolies, scam artists and robocallers,” and “Medicaid provider and nursing home fraudsters.”

AI, technology, and privacy. Kulewicz’s comments on data privacy and “algorithmic decision-makers” signal potential focus on data collection, cybersecurity and privacy, and AI-based decision-making.

Consumer protection and competition. Kulewicz emphasized a focus on addressing rising prices for necessities such as groceries, fuel, and utilities, as well as robocalls, scams, and Medicaid and nursing home fraud.

Utilities. He has said he will focus on accountability at the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio as a priority.

Federal and multistate litigation. Kulewicz has criticized the office’s direction under former AG Dave Yost, saying he would have “far less interest in taking part in culture war cases around the nation.” Consistent with other new Democratic AGs, we expect Ohio to step back from national Republican-led multistate litigation and instead selectively join Democratic or bipartisan coalitions in consumer protection and antitrust cases.

AG-elect Kulewicz is a 44-year member of the Columbus-based law firm Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease LLP.

Texas

Texas voters elected Democratic State Senator Nathan Johnson as AG, defeating Republican State Senator Mayes Middleton by roughly seven points. AG-elect Johnson will be the first Democratic AG in Texas since Dan Morales left the office in 1999. He replaces Ken Paxton, who ran for US Senate and lost. Johnson ran on a “back-to-basics” platform of public safety, consumer protection, and anti-corruption. His stated top priority is ending the use of the office as a “publicly-funded law firm” for one political faction and rebuilding its staff.

AI and technology. Johnson’s focus on antitrust and AI scams suggests continued attention to tech, pricing, and market consolidation, but with a different lens than Paxton’s.

Consumer protection and competition. Johnson has also identified consumer protection and the enforcement of market-competition laws as his second priority, after reforming the office itself. He has said he will use state and federal antitrust law and other business-practice laws against market consolidation, predatory pricing, fraud, and scams.

Federal and multistate litigation. Under Paxton, the office was a hub for conservative multistate litigation and filed more than 100 suits against the Biden Administration. Johnson pledged to push back on federal overreach, which means Texans will see an AG’s office opposed to Trump Administration policies for the first time. Clients should expect Johnson to move Texas away from the role it played under AG Paxton as a close partner of the Trump Administration and a leader of Republican multistate initiatives. He may also join Democratic-led coalitions on consumer protection, antitrust, and, potentially, challenges to federal action.

AG-elect Johnson is a commercial litigator and mediator in the Dallas office of Thompson Coburn LLP. He has also served in the state Senate since 2019, where he passed bills including 2026 legislation establishing state oversight of data brokers and 2025 legislation authorizing the AG to prosecute AI-enabled scams.

New AGs in Continuing-Party States

Alabama

Alabama voters elected Republican Katherine Robertson as AG over Democratic former State Representative Jeff McLaughlin. She succeeds Steve Marshall, who has held the office since 2017, was term-limited, and finished third in the Republican US Senate primary. She ran on continuity, saying she wants to make the office more effective while maintaining its current priorities, and that her “goal is to be the most effective and most conservative AG in the country.” After the election, Robertson said she would bring her experience in criminal, consumer protection, and constitutional defense cases to the job.

AI, technology, and privacy. Robertson has said regulation of license-plate cameras will be on her 2027 legislative agenda. Her stated aim is to protect privacy while keeping the cameras as a law enforcement tool, and she said, “I really want Alabama to lead the nation in that conversation.”

Federal and multistate litigation. Robertson’s campaign noted that she helped lead the office’s fights “against Joe Biden’s federal overreach” and on women’s sports, free speech, and abortion. She has said multistate litigation is core to the job: “I don’t see national lawsuits as something separate in any way from the in-state work,” and those cases can address “wrongs done to either Alabama’s consumers or to our state sovereignty as a whole.”

AG-elect Robertson began her public service in Washington as clerk and counsel to Senator Jeff Sessions on the US Senate Judiciary Committee. She later served as Vice President of the Alabama Policy Institute, and was Chief Counsel to AG Steve Marshall for nearly a decade.

Michigan

Michigan voters elected Democrat Eli Savit as AG over Republican Doug Lloyd by nearly eight points. He will succeed term-limited AG Dana Nessel, preserving Democratic control of an office the party has held since 2019. His victory was part of a broader Democratic sweep of Michigan’s statewide executive offices and legislative chambers. Savit campaigned on consumer protection, workers’ rights, environmental enforcement, civil rights, reproductive freedom, and public safety.

AI, technology, and privacy. Savit pledged to use the AG’s rulemaking authority under the Michigan Consumer Protection Act during his first 100 days to issue rules addressing the misuse of artificial intelligence. Those rules could target AI-driven pricing and deceptive marketing. He also identified regulating AI products that could harm children as a priority.

Consumer protection and competition. Savit pledged to litigate against price gouging, deceptive business practices, and other consumer abuses.

Labor and employment. Savit also campaigned to combat wage theft, payroll fraud, labor trafficking, and unsafe working conditions.

Environment, energy, and utilities. Environmental and utility matters are likely to remain prominent. Savit pledged to hold corporate polluters accountable, continue Michigan’s litigation concerning Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline, oppose utility price gouging, and protect residential customers from bearing the energy costs associated with data centers.

Federal and multistate litigation. He also said he would sue the federal government when necessary to protect Michigan elections, public funding, and constitutional rights.

AG-elect Savit is an experienced public law attorney: he was elected the County Prosecutor in 2020, and previously served as Assistant City Counsel for the City of Detroit. As county prosecutor, Savit created units focused on economic justice and conviction integrity and expungement. While at the City of Detroit, Savit led litigation against the opioid industry. He is also a lecturer at the University of Michigan Law School and is a former law clerk for US Supreme Court Justices Sandra Day O’Connor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

Nevada

Democratic State Senate Majority Leader Nicole Cannizzaro was elected as Nevada AG, defeating Republican Adriana Guzmán Fralick, former chair of Nevada’s Cannabis Compliance Board. AG-elect Cannizzaro’s stated first-year priorities are protecting children online, cracking down on financial fraud schemes that target vulnerable Nevadans, and targeting organized retail theft.

AI, technology, and privacy. Cannizzaro’s focus on children’s online safety, AI, housing, and data centers suggests continued scrutiny of technology platforms, institutional homebuyers, and large energy and water users.

Consumer protection and competition. Cannizzaro has also pledged to bring consumer protection cases against corporations for price fixing and unfair trade practices. Her focus on pricing signals more focus on price-fixing, personalized pricing (so-called “surveillance” pricing), and consumer fraud.

Energy and data centers. During the campaign, Cannizzaro released a plan for how the office would handle the rapid growth of data centers in the state.

Federal and multistate litigation. How often the AG’s office should sue the federal government was a central issue in the Nevada race, and Cannizzaro said she would “absolutely” sue the Trump Administration, protect reproductive rights in court, including if the federal government or other states try to infringe on them, and be open to challenging the recently announced cuts to Nevada’s Colorado River water allocation.

AG-elect Cannizzaro previously served as a prosecutor in the Clark County District Attorney’s Office, where she became Chief Deputy District Attorney in the Gang Unit. She has served in the Nevada Senate since 2016, and in 2019 she became the first woman to serve as Senate Majority Leader.

Oklahoma

Republican Jon Echols defeated Democrat Nick Coffey with about 55% of the vote. Echols succeeds AG Gentner Drummond, who ran for governor but narrowly lost the Republican primary. AG-elect Echols ran as the “public safety candidate,” with illegal immigration, defending the “conservative way of life,” fighting fentanyl, and shutting down illegal marijuana grows as his top priorities. Current AG Drummond often clashed with outgoing Governor Kevin Stitt. AG-elect Echols, by contrast, has said he expects to work closely with the next governor and to raise any disagreements privately first.

Consumer protection and competition. For businesses, the key question is continuity. Under Drummond, Oklahoma brought high-profile consumer protection and corporate cases, including suits against Roblox and Allstate. Echols’s consumer protection background suggests that enforcement will continue.

Environment and energy. Echols has pledged to protect Oklahoma farmland from foreign adversaries, support the Trump Administration’s Environmental Protection Agency, and oppose “environmental extremists” targeting the state’s energy industry. His stated priorities point toward criminal enforcement, alignment with federal policy, and support for the energy sector rather than environmental litigation.

Healthcare. Echols has argued that rebates under the federal 340B drug program are being siphoned off by providers instead of reaching low-income patients.

AG-elect Echols served 12 years in the Oklahoma House, eight of them as majority floor leader, the longest anyone has held that role. He practices family law in Oklahoma City and has co-founded healthcare and construction companies. In the legislature, he wrote the bill creating the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority and a 2023 law giving the AG full authority to enforce the state’s medical marijuana laws, as well as the state’s 2019 “Constitutional Carry” law.

Rhode Island

Rhode Island voters elected Democrat Kim Ahern as AG, defeating Republican Alan Gordon by nearly 33 points. Ahern will succeed term-limited Democratic AG Peter Neronha, maintaining Democratic control of the office. Ahern will become Rhode Island’s first Democratic woman elected AG and the second woman overall to hold the office. Ahern ran on consumer protection, healthcare oversight and challenging federal policies she considers unlawful. Ahern said her top priority would be to establish a Reproductive Justice Unit within the AG’s Office to protect reproductive and abortion rights. Ahern’s victory signals continuity with the active healthcare and consumer protection enforcement posture of outgoing AG Peter Neronha’s Administration, with potential expansion into emerging technology issues.

AI, technology, and privacy. Ahern said she will “prosecute platforms that violate data privacy laws, promote harmful algorithmic content, or fail to protect minors,” and ensure that “Rhode Island is leading the charge to protect children from AI-generated deepfakes and the potential super-charging of other digital harms.”

Consumer protection and competition. She pledged to make enforcement “a top priority” and to go after “landlords who jack up rents through price fixing; grocery stores that price gouge shoppers; or businesses tagging junk fees on to our daily purchases.”

Healthcare and utilities. Ahern has also pledged to closely scrutinize hospital and healthcare mergers, including by “blocking deals that prioritize profits over patients,” and to increase the office’s interventions in utility rate cases.

Federal and multistate litigation. She has committed to “not hesitate to take the Trump administration to court” when it oversteps its authority.

AG-elect Ahern served nine years as a special assistant AG under three attorneys general, including in the Special Victims Unit, where her campaign says she prosecuted more than 1,000 cases. She then served as deputy counsel to Governor Gina Raimondo and deputy chief of staff to Governor Dan McKee. In 2023, she became chair of the new Cannabis Control Commission, and she resigned in October 2025 to run for AG.

South Carolina

Republican David Stumbo was elected as South Carolina AG. Stumbo replaces Alan Wilson, who had held the office since January 2011 and was elected governor. South Carolina departed from the straight-ticket voting seen elsewhere this cycle: Republicans won all six statewide office races, yet voters also elected Democrat Annie Andrews to the US Senate with roughly 50.7% of the vote.

AI, technology, and privacy. Stumbo’s focus on internet crimes against children could also mean continued scrutiny of technology platforms on child safety.

Public safety. Stumbo’s stated top priority is leading the state’s criminal justice system, which he describes as the AG’s primary job under the state constitution. He has called for stronger bond laws to keep potentially dangerous defendants in custody and has pointed to gang legislation in North Carolina and Georgia as models for South Carolina.

Federal and multistate litigation. His agenda suggests the office will largely continue Wilson’s approach, including participation in Republican-led multistate efforts and challenges to federal action.

Stumbo has worked as a prosecutor for more than two decades and currently serves as Solicitor for the state’s Eighth Judicial Circuit (comprising several upstate counties) and previously served as an assistant AG. Before he was elected solicitor, he worked in private practice.

Alaska’s next AG will be appointed by the Governor, subject to legislative confirmation, and Maine’s next AG will be selected by the state legislature.

***

As described above, the new group of AGs that will take office in January comes with clear mandates and ambitious enforcement agendas. Some flipped seats, and others succeed AGs from their own party. Across both groups, the incoming AGs are signaling sustained or expanded scrutiny of pricing, competition, data privacy, AI, and children’s online safety. They are also signaling that multistate litigation will remain a central tool, whether used against the federal government or alongside it. The flips in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, and Texas will also shift the balance among multistate coalitions. Companies may face new or growing Democratic-led investigations in states that were recently aligned with Republican-led efforts.

New AGs often move quickly to set the tone for their tenure. They may reorganize enforcement divisions, create new units, issue rules or guidance, and pursue high-profile matters that show they are delivering on campaign promises. Companies should use this transition period to assess the new state AG landscape and:

assess their potential exposure in states with new AGs;

review pending investigations, civil investigative demands (CIDs), and settlement negotiations to which new leadership may take a different approach; and

prepare for engagement with incoming AGs and their senior staff.

WilmerHale’s bipartisan State Attorneys General Practice draws on attorneys who have served at the most senior levels of state AG offices and federal administrations of both major parties. title: Turkey to push for 'electrification' drive at COP31 as climate threats mount - France 24
description:
More than 100,000 people are expected at the UN's two-week climate negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.
'Implementation COP' Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference.
The European Union has called for "clean" electrification – a term that could spark debate over the role of fossil fuels in the Turkish initiative.
COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.
Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary "roadmap" with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.
text:
Nearly 200 nations gather for the COP31 summit in Turkey on Monday but tensions over geopolitics, finance and fossil fuels are tempering expectations of a major breakthrough in tackling the climate crisis.

More than 100,000 people are expected at the UN's two-week climate negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.

Tougher action on fossil fuels – the main driver of climate change – appears unlikely and budget-strapped developed countries are reluctant to commit more money to help developing nations cope with climate impact.

Read moreEl Nino set to intensify before peaking in December, UN warns

An energy crisis and cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the war in the Middle East, are also looming over the gathering.

"This is not going to be the COP that changes the world," said Paul Watkinson, France's former chief negotiator at climate summits.

"It's an intermediate COP in many ways. But it is an important conference and it does need to make sure it makes progress," he said.

A senior EU official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, also tempered expectations, adding: "We cannot expect a revolution in terms of climate action from the Antalya COP."

The talks follow deadly floods in Nepal, searing heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia.

Read moreMore than half of Europe faced intense summer heat stress, EU monitor says

An exceptionally strong El Nino climate phenomenon is forecast to peak later this year, adding to extreme weather and possibly helping to make 2026 or 2027 the hottest year on record.

The outlook is increasingly bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above preindustrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.

'Implementation COP'

Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference.

"COP31 comes at a difficult time for the world," said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen. "Reaching consensus among nearly 200 countries will not be easy but cooperation remains essential."

COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, said the conference would strive "to turn the commitments of past COPs into real results".

Turkey is promoting an "action agenda" alongside the formal negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.

Its centrepiece is an "electrification" drive to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35 percent by 2035.

"This year's energy crisis has shocked us out of our complacency," Kurum said. "Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions."

Turkey and Australia also want electrification to appear in a "cover decision" – an overarching political statement negotiated by consensus.

The European Union has called for "clean" electrification – a term that could spark debate over the role of fossil fuels in the Turkish initiative.

The EU official suggested the bloc might be willing to find a compromise.

"The word 'clean' may be difficult for some. There may be other ways of formulating this without having it so explicit," the official said.

Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think tank E3G, said the Turkish COP31 presidency's proposal was "carefully worded".

It is "quite an open pledge that I think is going to enable quite a few countries to come on board", Cassel said.

Read moreThree-quarters of world's displaced people face severe climate risks, UN says

Money fight

Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in 2023, but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.

COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.

Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary "roadmap" with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.

Observers say Turkey and Australia are keen to avoid a repeat of last year's fossil fuel fight.

But a feud looms over wealthy nations' unfulfilled financial commitments to help developing countries deal with climate change.

The group of African negotiators is demanding that a pledge to triple adaptation finance – money to cope with the worsening impacts of climate change – be added to the negotiation agenda.

Recent elections, meanwhile, have given climate campaigners a boost, with Democrats seizing control of the US Congress in a setback to US President Donald Trump, who calls global warming a hoax.

A US congressional delegation will attend COP31, but the Trump administration is not taking part in the negotiations.

Fresh from his re-election win over conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will travel to Antalya next week.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Published on: Nov 6, 2026

From a single global identity for its heritage brands to EV infrastructure data and bias-free site planning, Dow Jones Energy is building a trusted one-stop source for fuel and convenience retailers.

MobilityPlaza sat down with four members of the Dow Jones Energy team at the 2026 NACS Show in Las Vegas to discuss the company’s new global business identity and the data and tools it is bringing to fuel retailers.

The new identity gathers the group’s specialist brands under one roof: OPIS, Axxis, Eco-Movement and A2i in the fuel space, alongside Chemical Market Analytics and McCloskey more broadly. “Each of these businesses have earned trust through operating in this space for decades,” said Bryan Schutt, Senior Vice President, Head of Strategy and Operations.

E-mobility is a growing part of that offer. Dow Jones Energy has sold data to the automotive industry for years, but Jean Cherbonnier, Regional Director, sees demand accelerating among fuel retailers since the acquisition of Netherlands-based Eco-Movement a year ago. Retailers now use its global EV infrastructure data to benchmark the market, plan investments and compare charging prices. Europe is growing fast, with electric cars passing a quarter of the market, while US growth slowed after federal tax credits ended. Yet the US installed base keeps expanding, and more retailers want chargers on their own forecourts. “With EV, they can attract people who want to recharge and can spend easily 20 minutes on their premises,” Cherbonnier said, time that often ends with a visit to the c-store.

On the fuel side, pressure on volumes and margins makes reliable data a daily necessity. “You have to thread that needle every single day with all of your products at all of your stations,” said Brent Eubanks, Senior Software Sales Executive. He noted that this year’s volatility has been driven by wars rather than hurricanes, forcing retailers to adapt over a longer period, while Dow Jones Energy’s benchmarks help them measure how they are performing.

For site investment, the company offers LocationPro, a software platform that models what makes a location successful. Its main use case is guiding retailers on where to build new sites, a major investment that is costly to get wrong, but it also suggests improvements for every existing location. Ian Thompson, Executive Director, said the tool counters the gut feel and confirmation bias that often shape these decisions. “What LocationPro does is take away all of that emotion, all of that bias, and present the user with another lens through which to make the decision,” he said. The final call, he added, always stays with the user.

title: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer - Greenfield Indiana
description:
An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana.
Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.
When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part.
Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.
Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.
text:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely.

Winter also brings severe smog to parts of Pakistan and China, where warmer air can act as a lid, trapping colder air and pollution near the ground. In eastern Europe, burning coal and wood to heat homes also adds to winter pollution. Western Hemisphere countries, meanwhile, face their own seasonal air-quality problems, as summer wildfires send smoke across vast areas of the United States and Canada.

Experts say no matter where you live or when you face pollution, simple steps such as checking the air quality index, wearing a well-fitting mask and using air purifiers can reduce exposure to harmful pollutants.

An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana. Fireworks traditionally set off during the holiday, which starts Sunday, can make polluted air more dangerous.

As Diwali approaches, here are ways to reduce exposure to polluted air.

Check the air before heading out

Fireworks add a sharp burst of pollution to a much bigger problem. Across India, Pakistan and other parts of South Asia, traffic, factories, dust from construction and burning of crop residues and waste foul the air. Weak winds and stagnant winter air allow that pollution to build up.

“Poor air quality is our all-year-round problem in our country,” said Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance. Narayan said firecrackers add to the problem.

India’s air quality index turns pollution measurements into a health warning. AQI readings of 201–300 mean “poor,” 301–400 “very poor” and 401–500 “severe.” Severe levels can harm even healthy people.

Check pollution levels on government or privately run websites before heading outdoors. Look for data from a nearby monitoring station and the time of its last update. A citywide average can conceal a polluted neighborhood.

The problem is especially bad in Delhi, where fine particle pollution averaged about 19 times the World Health Organization’s annual guideline last year. Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.

City authorities have responded with temporary construction, industrial and vehicle restrictions. Public health experts said such measures often fail to address the root causes. The city of more than 20 million people is also implementing a long-term plan to promote use of electric vehicles.

Make your mask fit

Dr. Arvind Kumar, a chest surgeon at Medanta hospital near Delhi and founder trustee of the Lung Care Foundation, recommends using properly fitted N95 or N99 masks outdoors during periods of heavy pollution. These masks are available at pharmacies, hardware stores and online retailers.

N95 filters are designed to capture at least 95% of airborne particles; N99 filters are made to capture at least 99%. The particle respirator masks do not filter harmful gases.

Cover your nose, mouth and chin. Shape the nose clip and check the seal every time. Facial hair can break that seal. The aim, Kumar said, is to ensure “all the breathing is through the mask and not around the mask.”

Replace disposable masks when dirty, damaged or hard to breathe through. Never put a mask on a child younger than 2. People with heart or lung disease should seek medical advice about mask use.

Loose surgical masks, cloth masks and scarves offer unreliable protection against fine particles.

Kumar said pollution can cause persistent coughing, inflame the airways and trigger asthma-like attacks. He also cited increased risks of pneumonia, heart attacks and strokes, while linking prolonged exposure to impaired lung development in children and lung cancer.

Kumar said people should avoid strenuous exercise outdoors during heavy pollution, including early mornings, when pollution levels can be high.

Match the purifier to the room

Using the right air purifiers indoors can help. The devices draw in air to filter out pollutants, then recirculate the cleaner air.

A purifier needs enough capacity to clean the air of the room where it runs. Look for a high-efficiency particulate air, or HEPA, filter. Then check its clean air delivery rate, which is the volume of filtered air it supplies.

Place the purifier where you spend the most time, such as the bedroom. Keep its airflow clear and run it consistently.

HEPA filters trap particles. Substantial activated-carbon filters can remove some gases. No purifier removes every pollutant. Avoid machines that deliberately produce ozone, which irritates the lungs.

Cleaner indoor air reduces exposure, but a purifier cannot eliminate pollution’s health risks, Kumar said.

Celebrate with less smoke

Kumar said it’s important to avoid incense, mosquito coils and candles. Their particles can linger indoors for hours, especially in poorly ventilated rooms, while fireworks pollution can persist overnight, depending on the weather. When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part. Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.

“If one wants to celebrate and really enjoy the festival of Diwali, avoid bursting firecrackers,” said Narayan, the public health expert.

India’s health ministry also recommends reducing smoky cooking and using a kitchen exhaust that vents outdoors. Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.

Personal precautions have limits. Narayan said people who earn their livelihoods outdoors cannot simply stay home. Many families also cannot afford air purifiers.

She called for sustained action on pollution sources and affordable health care for those already suffering. Masks and filters can reduce exposure, but lasting protection requires governments to clean the air.

“It’s our responsibility to hold our governments accountable,” Narayan said. “There’s no other way about it.”
