text:
Republicans have controlled the Pennsylvania Senate for more than 30 years, but that changed on Tuesday. Voters flipped four seats to the Democrats, handing the party a rare trifecta: single-party control of the Governor’s office and the General Assembly.

LISTEN to the story

Audio Player

Longtime environmental advocate: It’s the energy bills

David Hess has been working on environmental policy and advocacy in Pennsylvania since the 1980s, and thinks the rising cost of energy is a key reason for the Democratic victories in Tuesday’s election.

“It had everything to do with the concerns people had about… the electric and natural gas bills that they’re getting, the price of gasoline,” he said. “It had to do, in particular, with data centers.”

Hess, who is a former secretary of the state Department of Environmental Protection, points out that the four Republican senators who lost all had data center projects in their districts. Data centers use a lot of power, and that has led to higher energy prices. According to an independent analysis, Pennsylvania homeowners are paying an average of 20% more for electricity than they were two years ago.

Pennsylvania Republicans have blamed the price hikes on climate policies in other states and Governor Shapiro’s electric grid policies.

Now that Democrats are taking control, Hess advises them to focus on reducing those costs by diversifying energy sources.

“The Republicans had a one energy source policy, that was natural gas. And to put more eggs in that basket just wasn’t going to work at all to reduce costs,” he said. “You need a variety of generation sources to do that.”

With a trifecta, Pennsylvania Democrats would pass energy reforms and rein in data centers

How to increase alternative energy sources

A recent report found that Pennsylvania ranks near the bottom of states in adding renewable energy to the electric grid. The state gets 5% of its electricity from renewable energy, compared with 37% in Texas, another gas-producing state.

Democrats have a chance to change that, said Sharon Pillar, founder and director of the non-profit Pennsylvania Solar Center.

Pennsylvania requires utilities to get only 0.5% of their electricity from solar energy, an amount that hasn’t changed since 2004.

Pillar wants the state to increase that amount because she says it will mean more energy and will also help the economy.

“We work with a lot of companies; they’re ready to go,” Pillar said. “They’ve been waiting on Pennsylvania for many years, and I think they’ll be very excited to come and invest billions of dollars into Pennsylvania.”

Pillar also wants lawmakers to approve community solar, which allows people who don’t have rooftop solar to buy energy from a nearby array.

Advocates for renewable energy, like Elizabeth Fiedler, a Democrat from South Philadelphia who chairs the House Energy Committee, also see a need for state investment in local electric grids.

“We need to do everything we can to get more energy online,” she said.

Fiedler supports a bill to allow Pennsylvanians to install balcony solar, which are solar panels that can be plugged into a wall outlet, as well as legislation to expand battery storage, so renewable energy can be used on demand.

“That’s super important because in just a couple of years there are predictions that we’re going to start to have major power outages,” Fiedler said. “We’ve got to do everything we can to make sure we’re using all the energy we have in a very wise way.”

Fiedler said the Democratic-controlled House already approved many bills to address these issues, but they stalled in the Republican-controlled Senate. Now she expects things to be different.

“We are ready to go, and that includes a bunch of bills that will lower people’s bills, lower the cost of energy for regular folks in Pennsylvania,” Fiedler said.

In a speech Wednesday, after the election results were finalized, newly-reelected Governor Josh Shapiro outlined top priorities for his second term, including mass transit funding, raising the minimum wage, codifying abortion rights and investing in housing.

David Hess hopes Democrats also stay focused on energy costs. He said the clock is already ticking on their leadership.

“If the Democrats get sidetracked on a whole bunch of other issues on their agenda without addressing stuff that’s right in front of their face and drove these results, I think they’re really missing an opportunity,” he said.

Gov. Shapiro said he and top-ranking Democrats in the General Assembly will release an agenda for their first 100 days of 2027 in the coming weeks.

description:

text:
CAMEROON – As United Nations climate talks kick off in Turkey on Monday, Secretary-General António Guterres has an urgent message for world leaders: “This is a moment of truth.”

He's delivered variations of this ominous warning about climate change, caused by the burning of fossil fuels like oil and gas, in the past decade, often with increasingly hyperbolic language. Three years ago, he even said, “the era of global boiling has arrived, " referring to rising temperatures and increasing extreme weather, both results of climate change.

But this time, it will be his last global warming sermon as head of the United Nations as his second and last term expires at the end of the year. And the sense of urgency is palpable in a world with worsening killer heat waves, storms, floods and droughts amid ever higher temperatures and, on top of all of it, El Niño, a naturally occurring climate pattern that scrambles weather systems around the globe.

“This is a moment of truths. We can no longer wait, we can no longer have endless discussions in which everybody tries to push the responsibility to someone else. Everybody must do more, everybody must do more now,” Guterres said he will tell leaders of the U.N. climate conference, known as COP31, scheduled Nov. 9-20.

The “moment of truth” message weighs so heavily that the Secretary-General used the phrase three times in 20 minutes during a recent exclusive interview with The Associated Press from his 38th floor conference room at U.N. headquarters. He discussed his one last push in the fight against climate change and a ten-year tenure where he became one of the most visible advocates urging often recalcitrant countries to do more to reduce their emissions of heat-trapping gases.

One of the most difficult days

The gravity of global warming reality also weighs heavily as he recalled his personal climate moment of truth. It was, he said, “one of the most difficult days of my life.”

It came last year when he consulted with scientists before a major speech on climate. As he had for nine years, Guterres was going to insist that the 2015 Paris Agreement's main goal — limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) since pre-industrial times — was still alive. He was going to say the world needs to do far more to keep below that threshold, and that it was doable.

“Scientists told me you cannot say that because that's no longer true,” said Guterres, an engineer before his political career. Too much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, the result of burning fossil fuels, had been released into the atmosphere.

“That was an enormous shock for me,” he said. Now the U.N. is trying to limit how much past that threshold the world heads.

It felt like a failure, Guterres said.

“But it's not the world that's failed, it's the political leadership that's failed,” Guterres said. Protecting the planet, he said, requires a long-term strategic view. Yet in many political systems “there is no strategic view. And policies change frequently, not allowing the kind of constant determined investment that is necessary," Guterres said.

He pointed to his tenure as Portugal's prime minister in the late 1990s to show it's possible to invest long term in a greener future. He added that a worldwide boom in wind and solar power as cheaper alternatives to fossil fuels gives him hope.

With wars raging in Ukraine and Iran and worries about artificial intelligence — which he also tried to rally world leaders around — there are a lot of threats out there, Guterres said.

“The problem is that all these things are getting combined,” Guterres said, noting the huge electricity and water consumption and carbon emissions of AI.

War-related energy shocks show that relying on fossil fuels is a fundamental security problem, he said.

Warning of a disaster that then came

Three years ago, Guterres toured the highest peaks of Nepal, warning of a future with swollen glacier-fed lakes bursting and devastating floods and landslides.

“I am here today to cry out from the rooftop of the world: Stop the madness,” Guterres said in 2023. “The glaciers are retreating, but we cannot,” he said. “We must end the fossil fuel age.”

“Unfortunately they came sooner than what I expected,” he recalled in the interview. Floods in August killed more than 1,400 people with another 5,600 missing. Scientists said climate change played a role in the disasters.

Guterres said someone needs to pay to help the victims of climate change, who often didn't cause the problem.

“Fossil fuel companies are making huge profits and obviously those windfall profits should be taxed and those taxes should be applied in supporting the countries that are having the more dramatic impacts of climate change," Guterres said.

Talking earlier this month with a science team on a drifting platform in the middle of the Arctic Ocean, Guterres mentioned that his trip to Mount Everest and chats with researchers changed him. He said the conversations created "a sense of fury in relation to those who go on, if not denying, at least refusing to take the measures that are necessary to stop this madness.”

Praised as a climate champion despite limitations

"António Guterres has consistently been eloquent, forceful and right on target in all of his many statements and initiatives to address the climate crisis," former U.S. Vice President Al Gore said. “He’s been so active on this issue because he understands clearly that it is the greatest challenge facing humanity.”

European Climate Foundation CEO Laurence Tubiana, who presided over the negotiations that resulted in the Paris Agreement, said Guterres “has done what he could, even pushing the ball much, much farther than any other SG, to the point that he may have been represented in a very adversarial context.”

Because nations don't have to do what the U.N. or its leaders ask and superpowers have veto authority, Guterres said his position as secretary-general “has no real power. We have not much money you know. But there is one thing we have: A voice."

That's why he simply has three words of advice to whoever succeeds him: “Tell the truth.” The U.N. Security Council is still deciding on who will be the next secretary-general.

The one message Guterres said he wants the public to remember on climate change: “Take it seriously because it is an existential threat. And the first thing we need to fight is for our own lives.”

NICE VIEW 👌 You’re looking straight down the core of our nation’s oldest nuclear power plant – Nine Mile Point in Oswego, NY. This was taken during a previous refueling outage that typically happens every 18-to-24 months at plants across the country. You can tell straight away that this is a boiling water reactor due to the number of assemblies and their checkerboard loading pattern. The shiny squares are the tops of fresh fuel assemblies that are being loaded into the core for the first time. The darker ones are irradiated fuel bundles that have already been through at least one fuel cycle and typically remain in the core for 3-to-5 years. The blue glow you see is coming from the irradiated fuel assemblies and is caused by a phenomenon known as Cherenkov radiation. It happens when electrically charged particles travel faster than the speed of light in that same medium, which in this case is water. The refueling bridge above the core travels back and forth between the fuel pool and the core to swap out old fuel and reposition the existing assemblies to maximize the efficiency of the reactor. 🎥: Constellation

NUCLEAR 101 (Nuclear Science Week Edition!) ⚛️: The sodium-cooled fast reactor uses liquid metal (sodium) as a coolant instead of water that is typically used in U.S. commercial power plants. This allows the coolant to operate at higher temperatures and lower pressures than current reactors—improving the efficiency of the system. Fast reactors use fast-moving neutrons that could allow them to operate on both fissile material and used fuel from current reactors to produce electricity.

text:
Overall, nationwide ballot measures will provide about $31 billion in transit funding, said Jessica Grennan, executive director of the APTA Center for Transportation Excellence, a project of the American Public Transportation Association, in a post-election webinar Nov. 5.

“Transit has been and remains popular” regardless of demographics or political makeup of a region, she said, noting that the message of transit being key to less congestion, more job opportunities and better connections was key.

Ward McCarragher, APTA vice president for government affairs and advocacy, said that despite the incoming Democratic congressional majority, bipartisanship remains key. Noting that only four House and 10 Senate Republicans in 2020 supported the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act IIJA, “'just reauthorize it’ isn’t an effective message." he said, emphasizing that transit’s role in increasing affordability for Americans will be more effective.

APTA legislative goals include restoring Inflation Reduction Act energy tax credits, which involve clean energy transit, and rescinding Trump administration tariffs.

Webinar panelists emphasized lessons learned from previous failed ballot measures—engage stakeholders, build a coalition and keep the message consistent, transparent and focused.

Bob Powers, general manager of Bay Area Rapid Transit, said it conveyed to voters what service would look like if Proposition RTM did not pass, and emphasized that its priorities were what riders want—safety, on-time performance and cleanliness. “I put out an alternative service plan that was crystal-clear,” he said. Without the funding, stations and route segments would close, and remaining service would be curtailed.

Voters passed the measure with 62% support. A 14-year sales tax will inject $14 billion for that system as well as for Caltrain, AC Transit and Muni.

Andrew Fremier, executive director of the Bay Area Metropolitan Transportation Commission, noted that “we convened a broad set of stakeholders to tell us what message would work” for Stronger Muni For All, a 15-year parcel tax proposition that funds $2.4 billion to close the agency operations budget gap and improve service. The agency will conduct regular financial efficiency reviews. “We can’t just go back to voters time and time again” and ask for more taxes, he said.

The measure passed with 72% of the vote.

Julie Kirshbaum, Director of Transportation for the San Francisco Metropolitan Transportation Association, said “it took a huge coalition that understood the importance of transit.” Passage creates “a mandate to continue to invest in what customers care about: safety, cleanliness and reliability.”

Ron Mitchum, executive director of the Charleston [S.C} Area Regional Transportation Authority, also emphasized stakeholder engagement, which was key to passage of a 25-year, half-cent sales tax that will provide $860-million for transit. The rest of the $4.25 billion expected revenue will fund highways and green spaces.

The agency emphasized interconnection of transit systems with highways and green spaces, noting that highway flood mitigation projects will also reduce flood disruptions to transit routes and that transit projects can result in acquisitions of land that could become green space. “We have competing interests but have learned to come together, and encourage people to understand how we help each other,” he said.

On the federal level, Ward noted that highway and transit programs would shut if Congress does not take some action by Dec. 12. “We don’t know how [the outgoing Congress] will approach December,” he said, although “a bipartisan goal is to finish full-year bills while this Congress is still in place.”

title: The Cop31 climate summit is betting on electrification – but still needs a plan to ditch fossil fuels
description:
Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels.
Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply.
It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021.
At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda.
This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels?
text:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, will get underway in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9. One of its key objectives is to boost electrification across the global economy – replacing petrol and diesel vehicles, gas boilers and some industrial processes that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives.

The summit’s host, Turkey, has set a target of 35% of energy demand being met by electricity by 2035, up from around 20% today. Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels.

Without doubt, electrification is essential to curtailing greenhouse gas emissions, and is already gathering pace. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has declared we are living in the “age of electricity”, and if stated policy pledges hold, global electrification rates will hit 31% by 2050. The Cop31’s focus on electrification hopes to build upon and accelerate this existing trend.

But electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain: the continued expansion of fossil fuel production, and growing geopolitical competition over clean technologies where the latter is increasingly shaping governments’ climate and energy policies, as they struggle to compete with dominant “electrostates” such as China.

Silence on supply

The Australian climate minister and Cop31’s president of negotiations has described electrification and fossil fuel reduction as “different sides of the same coin”. But they are not interchangeable. Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply.

By 2030, governments are planning to produce more than double the amount of fossil fuels than would be consistent with limiting warning to 1.5°C. More concerning is that this assessment was made before the conflict and disruption in the Middle East, which has caused the US, Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada and other fossil fuel producers to increase output in the name of energy security. The UK, meanwhile, has approved the Jackdaw gasfield in a purported bid to protect jobs and keep homes warm.

The 35-by-35 target is also silent on where that additional electricity will come from. After all, a country could in theory increase its rate of electrification by burning more fossil fuels (imagine a country where every car was electric, but all that electricity came from coal).

A genuine energy transition

What’s needed is the two-pronged approach of electrifying economies while simultaneously phasing out fossil fuels and reducing their supply. This will ensure capital is reallocated to renewable energy for electrification. Governments can do this nationally or through international initiatives such as the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance, the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and the Cop-adjacent conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

Skirting the fossil fuel issue is nothing new at these summits. It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021. And even then it only passed with calls to “phasedown” unabated coal power and phase-out “inefficient” fossil fuel subsidies.

At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda. Brazil has published an extensive voluntary “roadmap” to guide governments’ phase-out efforts, but this sits outside the formal negotiations and lacks timelines.

This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels?

Just electrify everything

Even growing demand for electricity does not guarantee a clean energy transition. The data centre boom in the US and beyond, for instance, is driving the use of gas and coal to generate electricity. The International Gas Union, a lobby group for natural gas producers, is explicitly positioning gas as a way to meet growing demand from data centres and AI.

Increasing electrification looks relatively straightforward: just encourage more renewable energy production and electric vehicles. Yet, for most of the world, this would mean overcoming security and trade tensions with China, whose dominance in clean technologies, manufacturing and rare earth processing makes it a lynchpin electrostate in a world hoping to electrify everything.

China’s dominance is near total. For the component materials of solar panels, in 2024 China controlled 93% of global polysilicon processing, 97% of wafer manufacturing – making the thin slices of silicon that form the basis of solar panels – 92% of solar cell manufacturing and 86% of solar module production. It also produced more than 80% of electric vehicle batteries in 2025. According to the IEA, China is dominant across 19 of 20 energy-related strategic minerals, averaging over 70% of processing control. Achieving global electrification targets will therefore require continued access to Chinese technologies, products and raw materials.

This runs counter to almost two decades of western policy aimed at protecting domestic industries from Chinese competition and restricting China’s technological development, most notably with semi-conductors. While these efforts have largely failed to contain Chinese innovation, an overreliance on Chinese clean technologies is increasingly seen as a “serious risk” to Europe’s economic and national security. European governments have responded with tariffs and restrictions on Chinese imports and investments, while seeking to build up their own manufacturing capacity.

Governments face a difficult dilemma. Opening their economies further to Chinese technologies could mean unpicking trade protections developed over years and create new dependencies, while refusing to cooperate with China risks slowing electrification and may even drive some governments to abandon climate and energy policies altogether because they cannot compete.

While the drive towards electrification at Cop31 is to be welcomed, it cannot be a substitute for the harder political task of securing binding commitments to phase out fossil fuels, fast and fairly.

title: New Yorkers Urge Congress to Reject Environmental Rollbacks in Senate Permitting Bill
description:
In a new letter to Congress, New Yorkers raise concerns that the Senate permitting reform deal would weaken longstanding safeguards under the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act, National Environmental Policy Act, and other bedrock environmental laws.
The Endangered Species Act, supported by 84% of Americans across political ideology, is the nation’s strongest, most effective law for preventing extinction and protecting the natural systems all life depends on.
Current Senate Majority Leader Thune of South Dakota scheduled the Senate permitting reform deal for a vote on November 9, bypassing typical hearing and markup processes that allow for consideration and expert review.
Ahead of the vote, Democrat House Leader Jeffries, representative for New York’s 8th Congressional district and the presumptive Speaker of the House for the new Congress, said he opposes passing the Senate permitting reform deal into law.
Senate Minority Leader Schumer, a New York senator and presumptive Senate Majority Leader in the new Congress, has not indicated his position on the deal.
text:
New Yorkers from across the state are calling on Congress to reject sweeping environmental rollbacks in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (S. 5653), warning that the legislation would weaken protections for endangered wildlife, clean water, healthy ecosystems, and communities across New York.

From the Adirondacks and Catskills to New York City, Long Island, Niagara Falls, and the shores of Lake America, New York’s forests, rivers, wetlands, beaches, and estuaries are home to some of the nation’s most vulnerable wildlife. The federally threatened piping plover, an important indicator of a healthy ecosystem, nests along beaches in Suffolk, Nassau, and Queens counties, sharing these coastal ecosystems with species including black skimmers, American oystercatchers, terns, and federally threatened seabeach amaranth. New York’s waterways also provide habitat for federally protected Atlantic and shortnose sturgeon and bog turtles. These vulnerable species and landscapes are part of New York’s heritage and support recreation, fisheries, tourism, coastal resilience, and communities statewide.

In a new letter to Congress, New Yorkers raise concerns that the Senate permitting reform deal would weaken longstanding safeguards under the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act, National Environmental Policy Act, and other bedrock environmental laws. While the Senate permitting reform deal has been presented as an effort to modernize interstate transmission permitting, the letter urges Congress to ensure that efforts to build needed infrastructure and energy projects do not come at the expense of science-based wildlife protections, clean water, or the public’s ability to participate in decisions affecting their communities.

“The Endangered Species Act is America’s strongest, most effective law for preventing extinction, and its science-based protections have made a real difference for wildlife and the places we all depend on,” said Susan Holmes, executive director of the Endangered Species Coalition. “New Yorkers know that we do not have to choose between responsible development and protecting clean water, healthy ecosystems, and wildlife for future generations. Congress should defend these safeguards while working toward solutions that allow communities and wildlife to thrive.”

The letter highlights concerns about provisions in the Senate permitting reform deal that could weaken some of the Endangered Species Act’s most important safeguards, including requirements that decisions be grounded in the best available science, removing federal agencies from review of industry impacts on threatened and endangered species and moving that authority to state agencies, and access to public accountability through the courts.

“We need a consistent and committed application of the Endangered Species Act across all states wherever and whenever imperiled species like piping plovers are found,” said Chris Allieri, executive director, NYC Plover Project. “The ESA is the federal law of the land and was never meant to be something left to state agencies, many of which are cash-strapped and at the whim of the political winds across state capitols and legislatures from Bismarck to Tallahassee. If this dangerous bill becomes law, states could assume all ESA consultations, not only those for clean energy, but any industry activity – oil and gas leases, data centers, timber sales, beach dredging, and space exploration.”

The Endangered Species Coalition and New York signers are urging members of Congress to reject the Senate permitting reform deal and uphold the bedrock environmental laws’ (e.g., ESA, Clean Water Act, and NEPA) science-based framework to protect vulnerable species and habitats that are deeply connected to our public health, economy, and society.

The Endangered Species Act, supported by 84% of Americans across political ideology, is the nation’s strongest, most effective law for preventing extinction and protecting the natural systems all life depends on. The law has prevented extinction for 99% of the species it protects.

Current Senate Majority Leader Thune of South Dakota scheduled the Senate permitting reform deal for a vote on November 9, bypassing typical hearing and markup processes that allow for consideration and expert review. Ahead of the vote, Democrat House Leader Jeffries, representative for New York’s 8th Congressional district and the presumptive Speaker of the House for the new Congress, said he opposes passing the Senate permitting reform deal into law. Senate Minority Leader Schumer, a New York senator and presumptive Senate Majority Leader in the new Congress, has not indicated his position on the deal.

text:
The recent midterm elections brought historic voter turnout in the midst of rising costs of gas, groceries, and energy.

In the Mountain West, residents saw a historically dry summer and severe wildfire conditions, followed by an abnormally wet fall and destructive floods in the Four Corners region this autumn.

Max Boykoff is a faculty member in environmental studies at the University of Colorado Boulder. He’s also director of the SPIKE Center for Sustainability Education, and a fellow in the Cooperative Institute for Research and Environmental Sciences. He says concerns about human-caused climate change were on the ballot, even if those words weren’t explicitly used on the campaign trail.

Rocky Mountain Community Radio’s Caroline Llanes spoke with Boykoff to break down the election results.

Editor’s note: this transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

Caroline Llanes: Let's start off by looking at the national picture. Obviously, the headlines were this “blue tsunami,” this really stunning rebuke of the GOP and the Trump administration's policies. Where do you see climate and environmental issues playing into that, if at all?

Max Boykoff: Yeah, I think it would be overreaching to say that this was a green wave. I think that the questions that were really raised in a lot of what I'm hearing about early voter turnout and some of the issues that are important to them, cross several different important issues. Could we connect the dots back to the considerations around climate, environment, sustainability? Definitely. But I think that in voters' minds themselves, at least what I've been picking up on and learning, that climate, environment, sustainability are within this larger turnout.

So the blue tsunami, there's lots of different synonyms that we could think of to describe what was a really strong perspective and voice collectively from voters in this country that did think about and speak to many important issues. I've been taking a look at a few others' takes on this and just thinking about affordability as it relates back to carbon-based fuels, energy sources, that affordability then can be seen as a climate/environment/sustainability set of questions.

But that may not have been directly on voters' minds as they were going to the polls.

Llanes: Let's zoom in a little bit to some of the election results here in Colorado. We had some climate-related issues on the ballot this year; I'm wondering what you make of some of those results.

Boykoff: Picking up on Amendment 82, thinking about the right to natural gas, I mean, it was resoundingly a “no.” And so that's very interesting, and I think that those are data points about collective voice. But at the same time, with the ballot measure on passenger rail, that was a resounding “yes.” And so in these times of affordability challenges at the forefront, of costs of prices and such, that a decision collectively to move forward with funding passenger rail expansion is a signal from the Colorado voters.

Llanes: Thinking about the candidate piece of things, did you see climate coming up for candidates in Colorado races?

Boykoff: Yeah, I think that the kinds of conversations that candidates forge with their constituents can be really different: if you're having a conversation in Greeley, if you're having a conversation in Grand Junction, if you're having a conversation in Boulder, Colorado. And so where climate change, environment, sustainability explicitly show up are important to a certain extent, that we don't want to shy away from those challenges, but they can also be discussed in other ways.

And so, you know, if I'm living out in Greeley and I'm paying a lot for gas and paying a lot for diesel in the business that I'm running, that can be seen as a conversation relating to those topics, we could talk about it in those terms. If we're talking in Grand Junction about high food prices and the cost of our groceries, we can have that conversation and, importantly, have that resonance with folks there. But, are we explicit about climate change, environment sustainability? You know, maybe that comes a bit later in these ongoing conversations.

Overall, as a state, if we're talking about utilities and the cost of utilities, those are discussions that are resonant here in Boulder, Colorado, where I am and across the state. But the linkages there in a place like— as I know the constituents in Boulder can make those connections much more readily and the candidates then choose to do that because they know that that's a connection that's on voters' minds in those places.

Llanes: So obviously a big statement from voters this election, and we're going to have a new Congress, a big change in the political makeup in the House and the Senate. Do you see this new Congress being able to make progress on climate issues, or maybe being able to undo some of the rollbacks on climate policy that we've seen in the past couple of years?

Boykoff: I think that's a great set of questions. I think that this is a new moment, as, you know, a lot of people have indicated, record turnout overall, record turnout in those who have said in the exit polling that they care about climate change (and the) environment. Those voters have, in those exit polls—some of the early returns, some of the early voting polls—have said that voters want their political leaders to talk about climate change and the environment more, and not less.

There's also indications that voters worry about corruption, worry about giveaways to the fossil fuel industry, and the costs of that instead of stronger regulations. And so, with those indications that where climate-related issues are— the ways in which we're moving about and living and meeting our livelihood needs, candidates need to talk about them more, and some of the early voting exit polls are indicating that that was a part of voters' decision making.” That comes from the Environmental Voter Project, which has got some really good insights about how to make sense of what's just happened.

Going forward then, to your, the other part, another part of your question is that as we move forward, we are much more capably set to address the climate, environment, and sustainability. That's not about partisanship, necessarily. It doesn't have to be. It's about evaluating candidates—now elected officials’—priorities as they relate to these intersecting sets of issues on voters' minds, of challenges in their daily lives. And so we're seeing new capacity that is collective. Colorado has maybe gone more strong in those directions, but we see it in Arizona and Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, where I'm from.

We're seeing that those who have expressed their interest in addressing these issues are now in these elected positions, and so it gives overall, at a national level, opportunities to then address things in Congress. You had asked about that: their spring budget resolution that's coming, the fall appropriations bills that are coming, there's going to be a different stance than there was just in the previous Congress.

Llanes: After the results of this election, how are you thinking about how climate is going to play a role in future elections?

Boykoff: On my mind is thinking about new voters, thinking about university-age students that I interact with, that I teach here at the University of Colorado Boulder, and how they're growing into this world and how they're experiencing climate change. They're experiencing environmental challenges. They're experiencing where they sit within these spaces of decision making around sustainability and unsustainability. And so as we're seeing this, what's being called the “blue wave” now, and as we're seeing these changes in voter turnout in voter decision making, on the horizon is a whole new generation of decision makers.

I was born into a world where it wasn't until high school into college that I really started to get my head around climate change and environment. Young people that are voting today, my own kids that are in their 20s, are now making these voting decisions because they've been born into a world where this has already been part of a conversation. They may have had experiences, they may have a lot of emotions around their anxieties about moving into a world as an adult. And so what we're seeing as a “blue wave” now may be a part of something bigger that we're going to continue to see as the next election cycles come forward.

Llanes: Well, Max, thank you so much for taking the time to talk with Rocky Mountain Community Radio.

Boykoff: You bet.

text:
Four refining lines and 189 jobs are planned at the former RCA plant.

To help expand domestic refining of rare earths and other critical minerals, ReElement Technologies Corp.'s Marion, Indiana, project is being supported by a $46 million allocation under the federal New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) program.

Established to bring metal-refining technology developed at Purdue University into commercial use, Indiana-based ReElement Technologies has focused on recovering rare earths and other critical minerals from mined concentrates, recycled materials, and industrial byproducts.

Using a separation method widely employed in pharmaceutical manufacturing, the company developed modular production lines that could be expanded as suitable feedstocks became available and customer demand increased, allowing refining capacity to grow without requiring large-scale investments all at once.

Having developed and tested its refining process at a smaller commercial qualification facility in Noblesville, Indiana, ReElement selected the former RCA-Thomson electronics plant in Marion for its first large-scale refinery in 2023, acquiring an industrial campus covering roughly 17 hectares (42 acres).

Outlined in June, the first phase of development called for four production lines – separate systems for germanium, gallium, light rare earth elements, and heavy rare earths – with ReElement projecting combined annual refining capacity of more than 16,000 metric tons once all lines were commissioned.

Supporting that expansion, the U.S. Department of War in July announced a $25 million investment intended to help pay for equipment, installation, and working capital as ReElement increased its ability to refine rare earths and other defense-related critical minerals.

Progress continued in August, when the company commissioned a commercial-scale germanium production column at Marion and later received an air permit covering the installation, commissioning, and operation of all four planned refining lines.

Now, the company's development at Marion is being supported by NMTC, a program administered by the U.S. Treasury's Community Development Financial Institutions Fund that encourages private investment in eligible low-income communities by awarding tax-credit allocations to specialized financial organizations known as Community Development Entities.

Those organizations raise capital from private investors, who receive federal tax credits, and direct the money into qualifying businesses.

Under the November arrangement, the $46 million allocation supported tax-credit-backed financing for equipment and working capital during Marion's first phase, rather than representing a direct cash grant of that amount to ReElement.

By using the financing alongside other capital sources, the company sought to reduce funding costs and retain flexibility without issuing additional shares.

Alongside the planned equipment investment, the first phase was expected to create 189 advanced manufacturing jobs in Marion, with approximately 90% of those positions expected to be accessible to workers holding a high school diploma.

To prepare workers for those jobs, a $2.1 million commitment to workforce training and development is intended to support career pathways that could include apprenticeships, two-year degree programs, and advanced technical certifications.

"Building resilient U.S. critical-mineral supply chains requires disciplined investment in both advanced refining capacity and the people who will operate it," said ReElement CFO Kirk Taylor. "This NMTC-supported financing demonstrates how we are pursuing capital-efficient, non-dilutive funding to expand our domestic manufacturing platform while supporting meaningful job creation, competitive wages, and accessible pathways to long-term careers in Marion."

text:
A natural gas utility in Vermont struck a first-in-the-nation deal that will soon be saving customers money by turning to geothermal energy.

Vermont Gas launched the state’s “first community-scale geothermal project,” something the company’s CEO called one of the best solutions for lowering energy costs and one that many homeowners across the country hope to see in other areas.

These systems can indeed provide serious savings. A case study published by the DoE on an apartment complex in New York found that its geothermal heat pumps helped reduce energy costs by 40.7% across the 72-unit site.

Opened back in 2016, residents have seen average annual cost savings of approximately $24,000 per year, by now reaching a staggering quarter-million dollars in savings.

To that end, Vermont Gas has partnered with geothermal developer Dandelion Energy to install super efficient geothermal heating and cooling to the 44-unit Riggs Meadow affordable housing development in Hinesburg.

Drilling down into heated pockets of water below the Earth will begin in early 2027, while residents will be able to move in by year’s end.

The more high-profile geothermal installations in the US typically power large infrastructure, like Fervo Energy’s Corsac Station that ultimately serves Google-owned data centers. Yet others see the technology as ideal for utilities in modest-income housing.

In Detroit’s Virginia Park, the 27-unit Merrill Place II housing development for low and middle-income earners was designed with a geothermal heating and cooling system that, according to a release from the Mayor’s office, will make these utilities “free.”

“Our tenants are not billed separately for heating and cooling, which removes one of the most unpredictable and burdensome household expenses,” explained Sauda Ahmad-Green, lead developer on the project.

“That stability matters. It allows families to plan, to breathe a little easier, and to focus on building their futures instead of worrying about utility spikes.”

According to Dandelion Energy’s CEO Dan Yates, the Riggs Meadow development will be the first in the country where a utility—in this case natural gas—will directly own the geothermal installations, which they will operate as if they were gas lines.

GEOTHERMAL DEVELOPMENTS: UK’s First Geothermal Power Plant Begins Using Underground Heat to Power 10K Homes

This not only saves the builder the cost of putting the gas lines in, but allows Dandelion to leverage Vermont Gas’ much more favorable financing conditions to fund the project.

On a more technical level, the project will also provide individual loops—that is, a network of buried pipes that transfers heat between a building and the ground—to each individual house rather than together as a single system.

It will allow more frugal residents to take their energy savings to the next level, rather than being on the hook for their neighbors’ energy consumption. Single-system installations apparently dominated the early geothermal utility landscape, but are often far too expensive for community-level projects.

“Vermont Gas is really breaking ground here in taking a different approach to implementation of these systems,” Yates said in an interview with Engineering News Record.

GEOTHERMAL POWER: Giant 2-GW Geothermal Project in Utah Gains Federal Approval

Unlike geothermal electricity, geothermal heating and cooling require much shallower boreholes which can be managed in residential areas without much trouble. For instance, the New York apartment complex needed holes a mere 250 feet down.

“As Vermont looks to rapidly build housing to meet demand, our teams are eager to incorporate geothermal into our product portfolio to give more choices to home builders and customers,” said Neale Lunderville, president and CEO of Vermont Gas.

text:
In recent months, thousands of Americans have flooded municipal government buildings to testify against the construction of AI data centers in their communities.

According to a May 2026 Gallup poll, 7 out of 10 people oppose the construction of data centers in their local area, citing grave concerns over their environmental impact, water consumption, noise, and potential health risks. A Blue Rose Research poll from December 2025 found that Americans would rather live near prisons or nuclear power plants than data centers.

“Overcoming this opposition stands as a major hurdle in the expansion of AI computing,” noted Gallup Senior Editor Jeffrey M. Jones. “The intensity of opposition means that proposed data centers are likely to spur grassroots activism from local residents as well as legal challenges.”

Many of those challenges have proven successful, as more than 500 jurisdictions have approved moratoriums or bans even before the midterms. That trend was extended during this week’s elections, where data center-related questions appeared on the ballot in 13 states: 40 out of 41 ballot measures placing restrictions on data centers were passed throughout the country.

In many cases, the results were not close: 77 percent of voters in Edgewater, Florida, approved a ban on new data centers, while 82 percent of voters in Alhambra, California, endorsed one. Ohio, which had more data center-related questions on its ballots than any other state, saw voters pass outright bans in 11 municipalities, while another seven approved further regulations on them.

“Tuesday’s election was a historically bad night for the Republican Party,” declared the Boston Globe. “It might have been even worse for big tech and their plans to spend trillions of dollars building AI data centers.”

Anger over data centers certainly wasn’t limited to local ballot questions. Polling suggests that it helped determine the results of major races amid the Democratic Party’s historic “blue wave.” Exit polling from NBC News reveals that 56 percent of voters identified data centers and AI as a “crucial or major factor” in their vote.

Chief among these contests was the Ohio Senate race, where incumbent Republican Sen. John Husted was ousted by Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Husted was backed by powerful tech giants like Oracle’s Larry Ellison and Safra Catz; and a cryptocurrency PAC, funded by companies like Coinbase, spent $55 million trying to stomp out Brown’s challenge.

The Brown campaign consistently highlighted these ties during the campaign, running ads that referred to Husted as “the face of data centers in Ohio” and bankrolling billboards that directed voters to a website which details how Husted is the “chief reason” that 226 data centers exist in the state.

An internal National Republican Senatorial Committee memo, originally reported on by Axios, showed that Brown’s attacks were working and causing Republican anxiety over not just the Ohio race, but the GOP’s relationship with data centers more broadly.

“More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” it read. “If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”

In Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned on a data center moratorium, ousted Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott. Abbott embraced guardrails on the facilities leading up to the election, but for years he welcomed their construction in the state and, in 2025, he declared Texas to be the “epicenter of AI development.”

“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist who works on AI, told WIRED.

Tech magnate and GOP mega-donor Elon Musk dumped $224 million into the Texas elections in a failed effort to keep it red. After the Democrats prevailed, Musk, who had plans to construct multiple data centers across his adopted home state, tweeted: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

Immediately after the election, Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) released a statement calling on incoming House members to make AI regulation a top priority and for AI company CEOs to testify before the chamber.

“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” said Casar.

Georgia’s Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms and Ohio’s Governor-elect Amy Acton have also endorsed moratoriums, and Annie Andrews’s victory in South Carolina is another blow to the AI industry, which spent heavily in support of short-time incumbent Sen. Darline Graham.

Like Flock cameras and support for Israel, data centers are an issue that cuts across party lines and upends our perception of partisanship. In May 2026, Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed SB 484, which “protects ratepayers, the environment, and local communities from harm caused by hyperscale data centers.”

“These are much-needed protections for taxpayers and our natural resources,” said DeSantis at the time.

Even President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly touted the benefits of data centers, has modified his stance in recent months, seemingly aware that much of his base is skeptical about further construction.

In a Truth Social post days before the election, Trump called on AI companies to pay impacted communities a “dividend” in exchange for a data center’s construction.

“I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck,” claimed the president, who provided no proof that this has ever happened.

Amid the growing resistance, tech companies have also shifted their approach.

Amazon has pledged to improve the environmental rating of its backup data center generators and to disclose more information about their water use. OpenAI has rebranded its data centers as “compute campuses.” Companies like Google have announced that they will stop requiring government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements in an effort to increase transparency within communities.

Sam Burleigh, who helped found an organization aimed at stopping an Amazon-backed data center project in Pennsylvania, told the Associated Press that such efforts are merely “propaganda.”

title: Texas Matters: The State Board of Education flips. Will a blue Texas go green? And how ...
description:
The election results from Tuesday, Nov. 3, just kept getting more remarkable for Texas Democrats this week.
Democrats now appear poised to take control of the Texas State Board of Education.
The State Board of Education determines the curriculum standards for Texas public schools.
It approves instructional materials, helps oversee charter schools and manages billions of dollars in public education investments.
Now, with a possible Democratic majority, Texas could be entering a new era in public education.
text:
The election results from Tuesday, Nov. 3, just kept getting more remarkable for Texas Democrats this week.

First came the news that James Talarico had won the U.S. Senate race, ending more than three decades of Republican victories for that seat.

Then Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott, and Vikki Goodwin unseated Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick.

And the Democratic victories continued down the ballot — with Democrats winning the races for attorney general, comptroller, land commissioner, agriculture commissioner and railroad commissioner.

Then came another historic development. Democrats won control of the Texas House of Representatives for the first time since 2002 — although Republicans retained their majority in the state Senate.

But there was another major political shift that received far less attention on election night — and it could have profound consequences for what millions of Texas children learn in public schools.

Democrats now appear poised to take control of the Texas State Board of Education.

Republicans entered the election holding 11 of the board's 15 seats, with Democrats holding just four. But after Tuesday's voting, Democrats are on track to hold an eight-to-seven majority. One exceptionally close race still faces the possibility of a recount.

It would be the first Democratic majority on the board in more than 30 years.

And this is no small matter.

The State Board of Education determines the curriculum standards for Texas public schools. It decides what students are expected to learn about American history, slavery, civil rights, science and religion. It approves instructional materials, helps oversee charter schools and manages billions of dollars in public education investments.

For years, the Republican-controlled board has been at the center of national controversies over how history is taught, the role of Christianity in public education and whether political ideology is influencing classroom instruction.

Now, with a possible Democratic majority, Texas could be entering a new era in public education.

But how much can actually change? Could controversial curriculum decisions be reversed? And what would a Democratic-controlled board mean for students, teachers and parents?

Joining us to discuss this historic election and what comes next is Felicia Martin, executive director of the Texas Freedom Network, an organization that has closely monitored the State Board of Education and advocated for accurate, inclusive public school curricula.

Does a blue Texas mean a green Texas?

Does turning Texas blue mean Texas will go green?

For more than three decades, Texas has been governed by Republicans who have largely championed the oil and gas industry, resisted tougher environmental regulations, and made expanding fossil fuel production a central part of the state's economic policy.

But the election of Nov. 3 has dramatically changed the political landscape.

For environmental advocates, this could be a once-in-a-generation opportunity to change how Texas protects its air, water, land and communities.

And the challenges are enormous.

Texas is the nation's leading producer of oil and natural gas. It's also a national leader in wind and solar energy. The state faces worsening drought, extreme heat, increasingly destructive floods, industrial pollution and growing demands on its electricity grid and water supplies from the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence data centers.

For years, environmental organizations have accused Texas regulators of putting corporate profits ahead of public health and allowing polluters to operate with inadequate oversight.

Now those organizations are demanding action.

The Sierra Club and more than a dozen other Texas organizations have issued a joint statement calling on the incoming Democratic leadership to build a cleaner energy economy, hold polluting industries accountable, lower utility bills and restore local communities' ability to influence decisions that affect their health and environment.

But will a change in political leadership actually produce a fundamental change in environmental policy? Can Texas remain an energy powerhouse while becoming a national leader in environmental protection? And how much can Democrats accomplish with Republicans still controlling the state Senate?

Joining us to discuss this historic opportunity — and the challenges ahead — is David Cortez, director of the Sierra Club's Lone Star Chapter.

Elon Musk loses election

Elon Musk wasn't on the ballot Tuesday, but he may have been one of the biggest losers in the election.

The world's richest man poured hundreds of millions of dollars into electing Republicans, including candidates here in Texas. But despite his enormous wealth and political influence, voters delivered a sweeping rejection of many of the candidates he supported.

And that outcome didn't happen without a fight.

Grassroots organizations across Texas worked to educate voters about Musk's political spending, his influence over government, and the policies they say benefit billionaires at the expense of working people.

One of those organizations is VOCAL-TX, which has been organizing communities and raising awareness about the growing political power of Musk and other wealthy tech executives.

Now, with the election over, VOCAL-TX is holding an election after-party in Austin this Saturday to celebrate what organizers see as a rejection of Musk's attempt to buy political influence.

But did voters really reject Elon Musk? And what happens to his political power in Texas now that Democrats are preparing to take control of state government?

Joining us to talk about that is Paulette Soltani, an organizer with VOCAL-TX.

text:
AUSTIN, Texas — It looks like the end of the road for the Cybertruck.

Elon Musk said Friday that Tesla will wind down production of the vehicle at its factory in Austin, Texas, the only plant that makes the truck.

The change will start "around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk, Tesla's CEO, posted on his social media platform X.

It wasn't immediately clear if Tesla plans to switch Cybertruck production to another factory or phase it out entirely, though the Cybertruck's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest that the vehicle had reached its end.

"Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Morrill posted on X.

The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk, who has often described the Cybertruck as his favorite vehicle. On Tuesday, he saw the nearly $500 million in campaign contributions he made in the midterm elections go for naught amid a resounding defeat for Republican candidates.

The subsequent sell-off in AI stocks battered shares of Tesla and SpaceX, his two public companies, both of which fell more than 12% in the first two days of trading since the midterms. That has decreased Musk's net worth by $113 billion, according to Bloomberg's Billionaires Index, although he is still by far the richest person on the planet. That two-day drop alone is nearly the net worth of Microsoft founder Bill Gates, whose holdings equal $123 billion.

Fans of Tesla and Musk loved the Cybertruck's distinctive design. But its social media critics thought otherwise, referring to it as "dumpster chic," and the vehicle was ultimately an underperformer.

At Tesla's 2023 shareholder meeting, Musk said that his "reasonable guess" was that Tesla would be making 500,000 Cybertrucks a year. While Tesla has never broken out its sales of the Cybertruck separately, the company has reported sales of "other models" this year at fewer than 37,000. That metric is for cars other than its best-selling Model 3 and Model Y, and includes sales of Tesla's discontinued Model S and Model X.

Tesla has one other auto plant in the United States, in California. Musk halted production of his two most expensive models, the Model S and Model X, at that plant to make room for production of the human robots, Optimus, the company intends to sell.

Musk has made clear that the future of Tesla will be providing rides in the company's still nascent robotaxi service and humanoid robots, not selling electric vehicles. But both ambitious plans have thus far proven to be far more promise than reality.

Musk has said that Tesla would soon be making its Cybercab — a small vehicle with room for only two people and no steering wheel, accelerator or brake pedals — in greater number than all its other vehicles combined. He also promised that the company's robotaxi service would be providing fully autonomous rides to half the country by the end of last year.

However, the service is currently only available in seven cities — four in Texas and three in Florida – which is behind competing services like Alphabet-unit Waymo. Tesla has yet to break out the profits or revenue from the service in its quarterly report, suggesting it may be losing money. And it has proven difficult to get regulatory approval from local governments to allow self-driving vehicles on the roads.

Humanoid robots are also not yet available for sale. Musk said on a recent earnings call that Tesla is still working on some of the technology, such as getting the robots' hands to work.

text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks with leaders of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, May 24, 2023. Photo: Jewish Democratic Council of America via Flickr / CC BY 2.0 / Cropped from Original

(The Center Square) – Despite broad bipartisan support of the U.S. Senate’s permitting reform bill, which aims to expedite energy projects and lower electricity costs, Democratic leadership in the House is now demanding more concessions.

Senate leaders were hoping to hold a vote on the long-awaited Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act during the upcoming lame-duck session, the last eight weeks of the 119th Congress.

The primary purpose of the 417-page bill is to expedite the permitting approval process for energy-related projects – such as natural gas pipelines, drilling and mining, and data center infrastructure – primarily by scaling back environmental and judicial reviews.

Permitting-associated expenses cost manufacturers a cumulative $12.1 billion per year, according to the National Association of Manufacturers. By expediting the timelines that contribute to higher permitting costs, the BAAJA would cut that number by 35%, saving manufacturers $4.2 billion per year, NAM says.

Supporters of BAAJA say it will increase energy supply, reduce Americans’ electric bills, and create more jobs as the country enters a new era of energy demand.

Monumental election wins, however, have galvanized some Democrats to push for changes, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is set to become House speaker in January.

Jeffries said the bill “falls short in several areas,” specifically naming environmental and tribal protections in his post-election comments to Politico.

Jeffries’ remarks echo the concerns of BAAJA-critical organizations, who argue the bill in its current form would trample state and community rights by limiting litigation and local input, erode environmental safeguards, and make it more difficult for states and tribes to oppose federal projects and data centers.

Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., wants lawmakers to hold a hearing on the bill and allow amendments to be introduced before holding a vote.

“House Democrats support, and will deliver, responsible permitting reform. But as Speaker-elect Jeffries said today, and as some of us have said for weeks, we must have a chance to fix the most glaring flaws in BAAJA,” Huffman posted Thursday on social media.

But with Democrats having campaigned largely on affordability promises, some view the results as even more of a reason to pass legislation targeting energy costs as soon as possible, rather than make ultimatums.

“Modernizing our permitting process is an important way to lower utility costs, create good-paying local jobs, and secure our energy future, and we need to get it done,” Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., said in a statement Friday explicitly breaking with Jeffries.

“Standing up for working families means getting this done the right way and ensuring we don't repeat mistakes of the past,” Davids added. “I am working with House and Senate leaders in both parties to fix these provisions so we can pass a bill that lowers everyday costs, respects Tribal nations, and protects our environment.”

Without faster buildout of high-voltage transmission lines, additional power generation facilities, and other energy infrastructure, the U.S. demand for energy will overtake supply within the next ten years, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation.

The Trump administration has been bullish about restoring the country’s nuclear energy sector to its former glory, but growing the country’s nuclear energy capacity raises a new problem – where to source the nuclear fuel to power it.
The geopolitical risks inherent to current nuclear fuel supply chains represent a key and growing concern.
The world’s nuclear energy fuel supply chains are extremely geopolitically fraught.
The country is indeed getting closer to establishing nuclear fuel independence – but it still has a long way to go.
At present, a whopping 93 percent of the United States’ raw uranium for nuclear fuel is coming from foreign markets.
text:
The United States boasts the largest nuclear power production capacity in the world, but decades of insufficient funding and policy support is now posing an existential threat to the ageing sector. In the past decade, the United States has added just one new nuclear power plant to its fleet, while many more plants are drawing close to being decommissioned, at a time when clean, round-the-clock energy production has never been more needed. The Trump administration has been bullish about restoring the country’s nuclear energy sector to its former glory, but growing the country’s nuclear energy capacity raises a new problem – where to source the nuclear fuel to power it.

Countries around the world are racing to build up nuclear power capacity as the artificial intelligence boom places unprecedented strain on global power supplies, the war in Iran sustains volatility in oil and gas markets, and decarbonization deadlines draw nearer. As a result, competition over scarce enriched uranium supplies has ramped up at a rapid pace. As a result, U.S. nuclear energy now “faces fuel supply chain vulnerabilities, with tight uranium supplies, geopolitical risks, and rising costs,” threatening both existing reactors and advanced reactor development, according to a January report from Stanford Energy.

The geopolitical risks inherent to current nuclear fuel supply chains represent a key and growing concern. The world’s nuclear energy fuel supply chains are extremely geopolitically fraught. At present, just five plants in the entire world operate large-scale uranium conversion, and nearly half of global enrichment capacity is controlled by Russia. And if Russia decides to cut the United States off, or vice versa, the alternative could be even worse.

“The West needs more converted uranium than it can process, and cutting off Russian supply could leave its reactors dependent on a single Chinese facility,” an article from the National Interest warned earlier this week.

ADVERTISEMENT

In recent years, leadership in the United States has made considerable inroads toward building up domestic uranium production and conversion capabilities, as it has benefited from being one of the rare forms of energy supported by both the Trump and Biden administrations. Just last month, the National Enrichment Facility, located in Eunice, New Mexico, announced that its planned expansion is ahead of schedule and on budget. Currently, the singular plant converts enough uranium to cover about one-third of U.S. enriched uranium demand, with plans to raise enrichment output by more than 50 percent to reach 7 million separative work units (SWUs) as reactor demand grows.

The country is indeed getting closer to establishing nuclear fuel independence – but it still has a long way to go. And in today’s geopolitical climate, no one knows just how much time we have before a supply chain snag could cause the next global energy crisis. At present, a whopping 93 percent of the United States’ raw uranium for nuclear fuel is coming from foreign markets. If those supply chains dry up, it won’t matter how much uranium the country is capable of enriching.

And the issue is not limited to the United States alone, but to Western nuclear power markets in general. “To keep the lights on in the West every year, the nuclear reactor fleet requires approximately 44,000 metric tons of uranium feedstock. Western supply lines [including the United States, Canada, and France] are estimated to have processing capability of just 34,000 metric tons when fully operational,” the National Interest details. “Traditionally, reactors have relied on Russian or Chinese fuel producers to make up the shortfall, but as global trade corridors constrict and relationships become contentious, over-reliance on Russian or Chinese nuclear fuel could represent a serious national security risk.”

By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead - PBS
description:

text:
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — After a campaign season filled with outrage against artificial intelligence data centers, the midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry's biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown.

Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, and it wasn't among the top issues for most voters. But hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of many candidates, including the Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Nevada and Iowa, many of which are data center hot spots.

Skepticism of data centers, and their impact on electricity prices, often blended with the fight for affordability — a key campaign talking point for Democrats.

In Texas, Clayton Tucker, the first Democrat elected state agriculture commissioner since 1986, said his pledge to fight data center development was critical to his victory. Everywhere he went, he said, ranchers worried that data centers posed an existential threat to their dwindling water supplies.

"You know, there's an old saying around here that 'whiskey's for drinking and water's for fighting,'" Tucker told The Associated Press. "And that's exactly what happened."

Data centers were a persistent bogeyman in attack ads

According to data from AdImpact, campaigns large and small spent more than $380 million on television ads mentioning data centers. Democrats outspent Republicans on the topic by a more than 3-to-1 ratio.

Sweeping wins by Democrats could have far-reaching implications for data centers. Besides taking control of Congress, Democrats flipped at least five governors' offices and took full control of state governments in five more states: Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Nevada and Michigan.

Data Center Watch, a project of AI security consultancy 10a Labs, said it tracked winning candidates for Congress and governorships and found the vast majority had expressed support for stronger regulation or even a moratorium.

Among governors, 32 of the 34 victorious candidates in races where AP called a winner support stronger regulation or restrictions. Twelve of the 34 support bans or moratoriums, it said.

During the campaign, Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley, a Democrat, changed his position under pressure from his Republican opponent to take a harder line against data centers. Initially opposed to any moratorium, Crowley later said he supported one as well as abolishing the state's sales tax exemption for data center operators and developers.

In an interview Thursday with AP, Crowley said he's having discussions now about what he'll propose once he takes office.

In the mix are things like requiring developers to disclose more about their water and energy consumption, ensuring a community supports a project before it can go forward and insulating ratepayers and taxpayers from the energy costs of the projects, Crowley said.

The industry sees a need to build trust

AI giant OpenAI published a framework Thursday enumerating new commitments to the communities where it develops data centers. The company said it was asking federal, state and local policymakers to write "clear rules for how the industry builds."

"Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared," the post said.

An industry association, the Data Center Coalition, echoed the sentiment that developers need to keep trying to build trust with public officials and communities. A coalition official, Dan Diorio, said the industry is aware many midterm winners have vowed to impose a moratorium.

"We should expect them to want to deliver on those promises, but there are going to be real world consequences of that," Diorio said in an interview.

Those consequences, Diorio said, could include host communities missing out on tax revenue or payments from tech companies. Data centers are also driving a broader economic expansion that encourages investment in domestic manufacturing, he said.

Wall Street sees red lights ahead after the election

The election of data center skeptics adds challenges to stock markets riding high on the AI boom.

On Thursday, the Nasdaq, which is full of AI-related and other tech stocks, sank 11% below its all-time high amid worries that data center construction may slow because it's getting costlier to borrow money.

AI data center construction is driving much of the U.S. economy's growth, and any slowdown could have a broader chilling effect.

In an analyst report, Morgan Stanley said decisive results for Democrats carry "greater expectations for data center restrictions" that, under new state regulations, could "split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without."

It singled out Texas' election of Democrat Gina Hinojosa for governor as the "most important election result" for data center development. Hinojosa has said she'd block a permit for a data center if it wasn't a good deal for Texans or residents hadn't gotten a say in the matter. She defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who had touted Texas as "the epicenter of AI development" before trying to clamp down on it late in the campaign.

Morgan Stanley also said Ohio's election of Democrat Dr. Amy Acton as governor "creates significant risk of data center project delays in the state." Acton has pledged to block a data center project unless it meets certain standards.

Local elections didn't go well for data centers, either

Voters in local referendums cast ballots overwhelmingly in favor of restricting data centers, according to an analysis by polling and data science firm Redbud Consulting.

Redbud tracked 47 referendums in 44 municipalities in 12 states, including 21 in Ohio alone, eight in Maine, seven in Illinois and four in Kansas. Restrictions were approved in 44 of the 45 elections where counting was complete, Redbud reported.

Most voters don't want a data center built near them

About three-quarters of U.S. voters oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, according to The AP Voter Poll.

In red and blue states alike, majorities of voters were opposed to adding a data center where they live.

Support was higher in some traditionally red states, including Wyoming, West Virginia, Louisiana and Mississippi. In Texas, voters in the Senate race were similarly likely to say they oppose a new data center being built in their community.

Despite voters' deep opposition to data centers near them, The AP Voter Poll suggests it was not a particularly motivating issue in this election.

About one-quarter of U.S. voters said AI data centers were "crucial" to their vote for Congress, which is well below the shares that said government corruption or the cost of living were highly important to their vote.

The stakes were especially high in Texas

Texas is poised to overtake northern Virginia as the largest global data center market by 2030, according to a report by commercial real estate giant JLL.

In the campaign, Hinojosa aggressively attacked Abbott as having rolled out the welcome mat for data centers.

Stephen Sanders, a Republican who co-founded a data center protest group in Lubbock, said Texans were especially attuned to the issue because of talk that data centers pose a threat to their electricity and water in the drought-stricken state.

"I would say data centers were on the ballot," Sanders said.

Associated Press reporters Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.
