text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act.

The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican party.

When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year.

Strictly speaking, concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act and report emissions of these pollutants under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability and Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. But through a deal crafted in tandem with the EPA and the livestock industry, they’ve been given amnesty from doing so for more than 20 years.

The arrangement goes back to the early 2000s when the agency attempted to prosecute CAFOs for exceeding limits on some of these pollutants. The industry pushed back, arguing there was no adequate way of measuring them. So the agency worked with industry groups to develop what was dubbed the Air Consent Agreement, through which the EPA granted thousands of CAFOs safe harbor from legal action in exchange for their participation in a study that was funded by the industry.

The goal of the study, the agency said, was to develop tools and models that CAFOs could use to “determine whether they emit pollutants at levels that require them to apply for permits under the CAA or submit notifications under CERCLA or EPCRA” and “produce a scientifically sound basis for measuring and estimating air emissions” from these facilities.

But since the adoption of the agreement in 2005, the agency has failed to produce any air “emissions estimating methodologies,” even prompting a 2017 report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General that faulted it for slow-walking the process.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration and Congress have also gutted reporting requirements for factory farms to report air pollutants under CERCLA, also known as the Superfund Act, and EPCRA.

“As EPA has been saying it’s proceeding with this plan, it’s been dismantling all of its own tools to regulate emissions,” said Tarah Heinzen, the legal director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, which has tracked the proceedings from the beginning and filed dozens of lawsuits attempting to push regulators to control pollution from CAFOs. “Now it has announced it has no intention, basically, of ever holding factory farms accountable under the Clean Air Act, either.”

In its Oct. 30 announcement, the agency noted that in the two decades since the study, known as the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study, was conducted, many farms have modernized their barns and manure systems.

“Good science requires good data, and these data are too old and too limited to support methods that farms could rely on,” said Abigale Tardif, the acting assistant administrator for the agency’s Office of Air and Radiation, in a statement. “We would rather tell farmers that plainly than issue numbers we cannot stand behind.”

Rob Brenneman, president of the National Pork Producers Council, which has long pushed for the decision, said in a statement: “This move confirms what farmers have long known: Every farm is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all model to apply to them.”

Heinzen noted that the agency’s decision simply means that this administration has no intention of regulating air emissions from CAFOs, but for now, the Clean Air Act still requires permits for facilities that exceed emissions thresholds. The amnesty granted to these facilities will no longer be in effect now that the agreement has concluded.

“There’s no EPA-issued methodology to estimate emissions,” she said. “That doesn’t mean that there aren’t good studies out there of emissions from different types of animal feeding operations that can be used.”

Heinzen pointed to California, which has models for livestock emissions that it uses to enforce its own air regulations. “We just don’t have one set of national emissions factors from EPA,” Heinzen said. “That does not absolve these factory farms from their obligation to comply with federal law.”

Still, under this administration, it’s clear air emissions from factory farms won’t be measured and monitored any time soon. “No one’s going to estimate anything,” Heinzen noted. “As EPA said in its press release, we’re certainly not about to try to enforce the law.”

The Air Compliance Agreement did not extend to methane. The U.S. livestock industry is the single-biggest source of methane in the country, but Congress effectively blocks livestock facilities from reporting methane emissions in annual spending bills.

text:
Under the new plan, industrial companies can offset their emissions by funding commercial vehicle upgrades or other mitigation efforts in other industrial facilities.

The EPA praised the county's new scheme, while one critic said it fails to require businesses to curb their own emissions in the first place — essentially it's a license to pollute.

Maricopa County's air quality is one of the worst in the country and exceeds federal limits per the Clean Air Act.

Maricopa County is a rapidly growing industrial hub and the region ranks among the worst in the country for air pollution.

But the county has no plans to stop developing. To accommodate more growth without adding to the air quality problem, the county has expanded the menu of options for developers coming online to offset their emissions. Permit seekers can now look to commercial vehicles, public transit and car manufacturers to counterbalance their own air pollution.

On Nov. 5, the Environmental Protection Agency approved the plan.

The new policy enlists industry to be part of the solution and still grow, said Kate Brophy McGee, chair of the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors and District 3 representative.

“It is an incentive for them so that they can continue to employ people, so that they can continue to operate and to do it in a manner which in effect cleans up our air,” she said.

Tackling vehicle emissions

Before large industrial facilities like power plants and manufacturers can operate, they need to seek preconstruction permits from authorities. These permits usually carry environmental regulations, such as limits on the amount of pollutants applicants can emit in accordance with the Clean Air Act.

To meet these caps, businesses can restrict their own footprint or sponsor other permit holders to tamp down on their pollution.

Maricopa County’s Air Quality Department allows companies to trade what are called emissions reduction credits, which are a company’s total allowable emissions. Those who come under the regulatory limit can sell some of their credits to those that overshoot, allowing the extra pollution from one player to be canceled out by another with emissive room to spare.

Traditionally, the county has allowed permit applicants to trade with already permitted stationary sources, funding initiatives such as installing air scrubbers in factory smokestacks or improving industrial furnaces so they have a smaller environmental burden. But these permits can be challenging to find or economically infeasible to obtain.

Now, the new air quality plan allows companies to buy credits from “mobile sources” — manufacturers and commercial owners of vehicle fleets. Initiatives that could qualify include funding efficiency upgrades to garbage trucks, replacing aging fleets of cars or the electrification of municipal buses.

Representatives of the EPA lauded the county’s plan.

“It's really a win-win,” said Michael Martucci, the EPA administrator for Region 9 that encompasses the Southwestern states, Hawaii and Pacific territories. “It allows business and industry to grow in a place where they would otherwise be restricted.”

Martucci added that industry has already expressed interest.

Is it a license to pollute?

The plan has drawn skepticism about how much it could do for the Valley’s air quality. Echoing criticisms of existing carbon-trading schemes, one expert said this program could similarly give prospective developers a license to pollute, a way of punting their carbon-curbing responsibility to other polluters.

“Providing more flexibility to trade emission credits in or near non-attainment areas is not in the best interest of air quality or public health,” said Diane Brown, executive director of the nonprofit Arizona Public Interest Research Group. “While additional funds to mitigate air quality issues can be helpful, it is far better to reduce emissions at the source versus creating a system that leads to trading.”

So, instead of polluters reining in their own emissions, they now have more flexibility to pay to make it someone else’s problem.

Residents living near the original permit holder won’t get to enjoy the air quality benefits if mitigation is outsourced to another company located elsewhere, Brown said.

She said Maricopa County needs to beef up its permitting requirements rather than letting companies get around proper caps on emissions. For starters, the county could set stricter limits on emissions for everyone.

Maricopa County is already out of compliance with the Clean Air Act. Part of the reason is topographic — Phoenix sits in a valley, where haze can accumulate as if in a sump. Local government officials have also claimed that contaminants waft in from other states and across international borders, and are out of their hands to control.

In March, the EPA chose not to upgrade the severity of the Phoenix-Mesa area’s nonattainment status from “moderate” to “serious,” where it should be according to federal standards. A “serious” label would have forced local officials to do more to cut down on pollution.

In 2026, the American Lung Association rated Maricopa County a grade of F for its ozone and particle pollution, whose levels are far higher than any other county in Arizona.

The credit trading expansion won’t exacerbate pollution levels, the EPA estimates, and potentially whittle them down in the long run. “It's meant to make sure you're still making incremental progress,” said Lisa Beckham, a supervisory environmental engineer at the EPA who worked with Maricopa County on modifying the credit plan.

Still, any concern that tighter air quality regulations might hobble economic growth means little if local communities don’t have clean air and an environment to live in, Brown said.

“Air quality and public health should not be sacrificed for the purpose of growing the economy,” she added.

title: Mamdani and Hochul promise a new day for Puerto Rico after Democrats sweep midterms
description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul have pledged more support for Puerto Rico as it remains mired in multiple crises. They asserted during a
text:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul, right, and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, left, arrive at a campaign stop, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026, in the Brooklyn borough of New York.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul pledged more support for Puerto Rico on Friday as it remains mired in multiple crises, asserting during a trip to the island that the sweeping Democratic win in the U.S. midterm elections will be a boon for the U.S. territory.

“There’s a potential in that we can finally start to deliver for working-class people across this country,” Mamdani said. “What we heard today was the fact that so often what’s described as a natural crisis here in Puerto Rico is in fact a political crisis, one that is the result of political choices.”

Hochul said the election results represent “a whole new day” for Puerto Rico and warned that the federal government will be held responsible.



“What we’ve seen over the last two years is really an abandonment of that commitment," she said. "And we hope to have all those wounds heal, making sure that we continue bringing resources for resiliency, energy projects, building up the grid, as well as healthcare being restored, nutrition programs.”

Mamdani and Hochul are part of a group of New York government officials who are in Puerto Rico for a four-day, annual conference. They met with local nonprofits on Friday as officials announced a $280,000 partnership to help the island confront emergencies.

The partnership between Hispanic Federation and the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York comes as Puerto Rico struggles with chronic power outages and intermittent water shortages while it tries to rebuild from Hurricane Maria and other disasters.

The nonprofit Hispanic Federation said the money would equip 10 community-run resiliency hubs across the island with increased water storage capacity; some also would receive rain-collection systems, kitchen infrastructure and solar power with battery storage.

“We have to start working with the leadership to make sure that the Puerto Rico agenda is not forgotten,” Frankie Miranda, president and CEO of Hispanic Federation, told The Associated Press.

“In Puerto Rico, there are still some huge challenges," he said. “All the public policies have been so harmful to Puerto Rico.”

The announcement comes months after the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump canceled solar projects in Puerto Rico that were supposed to help thousands of low-income families. One project, worth $400 million, would have seen the installation of solar and battery storage systems in low-income homes and those with medical needs.

The U.S. Department of Energy has said the money initially slated for solar projects would instead be used to help maintain Puerto Rico’s crumbling power grid, which was razed by Hurricane Maria in September 2017. The grid, however, was already weakened given a lack of maintenance and investment.

The decisions prompted outrage on the island as federal support for solar projects fades .

Last week, six Puerto Rico residents sued the U.S. Energy Department and its secretary, Chris Wright, following the scrapping of a $1 billion federally funded program to provide solar power and battery storage to those who most needed it.

“The cost of such systems remains out of reach for the majority of Puerto Ricans,” the lawsuit stated.

Among those suing is 63-year-old Arecibo resident Ileana Ríos, who is diabetic and needs to refrigerate her insulin. Meanwhile, her son has asthma and needs to use a nebulizer, which requires electricity.

The lawsuit noted that Ríos “regularly loses power when the weather is stable and always loses power during storms, sometimes for several weeks at a time.”

The other residents who sued also have serious health conditions and need equipment or medications that rely on electricity.

The lawsuit requests that a judge order the U.S. Energy Department to reinstate the grant program, among other things. The agency said in a brief statement Friday that it is working closely with Puerto Rico's governor to stabilize the island's power grid as it criticized the previous administration for “advancing their Green New Scam agenda over helping Puerto Rico build an affordable, reliable, and secure electrical grid.”

The funding loss has been a blow to nonprofits and others who faced months of uncertainty and confusion as they awaited the Trump administration’s decision on whether and how it would continue the program.

“We had a lot of uncertainty. ... At some points it just felt like we were talking to no one," said Sybelle Rodriguez del Valle, director of operations at the energy resilience nonprofit Barrio Eléctrico, which was part of the U.S. Energy Department program.

Barrio Eléctrico provides electric service to more than 500 families and was poised to provide resilient energy for 1,200 families with funds from the federal program. It had only completed about one-third of its projects before the program ended, losing an estimated $16 million to $20 million in funding.

Associated Press reporter Gabriela Aoun Angueira contributed to this report.

As one carbon storage project struggled after another, Benson and other academic researchers continued to insist they could flourish.
text:
This article was first published by ProPublica, co-published with Drilled.

In the spring of 2005, the United Nations convened more than 100 of the world’s top scientists in the medieval town of Oviedo, Spain. They were there to finish writing a paradigm-shifting report about a technology that they hoped could help stop climate change.

To celebrate the report’s impending completion, the meeting’s hosts handed out bottles of cava, Spanish sparkling wine, with tongue-in-cheek labels stating that they were to be opened only by those who truly believed it could work.

Belief was necessary because the technology — carbon capture and storage, or CCS — had barely been tested. The idea was simple: strip carbon dioxide from smokestacks before it could flow into the air and warm the planet. Then pump it into a porous part of the Earth’s crust and leave it there. Forever.

The experts in Oviedo had stacks of papers proving that parts of the process worked. But major questions remained about how much space exists inside the Earth to store the CO2, how effectively it could be monitored and whether the poisonous, concentrated gas would reliably stay underground.

Tasked with wrangling roughly three dozen of those scientists toward consensus was Sally Benson, a geoscientist from Lawrence Berkeley National Lab who was co-leading the report’s chapter on underground storage of carbon. After a quarter-century of studying how fluids and gases move beneath Earth’s surface, she was an unimpeachable authority on the subject. She was also a savvy and diplomatic leader, skilled at managing rooms full of big egos and big tempers. It was proving handy in a process that had at times devolved into unruly debate.

The scientists had clashed for years over what the report should say, first at a meeting in Canada, then in Norway, Australia and Brazil. The evidence was scant. Three large-scale experiments were underway, but only one — a Norwegian operation that captured carbon from a natural gas field and pumped it under the bed of the North Sea — had rigorously tested permanent storage. There, the injected CO2 astonished engineers when it floated 700 feet upward through a series of geologic formations. To their relief, it hit a ceiling of shale that kept it underground, and the project was deemed a success. But with so little to go on, the scientists warned in their first draft that any broad statement about leakage risk would be “almost meaningless.”

The researchers were in Oviedo only because Saudi Arabia and other oil-exporting countries had pressured the U.N. to write the report despite the paucity of evidence, according to U.N. officials and records. The oil, gas and coal industries had spent years casting doubt on climate change while quietly fretting that policies to address it would one day put them out of business. The industry, documents show, saw CCS as a way to forestall that outcome, allowing the world to keep burning fossil fuels while simply burying the pollution underground. A U.N. report would bring the technology into the mainstream.

In turn, the U.N. hoped such a report would draw the oil-producing nations into its search for climate solutions. So despite objections from some nations and environmental organizations, which warned that the report would distract from the imperative to phase out fossil fuels, the U.N.’s preeminent climate science authority, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, went ahead. And for the first time, it invited a large contingent of industry researchers to join the scientists in writing the report, as well as several representatives from environmental groups. Benson’s chapter included authors and editors from Shell, Chevron and Saudi Aramco.

The process that followed would make some of the chapter’s scientists uneasy. The IPCC’s procedures stated that reports should assess the existing research on a topic based on peer-reviewed literature and that exceptions must be reviewed and clearly cited.

Bert Metz, one of the highest-ranking U.N. officials at the meeting, was pressing the group to come up with more definitive language about CCS’ potential. The report would be better if it could offer hard numbers, even where none existed in the literature: Precisely how many gigatons of storage capacity did the planet likely have? How long would a well-designed reservoir hold the CO2 injected into it? More than a year? A thousand years?

With so little evidence to work with, David Keith, a Canadian physicist, proposed a workaround: The authors could conduct an “expert elicitation,” taking an anonymous survey about what they expected the evidence to eventually show.

At first, not everyone was willing to go along. Some scientists worried that making what amounted to educated guesses would mislead the public, they told Drilled and ProPublica. Benson and Metz, though, both argued that on such an important matter informed advice was better than nothing.

In the end, the group agreed to take the survey and to keep it off the record — they would “burn it afterward,” Keith recounted, making no mention of it in the official report. When the meeting concluded, some of the scientists popped their bottles of cava in celebration.

“It’s not the hard science that you would prefer, obviously,” Metz would later tell Drilled and ProPublica.

Five months later, the IPCC published its special report, which would help legitimize CCS for a generation.

The 431-page document portrayed CCS as a potential savior for the climate that could enable countries “to continue to include fossil fuels in their energy mix.” It stated that using CCS could lower the cost of stabilizing global CO2 concentrations by at least 30% and that if fully supported by policy, it could account for as much as 55% of the world’s efforts to limit climate change through this century.

It acknowledged that there were still gaps in research and experience with the technology — offering extensive detail deep within its pages about the challenges and uncertainties of piecing together separate but proven steps in the CCS process. But its summary stated that “there are no major technical or knowledge barriers” to storing captured CO2 underground.

All of those assertions, however, rested on the critical determinations made by the scientists handling the storage chapter.

Benson’s group wrote that the planet offered vast CO2 storage capacity. Storage sites that were well selected and well managed, they said, were likely to retain 99% of the carbon pumped into them for at least 1,000 years.

A Consequential Decision

The scientists’ conclusions that day in Spain have had profound, compounding consequences.

The special report has been cited in thousands of academic papers, in legislative testimony and in media coverage validating carbon capture and storage as a realistic solution to global warming.

When climate forecasters built models, their calculations assumed CCS would work. When governments and corporations began making so-called “net zero” pledges, promising to subtract as much CO2 from the atmosphere as they add, they assumed CCS would work. When policymakers gave energy companies billions of dollars in public funds to develop “clean coal,” they assumed CCS would work.

These presumptions shifted the world’s discourse from how to limit carbon pollution to how to remove it from the atmosphere after the fact.

Enthusiasm for the technology has only grown. This spring, California embarked on one of the world’s largest carbon burial endeavors yet. While President Donald Trump eviscerated most programs addressing the climate, he has expanded subsidies for CCS. There are more than 100 applications for storage sites pending in the U.S. alone. U.N. analyses suggest that to achieve environmental goals, a CCS industry the size of the entire global oil production industry would have to be built by 2050.

But 21 years after Oviedo, a staggering gap lies between expectations for the technology and its operational reality. Since 1996, just 12 large-scale geological storage projects have been constructed. Collectively, they bury less CO2 than a single power plant can emit in a year, according to our analysis of sites listed in an International Energy Agency database. Seven of them have faced technical, financial or performance issues. An investigation by Drilled and ProPublica found there’s reason to doubt carbon capture and storage will ever succeed at the scale needed to offer a significant climate solution.

History is full of audacious technological leaps — moments when visionary engineering solved seemingly intractable problems. Scientists told Drilled and ProPublica that they have devoted themselves to studying CCS in that spirit, hoping a grand techno-fix could help the world solve the climate crisis without a painful overhaul of the global energy system.

But that ambition did not exist in isolation. It was bankrolled in large part by companies that stood to profit from its success.

Industry documents show that oil company executives have long seen CCS as a way to hedge against climate regulation, greenwash their brands and preserve their core business. Internal Exxon documents obtained by Drilled and ProPublica show that in 1988, the company determined that any climate research Exxon supported should serve the dual purposes of protecting the value of its oil, gas and coal while preserving the company’s business options; the company would eventually become one of the world’s major funders of CCS research.

Later, the American Petroleum Institute would write in internal communications that the industry’s “license to operate” depended on companies lowering climate pollution, and CCS, it wrote, “enables the use of petroleum and natural gas by providing an opportunity to capture and/or offset emissions.” And at a 2023 prominent oil industry conference in Houston, the CEO of Occidental Petroleum, Vicki Hollub, would explain that a novel form of CCS that sucks carbon directly from the air “is going to be the technology that helps to preserve our industry over time.”

For many university faculty, the rewards for studying the industry’s favored climate solution have been numerous, opening opportunities, funding papers and raising their profiles. Benson is a clear example. When the IPCC was awarded in 2007 with the Nobel Peace Prize for its climate work, she and her co-authors were recognized among the scientists who contributed. When Stanford University sought a new director for its ExxonMobil-funded climate research center, it tapped her. When President Joe Biden prioritized climate policy, he brought Benson into the White House.

Keith, the Canadian physicist, benefited from oil industry interest in a different way: He developed technology to capture CO2. Occidental Petroleum paid more than $1 billion to buy the company he founded.

There is no evidence that Benson, widely described by colleagues as scrupulous, skewed her scientific findings to suit the interests of her industry patrons, and Benson has described CCS’ flaws in her publications.

However, in speeches, presentations and even congressional testimony, she has been a dogged champion of CCS technology, time and again describing it as safe and ready for large-scale deployment, despite having a ringside view to its many setbacks.

She has frequently referenced the most affirmative statements from her group’s work in Oviedo as evidence. But the methodology Benson and her co-authors used to reach those conclusions 21 years ago has not been generally understood. When Drilled and ProPublica told prominent climate researchers about the expert elicitation process, several were disconcerted to learn that there was so little scientific basis for the report’s conclusion that 99% of CO2 was likely to remain underground.

A survey, said Oliver Geden, a vice chair of the IPCC’s forthcoming climate assessment, was “an inappropriate way of assessing the literature.”

Authors “are not supposed to do original research. They’re supposed to just collect what’s out there,” said Roger Cooke, who was a lead author on a subsequent IPCC report. Cooke said expert elicitation, done rigorously, can be valuable, but “just asking a bunch of experts to give their best guess is one of the worst things you can do.”

In a detailed written response, Benson said she did not believe that the survey undertaken in 2005 violated IPCC norms and said the group’s leadership was aware of the process. She disputed that the approach amounted to an informed guess and said that “there was an enormous amount of data” to draw on. The group was trying to agree on the best language to synthesize evidence detailed deeper in the report. She rejected the notion that her research or career were influenced by industry funding, writing that she has worked “tirelessly for 30 years on CCS and other climate solutions” in a sincere effort to combat an escalating planetary crisis. And, she offered, she views CCS as one valuable tool among many needed to address climate change.

Keith said the goal of the expert elicitation was not to seek precision, but to provide a sense of the orders of magnitude of the capacity and risks, “because that’s what’s relevant to public policy.” He said even sites with problems haven’t leaked large amounts of CO2 and that the report’s broad statements “have stood the test of time.” The chapter authors’ confidence in CCS doesn’t suggest “that a bunch of us are tools of the fossil fuel industry.”

The IPCC declined to comment on specific questions about how the report came about. “We are not in a position to comment on individual recollections,” a spokesperson wrote about the expert elicitation. However, they said that the group’s process was in keeping with the organization’s procedures at the time and that it reflected contemporaneous understanding of the technology. The IPCC did not directly respond to the assertion that the authors conducted what amounts to new research during the writing process, and it did not provide requested records that would detail the scientists’ vote. “The IPCC’s role is to assess the full range of available scientific knowledge,” the statement said. Metz referred to the IPCC’s response.

Chevron, Shell and Saudi Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

Drilled and ProPublica spoke with more than 100 experts on carbon capture, climate modeling and influence in academia, including a dozen people who attended the Oviedo meeting. We compiled records of geologic storage tests and surveyed an extensive body of peer-reviewed literature. This investigation is part of a broader examination into how fossil fuel industry funding of climate research has shaped climate policy, solutions and public understanding. It follows our report in June about a BP-funded program at Princeton University and the oil company’s role in crafting one of the program’s most influential climate papers.

Since Benson and her co-authors met in Oviedo, weather catastrophes have multiplied, oceans have acidified and the amount of carbon in the atmosphere has soared. In September, the U.N. released an urgent new report declaring that the race to avert disruptive warming has been all but lost. It concluded that “overshoot” — the notion that temperatures will rise above the world’s adopted goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming — is now a certainty.

Carbon capture and storage, it said, is one of the only ways to bring those temperatures back down.

Looking at a Failure and Calling It Triumph

Just a few days before the meeting in Oviedo, BP put Benson and a handful of other scientists on a chartered flight from London to Algeria. Their destination: the world’s second major geologic carbon storage experiment, in the Sahara.

The British oil giant, along with the state-owned oil companies of Algeria and Norway, had begun to drill for gas at a new field named for a nearby oasis called In Salah. Most natural gas comes out of the ground as a cocktail of methane and CO2. The CO2 must be stripped out and is usually vented into the sky. But at In Salah, the companies saw an opportunity to try out a greener process — one that could become big business.

Earth’s crust is a layer cake of rock. Some layers, like sandstone, contain honeycombed pores capable of holding CO2, while others, like mudstone, can act as impermeable seals, trapping the buoyant gas underground.

That layer cake is impossible to precisely chart from the surface, but engineers sent sound waves into the ground and interpreted what echoed up into rough maps. They learned their target sandstone reservoir sat below a 3,000-foot-thick brick of mudstone they believed would be impermeable. They also learned the sandstone was “tight” — less honeycombed than they had hoped — but still capable of holding gas. So they had begun to inject the CO2.

The plane landed on a sand-strewn strip circled by jeep tracks and rocky plateaus. A photograph shows Benson, medium height, her blond bob tucked beneath a hard hat, standing in the desert alongside a BP-funded physicist from Princeton named Robert Socolow and seven other men in front of a well that was pushing CO2 under the desert. In Salah had been operating for less than a year but seemed to be going smoothly.

Afterward, Benson traveled to Oviedo to finish drafting the special report, which listed In Salah among key sites that “indicate that it is feasible to store CO2” underground at significant scale.

That assessment has not held up.

Energy companies had first begun pumping CO2 into the ground commercially in the 1970s, when they realized it would loosen up stubborn crude oil, sometimes doubling an oil field’s output. They called it “enhanced oil recovery,” and though they didn’t try to lock the CO2 in place, much of it seemed to stay underground.

The idea to use carbon injection as a climate fix came a few years later from an Italian physicist named Cesare Marchetti, who suggested disposing of carbon deep in the ocean or underground. In the 1980s Exxon tried, and gave up on, efforts to develop the idea. And it wasn’t until 1996 when the first large-scale CCS project — the operation in the North Sea — began.

In a recent interview inside her narrow, fluorescent-lit office at Stanford University’s earth sciences building, Benson said it was shortly after that that she first heard of CCS. A colleague at the Department of Energy had sent her a slide deck by Princeton’s Socolow about the technology. “I was like, ‘I think this is nuts,’” she told Drilled and ProPublica.

“I just couldn’t really picture it working at scale.”

But, as both an idealist and a pragmatist, she was drawn to the potential for science to solve difficult environmental problems. She made a crude calculation of how much CO2 might fit beneath California and was surprised by the answer: a lot. At least in theory. And it changed her mind.

As Benson became one of CCS’ leading experts and champions, she increasingly found herself in rooms full of oil industry veterans. In 2000, she helped establish a partnership between the Department of Energy and companies including Chevron, Texaco and BP. That program had a focused mission: make large-scale geological storage an operational reality by 2015.

In 2002, Benson was asked to sit on the advisory council of a new BP and Ford Motor Co.-funded climate research center at Princeton University. At a summit there the following year, Benson expressed concern that focusing on leaks could undermine public support for CCS, according to meeting records and the account of another person in attendance.

“Need to present optimistic estimates,” the minutes recapping her presentation say.

By 2007, Benson was helping to run her own industry-funded research center. A few years earlier, ExxonMobil CEO Lee Raymond, a thunderous voice of climate denial, had put up $100 million of the company’s money to fund climate and energy work at Stanford University. With another $125 million from three other companies, Stanford’s Global Climate and Energy Project became one of the best-funded climate research centers in America.

The donation came with strings: ExxonMobil and the other sponsors had veto power over which research projects received funding.

Students and activists protested the funding structure, accusing ExxonMobil of retracing the path of tobacco companies, which paid for scientific work on obscure causes of cancer as a distraction from their culpability.

Benson defended the arrangement ardently and often. ExxonMobil and the other sponsors approved every grant that Stanford recommended, never exercising their veto power, she said. Reporting by Drilled and ProPublica did not contradict that assertion. Benson also pointed to the fact that the program funded an array of research, including on renewable energy.

In an interview and written response, Benson said researchers who take funding from oil companies are motivated not by corporate agendas, but by genuine interest in the work. The funding underwrites the inquiry, she said, not its conclusions. Where there’s “alignment,” she added, the industry support can be “amazingly catalytic and helpful.”

In response to a request for comment, Stanford University directed Drilled and ProPublica to former law school dean Paul Brest, who led a committee that reviewed energy research funding at the school. Brest said that faculty have a right to seek any funding they choose, so long as sponsors cannot direct the work.

Most important to Benson was that scientists and their students have the opportunity to research matters of great consequence. She has published more than 50 papers on geologic carbon storage since joining Stanford, most of them highly technical evaluations of CCS that reiterated its importance to reducing emissions, and many underwritten by ExxonMobil and other industry sources. “I don’t know anybody else,” she told Drilled and ProPublica, “who would eventually provide, you know, $225 million of funding” to study climate solutions.

But whether researchers intended to serve their funders’ agenda on CCS or not, some say the effect has been undeniable. “It seems like a credible solution because you have credible people at credible institutions working on it,” said Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard historian of science and an expert in corporate influence.

Benson was still getting settled into her new job at Stanford when the project in Algeria ran into major problems.

On a 118-degree day in 2007, In Salah’s inspectors heard CO2 whistling through the top of an abandoned oil well nearly a mile from the nearest injection site. Engineers had believed it would take years before the CO2 plume could spread so far underground, but the gas had cracked through the sandstoneand found a new path.

To stop the leak, workers poured cement into the well, plugging it permanently. But soon a second problem arose: Satellite data revealed the desert floor above the injection sites had bulged. When project engineers again used sound waves and other tools to map the layers underground, they arrived at an alarming discovery: Pressurized CO2 had sent cracks a quarter of the way up through the 3000-foot-thick layer of mudstone. If it breached the rest, it could leach into the pan-Saharan aquifer, acidifying a source of drinking water millions of people depend on.

BP and its partners eventually summoned Benson and the other science advisers to London. The dangerous gas, they could now see, was moving in ways they had predicted it could not. Nonetheless, the advisers suggested that injection proceed temporarily to see whether it could safely be done under lower pressure and with careful monitoring.

But the Algerians had had enough. In 2011 BP and its partners stopped injection, and in 2012 they quietly scrapped the project.

Benson would later describe In Salah as a technical failure but a triumph of detection. “It was monitored and people found a problem,” she told Drilled and ProPublica.

“Then,” she added, they “learned from it.”

More Problems, More Dependence

As she did in Oviedo, Benson still maintains that the fundamental mechanics of CCS are well enough understood to know that it can work.

As proof that geologic formations can handle high-pressure gas, she points to the natural gas industry, which injects large amounts of its product back underground for temporary storage.

She also points to enhanced oil recovery. Over the last 40 years, American companies have injected 100 times more CO2 into drilling fields as a way to extract more oil than they have into what CCS industry insiders call “dedicated” CO2 storage reservoirs. There are few reports of accidents or leaks at these sites.

Unlike dedicated CO2 storage, though, enhanced oil recovery is less likely to cause pressure to build up underground, because the CO2 pumped in fills space left by the oil that’s forced out. (These sites also can result in a net addition of CO2 in the atmosphere, since they wind up producing still more oil.)

The record of the industry’s largest CCS sites — ones designed solely to help the climate — has been far more troubled.

Around the time In Salah shut down, the world’s third large project — a Norwegian site named Snøhvit several hundred miles north of the Arctic Circle — also met critical obstacles. When injection began in 2008, engineers had calculated the site would have an 18-year capacity. But they had radically overestimated how much CO2 it could absorb and had to relocate the project after just three years.

In the U.S., a decadelong effort to build a “clean coal” power plant outfitted with CCS proved impossible within a reasonable budget and was abandoned in 2015 — but not before the government had spent $378 million in taxpayer money. Benson was on the project’s advisory board for part of that time.

That year in Canada, Shell opened a $1 billion carbon capture and storage facility — also largely paid for by the country’s taxpayers — connected to open-pit oil sands mines. The industry routinely promises that plants like this one, called Quest, capture at least 90% of emissions. But at Quest, once the energy required for the capture process itself is accounted for, the capture rate instead has hovered around 68%, according to a report by the research group Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. It has also caused hundreds of microearthquakes.

Shell did not respond to a request for comment.

As one carbon storage project struggled after another, Benson and other academic researchers continued to insist they could flourish.

In a keynote speech at a 2018 conference in Sweden, Benson showed a slide with a map of CCS facilities across the world, most of which were enhanced oil recovery sites. Her map included In Salah, which had shuttered. And it included another project, in Australia, which had yet to open. “The operations have been very good at all of these projects. And they’ve gone well in terms of safety,” she said.

She also showed a slide pointing to the 2005 U.N. special report’s statement that an “appropriately selected,” well-managed reservoir would likely retain 99% of its carbon for more than 1,000 years. “This was an expression that if you find the right site, the CO2 should be permanently stored,” she said.

In a written response, she said she continues to cite the 21-year-old special report’s conclusions on leakage because “the methodology was sound then and remains so.” Benson said that she is careful to qualify her characterizations and show evidence in her presentations, and that during her presentation in Sweden she did so. She did not directly address the status of projects portrayed in her map.

When the Australian project, called Gorgon, did open the following year, it turned out to be the biggest CCS fiasco yet. Australia had allowed Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell to drill a major new natural gas field there with the requirement that the companies buried at least 80% of the CO2 that came out of the ground with it. It was billed as the world’s largest CCS operation.

Instead, it has been plagued by clogged injection wells and underground pressure spikes. In their operating year ending in 2025, the companies were able to inject just a quarter of the CO2 collected there. Since they vent the remainder, Gorgon, once billed as a model for climate solutions, became the largest single source of industrial carbon pollution on the continent.

“Like any pioneering endeavour, it takes time to optimise a new system to ensure it performs reliably over 40-plus years of operation,” a Chevron spokesperson wrote in an emailed response. “We realise that people refer to the challenges at Gorgon in an attempt to discredit CCS, however, as we have shown, we can capture and store greenhouse gas at scale.” Shell and ExxonMobil did not respond to requests for comment.

An Idea Takes Root

While operators struggled to prove CCS could be viable, the world became dependent on it working.

As soon as the IPCC published the 2005 report, climate modelers that help assess the most economic ways to limit global warming began folding CCS into their calculations.

They projected not only that CCS could stop billions of tons of emissions from reaching the sky, but that it could suck old carbon pollution out of the atmosphere. They adopted a theory that supposed vast fields of switchgrass or fast-growing willow could absorb carbon into their stalks and leaves, and when those plants were harvested and burned for electricity, their emissions, too, would be captured and buried.

The modelers incorporated this subtractive approach so prodigiously that, on paper, they could reverse climate change. Global temperatures could overshoot targets in the short term, so long as enough carbon was eventually sucked back out of the air to bring those temperatures back down.

World leaders embraced the wiggle room this theory provided them. When they signed the U.N. Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, pledging to keep warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, they counted on these so-called negative emissions among the key tools that could make it possible. In 2018, when the IPCC published a special report on how to reach that goal, 89 out of its 90 scenarios included using large-scale CCS.

Now, in its latest report, the U.N. says that it is virtually impossible to still get to a 1.5 C future — or anything close — without removing carbon from the atmosphere. There are several ways to do that — reforestation and the use of minerals spread on fields to absorb carbon, for instance. But these methods are either small scale or even less proven than CCS.

By 2015, the tantalizing idea of “negative emissions” was showing up in new, mainstream ways. “Net zero” pledges to one day offset carbon emissions began rolling in from most of the world’s nations, as well as cities like Omaha, Nebraska; the band Coldplay; ice cream chains; funeral homes; and even ExxonMobil.

But real-world CCS projects have not met the moment.

To scale the technology as much as U.N. analyses suggest is needed to limit warming to 2 C would require not only a technological feat but almost unimaginable resources, Drilled and ProPublica found. Carbon dioxide injection would have to almost immediately increase by more than 400 times. That would require more than 2,000 new geological waste sites to be established — a new large-scale CCS project put into operation every four days, on average, for the next 25 years.

To move the CO2 to those sites would require 68,000 miles of specialized pipeline in the U.S. alone. Globally, at least 85 custom-built tankers would be needed to carry the high-pressure gas safely across oceans. Just four exist.

And if all of that were accomplished, the effort would come at an almost inconceivable cost: tens of trillions of dollars.

“Fuck, OK, It’s Harder Than We Thought”

At Benson’s office at Stanford, in a building where rocks painstakingly collected from field sites fill cabinets in the halls, the Society of Petroleum Engineers hosts Friday socials — beer and snacks provided — and the adjacent courtyard is named after the oil company Arco.

Inside, propped on a stack of boxes, is a framed copy of Biden’s keystone climate legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act. On it, national climate adviser Ali Zaidi scrawled in blue sharpie, “Thank you, Sally, for helping truly transform our energy & climate future!”

Benson returned to Stanford after a nearly two-year stint in Biden’s White House as the head of the energy division of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, where she says she provided periodic scientific advice as the act was being pushed through Congress. One of the most ambitious climate policy efforts in history, it offered a large set of incentives for CCS, which the fossil fuel industry had lobbied for intensely.

But even while oil industry leaders have pushed the world to embrace CCS, behind closed doors, they have remained skeptical of its potential as a climate solution.

In 2007, as ExxonMobil funded Benson’s center at Stanford, its former CEO Raymond told a room full of industry leaders that carbon storage might be considered “kind of the Holy Grail.” Executing it, though, would be “a whole different animal” than injecting carbon underground for enhanced oil recovery. “You can’t assume that’s going to happen. And the cost is going to be very, very significant.”

A 2011 internal slide deck from BP stated that while carbon storage would allow fossil fuels to remain the world’s dominant source of energy, “the pace of CCS development has been slow and the future pace remains uncertain.” And in a 2018 internal presentation, ExxonMobil predicted hardly any CCS would be deployed by 2050, even as it modeled that global CO2 emissions from energy production would continue to skyrocket.

Yet the industry saw brand value in encouraging CCS anyway. An ExxonMobil document from 2021 describes a public relations campaign to persuade the political and financial “elites” to “believe ExxonMobil is committed to helping solve climate change,” in part by proving its efforts on CCS will “play an indispensable role” in a greener economy.

For her part, Benson still has faith in the technology’s viability, despite the failures. “These are big projects, right? The idea that everything goes exactly according to plan, especially for these first-of-a-kind projects — it’s unrealistic.”

As proof that CCS is on the rise, she pointed to 77 operating CCS projects identified in a report by the industry group the Global CCS Institute and said that another report demonstrated a tenfold growth in CO2 injected underground since 2005.

When ProPublica and Drilled reviewed that same data, however, and excluded the enhanced oil recovery projects, we found just eight operating large-scale carbon burial projects on that list (10 using the group’s more recent data), and half the increase in annual injections that Benson stated.

Experts interviewed for this story insisted — often in an anguished timbre — that CCS simply must work because decades of delay have foreclosed other paths to a stable climatic future.

But just because the world now needs CCS to work doesn’t mean it can.

“It’s always some issue,” said Glen Peters, a senior researcher at the Cicero Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “I think there’s been a lack of willingness for the community to say, ‘Fuck, OK, it’s harder than we thought.’”

The latest CCS effort got underway this spring, in California, when the oil company California Resources Corp. began injecting CO2 beneath the state’s Central Valley.

California — long a vanguard of environmental policy — has embraced the technology. In 2021, as it was formulating a plan for how the state should reach its climate targets, the California Air Resources Board invited Benson to give a presentation on the role CCS could play.

“The fraction of CO2 retained underground is likely to be very high,” she told the board, again pointing to the 2005 special report: “This study said 99% over 1,000 years.”

The board set the ambitious goal of burying more than 100 million tons of CO2 a year by 2045, more than all the carbon that has ever been geologically stored around the world combined. Since it opened in May, the new project has injected just 7% of its advertised capacity, but California Resources Corp. is now seeking permits for eight more CCS projects across California, and other oil and gas companies have proposed four more, including two that Stanford is directly involved with.

California Resources Corp., in a written response, said the company is injecting the amount it had planned for early operations and will increase to capacity as the project develops.

Could California truly be burying 100 million tons of CO2 a year by 2045? For the first time, in an interview, Benson was hesitant to commit. “I think it’s very challenging,” she said. “That’s a lot of infrastructure, a lot of money, a lot of projects.”

Asked a second time, she once again demurred. “Oh gosh. If we really set our mind to it. If we could wave a wand.”

title: Phoenix Tailings prepares to open rare earth separation facility at Eastman Business Park
description:
Greece, N.Y. — Phoenix Tailings is preparing to open a rare earth separation facility in the Rochester area.
Kathy Hochul announced Oct. 20 that the Massachusetts-based company chose Eastman Business Park for a new $375 million, 500,000-square-foot facility that will process metals used in the production of electric vehicles, electronics and defense equipment.
The company announced Thursday that the facility, located off Lexington Avenue, will benefit from an estimated $54.2 million in state, local and infrastructure incentives.

text:
Greece, N.Y. — Phoenix Tailings is preparing to open a rare earth separation facility in the Rochester area.

Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Oct. 20 that the Massachusetts-based company chose Eastman Business Park for a new $375 million, 500,000-square-foot facility that will process metals used in the production of electric vehicles, electronics and defense equipment.

The company announced Thursday that the facility, located off Lexington Avenue, will benefit from an estimated $54.2 million in state, local and infrastructure incentives.

"Part of the incentive with the state and local community is to upgrade that building and make it more suitable for what we need to do to make an ecosystem to move fast," CEO Nick Myers said. "But we are not building buildings. We are building major metal production. That's the key thing."

The company said production on the facility will ramp up in 2027, with full production planned for 2028. It's expected to bring 90 jobs at launch, and more than 200 when fully operational.

description:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) will fund $237 million for opportunities to expand domestic manufacturing and strengthen supply chains for critical electric grid components.
The funding opportunity, called Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance (Grid SCALED), is the first under DOE's Grid Supply Chain Program.
The program is authorized to provide up to $375 million to strengthen domestic supply chains for the manufacturing of distribution and power transformers, grid components and materials.
DOE anticipates additional funding announcements in 2027 to strengthen domestic supply chains for next-generation technologies, including solid-state transformers, and promote common equipment configurations to streamline manufacturing.
We’re putting American ingenuity to work, developing next-generation grid technologies that strengthen our domestic supply chain, help lower costs, and make our grid more reliable.
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) will fund $237 million for opportunities to expand domestic manufacturing and strengthen supply chains for critical electric grid components. The investment is expected to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers, lower electricity costs and improve grid reliability.

The funding will support projects in two areas:

Equipment refurbishment and reuse: Up to $50 million will support projects that promote the refurbishment and reuse of existing grid equipment and materials.

Domestic materials and components: Up to $187 million will support projects that increase the use of alternative materials and subcomponents sourced and manufactured in the U.S.

The funding opportunity, called Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance (Grid SCALED), is the first under DOE's Grid Supply Chain Program. The program is authorized to provide up to $375 million to strengthen domestic supply chains for the manufacturing of distribution and power transformers, grid components and materials.

DOE anticipates additional funding announcements in 2027 to strengthen domestic supply chains for next-generation technologies, including solid-state transformers, and promote common equipment configurations to streamline manufacturing.

Applicants must submit a concept paper by Nov. 20, 2026, to qualify to submit a full application. Full applications are due Feb. 8, 2027.

Critical equipment and components

In a recent quote, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, said, “President Trump is bringing American industry and manufacturing back home, including the critical equipment and components needed to power our nation. The Energy Department is investing in American-made technologies and modernizing our grid to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and deliver affordable, reliable, electricity.”

Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza, added, “America should never have to rely on foreign suppliers to keep the lights on. We’re putting American ingenuity to work, developing next-generation grid technologies that strengthen our domestic supply chain, help lower costs, and make our grid more reliable. The power to secure our energy future should be in our own hands.”

text:
Aurrigo International plc is set to deploy its technology into a live UK port for the first time after receiving up to USD$133,000 (£100,000) in funding. The company will trial its Auto-Shuttle electric vehicle at Portsmouth International Port to prove driverless tech can operate safely and reliably in a live, mixed-traffic port environment.

Backed by the Connected Places Catapult's Freight Innovation Fund, the project will transport people, baggage and freight on a 1km journey portside. These activities will generate evidence on reliability, journey times, interventions, energy use and integration, providing transferable learning for future freight operations and proving out a host of environmental, cost and operational savings.

Auto-Shuttle is an electric powered autonomous transit vehicle, which has been fitted with more than 20 different LIDARs and sensors to help it navigate complex and shared paths/roads.

Portsmouth International Port contributes USD$534 million (£400m) to the national economy and supports 5200 jobs across the UK. It handles roughly 2.9m tonnes of goods, worth an estimated USD$10 billion (£7.5bn), every year and is home to both cruise ships and regular ferry/channel island routes.

The Freight Innovation Fund is delivered by Connected Places Catapult on behalf of the Department for Transport. Each SME selected for the Accelerator Programme receives up to USD$133,000 (£10,000) to develop a detailed trial proposal. The next phase sees up to eight of the bids selecting to deploy their solutions at a port or logistic hub, with further funding awarded of up to USD$133,000 (£10,000) each.

It accelerates investment and, builds on Canada's energy and natural resource advantage, and helps Canadians get ahead. Budget 2026: Masters of our destiny builds on Canada's strengths to create a stronger, more independent, more competitive, and more affordable economy. It is a plan for growth that puts people at its heart and strengthens Canada's sovereignty and unity.

It accelerates investment, builds on Canada's energy and natural resource advantage, and helps Canadians get ahead. It invests in our communities, culture and natural heritage, advances reconciliation, and strengthens our sovereignty and security. And it does so with the fiscal discipline needed to build a stronger Canada for the future.

Budget 2026 catalyses growth:

Canada Strong Notes: Allowing Canadians to invest directly in the $25 billion Canada Strong Fund and gain a stake in nation-building projects.

Canada Growth Incentive: Helping high-potential businesses attract investment, scale and keep more capital in Canada, through a new tax exemption on up to $15 million in capital gains from eligible investments and an enhanced small business rollover.

Major Projects: Fully funding the Mackenzie Valley Highway, an 800 km all-season road in the Northwest Territories, and creating an entity with the expertise and resources to deliver major projects such as the Mackenzie Valley Highway and Taltson Hydro Expansion projects.

Productivity Mega Deduction: Strengthening Canada's tax competitiveness by lowering the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from 13% to 6.4%, encouraging businesses to invest, expand and increase productivity.

Invest in Canada: Expanding Invest in Canada to support its leadership role in investment attraction and delivering future Canada Investment Summits.

Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expansion: Investing $930 million to expand the SR&ED tax incentive program to include certain commercialisation expenses, helping Canadian businesses develop and bring to market new technologies.

Power Canada Strong – National Electricity Strategy: Investing over $50 billion to support the goal of doubling electricity grid capacity by 2050 to meet growing demand, while accelerating electrification.

Nuclear Energy: Investing $518.5 million in the Nuclear Energy Strategy to strengthen domestic supply chains and Canada's position as a global energy superpower.

Canada's electric vehicle charging infrastructure: Investing just over $634 million to make it easier and more convenient for Canadians to drive electric vehicles, including by supporting over 55,000 additional electric vehicle chargers in areas where the infrastructure is needed most.

Critical Minerals: Investing $2.3 billion in the Critical Minerals Strategy to promote domestic production and processing capacity and strengthen Canada's economic resilience.

Forest Sector Transformation Strategy: Providing $6.5 billion over six years, on a cash basis, to transform Canada's forest sector by strengthening fibre supply, modernizing facilities and boosting productivity, and supporting new large-scale projects and major transformations of existing facilities, from biorefineries and biofuel facilities to other facilities producing innovative forest products.

Budget 2026 Delivers for People:

2027 Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit Supplement: Introducing a one-time 50% increase for the 2026-27 benefit year delivered in early 2027, providing up to $339 for a single person without children and up to $679 for a couple with two children.

Nutrition North Canada: Expanding and stabilising funding for Nutrition North Canada and associated initiatives to lower the cost of imported foods and support local food harvesting and distribution initiatives in remote northern communities.

Refundable Canada Caregiver Credit: Supporting caregivers who help people in need remain in their homes and communities with a fully refundable tax credit that could lift 15,000 individuals out of poverty. Caregivers would receive up to $1,260 annually (for 2027, indexed thereafter).

Building the homes Canada needs: Investing $44.7 billion over 11 years on a cash basis to put Canada on a path to end homelessness within 10 years, expand non-market housing, and build a housing market that works for all.

Mental health and home and community care: Providing $1.2 billion in 2027-28 to extend federal funding agreements with the provinces and territories for mental health and addictions services and home and community care, helping Canadians access support, regardless of their ability to pay.

Build Canada Workers Benefit: Introducing the Build Canada Workers Benefit to keep more money in workers' pockets. Altogether, the enhanced benefit would help lift an estimated 240,000 people out of poverty.

National Heat Pump Rebate: Investing more than $2 billion to help up to 820,000 households switch to heat pumps. Together with other measures to improve energy efficiency, including retrofits in multi-unit residential buildings, these investments are projected to save Canadians more than $1 billion a year on energy bills once fully implemented.

More affordable mortgages: Establishing new regulations to enhance publicly available information on insured mortgage rates, allowing more Canadians to compare and shop for the best available rates.

Tax simplification: Launching the most ambitious effort in a generation to improve Canada's tax system, making it easier for Canadians to file, claim, and access the tax relief and benefits they are entitled to.

text:
“By being first in the G7 to build small modular reactors, Ontario is securing a first-mover advantage that translates into real contracts and good-paying jobs,” said Stephen Lecce, Minister of Energy and Mines. “Ontario industries are emerging at the centre of the global nuclear build-out, and this leadership is delivering wins for Canada’s economy and vital contracts for Canadian businesses. Nuclear energy is tariff-proof, which is why we are building at scale and for future generations. Our government’s efforts are turning best-in-class nuclear expertise into a competitive advantage, creating more than 18,000 jobs when we need them most.”

Ontario’s nuclear industry is tariff-proof and recession-proof. As global uncertainty and U.S. tariffs put pressure on the province’s key industries, the DNNP is opening new markets for tariff-impacted sectors, including steel and concrete. For example, as part of the 14 contracts announced today, Oakville-based Hooper Welding is supplying steel for structural modules used to build the DNNP, while Toronto-based St. Mary’s Cement is supplying concrete and operating a high-density concrete batch plant for the project.

More than 100 Canadian companies have already signed agreements with Ontario Power Generation (OPG) to deliver this first-of-a-kind project, establishing themselves as leaders in the growing domestic and global markets for new nuclear technologies. These companies are helping build the expertise, capacity and skilled workforce needed to deliver major nuclear projects at home and compete for opportunities in growing markets around the world.

As countries around the world undergo a major nuclear resurgence in search of reliable, affordable and secure electricity, Ontario’s first-mover advantage is making it the partner of choice to build the components these projects need. This advantage has secured new domestic manufacturing investment in Ontario, including Velan’s planned facility in Durham Region to build critical safety valves for SMRs in Europe, and BWXT Canada’s agreement to manufacture key SMR components in Ontario for Poland.

“Ontario is choosing to build out a secure, prosperous and energy-efficient future with Ontario companies driving growth across the province," said Robert Dietrich, Chief Financial Officer, Armstrong Fluid Technology. “Armstrong Fluid Technology has been delivering on these priorities since 1934. As a 100 per cent Canadian-owned supplier, Armstrong is proud to provide leading optimization technology to make buildings and critical infrastructure in Canada and around the world more energy efficient and sustainable for a net-zero future.”

Once complete, the four SMR units at the DNNP will deliver 1,200 megawatts (MW) of reliable, clean electricity, enough to power approximately 1.2 million homes. The construction, operation and maintenance of the four SMR units will add $38.5 billion to Canada’s GDP over the next 65 years. The government has worked with OPG to ensure that 80 per cent of project spending goes to Ontario companies, helping anchor the economic benefits of this generational investment in the province. The construction and operations will protect Ontario workers and jobs by sustaining an estimated 3,800 highly-skilled, good-paying jobs for the next 65 years.

SMRs play a central role in Energy for Generations, the government’s first-ever integrated energy plan to ensure Ontario has the reliable, affordable power it needs to power new homes and drive economic growth. The government’s integrated approach and record investments in energy infrastructure are also providing the certainty needed for Indigenous communities, municipalities, businesses and industry partners to invest confidently in Ontario’s future. With a clear path forward, the plan is not only meeting the demands of today, but it is protecting jobs, supporting workers and powering economic growth for generations to come.

description:

The bill’s provisions on transmission and ratepayer protections are strong and sorely needed, and they ought to be enacted.
“The bill seriously weakens the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act and guts the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
And the bill would make it significantly more difficult to moderate, regulate, or alter these actions later, regardless of what public health, climate destruction, or public sentiment demand.
Regardless of what the law says, we expect him to spend two more years on his reckless and costly fossil-fuel building spree while working to block clean energy.
text:
WASHINGTON — Next week, the U.S. Senate is set to debate and vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) (S. 5653), a compromise permitting reform deal. Ahead of the planned vote, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program, issued the following statement:

“We appreciate the effort and care Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich put into reaching a compromise to facilitate the buildout of desperately needed clean energy and protect ratepayers from Big Tech’s voracious data center binge. The bill’s provisions on transmission and ratepayer protections are strong and sorely needed, and they ought to be enacted. Unfortunately, the bill’s drawbacks are greater, more immediate, and more certain.

“The bill seriously weakens the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act and guts the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It fast-tracks the permitting of all manner of projects, then makes it virtually impossible to regulate or arguably even enforce existing rules against them, without an act of Congress. Among other effects, the bill will open the door to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a hasty and reckless buildout of data centers powered by fossil gas. And the bill would make it significantly more difficult to moderate, regulate, or alter these actions later, regardless of what public health, climate destruction, or public sentiment demand. The bill also includes massive giveaways to the mining industry.

“There is also the question of President Trump’s implementation. We do not trust that he will abide by the letter or intent of the law. Regardless of what the law says, we expect him to spend two more years on his reckless and costly fossil-fuel building spree while working to block clean energy. Under BAAJA, his actions will form most of the baseline by which courts assess whether future administrations are discriminating against a given form of energy.

“In the November 3 elections, voters across the country resoundingly rejected data centers. This is not the time to pass a bill that enables Big Tech to charge forward with them, powered by fossil fuels, over the objection of local communities.

“No less important, the makeup of Congress will change substantially in January. It is likely a much better deal can be reached then—one that enacts the laudable and important provisions in this bill, and more, without so many sacrifices.”

text:
This is the second commercial contract between the two companies for nuclear island engineering and design: in April, Fluor entered into a contract with X-energy to support the company's first proposed Xe-100 project at Dow's UCC Seadrift Operations in south Texas under the US Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program. The latest agreement builds on Fluor's ongoing work for the Texas project, the companies said, enabling them to incorporate learnings from one project into the next, with the aim of targeting long-term cost and schedule reductions through standardisation and repeatable project execution.

The Cascade facility is expected to deploy four of X-energy's Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled reactors, each with a capacity of 80 MWe, for a total capacity of 320 MWe, with the potential to scale to a total of 12 units.

Under the agreement, Fluor will provide engineering, design development, supply chain, estimating and project control services for the nuclear island scope of the Cascade facility. The value of the contract has not been disclosed, but Fluor said it will "recognise" the value in the third quarter.

Cascade Nuclear Partners, a joint venture of Kiewit Nuclear Solutions, Black & Veatch, and Aecon, is responsible for the conventional island and integrating requirements across the plant to support potential future phases of the project.

"Advanced nuclear technologies are poised to play a critical role in meeting growing energy demand while supporting decarbonisation goals," Fluor's Business Group President of Energy Solutions Pierre Bechelany said. "The Cascade Advanced Energy Facility represents an important step forward in the deployment of next-generation nuclear energy. Fluor is proud to bring decades of nuclear expertise and project execution experience to support X-energy and its partners in advancing this innovative project."

The Cascade facility is the first project in a collaboration between X-energy and Amazon launched in 2024, with the goal of deploying 5 GW of new nuclear capacity by 2039: utility American Electric Power and X-energy signed a joint development agreement to evaluate the potential second project, for 960 MWe of capacity at a former coal plant site in Indiana, in October.

Opponents however, cite the damage that would result from weakening the rules and the loss of recaptured gas.

“You can look at satellite feeds and see fossil fuel’s massive methane leaks that they’ve lied about for years. Rolling back methane pollution standards, Trump’s EPA once again delivers pay-to-play payback to [his] fossil fuel donors,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), in a statement, adding that the rule would increase energy bills as well as insurance costs from climate-change fueled disasters like flooding and fires.

State-level Responses

Some states are moving to setting their own standards, with nine adopting policies to regulate methane emissions in recent years, according to the State Climate Policy Dashboard database.

Colorado is the latest, finalizing regulation in September that mirrors much of the Biden-era rulemaking, as well as a separate prohibition on flaring.

The Biden administration introduced its proposed methane rule in 2023, which sought to reduce methane emissions through methods that included monitoring for leaks, setting zero emissions standards for certain equipment and eliminating gas venting. LAZ Parking and EverCharge, a subsidiary of indiGOtech (GO), have announced a joint venture to offer EV charging services for apartment and condominium residents. The partnership combines LAZ’s parking and real estate operations with EverCharge’s SmartPower management technology.

LAZ operates approximately 2.1 million parking spaces at 5,700 locations in 639 cities in the US and Canada. The company has established relationships with property owners and operators.

EverCharge’s SmartPower technology allows multiple chargers to share a building’s available electrical capacity, enabling up to five times as many charging ports to operate using the same power supply, compared to unmanaged charging. This can allow more residents to charge their vehicles without requiring major electrical upgrades.

EverCharge operates some 10,000 charging ports at over 1,000 multifamily residential sites.

The two companies plan to offer a multifamily charging service that provides charging solutions for residents without requiring property owners to manage the installation and operating process.

“LAZ has always been about more than parking,” said Alan Lazowski, Chairman and CEO of LAZ. “The future is charging right where people park. Our joint venture with GO expands our charging network to 25,000 ports in North America, and we’re just getting started. Our broader relationship with GO also gives us the opportunity to explore how the places we operate can evolve alongside electric and autonomous vehicles.”

“Multifamily dwelling charging represents one of the largest infrastructure opportunities in the transition to electric transportation,” said John Lin, CEO of EverCharge. “We’re a leader in deploying intelligent charging for this market, and we’re working with LAZ to bring our platform to more properties and drivers.”

Tire wear limits will also be introduced gradually to reduce microplastic pollution.
