title: Why Tesla is ending Cybertruck production for Cybercab - USA Today
description:
Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in mid-2027 to increase production of its Cybercab.
The decline in Cybertruck sales coincides with a broader 30% drop in overall electric vehicle sales.
"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk wrote.
The comments come as Tesla's Cybertruck sales have fallen 28% so far in 2026, according to new data released by Cox Automotive.
Why is Tesla shutting down Cybertruck production?
text:
Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in mid-2027 to increase production of its Cybercab.

Cybertruck sales have fallen 28% in 2026, according to data from Cox Automotive.

The decline in Cybertruck sales coincides with a broader 30% drop in overall electric vehicle sales.

Tesla is winding down production of its unconventional Cybertruck electric pickup truck to focus on the Cybercab, the company's CEO Elon Musk said in a Nov. 6 X post.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk wrote.

The comments come as Tesla's Cybertruck sales have fallen 28% so far in 2026, according to new data released by Cox Automotive.

Tesla is planning to expand its Robotaxi service to a "dozen or so states" by the end of the year, CEO Elon Musk told investors as his company was reporting first-quarter earnings on April 22.

Tesla said on its website that Cybercab will be a "purpose-built fully autonomous vehicle, will offer rides in your area in the future."

Musk has also said the robotaxi will be a big part in his company's "overall shift to an autonomous future."

Why is Tesla shutting down Cybertruck production?

Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in first three months of 2026, compared to 16,097 in the first three months of last year.

The vehicle was first introduced for the 2024 model year.

The Cybertruck sales decline came as overall electric car sales fell in the last few years, following President Donald Trump and Congress eliminating a popular EV $7,500 tax credit.

Carmakers sold 725,888 electric cars in the first nine months of 2026, according to data released Oct. 12 by Cox Automotive, which was down 30% from the over 1 million EVs they sold through the same period last year.

What to know about Tesla's Cybercab?

Tesla revealed in documents submitted to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in May that the Cybercab will have a fully electric motor. It will weigh 3,113 pounds and have a 48 kWh lithium-ion battery with a charge depleting range of about 418 miles.

Tesla said the Cybercab will be all-wheel drive and have 219 horsepower. The vehicle will have regenerative braking that is commonplace on most fully electric cars.

How will riding in Tesla Cybercab compare to the experience of being an Uber or Lyft passenger?

Tesla said rides in Cybercab robotaxi will be ordered using a cell phone app that is similar to the ones riders use now to search for Uber and Lyft rides.

The company says drivers will have create an account, and the app is currently only available on Apple iOS devices.

Tesla says drivers will wait for their Cybercab rides at a designated pickup location, and they will notified when the car arrives via the app. But there's one catch: In a Tesla Cybercab, there will no human driver behind the wheel to greet when you open the door.

Tesla says passengers will simply tap a "Start Ride" button when they enter the Cybercab cars to get their trip going. The company said riders will be able to personalize their Robotaxi experience with different features such as climate settings and seat position. They will also be able to stream much the Robotaxi app, and certain driver profile settings will carry over for Tesla vehicle owners.

It's an experience Zoox and Waymo riders have already grown accustomed to in select U.S. markets, providing some ready-made competition as Tesla enters the autonomous rideshare game.

What has Musk said about the future of the Cybertruck?

Musk told investors on Tesla's Jan. 28 earnings call that its unconventional Cybertruck electric pickup truck may be heading for an autonomous, commercial future.

In response to a question about whether he would be willing to design "a more conventional looking pickup" given the sluggish Cybertruck sales, Musk said on the January earnings call, "We will transition the Cybertruck line to just a fully autonomous vehicle."

"There’s obviously a market there for cargo delivery, like say like localized cargo delivery with a city, with a few hundred miles something like that," Musk said. "There’s a lot of cargo that needs to move locally within a city, an autonomous Cybertruck could be very useful for that."

Industry analysts have noted the impact of Musk's work with Trump in 2025 and staunch conservative political stances on the sales performance of the company's cars.

The Cybertruck in particular launched during the height of the 2024 presidential campaign, when Musk vocally supported Trump, and the cars became a symbol for some of shoppers' alignment with Musk and Trump's politics.

According to a November 2025 Yale University study, Tesla sold 1 million-1.26 million fewer vehicles between October 2022 and April 2025 than it otherwise would have without what the study's authors dubbed the "Musk partisan effect." The study found Musk's public political stances also helped to increase the sales of other automakers' electric and hybrid vehicles by 17-22% as drivers who were opposed to the CEO's politics fled to other EV manufacturers.

According to a poll released on Jan. 12 by EVs for All America, an advocacy group that works with car manufacturers to push U.S. and state lawmakers to adopt EV-friendly policies, 44% of people who said they are seriously considering buying an EV had a mostly unfavorable opinion of Musk.

name: Congress
title: Advice for California's Next Governor: Transportation - Legal Planet
description:
In this post, I’ll discuss our clean transportation strategies.
So what should Governor-Elect Becerra prioritize in this sector that impacts quality of life, job access, affordability, economic development, air quality, and climate change?
The Trump Administration and Congress have attacked California’s clean vehicle regulations.
Through support for litigation, partnership with the new Congress, and ambitious leadership at the California Air Resources Board, the Governor can help overcome this roadblock.
As the incoming Becerra Administration takes shape, transportation policy presents a key opportunity to address environmental and cost of living concerns together.
text:
Recommendations from CLEE’s policy roadmap for the incoming administration

Tuesday’s elections delivered a nationwide sweep of results with positive potential for climate and environmental policy.

The new Congress will have power to slow or reverse some of the Trump Administration’s attacks on federal clean air and clean water policy and the opportunity to reinstate some clean energy tax credits. State legislatures and governorships in places like Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas can tackle the data center question with an eye toward protection of communities and the environment. Even nationally low-profile bodies like the Georgia Public Service Commission will have the power to shift energy regulation more in favor of consumers and climate.

While these topics did not dominate the national conversation, the cost of gas and diesel–which sits at the core of the climate effort–did. And while the results here in California are perhaps not as surprising as the rest of the country, the environmental policy stakes of the leadership transition remain high.

As my CLEE colleague Louise Bedsworth discussed last week, CLEE and a group of expert partners developed a suite of environmental policy recommendations for the incoming governor, on topics ranging from electricity affordability to water sustainability. With Xavier Becerra now confirmed in that role, we will highlight groups of these recommendations in a series of posts over the coming weeks. In this post, I’ll discuss our clean transportation strategies.

Transportation was not a top issue during the gubernatorial race (though it’s difficult to say what was a top issue in this race) aside from the rising cost of gas and diesel resulting from the Iran War. Steve Hilton promised $3 gas and to dismantle the DMV (?), Becerra promised to stabilize prices and also indicated openness to relaxing vehicle electrification standards, they disagreed about the gas tax and replacements, and that was about it.

However, transportation was on the California ballot on Tuesday. Bay area residents approved Regional Measure RTM, which will provide nearly $1 billion per year to funding BART, Caltrain, SF Muni, and AC Transit service via a sales tax increase. San Francisco voters also approved Proposition H, a parcel tax that will raise an additional $160 million per year for SF Muni service. Meanwhile, Fresno voters appear to have rejected Measure S, which would have raised about $250 million per year for local transit services.

Despite a lack of candidate attention, transportation is perhaps the top climate issue for voters when viewed holistically: how we get around determines how we live. Access to a car or to quality transit is a key determinant of economic opportunity and quality of life. Overlong commutes dominate the weeks of far too many Californians who lack the latter but are priced out of urban centers. High fuel and insurance costs can displace other life necessities. And cars and trucks are the leading contributors to our climate and air quality crises.

So what should Governor-Elect Becerra prioritize in this sector that impacts quality of life, job access, affordability, economic development, air quality, and climate change? CLEE and our partners offered key strategies such as:

Facilitate leadership and coordination across transportation agencies. California spreads state authority for transportation matters across nearly a dozen agencies, ranging from Caltrans (highway construction and transportation planning) to the California Air Resources Board (vehicle emissions regulation and incentive funding) to the Governor’s Office of Business and Economic Development (clean vehicle market development and charging strategies). The Governor appoints leadership at all of these agencies and can direct them to take coordinated action prioritizing mobility, affordability, and emissions reduction.

Renew California leadership on vehicle electrification and explore legal innovations. The Trump Administration and Congress have attacked California’s clean vehicle regulations. Through support for litigation, partnership with the new Congress, and ambitious leadership at the California Air Resources Board, the Governor can help overcome this roadblock. Policies that focus on the cost and resilience benefits of grid-integrated vehicle batteries, address air quality within the often low-income districts that suffer from the air pollution from truck and logistics traffic, and consumer protection for drivers including EV buyers should be at the top of the list.

Preserve and expand public transit funding. Tuesday’s measures in the Bay Area provide a needed lifeline, but California’s public transit systems are suffering from low ridership and funding cuts across the board. Ensuring these systems–major rail networks like BART and LA Metro as well as rural bus services–maintain service is vital for both our sustainability goals and economic opportunity for those who do not have automobile access. The Governor can both support this baseline funding and work with the Legislature to expand service to serve communities and reduce emissions across the state.

These are just a few among many subject-matter recommendations we’ll be sharing in the coming weeks. As the incoming Becerra Administration takes shape, transportation policy presents a key opportunity to address environmental and cost of living concerns together. Doing so can continue California’s long record of leadership on this issue while shaping a new era of clean, equitable mobility.

name: Clean Energy
title: Why Countries Need National Plans to Manage the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF)
description:
This article makes the case for why countries need explicit planning for the transition away from fossil fuels, what these plans could address, and what considerations should shape countries’ plans.
These could include climate planning tools such as updated NDCs or just transition plans to core economic and sectoral plans such as long-term development strategies, national energy plans, or other national planning instruments.
Planning the transition away from fossil fuels can expand the scope for national planning and ask the questions that clean energy plans often leave unanswered.
Malaysia’s National Energy Transition Roadmap, published in 2023, is designed around the trilemma of energy security, affordability and environmental sustainability.
Whether pursued through roadmaps, NDCs, long-term strategies or other national planning tools, national TAFF planning can also inform wider debates on development, finance and economic resilience.
text:
In the span of just a few years, governments have watched a war in Ukraine upend Europe's gas supply and a war between the United States and Iran threaten the Strait of Hormuz, which carries a fifth of the world's oil. The pattern is hard to miss: Fossil-fuel dependence has become a recurring source of economic pain and strategic vulnerability.

While clean energy deployment has accelerated, few governments have developed explicit plans for managing fossil fuel consumption and, where relevant, shifts in fossil fuel demand and production. This matters because fossil fuel demand does not automatically fall when clean energy grows. Rapid growth in the absolute amount, or even the share, of clean energy may not lead directly to a decline in fossils, but rather serve at least partly to meet rising energy demand (from cooling, industrialization or data centers). Without such planning, governments risk treating fossil fuel decline as a by-product of clean energy growth rather than as a structural, economy-wide transformation that must be deliberately managed.

National planning for transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) can therefore set out how national fossil fuel use will evolve; how existing energy transition strategies can be integrated into a coherent whole; and how governments will manage the fiscal, infrastructure, investment and social dimensions of the transition. Given the necessary scale of the transformation over the coming decades and the uncertainties around how it will unfold, governments need plans that provide a long-term direction while enabling them to anticipate emerging risks and adapt to changing circumstances. While planning alone will not deliver the transition, it is a vital stepping stone to integrating such plans into more economic and sectoral planning, policies and investment choices.

This article makes the case for why countries need explicit planning for the transition away from fossil fuels, what these plans could address, and what considerations should shape countries’ plans. It also explores how COP31 and other international forums could help advance this agenda.

What Is National TAFF Planning and Why Is It Important?

National TAFF planning sets out how fossil fuel consumption and, where relevant, production, will evolve, how clean alternatives will scale, and how the macro-fiscal, social, infrastructure, and investment consequences of that shift will be managed.

Planning for the transition can be done through standalone plans or roadmaps, or embedded in a variety of policy instruments. These could include climate planning tools such as updated NDCs or just transition plans to core economic and sectoral plans such as long-term development strategies, national energy plans, or other national planning instruments. Regardless of the approach, TAFF planning needs to address the difficult choices and trade-offs that countries face in managing the transition alongside their broader economic and development implications.

TAFF plans can serve three practical functions. First, they can improve policy coherence by linking separate climate, energy, fiscal, industrial and just transition strategies in a common framework. Second, they can support domestic coordination by giving ministries and other stakeholders a shared reference point for making decisions that may otherwise be made in silos. And third, they can provide clear signals to investors and trading partners, helping reduce policy uncertainty and showing that a country is not only expanding clean energy, but also deliberately managing its fossil fuel dependence.

Why Are Existing Climate and Energy Plans Not Enough?

Most existing climate and energy plans miss the mark, focusing more on building the “clean” energy system than on governing the decline of fossil fuel systems. For example, WRI analysis finds that while many NDCs seek to expand clean energy, few explicitly focus on policies for the shifts away from fossil fuel use and production.

Some NDCs and other national plans include commitments to increase the share of non-fossil energy use, providing a helpful sense of direction for reducing fossil fuel dependence. But clean energy plans mainly focus on renewables, grids, storage, efficiency and electrification without necessarily addressing how existing fossil fuel systems will be managed.

Planning the transition away from fossil fuels can expand the scope for national planning and ask the questions that clean energy plans often leave unanswered. These include specific sectoral issues involving fossil-based power plants or oil demand for transport, as well as critical issues with the political economy and broader economic and social implications such as public revenues, subsidies, employment, regional economic impacts and decommissioning liabilities. A solar or wind energy target by itself does not tell a country how workers will transition or how changing fossil revenues will be managed.

Focusing on expanding clean energy can often draw more political support because it promises new investment, industries and jobs — all essential objectives. But planning for TAFF can be politically valuable by making the challenges and opportunities visible early and then addressing them squarely. Managing the transition also requires governments to confront risks that may emerge unevenly or abruptly as the energy system evolves. Volatile global markets, shifting demand and infrastructure tipping points can create sudden economic and social pressures, requiring ministries to develop stronger capabilities for anticipating, stress-testing and managing transition risks. Planning for TAFF can help make these vulnerabilities visible early, identify economic diversification opportunities, sequence reforms, develop support measures, and build broader coalitions around a managed transition rather than through fragmented policies and short-term crisis response.

Existing Plans Provide a Starting Point

National TAFF planning does not need to be built from scratch. Many countries already have parts of the architecture in place through NDCs, long-term strategies, plans to decarbonize power systems, subsidy reforms and just transition frameworks. IISD notes that at least 46 countries already have power-sector decarbonization plans. A growing number also have demand-side or decommissioning frameworks. The challenge is less about creating an entirely new planning tool than about integrating existing policies into a coherent framework that explicitly addresses the transition away from fossil fuels.

Countries are approaching this challenge in different ways, from explicit national TAFF roadmaps to broader energy transition strategies that provide important building blocks:

France, the Netherlands and Germany were the first three countries to develop a more explicit national TAFF roadmap in 2026. France’s TAFF roadmap, released at the Santa Marta conference, brings existing national climate and energy commitments under a fossil-fuel specific roadmap and sets end-of-consumption targets for coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and fossil gas by 2050 for energy purposes. The Dutch roadmap brings together existing and planned measures across different fossil fuels while stopping short of setting a single phase-out date. Germany’s roadmap also builds largely on its existing climate and sectoral policies and sets out how these contribute to transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045.

Colombia’s Just Energy Transition Roadmap in 2025 defines decarbonization trajectories and covers hydrocarbons, mining, electricity, new energy and demand management. It was built through a broad social-dialogue process involving communities, business and sectoral actors.

The United Kingdom’s carbon budget and clean power plans provide examples of economy-wide delivery and power-sector transformation, while its North Sea strategy engages more directly with the future of domestic oil and gas production.

Malaysia’s National Energy Transition Roadmap, published in 2023, is designed around the trilemma of energy security, affordability and environmental sustainability.

Ghana’s long-term energy transition framework and investment plan outlines a pathway to net-zero by 2060, across oil and gas, transport, cooking, industry and power.

At the regional level, Pacific Island countries have also begun developing a similar approach. Six Pacific governments adopted the Tassiriki Call for a Fossil Fuel Free Pacific in April 2026, setting out a common vision for 100% renewable energy and a just transition away from fossil fuels. Pacific ministers are now taking this forward through work on a regional TAFF roadmap. Other countries are beginning to explore similar approaches, with support from the NDC Partnership and Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance (BOGA).

None of these examples is a perfect template. But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan. National TAFF planning can help advance these pieces, identify what is missing, and ensure that the transition away from fossil fuels is treated not as an assumed by-product of clean energy deployment, but as an explicit and governed process.

What Questions Should TAFF Plans Answer?

There is no single template for national TAFF planning. Countries differ widely in their energy systems, economic structures, levels of development and exposure to fossil fuels. As a result, its design will necessarily vary and should reflect principles of equity and national circumstances while maintaining ownership, credibility and coherence. Emerging guidance, including recent guidance by IISD, suggest that credible TAFF planning needs to answer five core questions:

How will fossil fuel use and, where relevant, production evolve? Credible TAFF planning can set goals and a clear direction of travel while recognizing that countries will move at different speeds depending on national circumstances. In many developing countries, the pathways must also account for rising energy demand, access and affordability — where the transition must be designed as a development strategy as much as a decarbonization one, including through expanding clean, decentralized energy access. Goals may take the form of fuel-specific benchmarks, sectoral milestones or qualitative transition objectives, but their purpose is to provide a reference point against which policy, finance, governance, infrastructure and just transition measures can be designed and assessed.

How will the transition be financed and linked to economic diversification? TAFF plans can identify the investment needed to implement the transition, including for industrial conversion, decommissioning and site rehabilitation, worker support and regional diversification. It can also help prioritize investments, determine the respective roles of public, private, domestic and international finance, identify the enabling policies and institutions, support project pipeline development and specify appropriate financing instruments. For fossil fuel-dependent economies, this financing framework needs to be linked to a broader economic diversification strategy: identifying new sectors, export opportunities and domestic industries that can absorb capital and labor losses as fossil fuel revenues and jobs shifts. For many developing countries, high costs of capital can constrain investment in clean alternatives, making concessional finance, guarantees and other risk-sharing instruments particularly important. Fossil fuel-exporting economies face an additional challenge: financing economic diversification as export earnings, revenues and associated economic activity change.

How will macroeconomic and fiscal risks be managed? For exporting countries, this means explicitly addressing how revenues tied to extraction and exports will be replaced as fossil fuel income changes. Fossil fuel importers may also see changes in tax revenues and continued exposure to external price shocks. Geopolitical conflicts can fuel “fossilflation,” or fossil fuel-driven inflation that raises living costs and risks interest rate hikes, potentially constraining investment in clean energy. Central banks therefore have an important role in assessing these risks and their implications for monetary policy and financial stability. TAFF planning can help governments identify where these vulnerabilities lie, assess how they may evolve over time, and put in place the macroeconomic and fiscal measures needed to manage the transition without majorly destabilizing public finances or the broader economy.

How will workers, households, communities and regions be supported? TAFF plans should identify which workers, industries and regions face the impact of the transition. They should set out how these groups will be supported to ensure that economic restructuring does not deepen existing inequalities but instead minimizes costs, supports equitable sharing of opportunities and promotes decent work. This includes provisions for reskilling, retraining, early retirement, social protection, community investment and regional economic diversification, as well as reforms to fossil fuel subsidies that protect affordability and provide better- targeted support to vulnerable households. Participatory processes are also key. Meaningful engagements with workers and communities to build trust and ensure they have a role in shaping decisions for better outcomes, particularly in regions most exposed to transition impacts, are both important for procedural justice and political durability.

Who will be responsible for implementation and accountability? Making any plan operational requires cross-ministerial coordination, bringing finance, energy, industry, labor and regional subnational stakeholders under a shared framework, as well as clear institutional ownership, review cycles and robust monitoring systems. Such monitoring systems can track indicators related to changing fiscal and macroeconomic exposure to fossil fuels, shifts in economic and labor structures, adequacy of social safety nets for affected communities, availability of workforce transition programs, investment in cleaner economic sectors as well as small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and more. In large and regionally diverse economies, national TAFF planning should also be informed by subnational actors.

What Should Shape the Design of TAFF Planning?

Having the right content in a TAFF plan is one thing; whether it can be implemented depends on the political, financial and institutional realities countries actually face, as well as the wider global environment in which the transition unfolds. Countries will be managing these shifts amid volatile fossil fuel markets, geopolitical tensions, trade disruptions and rapidly changing energy value chains. TAFF planning therefore needs to be both grounded in domestic realities and robust enough to adapt as external conditions change.

Finance is often the most immediate constraint. For many developing economies, high debt burdens and the cost of capital limit their ability to invest in clean alternatives and economic diversification. Credible TAFF planning will therefore depend on these countries increasing their fiscal space and reducing the cost of capital, whether through debt restructuring or relief, recognition of a well-managed transition strategy in their credit rating, receiving concessional finance and international support, access to other forms of lower-cost capital and availability of risk-sharing arrangements such as guarantees.

Political economy is equally important. Subsidy reform, plant closures and industrial restructuring create visible losses, often before benefits arrive. Governments that have not prepared the ground politically will struggle to sustain them. Credible planning therefore needs to sequence reforms carefully, communicate clearly, bring incumbent industries and trade unions on board, and provide targeted protections for vulnerable workers and households.

Equity between countries should also shape TAFF planning from the outset. TAFF will not unfold at the same pace or in the same way across countries. For many developing and fossil fuel-dependent economies, the feasibility of transitioning will depend on energy access, fiscal space (including debt sustainability, access to international public and private finance, and domestic resources), and the ability to diversify before revenues fall. TAFF planning should therefore identify who is affected, who participates, how costs and benefits are shared, and how national circumstances shape the pace and sequencing of the fossil fuel transition.

Finally, implementation depends on state capacity and coordination. The transition is inherently complex and involves a large set of actors: line ministries, subnational governments, central banks, private investors, energy companies, workers and communities. Durable and decentralized governance structures, political buy-in, and stakeholder and community engagement are necessary for an effective governance of the transition.

What’s Next for National TAFF Planning?

Political momentum behind TAFF is building. At COP30 in Belem, more than 80 governments supported a global roadmap on transitioning away from fossil fuels. While the final negotiated decision did not include one due to a lack of consensus, the Brazilian COP30 Presidency committed to developing its own global TAFF roadmap, which they published just ahead of COP31. In April 2026, Colombia and the Netherlands hosted the first Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, which brought together 57 countries to discuss practical ways to manage the transition.

Under the Turkiye-Australia COP partnership, COP31 is explicitly being framed as an “Implementation COP,” with climate finance and the energy transition among its priority areas. That creates a natural opening for further progress on taking practical steps to transition away from fossil fuels.

Given the lack of consensus at COP30, COP31 may be better suited for advancing national TAFF planning through voluntary participation and coalition building rather than relying solely on a negotiated outcome. For example, a coalition of countries could arrive at COP31 with completed TAFF plans in hand, whether standalone roadmaps or embedded in existing plans and policy instruments, or with a commitment to produce them by COP32 in Ethiopia. Such a coalition should not be limited to a group of countries that are able to move fastest. Its credibility will depend on whether it includes, or at least creates space for, fossil fuel-dependent developing countries whose transitions require more finance, fiscal space, coalition-building and time.

These outcomes would not create new obligations. But they would help turn the political language of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” into something more concrete: country-owned strategies that show how governments intend to deliberately manage the fossil side of the transition in ways that are orderly, just, equitable and economically credible. COP32 in Ethiopia next year would then provide a useful checkpoint for assessing whether that planning effort is spreading beyond first movers.

Nor should this agenda of national TAFF planning remain confined to the COP process. The next TAFF conference, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland in the spring of 2027, could provide another opportunity for countries to present TAFF plans and announce commitments to develop them. More broadly, the fiscal and macroeconomic stakes of the transition are also increasingly relevant in other forums such as G20 discussions, BRICS and regional forums. Whether pursued through roadmaps, NDCs, long-term strategies or other national planning tools, national TAFF planning can also inform wider debates on development, finance and economic resilience.

text:
Transmission projects could become much easier to build.

Originally published in the Washington Post by Zachary Liscow, a professor at Yale Law School and former chief economist at the Office of Management and Budget, and Joseph Shapiro, a professor at the Energy Institute at Haas.

As the Senate takes up a landmark permitting bill next week, lawmakers will be asking themselves a simple question: What happens if we make it easier to build interstate power lines? They don’t have to wonder about the answer. Congress ran a version of that experiment nearly 80 years ago.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the most comprehensive permitting overhaul Congress has ever seriously considered. Nineteen former economic and national security officials, including former treasury secretaries Janet L. Yellen and Steven Mnuchin, sent a letter to congressional leaders calling the bill “the most significant bipartisan legislative effort that Congress has undertaken in decades” to address America’s permitting challenges.

“Our inability to build threatens our national security and economic growth,” they wrote. It takes more than four years for a new power plant to move from requesting grid connection to producing power, more than double the wait time in the early 2000s. Families pay for these delays when cheap power can’t reach them.

The bill’s opponents have raised environmental concerns, and senators are weighing those against the legislation’s potential upsides — one of which is the effect of removing barriers to transmission-line construction. So far, most estimates of that payoff have come from models making forward-looking guesses.

But better evidence comes from an earlier time Congress tried this.

In 1947, Congress gave natural gas pipeline companies the power of federal eminent domain, preventing a single state from blocking the construction of a pipeline running through it. Oil pipeline companies were not granted the same power.

Both industries were riding the same postwar boom. But, according to calculations in our new paper with Heidi Williams, annual additions to gas pipeline mileage rose to nearly six times the pre-1947 baseline, while oil pipeline construction stayed steady. Congress gave long-distance gas infrastructure a federal override, and construction boomed.

Today, electric transmission works the way oil pipelines did then. An interstate gas pipeline has its route approved by one federal regulator often with the authority to largely override a holdout state. An interstate power line, however, typically needs approval from every state it crosses. That gives each state a veto over projects in which the benefits often flow mostly to its neighbors.

New England has experienced the consequences. In 2016, Massachusetts attempted to import Canadian hydropower. New Hampshire, which would have hosted the power lines without getting the same influx of cheap energy, rejected it. A second route through Maine was blocked in a referendum and didn’t deliver power until January. Meanwhile, Massachusetts households paid some of the highest electricity prices in the country.

Texas is an example of what construction looks like when other states can’t interfere. Its grid sits almost entirely inside its own borders. In 2005, Texas set out to connect its windiest regions to its biggest cities, ultimately stringing more than 3,500 miles of transmission. Between 2009 and 2014, the share of wind power going to waste fell from 17 percent to 0.5 percent. The new wind power also cut the premium that fossil fuel plants could charge at peak hours, reducing their excess profits by $237 million a year, according to one study. Texas now generates more wind and solar power than any other state, nearly twice California’s total in 2024.

Some environmental advocates will read the 1947 history as a warning: Give Washington a veto over states, and you get more fossil fuel infrastructure. But they have it backward. Since 1947, interstate gas pipelines have been able to use federal eminent domain to bypass holdout states. Because transmission lines don’t have the same override, today’s siting rules tilt toward gas and away from renewable energy.

A gas plant can be built near the city it serves, with its fuel arriving by pipeline. But the best wind and solar resources are often hundreds of miles from population centers, and their power has to travel by transmission line. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, roughly 85 percent of the generation and storage capacity seeking to connect to the grid is from solar, wind and batteries. How much of those clean-energy resources get tapped depends heavily on whether transmission lines can be built.

For nearly 80 years, gas pipelines have been able to get past holdout states. Beginning Nov. 9, senators will decide whether power lines can, too.

text:
This past October was the warmest on record, about 1.76 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than temperatures before the widespread burning of fossil fuels began driving climate change. As we head into what is expected to be another historically warm winter, mitigating the worst impacts of the climate crisis has never been more urgent.

The Senate’s proposed permitting bill, the so-called Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), purports to accelerate clean energy deployment with the scale and speed needed to fight the climate crisis. But the stakes are too high not to fully examine whether the bill’s handouts to the oil and gas industry (among other industries) will cancel progress made elsewhere.

The bill threatens to create a set of laws under which oil and gas development essentially becomes untouchable.

Provisions in Sec. 1401 that seek to guarantee “project certainty” are highly problematic because they will make federal oil-and-gas leases virtually impossible to overturn, even if they’re issued in violation of law. While proponents of the bill emphasize that it covers “permits,” it’s important to note that the language is much broader, covering federal “authorizations,” “permits,” “records of decision,” and “any other approval or order” necessary for a project. Courts would likely view an oil and gas lease to be a federal authorization necessary for a fossil-fuel company to obtain the right to extract oil and gas on federal lands or waters. Thus, the certainty provisions can be read to cover federal oil and gas leases just as they would other federal approvals.

Two examples of what this could mean in practice are the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska and Chaco Canyon National Historic Park in New Mexico. Both places hold enormous cultural and historic significance to Tribal stakeholders with ancestral ties to those lands. Because of the permitting bill’s “project certainty” provisions, oil and gas leasing decisions made in either the Arctic Refuge or Chaco Canyon would be incredibly hard, if not impossible, for a future administration to undo. Even if it were possible, you can’t re-create a cultural landscape once it’s been industrialized.

Moreover, the Trump administration is proposing to vastly expand offshore oil and gas leasing to areas, such as the California and Florida coasts, where public opinion overwhelmingly opposes it. By making federal approvals so difficult to reverse, the bill’s “project certainty” provisions would leave states and local communities with very little ability to stop this destructive fossil fuel development.

There’s a difference between providing certainty for lawful decisions and making federal actions effectively irreversible. Congress can promote predictability without eliminating agencies’ ability to correct mistakes, respond to new information, protect cultural resources, and comply with court rulings. This bill goes far beyond certainty and risks creating permanence, even for deeply flawed decisions.

Sec. 1402 of the bill would create a disturbing new system where the oil industry can claim it is the “victim” and get paid for it.

To understand this provision, it’s useful to reflect on the concept of “disparate impacts” from the world of environmental justice. The phrase conveys the reality that many communities are overly burdened by industrial pollution; most often, lower-income communities of color shoulder a disproportionate burden compared with whiter and more affluent neighborhoods. One of the most prominent clusters of disproportionately impacted communities is along the Gulf Coast, where oil refineries and petrochemical facilities process raw products shipped in by oil tankers from offshore oil-drilling platforms. Because of the massive volume of toxic pollutants released into the air, such as benzene, formaldehyde, and chloroprene, nearby residents face a localized cancer risk that is up to 50 times higher than the national average.

Under this bill, the fossil fuel industry would be able to sue a future administration for so-called “disparate treatment” if it is not awarded a similar number of federal permits for fossil fuel development projects as it received under the Trump administration. A company could argue in court that it was treated differently from other energy projects and seek compensation from taxpayers for the project’s expected value. As a result, taxpayers could be on the hook for paying companies not to develop based on future losses calculated solely by that company.

The bill tilts the playing field even further toward approving oil and gas projects by establishing a five-year “lookback” period as the baseline for determining whether oil and gas companies have been treated “unfairly.”

The difference between the Trump administration’s approach and past administrations is significant. For example, in 2024, the Biden administration finalized a federal offshore drilling program with just three lease sales. In 2025, the Trump administration proposed 34(!) offshore lease sales, including in coastal areas that have never been offered for leasing.

By using this period as the benchmark, the bill effectively enshrines the Trump administration’s unusually aggressive leasing approach as the “appropriate level of oil and gas development” standard against which future decisions will be judged. This so-called “disparate impact” provision would allow oil companies to seek taxpayer-funded compensation by claiming they were harmed whenever a future administration approves fewer permits or leases than those being given to other industries, such as wind or other renewable industries.

There is way, way more.

The bill proposes major changes to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), enacted in 1970 after the Santa Barbara oil spill to prevent similar disasters from happening ever again. The bill would severely limit communities’ ability to have their concerns heard and considered during the decision-making process as required under NEPA. Under BAAJA, many fossil fuel projects are exempted entirely from the NEPA statute. If BAAJA passes, there will be minimal review, no opportunity for public input, and even courts will have little ability to stop projects that fail to comply with the law.

Similarly, changes to the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) will make it far more likely that oil-and-gas companies will simply ignore the process of consulting with tribes to learn how their plans might adversely affect cultural resources – a process currently required by law. BAAJA’s proposed changes to NEPA, the NHPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act would reduce public input, Tribal consultation, wildlife and clean water protections, and state and Tribal authority over harmful projects. These are just a few of the many anti-environmental provisions in this bill.

Every member of Congress is aware that rising carbon-dioxide emissions lead to a hotter planet. When a bill includes this many handouts to the oil and gas industry, it begs the question of whether provisions that shield fossil fuel projects from meaningful review and challenge will outweigh any clean energy benefits the bill contemplates.

From our point of view, the answer is a resounding No.

text:
Will Democrats’ midterms triumph put wind back in sails of the renewables sector?

After years as collateral damage in Donald Trump’s war on climate action, the Democrats’ sweeping triumph in the US midterm elections has emerged as a victory for the global renewable energy industry too. Across the world’s financial centres the market value of renewable energy developers climbed as the election results confirmed the Republicans had lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives. For the world’s largest offshore wind developer, Ørsted , the shift in power could spell a reprieve from the White House’s assaults on the Danish company’s multibillion-dollar offshore wind investments off the north-east US coast. Ørsted’s market value jumped by almost 10% within hours of the Democratic victory, before closing nearly 5% higher.

The share price of other European renewables companies active in the US also climbed. Portugal’s EDP Renewables and the French utility Engie rose by more than 3%. Shares in Germany’s RWE added about 1%. The clean energy market rally marks a modest boost for Ørsted, which has lost more than 70% of its market value since Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and resumed his salvoes against the industry as it struggled against fast-rising interest rates and supply chain pressures.

The White House has levelled multiple stop-orders against Ørsted’s Revolution Wind project since the re-election of Trump, a vocal supporter of the fossil fuel industry , who has repeatedly opposed the development of “ ugly, costly and inefficient ” windfarms in the US and abroad. View image in fullscreen Rotor blades and other parts for Ørsted’s Revolution Wind project, which has faced multiple stop-orders from the White House since Trump’s re-election Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters The impact has been chilling for the burgeoning US renewables sector too.

The US is home to renewable energy projects with a combined capacity of 388 gigawatts, or enough to power more than 83m American homes. The sector also directly employs more than 400,000 people across the country. This fleet of wind, solar, hydro and geothermal power projects has made up about 30% of the electricity generated across the US this year – well below the 50% share across the EU and China’s 40%. While there is no binding US-wide clean energy target, there are 24 states, plus the District of Columbia, with plans to achieve 100% clean electricity or net zero carbon emissions between 2035 and 2050.

But there has been growing disquiet over whether the forecast surge in electricity-hungry AI datacentres poses a threat to green targets by increasing the US reliance on gas power plants – and energy costs. “This was unquestioningly an energy election,” said Brenda Shaffer, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global Energy Center. Rising concerns over energy costs and the looming impact of datacentres on energy supplies had played a key role in Republican defeat, she said.

The Democrats’ decisive control of the US House of Representatives and its majority in the Senate may reduce the risk of further political interference and bring fresh confidence to the US renewable energy industry, according to market analysts. The Democratic house would be able to block further repeals of solar and wind tax credits, said Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist at the consultancy Rystad Energy. Battery storage credits would also now have a stronger defender in budget negotiations, and the administration’s roughly $4bn in offshore wind lease buybacks would face greater scrutiny, he added. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion While it was too early to call this a turning point for US offshore wind, said Tancrede Fulop, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar in the Netherlands, the election outcome might lower the risk of further regulatory disruption and provide a more stable backdrop for projects under development.

“For companies that have spent the past few years dealing with regulatory delays and shifting political priorities, a more supportive backdrop should provide some much-needed confidence around projects already under development,” he said. This in turn may ease investor jitters around regulatory uncertainty and support confidence in future project returns, according to analysts at Barclays, which could make new US renewable energy projects cheaper to finance.

The future was even brighter for developers hoping to build new onshore renewable energy projects, including batteries, which are typically decided at state level, said Shaffer. A string of Republican states have turned blue – including Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina – potentially ushering in greater support for clean energy investments. The “blue wave” had made it clear that “affordable, reliable power is a priority”, according to Jason Grumet, the chief executive of the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

Earlier in May, Meta and EDPR NA announced the deal. Under the agreement, the tech company signed a pact to support the clean energy the latter produces. Cypress Knee is the third such project among them, with Meta’s commitment to buy 545 MW from EDPR NA.

​To offset its carbon emissions, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company pledges long-term power purchases of cleaner energy. This contributes to the company’s larger goal of matching 100 percent of its annual electricity use with renewable energy generation.

​Beyond providing reliable energy to support America’s power grid, the Kansas project is expected to boost jobs and strengthen the state’s economy.

​”As energy demand continues to rise, projects like Cypress Knee Solar help strengthen grid reliability while creating jobs, generating meaningful local revenue, and delivering long-term benefits to the communities that host them,” said EDPR NA CEO Sandhya Ganapathy.

​The company estimates that the new solar farm project, once completed, is likely to bring $25 million in revenue over its lifetime.

Meta’s previous solar power purchases

​Last month, the Silicon Valley company also bought long-term power purchase agreements for a 203 MW solar project in Indiana from the Spanish renewable energy company Zelestra.

​The project is being built on reclaimed land from former coal mining operations in southwest Indiana and is expected to go live by 2027.

​More and more data centers are being built across the country to provide services such as instant search results and streaming videos to hundreds of followers on social media platforms, and they are massive consumers of electricity. With the recent addition of artificial intelligence (AI) services, tech companies are building even larger data centers to train and run AI models in the future.

​To counter their energy consumption needs from fossil fuels, the tech giants are investing in sustainable energy generation.

​Two years ago, Meta secured 300 MW of clean solar energy for its Texan data center from a Boston-based renewable energy supplier, Longroad Energy.

text:
The following blog is part of a series examining specific provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Clean Air Task Force is taking a close look at the bill to identify opportunities to strengthen its provisions, address potential gaps, and improve its effectiveness in meeting the country’s energy needs reliably and affordably.

As electricity demand grows and discussions around permitting and energy infrastructure continue, improving the process for connecting new generation to the grid will be increasingly important to meeting the country’s energy needs. CATF’s new report on interconnection queue reform does a deep dive into key principles necessary for getting new energy resources online more quickly and efficiently, and evaluates how several existing planning processes measure up to these ideals. The analysis offers a practical framework for policymakers, regulators, and grid operators to reduce unnecessary delays, improve planning, and make more efficient use of existing grid infrastructure.

Provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) point toward a better interconnection framework. In particular, the bill’s consolidated planning provisions align with CATF’s view that linking interconnection planning with transmission planning processes will improve system outcomes. However, providing additional resources and clearer direction to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) is needed to improve the odds of implementing BAAJA successfully, particularly given the challenges facing independent agency action in a post-Slaughter, post-Loper Bright, and post-Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) world.

We therefore recommend that Congress build on existing BAAJA text to provide FERC with more detailed direction to implement policies most likely to improve interconnection outcomes. Below, we outline suggested improvements with explanations for each. These recommendations are intended to provide extra detail and clarity for FERC, transmission planners, and courts, increasing the odds that this critical reform will succeed in unlocking stalled interconnection queues.

***

The draft BAAJA bill text as of November 5, 2026, includes a short provision requiring a “Consolidated Planning Process” (CPP), as a new section 318 in the Federal Power Act. The bill text provides that within 18 months of its enactment, FERC must issue a rule requiring each transmission planning region to “file a consolidated interconnection and regional transmission planning process that –

Jointly evaluates electric transmission facilities and the generating capacity reasonably anticipated to be needed to meet future forecasted demand and forecasted generation over the next 20 years;

Routinely identifies and publishes resource and fuel-neutral planned interconnection locations for generating capacity and an upfront, fixed, zonal, per-megawatt cost for each planned interconnection location; and

Establishes a streamlined generator cluster study process with a single decision point, meaningful and nonrefundable financial security, and withdrawal penalties sufficient to deter speculative projects.”

Transmission planning regions would be required to submit their consolidated planning process to FERC within two years of the bill passing and would be required to update the plan at least every two years.

This provision may be intended to model the Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP’s) own Consolidated Planning Process, which we rated highly when we evaluated it in our report against key interconnection reform principles. When applying those same principles to BAAJA’s provision, we find the provision needs additional specificity to receive the same high marks. CPP is a detailed program that combines holistic, scenario-based long-term transmission and interconnection planning. The combined program assesses how numerous factors will influence transmission and interconnection needs, evaluates the costs and benefits of potential solutions, and sets procedures for project selection and cost allocation. SPP’s program essentially combines, streamlines, and improves the transmission and interconnection planning requirements under FERC Orders 1920 and 2023. BAAJA’s CPP, in contrast, currently lacks the same level of detail. As a result, the program’s impact will depend on FERC’s discretionary implementation (and, to the extent FERC’s action under the provision is ever challenged, the discretion of a reviewing court).

Our research shows that transmission and interconnection planning should ideally be consolidated and co-developed. The BAAJA CPP provision is in an entirely separate section from, and makes no reference to, BAAJA’s regional and interregional transmission sections. It also does not reference existing 20-year transmission and interconnection planning requirements under FERC Orders 1920 and 2023 – nor the SPP CPP itself. Rather, it mandates that FERC issue a new rule meeting BAAJA’s specific requirements – creating the possibility of an additional, specialized process added to all the others, instead of streamlining multiple existing planning processes into one combined process.

Additionally, unlike the more comprehensive language found in BAAJA’s other transmission provisions, the BAAJA CPP establishes three broad requirements but leaves all necessary details on how to meet these requirements to FERC.

For example, BAAJA’s CPP provision does not explicitly require transmission providers to use Order 1920 long-term transmission planning in their consolidated plans. It also contains a number of essential yet undefined terms such as “evaluates,” “reasonably anticipated,” “forecasted,” and “planned interconnection location,” and does not require the study of interconnection needs per se. Subparagraph (2) (see above) does not actually require the planned interconnection locations to be informed by the results of the evaluation in subparagraph (1), nor does it provide any basis for selecting the locations or allocating their costs. And while planning regions must “routinely” identify planned interconnection locations, that timeline is unbounded. Because most transmission owners profit by building more, not less, they have strong economic incentives to minimize the efficiency of transmission and interconnection processes. Consequently, BAAJA CPP’s lack of detail and clear requirements enables incumbent transmission owners to legally comply with its requirements through a bare minimum of effort that largely preserves the status quo.

These examples illustrate a broader issue with BAAJA’s approach given institutional constraints: insufficient detail may hinder implementation of an otherwise well-intended provision. Particularly in the context of the energy system, certainty that survives administrations is critical, as building out the grid takes years and involves long-term planning. To provide that certainty, laws must use clear, specific language that mandates good planning practices; otherwise, consumers and industry will not be able to rely on it. Recent Supreme Court decisions underscore this point.

After Loper Bright,1 courts (rather than agencies with subject matter expertise) interpret ambiguous language in statutes. As a result, Congress must—even moreso now than before Loper Bright—use unambiguous, precise language in statutes or risk ceding the law’s core meaning to the judiciary. And the Supreme Court’s decision in Slaughter2 called into question the independence of agencies like FERC, which has maintained some core policy consistency across administrations. Indeed, even before Slaughter, FERC has seen wide swings in policy-based rulemaking between administrations that have had significant impacts on the energy system, such as the expansion of Minimum Offer Price Rules that artificially elevated the capacity market prices of state supported clean energy generation in 2018 and 2019 that were rescinded in 2021. To avoid policy swings in areas that require long-term certainty and durability, Congress must provide agencies with concise, unambiguous instructions that limit discretionary interpretation.

Congress can strengthen the current Consolidated Planning Process section with just a few edits. Below is a sample redline, followed by explanations of the edits.

‘‘(a) CONSOLIDATED GENERATION AND TRANSMISSION PLANNING.—Not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (referred to in this section as the ‘Commission’) shall issue a rule requiring each transmission planning region (as defined in section 225(a)) to file a:

(1) consolidate interconnection and Order 1920 regional transmission planning into one process that—

‘‘(A) no less than every 3 years, as part of the Order 1920 planning process, jointly evaluates electric transmission facilities and interconnection needs necessary to efficiently and rapidly connect the generating capacity reasonably anticipated to be needed to meet future forecasted demand and forecasted generation over the next 20 years; and

‘‘(B) routinely uses this joint evaluation to identifyies and, assess, and select locations on the grid for interconnection facilities that maximize the efficient connection of multiple generating resources, and annually publishes these locations as resource and fuel-neutral “planned interconnection locations” for generating capacity, and an upfront, fixed, zonal, per-megawatt cost for each planned interconnection location, before the interconnection application window opens; and

‘‘(2) an amended interconnection application process with establishes a streamlined generator cluster study process with a single decision point, meaningful and nonrefundable financial security, and withdrawal penalties sufficient to deter speculative projects.

Explanation of suggested redline edits:

First, given that the purpose of consolidated planning is to efficiently combine long-term transmission planning and interconnection planning, Congress should clarify that planners must use the existing Order 1920 long-term planning to evaluate transmission and generation, such that it is all one “consolidated” process—as SPP does. This clarifies that transmission providers should not create a separate transmission planning process, as the current draft suggests.

Second, Congress should set firm planning intervals, rather than using the more open-ended term, “routinely.” A 3-year requirement mirrors the SPP CPP cycle, which does a consolidated transmission and interconnection planning evaluation (using 1920) every 3 years.

Third, in new subparagraphs (A) and (B) above, it is critical to require use of the combined planning process to identify and select the planned interconnection locations, which the current draft does not connect. Such a disconnect opens the door for transmission providers to minimize the number of interconnection points or place them in a way that favors some resources or customers over others, independent of holistic system needs.

Fourth, because the current version does not define “planned interconnection location,” it is not clear what that term means and leaves it up to FERC or planners to decide. We therefore propose defining “planned interconnection locations” in paragraph (B) as “locations on the grid that most efficiently connect multiple generating resources.”

Fifth, we also propose clarifying that planned interconnection locations should be updated and published annually. This mirrors SPP’s CPP, which updates its planned interconnection locations as part of its annual CPP-10 (10-year planning horizon) process. It is important to require planning regions to identify and update these locations at set intervals, since interconnection application periods are often annual.

Sixth, Congress should explicitly require upfront costs to be set and published before the interconnection application opens—which is a central feature of SPP’s process. Ensuring applicants know whether they can meet the requirements of interconnection is a core need to speed connection and lessen queue withdrawals.

Finally, new subparagraph (2) recognizes that the interconnection application process itself will be separate from consolidated interconnection and transmission planning. Putting the number (2) here (and a (1) above) means FERC is still directed to issue one rule, but transmission planning regions are directed to do two things: (1) submit one consolidated Order 1920-based transmission and interconnection planning process; and (2) submit an amended interconnection application process.

* * * *

Our suggested edits follow from decades of litigation experience demonstrating that every word matters when it comes to building durable policies that all stakeholders can rely on and safely invest in—a goal we all share. As our report details, consolidated planning by organizations like SPP and CAISO can dramatically improve interconnection planning and implementation. Making this a national requirement would be a massive win for everyone—but only if we get it right.

CATF looks forward to working with Congress, FERC, and other stakeholders to advance these recommendations and develop an interconnection framework that gets new energy resources online more efficiently, makes better use of existing grid infrastructure, and helps meet the country’s growing energy needs.

title: National Review: Congress Seeks a Shot Clock on the Permitting Fast Lane
description:
Congress is on the verge of fixing one of the strangest defects in federal permitting: an environmental review designed to be fast that has no time limitation.
The bill was introduced only six weeks after new research from the Pacific Legal Foundation (PLF) identified essentially the same flaw in federal geothermal permitting.
Congress missed on solving this problem the last time it reformed the federal permitting system.
CXs are supposed to reduce the time and burden of federal review for projects unlikely to have significant environmental effects.
Congress deserves credit for identifying an erroneous feature of federal permitting and proposing a fix.
text:
Congress is on the verge of fixing one of the strangest defects in federal permitting: an environmental review designed to be fast that has no time limitation.

Introduced on September 30, the Senate’s new Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would, among many other permitting changes, impose a one-year deadline on federal permitting decisions for certain energy and infrastructure projects that do not require an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.

The bill was introduced only six weeks after new research from the Pacific Legal Foundation (PLF) identified essentially the same flaw in federal geothermal permitting. The study found that the supposed “fast lane” under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) — categorical exclusions (CXs) — sometimes took longer than Congress ordinarily allows the more intensive environmental assessment process to take.

Congress missed on solving this problem the last time it reformed the federal permitting system. In 2023, the Fiscal Responsibility Act imposed a one-year deadline on environmental assessments and a two-year deadline on environmental impact statements. But it left CXs, which are assumed to be much faster than the other two processes, without any deadline at all.

CXs are supposed to reduce the time and burden of federal review for projects unlikely to have significant environmental effects. In fact, the Trump administration recently issued a CX-first policy intended to relieve “excessive permitting burdens” and “help decrease project delays.” Yet today, a project placed in the CX fast lane can theoretically remain there longer than a project subjected to a far more intensive review.

And that happens.

PLF examined 133 geothermal exploration projects, including 88 approved through CXs. Eighteen percent of those CXs took more than 200 days to approve, 8 percent took more than a year, and 6 percent took more than a year and 100 days.

At first glance, one might assume that projects facing the longest delays were unusually large or environmentally consequential. But the available data suggest otherwise.

The PLF study found virtually no relationship between delay and project size. Among CXs, neither the amount of land disturbed nor the number of wells drilled meaningfully predicted how long review would take. Moreover, CXs are available precisely because an agency has determined that the activity is unlikely to have significant environmental effects.

Consider Nevada’s Hinds Temperature Survey. The project proposed taking basic subsurface temperature measurements at 35 locations. A vehicle would drive a 1.5-inch-wide steel rod roughly 50 feet into the ground to measure underground heat. The rod would then be removed, allowing the hole to collapse naturally or be filled. It required no new roads and would disturb less than one square meter of ground in total — about the size of a bath towel. Yet federal approval took one year and 182 days.

That is not careful environmental review scaling with project scope and intensity. At the very least, we should question whether long reviews simply reflect greater environmental risk.

CX delays likely make energy more expensive for Americans than it otherwise would be. Every project in the PLF study was geothermal exploration — the early work needed to locate and test geothermal resources that can provide clean, around-the-clock electricity. But permitting barriers make that exploration slower and more expensive. A Department of Energy analysis found that faster permitting alone could more than double geothermal capacity by 2050. Beyond geothermal, studies have found that permitting delays constrain a wide variety of energy infrastructure, contributing to higher costs and greater price volatility for consumers.

Enter the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the bipartisan permitting bill now reviving hopes for faster infrastructure development and cheaper energy.

For projects involving federal permits or authorizations but no environmental assessment or impact statement, the BAAJA would require agencies to make their permitting decisions within one year. Projects that avoid the National Environmental Policy Act’s more intensive forms of review would finally get a time limit of their own.

A one-year deadline is not perfect. Small projects searching for reliable, clean energy that are unlikely to affect the environment should ideally obtain government approval in a matter of months, if that. But one year is still a dramatic improvement over the open-ended timetable that exists today.

Congress deserves credit for identifying an erroneous feature of federal permitting and proposing a fix. Now it must follow through: preserve this important provision of the bill and pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

text:
A rare-earth facility to be built at the former Kodak Park is in line for $54.2 million in combined state and local government assistance.

Much of the package aiding Massachusetts-based Phoenix Tailings consists of tax credits and exemptions, rather than direct funding, according to the company. The total does not include investment to upgrade power infrastructure by RED-Rochester, which oversees park utilities. The railroad spur serving the 1600 Lexington Ave. facility also will require investment.

The forthcoming facility, announced last month, would cull the highly sought-after metals from mine waste and other industrial sources at an Eastman Business Park industrial warehouse complex in Greece.

Phoenix's capital outlay is estimated at $375 million, according to Gov. Kathy Hochul. But the company estimates its total costs, including needed chemicals and other operational expenses, at $600 million.

The combined public commitment, announced by Phoenix on Thursday, "underscores New York’s commitment to the project and bipartisan support for expanding U.S. production of critical materials," a company statement read.

Those rare earth metals are key in the production of electric vehicles, electronics, and defense equipment, but China currently controls most of the supply.

Local operations are scheduled to ramp up in 2027, with full production planned for 2028. The Eastman Business Park facility is projected to support 90 jobs at launch, and more than 200 when fully operational.

The award breaks down in general terms as follows:

Up to $3 million in performance-based tax credits through Empire State Development’s Excelsior Jobs Program

$15.9 million in New York State investment tax credits.

$35.3 million in tax savings on eligible equipment and construction materials, including local tax breaks, along with anticipated funding for power infrastructure improvements serving the project.

The company anticipates additional support for equipment purchases and workforce training through county programs.

Phoenix's Greece facility is part of the company's larger $1.2 billion "Freedom Project" described as "an integrated separation-and-metallization platform designed to close a critical gap in U.S. midstream rare earth processing capacity.

The Trump administration has additionally committed more than $550 million combined to support the company.

“Building America’s rare earth supply chain is a national security imperative and bipartisan government priority,” Phoenix Chief Strategy Officer Pat Kumashiro said in a prepared statement. “We are excited to see federal, state, and local stakeholders collaborate to support domestic production of the critical materials America needs.”

The company statement described Freedom Separation as "designed to process more than 18,000 tons of rare earth feedstock annually, producing more than 4,400 tons of separated rare earth oxides at full capacity for downstream production."

The project, the company said, "is designed to strengthen access to domestic processing for America and her allies while reducing reliance on foreign supply chains and advancing environmentally responsible production."

text:
As Americans prepare Thanksgiving meals, stock their refrigerators and eventually clear their plates, much of the food that goes uneaten will end up discarded. But food that can’t be eaten doesn’t have to go to waste entirely. Across the country, biogas capture facilities are recycling discarded food into renewable energy ─ and new research from the American Biogas Council finds that the opportunity to do more is enormous.

Food waste naturally produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC’s research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states that produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. Another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually, and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC’s expanded research this year uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory. The increase of 73% over last year’s count reflects a more complete picture of the industry.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” said Patrick Serfass, executive director of the American Biogas Council. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

Food waste is already producing energy across America

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. Some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing. Others process retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process pre-consumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing. Another 43 facilities handle retail food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

Most facilities use their biogas to generate electricity and heat. In fact, 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both. Another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

A growing industry, with bigger projects and more investment

Food-waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32% of the sector’s annual biogas production and 45% of its total investment. On average, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.
