text:
TEXAS — Tesla is considering a potential $10 billion deal that could bring nearly 10,000 jobs and thousands of dollars in revenue to Fort Bend County. It involves the construction of what officials call the largest single solar cell manufacturing site in the country.

In January, Tesla CEO Elon Musk shared plans for solar manufacturing.

“The SpaceX and Tesla teams both separately are working to build to 100 gigawatts a year of solar power in the U.S., and of manufactured solar power,” Musk said.

Months later, the Fort Bend County Commissioners Court approved a tax abatement agreement for Tesla’s Project Crystal Sun.

The electric vehicle and clean energy company proposed building a $10 billion solar cell manufacturing plant on more than 3,000 acres of land near Richmond. Officials say the potential 30-year agreement would create more than 9,700 permanent jobs paying at least $55 an hour.

The Lamar Consolidated Independent School District approved tax incentives for Tesla in September. Supporters say the plant would provide job opportunities for local students and residents. However, there’s no guarantee Tesla will build the plant at the proposed location at FM 1994 and FM 762 near Needville in Fort Bend County. The company says the county is competing with another location outside of Texas.

Spectrum News looked at documents to see how the agreement would work if Fort Bend lands the deal. They show the county agrees to waive property taxes for machinery and equipment and eliminate inventory-related taxes for 10 years. We also learned the Lamar CISD approved tax incentives through the fairly new Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act (JETI), which requires Tesla to pay full debt service taxes on voter-approved bonds and pay half of the taxes used to fund day-to-day operations.

Neighbors like Daniel Saffron say not everything is written in fine print.

“It’s gonna leave local taxpayers to hold the financial bag on day one,” Saffron said. “There’s no promises to protect the environment that it’s being built on. There are no promises to rebuild any of the infrastructure around it. They say they have this water recycling system, but there’s no specifics behind it.”

Carlos Guzman, the county’s economic opportunity and development agency director, says that the infrastructure, workforce and proximity to Houston are what sparked Tesla’s interest in Fort Bend.

“If it were to locate here in Fort Bend County, we fully expect to have other companies start looking to set up shop as close as possible,” Guzman said, adding that once Gov. Greg Abbott signs off, Tesla will make its decision. “We’re very excited. I hope we get selected because I know it would change the trajectory of this county.”

In the meantime, opponents of the tax incentive program hope industrial expansion won’t strip away the soul of Fort Bend County.

“Anytime there’s a new bill, there’s paperwork, there’s loopholes that people find,” said Saffron, referring to JETI.

If Fort Bend is selected, construction could start this year.

title: Business leaders urge COP31 Presidency to commit to global action on clean electrification ...
description:
The signatories ask the Presidency to place two priorities at the centre of the COP31 outcome: Accelerate clean electrification by backing the target of 35% electrification by 2035 and developing country strategies to deliver it.
The letter pushes back against a growing discourse suggesting the Paris goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C is out of reach.
"Keeping global warming well below 2°C is still vital and still possible," said Adair Turner, Co-Chair of the Energy Transitions Commission.
"Clean electrification has momentum, like a boulder rolling downhill.
What the ETC's new analysis shows Clean electrification can deliver the biggest cut to projected warming, to around 2.3°C.
text:
Global warming will reach 2.6°C by 2100 if no new policy support is offered and technologies are adopted only when they become cost-competitive, say signatories of a letter published today.

Clean electrification, with electricity meeting over 50% of final energy demand by mid-century, and phasing down coal use for electricity generation could cut projected warming to around 2.3°C, with low or no cost.

But projected temperatures will not reach below 2°C without action to decarbonise heavy industry, aviation and shipping, deeply cut methane emissions and end deforestation.

Combined, these five priority action areas could reduce warming to around 1.8°C – but this is not cost-free and requires policy support.

Exponential growth in carbon removals is required to bring potential warming down to 1.5°C.

LONDON, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Over 30 members of the Energy Transitions Commission (ETC) today urge COP31 President Murat Kurum and President of Negotiations Chris Bowen to put clean electrification and the hard-to-electrify sectors at the centre of the climate summit's outcome, as new ETC analysis shows current policies leave the world on course for 2.6°C of warming.

Their letter, published today alongside the ETC briefing Still vital, still possible: How governments and businesses can work together to limit global warming, comes days before negotiators gather in Türkiye. Signatories include ETC Commissioners from Arup, Envision, Grantham Research Institute (LSE), Octopus Energy, Rothschild, Schneider Electric, Tata Steel, and Vattenfall alongside other leaders from clean power and utilities, heavy industry, transport, and finance.

The signatories ask the Presidency to place two priorities at the centre of the COP31 outcome:

Accelerate clean electrification by backing the target of 35% electrification by 2035 and developing country strategies to deliver it.

Act on the hard-to-electrify sectors by committing globally to faster decarbonisation of steel, cement, aluminium, chemicals, aviation and shipping, including through carbon prices.

The letter pushes back against a growing discourse suggesting the Paris goal of limiting global warming to well below 2°C is out of reach. It argues this narrative risks weakening climate policy and corporate commitments just as clean technologies reach scale. Conversely, strong commitments on clean electrification and the hard-to-electrify sectors could relaunch the 'ambition loop' of policy, private investment and falling technology costs that followed the Paris Agreement and already curbed future warming projections from upper bounds of 4°C to 2.6°C.

"Keeping global warming well below 2°C is still vital and still possible," said Adair Turner, Co-Chair of the Energy Transitions Commission. "Costs of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles have fallen faster than forecast 10 years back, reducing the danger of catastrophic global warming above 3°C. But with unchanged policies, we're still on track to about 2.6°C by 2100. To keep well below 2°C, we must turbocharge clean electrification which in many applications will deliver both lower emissions and lower costs. But we must also meet more difficult challenges – reducing the utilisation of existing coal plants; decarbonising heavy industry, shipping and aviation; and radically reducing methane emissions from fossil fuel production and agriculture. In many cases, this will entail accepting some increased costs, but these costs are far less than the cost of unchecked climate change."

"Clean electrification has momentum, like a boulder rolling downhill. We need to clear its path with faster grids and permitting for it to accelerate. Heavy industry, methane, deforestation and removals are like boulders stuck at the foot of the hill, needing carbon prices and finance to push them uphill. Move both and we take almost a degree off future warming with a huge impact: fewer wildfires, floods and failed harvests, and a lower risk of irreversible tipping points," said Jules Kortenhorst, Co-Chair of the Energy Transitions Commission.

What the ETC's new analysis shows

Clean electrification can deliver the biggest cut to projected warming, to around 2.3°C. That involves building the new energy system and phasing out the old: electricity's share of final energy rises from 20% to over 50% by 2050, and coal falls to under 5% of power. Past forecasts underestimated falling solar and battery costs, so faster electrification could cut bills and emissions. Only early coal retirement carries a clear cost.

Decarbonising heavy industry, aviation and shipping can remove about 0.2°C, but faces a green premium. However, green steel costs around 45% more than conventional steel, but only adds around 1.2% to the price of a car. Carbon prices of around $100 per tonne, close to EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices today and in the coming years, would drive decarbonisation of steel and cement; aviation and shipping need $200–300 per tonne.

A cut of around 45% in annual fossil, agricultural and waste methane emissions by 2050 removes about 0.2°C. Ending deforestation by 2035 removes a further 0.07°C.

Returning warming to 1.5°C by 2100 is more costly, requiring over 500 Gt of CO₂ removals this century, costing over $500 billion a year, or about 0.4% of today's global GDP. Today, purchased removals total less than 20 Mt per year.

Download the briefing.

The ETC is a global coalition of leaders from energy producers, energy-intensive industries, technology providers, finance and environmental NGOs, committed to achieving net-zero emissions by mid-century, in line with the Paris climate objective of limiting global warming to well below 2°C and ideally to 1.5°C. The ETC is hosted by Systemiq Ltd.

name: Congress
title: Real Clear Energy: Permitting Reform Could Be a Victory for the Environment
description:
This might be reasonable if foregoing natural resources altogether were an option.
Indeed, living itself requires the disturbance of land and use of natural resources in some form.
That is why four senators just unveiled a major permitting bill aimed at accelerating energy and resource development by streamlining environmental reviews.
A blocked resource project can be celebrated as an environmental victory at home even as foreign landscapes continue supplying the same resource.
So long as we continue to need natural resources, wouldn’t it be more just for Americans to develop our own abundant resources?
text:
America has the seventh-largest known unmined copper reserves in the world. Those reserves alone could meet current U.S. demand for more than two decades, supplying the copper needed for electricity, buildings, and other critical infrastructure. Yet we still import 57% of the copper we use—much of it from Chile.

American environmentalism often asks us to leave valuable resources untouched for the sake of protecting the landscapes housing them. This might be reasonable if foregoing natural resources altogether were an option. But it is not. Modern society depends on natural resources. Indeed, living itself requires the disturbance of land and use of natural resources in some form.

That is why four senators just unveiled a major permitting bill aimed at accelerating energy and resource development by streamlining environmental reviews. Many environmental groups pushed back. Some warn the bill would weaken the environmental authority “used to stop projects like the Pebble [copper] Mine in Alaska.”

The environmentalists’ concern is straightforward. Development comes with environmental costs. But so does refusing to develop the resources we continue to consume. Therein lies a lesson that American environmentalism has yet to learn: moral victories for some are not moral victories for all. A blocked resource project can be celebrated as an environmental victory at home even as foreign landscapes continue supplying the same resource.

Enormous mines operate in the Atacama Desert, the driest non-polar place on Earth. In Antofagasta, mining accounts for nearly half of all water consumed, further depleting the region’s scarce groundwater. Copper production also requires moving immense amounts of rock, storing mine waste, and permanently altering portions of the landscape.

Chile’s environment has been altered to extract the copper making American life possible. To read this article, turn on the lights, or drive a car, we depend on copper extracted in Chile.

But that dynamic is not inevitable. America has abundant copper of its own. In some cases, we elect to leave viable deposits underground — often for environmental reasons. Chile, by contrast, has been more willing to extract its copper. And Americans benefit.

Consider Pebble Mine, the very proposed copper project that environmental groups cite both as an example of what current permitting laws can stop and as a reason Congress should reject permitting reform.

Pebble sits atop an enormous copper, gold, and molybdenum deposit in Alaska. Copper is critical for nearly everything electric, gold for many electronic devices, and molybdenum for construction. But in 2023, a federal agency used a rarely invoked provision of the Clean Water Act to effectively restrict development of the deposit.

That decision may have protected a portion of American nature, but it left our demand for copper unchanged. So long as we continue to need natural resources, wouldn’t it be more just for Americans to develop our own abundant resources?

Doing so would not entail rubber-stamping every project. As New Mexico Senator Martin Heinrich, one of the bill’s authors, put it, the goal is “to have the same standards, but to get to ‘yes’ — or if it’s a bad project, get to ‘no’ — a whole lot faster.”

Currently, federal permitting burdens can delay domestic resource production for decades—or prevent it altogether—as found by a recent suite of research from Pacific Legal Foundation.

PLF’s review of major mining projects found that some of the very burdens Congress is now looking to fix can trap mineral deposits underground for decades. One copper-nickel project, for example, has been stalled by regulations for more than 20 years. Across the country, opening a new mine takes an average of 29 years.

Separate PLF research found major mineral deposits locked away on federal lands (often for environmental reasons), including nickel equal to roughly 56 years of current U.S. production and copper equal to more than five years.

But what if developing those resources could reduce pressure on islands in Indonesia and deserts in Chile while helping power America’s economy and meet environmentalists’ climate goals?

Both nickel and copper are crucial for everything electric and environmentalists’ decarbonization goals, and a significant copper supply shortage driven by increasing electrification is projected by 2035. The problem is not that copper does not exist — it is that too little is being developed.

Yet a coalition of environmental groups has mobilized to stop the permitting bill. In a leaked strategy call, organizers discussed spurring opposition to the bill while hiding their strategy from the senators involved. One organizer said the goal is “to stop this bill, not to make it better.”

Before decrying permitting reform’s potential environmental effects, objectors should consider the consequences of continuing to rely on foreign countries to produce the materials American environmental policy makes exceedingly difficult to produce at home.

text:
WASHINGTON – Nov. 6, 2026 | Verra has approved the first carbon credits under its carbon capture and storage (CCS) methodology for a project in northern Texas. Credits can now be issued to the Barnett Zero Project (Verra Project 6016) in the city of Bridgeport. The project captures CO2 separated from raw natural gas at a processing plant, then compresses the CO2 and stores it permanently in an injection well nearby.

The credits were generated under Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) methodology VM0049 Carbon Capture and Storage v1.0, which establishes criteria and procedures for quantifying greenhouse gas emission reductions and carbon dioxide removals from projects that capture CO2 and store it permanently.

The project was developed by BKV Corporation (NYSE:BKV) and verified by the independent validation/verification body (VVB), GHD Limited. It uses module VMD0062 CO2 Capture from Natural Gas Processing together with VM0049 to account for the emissions impact of diverting CO2 separated from natural gas streams and storing it permanently. The module addresses a specific and largely unavoidable emissions source from an energy source that will continue to be relied on as part of the net-zero transition.

“The approval of the first credits under Verra’s CCS methodology is an important milestone for BKV and for the broader carbon management industry,” said Chris Kalnin, Chief Executive Officer of BKV. “Meeting Verra’s rigorous standards demonstrates that permanently sequestering CO2 from natural gas processing can be credibly measured, independently certified and recognized through a robust market framework. This achievement reflects BKV’s commitment to advancing practical emissions solutions across our operations and delivering lower-carbon energy to our customers through our closed-loop business model.”

ICVCM Approval

VM0049 and modules VMD0056 to VMD0059 were recently approved by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM) as meeting the Core Carbon Principles (CCPs). VMD0062 is currently being reviewed by the ICVCM.

Featured image: The cover of the federal budget depicts the Churchill Falls and Full Island electricity project.
text:
Ottawa, ON — The Federal Budget, Masters of our Destiny, and its implementation of the National Electricity Strategy, is a landmark commitment that recognizes electricity as the foundation of Canada’s economic growth. It’s a welcome green wallet but some environmental experts are concerned.

Through investments exceeding $50 billion, the federal government has taken a significant step toward its goal of doubling Canada’s electricity system by 2050 while accelerating electrification and strengthening Canada’s position as an energy superpower.

“Being masters of our destiny is about having the confidence to build on our strengths and shape our own future,” said François-Philippe Champagne, the federal Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “Canada has the resources, talent and ambition to succeed. Budget 2026 builds on those strengths by unlocking investment, building more at home, strengthening our energy and natural resource advantage, and helping Canadian businesses grow and compete on the world stage. That’s how we will create good jobs, make life more affordable, and build a stronger, more resilient and more united Canada for generations to come.”

François-Philippe Champagne, the federal Minister of Finance and National Revenue presents the federal budget in the House of Commons on November 5, 2026. Credit: Government of Canada.

The federal budget aims to super charge the economy and support sovereignty in the following ways:

Lower deficits

Direct program spending growth lowered from 8% to 2%

Kickstarting Investment Supercycle

$400B capital investments over 6 years

$22B of new affordability measures

Supercharging the clean economy

The budget is paired with Powering Canada Strong: From Strategy to Action, the federal action plan to double Canada’s electricity system by 2050, backed by $52 billion in new funding. The plan includes nearly $4 billion to expand electricity infrastructure and renewable energy, including new funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program. It also draws on Clean Power Nation research showing up to $100 billion in Canadian manufacturing opportunities for wind, solar and battery technologies.

The budget delivers on that vision by supporting infrastructure needed to power a growing economy, including:

Positioning electricity investment as an affordability measure, with electrification helping to reduce Canadians’ overall “energy wallet”

More than $50 billion in support of the National Electricity Strategy and the goal of doubling Canada’s electricity system by 2050, which includes:

Extension of the Clean Electricity and Clean Technology Investment Tax Credit to 2040, providing long-term certainty for investors and utilities

Expanding the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to include critical intra-provincial transmission

Funding of nearly $4 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28, to support electricity infrastructure expansion, renewable energy and priority electricity sector projects across Canada, including new funding for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program

Advancing projects such as the Taltson Hydro, Mayo Hydro Facility and Atlin Hydro

Announcing the implementation of the EIFEL exception for utilities, including expanding the Utility exception to including holding companies

Green Wallet, Grey Areas: Comments from the industry

Electricity Canada emphasizes that growing and modernizing Canada’s electricity system is a nation-building endeavour and welcomes the significant commitments to Canada’s electricity future.

“By investing more than $50 billion through the National Electricity Strategy and providing long-term certainty through measures such as extending the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to 2040, the federal government has demonstrated the bold leadership required to meet a challenge that will define Canada’s economic future. It recognizes that Canada must finance the build, modernize regulatory processes, adapt to a rapidly evolving grid shaped by electrification, artificial intelligence, data centres, and industrial growth, and ensure the electricity system can support the country’s broader economic ambitions,” said Josée Guibord, President and CEO of Electricity Canada.

“We commend the government for thinking at the scale this moment demands. The focus now must be delivery. Canada must move with urgency to turn financing into projects, approvals into construction, and ambition into infrastructure. Success will ultimately be measured not by what was announced today, but by the generation, transmission, and distribution assets we build together over the coming decades.”

The Canadian Renewable Energy Association (CanREA) welcomes Budget 2026 and federal advocacy to build more affordable electricity for Canadians.

“This is a strong budget for affordable, reliable electricity, and we’re proud to see key Clean Power Nation recommendations adopted,” said Vittoria Bellissimo, CanREA’s President and CEO. “Affordability is Canadians’ top priority, and wind, solar and energy storage deliver affordable, clean power quickly. The federal government has shown vision by extending tax credits to 2040, giving investors the certainty to build more projects, create jobs and strengthen Canada’s renewable energy industry.”

The Canada Energy Regulator projects that electricity demand could grow by 26% to 85% by 2050. About 24 GW of wind, solar and energy storage is already being procured across Canada, and with stable, competitive policies, the sector could attract up to $200 billion in investment by the mid-2030s and support 250,000 to 350,000 job-years.

“Transmission connects the lowest-cost new power to the people and businesses who need it,” said Bellissimo. “Extending the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to high-voltage transmission within provinces is a smart, practical move. It lowers the cost of building those lines, and that helps keep power bills down for families and businesses.”

Marine Renewables Canada (MRC), the national association representing offshore wind, tidal, wave, and river current energy, also applauds the budget and says the proposed extension of the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits (ITCs) through 2040 marks a significant milestone in MRC’s sustained advocacy for the long-term investment certainty needed to advance Canada’s marine renewable energy sector.

“Budget 2026 recognizes that building Canada’s electricity system is fundamental to our energy security and economic competitiveness,” said Elisa Obermann, Chief Executive Officer of MRC. “MRC has advocated for extending clean energy investment tax credits through 2040 because developers and investors need certainty that reflects the time required to bring projects into operation. Together with investments in transmission, renewable energy, and community capacity, this proposal would help create the conditions to advance Canada’s marine renewable energy sector.”

The David Suzuki Foundation also welcomes the clean electricity investments.

“For over five years we’ve advocated alongside dozens of allied groups and tens of thousands of people throughout Canada for this level of clean electricity investment. It’s a hard-fought, generational win, and now all people living in Canada can reap the benefits,” said Stephen Thomas, Clean Energy Manager at the David Suzuki Foundation.

“Investments in affordable, reliable, clean electricity will save households money on their energy bills and secure our economy for the long term. It will create over a million good jobs, it can use Canadian steel and aluminum, and it supports the leadership of Indigenous communities to build renewable projects on their territories. If we want more affordability and a resilient economy, we need to get serious about building clean electricity throughout Canada and reducing reliance on volatile fossil fuels for our energy needs and economic strength.”

However, the Foundation warns that continued backing for polluting fossil fuel projects, keeping gas on the grid and environmental rollbacks puts this progress at risk. Lisa Gue, national policy manager at David Suzuki Foundation, said: “Gaps remain when it comes to scaling up funding to meet Canada’s nature commitments and tackling plastic pollution. With the government investing in expanding forestry and mining, we need strong legal guardrails to protect nature and uphold Indigenous rights, yet in Bill C-39 the government is proposing to unravel these very protections.”

Similarly, Climate Action Network Canada and its member organizations has concerns about the impacts to Canadian communities and the ongoing support for oil and gas.

“The result of years of advocacy for consequential investments in renewables and electricity transmission can be found on the cover of the 2026 budget. An electrified economy based on renewables can help lower Canadians’ energy bills, boost our independence and ensure our resilience to external shocks — whether extreme weather or volatile fuel prices. The next step is ensuring that projects get built right, with communities, Indigenous Peoples and civil society taking part of the process from the beginning,” said Caroline Brouillette, Executive Director of Climate Action Network Canada.

“Investments and regulations should go hand in hand. The cover of this year’s budget tells only half of the story. Building a net-zero economy requires action to diversify away from costly infrastructure that risks holding us back. The Carney government continues to prioritize costly fossil fuel projects that risk leaving Canada behind, like subsidizing the Pacific Link Pipeline and creating new incentives that continue to benefit the expansion of oil and gas.”

The International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD) also states its concerns, citing that the positive signals of the budget are offset by the decision to direct more tax dollars to oil and gas, further fuelling climate change. The budget increases fossil fuel production subsidies by offering tax breaks for constructing new liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities while at the same time extending an existing investment tax credit for carbon capture and storage. These subsidies lock-in new and expanded fossil fuel production and, in the case of LNG, violate the Canadian government’s own policy to avoid new inefficient fossil fuel subsidies. This diverts scarce resources away from low-carbon innovation in a world where rapidly expanding renewable energy is driving down global demand for oil and gas.

“Committing to build a low-carbon economy while at the same time subsidizing a growing fossil fuel industry is like trying to drive forward while the gearshift is in reverse,” says Nichole Dusyk, Senior Policy Advisor and Lead, Canada Energy team at IISD. “By funding and relying on carbon capture and storage and LNG as ‘climate solutions,’ the federal government is sapping resources from real, globally competitive climate solutions.”

State of the current economy

Despite a challenging global environment, the Canadian economy has shown resilience:

Canada’s economy grew by 3.3% in the second quarter, the fastest pace in the G7.

The IMF expects Canada to be the second-fastest growing economy in the G7 in 2027.

Canada is expected to maintain one of the lowest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the G7, signaling fiscal strength and the capacity to invest in the future.

More Canadians are benefitting from labour market strength. Over the past year, Canada’s economy has added 214,000 jobs in private employment, while the unemployment rate has fallen to 6.5%, near its lowest level in two years.

Since the end of 2024, Canada has also created nearly twice as many jobs per capita as the United States.

text:
Lehigh has received $1.6 million to participate in the “Commonwealth of Pennsylvania EGS Pilot Demonstration,” a U.S. Department of Energy-funded project led by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP).

The total project budget is about $14 million. The “EGS” stands for enhanced geothermal system.

“This project shows what’s possible when faculty work across disciplinary and college boundaries,” said Robert Flowers, Herbert J. and Ann L. Siegel Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences.

“Earth scientists from the College of Arts and Sciences and engineers from the P.C. Rossin College of Engineering and Applied Science are bringing complementary expertise to a problem neither could solve alone.

“Research like this matters because discoveries don't stay in the lab. It’s designed to bring new possibilities to Pennsylvania communities, and it reflects Lehigh’s commitment to scholarship that serves the people and places around us.”

The goal is to generate one megawatt of electricity from a low-enthalpy, underperforming Marcellus Shale gas well in Indiana County, Pennsylvania.

The project will draw heat from an underperforming natural gas well by circulating water at depth, and then bring that heated water to the surface.

That heated water energy will produce electricity for the local grid and supply direct-use heat to nearby homes and businesses.

“Pennsylvania’s conventional hydrocarbon industry, followed by the shale oil and gas revolution left behind a vast network of wells and related infrastructure ,” said Frank Pazzaglia, professor of Earth and environmental sciences in Lehigh’s College of Arts and Sciences and the principal investigator. “This project asks whether we can give that infrastructure a second life as a clean, renewable energy source.”

The pilot will use a deep existing unconventional gas well in Indiana County, PA where the geology is favorable for tapping geothermal resources.

The well is operated by CNX Green Ventures, an Appalachian oil and gas producer.

“Repurposing abandoned hydrocarbon wells for low-enthalpy geothermal mining represents an economic and environmental opportunity, transforming the methane-leaking liability into a predictable source of clean, local energy,” said Carlos Romero, professor of mechanical engineering and mechanics in the Rossin College and director of Lehigh’s Energy Research Center.

Project leaders say the approach could also create opportunities for displaced oil, gas, and coal workers, whose subsurface experience transfers directly to the geothermal industry.

By extending the useful life of existing wells, the project aims to stimulate geothermal energy development, particularly in the eastern US where geothermal resources are more restricted than in the western US, and demonstrate that the approach is portable.

“The project is a chance to train the next generation of scientists and engineers while helping to show that geothermal energy can work in places many people wouldn’t expect,” Pazzaglia said.

Lehigh’s funding will support five researchers and students from two units.

The Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences (EES) will include three principal investigators, a postdoctoral researcher and a graduate student, while the Energy Research Center will include two principal investigators and a graduate student.

Project personnel from Lehigh include Frank Pazzaglia; Steve Peters, associate professor of EES; Anne Meltzer, professor of EES; Carlos Romero and Muhannad Suleiman, professor of civil and environmental engineering.

DEP is the project lead, working in coordination with the Pennsylvania Geological Survey. Partners include Gradient Geothermal Inc., Teverra Inc., Idaho National Laboratory, CNX Green Ventures, and Seequent, in addition to Lehigh University.

text:
[BENGALURU] Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of 2027, chief executive officer Elon Musk said on Friday (Nov 6), as the futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks struggles to win mass market appeal.

Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly-launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions.

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker’s Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model’s specialised components.

Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours.

“Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time,” Musk said in response to a user on X, calling the model the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made” and the wind-down the “end of an era”.

“Polarising” technology

Musk had, during Cybertruck’s launch in 2023, touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford. But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations.

Often described as polarising, Cybertruck’s unorthodox sharp-edged stainless steel design has limited its prospects outside the US.

Regulatory approval became difficult to come by in parts of Europe, depriving Tesla of major markets that could have helped turn the pickup into a higher-volume product.

The model has also faced multiple recalls and quality-control issues, while Tesla has repeatedly revised prices.

Tesla does not officially disclose individual sales figures for the Cybertruck. Instead, the automaker groups it into an “Other Models” category, which accounted for just 8,295 deliveries in the third quarter, down from 12,364 deliveries in the second quarter.

“Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

Musk’s new bet

The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk’s key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an artificial intelligence and robotics company.

He has said he sees it as Tesla’s main autonomous model within a larger driverless network and that it will eventually be the company’s highest-volume vehicle, supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Musk’s self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September.

However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency’s questions on whether it properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. REUTERS

text:
When leaders, innovators and energy stakeholders gathered at the Coastal Center, it wasn’t just a routine conference. The event marked a milestone for Future Use of Energy in Louisiana, a statewide engine driving the future of energy transition, traditional manufacturing and carbon management.

While the conference has already concluded, its echoes are reshaping what it means to study energy, management and environmental resilience right here in Thibodaux.

What is FUEL and Why is it Vital to the Coast?

FUEL is a collaborative coalition anchored by major research institutions, industry partners and economic developers. Backed by historic support, including a landmark National Science Foundation Regional Innovation Engines award, FUEL is designed to transition Louisiana from powering the nation through legacy oil and gas to leading the world in next-generation energy technologies, carbon capture and grid modernization.

For Thibodaux, sitting squarely in the bayou region, this mission is personal. Our local geography makes us both a frontline witness to coastal changes and the beating heart of the state’s energy infrastructure.

Hosting a FUEL-centered event at the Coastal Center bridges high-level statewide policy with the physical reality of our coastline. It acknowledges that the solutions to coastal protection, energy security and economic longevity must be engineered, managed and sustained right here in south Louisiana.

Igniting a Venture Studio Model: Innovation in Action

The timing of the Coastal Center conference closely mirrors FUEL’s rollout of its brand-new FUEL Venture Studio and its appointment of inaugural Innovator-in-Residence Daryl Roy.

Rather than just offering traditional grants to pre-existing companies, this venture studio model actively builds new startups from the ground up. By pairing cutting-edge academic research, like that coming out of university labs, with seasoned operators, private investors and corporate partners, FUEL is actively creating companies focused on carbon management and modernized infrastructure.

Bringing conversations around this model to Thibodaux signals a shift from textbook theory to market-driven execution. It answers why the conference happened, to root high-tech entrepreneurship directly in the communities most impacted by shifts in the energy sector.

What This Means for Nicholls Students

For students studying energy management, business and environmental science at Nicholls, these developments translate directly into career momentum. Hosting high-level regional conferences right in their backyard at the Coastal Center gives students a front-row seat to network directly with the policymakers, startup founders and corporate leaders steering Louisiana’s economic future.

As FUEL builds a venture studio to commercialize new technologies, students are positioned at the doorstep of an emerging job market focused on keeping high-paying careers, intellectual property and startup creation within the state.

Because modern energy management has expanded beyond traditional extraction to complex landscapes, carbon management economics and sustainable infrastructure, witnessing statewide initiatives like FUEL unfold on campus ensures that student coursework aligns in real time with the skill sets regional employers are hunting for.

The conference at the Coastal Center may have passed, but its impact is just beginning to ripple across campus. For Nicholls students, it’s a clear reminder: the future of energy isn’t being written in a distant boardroom–it’s being engineered right down the bayou.

text:
Democrats Swept Congress and Won in Red States. Here Are the Races That Matter Most for Decarbonization, Disasters, and Data Centers.

The Democratic Party won a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections. As of Wednesday morning, the party had secured control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. The sweep will have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Now, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could even impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats will also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump will have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down. With majorities in the Senate and the House, the party could even seek to reimpose some of the clean energy tax credits that Republicans rescinded last year.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats gained full control of the state government in Wisconsin, Arizona, and Pennsylvania, according to election analysts, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow the passage of meaningful climate policy in much of the country for the first time. In Pennsylvania, for instance, state House Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the Public Service Commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In state races in Texas and Ohio, and in bellwether House districts like one in central Pennsylvania, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

House Democrats Could Make the Trump Administration Spend Money on the Climate

Upon taking office, the Trump administration attempted to withhold billions of dollars in climate money, much of it from the landmark Inflation Reduction Act signed into law by Joe Biden in 2022. These freezes threw a number of major climate projects into limbo — the Department of Energy halted experimental projects for hydrogen production in Pennsylvania and decarbonized cement in California, while the Environmental Protection Agency froze a $7 billion community solar program.

Those days may soon be over. Chellie Pingree, the lead Democrat who oversees funding for the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, says that she has prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin. She also intends to use the power of the purse to force the administration to spend climate money. Funding bills could include provisions that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.

“We can put a lot more teeth into the next appropriations bill,” she said. “We can say, ‘OK, fine, if you’re not going to spend the money, we have the power to withhold other funding.’”

— Jake Bittle

Texas Elects a Democratic Senator for the First Time in Nearly 40 Years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

A Wildland Firefighter Endorsed by AOC Wins a House Seat in Montana

Montana is on track to send a Democrat to the House of Representatives for the first time in over 30 years. Sam Forstag, a former wildland firefighter and union leader, claimed victory in the state’s competitive western district seat over Republican Aaron Flint, who conceded the race early Wednesday morning. The Associated Press estimates that 13 percent of ballots remain uncounted as of midday Wednesday.

Forstag ran his campaign on the affordability issues facing many Montanans and emphasized rising power bills, the need for data center regulation, and protecting public lands from attacks. The 31-year-old decided to run for office after experiencing Trump’s massive cuts to federal land management agencies, including wildland firefighting. Forstag received early endorsements from Representative Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

In an interview with Montana Free Press in October, Forstag said he wanted to “invest in transmission” and ensure “next-generation energy projects, wind and solar, have the actual resources that they need to get off the ground.”

— Ellis Juhlin

Two Climate Hawks Survive Republican Redistricting

Their districts were redrawn to eliminate them, but voters in Florida’s 14th and Ohio’s 9th districts respectively reelected Kathy Castor and Marcy Kaptur anyway.

Castor — referred to as a “climate hawk” by Politico — has spent much of her long career in Congress raising the alarm about climate change. Between 2019 and 2022 she chaired the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis, and has otherwise made reducing carbon pollution and preparing communities for climate impacts central to her legislative agenda. In March, she backed the Energy Bills Relief Act, which proposed restoring energy upgrade tax credits and connecting more clean energy to the grid. She has also strongly opposed data centers in the Tampa area that she serves, warning that the facilities could drive up her constituents’ utility costs while straining local water supplies.

Kaptur is the longest-serving woman in the House. She has been a leading opponent of the Department of Energy’s efforts to redirect Inflation Reduction Act money away from clean energy and toward fossil fuels. She has alleged that these redirections violate federal law, and would likely lead investigations into the Energy Department’s actions in a Democratic-controlled Congress. The Ohio state Legislature redrew her district to encompass more conservative areas along Lake Erie, but she held on to her seat comfortably.

— Jake Bittle and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A Democrat Will Become a Texas Oil and Gas Regulator

Stunning results are still coming in from the Lone Star State. For the first time in over 30 years, a Democrat has won a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, the regulatory agency that oversees the state’s oil and gas industry. Jon Rosenthal defeated Republican candidate Bo French, who made a racist social media post about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game that drew national bipartisan backlash.

“To the dude that posted the online poll last summer, asking who’s a bigger threat to America and the only two choices were Muslims and Jews — tonight this Jewish engineer sent that motherf*cker home,” said Rosenthal in his victory speech, referring to another racist post by French.

Rosenthal asserts that good jobs and clean air can — and must — coexist. He supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy and capturing natural gas. He also wants to “turbocharge” the plugging of inactive oil and gas wells, which leak methane. The Railroad Commission is currently considering rules on that, spurred by state legislation passed last year.

Rosenthal will join two Republican commissioners, meaning it’s likely he will be outvoted on many issues.

— Celeste Guajardo

Democrats Flip Control of Georgia Utility Commission for the First Time in Decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

Public Transit Wins in Multiple States

After years of financial woes and operating deficits, some residents of the California Bay Area were concerned that this year’s midterms might signal the downfall of public rail options in the region, leaving them stuck in its infamous traffic. But the Regional Transit Measure, which sought to enact a sales tax to fund local transit agencies for another 14 years, easily won a majority vote. It is expected to raise $1 billion each year to keep trains up and running.

Colorado rail supporters have also claimed victory for Measure 7A, which will establish a permanent sales tax to extend Colorado Connector passenger trains between Pueblo and Fort Collins. The coalition that campaigned for the measure argued that the expanded railway would reduce emissions equivalent to 29,000 cars in the area.

Other states had transit wins, too: More than 70 percent of voters said yes to Seattle’s Proposition 1, which would double the dedicated transit tax and support more frequent bus service. And Lawrence, Kansas, increased its transit sale tax to fund service for another 10 years.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Public Transit Wins in Multiple States

Colorado voters roundly rejected an effort to enshrine a right to natural gas in the state Constitution, which would have been a first in the country. Amendment 82 proposed giving homes and businesses a right to use gas stoves for cooking and heating, as well as giving distributors and utilities a right to sell the fossil fuel. Since the Constitution trumps all else, the ballot measure’s approval could have jeopardized local and state efforts to shift away from fossil fuels and electrify buildings, prompting court challenges to climate policies. The measure also raised concerns that it could protect access to natural gas for power-hungry data centers.

Only 46 percent of voters supported Amendment 82 as of late Wednesday morning, far beneath the 55 percent a constitutional amendment needs to pass. That protects the Colorado Public Utilities Commission’s Clean Heat Plan, which requires utilities to cut natural gas emissions by 41 percent by 2035.

— Kate Yoder

A Flip in an Area Devastated by Helene

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait — not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House District, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

— Jake Bittle

An Ex-Sunrise Activist Wins in Michigan

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement, has prevailed in a razor’s-edge House of Representatives race in central Michigan. Lawrence, a 36-year-old progressive, ousted freshman Republican Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, a bellwether area encompassing Lansing and its suburbs. He made opposition to data centers a focal point of his campaign, calling for a national moratorium on data center development. He also aligned himself with activists and residents who have opposed large-scale renewable energy projects in the Lansing area. In an interview with Grist last month, Lawrence said that many utility-scale solar projects don’t benefit the communities around them.

— Jake Bittle

Democrats Win After Attacking Republicans on Data Centers

In one of the night’s biggest upsets, Texas state Representative Gina Hinojosa ousted incumbent Governor Greg Abbott after campaigning on a data center moratorium and accusing Abbott of selling out to the tech industry.

And at least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. (Bresnahan has owned stock in data center companies.) And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over incumbent Darline Graham after Andrews highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million dollars on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions, but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona, Sachi Kitajima Mulkey, and Jake Bittle

Data Centers Upend Municipal Politics

Further down the ballot, it’s hard to find a place where data centers didn’t lose. In addition to the marquee congressional and governor’s races where voter sentiment about the AI boom may have helped oust Republican incumbents, dozens of towns and cities passed pauses or bans on data center development, according to The Washington Post. In many cases, these restrictions passed by enormous margins — in Sunbury, Ohio, where Amazon proposed a $2 billion project, voters rejected the facilities by an almost 60-point margin.

The AI issue also upended local elections, and perhaps the best example is in Pine Island, Minnesota. Google has proposed building a large new data center there, one that would be powered exclusively by clean energy and would include big subsidies for electric ratepayers. But voter outrage over the project caused a previous mayor to resign and led a first-time politician to mount a campaign against the interim replacement. That challenger, Mark Lang, won with well over 60 percent of the vote.

— Jake Bittle

A FEMA Defender Sails to Victory in Florida

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th Congressional District. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, Cabinet-level agency — just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance, and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Michigan Gets Utility Money Out of Politics

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it aims to do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision in 2010. Shortly before midnight on Tuesday, a conservative policy group sued the state in federal court, saying that everyone from journalists to nonprofit organizations could lose speech and privacy rights under the new measure. And while experts said the measure likely won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

— Vivian La

A Governor Who at Least Acknowledges Climate Change in Florida

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th Congressional District, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent Cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A MAGA Loyalist Who Says No To Drilling in Florida

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Florida Governor Ron DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

This story has been updated with analysis of additional races and trends.

This story was previously published by Grist on November 4, 2026.

text:
Governor Newsom prioritized cleaning up neighborhoods impacted by decades of Exide pollution, investing more than $500 million in one of the largest residential lead cleanups in U.S. history.

California has completed cleanup at:

🏡 6,495 residential parcels

🛣️ 7,818 parkways

✏️ 12 schools

🧑‍🧑‍🧒 68 childcare centers

🛝 5 parks

“Clean air, soil and water should be basic rights. That’s why California is committed to cleaning up the decades of pollution left behind by Exide, affecting far too many families and communities,” said Secretary for Environmental Protection, Yana Garcia. “The investments made by this administration mean that in Southeast Los Angeles, nearly 6,500 families have cleaner properties, and impacted communities have safer childcare centers, schools and parks where they can safely live, work and play.”

“DTSC is delivering real and measurable progress for families living near the former Exide facility,” said DTSC Director Katherine Butler. “Every home we clean brings communities closer to the safe, healthy future they deserve after decades of industrial pollution. California remains steadfast in completing this cleanup thoroughly, safely, and with full transparency.”

How we got here

The former Exide facility in Vernon, located five miles southeast of downtown Los Angeles, operated for decades, recycling lead-acid batteries. In 2002, DTSC required Exide to investigate and clean up releases from its operations. In 2014, testing revealed elevated lead levels in nearby residential soil. In 2015, DTSC ordered Exide to withdraw a pending permit to operate, effectively closing the facility. Cleanup has continued ever since.

When a federal bankruptcy court later allowed Exide to abandon the site, Governor Newsom condemned the decision, declaring that California would continue fighting to hold Exide and its creditors accountable for poisoning the residential parcels, playgrounds and backyards surrounding the facility.

Since then, California has made sustained investments to accelerate cleanup and protect surrounding communities, including major state funding in 2021 for demolition, site cleanup and residential remediation, additional funding in 2023 for parkway cleanup, and continued funding to clean more contaminated residential parcels. The Newsom administration also took decisive steps to request the addition of the former Exide facility to the federal Superfund National Priorities List that, if successful, would bring additional federal resources to one of the largest contamination cleanups in U.S. history.

Today’s progress reflects years of work by the state and community partners to clean contaminated soil, protect families, and address what Governor Newsom has called Exide’s “toxic legacy” and a “decades-long injustice.”

How the cleanup works

California conducts comprehensive soil sampling to guide cleanup decisions. Initial sampling identifies properties eligible for cleanup, while spot-check verification and retrospective sampling confirm that completed work meets the state’s high standards.

To date, DTSC has performed sampling of 10,028 parcels to determine cleanup priority. 9,016 parcels have been identified as eligible for further remediation (about 80% of those contacted have granted DTSC access), based on soil lead concentration greater than 80 parts per million and/or a single sample greater than 1,000 ppm. DTSC conducted verification and retrospective sampling on 623 properties.

text:
ISTANBUL (AP) — The Turkish energy minister has laid out plans for his country to wean itself away from coal and other fossil fuels as it prepares to host the COP31 climate change summit.

World leaders are due to arrive next week in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, and Turkey’s hosting of the annual environmental conference has thrown a spotlight on its own coal, oil and gas usage.

Turkey is Europe’s largest coal power generator, according to energy think tank Ember. The Turkish Energy Ministry says coal remained its largest source of power last year, accounting for 33% of generation. The share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed the National Energy Plan 2040 to reporters in a presentation made public Friday, in which he said Turkey would aim to transition from coal to cleaner energy sources — a process known as electrification. This would help it fulfil its pledge to reach net zero emissions by 2053.

“When we reach 2040 we are going to reduce our emissions by 40%. This big change in electrification will make this happen,” he said, adding that the use of solar and wind energy sources would more than quadruple over the next 13 years.

“Our aim is to reach 36% electrification by the year 2040,” he told a news conference in Istanbul. Using transport as an example, Bayraktar said the number of electric cars on Turkey’s roads would increase from around 500,000 to 20 million in the next 13 years.

The aim of the plan is to produce a “paradigm shift” in how energy is used in Turkey. “We have a huge project list ahead of us,” the minister added.

Huge level of investment needed

Such a shift, however, would require a huge level of investment — $500 billion in the next 13 years, some $210 billion of which would come from Turkish public sector companies with much of the rest from foreign investment.

“If the world is serious about carbon neutrality and if we would like to fund (fighting) climate change and global warming, we need to find the money,” Bayraktar said. “Everyone needs to take some responsibility and provide money for that.”

He also emphasized the importance of a transition from coal to clean energy that would not negatively impact communities reliant on mines and power stations for employment.

“We are looking for a just transition from coal to relatively cleaner sources of energy… but we need coal for security of supply,” he said.

“Equally important is that (coal mining) is providing at least 30,000 to 40,000 people with employment and labor opportunities. How are we going to make these miners into AI experts or high-tech experts? It’s not going to be easy. We need a just transition period.”

Despite aiming to break away from coal, Turkey will remain tied to other fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, for the foreseeable future.

Turkey recently started drilling gas reserves in the Black Sea and Bayraktar said production would double to 7.5 billion cubic meters annually in the coming years.

Growing nuclear power

Another key area would be nuclear power. The Akkuyu nuclear power plant on the Mediterranean coast is nearing operation and there are plans for another nuclear station by the Black Sea.

These would contribute towards the “very ambitious target” of Turkey becoming energy independent by 2040, Bayraktar said.

Turning to the “turbulent times” facing energy markets, Bayraktar described how sanctions around the wars in Ukraine and Iran were impeding efforts to fight global warming.

“We are trying to become carbon neutral in less than three decades’ time and with all these difficulties it’s very difficult to achieve this,” he said.

According to the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, Turkey’s climate targets and policies are “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared with the early 1800s.

Looking ahead to COP31, Bayraktar said his key message would be for countries to adopt “responsive and realistic policies” to achieve carbon neutrality.

Legislation to lower energy bills and speed up permitting for clean energy projects will likely be one of the top 10 priorities when Democrats regain control of the U.S. Congress in early January, Rep. Sean Casten (D-IL) told a triumphant media briefing Nov. 4, just hours after Donald Trump’s crushing and historic defeat in midterm elections.

I’m awake, barely,” said Casten (D-IL), a former clean energy entrepreneur first elected to Congress in 2019. “I think we’re all still processing the victory from last night.”

“The American people made their voices heard at the polls by resoundingly rejecting the destructive, corrupt actions of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran, the attacks on clean energy that have driven up costs for everyday people, and while they’re doing this, they’re boosting the profits of fossil fuel polluters,” said Gretchen Goldman, president of the Union of Concerned Scientists.

“Polling has showed that voters across the country are concerned about affordability,” Goldman added. “There’ve been news stories about regular people going without medicine and even food to fill their gas tanks. And yet the Trump administration has moved full speed ahead with repealing popular vehicle emission standards, among the strongest policies we’ve had to curb fossil fuel pollution and save drivers money at the pump.”

While Democrats in the House of Representatives are still working through their initial priorities for early 2027, energy affordability will be high on the list, with more than 160 legislators already signed on to support an Energy Bills Relief Act, Casten said. The bill will focus on “changing the incentives so that energy producers can make money by working to the benefit of energy consumers and lowering costs, which is not the way our regulatory structure works right now.”

At the same time, the veteran legislator didn’t minimize the challenge of trying to get anything done in Washington when Trump has already pledged to become “Mr. Veto” if Democrats won the midterms.

“We don’t have veto-proof majorities in the House or Senate, in spite of all the wins we had last night,” he told reporters. So “it’s important for us to put forward an agenda to try to get it passed, to not shy away from our values, but I think the strongest tools we’re going to have will be in appropriations and in oversight,” using Congressional authority to shift spending and “shine a light on some of the horrific things this administration has done.”

The Union of Concerned Scientists has tracked 625 attacks on science by the Trump administration over the last two years, and “each brazen attack served as a catalyst to mobilize scientists and science supporters across the country,” Goldman added. “But now we have more science champions in Congress, making it possible to limit the administration’s worst excesses and to hold them accountable for harms they’ve caused at home and on the global stage.”

As this story went to virtual press, Democrats had seized 54 of the seats in the 100-member U.S. Senate with races in Mississippi and Alaska still too close to call, and latest projections showed an overwhelming 259-176 Democratic Party margin in the House of Representatives. The early days since the polls closed have seen furious speculation about what’s next—for intensive Congressional investigations of Trump’s family and political cronies and attempts to roll back many of his most egregious policies, nowhere more urgently than on climate change and energy.

An ‘Important Diplomatic Function’ at COP31

But the change in tone stemming from the midterms might become evident as soon as next week, long before the new Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, when this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, convenes in Antalya, Türkiye.

“In the immediate term, we have a really important diplomatic function,” Casten said. “There are going to be about 20 of us going to the COP. We will not of course be in the majority [in Congress] at that point, but we will be received with the understanding of what just happened. We will be the entirety of the United States federal delegation in Türkiye, which makes our role very important.”

Those delegates will have to step carefully, he conceded, because “the rest of the world knows that the United States is the country that failed to ratify Kyoto. We’re the country that dropped out of [the Paris climate agreement], not once, but twice. But I think also there’s real value in us being able to convey to the world that America has spoken, and that so many of the challenges we face are the same,” from climate refugees on the move to the way climate change distorts and destabilizes financial systems.

Something else the U.S. has in common with other countries, Casten added, is the large share of the economy that rises or falls with the price of oil.

“Speaker [Mike] Johnson (R-LA) represents a district that wants people to consume as much natural gas as possible, pay as much as possible for that natural gas, and to force the export of LNG to the rest of the world,” he said. The likely incoming Speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), “has a very different set of values from his constituents. But I think we can approach this moment with an empathy to realize that the climate demands action, the economy demands action, the rest of the world is already making that transition… but we need to do that with an appropriate amount of empathy and an appropriate amount of urgency.”

Goldman described the latest science on climate change as “sobering”, with decades of “insufficient policy-maker action and fossil fuel industry duplicity” now making it inevitable that humanity will overshoot a 1.5°C limit on average global warming.

“People in the U.S. and around the world are experiencing the deadly and costly effects of those rising temperatures,” she said, and “public polling routinely shows that voters across the country support common sense, science-backed policies to keep their families and communities safe”—including 75% of registered voters in the U.S. who say they want to see carbon dioxide regulated.

The Momentum is Local

While change in Washington, DC will be slower and less decisive while Trump is still in office, much of the momentum will come from state and local governments—just as it has over the last two years, only more so. Democrats are now the governors of 30 of the 50 states, and former Washington State governor Jay Inslee said 22 states now have Democratic “trifectas”, where one party holds the state house, senate, and governor’s office. That makes it easier for them to enact policies that accelerate their response to climate change and adoption of clean energy.

Inslee said voters’ “Titanic rejection of a climate denying president” will “change the course of America and allow us again to assume a leadership role in developing a clean energy economy, for us and the rest of the world.” Importantly, he said the winning Democratic candidates ran on a dual platform of cutting energy costs and adopting solutions that will also reduce climate pollution.

So “it was a two-fer, and Americans responded.”

That dynamic will clear the way for Congressional Democrats to pursue “as aggressive a policy as possible to get Americans access to electric vehicles and heat pumps and solar and wind,” Inslee said. But “we don’t even have to wait for Congress because we have six or seven new governors, six new trifectas… 30 states with democratic governors,” and “every single one of them are engines of clean energy development.”

Those jurisdictions are referred to as “subnational” governments in COP-speak, Inslee added. But “they’re actually super-nationals, because states can move the ball, and we’re with you. The U.S. Climate Alliance is alive and kicking, and you’re going to see progress on a fairly rapid basis starting in January.”

Casten added that state public service commissions often “have a lot more control over the incentives to bring cheaper, cleaner sources on the grid than we do at the federal level. Now, “there’s a huge opportunity for oversight in terms of defence and security investments in the U.S. and how cuts have been made to considerations of climate as a security issue,” she said.

She cited the U.S. National Defense Authorization Act as one of the available pathways for climate security investments. Congress set a definition of climate security during Trump’s first term, and “there’s a recognition that cleantech is a competitive advantage for the United States, that wildfires are straining our military and National Guard regularly, that we need better proactive investments.
