text:
A Kern County judge ruled that approval of California’s first operating carbon capture and storage project — a technology the state is counting on to meet its climate goals — violated state environmental law and must be set aside.

Judge Marcos Camacho found that environmental review of California Resources Corp.’s TerraVault project, which Kern County supervisors approved in October 2024, fell short in several ways. Among them, it failed to analyze the industries expected to supply the project with carbon dioxide.

Because the judgment is not yet final, it’s not clear when CRC must stop injecting carbon dioxide and suspend the facility’s operations. A real-time project tracker on the company’s website indicates that carbon injection continues.

Carbon TerraVault 1 — the first of at least nine carbon storage projects the company plans around the state — is designed to collect up to 46 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to CRC. The company is injecting carbon deep underground in a Kern County oil field to keep it from warming the atmosphere. The project began operating earlier this year after a lengthy and controversial approval process.

Kern County policymakers hoped the project — and others that might crop up nearby to send carbon to the reservoirs — would provide a much-needed infusion to the county’s oil-dependent economy as California moves away from fossil fuels.

More than 15 similar projects are under development in California, according to a map from the Clean Air Task Force. But for many communities, siting those projects can be a hard sell because of uncertainty and mistrust, and some residents near the project have raised concerns about air pollution and carbon dioxide leaking from the reservoirs or the pipelines feeding it.

What the court found

Environmental groups sued over TerraVault 1 in 2024, alleging the project’s environmental impact report did not adequately consider cumulative environmental and greenhouse gas impacts, among other issues, in violation of the California Environmental Quality Act. Camacho sided with them on several counts.

Among the most significant issues was the potential that polluting facilities could crop up near the storage reservoirs. CRC’s environmental assessment laid out eight industries, such as hydrogen, cement and steel manufacturing, that could someday ferry carbon dioxide to the depleted reservoirs in the Elk Hills oil field. But the review didn’t look at how those plants could affect the surrounding area. The project currently stores only carbon dioxide that CRC strips from gas the company draws from its own oil field.

Leaving out those likely sources, Camacho wrote, “infects the informational foundation for the whole Project.”

Michelle Ghafar, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represented two of the plaintiffs, called the ruling “a pretty resounding win.”

“I was really struck by the decision, which basically said that there are errors running throughout the entire document,” she said.

CRC did not respond to emailed questions about whether it will appeal, how long the reapplication process may take, or if it will suspend project operations.

Company president and CEO Francisco Leon said in a statement that the order “is a step in the wrong direction for addressing the impacts of climate change and reflects the weaponization of CEQA by a narrow group of special interests.” The company plans to “aggressively pursue all available options to protect and advance this important project,” the statement said.

What comes next

Plaintiffs, including the Central California Environmental Justice Network, Committee for a Better Shafter and the Center for Biological Diversity, will now prepare a proposed judgment for the court’s approval. They say CRC must suspend operations while the company reanalyzes the project’s impacts and the county reconsiders it. That could take several months or several years, according to Ethan Elkind, director of the climate program at UC Berkeley’s Center for Law, Energy & the Environment.

In a regulatory filing, CRC said Camacho’s ruling was not final and its effect on existing operations was uncertain. A spokesperson for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, which approves carbon injection permits in California, said the court ruling has no impact on CRC’s federal permit approvals. A Kern County planning department representative did not reply to requests for comment.

Ileana Navarro, a policy associate at the Central California Environmental Justice Network, called the ruling “a breath of fresh air, both figuratively and literally,” for nearby communities.

“You’re asking community members to gamble their communities, neighborhoods, health and safety on projects that don’t really have a track record,” Elkind said. “That’s always difficult.”

The ruling came as voters weighed Proposition 45, which would set deadlines for environmental reviews and lawsuits on certain “essential” projects — a category that explicitly includes carbon capture and storage — and bar courts from ordering approvals rescinded.

Supporters said the measure would speed construction of housing and infrastructure; opponents said it would weaken environmental protections. It was trailing in early returns.

Ghafar said the ruling shows why the state’s environmental review law remains an important tool. “We need the law now more than ever,” she said.

title: New DOE-Backed Study Puts a Price Tag on Power Outages for Rural Electric Co-op Members
description:
Understanding what power interruptions actually cost consumers is essential to making smart decisions about grid investments.
But the surveys behind the original tool are aging (some more than 25 years old), and they leave out large parts of the country, including many rural communities served by electric cooperatives.
To close that gap, the Department of Energy's Office of Electricity partnered with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Resource Innovations, and the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) to survey members of 18 electric cooperatives across the Southeast, Great Plains/Upper Midwest, and Intermountain West.
A single momentary interruption cost residential members an average of $2, while a single 24-hour outage cost an average of $54.
The study also found that rural cooperative members have higher rates of backup generator adoption.
text:
Understanding what power interruptions actually cost consumers is essential to making smart decisions about grid investments. That's the idea behind the Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE) Calculator, a free online tool that utilities and regulators have relied on for over a decade to weigh the benefits of reliability and resilience upgrades. But the surveys behind the original tool are aging (some more than 25 years old), and they leave out large parts of the country, including many rural communities served by electric cooperatives.

To close that gap, the Department of Energy's Office of Electricity partnered with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Resource Innovations, and the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) to survey members of 18 electric cooperatives across the Southeast, Great Plains/Upper Midwest, and Intermountain West. Over the course of 2025, more than 1,300 residential and non-residential co-op members answered detailed questions about what different lengths of power interruptions—from a momentary interruption lasting less than 5 minutes to a full 24-hour interruption—would cost them.

The results confirm what many customers already sense: even short outages add up fast. A single momentary interruption cost residential members an average of $2, while a single 24-hour outage cost an average of $54. For businesses, those same outages cost $1,283 and $15,106 on average.

The survey also found that advance warning genuinely helps households said 24 to 48 hours' notice was enough to meaningfully soften an outage's impact, and businesses reported cost reductions of 27% to 59% when they knew ahead of time.

The study also found that rural cooperative members have higher rates of backup generator adoption. About 31% of residential respondents and 20% of non-residential respondents indicated they have backup generators installed. For comparison, 17% of residential and 14% of non-residential customers of investor-owned utilities reported owning backup generators as part of the broader initiative to update the Calculator.

And when asked how they'd cope with a three-day outage, 42% of residential respondents said they'd relocate some or all family members, while 65% of businesses said they'd simply shut down for the duration.

These findings will feed into the next major update of the Calculator, expected in early 2027, giving utilities—especially rural cooperatives that have historically been underrepresented in this kind of research—better data to justify investments that keep the lights on. It's another example of how the Office of Electricity's research partnerships help translate real customer experiences into the kind of evidence that supports a more reliable, resilient, and affordable grid for all Americans.

name: American Energy
title: Barry Schiller: A bill in Congress would speed up project approval. Is this good or bad?
description:
From its name, it certainly sounds like a good thing, but it has actually split the environmental movement.
It is a 417-page bill with 4 sponsors, two from each party, one of whom is our own Sheldon Whitehouse, long a climate leader.
The bill purports to be about permitting reform, intended to reduce delays so the U.S. can build projects more quickly, especially in energy.
Rhode Island Senator Sheldon Whitehouse is thinking of renewable energy, and is quoted in the press release saying Americans “want lower energy bills, and they want more clean energy.
If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share.
text:
Have you heard about the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act,” S5653, introduced in the United States Senate? From its name, it certainly sounds like a good thing, but it has actually split the environmental movement.

It is a 417-page bill with 4 sponsors, two from each party, one of whom is our own Sheldon Whitehouse, long a climate leader. The bill purports to be about permitting reform, intended to reduce delays so the U.S. can build projects more quickly, especially in energy.

Rhode Island Senator Sheldon Whitehouse is thinking of renewable energy, and is quoted in the press release saying Americans “want lower energy bills, and they want more clean energy. Our permitting reform plan gets us a long way toward both of those goals. If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share. Like all major pieces of bipartisan legislation, this bill is a compromise. We believe it is a compromise that will result in a brighter, cleaner, more affordable future.”

Renewable energy firms, worried about getting transmission lines built, support the bill, as does the Citizens Climate Lobby, which claims it will “unlock a huge amount of clean energy development.” But because the bill can also speed up fossil fuel development, it has support from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the National Mining Association, natural gas interests, and apparently the Trump administration, which wants to speed up projects like oil wells, coal mines, gas pipelines, and nuclear energy.

But some environmental groups oppose it, as the bill limits time for public comment, restricts judicial remedies, and narrows the scope of environmental review. The New York Times summary of the bill says “it puts new limits on landmark environmental laws such as the Clean Water and Endangered Species Acts.” The latter inspired a 4-page letter signed by more than 200 environmental groups, including Friends of the Earth, the Western Environmental Law Center, and the Center for Biological Diversity, detailing why the bill is objectionable. That last group says, “The U.S. Senate will soon vote on a massive legislative package that puts polluters, fossil fuel executives, mining companies, and Big Tech ahead of endangered wildlife, clean water, public lands, Tribal rights, and the people left to deal with the consequences. It contains 77 distinct environmental attacks. And North Atlantic right whales, monarch butterflies, manatees, spotted owls, and countless other species could pay the steepest possible price. This legislation dismantles critical environmental safeguards so powerful industries can push through destructive projects as quickly as they can — with less public oversight and fewer legal protections. This legislation is the most dangerous attack on wildlife and environmental protections.”

I can’t read and understand a 417-page bill, so I rely on others to. But thinking about our actual Rhode Island environmental history and what we face now, I note community opposition stopped proposals for an oil refinery on Narragansett Bay (why Save The Bay was formed), a polluting incinerator in North Kingstown, a coal plant in East Providence, nuclear power plants at Rome Point and in Charlestown, a new gas power plant in Burrillville, plus plans to slash interstate highways across the Scituate watershed and South County. In all those cases, the establishment mostly wanted the projects, but community opposition prevailed (with the help of allies in government). What “good” projects were stopped by community opposition? I can think of a few bike paths (the latest in Johnston), but not much else.

And what do we face now? Opposition to offshore wind isn’t due to community opposition, but to the current Federal regime. We do face a proposed gas pipeline expansion, data centers, LNG infrastructure, incineration, maybe coastal drilling for oil.... with the current Federal administration pushing them, these are the things that will most likely actually happen - plus our public lands in other states turned over to fossil fuel interests.

I’ll add that some local opposition to “solar farms” that destroy woodland, or transmission lines that slice through mountains, is not to be dismissed lightly. “Flooding the grid” with renewable energy isn’t without significant impacts, and the bill seems devoid of incentives to conserve, increase efficiency, or use less energy. So though I’m doubtful about it, I encourage discussion of the issue, especially since Senator Whitehouse is so involved and the Senate could start considering the bill as early as next week. I frankly don’t see why any Democratic Senator would want to work on the bill in the current Congress when they will have much more influence in just two months. I think it is worth considering calling Senators Reed and Whitehouse about this issue.

The lawmakers FOX 2 spoke with say they are still wrapping their heads around what the new legislation could look like. But some AI companies are already making their own policy changes in response to Washington’s new direction.

OpenAI released a new series of data center commitments—vowing to pay full electricity and infrastructure costs at its facilities, alongside new environmental protection plans.

It comes as Democrats in the incoming congressional majority push for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction, citing grid strain, public safety, and job loss concerns. Lawmakers are also demanding mandatory safety frameworks and calling on Big Tech CEOs to testify.

What they're saying:

FOX 2 asked industry experts what these potential new regulations could look like.

"My expectation is that they will put up some legislation similar to what we’ve seen from states like Illinois and California to maybe prevent larger companies from taking advantage of the leeway that they’ve had in AI for the past few years," said AI expert Joe Tavares.

"Well, we’re always going to try to protect the people, right? So we are looking at how do we protect energy, how do we protect water, how do we protect communities, noise regulations," said Awecomm CEO Brent Yax. "I assume we are going to see more of that. I hope we don’t see a moratorium because I think that slows us down quite a bit, but I do hope we see those regulations and see other states regulate this while building, and not slow down economic development."

This push is playing out at the grassroots level, too—voters approved dozens of local ballot measures nationwide this week to delay or ban new data centers over noise and rising utility rates.

Phoenix Tailings‘ planned $375 million rare earth separation facility at Eastman Business Park has been awarded $54.2 million in state, local and infrastructure incentives.

The incentive package for the company’s Freedom Project combines state tax credits, local tax benefits and anticipated infrastructure funding. It includes up to $3 million in performance-based tax credits through Empire State Development‘s Excelsior Jobs Program and roughly $15.9 million in separate New York state investment tax credits.

Another $35.3 million in projected benefits consists of tax savings on eligible equipment and construction materials, along with anticipated funding for power infrastructure improvements serving the facility.

“We do not celebrate progress by announcing we’ve built a floor or a wall. Success is producing the rare earth metals and oxides that power America and our allies,” said Nick Myers, co-founder and CEO of Phoenix Tailings. “Support from the Town of Greece, Greater Rochester Enterprise and New York State helps us upgrade the existing buildings and infrastructure at Eastman Business Park to bring production online faster for America.”

Additional Monroe County programs are expected to support equipment purchases and workforce training. The incentives are subject to applicable eligibility and performance requirements, approvals and final award terms.

The financial support is expected to reduce project costs and allow Phoenix Tailings to direct more capital toward processing equipment, production capacity and hiring local workers, its leaders said.

“This is about making sure the next generation of American innovation is built right here in Rochester, by American workers,” U.S. Rep. Joe Morelle said.

The incentive package also builds on a previously announced conditional loan from the U.S. Department of War for the Freedom Project.

State and local partners, including Monroe County and RED-Rochester, are helping advance the development through site preparation, permitting and access to the region’s manufacturing workforce.

The planned 500,000-square-foot facility will process rare earth materials used in electric vehicles, electronics and defense equipment. The materials are considered strategically important to U.S. manufacturing and national security, with much of the world’s rare earth separation capacity currently concentrated in China.

Phoenix Tailings plans to begin some operations at Eastman Business Park in 2027, with full production expected in 2028.

text:
More than 100,000 people are expected at the UN's two-week climate negotiations in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya.

Tougher action on fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change, appears unlikely and budget-strapped developed countries are reluctant to commit more money to help developing nations cope with climate impacts.

An energy crisis and cost-of-living pressures, fuelled by the war in the Middle East, are also looming over the gathering.

"This is not going to be the COP that changes the world," said Paul Watkinson, France's former chief negotiator at climate summits.

"It's an intermediate COP in many ways. But it is an important conference and it does need to make sure it makes progress," he said.

The talks follow deadly floods in Nepal, searing heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia.

An exceptionally strong El Nino climate phenomenon is forecast to peak later this year, adding to extreme weather and possibly helping to make 2026 or 2027 the hottest year on record.

The outlook is increasingly bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above preindustrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.

'Implementation COP'

Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference.

"COP31 comes at a difficult time for the world," said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen.

"Reaching consensus among nearly 200 countries will not be easy but cooperation remains essential," Bowen said.

COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, said the conference would strive "to turn the commitments of past COPs into real results".

Turkey is promoting an "action agenda" alongside the formal negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.

Its centrepiece is an "electrification" drive to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35 percent by 2035.

"This year's energy crisis has shocked us out of our complacency," Kurum said. "Electrification is the answer. It protects communities from volatile global markets and cuts emissions."

Turkey and Australia also want electrification to appear in a "cover decision" -- an overarching political statement negotiated by consensus and reflecting the main outcomes of the summit.

The European Union has called for "clean" electrification -- a term that could spark debate over the role of fossil fuels in the Turkish initiative.

"The Turkish COP31 presidency's electrification pledge was quite carefully worded in its language," said Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert at think tank E3G.

It is "quite an open pledge that I think is going to enable quite a few countries to come on board", Cassel said, noting that the initiative refers to "diverse and sustainable energy sources".

Money fight

Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.

COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.

Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary "roadmap" with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.

Observers say Turkey and Australia are keen to avoid a repeat of last year's fossil fuel fight at COP31.

But a feud looms over wealthy nations' unfulfilled financial commitments to help developing countries adapt to climate change and shift to cleaner energy.

The group of African negotiators are demanding that a pledge to triple adaptation finance -- money to cope with the worsening impacts of climate change -- be added to the negotiation agenda.

Recent elections have given climate campaigners a boost, with Democrats seizing control of the US Congress in a setback to President Donald Trump, who calls global warming a hoax.

A US congressional delegation will attend COP31, but the Trump administration is not taking part in the negotiations.

Fresh from his re-election win over conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will travel to Antalya next week.

title: Q&A: EPA's Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solution One Year After Reset
description:
ORD was previously headed by an Assistant Administrator and OASES now falls directly under the EPA Office of Administrator.
Q: What is the mission of the Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions at EPA?
OASES leads the agency’s gold-standard science enterprise and provides innovative applied science and environmental solutions that support the agency’s policy and regulatory decisions.
Q: Tell me a little bit about the Gulf Coast Environmental Science Laboratory, how many people work there and what work they do?
The Gulf Coast Environmental Science Laboratory houses the Gulf Coastal Science Branch within the OASES Coastal Science Solutions Division as well as a handful of staff from other EPA offices.
text:
The Florida Specifier recently interviewed Teresa Booeshaghi, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Associate Administrator of OASES, a year after the agency restructured, creating the office, refocusing its mission on research and collapsing the Office of Research and Development. ORD was previously headed by an Assistant Administrator and OASES now falls directly under the EPA Office of Administrator. Booeshaghi previously served as Florida DEP’s Deputy Director of the Division of Waste Management. Below is the question and answer interview.

Q: What is the mission of the Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions at EPA?

EPA’s mission is to protect human health and the environment. OASES leads the agency’s gold-standard science enterprise and provides innovative applied science and environmental solutions that support the agency’s policy and regulatory decisions. OASES partners with the program offices and regions to establish priorities and science needs that are in line with our statutory authorities and ensure that we’re able to provide clean air, clean water, and clean land to all Americans.

Q: How has the mission of OASES changed after the reorganization involving the Office of Research and Development?

Over the past year and a half, EPA has undertaken a strategic restructuring effort that ensures rigorous, evidence-based science will continue to guide decision-making at the agency.

As part of that reorganization, EPA moved hundreds of scientists into our program offices, closer to the real-world regulatory work and established OASES within the Office of the Administrator to provide critical oversight of the agency’s scientific enterprise.

In addition to our science coordination role, OASES also conducts applied research that is closely coordinated with our partners across the agency to directly advance the agency’s statutory requirements. Our goal is to prioritize practical, solution-oriented research. OASES also supports cooperative federalism through collaboration with states and Tribes.

Q: What impacts have you seen in operations since the reorganization was announced and implementation began?

I was appointed as the OASES Associate Administrator and EPA’s Agency Science Advisor in April 2026, 6 months following the implementation of OASES. Since that time, I have seen many benefits to the revitalized structure.

Bringing scientists into the program offices they support has strengthened the engagement between researchers and decision makers, helping to ensure science is the backbone of every decision the agency makes.

OASES’ placement in the Administrator’s Office has helped to elevate the visibility of science across the agency, enhance scientific consistency, and strengthen our connections to agency priorities. It provides a direct line of communication between our science enterprise and senior leadership while also giving us a birds-eye-view of the agency’s programs and scientific needs.

Q: How will OASES meet EPA’s mission?

It already is! OASES has an important role when it comes to fulfilling EPA’s mission of protecting human health and the environment.

OASES was established in the Office of the Administrator to assist in coordinating and overseeing EPA’s science enterprise, aligning our applied research tightly with the needs of Air, Water, Land and Emergency Management, and Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention program offices who are responsible for carrying out EPA’s statutory obligations.

Our office is doing important work to promote public health protection in EPA rulemaking, policies, enforcement actions, and research. OASES is also working on applied science activities that deliver solutions for responding to environmental emergencies; identifying potential health and ecosystem effects; remediating contamination; monitoring, protecting, and restoring environment, and informing waste and materials management decisions.

I can share many examples of how ongoing OASES work is making a real impact toward meeting EPA’s mission, but I’ll take this opportunity to share just one here. Lead remains a real problem for millions of Americans. EPA researchers have installed a lead service line identification test bed at our regional research laboratory in Edison, New Jersey. There, EPA is evaluating emerging lead service line identification technologies under controlled, consistent conditions. This helps identify what emerging minimally invasive methods are reliable for locating and classifying lead service lines in communities, with the ultimate goal of replacing them and safeguarding public health. I’m looking forward to visiting Edison in a few weeks to see the testbed for myself.

Q: Tell me a little bit about the Gulf Coast Environmental Science Laboratory, how many people work there and what work they do?

The Gulf Coast Environmental Science Laboratory houses the Gulf Coastal Science Branch within the OASES Coastal Science Solutions Division as well as a handful of staff from other EPA offices.

The lab is home to a workforce of approximately 65 staff – federal scientists, professional staff, research fellows, IT, operations and maintenance and security teams. The lab delivers applied collaborative research to inform decision-making aimed at protecting, remediating and restoring coastal resources to advance EPA’s statutory obligations to safeguard human health and the environment.

Q: Why is that facility located in Florida and does that give EPA a strategic benefit?

The laboratory in Gulf Breeze was initially established by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and later inherited by EPA in 1970. EPA is federally mandated to maintain a research facility in the southeastern area to conduct research, investigations, experiments, field demonstrations and more.

Beyond its original purpose, the facility’s location provides many distinct advantages. It is the only EPA research facility in the Gulf with specialized capabilities to study coastal ecosystems, watersheds, and how pollution and other human activities affect aquatic resources. The lab’s position also allows it to play an important role in research response for crisis events like hurricanes and oil spills.

The facility also has unique assets, like a 14,000 ft² wet laboratory for evaluating impacts of stressors on fresh and saltwater species; a 19,000 ft² chemistry, microbial, and molecular laboratory supporting analytical activities; a research fleet that includes offshore and nearshore vessels; and a Unit Dive Team for scientific dives and trainings.

Q: What type of research is happening there and how is that research being applied to EPA standards and other environmental projects?

There’s a lot of great research happening at our Gulf Breeze laboratory. Our scientists are combining fieldwork, laboratory studies, and computer modeling to better understand how pollution and other human activities affect aquatic ecosystems. That work is helping to inform water quality standards and environmental management decisions.

They are also developing new tools and methods to evaluate how effectively we can clean up contamination and restore damaged ecosystems.

Their work helps EPA better assess the health of aquatic ecosystems and protect our nation’s waters and the health of surrounding communities. Let me share a few examples:

In Pensacola Bay, our researchers are monitoring water quality, including low oxygen and changes in acidification. Understanding where these conditions occur and how long they last can help inform our goals of improving and protecting the Bay’s water quality.

In collaboration with local estuary programs, they are using environmental DNA or eDNA to learn more about fish and other aquatic species living in Pensacola and Perdido Bays. Living organisms constantly shed and excrete DNA into the environment, and by analyzing this material scientists can better understand local biodiversity (including endangered and invasive species) and create a clearer picture of the health of aquatic ecosystems.

The Gulf Breeze campus is also home to EPA’s only coral lab. EPA scientists are studying corals under controlled laboratory conditions so we can better understand how pollutants and other environmental stressors affect these important ecosystems. What makes this facility especially valuable is our ability to bring questions from the real world into the laboratory. We can recreate environmentally relevant conditions, carefully control exposures, and measure how corals respond. For example, our research has examined how sediment impacts coral systems. Our scientists are studying species-specific coral responses to sediment and working to further refine threshold values across multiple species. The research can have very practical applications. For example, understanding how corals respond to sediment can help inform operational approaches intended to reduce impacts associated with activities such as dredging.

Q: Do OASES and the Laboratory have connection with private industry to partner on solutions and if so, do you have any examples?

I have made it one of our program goals to increase public private partnerships in the coming year. Building relationships with private industry can help identify practical solutions that benefit both the environment and communities that depend on it. I believe that some of the best solutions come from bringing people together who may approach a challenge from different perspectives. Connecting with private industry is an important part of that. Businesses bring innovation, technical expertise and resources that can help us address environmental challenges in practical ways and often offer opportunities for mutual benefit.

OASES has multiple examples of these partnerships across the organization. Our scientists at the Gulf Breeze lab are partnering with private industry on a number of projects. They’re collaborating on models and data to support Total Maximum Daily Loads (TMDLs) development, partnering on contaminated sediment characterization and sediment dredging design, and collaborating with industry to develop and refine analytical protocols for critical emerging contaminants of concern for aquatic environments.

More broadly, across OASES, we are also partnering with private industry to advance the science and understanding on topics such as the thermal destruction of PFAS. By partnering with municipal and hazardous waste facilities to do facility-scale testing, we can evaluate how effective incineration is in treating PFAS, building on the pilot-scale testing that takes place at our labs. These tests, including one that took place in Florida, help us understand what happens when these waste-to-energy facilities process materials that contain PFAS.

Q: Even though you have a national role, is Florida still your favorite state and why do you say yes?

Without a doubt, Florida is still my favorite state. I spent 25 years living and raising my family there, so it will always hold a special place in my heart. Add sunshine, beautiful beaches and toes in the sand, and it’s an easy choice. And with a student at the University of Florida, I’m still very much invested in the state – Go Gators!

My national role has given me the opportunity to travel across the country and experience the incredible natural beauty and diversity of our states. It has also deepened my appreciation for the natural resources that make each state unique and reinforced how important it is to protect Florida, which is especially meaningful to me, both because of my years there and because of the responsibility we all share in preserving what makes it so special for future generations. Through my travels, I discovered Oregon, which is giving Florida a run for its money, but dipping my toes in the Pacific Ocean was a very different, and much chillier experience!

So yes, Florida still gets my vote, and I’m proud that my work allows me to help protect the state I still consider home.

text:
Robinson Carbon announced it will invest $16.3 million to establish a biochar manufacturing facility at England Airpark in Rapides Parish, 130 miles northwest of Baton Rouge, extending its family-owned wood products business into a new market more than 130 years after its founding in Louisiana.

Robinson Carbon is expected to create 42 direct new jobs. Louisiana Economic Development estimates the project will result in an additional 60 indirect new jobs, for a total of 102 potential new job opportunities in the Central Region. The project builds on Robinson Lumber Company’s longstanding Louisiana presence, with the fifth-generation family business expected to retain 22 existing positions.

“Louisiana has long been a leader in turning our natural resources into products used around the world,” LED Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois said. “For more than 130 years, the Robinson family has been part of that history, and we are grateful for their continued commitment to Louisiana. Their latest investment reflects how innovation is creating new possibilities across the sectors that have powered our economy for generations, strengthening our competitiveness while extending Louisiana’s foundational industries into new products and markets.”

The facility will operate two rotary drum pyrolysis reactors, converting approximately 100,000 metric tons of Southern Yellow Pine residuals annually into 16,500 metric tons of biochar. Robinson Carbon plans to source the material from nearby mills and produce biochar to customer specifications for agricultural, horticultural and pollution remediation applications. The company has relocated a pilot reactor from its New Albany, Indiana, manufacturing site to Alexandria, where it will be used to train employees ahead of full-scale production. Once certified under the Puro Standard, the facility is also expected to generate approximately 40,000 CO2 Removal Certificates annually, each representing one metric ton of carbon dioxide removed.

Robinson Lumber Company history

“My great-great-grandfather founded our company in New Orleans in 1893 selling Louisiana longleaf pine,” Robinson Carbon CEO Garner Robinson said. “Since then, the products have changed many times over, but our passion for wood products hasn’t. Biochar is an exciting opportunity to make something truly new out of wood, and we look forward to planting new roots in Central Louisiana. We are grateful to Governor Landry, Secretary Bourgeois, the LED team, and to our partners, for helping us bring this project home to Louisiana.”

Robinson Carbon is the carbon products arm of Robinson Lumber Company, a fifth-generation family business founded in New Orleans in 1893. Over more than 130 years, the company has expanded from selling Louisiana longleaf pine into international wood products manufacturing and distribution, with Robinson Carbon representing its entry into biochar production.

“Robinson Carbon’s investment reinforces England Airpark’s position as a competitive location for advanced manufacturing and industrial development,” England Economic and Industrial Development District Executive Director Ralph Hennessy said. “Our infrastructure, strategic location, and capacity for growth make England Airpark an ideal home for innovative companies like Robinson Carbon. We look forward to supporting the company’s continued success and expansion.”

Project timeline

Construction is expected to begin in November 2026, with production anticipated in the second quarter of 2027.

“Robinson Carbon’s $16.3 million investment is another example of how Central Louisiana is building on its traditional industry strengths to create new economic opportunities,” Louisiana Central President & CEO Chris Masingill said. “By connecting our region’s longstanding timber and wood products industry with innovative manufacturing technologies, this project strengthens our industrial base, creates high-quality jobs, and opens new markets for Louisiana’s natural resources. Investments like this demonstrate that Central Louisiana is well-positioned to compete for the next generation of industry while creating lasting economic opportunities for our people and communities.”

OTTAWA — CHRIS SEVERSON-BAKER, the Pembina Institute’s executive director, made the following statement in response to the federal government’s Budget 2026:

“Today’s federal budget marks a significant step forward for Canada’s path to electrification, including investments in transmission, electric vehicle charging networks, and reducing diesel dependence in northern communities. After decades of underinvesting in our electricity system, today’s budget recognizes the investment and breadth of action needed to build a more resilient, affordable, and secure system.

“These investments will help Canada tackle some of its biggest challenges, from economic competitiveness and energy security to affordability, job creation, and climate resilience. They also demonstrate a serious commitment to electrification as a foundation for a stronger economy and a more independent energy future.

“Today's budget is also an encouraging signal after a year that saw important climate and clean energy policies weakened or rolled back. Investments in electricity infrastructure, transportation electrification, and northern energy modernization can help restore momentum and provide greater certainty for workers, communities, and investors looking to participate in Canada's clean energy transition and reap the benefits of affordable and reliable energy."

Long term certainty on Clean Electricity and Clean Technology Investment Tax Credits by extending them from 2034 to 2040, costing $38.5 billion. This change supports projects that take many years to build, including transmission lines within and across provincial borders.

$1.6 billion over 10 years for energy reliability in the North, starting in 2027-28. This includes $713.8 million for renewable energy and capacity-building projects that help Indigenous, rural, and remote communities transition from diesel and fossil fuels to renewable energy sources, and $929.1 million to replace and upgrade aging electricity infrastructure in northern communities.

Significant investment in EV charging, with $634.2 million committed to charging infrastructure and related programs. Funding for more than 55,000 additional chargers will make it easier for Canadians to switch to electric vehicles and save on fuel costs. text:
Electric-vehicle developments this week included Tesla’s launch of unsupervised Robotaxi service in Fort Worth, a UBS upgrade of Rivian citing early R2 demand, and Citigroup’s third-quarter filing that showed increased stakes in some EV names while cutting positions in others.

Tesla Opens Unsupervised Robotaxi Service In Fort Worth

Tesla launched unsupervised Robotaxi rides in Fort Worth this week across an estimated 143-square-mile zone centered on downtown and extending toward Saginaw, White Settlement, Benbrook, Haltom City, and Forest Hill. It is Tesla’s seventh U.S. city with unsupervised rides and its fourth in Texas. The launch is the first new market in about three months. Rides are booked through the Robotaxi app with no safety monitor on board, consistent with other Texas operations. Tesla has not confirmed the initial vehicle mix or whether Cybercabs are included at launch.

Rivian Draws Wall Street Optimism

UBS upgraded Rivian to 'Buy' earlier this week, citing solid early R2 demand and a path toward positive automotive gross margins by year-end. The firm has a price target of $17 on the stock and noted that the recent selloff poses a buying opportunity.

In the third quarter, the first full quarter after the company started delivering the R2 SUV to customers, the company’s deliveries reached a record 19,248 vehicles, prompting the company to increase its full-year outlook to 67,000–70,000 vehicles.

Tesla’s Chinese Rival BYD Clocks Growth; Smaller Startups Report Mixed Performance

BYD, Tesla’s chief global rival, reported October new-energy vehicle sales of 490,168 units, up about 11% year over year, with strong overseas shipments near 170,000. Battery electric vehicle deliveries alone amounted to 305,743 units in the month.

Guangzhou-based EV startup XPeng, meanwhile, set a monthly delivery record of 50,237 vehicles in October, up about 20% year over year, with overseas volume also reaching a record.

Other China-based startups such as Nio and Li Auto, however, experienced a dip. NIO delivered 34,246 vehicles across its brands in October, below the 40,397 recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Li Auto delivered 29,025 vehicles, compared to 31,767 vehicles in October 2025.

Citigroup’s Auto Trades

According to a filing this week, Citigroup increased its Rivian stake by nearly 40% to about 8.56 million shares in the third quarter and more than doubled its Lucid position, raising holdings to roughly 4.25 million shares from about 2.06 million. It also raised its Tesla position by about 10%.

Citigroup, however, cut its XPeng holding by about 83% and reduced its Li Auto position while adding to NIO. The firm also exited its small position in California-based EV startup Faraday Future.

How Did Retail Traders React?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TSLA trended within the 'bearish' territory at the time of writing, while sentiment around RIVN, XPEV, and NIO was on the 'bullish' end. Sentiment around LCID and LI stayed 'neutral.'

While TSLA has dived a deep 14% thus far this week, RIVN, LI, and XPEV have clocked high single-digit gains.

title: Carbon-aware EV charging cuts emissions 1.62% without extra infrastructure
description:
Researchers report that a carbon-aware charging strategy, built on reinforcement learning and tested against real residential charging data, cut charging-related emissions by approximately 1.62% compared with uncontrolled charging, while delivering exactly the same amount of energy to the vehicles.
The carbon intensity figures represent operational average emission intensity, calculated as total CO2 emissions divided by total electricity generation at each time step.
The researchers solved a deterministic linear programming benchmark with perfect knowledge of future carbon intensity under the same constraints.
Subject of Research: Quantifying carbon emission reduction from carbon-aware electric vehicle charging in distribution power networks Article Title: Quantifying carbon emission reduction from carbon-aware electric vehicle charging in distribution power networks Article References: Hossen, M. S., Sarker, M. T., Ramasamy, G., & Eng, N. E. (2026).
Quantifying carbon emission reduction from carbon-aware electric vehicle charging in distribution power networks.
text:
Electric vehicle charging is often celebrated as a clean alternative to gasoline, but a new study shows that when and how those vehicles plug in can determine whether the technology actually trims carbon emissions. Researchers report that a carbon-aware charging strategy, built on reinforcement learning and tested against real residential charging data, cut charging-related emissions by approximately 1.62% compared with uncontrolled charging, while delivering exactly the same amount of energy to the vehicles. The striking part of the finding is what did not work: an intelligent charging controller that optimized scheduling without any carbon information produced zero emission reduction, matching the uncontrolled baseline to the kilogram.

The study, published in the journal Carbon Research, reconstructed real-world charging sessions from an urban residential charging site at hourly resolution. Each session record contained a start time, an end time, and the total energy delivered. The team converted timestamps to a unified format, removed incomplete or invalid entries, and then spread each session’s energy across the hours it overlapped, preserving total energy so that no artificial loss or gain entered the analysis. This hourly demand profile was then paired with time-varying grid carbon intensity data from the Malaysian Peninsula power system, obtained from publicly available hourly emission records and expressed in kilograms of CO2 per kilowatt-hour.

The carbon intensity figures represent operational average emission intensity, calculated as total CO2 emissions divided by total electricity generation at each time step. The authors note that lifecycle emissions from infrastructure, fuel extraction, battery manufacturing, and vehicle production were excluded, since those components are independent of charging time and cannot be influenced by scheduling decisions. The analysis therefore captures the emissions that charging coordination can actually change.

Three charging strategies were compared under identical energy delivery and network constraints. The baseline allowed vehicles to charge immediately upon connection. A carbon-unaware variant of the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm optimized charging subject to feeder capacity limits but ignored carbon intensity entirely. The proposed PPO-Carbon strategy explicitly incorporated grid carbon intensity into its reward function, penalizing emissions alongside feeder overload and charging delays. All three strategies delivered the same total energy of 53,740.38 kilowatt-hours over the evaluation horizon, ensuring that any difference in emissions arose purely from scheduling.

The results were unambiguous in their asymmetry. Uncontrolled charging produced 32,315.26 kilograms of CO2, with an average carbon intensity of 0.6013 kilograms per kilowatt-hour. The carbon-unaware PPO strategy produced identical figures, confirming that intelligent optimization alone does nothing for emissions when the objective ignores carbon. The carbon-aware strategy, by contrast, brought total emissions down to 31,793.24 kilograms and lowered the average intensity to 0.5916 kilograms per kilowatt-hour, a relative reduction of 1.62%, equivalent to roughly 522 kilograms of CO2 avoided.

The mechanism behind the reduction lies in a temporal mismatch the study quantified directly. Average grid carbon intensity during evening peak hours, defined as 18:00 to 22:00, measured 0.6789 kilograms of CO2 per kilowatt-hour, while off-peak intensity measured 0.5747 kilograms per kilowatt-hour, an 18.1% relative increase during peak periods. Residential charging commonly occurs in the evening when users return home, precisely when the grid relies more heavily on fossil-fuel generation. A representative month of data showed charging demand concentrated in the same hours when the grid was least clean, meaning a substantial share of uncontrolled charging happened at the worst possible times.

The carbon-aware controller did not simply delay charging uniformly. Hourly emission comparisons showed that reductions occurred predominantly during periods of elevated carbon intensity, particularly in the evenings, while emissions during cleaner hours closely tracked the baseline. Peak-period emissions fell from 9,330.80 kilograms under uncontrolled charging to 7,472.95 kilograms under the carbon-aware strategy, a pronounced drop, while off-peak emissions remained largely unchanged. This targeted shifting explains how the strategy achieved savings without curtailing energy or extending charging beyond users’ connection windows.

Statistical testing supported the finding. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test applied to paired daily aggregated emissions, chosen to reduce temporal autocorrelation in the hourly data, yielded a p-value of 0.002, indicating the reduction is significant at the 1% level. The team also checked robustness from several angles. A sensitivity analysis over the reward weighting coefficients showed that increasing the carbon weight monotonically reduced emissions, with diminishing returns once limited session flexibility was exhausted, and that the carbon-aware strategy consistently outperformed the baseline across realistic weight combinations. When Gaussian noise representing 5% and 10% forecast uncertainty was added to the carbon intensity signal, the reduction declined gradually but stayed above 1.4% and 1.2% respectively, showing the controller does not depend on perfect foresight.

How close does the learning approach come to the theoretical best? The researchers solved a deterministic linear programming benchmark with perfect knowledge of future carbon intensity under the same constraints. That optimum yielded 31,720.15 kilograms of CO2, only about 0.23% below what the PPO controller achieved. The small gap indicates the modest overall reduction is limited by the temporal flexibility of residential charging sessions and the actual variation in carbon intensity, not by algorithmic inefficiency. The authors also observed a trade-off: carbon-aware charging produced a slight increase in peak charging power, because the objective prioritizes emission reduction over peak load minimization and can concentrate charging in low-carbon intervals that are not the lowest-load periods.

The authors caution that the analysis covers a single urban residential feeder, which constrains the magnitude of achievable reductions, and that historical carbon intensity data may shift as renewable generation grows. Feeder constraints were modeled as an aggregate capacity limit, without detailed voltage regulation or power flow modeling, and electricity cost optimization was not considered. Even so, the study demonstrates a clear principle: emission savings from electric mobility depend on aligning charging with cleaner electricity hours, and that alignment requires carbon signals to be built directly into the control objective. Without them, even sophisticated learning-based scheduling leaves the carbon footprint untouched.

Subject of Research: Quantifying carbon emission reduction from carbon-aware electric vehicle charging in distribution power networks

Article Title: Quantifying carbon emission reduction from carbon-aware electric vehicle charging in distribution power networks

Article References: Hossen, M. S., Sarker, M. T., Ramasamy, G., & Eng, N. E. (2026). Quantifying carbon emission reduction from carbon-aware electric vehicle charging in distribution power networks. Carbon Research, 5(1), Article 43. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44246-026-00280-6

title: Democrats' state wins open the door for major clean energy progress - Canary Media
description:
At the state level, however, Democrats’ victories offer immediate opportunities to advance clean energy as well as energy affordability.
Some states that have already passed clean energy mandates are eyeing opportunities to go further.
Pennsylvania environmental groups are also tracking a dozen environmental or clean energy bills that have been blocked by Republicans in the state Senate.
Republicans in the Texas legislature have pushed a variety of pro–fossil fuel and anti–clean energy policies in recent years, though sometimes unsuccessfully.
The Trump administration has put its thumb on the scale for fossil fuels, weakening pollution restrictions on coal plants, forcing aging power plants to stay running, and directing massive investments to support new gas power plants, pipelines, and export terminals.
text:
Democrats’ historic wins in Tuesday’s midterm elections will give them control of Congress and a chance to combat the Trump administration’s anti-climate agenda, but the president’s veto power will limit their options.

At the state level, however, Democrats’ victories offer immediate opportunities to advance clean energy as well as energy affordability.

Democrats flipped governor’s seats in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas — and likely Alaska. They won control of both houses of state legislatures in five states where they did not previously have it — Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin — and their chances are looking good in Arizona as well. Come January, Democrats will have trifectas — hold the governor’s office and both houses of the legislature — in 21 or more states, up from 16, adding at least Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

States hold significant power over key facets of energy policy, including what kinds of power plants utilities can build or must shut down, how energy-efficient buildings must be, and how much pollution industries can emit.

“Almost every policy you can think of to decarbonize our economy, except maybe border adjustment taxes, can be done at a state level,” Jay Inslee, former governor of Washington state, said at a Wednesday press conference. His state has instituted some of the country’s most aggressive climate policies, including a carbon cap-and-invest regime, a 100% clean electricity standard, incentives for electric vehicles and EV chargers, and ​“the nation’s leading building code standards,” he said — all of which ​“could not be stopped by Donald Trump.”

Washington is one of about two dozen states with some form of policy calling for electricity to be 100% renewable, carbon-free, or carbon-neutral in the coming years. Almost all these policies were enacted because Democrats held sufficient political power to overcome Republican opposition.

When Democrats are in power at the state level, ​“we don’t even have to wait for Congress,” Inslee said.

How states can shape energy and climate policy

BloombergNEF highlighted this dynamic in a postelection memo, noting that newly empowered Democratic trifectas ​“should lead to policies boosting clean-tech sectors like renewables, energy storage, heat pumps and EVs.” Democratic state governments could also push through policies requiring data centers to use clean energy and curb costs for residents in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, and measures that would boost solar and battery development in Arizona and Nevada.

Some states that have already passed clean energy mandates are eyeing opportunities to go further. In Michigan, Democratic leaders are considering new climate and energy measures after fighting back efforts from House Republicans earlier this year to repeal the state’s 2040 target for 100% clean energy.

In Minnesota, two years of partisan deadlock in the state House held back efforts to expand virtual power plants and legalize plug-in solar, according to advocates promoting those policies. Now, bills will have a better chance to move forward.

Trish Demeter, managing director at clean energy trade group Advanced Energy United, highlighted other opportunities in a Thursday press conference, including in states where anger over data centers and rising utility bills has galvanized voters.

She pointed to Pennsylvania, where clean energy boosters are pushing a reform package meant to streamline the state’s ​“complicated and burdensome siting and permitting regime for building new large-scale wind, solar, and batteries.” Similar reforms have been gaining traction in other states that are struggling to build clean energy to meet growing demand for power, although those efforts face pushback from local communities.

Pennsylvania environmental groups are also tracking a dozen environmental or clean energy bills that have been blocked by Republicans in the state Senate. Among them are a legislative package backed by Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro that aims to impose pollution, clean-energy, and affordability requirements on data centers, and another that would expand access to distributed solar and other energy resources.

In Wisconsin, where Democrats have regained their first trifecta in 16 years, climate advocates are pushing for policies that will constrain utility spending on fossil-fueled power plants to serve data centers and promote solar, wind, and batteries instead. To this end, Advanced Energy United is lobbying Wisconsin Democrats to impose more-stringent utility planning regimes.

The breaking of Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas could also ​“constrain those states’ support for fossil fuels and restrictions on clean power,” BloombergNEF wrote. Republicans in the Texas legislature have pushed a variety of pro–fossil fuel and anti–clean energy policies in recent years, though sometimes unsuccessfully.

And in Georgia, Democratic candidates for the state’s Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, won a 3–2 majority after two decades of Republican control. That could position the PSC to work with Democratic Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms to push utility Georgia Power to expand consumer access to rooftop solar and energy efficiency and to prioritize clean energy and batteries instead of fossil gas–fired power plants to serve uncertain data center demand.

It’s the affordability, stupid

Governors and state lawmakers are most directly responsible for dealing with public outrage over high and rising electricity costs.

Last year, Democrats won governorships in New Jersey and Virginia in large part by committing to lowering utility bills, which they’ve sought to carry out in conjunction with aggressive climate programs. This year’s Democratic gubernatorial victors — including Bottoms of Georgia, Amy Acton of Ohio, and Gina Hinojosa of Texas — ran on promises to promote clean energy, bring down utility bills, and curb unchecked growth of power-hungry data centers.

These issues have risen to the top of voters’ concerns, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, a group that supports state and local pro-climate candidates. Of the 120 candidates her group backed this year, 86 had won election, nine had lost, and 24 were too close to call as of Wednesday morning.

“This was the affordability election,” she said during a press briefing her organization held. ​“Talking to voters across the country, utility bills, electricity prices, gas prices, affordability came up over and over and over.”

She added, ​“The good news is that climate solutions and clean energy solutions and affordability are the same.” Solar, wind, and batteries are cheaper and can be built faster than gas-fired power plants, and have made up more than 90% of new additions to the grid in the past several years.

The Trump administration has put its thumb on the scale for fossil fuels, weakening pollution restrictions on coal plants, forcing aging power plants to stay running, and directing massive investments to support new gas power plants, pipelines, and export terminals. But states regulate utilities that deliver electricity and gas to customers, and hold varying degrees of power to direct the mix of fossil-fueled and carbon-free resources those utilities rely on.

State regulators ​“have a lot more control over the incentives to bring cheaper, cleaner sources on the grid than we do at the federal level,” U.S. Rep. Sean Casten, an Illinois Democrat and outspoken climate champion, said at a press conference on Wednesday. ​“They’re the ones who set the interconnection rules. They’re in many cases the ones who are directly facilitating with the ISOs and RTOs,” the entities that oversee wholesale energy markets and regional grid operations for about two-thirds of the country. ​“They’re the ones who are making sure that you can actually monetize the value you create.”

Most of the country’s utilities have been backsliding on their carbon-cutting commitments over the past two years, primarily by delaying the closure of coal plants and dramatically expanding plans to build new gas-fired power plants. That shift in utility priorities has been largely driven by the seemingly insatiable demand for electricity from AI data centers.

text:
Toledo has quite a history when it comes to manufacturing items that contributed to major events.

“You are in a city that does things, that makes things, that’s not afraid to roll up its sleeves, get a little dirt and grease under its fingernails,” Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said Thursday at the Electric Vehicle Innovation Summit America 2026.

The international conference and exhibition at the Glass City Center brought together global leaders, policy makers, researchers, and industry pioneers to discuss the future of electric transport and mobility.

“We don’t just make automobiles, we invent them,” the mayor said. “The Jeep, for instance, was a military vehicle that helped win World War II, and we never stopped making them. There’s a lot of civic pride in something like that.”

Toledo also contributed to putting a man on the moon, he said.

“The elevators that took Neil Armstrong from the ground to the top of his Saturn V rocket were made by Haughton Elevator Company in Toledo. When the astronauts got to the moon, the visors of their space suits were made at the Libbey Owens Ford glass plant. I say all of this as a preamble that we are a prideful place that does things, makes things, and builds things,” Mr. Kapszukiewicz said.

“When it was time to build a machine that won World War II, when it was time to put a man on the moon, we were there,” the mayor said.

Topics of discussion during the multi-day event included hydrogen fuel, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving systems, and smart urban infrastructure. EVIS is headquartered in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, and chose northwest Ohio for its first summit in the United States.

“This is an international conversation that’s happening in Toledo,” said the mayor after the meeting. “Whenever you have leaders from all over the world coming together to have an important conversation — if it’s happening in Toledo — it’s a big deal for our city. This is a conversation about the future of electric vehicles, and Toledo’s not afraid of the future. There will be economic benefits for Toledo transitioning to electric mobility.”

Hesham Al Bahri, the event producer of EVIS America 2026, said Toledo was chosen to be the location for its first U.S. visit because it is based in “automotive alley.”

“Toledo has an automotive heritage. It is strategically located at the center of the automotive industry, close to Detroit. It’s a manufacturing hub for the industry,” he said.

Local partners, including the University of Toledo, Destination Toledo, the City of Toledo, and the Regional Growth Partnership helped the group come to the United States, Mr. Al Bahri said.

“They helped us make this happen. We hope it will generate more public awareness about electric vehicles and mobility,” he said.

“It fits in exactly with our automotive heritage,” said Dean Monske, president and CEO of the Regional Growth Partnership. “We’ve done new EV technology. We got together with a lot of partners, and they agreed they wanted to do this.”

“We’ve had a lot of friends from Michigan, from Detroit’s economic development corporation, and automotive suppliers, who came to the summit yesterday,” Mr. Monske said of the summit’s second day of events. “We may have had a little bit of a slowdown in the last couple of years when it comes to EVs, but the rest of the world is moving pretty quickly forward.”

EVIS is already committed to coming back to Toledo next September, he said.

“They’ve already signed a contract to come here. My guess is it’s going to be four to five times bigger across the spectrum. The quality of people who are here is phenomenal,” Mr. Monske said.

title: Carney's Electrification Budget Is a Breakthrough. Now Triple the Ambition - Energi.Media
description:
Budget 2026 puts electricity and electrification at the centre of Canada’s economic strategy.
The government understands that cheap, abundant, clean electricity is the foundation of industrial competitiveness, energy security and household affordability.
It follows, then, that Canada should be shooting for a much, much higher degree of electrification than this budget suggests.
Natural Resources Canada says federal support for electrification totals $115 billion through 2041–42, including $52 billion in new Budget 2026 commitments.
Mark Carney’s electricity budget is unlikely to significantly change the country’s trajectory.
text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has delivered the budget I’ve been waiting for. Budget 2026 puts electricity and electrification at the centre of Canada’s economic strategy. The government understands that cheap, abundant, clean electricity is the foundation of industrial competitiveness, energy security and household affordability. It understands that electric cars, heat pumps, and factories are part of one economic transformation. And it’s prepared to put serious federal money behind that vision.

For someone who’s spent years arguing that Canada should electrify its economy, this is a terrific budget.

But I’ve got one big complaint: The ambition isn’t nearly big enough.

Canada gets about 18 per cent of its end-use energy from electricity. That’s the starting line. But the math doesn’t match Carney’s ambition.

Canada consumes 600 TWh of electricity per year. I’ve done a rough calculation about how much new industry – pipelines, LNG< oil sands, mines, smelting and refining, manufacturing, to name the big ones – could be added by 2050, and the new load could easily be another 600 TWh. That would leave Canada using the same percentage of electricity it does today.

Meanwhile, other advanced economies are advancing at a rapid pace. The electrification rate for China, for example, 30 per cent and it’s rising by one percentage point per year. China could arrive at mid-century with a rate of 55 to 60 per cent.

The Prime Minister is correct that electrification is more efficient, lower cost, and that electric technologies make Canada more competitive. It follows, then, that Canada should be shooting for a much, much higher degree of electrification than this budget suggests.

An advanced economy that wants to compete in an increasingly electric world should be far more ambitious. The budget finally gets the direction right. Now the federal government needs a plan that matches the scale of the opportunity.

The Great Electricity Build-Out

Ottawa’s National Electricity Strategy, first released last spring, aims to double the country’s electricity system by 2050. Natural Resources Canada says federal support for electrification totals $115 billion through 2041–42, including $52 billion in new Budget 2026 commitments.

Those aren’t all cheques for new power plants: a large share consists of tax incentives spread over many years.

Still, the program is substantial. The government proposes extending the 30 per cent Clean Technology and 15 per cent Clean Electricity investment tax credits to 2040, at an estimated cost of $38.5 billion. High-voltage transmission lines within provinces would become eligible for the electricity credit. Another $4 billion would support electricity infrastructure, renewable energy and priority grid projects.

Nuclear power, hydroelectricity, offshore wind, northern energy systems, and interprovincial transmission are all in the mix. Projects already receiving federal backing include Darlington nuclear in Ontario, the North Coast Transmission Line in British Columbia, and Churchill Falls and Gull Island in Labrador.

And here’s where the arithmetic becomes uncomfortable.

Canada produces roughly 600 terawatt-hours of electricity annually. Doubling that would take us to about 1,200 TWh by mid-century, an additional 600 TWh. But expanding industries—everything from critical minerals processing and steel to hydrogen and data centres—could claim a staggering share of that new supply.

Consider a plausible scenario in which new industrial demand alone adds 600 TWh a year. The entire increase in generation would be spoken for before we dramatically electrified the rest of the economy. That’s a stress test, not a verified federal demand forecast, and we must avoid counting industrial demand twice.

But it exposes a crucial question: is doubling supply sufficient for both industrial expansion and mass electrification?

Ottawa needs to publish an integrated electricity-demand plan, sector by sector, that shows how much power its economic ambitions actually require. If the answer is more than twice today’s supply, the national target should rise.

Connecting the Country—and Making the Equipment

The budget recognizes that generation is only half the battle. Electricity has to get from dams, reactors, and wind farms to the communities and industries that need it.

Canada’s provincial grids are fragmented

Transmission links could allow provinces to share clean electricity, reduce the need for duplicate capacity and protect customers against disruptions. Ottawa proposes additional transmission support, planning work and new financing arrangements to avoid loading the entire cost of long-lived infrastructure onto today’s ratepayers.

The most encouraging part might be the industrial logic. Federal tax-credit bonuses of up to 10 percentage points for clean technology and five points for clean electricity are being considered for projects using Canadian-made components. Transformers, cables, batteries, turbines and digital controls could become major Canadian manufacturing opportunities.

That’s economic sovereignty in concrete form: building the infrastructure and building the industries that supply it. But these domestic-content bonuses are still subject to consultation. Ottawa will have to translate its intentions into orders, factories and jobs.

Heat Pumps: A Good Start, Not a Mass Transition

The government is also spending more than $2 billion on one million home retrofits. Its National Heat Pump Rebate is intended to support up to 820,000 households, helping them replace costly heating systems and lower energy bills. The government estimates annual savings exceeding $1 billion across its retrofit effort.

Excellent policy. Modest scale.

Using a working estimate of 17.4 million homes, 820,000 installations would represent about 5.7 per cent of the housing stock over eight years. And not every supported installation necessarily replaces a fossil-fuel heating system. The actual additional electrification would be smaller.

We replace furnaces and other heating equipment every year. That’s the opportunity: make the electric option easy and affordable whenever a household needs a new system. A serious national electrification program would move beyond a limited rebate pool toward sustained, mass-market adoption, supported by provincial utilities and installers.

Electric Vehicles Need the Same Ambition

Budget 2026 promises more charging infrastructure: over 55,000 additional federally supported chargers, backed by $587 million over five years, alongside support for EV affordability and Canadian automotive manufacturing.

Good. Range anxiety is real, especially in rural Canada, and dependable public charging matters. But chargers are only one part of the transition. Canadians also need affordable vehicles, straightforward home and workplace charging, and electricity prices that make switching attractive.

The government’s own action plan sees electric vehicles and heat pumps as the means of shrinking the household ‘energy wallet’—the combined bill for gasoline, natural gas, heating oil, propane and electricity.

As electricity takes a larger share, overall energy spending can fall because electric technologies use energy more efficiently.

That’s a compelling affordability argument. Ottawa should make it much more central to public policy.

Make the Vision Bigger

This graph sums up a big problem for Canada: The electrification of the national economy hasn’t changed for 35 years. Sure, we have a clean power supply, but the majority of Canada’s energy comes from gasoline and diesel for transportation and natural gas for heating.

Mark Carney’s electricity budget is unlikely to significantly change the country’s trajectory.

The Canadian Climate Institute is right to welcome this budget’s direction. Electricity investment can drive growth, lower emissions, and improve competitiveness. The federal government has finally connected those dots in a way that reaches far beyond climate policy.

But we shouldn’t confuse a breakthrough in thinking with a complete plan. Doubling electricity generation by 2050 is a major undertaking. It may also be too conservative. Electrifying a relatively small fraction of homes over eight years won’t transform the residential sector. And charging stations won’t electrify transportation by themselves.

Carney has given Canada a convincing economic destination. Now he needs to show the country what it will take to get there—and raise the ambition if the math demands it.

That’s my verdict on Budget 2026: a remarkable start, and a challenge to think much bigger.

text:
The Nvidia-backed cloud provider IREN said Thursday that a Microsoft-requested change to networking equipment resulted in delays to a massive data center project in Childress, Texas.

IREN said it now expects to reach $4 billion in operating annual recurring revenue by January or February, having previously targeted year-end.

The project comprises four phases, and IREN is building it under a $9.7 billion contract with Microsoft. After the first building was delivered in August, Microsoft requested relatively inexpensive changes to help support the latest AI models, IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts said Thursday on an earnings call.

"The data centers are practically done, and we're waiting for remaining equipment to arrive to finish commissioning," he said.

He said that IREN and Microsoft have a "great relationship."

Microsoft said last week that it spent $5 billion less than expected on AI infrastructure due to delays from third-party cloud providers. While it didn't name names, satellite images analyzed by research firm Aterio pointed to IREN and Nebius.

The delay underscores growing concerns about neoclouds, which rent AI compute to businesses and have been facing power shortages and construction setbacks.

Roberts said IREN is slowing expansion plans because of tougher financing conditions, though customer demand remains strong.

IREN shares plunged Thursday and rebounded in after-hours trading following its earnings report. The company reported $228 million in quarterly revenue and a net loss of $263 million.

Neoclouds like IREN are a key part of Nvidia's customer base, and Nvidia has supported many of them through investments and financial guarantees.

They give Nvidia access to a broader pool of customers beyond cloud giants like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, which buy Nvidia's chips and are also developing rival hardware of their own.
