text:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — A pair of lawsuits are challenging the constitutionality of Proposal 2.

On Tuesday, four out of five voters in Michigan cast their ballot in favor of the proposal, which restricts campaign contributions from companies like Consumers Energy and DTE Energy.

Hours after the race was called, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy — a conservative think tank in Midland County — filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan, claiming the proposal violates the First Amendment.

On Thursday, Consumers Energy filed a separate suit in the same court on similar grounds.

Proposal 2

Proposal 2 bans certain entities and people — 1) state-regulated electric and gas utility companies, 2) businesses with large state or local government contracts, 3) and certain people affiliated with these entities, including presidents, board members, lobbyists, and the immediate family members of these people — from making political contributions in certain state and local elections.

Proposal 2 also subjects more forms of communication to campaign finance laws in the state.

First, people who spend $5,000 or more a year to publicly communicate about a candidate within 100 days of an election must now report to the state their election-related communications — a term referred to as electioneering — and disclose information about the donors who financially supported their communication.

Second, people who spend $500 or more a year on communications that attack or defend a candidate are also subject to campaign finance laws in the state and must similarly disclose donor information.

Previously, those who spent $100 or more a year on these types of communications — a term referred to as independent expenditures — were subject to campaign finance laws, but only if they expressly advocated for an election result.

America Votes

What is Proposal 2 in Michigan? FOX 17 is breaking down the proposal

Sam Landstra

Mackinac Center for Public Policy

"This law is not aimed at a very narrow portion of campaign finance. It's aimed at everybody," said Patrick Wright, vice president of legal affairs for the Mackinac Center for Public Policy. "So, we call it a nasty tool, and I think that's a valid description."

Wright claims the language in Proposal 2, specifically as it relates to electioneering and independent expenditures, is "vague" and believes it could subject nonprofits, journalists and even private citizens to its campaign finance reform.

"If you spend $5,000, what does that mean?" Wright said. "What about somebody who writes an op-ed? What about somebody who talks on a Substack? What about somebody does a subscription newsletter?"

In its lawsuit, the Policy Center said its own communications "will likely fall under Proposal 2’s new definition of 'electioneering communications' or 'expenditures' thus triggering burdensome disclosure requirements and raising the risk that Mackinac and its supporters will face threats, harassment, and reprisal from those opposed to its advocacy."

Consumers Energy

While the lawsuit from the Mackinac Center does not challenge Proposal 2's restrictions on campaign contributions made by utility companies, the suit from Consumers Energy does take issue with this portion of proposal.

"This proposal unfairly targets a Michigan business, its Michigan employees and their family members from exercising their constitutionally protected rights to participate in the political process, while allowing out of state special interest groups and billionaires to continue flooding Michigan with political spending. Michiganders should not lose their First Amendment rights because of where they work," the utility company said in a statement to FOX 17.

Michiganders for Money out of Politics

Michiganders for Money out of Politics — the group that put Proposal 2 on the ballot — defended the measure to FOX 17 on Thursday.

"This is about Michiganders prioritizing a fair and transparent democracy where voters are the primary concern of their elected officials," said Christy McGillivray, co-chair for MMOP.

"I think it's totally predictable that the corporations that have benefited from pay-to-play politics, would prefer to keep the status quo," McGillivray said. "We are confident that we are as well prepared as we can be to prevail in court."

McGillivray also said the Mackinac Center was "grasping at straws" with its claims.

"They have to lie to people to make their case," she said. "What's going to happen with this is that voters will no longer see all sorts of dirty political ads on their screens that don't provide any disclosure about who's paying for them. That's what's going to happen."

text:
Australian conversion specialists Janus Electric have been celebrating a growing slate of orders for their Class 8 electric truck conversions, which ditch diesel in favor of advanced battery-swap electric power – but exactly how they’d deliver all those trucks was still a question. Now, we have an answer: Electrovaya will supply the batteries.

The concept of dropping an electric power unit into a Class 8 semi makes perfect sense, as most of these trucks are built as gliders. That is, rolling body and chassis without an engine and transmission that’s ready to receive power from Cummins, Detroit, International, or Volvo Penta. That’s the role that Janus Electric sees itself occupying, and it seems to be working.

Janus’ reservation book crept past 70 units this past summer, helped along in part by California’s HVIP Program and the US EPA’s Diesel Emission Reduction Act (DERA) Grants. When the HVIP voucher is combined with the Port of Los Angeles’ “Plus” support, customers can received up to $166,000 per truck conversion. Factor in the massive fuel savings of electric and the classic good looks of square-nose Western Star truck body, and it’s easy to see why they’d be a popular choice.

As Jerry Seinfeld taught us however, it’s one thing to take a reservation – it’s another thing to deliver. To help make it happen, Janus has inked a battery supply deal with Electrovaya that will see a $26 million initial purchase orders for Electrovaya battery packs to demand for Janus’ products in the US and Canada, along with the battery company purchasing approximately $1.4 million in Janus stock with (what seems to be) actual money.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

“Electrovaya is an important partner to Janus Electric, and we’re particularly pleased it has decided to invest directly in our business,” explains Ben Hutt, Managing Director and CEO of Janus Electric. “The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport.”

Loads of promise

The Janus Electric-repowered trucks carry a stout, 480 hp electric motor drawing power from a standard 310 kWh battery pack, with up to two battery packs (one on each side) of the truck. In practice, that gives the Janus trucks up to 370 miles of loaded range. After that, the batteries can be DC fast charged in under 90 minutes, or swapped for fresh ones in about four minutes without too much in the way of specialized equipment. That’s not just Janus’ killer app, it means that a battery supply deal like this one with a strategic partner who’s invested in the fledgling company’s success is such a huge deal.

“Reliable battery supply is critical to our growth,” adds Hutt, “and Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale. Both companies see considerable opportunity in this market, and we look forward to building on our partnership.”

For their part, Electrovoya executives seem to know their role here, and seem excited to be a part of what Janus is doing. “Class 8 trucking is one of the most exciting and demanding frontiers in electrification, and Janus has demonstrated real commercial traction with fleets in the US, Canada and Australia,” said Dr. Raj Das Gupta, CEO of Electrovaya. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations.”

Electrovaya will be expanding its American manufacturing capacity with lithium-ion cell, module, and battery pack production at its new, potentially BABA-compliant facility in Jamestown, New York, which is expected to come online in 2027.

text:
Rule 205 will improve air quality, enhance economic development

Maricopa County Air Quality Department is excited to announce a major milestone in the effort to lower emissions and enhance economic development.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) gave final approval today to the Maricopa County-authored Rule 205 which provides emission reduction credits to fleet owners who upgrade or replace high-emitting on-road vehicles.

“Rule 205 is a win-win for our residents, demonstrating that Maricopa County can prioritize both cleaner air and a strong economy,” said Maricopa County Board of Supervisors Chair Kate Brophy McGee, District 3. “By incentivizing rather than punishing job creators, this approach will deliver measurable improvements in air quality while creating new opportunities for businesses to invest and expand.”

Adopted in May 2025, Rule 205 allows fleet owners and operators to generate emission reduction credits (ERCs) by upgrading or replacing higher-emitting on-road vehicles with cleaner technologies. These credits can be used to offset emissions from new or expanding industrial sources, helping businesses meet Clean Air Act requirements under the nonattainment New Source Review program. With the EPA’s final approval, Maricopa County will be able to start using Rule 205 immediately to issue these credits to businesses.

"I applaud EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for working with Maricopa County to find Clean Air solutions that fit the unique needs of our region. It's proof we can partner with the federal government to streamline regulations while still protecting the quality of the air we breathe," said Vice Chair Debbie Lesko, District 4.

Final approval of Rule 205 comes just one month after the EPA announced proposed approval of Maricopa County Rule 204, which would provide an incentive for owners and operators of non-road vehicles like railroad locomotives and construction equipment to upgrade or replace high-emitting vehicles with cleaner technologies.

These rules are the first of their kinds in the country and position Maricopa County as a regional leader in effective, innovative government.

Taken together, they provide regulators and the business community with new options to meet federal air quality standards in ways that encourage economic development.

Whether longtime, non-traditional, or new voters, we must continue to argue for inclusive and participatory democracy to address climate change.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

The country feels different as the US midterm election results come rolling in. When all of the votes are counted, Democrats are set to win the national popular vote in all House races by about 13 percentage points. The voters have spoken in huge numbers: they want leaders who make everyday life a little bit easier.

Now the politicians must answer, and, essentially, they need to design policies that lower costs for ordinary people in the US. It’s not about revenge: revenge is too distinct from US consumers’ lived experiences.

Paul Krugman, the Nobel Prize-winning economist, says that one of the main things “Democrats need to do now is hold not just Trump’s officials, but also his enablers, accountable.” Representative Robert Garcia of California posted on social media in the same vein: “Lawyer Up” to the MAGA losers.

No, that’s playground antics. Instead, the next two years must demonstrate a willingness to listen to US citizens as each family struggles to make ends meet with groceries, household utilities, healthcare, and other daily costs.

Roy Cooper’s Senate campaign in North Carolina had a mantra that permeated every stop on his statewide tour: Make Stuff Cost Less.

That’s it.

James Talarico, Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper, among others, grounded their campaigns in economic populist agendas. They harangued against President Trump’s economic record and called out corruption for what it is — self-promotion over the interest of US citizens.

Georgia’s Senator-elect Jon Ossoff made Trump’s assault on the rule of law practical. In everyday terms he pointed out to voters how democracy and economic distress depend on each other. He argued that “corruption is why nothing works for ordinary people.”

We are ready as a nation to reintroduce the importance of science to accomplish these goals.

In a recent commentary in the journal, Nature, a group of authors argue that “science is an essential backbone of democracy.” Science as a source of discovery, expertise, and innovation is intertwined, they continue, with democracy as a set of institutions, rules, and procedures. They put forward three pillars through which science enables democracy:

establishing shared factual baselines;

aiding trust in institutions; and,

providing tools to adapt policies and organizations in response to changing circumstances.

Citizens have legitimate concerns, the scientists agree, “about economic restructuring, regional inequities, how migration is governed, technological changes, ageing populations, climate risks and geopolitical instability.” Then again, “expertise strengthens democratic legitimacy when it is transparent, diverse, independent and open to scrutiny — as prescribed by the rules of science.”

Democracy — when it lives up to its responsibility as the rule of law — contributes to a decrease in CO2 emissions. Climate change, like voting in a democracy, is a collective action problem — a conflict between the individual interest and the group interest.

How Can Embrace of Science Translate into a Populist Message?

Congress can look ahead and back science-based clean energy in a variety of ways, from policies to investment, all of which will address the affordability crisis, improve public health, and protect the environment, says Gretchen Colman, president of the Union of Concerned Scientists. That will include renewables and clean transportation, modernizing the power grid, protecting our air and water, and more.

Science-based legislating, Colman continues, must be based “on facts and evidence, not political whims. We’ll petition Congress to restore funding for science, protect federal science agencies, and re-establish safeguards for federal scientists to carry out their work and communicate about it free from political interference.”

A national return to scientific reasoning is underway. Gina Hinojosa, elected as the first Texas Democratic governor, has called for an immediate moratorium on data center development. She has accused developers of “raising our utility rates and depleting our water.” As reported on Bloomberg Green, she’s vowed to halt approvals until “a legislative session that puts Texans first so that we don’t have any more communities in Texas who are powerless against these global corporations.”

Indeed, the output of data centers must also be questioned. Few AI-generated findings are peer-reviewed or tested in laboratories. Talk about mixed messages! We return to a nostalgic past by foregrounding large language models that are programmed to present particular, narrow, and self-serving points of view — generally by billionaires seeking to protect their wealth. It’s time to tax these rare individuals accordingly, eliminate any incentives for their built structures, and require them to provide major renewable energy contributions to communities that house them.

Yes, energy plays an increasingly important role in today’s world. Instead of treating electrification as an option to move us toward decarbonization, it’s time to see it is essential — we need to electrify everything quickly. In the US, more than 60 state and local governments are similarly in court to seek damages from oil companies. These are the lawsuits that Democrats in Congress should be pursuing as complements to transitioning virtually all building, transportation, and industrial systems to electric. This means subsidizing heat pumps and EVs and solar panels and home battery storage — subsidies are far cheaper than funding wars for oil.

Final Thoughts

The ground-breaking election events have hoisted non-traditional candidates to levels of power and influence, as the New York Times chronicles:

The first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan;

the first Black female governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia;

the first openly gay male senator, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire;

the first Hispanic governors elected in Texas, Gina Hinojosa, and California, Xavier Becerra;

the first female governor of Ohio, Amy Acton; and,

the first female Native American governor, Deb Haaland of New Mexico.

Political analyst Chris Armitrage suggests another important positive trend. “The thing that lasts past January 2027 is the voter who had never voted in a midterm, did it in 2026, and now has the habit,” he concludes.

The urgency of climate change has brought democracy to a critical moment in time. Whether longtime, non-traditional, or new voters, we must continue to argue for inclusive and participatory democracy to address climate change. Shaped by democratic governance, a robust civil society, and innovative advocacy strategies, collective climate action can be a force for the right to a healthy planet.

name: Texas Environment
title: With New Control of State Legislatures, Democrats Have Decisions to Make
description:
Texas state Rep. Gene Wu, the Democratic minority leader in the state House, knows what it’s like to legislate under Republican control.
They flipped at least 10 chambers that were under Republican control, and likely two more.
The scale of the shift “exceeds all expectations,” says Tim Storey, CEO of the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL).
Pennsylvania Democrats flipped the state Senate Tuesday night, giving them a trifecta for the first time since the early 1990s.
But with a Republican majority in the Senate, it’s far from a free hand.
text:
By Jared Brey.

Texas state Rep. Gene Wu, the Democratic minority leader in the state House, knows what it’s like to legislate under Republican control. He’s done it for his entire political career in the state capital, which started in 2012. At first, it was mostly what Wu expected. Democrats couldn’t set the agenda or get many major bills through, but they ran some committees, negotiated legislation and went out for dinner with their Republican colleagues.

Something changed around the time Donald Trump was elected president in 2016, Wu says. As the Republican agenda became more hardline, the environment in the House became less collegial. Successive leaders sought to outflank each other on the right. The GOP ended the practice of letting Democrats chair some committees. When Republicans decided to vote on new legislative maps last summer, kicking off a frantic back-and-forth of mid-decade redistricting, they threatened to arrest some of the Democrats who had fled the state to deny them a quorum. Later they tried to have them removed from office. Along the way they passed plenty of legislation that Democrats considered harmful, offensive and even vindictive. One that sticks out to Wu is SB217, which bars people from certain countries, including China, where Wu was born, from owning property in Texas.

So when Democrats suddenly ended up winning control of the Texas House, along with the governor’s race and every statewide office for the first time in decades, it almost didn’t seem real.

“Maybe my expectations were tampered by years of failures — election cycle after election cycle of disappointments and trauma,” Wu says. “I was not prepared for the amplitude and the magnitude of the wave.”

Tuesday’s election was a rout for Democrats around the country. They won all eight of the state legislative chambers considered “toss-ups” by the University of Virginia Center for Politics. They won the ones that “leaned Republican” as well, including the New Hampshire Senate and the Georgia House. They flipped at least 10 chambers that were under Republican control, and likely two more. They got six new state trifectas — in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Arizona and Nevada — bringing their total to 22. They broke a few Republican trifectas and supermajorities. And they won some chambers, like the Texas House, that virtually no one predicted they’d win. They won enough governor’s races to give them a majority of states. They’ll start next year with more states under Democratic control than any time since the early 1980s.

The scale of the shift “exceeds all expectations,” says Tim Storey, CEO of the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL). For many decades, it was typical to see 11 or 12 chambers flip between parties every two-year cycle. But after the 2010 cycle, when Tea Party-powered Republicans flipped 20 chambers, the frequency of chamber flipping has ebbed, according to NCSL. Only a few chambers changed hands in the last few cycles. In addition to the new partisan majorities, there are at least 42 new leaders — house speakers and senate presidents mainly — of individual legislative chambers. The political pendulum swing is proof that advocates working in state capitals need to build relationships in both parties, no matter how solid a majority may seem.

“We always joke, what do you call the minority party leader?” Storey says. “Future Speaker.”

Democrats have decisions to make about how they’ll run legislatures, what kinds of policies they’ll prioritize, and how much disagreement they’ll tolerate within their own caucuses. Their agendas will likely look different depending on how long they’ve been locked out of power. Minnesota, for instance, last won a Democratic-Farmer-Labor (DFL) trifecta in 2022. The party used the 2023 session, under Gov. Tim Walz, to clear nearly the entire legislative agenda they’d built up since the last time they had control, a decade earlier. Minnesota state Sen. Scott Dibble told Governing in 2024 that the DFL had regretted being too cautious when it had a trifecta in 2013, because it quickly lost the majority and missed a chance to pass some of their priority legislation. So they didn’t leave anything out in 2023. The session was so momentous that some legislators retired after it was over.

Other majorities don’t have that kind of muscle memory, and to some extent Democrats can’t know how much of their success on Tuesday was an endorsement of their policy agenda versus a repudiation of Republican leadership. Pennsylvania Democrats flipped the state Senate Tuesday night, giving them a trifecta for the first time since the early 1990s. Alongside Gov. Josh Shapiro, a relatively moderate Democrat, they have outlined a backlog of priorities they want to pass: Raising the minimum wage, providing new mass transit funding, legalizing marijuana and other issues. They’re sorting out how much leeway they have.

“We are going to be fiscally responsible, fiscally conscious,” said state Sen. Jay Costa, the Democratic minority leader, in a press conference this week. “We’re going to make sure that we’re being thoughtful going forward because, you know, we don’t want to just have a majority for two years — we want to stick around a little while.”

Michigan Democrats won their trifecta back just a few years after they last had it. In that state, there’s no giant backlog of policy goals the caucus has been itching to pass, says Matt Grossman, a Michigan State University political scientist. The Legislature will adjust to working with the new governor, Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who campaigned more on competent administration than an ambitious policy agenda, Grossman says. The Legislature will have more leftwing Democrats, and fewer moderate Republicans. It’s possible, given the scale of Democrats’ win, that negotiations will rely less on distributing district-level benefits for every representative who signs onto a bill, as has happened in the recent past.

“When you have a small majority you need everybody, so that process is necessary,” Grossman says. “But when you have a bigger majority I’m not sure it is.”

With control of the House and a governor from the same party, Texas Democrats will have more say over the state’s policy agenda than they’ve had in generations. But with a Republican majority in the Senate, it’s far from a free hand. Wu says the party needs to focus on the affordability and quality-of-life measures that drove people to the polls, echoing Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa’s campaign message.

“The key for Democrats is not to be consumed by the Republicans’ desire to do red-meat culture war issues. I think the lesson we’ve learned from 2026 is to ignore their bullshit and just work,” Wu says. “Do the things you promised you would do. Do what people want and move on. It’s the Mamdani example: Ignore the naysayers, get it done, and then tell people what you did.”

It remains to be seen how Democratic leaders will run the Texas House, which they haven’t done since 2002. Will they turn the other cheek, and offer Republicans a chance to chair some of their committees? Wu, for one, doesn’t see why they would.

“I don’t think anybody has any desire to change the rules the Republicans shoved down our throats,” he says. “Democrats have to be tough. Democrats have to make sure there are consequences for bad behavior. That’s what’s been missing from our politics for a long time.”

Jared Brey is a senior staff writer for Governing. He can be found on Twitter at @jaredbrey.

text:
Austin energy startup Base Power is continuing its expansion in North Texas.

In August 2025, the company opened an office and warehouse in Grapevine with around 10 full-time employees. Today, it has more than 100 employees and more than 50% of its customer base in Dallas-Fort Worth. It also recently inked a deal with Dallas-based Hillwood Communities to offer its home battery backup system to nearly 6,500 homes in three North Texas communities.

“The original thesis, and the thesis still today, is that the U.S. grid needs a lot of help,” co-founder and COO Justin Lopas said during a presentation at the Venture Dallas conference Oct. 22. “It needs a lot more capacity, and we think we have a unique, novel way to add capacity to the grid quickly.”

Growth heats up

Investors are taking note of the growth. According to TechCrunch, Base Power raised $1 billion in a Series D round in August, less than a year after raising $1 billion in the previous round. The latest fundraise values the company at $13 billion.

Base Power is installing around 100 batteries at single-family homes a day, with 50 in the DFW area, Lopas said. By the end of the year, he expects the company will have deployed roughly a gigawatt-hour of capacity. Demand on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas grid hit a record 91.1 gigawatts on July 22, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Texas was an obvious choice for the company’s headquarters and initial growth, Lopas said, citing its status as an energy capital, its talent pool and its business climate.

“We’ve found that it is frankly easier and lower friction and better to do business in Texas than where we’ve started expanding outside of Texas,” he said. “This is the best place to do business in the country by far. There’s also just a huge market.”

How Base Power will work in Hillwood homes

Under the company’s deal with Hillwood Communities, new and existing homeowners in three neighborhoods — Treeline by Hillwood in Justin, Pecan Square by Hillwood in Northlake and Harvest by Hillwood in Argyle and Northlake — will be eligible for Base battery systems to provide power during outages. At full build-out, about 9,500 homes in the three subdivisions will have access to Base battery systems.

“From winter storms and extreme summer heat to tornadoes, North Texans know how quickly severe weather can disrupt daily life,” Andrew Pieper, senior vice president of Hillwood Communities, said in a statement announcing the program. “Through this partnership, we’re giving homeowners a cost-effective way to prepare for power outages while supporting the broader electric grid.”

Base offers its service through agreements with local utilities and electric cooperatives in areas where homeowners cannot choose their electricity provider. Elsewhere, the company serves as a retail electricity provider. Last year, Base qualified for ERCOT’s Aggregated Distributed Energy Resource program, which allows it to pool capacity from individual home batteries and sell it in the market.

With the Hillwood communities, Base is working with the electricity co-op CoServ. Hillwood homeowners will receive preferred pricing, according to the announcement. Base owns the batteries and provides any needed service. Its Base Core battery provides 39.2 kilowatt-hours and up to 36 hours of backup, depending on usage. The backup kicks in automatically when power goes out.

“We’re building energy infrastructure that can add capacity where people live,” Zach Dell, co-founder and CEO of Base Power and son of Dell Technologies founder Michael Dell, said in a statement. “Hillwood’s communities give us an opportunity to do that at scale. Together, we can put technology to work for thousands of households while supporting our grid.”

Hillwood and Base plan to extend the partnership beyond the three initial communities to future homes served by CoServ in Landmark by Hillwood in Denton and Lantern by Hillwood in Pilot Point. And the partners are looking toward further expansion.

“Building strong communities means thinking about the needs of our residents over the long term,” said Fred Balda, president of Hillwood Communities. “While we’re focusing on North Texas now, this partnership will evolve throughout our development platform where feasible, including our investments in Austin, Houston, Florida and the Northeast as Base is ready to serve those markets.”

title: Voters Have Spoken: No Dirty Data Centers - Earthjustice
description:
Voters in at least 38 jurisdictions and counting passed data center bans or restrictions, and exit polling shows that a majority of midterm voters considered artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers to be a major factor in their vote.
Data centers were at the center of countless races, including high-profile races like the Texas governorship and the Ohio Senate seat.
With its extremely targeted provisions for gas pipelines, BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.
With Tuesday’s election results, voters are clearly asking elected leaders to stop the build-out of dirty data centers.
Voters overwhelmingly approved data center restrictions, and elected leaders who ran on ensuring safeguards and accountability for data center development.
text:
No issue has activated more Americans in this historic election than opposition to the current data center build-out. And the current Congress faces an immediate test next week on whether they got the message.

Voters in at least 38 jurisdictions and counting passed data center bans or restrictions, and exit polling shows that a majority of midterm voters considered artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers to be a major factor in their vote. Data centers were at the center of countless races, including high-profile races like the Texas governorship and the Ohio Senate seat.

This historic election showed that voters are deeply skeptical about the way that data centers are getting built now and how the process is representative of what is not working for people in our country. Secret deals and corporate tricks. Sky-rocketing electricity bills. Air pollution and failures to protect water. Intolerable noise. The sheer scale of industrialization and loss of place. Not least of all: the raw power of the wealthiest companies in the world to speed past anything and anyone in their way.

Going into the election, voters overwhelming wanted more guardrails on data center development. A plurality wanted stronger regulations (39%), and another 25% wanted a moratorium on new data centers in their community; 22% even wanted a permanent ban. Large support for regulations and moratorium was consistent across those who self-identify as Democrats, Independents, and non-MAGA Republicans.

The data center backlash fueled the midterm election results. But before all the new members are sworn in, the old Congress is set to finish up some last-minute business.

A few days from now, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). Without major amendments that appear to be out of reach, a vote for this bill would ignore the message that voters around the county have just sent to Washington, D.C.

BAAJA is being promoted by its most vocal proponents as a bill to build new transmission lines to unleash clean energy, and that is critically important. We need to expand the grid and put it to much more effective use by addressing real transmission and interconnection bottlenecks.

But BAAJA is not only or even mostly a transmission bill. It is a sweeping overhaul of federal law. One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out. The speed-to-power rush for AI has become a rush to gas, and the industry is desperate to meet rising demand and lock in more gas consumption.

With its extremely targeted provisions for gas pipelines, BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers. Here’s the package: gutting federal environmental review, including an outright exclusion for pipeline expansions, rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act, blocking interference from States and Tribes, and prohibiting courts from issuing injunctions and other meaningful remedies. What this combination gives to the gas industry is an ultra fast-track for new and expanded gas pipelines that is insulated from court challenges and the kind of public opposition to data centers that is now expanding to associated pipeline projects.

Why does the fast-track matter so much? Some of the industry’s biggest players are poised to bring gas from hubs like the Marcellus Shale and the Permian Basin to fuel bigger and bigger data center complexes with gas. In a recent report with the Better Data Center Project, we identified 177 GW of planned gas capacity to power data centers on site or “behind the meter.” The scale of total and individual proposals is massive. As of August 2026, we identified nine proposed gas projects that are 4.5 GW or larger. If all are built, nine of the top 10 largest power plants in the U.S. would be data center gas projects.

From the perspective of AI hyperscalers, piping in gas for on-site power is the fastest, cheapest path to lock in power on a timeline and on terms that are most in their control. The only risk they have now is reliable gas capacity. BAAJA’s pipeline package would solve that problem for them immediately, sealing many deals that would enable the dirtiest version of the data center build-out to move even faster, while the transmission provisions that could enable more clean energy will take years.

With Tuesday’s election results, voters are clearly asking elected leaders to stop the build-out of dirty data centers. And, maybe more than anything else, people are demanding that government work for them. Instead, this bill gives more certainty to the most powerful AI and oil and gas companies, while dramatically weakening environmental protections and giving President Trump even greater license to drive his dangerous agenda and do damage that a future president will be unable to repair.

Data centers were on the ballot on Tuesday, and they lost. Across the country, voters came out to stop a “speed at all costs” build-out that is hurting communities and increasing costs and pollution. Voters overwhelmingly approved data center restrictions, and elected leaders who ran on ensuring safeguards and accountability for data center development. Super-charging gas-fired mega-data center projects is the opposite of that. Now is the time to make AI developers do better.

The share of new solar projects deployed with co-located battery storage this year is 16% — or about 41 GW — as of September, and may reach 19% by year’s end, said an Oct. 30 report from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. It is likely to pass 30% in the next two years, the agency estimated.

The trend has increased significantly over the last decade, as only around 2% of projects, or 5 GW, of new solar capacity was co-located with storage in 2017. In 2023, co-location jumped to 25% of projects, then fell over 2024 and 2025, according to EIA’s data — but is projected to pass 30% over the next two years, based on planned additions.

“When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices,” EIA’s report said. “Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease.”

“Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment,” EIA added.

An Oct. 22 report from the Solar Energy Industries Association found that from 2021 to 2026, “solar generation increased 421% in Texas and 90% in California, while battery storage capacity grew more than 26-fold in Texas and nearly sevenfold in California.”

When comparing the same June to August period, SEIA found that “CAISO used 2.5% more power than the same time in 2021 with an average wholesale electricity price 40% lower after accounting for inflation. ERCOT used 30.1% more power than the same time in 2021 with an average wholesale price 42% lower after accounting for inflation.”

EIA’s report noted that Southwest states “have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity.”

“As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage,” EIA said. “The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.”

title: Could putting AI data centers in space solve an environmental problem, or create a new one?
authors: Liz McLaughlin, WRAL Climate Change, Liz McLaughlin, WRAL Climate Change
description:
SpaceX is developing plans for much larger satellites that could eventually form a network of space-based data centers.
But so are the technical challenges and environmental risks, including new sources of space debris and light pollution.
Google is already testing AI in space In October, Google launched a refrigerator-sized satellite carrying AI chips as part of Project Suncatcher, an effort to develop solar-powered computing in orbit.
SpaceX is developing AI computing satellites with large solar arrays, radiators and laser communication links.
The early experiments demonstrate that AI computing can work in orbit.
text:
As communities push back against the enormous electricity and water demands of AI data centers, some of the world's biggest tech companies are pursuing an unusual solution: moving computing hundreds of miles above Earth.

Google has begun testing AI technology in orbit. SpaceX is developing plans for much larger satellites that could eventually form a network of space-based data centers.

The potential payoff is significant. But so are the technical challenges and environmental risks, including new sources of space debris and light pollution.

Google is already testing AI in space

In October, Google launched a refrigerator-sized satellite carrying AI chips as part of Project Suncatcher, an effort to develop solar-powered computing in orbit.

The satellite successfully generated and transmitted a haiku back to Earth:

Blue marble belowData streams in silent graceStarlight feeds my core

"Turns out, it is possible," said Travis Beals, Google's senior director leading Project Suncatcher, in a company video.

The experiment demonstrated that AI processors can operate in space. The next challenge is connecting multiple satellites to perform more demanding computing tasks. Google plans to test laser communication between two satellites in 2027.

The timing is significant. Global data center electricity demand is projected to roughly double by 2030, as communities across the country raise concerns about the industry's growing environmental footprint.

According to Google's estimates, solar panels in certain orbits could generate five to eight times as much electricity as comparable panels on Earth. Space-based computing could also reduce the need for some water-intensive cooling systems.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk sees similar potential.

"That avoids the need to build massive power plants on Earth and deal with cooling because cooling is actually much easier in space than it is on Earth," Musk said in a company presentation.

SpaceX is developing AI computing satellites with large solar arrays, radiators and laser communication links. The company has proposed a constellation that could eventually include as many as 1 million satellites, although that system has not been approved or deployed.

Why space isn't an easy solution

Despite the appeal of abundant solar power, putting computers in space doesn't eliminate the heat they produce.

"The heat is still generated from inside the circuits," said Dr. Arun Kannawadi, an assistant research professor of physics at Duke University. "You still need an effective way of like transferring that heat from inside the circuits to the exterior wall, and then it dissipates."

Without air to carry heat away, satellites need specialized cooling systems and radiators. Repairs could also require additional launches, while solar radiation can damage sensitive electronics.

"Even if you just put this in space, it's not going to be as efficient as you think it might be, just because the space is cold," Kannawadi said.

The risks extend beyond engineering.

Kannawadi, an observational astronomer, studies the universe using telescope images that are already affected by sunlight reflecting off satellites.

"They are kind of photobombing the images that we are trying to take," he said.

An October 2026 research paper modeled the impact of a hypothetical constellation approaching 1 million orbital data center satellites on the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile. Researchers projected substantial interference with astronomical observations, including dramatic increases in sky brightness under certain conditions.

Those are modeled scenarios, not effects observed from an existing space-based data center network.

Kannawadi also raised concerns about potential effects on wildlife if satellites significantly brighten the night sky, as well as the danger of collisions creating additional orbital debris.

"You end up having a lot more debris than you would have just from a smaller satellite," he said, warning that collisions could trigger a chain reaction.

The full environmental impact would also depend on the emissions and resources associated with manufacturing, launching, maintaining and eventually replacing the satellites.

North Carolina's energy demands aren't going away

Even if orbital computing becomes practical, it won't address the immediate demand for electricity from North Carolina's growing data center industry.

Duke Energy projects data centers could account for about 10% of its electricity sales across the Carolinas by 2030. The utility is planning billions of dollars in new power plants and infrastructure, including natural gas generation, to meet growing demand.

Those plans have raised questions about costs for residential customers and the environmental consequences of building additional fossil fuel infrastructure.

For now, the technology remains experimental. Google's next test is planned for 2027, while SpaceX is pursuing larger-scale satellite manufacturing.

text:
Fusion energy has long promised virtually limitless, low-carbon power by mimicking the physical reactions that fuel the Sun. But turning laboratory experiments into working power stations remains a huge problem. Connecting that power to the electrical grid is one of science’s greatest engineering challenges.

Now, an international pact aims to bridge that divide. Engineering firm Amentum has agreed to a strategic partnership with Japanese developer Kyoto Fusioneering. Under a new agreement, the two companies plan to combine their technical resources.

1/1Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE

Together, they will focus their work across Japan, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Their shared ambition is straightforward, which is to move fusion from experimental physics rigs into commercially viable power plants.

Building a commercial reactor is fundamentally a systems challenge. Reactors require specialized internal hardware that can endure conditions hotter than the solar core.

Combining industrial engineering with digital innovation

Kyoto Fusioneering supplies several of these critical technologies. These include plasma heating devices, advanced fuel-cycle equipment, and “breeding blankets” designed to generate tritium fuel within the reactor walls. Amentum, by contrast, brings the nuclear safety protocols, systems engineering, and large-scale delivery management needed to construct actual industrial facilities.

“Building a fusion power plant will depend on collaborations like this one,” said Kiyoshi Seko, president and chief operating officer of Kyoto Fusioneering. He noted that Amentum provides the scale of nuclear engineering experience that developers urgently need as projects advance toward physical construction.

More from Energy

See All

A major focus of the venture will be digital simulation. The teams intend to deploy artificial intelligence and digital engineering tools to model plant operations. In theory, testing virtual designs will cut down development cycles, predict equipment degradation, and avoid costly trial-and-error during physical builds.

The agreement comes amid rising momentum in Japan. Tokyo’s national fusion strategy has channeled substantial public backing into private demonstration ventures, giving firms like Kyoto Fusioneering a springboard to pursue joint ventures across western markets.

“This collaboration comes at a pivotal moment,” said Mark Whitney, president of Amentum’s energy and environment division, arguing that combining their specialisms will directly tackle the delivery hurdles stalling commercial deployment.

Extreme testing and reactor hardware trials

The initiative builds on Kyoto Fusioneering’s growing international testing footprint. In October, the company joined forces with the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in California, a testbed backed by the US Department of Energy.

Inside a fusion tokamak, operators face a brutal thermal dilemma. The core plasma must stay searingly hot for atomic nuclei to fuse, but the surrounding chamber walls must stay cool enough to avoid structural failure.

To help resolve this, Kyoto Fusioneering is supplying heat-resistant tiles for an advanced “divertor”—the exhaust component that expels waste heat and impurities from the plasma chamber. Alongside researchers from Columbia University, engineers will run extended operational tests on DIII-D’s reverse-D-shaped plasma.

Data gathered from those California trials will feed directly into US Department of Energy roadmaps. The measurements will help physicists assess plasma stability, validate computer models, and choose the resilient materials required for the world’s next generation of pilot plants.

text:
EPA faces pressure to restore 770 million biofuel credits as refinery exemptions threaten ethanol demand, farm income and rural economies across America.

Emily Trask is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural trade, policy, and agri-food markets, with a focus on U.S.-Latin America relations and their impact on global agribusiness.

Fuente: AgroLatam.com

Autor: AgroLatam.com

The Environmental Protection Agency faced mounting pressure from U.S. biofuel organizations on November 4, 2026, as industry leaders urged regulators to restore 770 million renewable fuel compliance credits affected by refinery exemptions. During a virtual hearing, ethanol and biodiesel representatives warned that leaving those obligations unaddressed could weaken demand for American corn and soybean oil. The dispute comes as farmers face difficult commodity markets, elevated input costs and shrinking profitability, making the Renewable Fuel Standard a critical issue for agricultural producers and rural economies.

The controversy follows EPA's decision to grant full or partial exemptions to 29 small refineries for their 2025 renewable fuel obligations. According to the agency's October proposal published in the Federal Register, the exemptions affected approximately 1.76 billion Renewable Identification Numbers, or RINs, compared with the 990 million initially projected. The unexpected difference of 770 million credits represents nearly 44% of the exempted volume. EPA is considering reallocating those additional obligations between 2026 and 2027 to prevent exemptions from undermining established renewable fuel requirements.

EPA's official breakdown shows that 34 refinery petitions were evaluated, resulting in 18 full exemptions, 11 partial exemptions, three denials and two ineligible applications. The decisions involved approximately 13.38 billion gallons of petroleum-based fuel associated with exempted refinery obligations. The agency is now considering two alternatives: distributing 385 million additional RINs to each of the 2026 and 2027 compliance years or assigning the entire 770 million to 2027. The timing could influence refinery credit purchases, renewable fuel production and agricultural feedstock demand.

Why EPA's Biofuel Decision Could Affect Farm Markets Through 2028

The American Coalition for Ethanol (ACE) strongly supported restoring the entire 770 million-credit shortfall. CEO Brian Jennings warned that failing to reallocate exempted obligations could reduce ethanol demand and economic opportunities for American farmers. He also contrasted strong refinery earnings with the financial challenges facing agricultural producers. Growth Energy supported full reallocation, arguing that EPA must account for unexpected exemptions to protect the Renewable Fuel Standard. Both organizations emphasized that predictable blending requirements are essential for ethanol investment, rural employment and long-term corn demand.

Clean Fuels Alliance America urged EPA to divide the additional credits equally between 2026 and 2027, arguing that regulatory certainty is necessary for biodiesel and renewable diesel producers. Vice President of Federal Affairs Kurt Kovarik called for a final decision before the end of 2026. The organization stressed that stable blending requirements support production planning and agricultural feedstock purchases. For soybean processors and renewable fuel manufacturers, uncertainty over future obligations can influence investment decisions, processing margins and demand throughout the supply chain.

Newsletter Sign Up.

Email:

In Iowa, Renewable Fuels Association leaders and state biofuel representatives raised concerns about the broader consequences of refinery exemptions. Iowa Renewable Fuels Association Executive Director Monte Shaw warned that assigning all 770 million credits to 2027 could allow qualifying compliance deficits to move into 2028, delaying the impact on renewable fuel demand. Shaw also reported that Iowa ethanol facilities previously affected by shutdowns and layoffs had returned to full operation. His testimony highlighted the importance of stable renewable fuel requirements for corn purchases, processing employment and rural economic activity.

The Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) also called for reforms to the small-refinery exemption program. President and CEO Geoff Cooper argued that relief intended for genuine economic hardship should not become a recurring regulatory benefit. He warned that excessive exemptions could weaken demand for newly produced renewable fuels and discourage investment. The controversy has also raised questions about refinery financial disclosures, with Iowa officials challenging potential inconsistencies between hardship claims and information provided to investors. Those concerns remain allegations rather than established findings of wrongdoing.

For American agriculture, the stakes extend beyond refinery compliance. Corn-based ethanol provides a major domestic market for U.S. grain, while biodiesel and renewable diesel support demand for soybean oil and other feedstocks. Changes in renewable fuel obligations can influence processing margins, commodity prices and investment decisions. However, reallocating RINs does not automatically guarantee additional physical fuel production or higher farmgate prices. Market outcomes will also depend on fuel consumption, existing credit supplies, refinery behavior, crop yields and broader agricultural supply and demand conditions.

A critical deadline is approaching. According to EPA's October 16 Federal Register notice, public comments on the proposal are due December 4, 2026. The agency has also considered extending the March 31, 2027, compliance deadline for 2026 renewable fuel requirements. The final decision will determine how the additional 770 million credits are distributed and when those obligations take effect. For corn growers, soybean producers and biofuel manufacturers, the outcome could influence domestic demand, regulatory certainty and agricultural investment heading into 2027 and potentially 2028.

New Analysis: Restarting Solar for All Could Cut Electric Bills 25% for a Million Households

Former EPA officials urge the agency to drop its threats to appeal, finding that a prompt restart could save families more than $450 million in the first year, while fighting in court could permanently shut out 410,000 households as solar tax credits expire.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — As American families face record-high electricity bills, a new report released today by the Environmental Protection Network (EPN) finds that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) could still help 1 million households cut their electric bills by about 25 percent if the agency complies with two federal court rulings and promptly restarts the $7 billion Solar for All program instead of appealing.

The issue brief, Restore Solar for All, prepared by former EPA officials, comes as the agency weighs whether to appeal two separate federal court rulings in Rhode Island and Washington, D.C. that found its August 2025 termination of the program unlawful. The government’s 60-day window to appeal the rulings closes in mid-November.

The new analysis examines how rising electricity prices, changes in federal solar tax credits, and delays caused by EPA’s termination have altered the program’s potential benefits and the urgency of restarting it.

“Families are skipping groceries to keep their lights on, yet restarting Solar for All could ultimately deliver more than $450 million a year in electricity bill savings,” said Michelle Roos, Executive Director of the Environmental Protection Network. “Two federal courts have now said EPA broke the law when it terminated Solar for All grants. Instead of keeping families in the dark, EPA should take this opportunity to help a million households cut their electricity bills.”

“Groundswell stands at the ready to restart our Southeast Rural Power Solar for All program,” said Michelle Moore, CEO, Groundswell. “I’m confident we could reach thousands of families across the Rural South with deep bill savings by this time next year.”

Key findings from the report:

1 million households could cut their electric bills by roughly 25 percent if EPA restarts the program promptly.

$458 million in first-year savings, or about $456 per household, which could grow if electricity rates continue to rise.

An appeal could put Solar for All savings out of reach for about 410,000 households. EPN’s modeling shows that if further delays prevent projects from qualifying for federal solar tax credits, the same $7 billion would reach about 40% fewer families.

EPN is calling on EPA to forgo an appeal, immediately restart Solar for All and give grantees the flexibility they need to get their systems operating before the deadline.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Climate Mobility Modeling and Policy Action
authors: Kayly Ober, Otoniel Ramos, Lawrence Huang, Debbra Goh
description:
The Role of Scenario Planning in Climate Mobility Modeling Quantitative modeling and scenario planning serve different purposes but are best treated as complementary, not incompatible.
Activists also have long used estimates of climate migration modeling to call for stronger climate action and migration policies.
Use Case 3: Project and Program Planning Beyond long-term planning, climate mobility modeling can inform near-term decisions about how and where policymakers and practitioners should invest in climate mobility programs.
As the field of climate mobility modeling grows, it will have to reckon with a structural methodological challenge.
Lawrence Huang Senior Policy Analyst, Migration Policy Institute Lawrence Huang is a senior policy analyst with the Migration Policy Institute.
text:
Introduction

Climate mobility, or the movement of people in the face of a rapidly changing climate, is not some future abstraction but rather a reality that governments are grappling with today. Governments are already deciding where to invest in adaptation and where to concede that it will not be enough, whether to plan relocation for exposed communities or wait for people to leave on their own, and how cities can absorb arrivals they did not anticipate. These choices are expensive, consequential, and, in some cases, irreversible. And yet policymakers are making many of these decisions without drawing from climate mobility–specific evidence. That needs to change.

Policymakers are not using this evidence partly because it is often generated by academics for academics. Moreover, for nearly three decades, much research on climate change and human mobility has revolved around a singular question, “How many people will move?,” which has produced starkly divergent answers—from tens of millions to more than a billion. The most widely circulated estimates have been borne from thin methodology, stripped of their assumptions in transit, and used in political arguments in ways the analysts did not intend.

Such critiques of these estimates have been well documented. But while projecting numbers of migrants is important, the debate over accuracy has largely obscured an equally valuable question: “How do these numbers actually help policymakers make climate mobility policy?”

In key stakeholder consultations with nineteen participants across four policymaking groups—bilateral and philanthropic donors, national governments, urban and local planners, and activists and civil society—we asked how they had encountered climate mobility projections, what decisions those projections informed, and what they need from modeling that they do not currently get. We found consistent demand for things that current models are largely not built to deliver.

This mismatch is not evidence of bad faith or bad science. Modelers face binding constraints: climate inputs are projected at decadal resolution, migration data are patchy or absent in the most climate-vulnerable places, and the methods that capture individual decisionmaking most convincingly are the least portable across geographies. And policymakers face constraints of their own: budget cycles, political headwinds, and the need to justify spending against competing priorities. Both sets of incentives and challenges are rational.

Therefore, meeting the demand for upgraded, more frequent modeling requires movement from both directions—in other words, a better understanding of both what modelers can provide and what policymakers require.

Building on the literature review undertaken by Kerilyn Schewel et al. (2024), we assess thirty-seven modeling approaches to future climate mobility, including white papers and institutional reports that, while not peer reviewed, include the projections policymakers are most likely to encounter. This paper defines climate mobility modeling as models with longer time horizons—excluding short-term forecasting and early warnings of mobility on scales of days to months, such as cyclone or drought warnings —and those that project movement, rather than the risk of displacement (see the “Basics” section below).

We first mapped the literature to understand what types of migration, geographies, hazards, and time frames the models cover and where there are gaps. This review revealed some imbalances in coverage. For instance, we found that eleven of the thirty-seven models (29 percent) focus on only two countries (Bangladesh and the United States). And nearly half (seventeen of thirty-seven) address internal migration only. Twenty-seven percent treat sea-level rise as the primary or sole hazard. Almost all of the models make projections to 2050 or later.

We then mapped how closely these models align with what policymakers need to know. In a resource-constrained world, policymakers may not need better numbers so much as they need to know which existing tool answers which question—and which questions are not yet answerable with existing models. In this paper, we assess the four dominant modeling approaches—gravity, computable general equilibrium, agent-based, and econometric—and map the models against the four primary use cases identified during our stakeholder consultations: (1) political buy-in and advocacy, (2) long-term strategic planning, (3) project and program design, and (4) local and community planning. Some of these use cases are well served by what already exists, but some are not.

Next, we set out what would have to change for models to serve policymakers better. The first is bridging a basic information gap—as the most academic models were the least likely to be on policymakers’ radars. Our consultations bore this out: The projections stakeholders knew best came from the World Bank, ProPublica, and First Street, not from scientific journals. In conclusion, we lay out seven priorities to help make modeling considerably more usable for policymakers and practitioners.
