text:
Carbon materials manufacturer JNTG will become the sole supplier of gas diffusion layers (GDLs) for Hyundai Motor’s hydrogen fuel cells. The fuel cells will be installed in Hyundai’s 2028-model hydrogen electric vehicles. GDLs accounted for just 6.5% of JNTG’s revenue in 2025, but their contribution is expected to increase as supplies expand from 2028.

JNTG has expanded rapidly over the past five years. Revenue is projected to exceed 100 billion won in 2026, compared with 5.7 billion won in 2021. In the first half of 2026 alone, the company generated 60.7 billion won, equivalent to about 84% of its full-year 2025 revenue of 72.4 billion won.

JNTG outlined its medium- to long-term growth targets and business plans at an initial public offering (IPO) press conference on Nov. 5. The company aims to raise up to 130 billion won through a Kosdaq listing and allocate more than half of the proceeds to capital expenditures.

JNTG processes carbon materials into key components for batteries and hydrogen fuel cells. Its main products include carbon electrodes for energy storage batteries and GDLs for fuel cells that generate electricity from hydrogen. It also supplies carbon substrates for distributed power generation and water electrolysis equipment.

GDLs distribute hydrogen and oxygen evenly to the catalyst layers inside fuel cells. They also remove water generated during electricity production and regulate internal moisture levels, affecting fuel cell output and durability.

JNTG manufactures GDLs by coating carbon substrates made from carbon fibers formed into paper-like sheets with a microporous layer. The company has developed a domestic alternative to previously imported automotive materials. It was selected as a GDL supplier for Hyundai Motor’s hydrogen electric vehicles and secured supply volumes covering the next six years. GDL revenue totaled 4.7 billion won out of JNTG’s 72.4 billion won in total revenue in 2025. Significant revenue growth is expected from 2028, when mass-production supplies to Hyundai begin. JNTG plans to use IPO proceeds to triple annual GDL production capacity from 1 million square meters to 3 million square meters.

Carbon electrodes are currently JNTG’s main revenue source, accounting for about 74%, or 53.9 billion won, of 2025 sales. The company supplies the materials to non-lithium battery manufacturers using vanadium, zinc and other materials. Overseas companies developing vanadium and other non-lithium batteries include CellCube and Invinity, while domestic developers include Standard Energy and H2.

JNTG began mass production of carbon electrodes in 2023. It added electric furnaces to accommodate customers’ requests for changes in raw materials and performance improvements. Material orders subsequently increased as customers automated their battery manufacturing processes and expanded production.

JNTG’s manufacturing competitiveness comes from continuous production technology that reduces processing time and costs. Competitors use batch processes in which carbon materials are heated in electric furnaces, cooled and then removed. JNTG instead uses a roll-to-roll process that continuously feeds materials through high-temperature electric furnaces. By eliminating repeated heating and cooling cycles, the process enables higher output in less time.

Annual carbon electrode production capacity currently stands at 2.4 million square meters. JNTG plans to expand it by about 50% to 3.6 million square meters through capital investment. Annual carbon substrate capacity for distributed power generation and water electrolysis will also increase from approximately 1 million to 1.5 million sheets. Investments will be made in stages based on customer demand forecasts and long-term supply agreements.

Revenue is expected to exceed 100 billion won in 2026, nearly 20 times the 5.7 billion won recorded in 2021. JNTG also expects to remain profitable for a second consecutive year. The company posted an operating profit of 21.3 billion won in 2025, reversing an operating loss of 4.9 billion won in 2024, and recorded an operating profit of 18.1 billion won in the first half of 2026.

JNTG plans to offer 4.3 million shares as part of its targeted Kosdaq listing in November 2026. The indicative IPO price range is 26,400 won to 31,900 won per share. Institutional bookbuilding runs from Nov. 3 to 9, followed by public subscriptions on Nov. 12 and 13. Daishin Securities is the lead underwriter, with NH Investment & Securities serving as co-underwriter.

text:
November 5, 2026

BY Erin Krueger

The Andersons Inc. on Nov. 3 released third quarter results, reporting that its renewables segment delivered strong earnings with improved ethanol and corn oil yields. During a Nov. 4 earnings call, company officials discussed the acquisition of three additional ethanol plants.

According to The Andersons, its renewables segment had a strong third quarter driven by efficient plant operations, higher coproduct values, and lower corn basis at the company’s eastern plants. Although board crush margins were lower quarter-over-quarter, overall plant profitability improved.

The renewables segment reported pretax income of $63 million for the third quarter. Cascade Nuclear Partners, a joint venture of Kiewit Nuclear Solutions Co., Black & Veatch, and Aecon, serves as Energy Northwest’s progressive design-builder, responsible for the conventional island and integrating requirements across the plant to support potential future phases of the project.

The agreement between X-energy and Fluor (the “Companies”) for the Cascade facility is their second commercial contract for nuclear island engineering and design, building on Fluor’s ongoing work for X-energy’s first proposed Xe-100 project in Texas under the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program. text:
This story is from Floodlight, a nonprofit newsroom that investigates the powers stalling climate action. Sign up for Floodlight’s newsletter here.

New Jersey’s largest planned AI data center, DataOne, has stirred controversy since day one.

Persistent noise complaints, unpermitted construction and a contentious zoning process have plagued the project since it broke ground last year, but it wasn’t until the state fined the company more than $1 million last month over its fleet of unpermitted gas-powered generators that DataOne became international news.

A new short documentary from Floodlight shows how a thermal drone investigation in August first brought these generators to light, and how the Vineland community reacted to learning what was spewing into their air.

“What am I breathing in? What am I being exposed to?” said Tiffany Leone-Vespa, who lives about a mile from the generator fleet. “It’s terrifying for me.”

Following New Jersey’s record fine against DataOne, Floodlight obtained public records showing the unpermitted generator fleet was capable of emitting staggering amounts of air pollution and had been operating for nearly a year before state regulators intervened. Floodlight also asked Ed Potosnak, commissioner for the state’s Department of Environmental Protection, why his agency was allowing the facility to continue running the generators despite the lack of permits.

As seen in the video, Potosnak refused to answer, instead suggesting to a Floodlight reporter that they set up a time for an interview. His office would later refuse that interview request.

Today, DataOne continues operating its fleet of generators as it works toward “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution,” according to its spokesperson.

Despite initially claiming they would apply for the necessary permits, the company has since requested a hearing to contest the state’s fine and argue the generators do not require permits.

Under the state’s enforcement order, DataOne has until November 6 to apply for the permits or stop operating them.

title: EPA approves Arizona county's first-in-nation emissions rule - The Center Square
description: (The Center Square) – A new rule approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency could help get high-polluting vehicles off the road and replaced with cleaner alternatives in Arizona's Maricopa
text:
Downtown Phoenix. Photo: Gabriel Valdez / Unsplash

(The Center Square) – A new rule approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency could help get high-polluting vehicles off the road and replaced with cleaner alternatives in Arizona's Maricopa County.

That’s because the EPA greenlit the municipality's Rule 205, a first-in-the-nation program allowing fleet owners and operators in the state's most populous county to generate Emission Reduction Credits by upgrading their vehicles with cleaner technologies.

Those credits can, in turn, be purchased by factory owners or others that are considered “stationary emissions sources” to offset any potential emission increases that come from expanded operations.

The newest rule is the brainchild of the Phoenix-based Maricopa County Air Quality Department, which reports to the county’s Board of Supervisors.

Board Chair Kate Brophy McGee told The Center Square on Thursday that the county’s newest emissions rule will allow business to expand in the region, without harming air quality.

Kate Brophy McGee, chair of the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, talks during a Phoenix news conference about the county's election, Nov. 2, 2026. Photo: Christopher Boan / The Center Square

She also noted no taxpayer dollars would be spent as part of the implementation of Rule 205, as was the case with Rule 204 , a similar policy that concerned non-road vehicles such as locomotives and construction equipment.

“Maricopa County has an incredible air quality division, and they are they're basically Department of Super Nerds,” Brophy McGee told The Center Square. "And we have been working on this as a county because we've been hovering on the edge of non-attainment for a long time, and a large part of it, I will tell you, is due to factors outside our control.”

When Brophy McGee talks of the county’s nonattainment status, she’s referencing stipulations put in place on municipalities by the Clean Air and Water Act.

Those regulations state areas that fail to meet certain air quality metrics must go through extra steps to approve permits for higher-emission projects, such as factories and data centers.

Maricopa County is ranked as a moderate nonattainment zone for ground-level ozone, which Brophy McGee attributes to Phoenix’s place at the bottom of the greater Salt River Valley.

“We’re in a bowl,” Brophy McGee said. “The particulates and things settle in the bowl, and then the sun comes along and heats it up. And that creates the ozone.

“But what (Rule 205) does is say, ‘Hey, the stuff that we're actually doing, the pollution that we're actually generating, let's cut back on that. And here's an incentive to do that’,” she added.

Mike Martucci , the EPA Pacific Southwest regional administrator, told The Center Square that the county’s newest air pollution rule has the potential to pay huge dividends for the quality of life for residents.

Martucci said anyone looking for a permit for a certain number of emissions per year would have to purchase that amount plus 15% more from those fleet operators. He said that would provide the operators with the money needed to overhaul their fleets and introduce more efficient vehicles that cut down on emissions in the long run.

He said credits are paid out to fleet operators depending on how much of an emissions upgrade they make. Those who exchange older diesel-powered trucks with newer versions are considered to be on one level for credits. But bus operators that go from diesel to compressed natural gas or electric-powered vehicles can reap greater benefits.

“At its core is a science-backed approach to make sure that we're maintaining that 115%,” Martucci told The Center Square.

Brophy McGee said Rule 205 has the potential to open new doors for manufacturers that are butting up against environmental emissions regulations, fueling the county’s economic aspirations, both in the short and long term.

“We have businesses who want to come here and build,” Brophy McGee said. “A high-profile example would be the Taiwan Semiconductor Co,, and in order to do that, they need air quality credits.”

The Arizona native cited the example of a beat-up tractor trailer that you’d see chugging along the interstate as a reason why Rule 205 is important. The rule is designed to incentivize fleet operators to get those trucks off the road and replaced by ones that operate more efficiently.

“They need [air quality credits], and we need to continue to meet the federal standards for clean air,” she said. “And so, businesses are incentivized to clean [their fleets] up and to get newer technologies to replace those old, on-road motor vehicles.”

Danny Seiden, president and CEO of the Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry, seconded Brophy McGee’s comments.

Seiden commended the EPA for finding a solution to the region’s environmental problems that doesn’t kneecap business development along the way, providing positive results for all involved.

“This is a big win for Arizona’s economy and another important step toward addressing the air quality challenges that have made it increasingly difficult for businesses to build and expand in Maricopa County,” Seiden told The Center Square. “For too long, the shortage of available emission reduction credits has been a major obstacle to new investment, even for companies committed to meeting stringent environmental standards.

“Rule 205 offers a practical, market-driven solution that helps remove that barrier while encouraging cleaner air,” he said.

description:
Canadians deserve better than having the Government of Canada hand another tax break to fossil fuel companies while leaving the public to foot the bill.
This appears to represent a new fossil fuel subsidy for the polluting oil and gas industry.
The $50 billion announced for the National Electrification Strategy is an important step toward Canada’s energy transition.
This investment in ocean protection is a drop in the bucket compared to the tax breaks for fossil fuel companies in this budget and anticipated future investment in fossil fuel infrastructure.

text:
Toronto | Treaty Lands and Territory of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation, and the traditional territory of the Anishinaabeg, the Haudenosaunee, and the Wendat – Keith Brooks, Programs Director at Environmental Defence, made the following statement in response to the 2026 Federal Budget (a detailed budget analysis follows):

“Budget 2026 appears to be an attempt to paper over this government’s pro-fossil fuel agenda by dangling investments in clean electricity. While $50 billion is a significant sum, it appears to be spread over the next 15 years. Meanwhile, the federal government has committed billions of dollars to new subsidies for LNG and to fund the majority of the “Pacific Link” pipeline (estimated to cost in excess of $40 billion). It has also pegged the cost of the Productivity Mega Deduction at $36 billion over the next five years, most of which will likely go toward oil and gas development.

It’s easy to say that Canada is still on track to achieve net-zero by 2050, but Budget 2026 does not lay out a plan to do so and does not earmark investments that would be required to turn this commitment into reality.”

EXPERT ANALYSIS:

Energy

With no restrictions on fossil fuels, the Productivity Mega Deduction could give a free ride to wealthy oil and gas companies to expand their production and shift all the risk onto Canadian taxpayers. Even the federal government’s own assessment cannot determine the deduction’s environmental impact. Canadians deserve better than having the Government of Canada hand another tax break to fossil fuel companies while leaving the public to foot the bill.

Since the Spring Economic Update, the Government of Canada has included $200 million until 2028-2029 in financial support for Woodfibre LNG, via Natural Resources Canada. This appears to represent a new fossil fuel subsidy for the polluting oil and gas industry.

The $50 billion announced for the National Electrification Strategy is an important step toward Canada’s energy transition. We welcome the extension of the Clean Electricity investment tax credit to 2040. However, the inclusion of natural gas electricity, as well as options for emissions offset, is concerning and would be a step backwards in Canada reducing emissions. More details on this strategy and how it will be implemented are needed.

The $740 million over four years for ocean protection is clearly meant to subdue concern for the Southern Resident Killer Whales that will be pushed towards extinction with the government’s proposal to finance and build the Pacific Link pipeline and designation of the Roberts Bank Terminal expansion as a Project of National interest under the Building Canada Act. This investment in ocean protection is a drop in the bucket compared to the tax breaks for fossil fuel companies in this budget and anticipated future investment in fossil fuel infrastructure.

Transportation:

The $578 million allocated for EV charging and additional funds for research and development are welcome, but a small amount of money considering transportation is one of the largest sources of emissions in Canada, second only to oil and gas production.

Canada dropped its Zero Emissions Vehicle Availability Standard and, while the government initially committed to achieving 75 per cent EV sales by 2035, it has not come forward with new tailpipe emissions standards but has realigned Canada’s tailpipe standards with the U.S. just last week, taking Canada further backward. This means that EVs will continue to be hard to access in Canada, forcing more Canadians to drive polluting cars that are increasingly expensive to fuel.

Plastic Pollution

Funding for federal action on plastics is renewed for another four years, with $22 million allocated for 2027-2028. This is good news for the environment and our health. It enables the government to continue to identify and eliminate unnecessary and harmful single-use plastics while supporting alternatives, including reuse and refill programs for packaging, and work with allies to finalize an effective global treaty to address plastic pollution.

ABOUT ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENCE (environmentaldefence.ca): Environmental Defence is a leading Canadian environmental advocacy organization that works with government, industry and individuals to defend clean water, a safe climate and healthy communities.

text:
Karen Feldscher

Amid their quest to expand artificial intelligence and cloud computing, tech companies are building hundreds of huge data centers across the U.S., along with gas-fired power plants to keep them running. According to Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health’s Gianluca Guidi, these plants could result in hundreds of millions of tons of climate-damaging emissions in the years to come.

Some estimates suggest that, because of these data center projects, the tech industry could become one of the world’s biggest emitters of greenhouse gases, according to a Nov. 2 Washington Post article. Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow in biostatistics, conducted an analysis for the Post on how much emissions would increase from these projects based on air permits, corporate disclosures, community presentations, and other materials. “AI may feel completely digital, immaterial, but its infrastructure is very physical. It needs land, power plants, transmission, water and fuel, and these choices can last for decades,” he said.

Among findings listed in the article:

Two gas projects planned by Amazon, which would power planned data centers in Texas and Pennsylvania, would produce more carbon pollution than the dirtiest coal plant in the country, located in Alabama—and would be equivalent to a 28.5% increase over Amazon’s current greenhouse-gas footprint.

Emissions from gas plants at a nearly six-square-mile data center in rural Louisiana, being built by Meta, would create more carbon emissions than all the emissions currently generated by the entire Meta corporation. The data center would consume as much electricity as three cities the size of New Orleans.

A Microsoft project in West Texas and a Google project in Wyoming, both involving gas plants, would consume five times as much electricity as every household in the latter state, and would vastly expand emissions. And an OpenAI data center in Pike County, Ohio, would emit more carbon pollution than the Microsoft and Google projects combined.

Guidi noted that, once built, these gas plants are likely to keep running for at least a generation, even if the AI boom fades. “Decisions being made for today’s data-center boom can shape emissions long after today’s generation of AI hardware is obsolete,” he said.

title: Three ways the 2026 midterm election could impact Michigan's environment
description:

Science and the environment Eli Savit won the Michigan Attorney General race.
text:
Somehow I spent Election Day reporting on snails. I don’t really understand how it happened either. While my colleagues were driving around Michigan covering events and reporting in from polling places and parties, speaking with Michiganders about this historic and dramatic Senate race, I was here in the office calling up scientists and gleefully shouting out snail facts.

Let’s talk about how some of the election results may impact environmental issues moving forward.

Data centers

Data centers were certainly on the ballot this election. They were a prominent talking point in the tight race for the House in Michigan’s 7th District, which William Lawrence won.

Democrat Jocelyn Benson was elected governor of Michigan. Her campaign stated support for a temporary moratorium on data centers. Her website calls for "requiring developers to prove prior to construction that the data center will not abuse natural resources - from water to land.” This statement is vague, so it’s hard to say at this point what that would mean in practice.

Garlin Gilchrist won the election for Michigan Secretary of State. In a statement to Planet Detroit, he listed flooding, poor air quality and extreme heat as environmental priorities for the state. He also emphasized data center companies’ responsibility for water use and water quality impacts.

Science and the environment

Eli Savit won the Michigan Attorney General race. He told Michigan Public’s Caoilinn Goss that environmental protections were something he cared about protecting as part of our democracy. Attorney generals have a key role in defending science and the environment. Earlier this year, Attorney General Dana Nessel joined other states in signing a letter opposing legislation that would have made government science funding processes more partisan.

A millage (a.k.a. a tax) was approved to help support the Detroit Zoo and several Detroit museums, including the Belle Isle Dossin Great Lakes Museum.

Energy

In Ann Arbor, Proposal E, which would have started the process of changing the city’s electric infrastructure to establish a municipal utility, narrowly failed to pass.

Eli Savit’s win may also be important for Michigan’s energy future. Current Attorney General Nessel filed multiple requests challenging the J.H. Campbell power plant, for example.

State-level challenges of the Trump administration environmental and energy regulation will continue to be incredibly important to watch. And how each candidate rises to their campaign promises, especially how those promises relate to our clean air and water, is something I’m personally interested in following as well.

Let's end on snails

One of the scientists I spoke with on Tuesday said she was super happy to talk about anything but the election. So in case you’re also exhausted from this election news cycle, I’ll just end with some mind-blowing facts about the invasive New Zealand mudsnails:

So far, all snails found in Michigan have been female.

They can reproduce asexually, so just one female snail arrival in a new location could herald a new era of snail dominance.

This snail’s shell has a little trapdoor that lets it duck inside and shut the door. Some of them have been found to survive inside a fish digestive tract using this! This means that they are incredible survivors and a terrible meal for fish.

Have more news for me? Have a hot tip? Send your ballot-based environmental concerns to furby@umich.edu.

‘Til next week,

Kate Furby, Senior Environment Reporter

text:
LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Consumers Energy and DTE Energy have filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block Proposal 2, the ballot measure Michigan voters approved that, in part, bans political campaign contributions from utility companies.

The utilities’ lawsuit follows a federal lawsuit filed by the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, which is seeking to block two parts of the proposal.

Utilities file lawsuit

The utilities’ joint lawsuit claims the proposal - which resoundingly passed with more than 80% of voters in favor - violates free speech by only targeting one side of the argument.

The lawsuit also claims Proposal 2 bans political giving without evidence of wrongdoing and punishes people simply by association. The utilities claim the rules are too vague and confusing.

DTE shared the following statement with News 10:

“DTE has long supported the right of Michiganders to lawfully participate in the political process and engage on issues that affect their families and communities regardless of their job. Our company is made up of 10,000 Michiganders whose fundamental right to free speech is under attack. They deserve the same rights as their friends and neighbors to support the candidates and issues they care about.”

News 10 has reached out to Consumers for a statement on the lawsuit and is awaiting response.

Read the full lawsuit below:

Mackinac Center challenges reporting rules

Hours after voters approved the proposal on Tuesday to amend the state’s Campaign Finance Act, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy filed its lawsuit. The proposal is known to many voters as the “Money Out of Politics” initiative. It bans some political donations from utilities and state contractors.

The Mackinac Center takes issue with the proposal’s expansion of campaign finance reporting rules and calls the measure a “Trojan horse.” The center claims in the lawsuit that part of Proposal 2 threatens free speech.

Patrick Wright, the center’s vice president of legal affairs, said the center is concerned about a rule that requires groups to disclose their donors if they spend a certain amount of money.

“This makes it very hard for people to know what they can say, when they can say it, and how they can say it,” Wright said.

“It’s going to lead to self-censorship, potentially,” Wright said.

“There’s maybe people that don’t want to get on these lists and be harassed. And so, it’s probably going to chill speech,” Wright said.

The Mackinac Center wants a judge to pause the rules before they take effect.

“America has been built on being able to dissent and express your mind. And this law makes it harder for people and less safe for people to do that,” Wright said.

Proposal 2 campaign responds

The campaign behind Proposal 2 said it expected this kind of action. In a statement, campaign manager Maura Cowley said she believes corporations against the proposal have been gearing up for a lawsuit all along.

Cowley said the campaign is confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny and is prepared to take on the challenge.

Read Cowley’s full statement below:

“This lawsuit is no surprise. The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before. On Tuesday, Michiganders spoke loud and clear, voting to pass Proposal 2 with an overwhelming majority and delivering a resounding mandate to end pay-to-play politics and put power back where it belongs – with the people. The bottom line is that we are confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this challenge.”

Defendants and next steps

The Mackinac Center’s lawsuit names Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Attorney General Dana Nessel as defendants because their offices enforce the state’s campaign finance law.

The center said it will ask for a temporary order or a preliminary injunction. A hearing is expected soon.

If there is no court injunction, Proposal 2 is set to go into effect 10 days after Michigan’s election results are certified. That is no later than Dec. 3.

After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.

In a post on X, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers. Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.

“National data center moratorium now,” he wrote in the post. “Americans don’t want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity’s future.”

In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, “Yes!”

According to the CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.

Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.

Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.

South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — “data center Darline.”

Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, “I do not work for data centers.”

title: Integrated resource planning is key to a cleaner, more affordable energy future - News and stories
description:

By looking at investments needs at a systems level, integrated resource planning helps utilities and regulators make sure they are building a system that is reliable, affordable and meets customers’ needs.

text:
By Christen Chappelle, Legal Intern & Jolette Westbrook, Director & Senior Attorney, Regulatory Solutions, Environmental Defense Fund

America’s electricity demand is surging, driven in part by data centers and industrial growth, while utilities face decisions that could lock in higher costs and pollution for decades. New research from Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy reveals just how dramatically the landscape is shifting. Fossil fuels accounted for just 5% of new U.S. power capacity in 2024. By 2030, that share could reach 70% if currently planned projects move forward.

States can meet this growing electricity demand without driving up bills, compromising reliability or sacrificing public health and environmental protections, using a process called integrated resource planning (IRP). By looking at investments needs at a systems level, integrated resource planning helps utilities and regulators make sure they are building a system that is reliable, affordable and meets customers’ needs.

What is integrated resource planning?

Integrated resource plans, or IRPs, are long-term roadmaps utilities develop, often with oversight from state energy regulators, to guide electricity investments. Well-designed IRPs forecast energy needs over roughly 10 to 20 years and compare ways to meet demand while considering cost, reliability, equity, environmental impacts and public health.

IRP requirements vary by state and depend in part on how electricity markets are structured. Utilities typically update their plans every two to four years, giving regulators and the public opportunities to evaluate whether their long-term strategies can deliver clean, affordable, reliable electricity. Regulators have varying levels of authority to review and influence these plans, and in most states, an IRP does not automatically approve future investments or their costs.

Why are IRPs important?

Effective integrated resource planning helps utilities and regulators look beyond immediate energy needs to make decisions that serve customers and communities for decades. By comparing options – from new power plants and renewable energy to energy efficiency, battery storage and programs that reduce demand during peak periods – IRPs can help identify more affordable, reliable and cleaner ways to meet future energy needs.

These decisions affect more than electricity supply. They shape household bills, local economies, air quality, public health, and progress toward climate goals. Just as important, the IRP process gives communities, advocates, and other stakeholders a voice in decisions that affect their lives. This participation helps ensure plans reflect the needs and priorities of the people they serve.

Nationwide, more than 40 states have formal IRP requirements that are typically updated every two to four years, and that number is growing. Table 1 shows differences in market structure, IRP planning requirements and status in a sampling of states.

Note: Planning status reflects three stages: Infancy means a formal commitment exists, but no plan has been completed. Underway means planning has begun. Robust indicates an established process with multiple planning cycles that inform energy decisions.

How to influence IRP outcomes

You don’t need to be an energy expert to have a say in decisions that affect your community. In Detroit, for example, a coalition of community and advocacy groups participated in an IRP proceeding and helped secure an $8 million commitment from DTE Energy to support a community-led program providing home repairs and energy efficiency improvements to help residents lower their electricity bills.

CONTACT Krystal Northey (Mountain Time) Lead, Public Affairs Canadian Climate Institute (226) 212-9883 Jaela Bernstien (Eastern Time) Senior Communications Specialist Canadian Climate Institute (226) 212-9883 About the Canadian Climate Institute The Canadian Climate Institute is Canada’s leading climate change policy research organization.
text:
OTTAWA—Dale Beugin, Executive Vice President of the Canadian Climate Institute, made the following statement in response to the federal government’s tabling of Budget 2026:

“While Budget 2026 is rooted in economic objectives, it recognizes that climate progress and economic goals can and should be mutually reinforcing. The budget lays out actions and public dollars for clean electricity and electrification. It establishes a broader framework for mapping progress in building a clean economy. In order to mobilize investment and transform goals into reality, the government’s next steps should be to finalize policy details and track progress in concrete terms.

“The budget reiterates the government’s commitment to net zero and defines a new framework for delivering on that goal; tracking progress will be critical. The categories are sound elements of a net zero transition: Building clean electricity, shifting to electricity, transforming energy systems to waste less energy, and innovating and scaling new technologies. This framework broadly aligns with new work the Climate Institute is launching soon on tracking concrete measures of progress toward clean growth. The next challenge will be tracking progress and ensuring the scale and pace of policy is proportional to the change necessary to deliver on net zero.

“The budget rightfully centres clean electricity and electrification as enablers of economic growth, affordability, and net zero. Alongside Budget 2026, the government published its updated National Electricity Strategy. Building on previous announcements, it commits $50 billion to double Canada’s electricity generation and build the transmission needed to connect Canadians and Canadian industries with the power they need. Notably, it proposes expanding eligibility for the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit to high-voltage intra-provincial electricity transmission, addressing critical pressure points identified by our analysis. It also opens the door to developing new financial mechanisms to share costs and risks with interested provinces and territories, reinforcing other policy approaches that can help scale electricity systems while moderating rate pressure.

“Budget 2026 also recognizes that electrification and energy efficiency are essential complements to expanding clean electricity. Proposed investments in deploying heat pumps, expanding charging networks for electric vehicles, and adoption of energy-saving technologies at industrial and manufacturing facilities can help unlock decarbonization while keeping energy costs affordable for consumers.

“The budget also makes some important steps forward on sustainable finance to catalyze private investment. In particular, the budget commits to using the Made-in-Canada sustainable investment guidelines for a new federal Sustainable Bond Framework. The Budget also highlights the Institute’s upcoming Sustainable Finance Conference in February 2027, which will continue to build momentum.

“Budget 2026 misses an opportunity to broadly advance climate preparedness. As the recent landmark federal report on climate impacts made clear, Canada can expect to see a wide range of increasingly severe extreme weather events. Escalating damages can only be lessened through targeted investments and policy changes in adaptation. As our research has consistently shown, funding for adaptation can more than pay for itself over time and help protect communities across the country. The budget does not mention the National Adaptation Strategy.

“Budget 2026 highlights several other important steps forward:

It expands support for critical mineral supply chains in Canada, helping to grow a nascent source of competitive advantage in the global clean economy.

It proposes significant new resources for innovation of new, emerging low-carbon technologies. As CCI has noted, achieving net zero will require both deploying “safe bets.” and developing new “wild card” technologies; this support can help unlock the latter.

It reiterates the importance of robust, certain industrial carbon pricing markets.

It reiterates that Clean Electricity Regulation will support net zero by 2050.

It also proposes support for increasing production of water bombers to support fighting wildfires both domestically and internationally.

text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (S.5653) was introduced last month, marking an ambitious bipartisan attempt to expedite the federal permitting process by reworking the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act, among others. In exchange, however, the bill would narrow occasions for full environmental review, as well as the grounds for revisiting approvals.

What the Bill Proposes

Faster Reviews

Under the bill, NEPA-based challenges to federal authorizations would bypass federal district courts. Instead, the circuit court where a project is constructed, expanded, or operated, would have original and exclusive jurisdiction over those claims. Claims would also have to be filed within 150 days by a party that previously submitted a “sufficiently detailed comment” during the public comment period, alleging a direct injury. Moreover, a court finding a NEPA violation could only remand the authorization to the agency, without vacatur or an injunction – i.e., the authorization would remain in effect during the remand. The bill would also allow federal agencies to skip further NEPA review when (1) a state or tribunal environmental review has already covered the project and serves a similar function, or (2) compliance with another federal law serves a similar function to NEPA compliance.

Eliminating district court review would give energy project developers more certainty by removing wait times for a definitive appellate ruling. Though there is no guarantee that cases would move faster simply because they are heard in the first instance by an appellate court. In fact, the bill directs the circuit courts to rule only “as expeditiously as possible” but sets no fixed deadline.

The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (covered by Goldberg Segalla’s ELM here: Supreme Court Cuts Down ‘Judicial Oak’ of NEPA; Energy and Infrastructure Developments Projected to Increase – Goldberg Segalla,) could, however, keep the circuit courts from being overwhelmed by NEPA litigation. The decision limited the scope of Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) review under NEPA by instructing federal agencies to consider only the environmental effects of the “project at hand,” and by holding that courts should “defer to an agency’s reasonable choices regarding the scope and contents of the EIS.”

The bill would codify a similar approach, directing courts to afford “substantial deference” to the agency on the scope and contents of an environmental review. In addition, Department of Air Force v. Prutehi Guahan (covered by Goldberg Segalla’s ELM here: Falling Leaves, Rising Questions: NEPA Returns to the Supreme Court – Goldberg Segalla), which was argued before the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this month, could further limit NEPA’s reach where it overlaps with arguably duplicative federal environmental regulations.

Questions do remain about the potential for parallel challenges and inconsistent results. The bill gives circuit courts supplemental jurisdiction over other claims related to the validity of a challenged authorization. However, in its current form, the bill does not expressly prevent, for example, Clean Water Act claims unconnected to NEPA from being heard in district court. The 150-day deadline to challenge NEPA decisions could also create timing issues for litigants as federal authorizations for a single project are not necessarily issued at the same time.

Project Certainty

The bill also proposes making issued permits harder to revoke. For projects with non-federal sponsors, federal agencies could not revoke, rescind, suspend, or alter federal authorizations or permits in effect on or after September 16, 2026, except in limited circumstances (e.g., a court orders the action, the permit holder materially breached the permit or violated the law, or new information shows a specific and urgent harm). Before acting, the agency would have to give the sponsor written notice explaining the action, its statutory authority, and the supporting evidence. If the sponsor challenged the action, the agency would bear the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that an exception applies.

Implications Moving Forward

For developers and lenders, the bill offers meaningful protection against policy swings between administrations, and the September 16, 2026 cutoff means the protection would cover permits already in effect. On the other side, agencies and public interest groups that petition to revisit environmental permits would have a narrower path to reopen a permit and would ultimately carry a heavier burden in court.

The bill has only just been referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, and its text will likely change as it moves through committee. Still, it paints a clear bipartisan permitting deal, and its potential implications could affect project developers, permit holders, and environmental groups with respect to projects in development and pending or anticipated litigation.

text:
Last summer, while on an assignment in Ethiopia, I found myself daydreaming while trapped in Addis Ababa’s rush hour traffic. Staring out from my gridlocked taxi, I was struck by something remarkable: on all four sides were vehicles produced by Chinese manufacturer BYD.

Except it wasn’t really that remarkable. For years now, BYDs have been a regular feature of my travels to even the most far-flung places, plying streets from Yerevan to Yangon and beyond. Last year, the firm, whose initials stand for “Build Your Dreams,” became the world’s top purveyor of EVs, selling 4.6 million vehicles across 120 countries and regions, while accruing revenue of $111 billion. It was perhaps more surprising I wasn’t sitting in a BYD myself.

“If you look at a lot of markets, we say, ‘there's been a boom in EVs,’” says Ilaria Mazzocco, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “Actually, it's just BYD. They're single-handedly creating markets in some countries, which is remarkable.”

Now the Shenzhen-based firm aims to overtake Toyota as the number one automaker by 2030—a feat that, at current sales figures, would require more than doubling its output. As China’s auto market cools amid a broader consumer slowdown, it’s an ambition that increasingly depends on swelling BYD's foreign business, which has already surpassed its domestic revenue.

Indeed, BYD’s runaway success overseas has contributed to a broader rethink of global trade policy, spurring barriers such as 27% tariffs in the E.U., 35% in Brazil, 40% in Turkey, and 100% in the U.S. On Oct. 12, the E.U. announced a 350,000-a-year quota would be imposed on hybrid EV imports from China in a move that is expected to halve their market share. The U.S. has gone further than tariffs and quotas, with the Pentagon in June labeling BYD as a “Chinese military company.”

Analysts say Europe’s restrictions on Chinese plug-in hybrid vehicles may become a template for protecting other industries exposed to what’s been dubbed “China shock 2.0,” from chemicals and medical equipment to wind turbines that critics say are heavily subsidized. As such, BYD has become an unwilling lightning rod for a fundamental rebalancing of global trade.

Li: We are working closely with them to check what's the reason, because we are a privately owned, publicly traded company. They say BYD is close to [the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology,] which is the industry authority to give approval of cars. Well, all car companies for sure always need to go to them, including Tesla. Every U.S. company needs to go there. So this reason isn’t very strong. The second they say that BYD has a manufacturing plant within an army industrial park. But different companies, including several American companies, are also there. It’s ridiculous.

The big challenge now is geopolitical. Every day, you wake up with headlines saying, ‘the U.K. is going to put a 45% tariff,’ and ‘the European Union is going to put another tariff.’ It’s all this scary news.

This is mainly triggered by political concerns. Because thinking about BYD or [other foreign] manufacturing in the region, we will hire local people. Then what's the difference? Sometimes when the revolution comes, people need a little time to digest. For us, we are a global company. We need to also make ourselves very strong [by hiring] local people.

One argument is that the whole of China's car industry was built on joint ventures, with Volkswagen and Audi and all these companies forced to partner with local firms to do business in China, which helped build up the domestic auto industry. Does it not make sense to reciprocate with joint ventures overseas?

It's a very different moment now, because when all those foreign companies came to China, the whole auto industry was weak. But China did open up for all the foreign brands to make tons of money over the past 20 years. They banked the profit from China. So now if we do a joint venture, can we make the same profit that they did in China? No, it's impossible. So it's a different moment because now the whole society, industry, has grown to be more open, to be a really consumer-driven, competitive market.

But without BYD, the Chinese auto industry would still be weak, because in these joint ventures the Chinese engineers had zero influence or knowledge with the car. Everything was decided by the foreign country. But when we started in the car industry, people went, ‘how can they do this?’ Then they also started to learn.

We need to focus on the domestic market, where we're going to get stronger. It is just like altitude training—training with extreme conditions! So we need to retain our number one position in China.

We are maybe 10 times more careful than other companies. Because everybody is watching us to see any mistake we make. We already use tech firms from overseas. Even our data center, our Cloud, uses Google.

BYD is in the leading position to develop a solid-state battery, but this kind of technology still needs some maturity for mass production. The industry wants to push for 2030, but I think now they need to postpone the schedule a little bit. But BYD will be the first one to make this happen.

You talk about BYD as being a pure technology company and your electronics arm already assembles a lot of the world’s smartphones and iPads. Now you're moving into humanoid robots, data centers, and other things. What's the next great leap you’re preparing for?

For cars, autonomous driving is already the big challenge. And second is about the ecosystem. For example, flash charging; all the charging capability we do is also a huge business. And then the third is robots. And then battery storage and the server and all the components among the server. So all this industry add-on together we already have a very strong position.

title: New Report Examines the Economics of Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels Ahead of COP31
description:
Research shows that pricing carbon can reduce emissions at a lower cost than conventional regulations, even in developing countries.
Second, the report recommends increasing funding for clean energy innovation, so low carbon energy become cheaper and more competitive.
Together, carbon pricing and innovation policies could limit warming to approximately 1.9°C by 2100 and achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2080.
These measures would help unlock investment in clean energy in emerging markets and developing countries and support sustainable growth.
“Making clean energy cheaper reduces the carbon price needed to achieve the same emissions reductions, making carbon pricing easier to implement and sustain.
text:
As negotiators prepare to meet for COP31, a new report builds on the roadmap for a just, orderly and equitable transition away from fossil fuels launched at last year’s COP. It examines the economic challenges involved in the transition and sets out concrete policy recommendations to accelerate it. The Economics of Climate Organisation (ECO), hosted at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) in collaboration with the COP30 Presidency, International Growth Centre (IGC) and the LSE Global School of Sustainability, held an event on 5 November bringing together leading economists and the COP30 Presidency team for the release of the report, The Economics of Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

“The extraordinary economists who came together at ECO have been contributing to the work of the COP30 Presidency since 2025, and the report launched today is a strong additional contribution. Their report has enriched the Roadmap the COP30 Presidency launched this week with sound economic analysis. The Roadmap makes the case that the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable, urgent and yet possible, and that every country can start now, from where it is,” says Ambassador André Corrêa do Lago, COP30 President and Co-chair of ECO.

The report identifies two key market failures holding back the transition: fossil fuels remain underpriced because their environmental and health costs are generally not reflected in market prices, while investment in clean-energy innovation remains insufficient. It estimates that, under current policies, the world is on track for approximately 3°C of warming by 2100. The consequences are substantial. For example, 2025’s global emissions by themselves will cause about $20 trillion of climate damages or roughly equal to 17% of global GDP.

“The cruelty of the climate arithmetic is that it is impossible to meet conventional climate targets without today’s poorer countries undertaking massive emissions reductions, yet these countries can least afford to do so,” says report co-author Michael Greenstone, the Milton Friedman Distinguished Service Professor in Economics and director of the University of Chicago’s Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth. “Unless they are incentivized to undertake robust carbon pricing or innovation causes clean energy to become cheaper than fossil fuels, they are unlikely to make these kinds of emissions cuts.”

The report recommends three policy responses. First, countries should put a price on carbon—whether through a tax or a cap-and-trade market—so fossil fuel prices reflect the damage they cause. Research shows that pricing carbon can reduce emissions at a lower cost than conventional regulations, even in developing countries. The report recommends that countries start by setting a carbon price for high-emitting sectors like energy, transport and polluting industries, then expand to land-use and other sectors. However, by itself, even an ambitious global carbon tax starting at $50 per tonne and rising 3 percent annually would leave the world on track for 2.2°C of warming by 2100, suggesting that carbon pricing by itself is not enough.

Second, the report recommends increasing funding for clean energy innovation, so low carbon energy become cheaper and more competitive. Together, carbon pricing and innovation policies could limit warming to approximately 1.9°C by 2100 and achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2080.

And finally, the report recommends policies to accelerate clean energy adoption, including phasing out fossil fuel subsidies, expanding preferential financing through international development banks and trade organizations, and lowering trade barriers. These measures would help unlock investment in clean energy in emerging markets and developing countries and support sustainable growth.

“Carbon pricing and clean energy innovation reinforce each other,” says report co-author and ECO Co-chair Robin Burgess, Professor of Economics at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) and director of IGC. “Making clean energy cheaper reduces the carbon price needed to achieve the same emissions reductions, making carbon pricing easier to implement and sustain. At the same time, carbon pricing creates a larger market for clean technologies, spurring further innovation.”

As countries come together at COP31 to discuss the next steps in the global transition away from fossil fuels, the report contributes to the ongoing policy discussion on how economic evidence can inform a just, orderly and equitable transition. It highlights the need to consider how carbon pricing, clean-energy innovation and the wider adoption of clean technologies can work together to accelerate the transition.

The report is supported by ECO, a global collaborative initiative bringing together economists and policymakers to advance climate research and strengthen the contribution of economic evidence to the design and implementation of climate policies. Launched in June 2026 by COP30 President Ambassador André Corrêa do Lago, ECO grew out of the COP30 Presidency Council on Economics, Finance and Climate.

title: ELECTION GUIDE: What companies can expect in a divided government
description:
Editor’s note: The Election Guide is drawn from recent BiGS articles explaining how the midterm election will impact business.

text:
Editor’s note: The Election Guide is drawn from recent BiGS articles explaining how the midterm election will impact business. You can see highlights of our coverage here, which include a more complete discussion of many issues.

The Democratic takeover of Congress, as well as key governorships and other state offices, will shift the landscape for American business, impacting everything from immigration to industrial policy in the next Congress.

Republicans will lose the ability to pass partisan federal bills. Democrats will gain the ability to hold hearings, launch investigations, influence budget decisions and push back on the Trump administration’s agenda. They can also pass legislation with Democratic priorities, though only bills with bipartisan support have any hope of becoming law, thanks to the president’s veto pen.

“In areas where everyone agrees, or where it is not a high-profile issue or a polarizing issue, there’s a chance there can be some movement on those, even with divided government,” says Benjamin Schneer, associate professor of public policy at the Harvard Kennedy School. “But I think the overall tenor will be very confrontational.”

To help companies navigate this new terrain, the Institute for Business in Global Society (BiGS) interviewed roughly two dozen experts around the U.S., including more than a dozen from Harvard Business School (HBS) and other schools across the university. Here’s what they see ahead.

COST OF LIVING

Affordability was a major issue for Americans, with U.S. tariffs and the Iran war increasing consumer costs and driving a nationwide call for policymakers to take action.

Bipartisan initiatives, such as cutting red tape in the housing market, could gain traction, according to Max Miller, an assistant professor at HBS who studies the impact of finance and economics on public policy. “Those kinds of policies could be effective in making at least housing, which is the biggest expense for most Americans, a little bit more affordable,” he says.

Democrats may also advance more partisan ideas, such as extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, capping the cost of some prescription drugs, and taxing oil company profits.

IMMIGRATION

Broad immigration reform is unlikely, but targeted policy changes may be possible. One example may be laws that allow workers to enter the country temporarily to help in industries where the labor supply is short, such as farming. “I am mildly optimistic that there might be partial fixes,” says HBS Assistant Professor Marco Tabellini, who studies how migration affects companies, politics, and economies.

Democrats may also try to pass legislation to protect the so-called Dreamers, who were brought into the U.S. without legal status by their parents when they were children, though that legislation will likely face opposition from the administration. Experts also expect Democrats to launch inquiries into policies and procedures at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY

The most consequential debate in industrial strategy may be a shift from first‑generation renewables such as wind and solar, where the parties disagree, to a second wave of policy focused on economic power and competitiveness (rather than just emissions), where the two sides may have more common ground.

The change in party control may also tweak which energy technologies receive political favor. For example, the most substantive shifts going forward could center on newer energy technologies such as green hydrogen and ammonia, advanced geothermal, next‑generation nuclear, transmission, and cleaner industrial processes.

But lawmakers must first give companies a stable landscape, says Christian Kaps, an assistant professor at HBS. “The U.S. policy environment is so volatile that a lot of companies are hesitant to make large capital investments,” he says.

IRAN WAR

The war in Iran was a driving issue in the election, in large part because voters were unhappy about rising gasoline and diesel prices. But it is not clear that the conflict will end anytime soon.

Both the House and Senate narrowly approved resolutions over the summer aimed at ending the war in Iran or convincing the president to seek congressional approval before continuing military action. But the White House brushed off the measures, which were largely symbolic.

Though Democrats will wield more power in the new Congress, Schneer says it will be difficult to stop the war. “Obviously, the effects of the war are not popular,” he says. “That hasn’t really mattered for Republicans, so far. They’re not reining in the war effort in a meaningful way. I do think the war is a partisan issue … and I would hesitate [to predict] they’d do a full about-face.”

TRADE

Though the administration’s tariff policy is well known for abrupt shifts and changes over the last two years, experts say the overall course is unlikely to change. Democrats are expected to hold hearings, call to relieve tariff burdens on allies, and put forth legislation to give Congress greater control, but the outcome of those efforts is uncertain.

Ebehi Iyoha, assistant professor at Harvard Business School who has studied how U.S. trade policy affects smaller companies and its impact more broadly, expects Democrats will also focus on the problems confronting small businesses, which have been hit hard by tariffs increases.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

Artificial intelligence could be an area where bipartisan legislation is possible because lawmakers in both parties worry about the technology’s effect on employment, personal privacy and child safety. While sweeping legislation is unlikely, experts say targeted reforms could gain traction. One example may be funding a Center for AI Standards and Innovation to balance innovation with national security concerns.

“Rarely do we create comprehensive, proactive regulation,” says Eugene Soltes, a professor at HBS who studies organizational cultures and the regulatory environment. “I think we can make meaningful progress on targeted regulations addressing AI-enabled fraud and consumer harm, where there is broad agreement across political and business communities about what constitutes unacceptable conduct. But developing a more comprehensive, forward-looking regulatory framework for AI is a much greater challenge. Historically, it often takes a significant crisis to create the political will and public consensus necessary for that kind of regulatory action.”

DATA CENTERS

Concerns that data centers increase electricity demands, raise costs and impact the environment will make them a focus of debate in coming months. While there are many things Congress and federal agencies could do, much of the debate and the policy that shapes it is expected to play out at the state and local level.

New York announced a one-year moratorium on data centers earlier this year. Data center policies were on the ballot this week in dozens of local jurisdictions across 10 states. John Macomber, a senior lecturer at HBS who studies climate adaptation and the future of cities, says these debates can be difficult.

“I think a lot of this has to do with what the community is trying to prioritize and who makes that decision, whether it is commissioners or voters or the governor or a consortium of business leaders,” he said in an interview earlier this year.

“There may be people who want to prioritize revenue to the community. There may be others more worried about preserving the character of the place as they know it. Still more are discomfited by the AI specter in general, in a way that other local industrial investments did not worry them. But the first question, if we are indeed all working together, is: What is it that are we all trying to accomplish together?”

RENEWABLE ENERGY

While Democrats generally support first-generation renewables such as wind and solar, experts say politics may take a backseat to economics as renewables become cheaper. “The reality is that these technologies have become important to the economic competitiveness and security of the country,” says HBS Professor Gunnar Trumbull, who studies how climate policy impacts companies and authored the book, A Concise Business Guide to Climate Change. “At their heart, they're bipartisan.”

Democrats also have signaled interest in defending remaining supports for storage technologies, geothermal, hydrogen and nuclear power while pushing transmission expansion, easier permitting for zero-emissions energy, and closer scrutiny of the surge in energy demand caused by data centers.

FOSSIL FUELS

With Democrats gaining power in Congress, coal may become a flashpoint in energy and climate policy.

The Trump administration has supported the industry, but that has not stopped a decades-long decline as coal struggles to compete with cheaper energy sources such as gas and renewables. The issue may be politically fraught for Democrats. They will be under pressure from the party’s environmental constituencies to respond with aggressive oversight, but at the same time risk alienating key communities in battleground states, where mining is part of local identity.

Democrats could be well-served to “think in a bipartisan way” and work out a “grand bargain” with Republicans that builds out both renewables and fossil fuel infrastructure, says Harvard Kennedy School Professor Dustin Tingley, who teaches an energy class at HBS and is a co-author of Uncertain Futures, which examines the challenges of fossil fuel producing regions. “It would be closer to being veto-proof,” he says.

ENERGY PERMITTING

Permitting reform could advance in the next Congress as a fragile bipartisan consensus builds. In late September, a deal was announced on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would accelerate federal approvals for major energy and infrastructure projects. But Congress didn’t vote on it before the election.

Surging demand for power from data centers and other sources is exposing grid bottlenecks and location issues, forcing both political parties to confront the mechanics of building projects. In a high‑demand era, queue times, transmission routes, and zoning may matter as much as choices about coal, gas, and renewables.

Republicans are focused on speeding approvals and narrowing environmental reviews and court challenges for oil, gas, pipelines, and other traditional energy projects. Democrats want to safeguard approvals for clean generation and interconnection projects and secure stronger environmental‑justice protections. Any compromises are likely to bundle elements of both.

DIVERSITY

Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives in the U.S. quickly retreated after Republicans took control of the White House and Congress in 2025. While experts say that is not likely to change substantially now that Democrats have a majority in Congress, the election did represent several high-profile victories for diversity.

Among them were the first Muslim senator (Michigan), the first Black female governor (Georgia), and the first openly gay male senator (New Hampshire). California and Texas elected their first Latino governors; Florida, Nevada and Wisconsin elected their first Black governors; Minnesota, Ohio and Tennessee elected their first female governors; and New Mexico elected the first female Native American governor. For the first time, women will occupy more than 100 seats in the House. If House Democrats select Representative Hakeem Jeffries as Speaker, which is widely expected, he will be the first Black Speaker of the House.

However, the current course on policy was set by executive orders, rule changes and political pressure, and cannot be easily reversed by Congress. “So much of this is at the discretion of the executive branch,” points out Edward Chang, an associate professor at HBS who studies DEI in organizations.

However, Siri Chilazi, senior researcher at the Women and Public Policy Program at the Harvard Kennedy School, notes that companies have recruiting needs regardless of politics. “[CEOs] need to hire the best person for the right role at the right time,” she says. “And that matters, whoever may be in the White House or Congress.”

GENDER

American women have been affected by federal policy in areas ranging from compensation to healthcare in recent years. But because many policies were enacted via executive order and court action rather than legislation, experts do not expect dramatic changes. “There is no enabling legislation for any of this,” says Sandra Sucher, a Harvard Business School professor

Democrats may hold oversight hearings on administration policy, and can block some Republican measures, such as limiting access to abortion medications. As Sucher put it, “with the overwhelming Democratic victory in the midterms, and the victory of female candidates, we will likely see substantial pushback against new measures, and attempts to block Republican measures that negatively affect women and families."

LGBTQ RIGHTS

President Trump’s focus on transgender Americans at the start of his second term had a severe impact on their rights ever since. Shortly after his inauguration, he signed executive orders that removed gender identity from federal policy. They banned trans troops in the military and led to the end of gender-affirming care coverage for federal workers.

Democrats' new power in Congress won't likely reverse those moves. But they can make new policies harder to enact without political repercussions. Diego Garcia Blum, program director for the Global LGBTQI+ Human Rights Program at Harvard Kennedy School's Carr Center for Human Rights Policy, says oversight will be the primary weapon for Democrats. “In real terms, meaning laws and policies, not much will change, because that is going to be determined by the president,” Blum says. “Their ability to enforce [executive orders] strongly may change because of the oversight power [Democrats] may have.”

EMPLOYEE OWNERSHIP

Employee ownership enjoys bipartisan support. Several weeks ahead of the midterms, the Retire Through Ownership Act, which reduces the legal risks associated with forming an Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP), became law. Several more pieces of legislation to make it easier for employees to own their companies could see action in the new Congress.

Possibilities include the Employee Ownership Representation Act, which would put representatives of employee-owned companies on a U.S. Department of Labor advisory panel on employee benefits, ensuring their views are considered; the Promotion and Expansion of Private Employee Ownership Act, a tax-deferral benefit for owners selling their companies to an S-Corporation ESOP; and the American Ownership and Resilience Act, which would use federal backing to help expand pools of private investment capital to fund employee ownership deals.

Harvard Business School Professor Nien-hê Hsieh, who studies employee ownership and serves as faculty co-director of The Ownership Project, says “For many voters, the election was not just about affordability, but more fundamentally about fairness and economic opportunity. A promising way to address these concerns would be to pass legislation to promote employee ownership.”

—BiGS writers Bill Ainsworth, Matthew Benjamin, Desmond Dodd, Petula Dvorak and Cindy Perman contributed to this report.

description:

text:
The offshore wind farm Revolution Wind is completely up and running — despite the Trump administration’s repeated and ongoing efforts to halt development of the $6.2 billion project.

On Thursday, the Danish energy giant Ørsted said its 704-megawatt wind farm near Connecticut and Rhode Island began ​“generating up to its full capacity” in October. Revolution Wind began producing smaller amounts of power in the spring, and the company installed the last of 65 turbines in September.

The project is the third U.S. utility-scale offshore wind farm to reach full commercial operations, after South Fork Wind near New York and Vineyard Wind near Massachusetts.

“Revolution Wind will provide enough electricity to power the equivalent of more than 350,000 New England homes, strengthening the region’s supply of affordable, reliable energy,” Ørsted said in an emailed statement after its quarterly earnings call. The company is selling the carbon-free electricity to three utilities in the area: Rhode Island Energy, Eversource Energy, and United Illuminating.

America’s once-burgeoning offshore wind industry has weathered a series of political attacks since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025. Before his second administration began, BloombergNEF projected that the U.S. would build 39 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035. Now, it expects just 5.9 GW to come online — an amount that reflects the handful of projects that were already completed or under construction at the start of last year.

Despite the diminished pipeline, the carbon-free energy source is still expected to help keep household utility bills in check across the U.S. Northeast, experts say. Revolution Wind and the country’s other completed projects have already played a key role in reducing grid stress during extreme weather events this year.

“Revolution Wind will provide an essential boost of utility-scale electricity to the power-hungry Northeast, delivering a substantial new source of generation, diversifying supply, and strengthening electric reliability for decades,” said Hillary Bright, executive director of offshore wind advocacy group Turn Forward, in a Thursday statement.

Ørsted hit its power milestone despite being forced to halt construction twice last year.

In August 2025, the Interior Department issued a stop-work order for Revolution Wind, due to unspecified national security threats. That order was tossed out by a federal judge one month later. But in late December, the administration issued new stop-work orders to all five offshore wind projects then under construction. Judges struck those orders down one by one — but not before developers had lost huge sums of money and nearly missed key project deadlines.

Revolution Wind still isn’t fully out of Trump’s crosshairs.

In October, the Interior Department asked a federal court for permission to reevaluate the agency’s 2023 approval of the wind farm’s construction and operations plan. While the move didn’t immediately affect the project’s activities, experts said it adds uncertainty around what is now a fully operational installation.

Meanwhile, Ørsted said it’s making progress on another offshore wind development, Sunrise Wind. The developer on Thursday said it has finished installing all of the wind-turbine foundations for the 924-MW project off the coast of Long Island, New York. That installation is expected to be fully operational in the second half of next year.

text:
The number of electric vehicles on Connecticut roads has soared since 2014, rising from 2,000 to 75,000 this year. Despite that increase, though, they still make up a small sliver of drivers overall.

The Census Bureau began interviewing Americans on the subject in 2025. Data from the state goes back further and provides more information, allowing a view into the popularity of different models. Are fully-electric cars really taking off? Have Elon Musk’s political dalliances hurt Tesla’s sales? And how many people are driving those weird-looking Cybertrucks, anyway?

Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.

Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.

ONLY 99¢

Last year, around 5% of Connecticut households said they owned or leased an electric car, according to the Census Bureau. Put another way, for every twenty garages on your street, one may be home to an EV. (Look for the person less frazzled by elevated gas prices.) That density of vehicles puts Connecticut at 14th nationally.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Loading...

That 5% figure obscures the much more interesting story about EV ownership in Connecticut. Despite cheaper models coming into the market, ownership remains a tale of haves and have-nots. Of all cars on Connecticut roads, around 3% are electric.

In Westport, though, 12% of passenger cars are electric vehicles, according to numbers published in July by the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection. The state’s wealthiest towns — Weston, New Canaan and Greenwich — all have roughly three times the share of EVs as the state overall.

Loading...

Compared to the state’s least wealthy towns, the divide widens. In New Britain, one of the towns with the lowest per-capita income, 1% of cars are electric. Electric vehicle ownership serves as a good proxy for wealth overall.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The types of electric vehicles on each towns roads also differ, although Teslas still dominate. In 2024, Teslas made up around 40% of Westport’s EVs. In New Britain, the share of Teslas was around 30%, even though it is still the most popular make. Less-expensive cars like the Chevrolet Bolt, the Toyota Prius and Toyota Rav4 made up a larger share of the EV fleet in less-wealthy towns that same year.

Loading...

2024 was also the year that Tesla CEO Elon Musk jumped into the world of politics, donating hundreds of millions of dollars to Republicans and taking a position with the Trump administration.

It doesn't seem to have hurt the company even in deep-blue Connecticut. Tesla registrations haven’t declined more than the electric vehicle industry overall, which hit a slump after President Donald Trump championed a law allowing a federal tax credit of $7,500 to expire in 2025. If anything, registrations for Teslas in Connecticut did slightly better than other brands.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Loading...

Still, the introduction of models from other carmakers ate into Tesla’s overall market share. The company's market share dropped five percentage points between 2023 and 2025. (It has remained relatively flat since.) The company had around 26,000 cars registered in Connecticut this year, fewer than 450 of which were Cybertrucks.

The decline in Tesla's market share may also be a function of the state's efforts to broaden access to electric vehicles. Through the state’s aptly named “CHEAPR” program, Connecticut has offered rebates to incentivize purchases by lower-income drivers. Some rebates shave as much as $4,500 from the sticker price of a new car, giving out more than $50 million since its inception in 2015, according to DEEP.

It is an effort to lower climate-warming emissions by replacing gas-powered cars with EVs. It may also diversify the types of drivers who can get behind their wheels.
