description:
The brand will spend the money on its current plant to expand engine production for support of hybrids and range-extended electric vehicles.
According to Alabama Governor Kay Ivey's office, the investment will also prepare Hyundai Motor Manufacturing Alabama for the refreshed Santa Fe and all-new Tucson.
It's clearly just one piece of a broader strategy moving forward for Hyundai in Alabama.
Hyundai already confirmed that the Santa Fe EREV will come out of the Alabama facility.
And, of course, how far the Santa Fe EREV can travel before its engine starts.
text:
Hyundai already offers gas, electric, and hybrid cars like the facelifted Tucson, but it's about to go further. In fact, it's doing so with an investment of nearly $450 million in Montgomery, Alabama. The brand will spend the money on its current plant to expand engine production for support of hybrids and range-extended electric vehicles. For buyers interested in electric propulsion who still want a gasoline backup, that factory work could soon pay off in the showroom.

According to Alabama Governor Kay Ivey's office, the investment will also prepare Hyundai Motor Manufacturing Alabama for the refreshed Santa Fe and all-new Tucson. Officials celebrated the announcement on October 28, tying the production upgrades to a broader expansion of the plant's powertrain capabilities. The governor also confirmed that hybrid versions of the next-gen Tucson will be part of the plant's future products. It's clearly just one piece of a broader strategy moving forward for Hyundai in Alabama.

The range-extender portion is especially interesting given market conditions. Hyundai already confirmed that the Santa Fe EREV will come out of the Alabama facility. It'll arrive at dealers in the first half of 2027 with an expected range of more than 600 miles. To achieve that range, the vehicle features a typical EV powertrain with a small ICE that runs solely to charge the battery pack. Notably, Hyundai hasn't announced a 600-mile battery-only Santa Fe. That said, it remains a manufacturer target, so buyers will have to wait for the production specifications and official ratings to see how the finished SUV measures up.

Ultimately, the benefit of vehicles like the Genesis GV90 EREV is obvious. Folks who want to run on battery power alone can do exactly that. Then, when the need calls for it, the combustion engine on board will charge the battery. Put another way, range anxiety will have no hold on the owner since charging simply requires a trip to the gas station. The downside is carrying around the additional mass associated with an electric drive system and combustion hardware, and the packaging and maintenance considerations that come with it.

The Alabama expansion fits a larger push for Hyundai. At its 2026 CEO Investor Day, the automaker said North America would offer more than 10 hybrid models by 2030, since hybrids account for half the regional sales mix. Production will span the Alabama operation and Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in Georgia. Hyundai also raised its North American parts sourcing target to 80% by the end of the decade. Building more electrified vehicles and the associated components in the region is a substantial part of the plan and should lessen the effect of tariffs.

Montgomery already employs around 4,200 people, according to state officials. The latest announcement ultimately broadens the work the facility can handle. The remaining questions are the ones buyers will care about most. How much will it cost and how efficient will it be? And, of course, how far the Santa Fe EREV can travel before its engine starts.

LONDON and SAN JOSE, CALIF., November 5, 2026 – NTT DATA, a global leader in AI, digital business and technology services, today announced an agreement with Bloom Energy (NYSE: BE), a global leader in power solutions, to deploy 900 megawatts (MW) of onsite power across multiple data center projects, globally.

Under the agreement, NTT Global Data Centers will use Bloom Energy’s fuel cell technology to support growing data center capacity and evolving AI infrastructure needs, with initial shipments starting in 2027. The agreement is Bloom Energy’s largest international project to date, and will help provide greater flexibility in bringing new capacity online as demand for digital infrastructure continues to grow.

As demand for AI infrastructure accelerates globally, access to clean and reliable power has become a strategic competitive advantage. Bloom’s fuel cells generate electricity without combustion, delivering highly reliable onsite power with low local air emissions, minimal water use and quiet operation. The modular systems can be deployed rapidly and expanded in phases, allowing power capacity to come online alongside data center construction and grow with increasingly power-dense AI workloads.

“Our clients are building AI capabilities at a pace the grid alone cannot always match, and speed to power has become one of the defining factors in delivering capacity when and where it’s needed,” said Doug Adams, CEO of NTT Global Data Centers. “Bloom’s onsite power gives us a reliable, scalable way to bring capacity online alongside construction, while honoring our commitment to the communities where we build and operate. Its fuel cells protect local air quality, use minimal water and run quietly, which matters to us just as much as the megawatts. This agreement gives us a foundation to power our clients’ growth across our global portfolio.”

“Companies that can secure power quickly will have a differentiated advantage and accelerated path to revenue,” said Aman Joshi, Executive Vice President and Chief Commercial Officer at Bloom Energy. “As AI compute makes its way from AI factories to deployment at scale for edge and inference use cases, we at Bloom are uniquely positioned to help our customers meet the moment by enabling time to power with highly reliable, cleaner power that meets AI workload requirements for the digital era. Biochar manufacturer Robinson Carbon plans to establish operations in Alexandria, Louisiana. The $16.3 million project is expected to create 42 jobs in Rapides Parish.

The investment will include the construction of a new manufacturing facility at England Airpark featuring two rotary drum pyrolysis reactors capable of converting approximately 100,000 metric tons of Southern Yellow Pine residuals annually into 16,500 metric tons of biochar. Production is scheduled to begin in 2027.

“My great-great-grandfather founded our company in New Orleans in 1893 selling Louisiana longleaf pine,” said Robinson Carbon CEO Garner Robinson. “Since then, the products have changed many times over, but our passion for wood products hasn’t. Biochar is an exciting opportunity to make something truly new out of wood, and we look forward to planting new roots in Central Louisiana. We are grateful to Governor Landry, Secretary Bourgeois, the LED team, and to our partners, for helping us bring this project home to Louisiana.”

To support the project, Louisiana Economic Development (LED) offered an incentives package that includes a $550,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements. The company is also expected to participate in the state's High Impact Jobs and Industrial Tax Exemption programs.

“Louisiana has long been a leader in turning our natural resources into products used around the world,” noted LED Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois. “For more than 130 years, the Robinson family has been part of that history, and we are grateful for their continued commitment to Louisiana. Their latest investment reflects how innovation is creating new possibilities across the sectors that have powered our economy for generations, strengthening our competitiveness while extending Louisiana’s foundational industries into new products and markets.”

Robinson Carbon, the carbon products division of Robinson Lumber Company, specializes in converting wood residuals into biochar for industrial and environmental applications.

“Robinson Carbon’s $16.3 million investment is another example of how Central Louisiana is building on its traditional industry strengths to create new economic opportunities,” added Louisiana Central President and CEO Chris Masingill. “By connecting our region’s longstanding timber and wood products industry with innovative manufacturing technologies, this project strengthens our industrial base, creates high-quality jobs, and opens new markets for Louisiana’s natural resources. “Robinson Carbon’s investment reinforces England Airpark’s position as a competitive location for advanced manufacturing and industrial development,” said England Economic and Industrial Development District Executive Director Ralph Hennessy. “Our infrastructure, strategic location, and capacity for growth make England Airpark an ideal home for innovative companies like Robinson Carbon. We look forward to supporting the company’s continued success and expansion.”

title: Preparing for Congressional Oversight in the 120th Congress: What Organizations Should Expect
description:
Incoming committee leaders, including Representative Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, and Senator Ron Wyden, have signaled that oversight will be a priority.
Congressional oversight of the executive branch is a routine feature of divided government, and both parties have exercised it when in the majority.

text:
Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. When the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, the new majority will chair every committee and control subpoena power, investigative budgets, and staff for the final two years of President Trump's term. Incoming committee leaders, including Representative Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, and Senator Ron Wyden, have signaled that oversight will be a priority. Congressional oversight of the executive branch is a routine feature of divided government, and both parties have exercised it when in the majority.

What May Happen

Expect oversight to begin rapidly and to come from several committees at once. Throughout 2026, Democratic ranking members sent minority letters, issued staff reports, and made document-preservation demands. The new majority is expected to build on these efforts, and the volume of oversight activity is likely to increase significantly. Subject matter has reportedly been divided among committees in advance. Announced priorities include:

Corporate interactions with the administration and the President's family, including cryptocurrency ventures, investment vehicles, White House-related donations, political committees, and other arrangements involving private-sector organizations and administration officials.

Federal contracts and government actions, including loans, tariff escalation or relief, merger approvals, government equity or "golden share" arrangements, and regulatory exemptions or preference involving companies that have engaged administration officials.

Consumer protection, affordability and pricing, including health care costs, surveillance pricing, and consumer financial services, as well as changes in the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) supervisory and enforcement priorities, junk fees, overdraft and credit card costs, medical debt reporting, "buy now, pay later" products, and earned wage access products.

Banking, "de-banking," cryptocurrency, illicit finance, including congressional scrutiny of financial institutions, digital assets, and related regulatory and enforcement policies.

Artificial intelligence (AI), including concerns about a potential investment "bubble" driven by debt-financed AI spending, the growing role of private credit and off-balance-sheet vehicles in funding that build-out, and the resulting exposure of banks, insurers, and retirement savers, as well as the rapid expansion of data centers needed to power AI and their effects on electricity rates, grid reliability, water use, and local communities.

Defense and Aerospace sectors will likely have various hearings and potential investigations in the 120th Congress as Democrats try to reign in the Trump administration, to include – review over the financial stake the United States government has taken in critical material suppliers via favorable loan and grant conditions from the Office of Strategic Capital; investigation into defense industry donations and how that may (or may not) have impacted contract/procurement decisions and investments; and the level of control companies have on critical weapons systems (space/airborne systems, AI, etc.) which puts the USG at various levels of risk.

Why Private-Sector Organizations May Receive Requests

Committee leaders expect the administration to contest document requests, primarily through litigation. They have indicated they may seek the same information from third parties: companies that communicated with, benefited from, or did business with the administration. A company need not be accused of wrongdoing to receive a letter or subpoena. Industries already drawing attention include technology and AI, financial services and private capital, cryptocurrency, pharmaceuticals and health insurance, energy, defense, and federal contracting.

Recent court decisions have also clarified the enforceability of congressional subpoenas. Courts have held that willful default on a congressional subpoena is a crime even when the witness relied on counsel's advice (United States v. Bannon, 101 F.4th 16 (D.C. Cir. 2024)) (subsequently vacated after the Justice Department moved to dismiss). They have held that only the President, not a subpoena recipient, can invoke executive privilege (United States v. Navarro, 182 F.4th 1005 (D.C. Cir. 2026)) (petition for certiorari filed on October 8, 2026). And they have held that a witness cannot sue to block a committee subpoena and must appear even if the witness plans to invoke the Fifth Amendment (de la Torre v. Cassidy, 185 F.4th 174 (D.C. Cir. 2026)). Contempt referrals depend on Justice Department discretion, and committees have other enforcement tools, including civil enforcement, public hearings, and referrals to state attorneys general. Some committee members have indicated they may coordinate with state attorneys general.

Congressional Investigations Are Not Litigation

In Congressional investigations, there is no judge, there are no rules of evidence, and there is no guaranteed protection for the attorney-client privilege or work product. Congress recognizes only the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination as a right. Documents can be made public, quoted selectively at hearings, or shared with regulators and plaintiffs' lawyers.

How to Prepare and Respond

These steps are advisable regardless of which party controls Congress and apply to any congressional inquiry.

Engage experienced counsel early. Counsel can direct internal reviews so they are more likely to remain privileged, evaluate a committee's authority and the scope of a request, negotiate with committee staff, and coordinate the response with any parallel regulatory, criminal, state, or civil matters. Decisions made in the first days often shape an entire investigation.

Assess exposure now. Under counsel's direction, identify all formal and informal communications with the White House and agencies, as well as government contracts, funding, approvals, donations, and sponsorships that may attract interest.

Preserve records, including text messages, collaboration platforms, and encrypted applications, and suspend automatic deletion, where appropriate.

Assemble a response team of legal, government affairs, compliance, and communications professionals, and brief the board and senior leadership.

Take every letter seriously. Minority and lame-duck letters preview the 2027 investigations. Ignoring them invites escalation. Early, good-faith engagement with staff to narrow requests is usually the most productive course.

Do not act alone on privilege. If a request reaches communications with the White House, counsel should address any privilege question with the committee and the White House Counsel's Office. A company cannot assert executive privilege on its own.

Looking Ahead

For companies facing congressional scrutiny by the 120th Congress, preparation is critical. The new majority has announced its priorities. Organizations that engage counsel, understand their exposure, and plan their response before the first letter arrives will be best positioned to respond.

Several developments will shape how these investigations unfold: the organization of committees and the use of subpoena authority when the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027; the Supreme Court's response to the pending petition for certiorari in United States v. Navarro on executive privilege; and the extent to which committee members coordinate with state attorneys general. Organizations should watch for letters from committee members in the coming weeks, which may signal the scope of 2027 inquiries. Because congressional investigations often overlap with policy, regulatory, and legal issues, organizations would be well served by working with counsel to understand how those pieces fit together to anticipate requests and respond in an informed way.

text:
EDF just launched “Coal Costs Americans,” an interactive tool that allows you to visualize the impacts of the Trump administration’s playbook to put its thumb on the scale for coal.

Those actions include forcing aging plants to keep running past their planned retirement dates, handing out free passes to get out of complying with clean air rules, direct payments and more. On our new site, you can learn about 187 coal plants, dig into which ones have received direct federal support, and learn how much these facilities are polluting and what it’s costing Americans.

The timing could not be more important. Recent EDF and Atlas Public Policy analysis found that the U.S. power pipeline is shifting toward more costly, polluting fossil fuels, reversing years of clean energy growth. At the same time, America’s coal fleet continues to age, with the average coal plant now 44 years old.

Rather than allowing these aging facilities to retire, Trump administration policies are helping keep many of these facilities online longer than utilities had planned. Coal remains one of the most expensive and polluting sources of electricity, yet federal support is extending the life of plants that were already on their way out. Here are some of the worst offenders:

The coal plant receiving the most measures of federal support

Unit 1 of the Craig coal plant in Colorado has received a presidential exemption from compliance with the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) and four extensions of its retirement date. The unit is 46 years old. Its repeated retirement extensions will cost ratepayers $82.4 million to pay for the unit’s continued operation and an estimated $2.2 to $2.8 million in health harms from the unit’s pollution during that time.

Craig is the only coal plant that has received three of the four types of federal support measures analyzed by EDF. The combination of a MATS exemption and retirement extensions means that Craig unit 1 gets to continue operating past its scheduled retirement date and continue to put Coloradans at risk.

The coal plants emitting the most harmful air pollution

Mercury

The Coal Creek plant in North Dakota emitted the most mercury of any U.S. coal plant in 2025 — 294.5 pounds. It also received a MATS exemption from the Trump administration.

Coal Creek burns lignite coal, a particularly dirty and inefficient power source. Lignite coal has higher mercury concentrations than other coal types and has a lower power content, meaning more of it needs to be burned to produce the same amount of energy, resulting in more pollution. This pollution is toxic; mercury causes brain damage in babies and is associated with heart disease.

Coal Creek is one of several large lignite-fired power plants operating in central North Dakota, alongside Antelope Valley, Coyote and Milton R. Young. This concentration of lignite generation means that residents are exposed not just to emissions from a single facility, but to pollution from an entire fleet of plants burning one of the dirtiest forms of coal in the country.

Sulfur dioxide

The 56-year-old Labadie plant in Missouri emitted 38,232 tons of sulfur dioxide in 2025, the most of any coal plant in the U.S. The Labadie plant also emitted the fourth most mercury of any coal plant in 2025 –167 pounds. Yet it too received a MATS exemption from the Trump administration.

Sulfur dioxide causes eye irritation, worsens asthma, increases susceptibility to respiratory infections, impacts the cardiovascular system, and contributes to acid rain as well as harmful soot pollution. Roughly 2,000 people live within three miles of Labadie, almost a quarter of whom are low-income.

Nitrogen oxides

Also in Missouri, the New Madrid coal plant emitted 14,335 tons of nitrogen oxides in 2025, the most of any coal plant in the U.S. Nitrogen oxides are a key contributor to smog pollution (also known as ground-level ozone). Exposure to nitrogen oxides can result in development and exacerbations of asthma and bronchitis and can lead to a higher risk of heart disease.

The coal plants that have been ordered to keep running past their retirement dates

Units at six coal plants have been ordered to remain online past their planned retirement dates, in some cases for more than a year. Utilities had already determined that retiring these units was in the best interest of their customers, yet they were forced to continue operating.

These extensions come at a cost. Keeping aging coal plants running longer than planned saddles customers with additional operating expenses while exposing communities to more harmful air pollution. Collectively, these extensions have already cost ratepayers $593 million and have resulted in over $850 million in health harms.

Rather than improving reliability for the power grid, many extended coal plants have either broken down or have not been running at all. For example, unit 18 at the R.M. Schahfer coal plant in Indiana has not been operating because of mechanical issues. The Centralia plant in Washington has produced virtually zero electricity since it was first extended last December.

Learn more about EDF’s legal challenges to these unlawful extensions and the harms they pose to Americans.

The coal plants that received direct payments from the U.S. Department of Energy

Through Department of Energy grants, the Trump administration is doing more than simply delaying coal retirements. It is directly investing taxpayer dollars into coal facilities across the country.

DOE has awarded $950 million to 24 coal plants, providing financial support to an industry that has struggled to compete economically against cheaper clean energy resources and natural gas. This taxpayer money extends the life of facilities that are imposing significant health and economic burdens on Americans, while delaying the replacement of cheaper, cleaner energy.

$107.54 million of this almost $1 billion has been given to build two new coal-fired power plants in Alaska and West Virginia – the first new coal plants to be constructed in over a decade. And the Trump administration awarded $78 million to Warrior Run, a Maryland plant that retired in 2024 because it could not produce energy economically. In fact, the grid operator called the plant “extraordinarily uneconomic.”

The Trump administration’s actions hurt us now, and later

The Trump administration’s efforts to prop up coal are a part of a broader set of policies aimed at tilting the market in favor of fossil fuels, threatening to reverse years of progress in reducing harmful pollution from power plants. Right as electricity demand surges, the Trump administration is delaying, blocking and cancelling low-cost wind and solar projects around the country. Recent analysis by EDF and Atlas Public Policy found that these lopsided policies are having an impact: planned fossil fuel power capacity surged 45% in just six months, with roughly 68 gigawatts expected to come online between 2026 and 2030 – nearly all from new natural gas. If these projects move forward, fossil fuels could account for 70% of new power capacity by 2030, compared to just 5% in 2024.

Keeping aging coal plants online, along with actions the Trump administration has taken to weaken pollution protections and make clean energy harder to build, risks locking Americans into higher electricity costs and more harmful air pollution for decades. Americans could pay the price twice: through higher energy bills and the health costs of increased air pollution.

title: How the midterms could unleash a new era for clean energy in these 3 states - Grist.org
description:

“It is impossible to overstate how monumental these results are,” said David Weiskopf, the senior policy director at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit that works to elect climate-focused candidates and pass state climate policy.
“This is just a massive opportunity to make progress.” Here’s how the election could open up the floodgates for new climate policy in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and Arizona.
Pennsylvania The Pennsylvania Senate has long been known to Democrats as the place where climate policy goes to die.
The Keystone State’s status as a large producer of both natural gas and coal also made it difficult to secure agreements within the Democratic Party on clean energy proposals.
text:
When Trump was elected both in 2016 and 2024, promising to make the federal government hostile to climate action, many climate advocates insisted that state and local governments would take up the mantle of pushing for clean energy. That’s the thesis of the “America Is All In” coalition, which brings together cities and states that have vowed to uphold America’s “climate commitments … [i]n the absence of federal leadership.” The unspoken caveat in these claims is that the states leading the way on climate policy are concentrated in a few liberal parts of the country, like New England and the West Coast.

The Democratic Party’s historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could change that. Democrats have secured control of both state legislative chambers and the governor’s mansion — also known as a “trifecta” — in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, three states that have spent years or decades under Republican or divided control. The three states have also lagged on support for clean energy. Democrats also restored trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan, and Nevada this week, but those are states where they last had unified control earlier this decade.

“It is impossible to overstate how monumental these results are,” said David Weiskopf, the senior policy director at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit that works to elect climate-focused candidates and pass state climate policy. He said that the six states where Democrats have secured trifectas would be one of the world’s largest emitters if they made up their own country, rivaling Canada and Saudi Arabia. “This is just a massive opportunity to make progress.”

Here’s how the election could open up the floodgates for new climate policy in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and Arizona.

Wisconsin

Compared to its neighbors in the Upper Midwest, Wisconsin has been far less ambitious when it comes to ditching fossil fuels in its power sector. While Michigan and Minnesota have both passed laws that mandate that the states get all their power from clean sources by 2040, Wisconsin set a measly 10 percent renewable electricity standard more than two decades ago. It blew past that goal but never set a new target. Unlike most other states, it doesn’t even require utilities to plan for what kinds of power plants they want to build. The state gets a larger share of its electricity from coal than its immediate neighbors.

Renewable energy advocates in the Badger State believe they can make some short-term gains with Democrats’ first trifecta since 2010. Erik Kanter, the policy director for the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, said he believes that the new legislature can agree on the “low-hanging fruit” of making utilities plan for the future, which he said will nudge more of them to build renewables rather than extending the lifespans of gas and coal plants. The Wisconsin legislature failed this year to pass a law that would require data centers to source their power from clean sources, and Kanter expects such a measure to pass once Democrats take control. The legislature will also likely renew programs like Knowles-Nelson, a longstanding fund for parks and ecosystem preservation, which once enjoyed bipartisan approval but has lost support from Republicans in recent years.

Weiskopf, of Climate Cabinet, believes that even more ambitious moves are in the offing. He expects Wisconsin’s new class of legislators to pursue a 100 percent clean electricity standard, filling what he calls a “Wisconsin-sized hole” in the Upper Midwest. Not only would that help to phase out coal in the state, it would also make it easier for neighboring states to meet their climate goals, since the whole region shares the same interconnected power grid.

Pennsylvania

The Pennsylvania Senate has long been known to Democrats as the place where climate policy goes to die. Even though the party managed to flip the lower house of the legislature a few years ago, Republican leaders in the upper chamber often refused to bring climate bills to a vote. The Keystone State’s status as a large producer of both natural gas and coal also made it difficult to secure agreements within the Democratic Party on clean energy proposals.

“You don’t want to let yourself fully imagine what it can be, because you’ve been let down in the past,” said Lindsey Williams, a state senator who represents a swath of the Pittsburgh metro area. “Now we’re in that moment of, wow, there’s so many things that we can accomplish.”

Every year since 2019, Williams has introduced a bill that would establish mandatory energy and water efficiency standards for appliances like ovens and showerheads, a measure she said could save consumers millions of dollars a year. The legislation has never moved forward — but she thinks it will in next year’s session.

She hopes Democrats will use their first trifecta since 1993 to advance a full-scope climate agenda. In addition to passing laws that would allow community solar and warehouse rooftop solar, Democratic lawmakers also want to pass a funding package for struggling mass transit systems like Philadelphia’s. The $1.5 billion infusion would help prevent the transit “death spiral” for those systems and would reduce reliance on gasoline-powered cars.

The state’s reelected centrist governor, Josh Shapiro, appears to be on board with at least some of these proposals. Although he withdrew the state from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, a Northeast-wide carbon pricing system, he has promised to create a similar cap-and-trade system for Pennsylvania itself if he can get legislative support. He has also named funding for mass transit as a leading item on his agenda for the new legislative session next year. But Democrats will have to be careful: While they will now control both chambers, they’ll have slim majorities in each, and may have just a narrow two-year window to pass climate policy before one flips back.

“We need to be brave and lead,” said Williams. “Yes, what are the low-hanging fruits, but what are the big ambitious things that we can get done this session?”

Arizona

The last time Democrats had a trifecta in the Grand Canyon State was in 1966, decades before the general public was even aware of global warming. The state has ample sunshine and wind, so its renewable energy industry has grown quickly over recent years, and its grid is cleaner than in regions like the Midwest. Furthermore, the many new-built suburbs of the Phoenix metroplex tend to be heated with electricity rather than natural gas. Yet Republicans in the state legislature have all but banned climate and environmental policy, prohibiting the state government from regulating greenhouse gas emissions or energy usage, and numerous climate and water bills have failed in recent years.

Lauren Kuby, a longtime Democratic legislator who represents the Phoenix suburb of Tempe, says she and her colleagues have a long wish list that spans several issues. Their first order of business is to reform the Arizona Corporation Commission, the state’s utility regulator, which Kuby says has been slow to embrace new technologies like solar and wind even as developers seek to build more of them. Legislators want to pass a law that would direct the commission to make utilities invest in solar, batteries, and “virtual power plants,” or networks of homes and businesses that coordinate their energy usage. As part of the reform, they might even change the commission’s name, taking out the “corporation” and replacing it with “public utilities.” The two Democrats who appear set to win seats on the commission will make these reforms easier to push through.

The legislature could also break long-standing logjams on the crucial issue of water — a scarce resource in a desert state where climate change is worsening droughts. Kuby and other senators have been trying for years to pass a bill that would regulate groundwater pumping in the state’s rural areas. These areas are home to massive dairies and alfalfa farms like Riverview and the Saudi-backed Fondomonte, which have been blamed for sinking land and dried-up residential wells. The bill has failed in several legislative sessions, but Kuby believes that some form of regulation can pass in the coming year, bringing an end to the water free-for-all in the desert areas outside Phoenix.

“That has been languishing and has not been heard in the legislature, even though we have agreement from a lot of Republicans on water and environmental protection,” said Kuby. Of the trifecta, she said, “It’s a game-changer.”

With millions of households already opting in to these smart features, VPPs are ready to start lowering household bills now.

That new capacity can be a powerful lever to bring down utility costs and pass those savings onto customers. But for these tools to deliver bill relief in the near-term, state leaders need to put them into action quickly. That means updating state policies so demand flexibility can be counted, compensated, and deployed to meet new demand, make better use of the grid, and help lower costs for households.

In this Frontier Forum, Everyday Electric’s Will Baker and Brattle’s Ryan Hledik will join Latitude’s Maeve Allsup to offer a practical guide to implementing VPPs at the state level. This event will unpack a new study from The Brattle Group, prepared for Everyday Electric, which found that a model utility-scale virtual power plant can reduce rate increases for average households by more than half.

Brattle’s research, which modeled the five-year trajectory of a utility-scale VPP, quantified the benefits across the utility ecosystem, and translated those efficiencies into household cost savings. With real-life case studies, Will and Ryan will put these insights into practical next-steps for regulators, policymakers, and utilities to lower residential energy costs in 2027.

text:
Louisiana voters approved seven of the 10 proposed amendments to the state constitution on Tuesday and rejected three, according to unofficial results.

The proposals covered property tax exemptions, bail for certain offenders, term limits for governors, retirement system funding, water line replacement and more.

Here is how each amendment fared statewide:

Amendment 1: Surviving spouse property tax exemption — Passed Amendment 1 allows the surviving spouse of a deceased veteran with a service-connected disability, who receives the additional property tax exemption, to make a one-time transfer of that exemption to a subsequent qualifying property. It passed with 74% of the vote. The change takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Amendment 2: Lower millage rate — Failed Amendment 2 would have allowed a local taxing authority to continue levying a lower millage rate without losing its ability to adjust to the maximum authorized millage rate from a prior year’s reassessment. It failed with 58% of voters opposed.

Amendment 3: Post-conviction bail — Passed Amendment 3 prohibits a defendant from being released on any post-conviction bail if convicted of an aggravated offense against a minor child. It passed with 68% of the vote.

Amendment 4: Governor term limit — Passed Amendment 4 prohibits a person who has served more than one and one-half terms as governor from being elected governor for any future term. It passed with 58% of the vote.

Amendment 5: Retirement system funds — Failed Amendment 5 would have authorized a state retirement system to apply any nonrecurring state money it receives to any of its unfunded accrued liability, rather than requiring that it go to the oldest. It failed with 62% of voters opposed.

Amendment 6: Property tax exemption for owners 65 and older — Passed Amendment 6 authorizes parishes and municipalities to extend an additional property tax exemption for homestead property owned and occupied by a person at least 65 years old who qualifies for the special assessment level. It passed with 64% of the vote. The change takes effect Jan. 1, 2028.

Amendment 7: Water service lines — Passed Amendment 7 allows political subdivisions to use public funds to identify, inventory, remove or replace drinking water service lines made of or affected by certain materials, as specified in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, on property owned by utility customers. It passed with 65% of the vote.

Amendment 8: Foreign adversary expropriation — Passed Amendment 8 prohibits the expropriation of property by a foreign adversary or an agent of a foreign adversary. It passed with 62% of the vote.

Amendment 9: Homestead special assessment income limit — Passed Amendment 9 increases the maximum income a person may receive and still qualify for the special assessment level for residential property receiving the homestead exemption. It passed with 58% of the vote. The change takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Amendment 10: Rehabilitated blighted property — Failed Amendment 10 would have allowed property tax exemptions for blighted or derelict properties that have been rehabilitated, and would have required the Legislature to enact laws providing for administration of the exemptions. It failed with 53% of voters opposed.

Results are unofficial until certified by the Louisiana Secretary of State.

By EVWorld.com AI Editorial Team

The 2026 midterms have changed the political landscape. The challenge now is turning voter dissatisfaction into a durable American energy strategy before the 2028 presidential election.

The political message emerging from the November midterms is difficult to ignore. Democrats have captured both chambers of Congress, Texas has delivered an extraordinary statewide reversal, and Republicans are confronting the consequences of an electorate increasingly concerned about economic performance, affordability and the direction of the country. For the Trump administration, the remaining two years of its term will be considerably more complicated.

But the election should not be interpreted as a blank check for Democrats to resurrect every element of the Biden administration's energy agenda. Nor should it be viewed as a mandate to abandon the policies that made American oil and natural gas production globally competitive. The opportunity is considerably more interesting: to construct an energy strategy that recognizes the economic value of competing technologies rather than treating energy policy as a partisan contest.

America needs more energy, not another ideological argument about which energy source deserves to survive.

The immediate challenge is restoring predictability to an industry that requires enormous capital investment and decades-long planning horizons. The 2025 reconciliation legislation accelerated the expiration of numerous electric vehicle, renewable energy and efficiency incentives. Whatever one's opinion of those subsidies, abruptly changing the rules creates uncertainty for manufacturers, utilities and investors. Reconsidering selected provisions on their economic merits should be part of Congress's agenda.

That does not mean simply reinstating every previous tax credit. It means establishing technology-neutral incentives that reward measurable results: dependable electricity, lower emissions, domestic manufacturing, improved efficiency and reduced dependence on vulnerable foreign supply chains.

Electricity affordability should become the centerpiece of this effort. Artificial intelligence, data centers, industrial reshoring and electrified transportation are creating new demands on an already complicated electrical grid. Consumers should not be expected to underwrite infrastructure investments primarily benefiting hyperscale technology companies. Large electricity users should bear an appropriate share of the generation, transmission and storage costs they create. At the same time, permitting reform must make it easier to build transmission lines, generating facilities and energy storage systems.

Nuclear power, natural gas, renewables, hydroelectricity and battery storage all have roles to play. The question is not which technology wins a political argument, but which combination delivers reliable electricity at competitive prices.

The Chinese EV Dilemma

Perhaps the most consequential test of America's commitment to competitive energy markets will be whether it permits Chinese electric vehicles to enter the American market.

Washington has effectively closed the door to Chinese-made connected passenger vehicles through a combination of tariffs and national security restrictions. The Commerce Department's connected vehicle rules restrict specified Chinese-linked software and hardware, while tariffs have made direct imports economically prohibitive. The security concerns are not imaginary. Modern vehicles collect enormous quantities of data, communicate continuously with external networks and increasingly incorporate autonomous driving capabilities.

But there is a difference between protecting national security and protecting domestic manufacturers from competition.

China has developed an extraordinary manufacturing advantage in electric vehicles, batteries and associated technologies. Its manufacturers can produce vehicles at prices that American and European competitors struggle to match. Keeping those products entirely outside the American market may protect existing manufacturers in the short term, but it also deprives consumers of potentially less expensive transportation and reduces competitive pressure on domestic companies to innovate.

The question deserves a more sophisticated answer than either unrestricted imports or a permanent prohibition.

Congress should develop a controlled-access framework that distinguishes genuine security risks from ordinary commercial competition. Independent software certification, restrictions on sensitive data transfers, domestic control of vehicle communications systems, cybersecurity audits and transparent supply chain requirements could provide a foundation for evaluating market access.

And the discussion should extend beyond passenger cars. Chinese electric buses, delivery vans, municipal vehicles, semis and other commercial equipment could offer substantial operating-cost advantages. American school districts, transit authorities and private fleet operators should not be forced to pay unnecessarily higher prices simply because policymakers have failed to develop a workable competitive framework.

Commercial vehicles require particular attention. Their procurement often involves taxpayer money, and their operating economics affect the cost of delivering goods and providing public services. National security restrictions may be justified for certain government and critical infrastructure applications, but those concerns should be evaluated separately from ordinary commercial purchasing.

There is also an alternative to simply importing finished vehicles: invite manufacturers to compete by establishing American factories, employing American workers and developing domestic supplier relationships. Such arrangements should require meaningful local investment, enforceable cybersecurity standards and protections against state-directed subsidies and unfair trade practices.

The objective should be to compete with China, not pretend it does not exist.

A More Durable Industrial Strategy

Electric transportation needs similar pragmatism. The EV market does not need another round of political mandates. It needs competitive vehicles, dependable charging infrastructure, affordable batteries and consumers who recognize the operating-cost advantages of electrification. Domestic battery manufacturing and critical mineral processing deserve attention as matters of industrial security.

The next two years offer an opportunity to establish measurable progress. Congress should concentrate on permitting reform, grid reliability, fair electricity pricing, domestic manufacturing and predictable investment rules. It should scrutinize federal energy spending for waste and favoritism, regardless of which party initiated the program. Where incentives produce demonstrable economic and public benefits, they deserve consideration. Where they fail, they should be reconsidered.

There is also a larger international dimension. China is not waiting for Washington to resolve its political disagreements. Its investments in electric vehicles, batteries, solar manufacturing and industrial electrification are building competitive advantages that will not disappear because American politicians change administrations. A country that repeatedly reverses its industrial priorities risks surrendering markets it helped create.

The 2028 Test

By 2028, voters should be able to judge competing energy strategies on something more substantial than promises about gasoline prices or declarations of climate virtue. They should be asking which approach delivered additional generating capacity, lower electricity costs, more competitive manufacturing, reliable transportation infrastructure and greater energy security.

For Democrats, congressional control creates an opportunity to demonstrate that a modern energy transition can be economically responsible rather than dependent on expanding federal subsidies. For Republicans, the challenge is demonstrating that an energy-abundance agenda can accommodate technological innovation without unnecessarily restricting competing industries.

Neither party has a monopoly on the answers.

The ultimate objective should not be the elimination of fossil fuels on an arbitrary political timetable, nor the preservation of yesterday's energy economy at the expense of tomorrow's technologies. It should be an increasingly diversified energy system in which innovation, competition and economic performance determine the winners.

The 2026 election has changed the political equation. Whether it produces a better American energy policy will depend on what Washington does with the next two years.

By 2028, the country should be debating results, not slogans.

title: Eugene clean energy tax on big retailers likely to pass | Local | kezi.com
description: Eugene’s Clean Energy Fund measure is on track to pass with more than 57% support, creating a 2% fee on gross profits for large corporations earning over $1 billion nationally,
text:
EUGENE, Ore. - The Eugene Clean Energy Fund is expected to pass after receiving more than 57% of the vote.

Measure 20-388 leads by just over 9,000 votes, as of the latest results. The measure would place a 2% fee on gross profits for corporations that make more than a billion dollars in profits nationwide, beginning in the 2027 tax year.

Zero locally owned businesses meet these criteria. The tax would be placed on large retailers like Walmart, Target and Amazon.

"What this measure is designed to do is to take from these billion-dollar corporations that are posting record profits year after year and redirect just a tiny portion of that money back into our community to create good paying jobs, to fight climate change, to make our utility bills more affordable," said Dylan Plummer, a spokesperson for Measure 20-388.

The revenue will be managed by a nine-member oversight board. The board includes one representative from Eugene City Council, one from EWEB, one from the Human Rights Commission, one from the Sustainability Commission and five at-large members.

Petitioners estimate the tax will generate at least $15 million annually. Revenue will be used to fund renewable energy projects.

"Whether it's expanding energy efficiency programs at EWEB or building out big renewable energy projects like community solar. There're all sorts of different projects we want to fund," Plummer said.

Those opposed to the measure say they're worried the fee will be passed on to consumers. Supporters say they don't expect that to happen.

"I think that on paper it's a really desirable and wonderful idea. Those costs have to be passed down somewhere," said Matt Bailey, a Eugene resident. And that's going to lead to people getting their hours cut on the job, job losses, higher prices.”

"There is no evidence to show that when Portland passed their clean energy fund that any of the costs were passed on to consumers, and we just respond that it's flatly false," Plummer said.

City council will have the final say on which projects receive funding. The city will have until 2030 to begin spending the money raised.

"People should be concerned about the prices they pay at these larger retailers. They should be concerned about the workers who rely on jobs from these major retailers," Bailey said.

Ultimately, petitioners say taking action to combat climate change outweighs any potential cost to businesses.

"We are not concerned about the impacts to these billion-dollar corporations. We're concerned about the impacts of climate change that it's having right now on Eugene residents," Plummer said.

Organizations behind the measure are holding a victory party at Gratitude Brewing in Eugene on Nov. 14. Community members are invited to share ideas on potential projects.

text:
Today, we are announcing our first data center in the state of Wyoming, in partnership with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power (AEP), and Related Digital. Google is making a long-term, $17 billion investment in the Cowboy State, designed to deliver lasting benefits for Laramie County families and businesses.

Our commitment to responsible growth

We’re committed to partnering with communities to build data centers the right way. We will pay for 100% of the power we use, and when we build data centers, we’ll cover the infrastructure needs directly driven by our growth.

The project is contracted with AEP to feature a first-of-its-kind, commercial-scale, 702 MW fuel cell development with carbon capture and storage (CCS) — the largest planned development of its kind to date. Fuel cells efficiently convert fuel, in this case natural gas, into electricity through a safe electrochemical reaction. The fuel cells for this project will be made in America by Bloom Energy and will help minimize emissions and water use in the production of energy for our data infrastructure.

The CCS technology will enable the capture and permanent geologic storage of a large majority of its carbon emissions at Tallgrass’s nearby Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub. This project builds on our first CCS project in the U.S. announced last fall, and brings our total contracted CCS capacity to nearly 1 gigawatt.

We are also sourcing power from gas generators operated by Tallgrass Energy and Black Hills Energy, and conducting a technical front-end engineering and design (FEED) study to evaluate fitting Tallgrass’s combined cycle turbines with CCS technology. Together, these efforts represent a novel approach to powering data centers efficiently, accelerating the commercialization of CCS, and creating pathways to reduce the carbon emissions associated with natural gas generation.

Water is another essential shared resource, and we remain deeply committed to using it responsibly and investing in local water replenishment efforts. Consistent with our water stewardship commitments for local communities, our Wyoming data center will be air-cooled to minimize strain on local water resources.

Investment in Cheyenne

We know being a part of the community means investing in the things that matter most to the people in it. Google and our partners have held numerous meetings, and are continuously engaging key stakeholders at the local and state level. Recently, we hosted a community meeting in downtown Cheyenne; we spoke to and met with more than 200 residents in Laramie County, gathering clear and constructive feedback on their priorities. Those include:

A holistic picture of the economic benefits of this project. We expect this project to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in local property taxes for Laramie County and School District 1. This is in addition to our community investment plans, which will focus on initiatives in K-12 education, workforce development, and pathways to accelerate Wyoming’s economy.

Requests for more information on career and job skilling opportunities. Through targeted grants, Google is partnering with key local institutions championing STEM education, supporting local entrepreneurs, and expanding skilled trades training across the state. We already hosted our first Community Day at the Cheyenne Children’s Museum, and we look forward to sharing more about our community partnerships in the coming weeks.

Data center growth supporting communities. A key concern from the community meeting stretches beyond the boundaries of our own project — how data center growth is impacting Cheyenne as a community. Building on our existing engagement efforts, Google, Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, Related Digital, AEP, and Bloom Energy are standing up a Community Council designed to develop common-sense solutions to support Cheyenne through this phase of growth.

Data centers power the technology America relies on — everything from online banking, to digital maps and wayfinding, to hospitals and 911 systems. Building on Google’s 20-year track record of data center development, our promise is to show up today and tomorrow for Cowboy State residents. We are excited to put down roots in Wyoming and look forward to working closely with the community for decades to come.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – The need to bring more power online quickly in the United States is growing amid rising electricity demand, decarbonization requirements, and concerns around energy affordability. The draft Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes provisions that aim to help address longstanding barriers to connecting new power to the grid, known as interconnection. A new report from Clean Air Task Force (CATF) examines opportunities to strengthen these provisions and improve the efficiency, affordability, and predictability of the interconnection process.

CATF’s report examines why interconnection processes across much of the country remain costly, inefficient, and time-intensive, and outlines practical reforms to reduce delays, improve planning, and make more efficient use of grid infrastructure. It establishes a set of principles for evaluating interconnection proposals, with the goal of bringing new generation online more quickly and lowering costs for consumers. In a companion piece, CATF assesses how BAAJA’s proposed Consolidated Planning Process (CPP) aligns with these principles and identifies opportunities to strengthen the bill’s approach.

“Today’s interconnection process creates a cycle of uncertainty that slows the deployment of new generation and raises costs for everyone,” said Wilson Ricks, Manager, Electricity at CATF. “Developers often enter the queue without knowing how much they will ultimately be asked to pay for grid upgrades or how long the process will take. When projects withdraw, grid operators frequently have to revisit studies for other projects, creating a domino effect of delays. Processes that provide greater upfront certainty or reduce the requirements for interconnection can help break that cycle.”

Long interconnection queues, years-long study timelines, uncertain network upgrade costs, and frequent project withdrawals have created significant delays in bringing new power online. In PJM, for example, projects that entered commercial operation in 2025 waited an average of eight years between submitting an interconnection request and beginning operation.

“Over the past several decades, efforts to expand and modernize the grid have too often been slowed by fragmented planning processes and growing interconnection backlogs,” said Veronica Saltzman, Attorney at CATF. “Interconnection reform is critical to meeting growing electricity demand affordably, and better coordination between transmission planning and interconnection can help ensure the grid is prepared to connect new resources where and when they’re needed.”

CATF’s report outlines seven principles to guide policymakers in designing more effective interconnection processes:

Ensure federal reforms work across diverse market structures. Reforms should address common constraints across U.S. electricity markets.

Link transmission and generator interconnection planning. Coordinate long-term grid planning with anticipated generation needs.

Clear queues and bring power online quickly. Simplify studies, improve timelines, and reduce uncertainty.

Allocate interconnection costs early, efficiently, and transparently. Establish predictable costs and fairly allocate upgrade expenses.

Identify and proactively use surplus grid capacity. Enable projects to connect where existing capacity can accommodate them.

Create a level playing field between incumbent generators and new entrants. Ensure fair access to transmission infrastructure.

Prioritize equal treatment across resource types and sizes. Improve the process without relying on preferential fast-tracking as a substitute for broader reform.

CATF’s analysis applies these principles to two interconnection frameworks: Southwest Power Pool’s CPP, approved by FERC in March 2026, and Connect-and-Manage, which is implemented in the Electricity Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market.

In the companion analysis, CATF evaluates BAAJA’s interconnection-related provisions against these principles, including its proposed “Consolidated Planning Process” requirement, and identifies opportunities for Congress to strengthen the legislation. CATF recommends clearer direction for integrating transmission and interconnection planning, establishing set planning cycles, and ensuring planned interconnection locations and associated costs are informed by long-term system needs.

“Long-term grid investments depend on durable, predictable rules,” said Alan Mitchell, Associate Director, Federal Policy at CATF. “BAAJA points in the right direction, but clearer Congressional direction will help ensure its reforms deliver coordinated planning, reduce delays, and lower costs for consumers.”

title: COP31 in Turkey: What to Expect at the 2026 UN Climate Summit
description:
Representatives from around the world will gather in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20 for the thirty-first Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
With the legacy of the Paris Agreement in question, COP31 President Murat Kurum has set the goal of moving beyond climate pledges to the concrete implementation of existing commitments.
In the United States, control over both chambers of Congress could decide if climate change regains prominence in national policymaking or not.
Climate change is also receiving less attention now than it was during the heady days of the Paris Agreement.
One thing that the COP process does well, however, is keeping the issue of climate change on the global agenda.
text:
Representatives from around the world will gather in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20 for the thirty-first Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Although it is an annual event, this year’s climate summit is notable for two reasons: first, it coincides with the tenth anniversary of the Paris Agreement entering into force; and second, the United States—the world’s second-largest and historically biggest emitter, which formally withdrew from the agreement at the start of this year—will not send an official delegation. (Members of Congress and U.S. businesses will still attend.)

With the legacy of the Paris Agreement in question, COP31 President Murat Kurum has set the goal of moving beyond climate pledges to the concrete implementation of existing commitments. Alongside the formal COP agenda, Kurum has introduced an Action Agenda organized around ten themes, including the clean energy transition and electrification, zero waste and methane reduction, and climate-resilient cities. The COP31 presidency has also put forward voluntary pledges, including a 35-by-35 pledge aimed at increasing electricity’s share of total energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035—up from 23 percent today—as well as a commitment encouraging countries, corporations, and investors to make artificial intelligence more sustainable.

There are achievements to be celebrated at COP31. When the Paris Agreement was negotiated in 2015, the world was on track to experience catastrophic warming of 3.7°C–4.8°C [PDF] (6.7°F–8.6°F) by 2100. Thanks to policy shifts and the growth of clean energy, including a spectacular increase in global solar capacity by 2025 to over ten times what it was in 2015, projected warming by the end of the century has fallen.

Under current policies, temperatures are now expected to rise by around 2.8°C (5.0°F), or around 2.6°C (4.7°F), if the most recent climate commitments are fully implemented. This is still an extremely dangerous level of warming, but bending the curve downward by a degree spares the Earth from some of the worst consequences of climate change. The heat is already beginning to bite: August 2026 joined July 2023 as the hottest month on record globally.

The summit in Antalya will cover familiar points of discussion from previous COPs, including climate finance, greater emissions reductions, and funding for loss and damage in countries that have contributed the least to climate change. Of these, finance will likely prove the most contentious issue on the formal negotiating agenda.

Climate finance. Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement states that developed countries “shall provide” financial resources to developing nations “with respect to both mitigation and adaptation”—but who pays, in what form, and how much are matters of long-standing debate. At COP31, developing nations will continue pressing developed countries to deliver on existing funding commitments, including the COP29 goal to mobilize at least $300 billion per year in climate finance by 2035 and the COP30 call to at least triple adaptation finance over the same period. Developed countries provided and mobilized a record $136.7 billion in climate finance in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Although developing nations are seeking faster and larger payouts and note that loans can add to debt distress, developed nations are under financial stress from increased fuel costs.

Fossil fuels. How to treat fossil fuels is a recurring point of contention at recent COPs. At COP30, the parties failed to formalize a roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels, even though the measure drew support from a broad coalition of more than eighty countries. The outcome of COP30—the Belém Political Package—omitted the words “fossil fuels” from the official text. Vulnerable nations, civil society groups, environmental nongovernmental organizations, and other actors viewed the omission as a major pullback from the Glasgow Climate Pact (COP26), which called for the phasedown of unabated coal power and phaseout of inefficient fossil fuel subsidies, and the United Arab Emirates Consensus (COP28), which explicitly called for transitioning away from fossil fuels. To quell the tension, the COP30 presidency published elements of a voluntary roadmap ahead of COP31.

Emissions reductions. The COP31 formal agenda includes the Mitigation Work Program, an initiative designed to accelerate emissions reductions. In a June lead-up meeting to COP31, however, nations could not agree on the terms of the initiative, including whether it should drive cuts or remain a space for dialogue. Negotiators have also clashed over the Global Goal on Adaptation, tussling over whether to reference the call to triple adaptation finance into the formal text and how to shape metrics and indicators to measure progress.

Other topics. Another issue likely to feature is the just transition mechanism agreed to be developed at COP30. The mechanism aims to strengthen cooperation and provide technical support to economies transitioning away from carbon-intensive industries. But questions remain over how the mechanism should operate in practice, and further dialogue on the topic is scheduled to take place at COP31.

Additionally, since COP26 in Glasgow, when the Global Methane Pledge was introduced, more than 150 countries have signed on to reduce methane emissions. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that is responsible for about 30 percent of global warming and plays a significant role in near-term heating. There are low-cost, readily available ways to cut methane, and doing so now would help slow the rate of heating. There are hopes that COP31 will help accelerate ambition to cut methane emissions, particularly in the oil and gas sectors.

The Paris Agreement’s stretch goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C (2.7°F) has slipped out of reach, according to the 2026 Emissions Gap Report by the UN Environment Program. The report finds that efforts to keep warming to well below 2°C (3.6°F) would require emissions to fall 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035, and 69 percent by 2040, compared with 2025 levels. Yet current national commitments will not yield that level of reduction. Beyond the lack of ambition shown by many countries, additional headwinds have emerged with the potential to push the 2°C goal even further out of reach.

One such headwind is the delay in science-based reporting. The second global stocktake—an inventory check of progress toward meeting the Paris Agreement’s goals—will begin at COP31, but the scientific process that underpins it is sputtering. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed body of scientists responsible for assessing the latest climate science, has failed to reach agreement on when it will finalize the next set of working-group reports. The IPCC had proposed publishing the reports in 2028, but member states were unable to agree on a timeline at a meeting in October. A group of countries, including China and Saudi Arabia, argued that more time was needed because the dominance of developed nations in climate science skewed IPCC findings.

Adding to the headwinds is uncertainty over the outcomes of national elections. In the United States, control over both chambers of Congress could decide if climate change regains prominence in national policymaking or not. In Europe, recent electoral gains by right-wing parties could see climate policies falling out of favor and new limits placed on climate-related action.

Climate change is also receiving less attention now than it was during the heady days of the Paris Agreement. Media coverage of the issue has declined over the last four years in several regions around the world, including Europe and North America, according to a study by the University of Colorado Boulder. And the number of journalists registered to attend the June lead-up meeting to COP31 reached its lowest level since 2021.

While the summit in Turkey is not the first COP to take place without the United States’ participation, the country’s continued absence comes during a consequential time for the COP process amid continuing questions about its effectiveness. The emphasis on implementation, present at COP30 as well, reflects a widespread concern that the summits’ outcomes are long on dialogue and commitment and short on concrete action. Those are fair criticisms.

One thing that the COP process does well, however, is keeping the issue of climate change on the global agenda. Every year, countries know that they will be expected to show up and, to some extent, lay bare what they have (or have not) accomplished on climate action. Moreover, the annual convening provides countries with an opportunity to build coalitions on pressing problems, such as accelerating efforts to cut methane.

COP31 isn’t expected to be characterized by one big outcome or breakthrough. But that nations continue to convene in this formal channel shows that climate action and the hope for a better future that it portends is not going away.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS (Nov. 5, 2026) — Dairyland Power Cooperative and Xcel Energy filed an application for a route permit with the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission this week for the Gopher to Badger Link Project.

The project is a new 765 kilovolt backbone transmission line that will strengthen grid reliability, reduce system congestion, and help ensure homes, farms, schools, hospitals and businesses have the reliable electricity they need as demand for power continues to grow in the coming decades.

“Energy needs are growing throughout eastern Minnesota and the surrounding region, and the Gopher to Badger transmission line, along with other key investments we’re making, will ensure our customers can power their homes, businesses and farms with the reliable electricity they depend on,” said Bria Shea, president, Xcel Energy–Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota. “Investing in a strong electric grid today means we can enable economic growth and support our thriving communities in Minnesota and throughout the Upper Midwest.”

Beginning in 2025, the Gopher to Badger Link project team began outreach to landowners, local government officials and community leaders, and state agencies to share information about the proposal and gather feedback on preliminary route options. The input helped shape the primary route identified from the North Rochester Substation near Pine Island to an area near Marion, Minn., where the transmission line will connect to an existing 161 kV corridor owned by Dairyland Power Cooperative. From there, the Gopher to Badger Link will follow that existing corridor as a double-circuit 765/161 kV transmission line, including where it crosses the Mississippi River into Wisconsin.

“The grid of the future starts with the investments we are making now,” said Ben Porath, executive vice president & chief operating officer, Dairyland Power Cooperative. “By using Dairyland’s existing transmission corridor, which has been in place for decades, we minimize impacts to landowners and the landscape while addressing regional reliability for current and future generations.”

In addition to enabling access to low-cost, diverse energy resources, which will keep energy costs low, the project will also deliver tax revenue for local communities to provide services to residents and create hundreds of good paying construction jobs.

The route permit application will be reviewed in conjunction with the Certificate of Need application, which was filed in February 2026. The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission will schedule public meetings and hearings throughout the project area, with a decision expected in 12 to 18 months.

###

Xcel Energy (NASDAQ: XEL) is a leading energy provider, dedicated to serving millions of customers with excellence. We make energy work better for customers, helping them thrive every day. That means always raising the bar — delivering better service and providing more reliable, resilient and sustainable energy.

We are committed to leading the clean energy transition, meeting our customers’ need for more, cleaner power, while keeping bills as low as possible. Because the people we serve depend on us to power their lives.

Headquartered in Minneapolis, we work every day to generate and distribute electricity and gas to customers across eight states: Minnesota, Colorado, Wisconsin, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, New Mexico and Texas. For more information, visit xcelenergy.com or follow us on X and Facebook.
