title: Meat-packer JBS faces complaints filed in Europe over alleged links to illegal Amazon deforestation
description:
In the filings, the group said Wednesday that JBS laundered proceeds connected to allegedly illegal deforestation in its Brazilian beef supply chain.
“Illegal deforestation of the Amazon is a crime, not a business model.
Indigenous communities and various civil society groups have been fighting corporate profiteering from this destruction for decades," said Bláithín Quigley, coordinator for the newly formed Transnational Legal Coalition, or TLC.
These transfers can enable “cattle laundering”: animals raised on illegally deforested land moved to compliant farms before slaughter, concealing their origins.
JBS has faced legal complaints in Brazil over illegal deforestation.
text:
MANAUS – A coalition of environmental and human rights advocacy groups has filed 14 legal complaints with European financial regulators and prosecutors against JBS, the world’s largest meat company, along with its banks, investment managers and advisers, accusing them of facilitating money laundering linked to alleged illegal Amazon deforestation.

In the filings, the group said Wednesday that JBS laundered proceeds connected to allegedly illegal deforestation in its Brazilian beef supply chain. The complaints were filed with financial regulators in Britain, Ireland, Germany and the Netherlands, as well as Britain’s National Crime Agency and Dutch bodies overseeing financial and legal professionals. A separate criminal referral against JBS’s Dutch parent company was filed with Dutch prosecutors.

The coalition hopes to prompt investigations and put financiers and advisers on notice about potential legal consequences of deforestation in JBS’s supply chain.

“Illegal deforestation of the Amazon is a crime, not a business model. Indigenous communities and various civil society groups have been fighting corporate profiteering from this destruction for decades," said Bláithín Quigley, coordinator for the newly formed Transnational Legal Coalition, or TLC.

The coalition “was formed to coordinate legal efforts to tackle involvement in serious environmental crime, across global value chains,” he added.

JBS said in a statement to The Associated Press that it had not received the data or methodology behind the allegations, preventing the company from independently evaluating the claims or responding to them.

“Since 2010, JBS has monitored its cattle suppliers in the Amazon. Using satellite imagery and geo-referencing, it assesses each transaction against industry-wide criteria set out in a protocol established by Brazil’s Federal Prosecution Office,” the company said.

“The system analyzes more than 600,000 square kilometers of Brazilian territory every day and automatically blocks farms with illegal deforestation, embargoed areas, overlap with Indigenous lands, quilombola territories or conservation units, or slave-like labor,” JBS added.

Aligned groups focus on JBS from Europe

The coalition of groups includes the Global Legal Action Network, the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights, Mighty Earth, FIND and a law professor from King’s College London.

The legal rationale for bringing the cases before European authorities is JBS' ties to financial institutions in Europe, not the continent's consumption of beef from JBS, according to the TLC. Around 70% of the beef produced in Brazil is consumed domestically. Of the country’s exports, official data show that the largest share goes to North America, with the U.S. at 21.5%. Europe accounted for 18.8% of Brazilian beef exports.

By turning to European authorities, the coalition hopes to use anti-money laundering laws to hold companies and their financial partners accountable for proceeds linked to alleged illegal deforestation. The complaints allege that JBS uses revenue from sales of such cattle to pay EU-based financiers and advisers, triggering obligations under anti-money laundering laws.

The group targeted Barclays, Standard Chartered and the London branches of Bank of Montreal and Banco do Brasil; Dutch banks Rabobank and ING; BlackRock Asset Management in Ireland and Germany; and JBS’s legal, accounting and auditing advisers in the Netherlands: Loyens & Loeff, EY and KPMG.

The AP contacted all the companies named in the complaints. Rabobank declined to comment on specific clients but said its policy bars financing deforestation, accepting new clients whose land has been illegally deforested since Jan. 1, 2018, or taking as collateral Amazon land deforested after that date, even when the clearing was legal. The bank added that it is committed to preventing and detecting money laundering and regularly strengthens its controls to protect the integrity of the financial system.

Banco do Brasil said it had not seen the complaint and that it complies with anti-money laundering rules, monitors environmental and social risks, and follows industry guidelines aimed at addressing illegal deforestation risks in the beef supply chain.

ING also said it has not seen the complaint and thus could not comment. The company said it works with high-risk clients in line with international standards while applying safeguards against financial crime, but it does not comment on individual client relationships.

KPMG said it has not been contacted or seen any document from TLC and therefore could not comment. The company added it complies with applicable anti-money laundering laws and professional obligations.

Loyens & Loeff and Standard Chartered said that they could not comment due to client confidentiality. BlackRock and Barclays also declined to comment.

Founded in Brazil in 1953, JBS operates in more than 180 countries and reported $86.2 billion in revenue in 2025, according to its U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filings. It began trading on the New York Stock Exchange in June 2025 while retaining a listing on Brazil’s B3 exchange. As part of the move, JBS incorporated in the Netherlands and moved its headquarters from Sao Paulo to Amsterdam.

Complaints relied on supply chain and deforestation data

The complaints argue that revenue from cattle raised on allegedly illegally cleared land constitutes criminal proceeds and that banks, investment managers and professional advisers failed to meet obligations to detect and report suspicious transactions. They draw on commissioned research by the nonprofit AidEnvironment, which monitors deforestation and supply chains. Researchers used Brazil’s mandatory animal health and movement records to identify farms linked to cattle purchased by JBS slaughterhouses, then cross-referenced those properties with official deforestation maps.

AidEnvironment’s analysis covered 21 JBS slaughterhouses across five states in Brazil’s Amazon region: Acre, Mato Grosso, Para, Rondonia and Tocantins. It identified 3,329 direct suppliers and 9,247 indirect suppliers.

Brazilian beef cattle generally pass through three stages -- breeding, rearing and fattening -- on one farm or across several properties. Direct suppliers sell cattle to slaughterhouses, while indirect suppliers breed or raise them earlier in life.

These transfers can enable “cattle laundering”: animals raised on illegally deforested land moved to compliant farms before slaughter, concealing their origins. Transfers are also routine in cattle production and do not, by themselves, indicate wrongdoing.

Brazil has made progress in reducing deforestation, but cattle ranching remains the main driver of it. Ranchers clear large swaths of forest so cattle can graze. Biodiversity is threatened as trees that absorb carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming, are replaced by cattle that emit methane, which also exacerbates the climate crisis.

JBS has faced legal complaints in Brazil over illegal deforestation. In October 2025, Rondonia’s government overruled its own state attorneys and rescinded a fine against JBS for trading cattle raised in a deforested protected area. The case followed a four-year investigation, but the state attorney general later said the fine relied on legislation no longer in force.

When the lawsuits were filed, JBS declined to comment on its operations in Rondonia. However, it cited an audit, published by Brazil's Federal Prosecution Service in 2023, that found 94% of its cattle purchases were from legal sources. When the audit was released, the company said it was working toward “100% compliance” while noting it worked with thousands of cattle sellers across the region.

text:
U.S. Oil and Gas Association President Tim Stewart is sounding the alarm over the potential fallout if the Lone Star State were to adopt California-style energy policies.

Stewart stressed that "the absolute worst thing that could happen to the United States economy would be to have California-style energy policy implemented in Texas."

During an appearance on "Big Money in the Morning," Thursday, Stewart explained how Texas adopting energy policies similar to those in California or Colorado could deal an economic blow to the state and the U.S. economy overall.

"It would have dire consequences for the U.S. economy when you take a $27 billion industry like ours in Texas and you begin to heavily overregulate it," he said.

Stewart's warning comes after Democrats made significant gains in Texas during Tuesday's midterm elections, including victories by Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico.

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

"When we saw that clean sweep of Democratic elections take place in Colorado, for example, in 2019, we've seen a 40% reduction, a 25 to 40% reduction in production in Colorado," he explained while discussing the effects of regulations.

"My big fear, and I've said this to my Texas friends, is what happens if Texas becomes Californicated. For example, it's, like, if you're a business in California, you don't like being regulated, you pick up and you move to Texas."

"We have to go where the actual resource is," Stewart said.

He explained how oil and gas companies from Colorado and California have moved their operations to Texas because of the availability of resources.

"We don't have any other place to go."

Stewart told FOX Business’ Dagen McDowell that Tuesday’s election was watched "very, very carefully" and that "alarm bells were going off" once the election results were in.

The U.S. Oil and Gas Association president highlighted Hinojosa's emphasis on data center and electricity costs rather than the oil and gas industry.

"I think she fully understands that $27 billion contribution to the economy and 1.4 million jobs is important," he said.

OIL GIANTS POST BILLIONS IN PROFITS AS AMERICANS FEEL PAIN AT THE PUMP

Stewart highlighted how outgoing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott approached energy policy and recognized the industry's economic importance, while also offering his outlook on the incoming Hinojosa administration.

"We anticipate that, again, that the governor-elect will understand how important the role that we play to her state, and we hope that she's willing to work with us."

"Governor Abbott supported an all-above approach. We hope that the governor-elect will do the same," he added.

title: Activists Hope Midterm Wins Set the Stage for Renewed Energy and Climate Policy
authors: britney, Marianne Lavelle, Dan Gearino, Chris Walker, Derek Seidman, C.J. Polychroniou, Sam Rosenthal, Sharon Zhang, Ali Harb, Orion Rummler
description:
Voters in Ohio, South Carolina and Texas — states Trump won by double digits two years ago — put Democrats over the top in the U.S. Senate.
Activists believe the result sets the stage for renewed environmental and climate policy, even though candidates seldom mentioned those issues by name in their campaigns.
Trump’s sagging approval became a millstone Republicans were forced to carry, as opponents attacked them for their complicity in an unpopular war that had caused U.S. energy prices to soar.
And the polling showed voters were more worried about the inflationary impact of Republican energy policies than Democratic climate policies.
(One example: Creating a Strategic Energy Affordability Reserve, drawing from windfall oil and gas profits.)
text:
Democrats on Tuesday won control of both houses of Congress and a decisive mandate to put a check on Donald Trump’s tumultuous presidency, a victory propelled by voter anger over high prices, corruption and the unchecked spread of data centers.

Some of the same concerns helped to lift Democrats to victories in statehouses, where they gained a majority of the country’s governorships for the first time in more than a decade.

Voters in Ohio, South Carolina and Texas — states Trump won by double digits two years ago — put Democrats over the top in the U.S. Senate. And the Democratic wave surmounted a seawall of money: the unprecedented spending the GOP’s tech industry allies poured into the races in recent weeks to protect the status quo and their freedom from regulation.

Activists believe the result sets the stage for renewed environmental and climate policy, even though candidates seldom mentioned those issues by name in their campaigns. They argue that any action Congress takes on voters’ top issues — soaring energy prices, undue industry influence and the surge of artificial intelligence infrastructure — will curb the upward trajectory of U.S. fossil fuel consumption that Trump has encouraged.

“Voters rejected the Trump administration’s failing energy policies, which have pushed electricity bills higher,” said David Kieve, president of EDF Action, the political arm of the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund, which invested $18 million in the midterms. “Families know that blocking clean energy raises rates. Paying companies to abandon wind projects, canceling grants meant to lower rural utility bills, and using emergency orders to keep coal plants running when cleaner, cheaper options are available all moved us in the wrong direction.”

A Broad Reaction to Republican Policies

A president’s party typically loses seats in Congress in midterm elections, and in the face of that history, Trump urged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The results indicated that voters listened. Trump’s sagging approval became a millstone Republicans were forced to carry, as opponents attacked them for their complicity in an unpopular war that had caused U.S. energy prices to soar. (The decision to unilaterally join Israel in airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28 resulted in “incalculable political damage for Trump’s party,” political pundit Charlie Cook wrote on the eve of the election.)

In unfortunate timing for Republicans, the U.S. oil industry last week reported its profits — $130 billion over the past six months, or triple the earnings of one year ago, all due to the war-related run-up in prices. On the campaign trail, Trump tried to frame the oil industry’s boon as a blessing for Americans.

“They’re making hundreds of billions of dollars — our country is — on oil,” Trump said at an Oct. 26 rally in Georgia. Trump said his advisers warned him not to mention that “because people are paying a little bit higher,” but he said he didn’t care how his words would be portrayed. “I don’t give a damn,” he said. “We’re making a freaking fortune!”

But Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) seemed to better capture the mood of his state’s voters in his last days of campaigning for reelection: “Under failed president Donald J. Trump, it costs more than ever in American history to fill up your truck, stock your fridge, visit the doctor or power your home.” Ossoff coasted to re-election as expected, and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated Republican Rick Jackson to win the Georgia governor’s race.

Opposition to data centers helped Democrats in many races, such as in Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback and defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Brown dubbed his opponent “the face of data centers,” and sought to tie Husted to tax breaks and other policies that have attracted the giant computing centers to Ohio.

Trump’s foes — including environmental groups — blanketed the airwaves in swing states and districts with ads tying the pain of high gasoline and electricity prices to cozy Republican relationships with oil and utility companies, tech giants and the insurance industry. “Voters are not simply frustrated, they’re angry at monopoly utility companies, Big Tech, and Big Oil, who are making record profits while families struggle,” said Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of LCV Victory Fund. The super PAC of the League of Conservation Voters became one of the leading outside issues groups supporting Democrats on both state and federal ballots, with a $110 million investment in the midterms.

Cabinet members like Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins fanned out into states like Iowa where Republicans were in deep trouble. They touted Trump deregulatory policies and offered aid to farmers. But pre-election polling showed key Trump administration messages on environmental protection fell flat. More than 70 percent of likely voters in Iowa, Ohio and Texas felt rollback of environmental regulations would have either no impact on making their lives more affordable or would make things more expensive, according to early October polling by The Cook Political Report, New River Strategies and GS Strategy Group.

And the polling showed voters were more worried about the inflationary impact of Republican energy policies than Democratic climate policies. About 60 percent blamed “Republicans’ support for the war with Iran, trade wars, and billions in giveaways for data centers” for high energy prices; only about 40 percent said they were more concerned about “Democrats’ radical environmental policies like the Green New Deal.”

James Talarico overcame a fusillade of tech industry money to become the first Democrat that Texas will send to the U.S. Senate in 33 years. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, alone contributed an unprecedented $445 million to super PACs, much of it to bolster Talarico’s scandal-plagued Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico made Musk’s effort to buy the seat an issue in the campaign, which resonated in a state that has been convulsed over the spread of Big Tech facilities.

Across the country, 56 percent of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their picks for Congress, according to polling by The Wall Street Journal. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, seeing the tidal wave of opposition grow, imposed a temporary moratorium on new facilities in Texas. But his moves were not enough to win him re-election. State Rep. Gina Hinojosa will become the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995.

After pulling off her surprise victory in the South Carolina Senate race, Democrat Annie Andrews spoke of the moment as a rebellion against the status quo. “You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington, D.C., that we will not bow down, that we will not back down, and we will chart our own course,” she told her supporters.

As Washington enters a period of divided government, governors and state legislatures will have an opportunity to lead on climate and energy policy in ways that the federal government won’t or can’t.

Democrats retained governors’ offices in Arizona, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, flipped control from Republicans in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, and were on track to add other wins in closely watched races.

“Because of your hard work, Ohio has chosen unity and decency over division and hate,” said Ohio Governor-elect Amy Acton, a former director of the state public health agency.

Democrats also won the two open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, a utility regulator, giving the party a 3-2 edge. The panel had been controlled by Republicans for decades and the new majority has an opportunity to address consumer concerns about rising utility bills.

Oversight Ahead

A key win for climate came early in the night with the re-election of Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), despite Florida Republicans’ failed efforts at redistricting to favor the GOP. Castor, who represents storm-prone Tampa, served as chair of the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis during Trump’s first term and has been leader of a project to develop a legislative agenda on the economy and environment for the new Congress. The so-called Thriving Economies Project unveiled a menu of 800 policy recommendations in September designed to win bipartisan support, many of them tapping into the concerns that animated voters in the midterms. (One example: Creating a Strategic Energy Affordability Reserve, drawing from windfall oil and gas profits.)

text:
Astemo Indiana plans to invest more than $11 million in its Muncie manufacturing operation, increasing production capabilities and supporting future growth.

The project includes additional injection molding capacity and a new assembly line for intake manifolds used in internal combustion engine and hybrid electric vehicle applications, according to a community announcement.

The Muncie City Council recently approved a five-year tax abatement to support the investment.

“We appreciate the support of the Economic Development Alliance and the Muncie community. This partnership reinforces Astemo’s commitment to investing in Muncie, supporting our employees and driving long-term growth," said Alejandro Navarro Lopez, vice president of operations at Astemo Americas.

Astemo's Muncie operation employs about 188 people

Astemo's Muncie facility was established in 1999 and employs about 188 associates. About 70% of the facility's employees live in Muncie, according to the announcement.

The Economic Development Alliance of Muncie-Delaware County worked with Astemo's local leadership in recent months to identify the company's growth goals and coordinate with local and state partners.

"Astemo's decision to expand its Muncie operation speaks to the strength of this facility, its workforce and our community," said Traci Lutton, vice president of economic development for the Economic Development Alliance of Muncie-Delaware County. "Manufacturing companies with national and global footprints continually evaluate where to place future production and investment. We're grateful Astemo continues to choose Muncie and Delaware County, and we're proud to support a company that has demonstrated such a long-term commitment to our community."

The project also aligns with a recently completed Economic Development Alliance study that identified advanced manufacturing focused on transportation equipment and mobility as a priority industry for Delaware County, according to the announcement.

Astemo plans to hire additional workers

Astemo expects to hire additional associates to support the manufacturing expansion. The company did not provide a hiring timeline or number of positions in the announcement.

People interested in jobs with Astemo can view openings and apply at careers.astemo.com/en.

Astemo Americas manufactures and markets engine management, electric powertrain and integrated vehicle controls for automotive manufacturers.

title: EPA Proposes Rollback of Methane Rules for Oil and Gas Industry | Legis1
description:

The agency's own modeling projects the changes would add 60 million short tons of methane emissions over that period.
Associated gas from oil wells: The 2024 rule generally required new oil wells to route associated gas to a sales line rather than routinely flare it, subject to specified exceptions.
§ 60.5400c establishes equipment leak standards for onshore natural gas processing plants under the emissions guidelines for existing sources in Subpart OOOOc.
§ 60.5400b establishes equipment leak standards for onshore natural gas processing plants under the new source performance standards in Subpart OOOOb.
text:
Why It Matters

Oil and gas companies, gas processing plants, and storage tank owners would face weaker methane emissions limits under an Environmental Protection Agency proposal to roll back parts of its 2024 regulations covering the crude oil and natural gas sector. ​

The rollback would weaken protections governing thousands of new sources and hundreds of thousands of existing sources in the crude oil and natural gas sector. EPA estimates the primary proposal would reduce equivalent annualized costs by approximately $2.7 billion per year over the 2027-2050 period. The agency's own modeling projects the changes would add 60 million short tons of methane emissions over that period.

The Big Picture

The agency says it "very likely underestimated costs because the actual costs of compliance are likely higher than the EPA anticipated in the March 2024 Final Rule." The proposal advances Executive Order 14154, "Unleashing American Energy," and Executive Order 14156, "Declaring a National Energy Emergency," both issued Jan. 20, 2025. Comments are due Dec. 16, and EPA is seeking comment on all requirements from the March 2024 final rule, not only those directly addressed in this proposal.

What Changes

Super Emitter Program: EPA proposes to rescind the program entirely, eliminating third-party certification, technology certification, and operator obligations to respond to notifications of methane emissions of 100 kilograms per hour or greater. Implementation had already been extended to Jan. 22, 2027, and has not yet taken effect.

Associated gas from oil wells: The 2024 rule generally required new oil wells to route associated gas to a sales line rather than routinely flare it, subject to specified exceptions. The proposal would replace that requirement with an option to route gas to a control device or flare achieving at least a 95% reduction in methane and volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions.

Well-site subcategories: EPA proposes two alternative approaches and would finalize one: a "marginal well site" subcategory for sites where all wells produce an average of 15 barrels of oil equivalent (boe) per day or less over the preceding 12 months, or a "conventional well" subcategory with reduced requirements for conventional wells. The agency states that wells producing 15 boe per day or less account for approximately 78%-80% of existing U.S. oil and natural gas wells but represented approximately 7% of total U.S. oil and natural gas production in 2024.

Gas processing facilities: Owners and operators would gain the option to conduct optical gas imaging surveys under Appendix K, an alternative not currently permitted under the existing standards.

The Law Now and After

Today, 40 C.F.R. § 60.5400c establishes equipment leak standards for onshore natural gas processing plants under the emissions guidelines for existing sources in Subpart OOOOc. The proposal would revise equipment leak requirements at gas processing facilities and provide additional compliance flexibility, including the use of optical gas imaging surveys under Appendix K.

Similarly, 40 C.F.R. § 60.5400b establishes equipment leak standards for onshore natural gas processing plants under the new source performance standards in Subpart OOOOb. EPA proposes changes affecting those standards, while the marginal well site and conventional well site subcategories would be established through separate provisions governing well sites.

The proposed revisions are not final. Existing requirements remain in place, subject to previously adopted compliance extensions.

Advertisement

The Fight Over the Rule

The American Petroleum Institute supported the proposal as a way to address compliance challenges, while the Environmental Defense Fund argued that capturing gas rather than losing it could offset compliance costs, NPR reported. Sierra Club campaign director Mahyar Sorour criticized the proposal as a giveaway to fossil fuel executives, Reuters reported.

CNBC reported that EPA's own modeling projected the proposal would add 60 million short tons of methane emissions from 2027 to 2050, while EPA estimated approximately $45 billion in savings over that period. The agency's regulatory impact analysis also projects increases of 17 million short tons of VOC emissions and 2.3 million short tons of hazardous air pollutant emissions under its primary proposal.

The Bottom Line

Comments are due Dec. 16 under docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0163. EPA has scheduled a virtual public hearing for Nov. 16, with advance registration for speakers closing Nov. 10. The agency is also requesting comments on its information collection provisions, which it can best ensure consideration of if the Office of Management and Budget receives them by Nov. 30.

text:
TUCSON, ARIZONA — Full-size trucks were the future of electric vehicle technology. Until they weren’t.

A year after General Motors Co.'s announcement in 2021 that it would phase out internal combustion engines by 2035, Chevrolet introduced the Silverado EV into the light-duty truck segment — the highest-volume segment in the U.S. auto market. From GMC to Ford to Ram, other Detroit truck brands also promised an EV pickup revolution with high torque for towing, battery range for long hauls, and big sales to gain credits for tightening government emissions mandates.

Four years later, the all-new, fifth-generation 2027 Chevy Silverado 1500 pickup unveiled to media in Arizona showcased four ICE powertrains, including two new V-8 engines and a segment-exclusive diesel engine. With anemic sales and reduced government mandates, the electric Silverado was nowhere to be seen.

From V-8s to diesel, ICE truck powertrains are resurgent. Ford and Ram have canceled their big EV trucks as the revolution has gone from boom to bust.

“We really wanted to appeal to the customers and provide them what they wanted,” Ryan Harrington, Chevy trucks senior marketing manager, said here. “We heard from our customers that they wanted to keep V-8s ... so it was important for us to continue to evolve and come up with powertrains that resonate with truck customers. The diesel is one of the most efficient full-size pickups on the road — especially when paired with the (optional) 34-gallon fuel tank, those customers are getting over 900 miles of range on one tank of fuel.”

The Silverado EV sold 5,327 units through the third quarter of 2026, a 43% decline from a year ago as consumer demand plateaued and government subsidies dried up. The electric pickup accounts for just 1% of Silverado’s 418,710 unit sales so far this year. Had it maintained 2025 sales, the EV pickup would only be 2% of Silverado sales.

The Detroit Three have all recorded big losses in their EV-related businesses. GM booked about $7.6 billion in losses for 2025, Ford Motor Co. recorded $19.5 billion in write-downs while nixing F-150 Lightning EV production, and Stellantis NV booked a $26 billion write-down while scaling back all-electric products in favor of gas models. An electric Ram truck prototype never made it to market.

“The reality of the sales potential of electric-powered trucks was clearly driven home to both Ford and General Motors over the past four years,” said Senior Auto Analyst Karl Brauer of iSeeCars.com. “They’ve decided to pivot away from all-electric vehicles back to vehicles they knew people would buy.”

GM has backed off on its plans to go all EV by 2035, now pledging a full lineup of gas and battery-powered vehicles from its Chevy, GMC, Buick and Cadillac brands. Harrington said Chevrolet is not giving up on light-duty electric pickup sales.

“There's still a great opportunity with EVs in the segment, especially with the architecture and the battery capabilities that the team has developed,” he said. “The 450 miles of range with the extended, max battery — there's still a big opportunity here, and we are still seeing sales with the production that we have. For consumers who want to go electric and need a pickup truck, we have an offering for them.”

The Silverado EV’s specs suffer compared to, for example, the standard, diesel-powered Work Truck that Chevy offers and that fleet customers buy in volume.

With a standard range of 283 miles, the all-wheel-drive electric Work Truck costs $56,095 with a towing capacity of 8,500 pounds. A comparable, AWD, $50,780, diesel Work Truck boasts 624 miles of range. Opt for the 34-gallon tank and that grows to 884 miles.

Assume 50% of range degradation for both the EV and diesel when towing, and range declines to 140 and 310 (440 with 34-gallon tank) miles, respectively.

“Gas and diesel trucks accomplish a lot of work without a major hassle to get the work accomplished,” said analyst Brauer. “Some people buy trucks purely for image, but the overwhelming majority of people who purchase trucks have work and travel in mind. It's not nearly as easy to accomplish things with an electric truck as it is an internal combustion-powered truck.

Fueling is also key to the pickup market and gas and diesel infrastructure is robust compared to electrics — with gas trucks quicker to refuel by a factor of 10. Fueling a gas tank to 100% takes five minutes vs. an hour for an electric model.

GM has leaned into the fact that many truck fleet operators store diesel tanks for fueling. In addition to the light duty, 3.0-liter, turbocharged 6-cylinder diesel, Chevrolet has introduced an all-new, 8.3-liter V-8 Duramax turbo-diesel for 2027 in its Heavy Duty trucks (not subject to U.S. emissions rules for light vehicles), making a record-for-GM trucks 1,230 pound-feet of torque for towing.

For fleet customers who own both HD and light-duty trucks, GM’s twin diesel offerings mean fleet customers don’t have to invest in alternative gas or charging infrastructure.

GM’s business model “is a good example of how unrealistic it is to assume that existing truck infrastructure built around diesels can easily be swapped out for electric vehicles,” said Brauer. “With light-duty diesel trucks like GM offers, it's easier to drag more segments into the existing diesel infrastructure than to destroy the . . . pipelines and everything that gets diesel fuel to where people want it to be and replace it with electric cable. Especially when, as anyone who bought an EV Lightning or Silverado discovered, you have less functional trucks.”

GM’s continued development of its signature pushrod V-8s is also significant.

With upgrades of nearly half-a-liter over the last generation V-8s, the new 5.7 and 6.6-liter engines gain 47 horsepower and 61 horsepower, respectively. Torque increases by 45 and 41. Despite the mass increase of the eight pistons, however, the engines are significantly lighter — and more space and cost-efficient — than adding more battery in an EV use case.

So space-efficient are Chevy’s pushrod V-8s that they are used in everything from the Corvette supercar to HD pickups.

“What the team's been able to do with this new-generation V-8 is fantastic,” said marketing chief Harrington. “The 5.7 is best-in-class max towing, and then the 6.6-liter is the most powerful Silverado ever.”

Henry Payne is auto critic for The Detroit News. Find him at hpayne@detroitnews.com or @HenryEPayne.

text:
Wärtsilä wins an order for dual-fuel engines and thrusters for Delfin's first FLNG vessel, built by Samsung Heavy Industries for service off Louisiana in 2030.

(P&GJ) — Wärtsilä has secured an order to supply the engines and thrusters for the first floating LNG (FLNG) vessel being built at Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI) for the Delfin LNG project off Louisiana, the company said Nov. 5. The order was booked in the second quarter.

The vessel will serve the Port Delfin LNG project, about 46 miles (40 nautical miles) off the coast of Louisiana, and will be supplied by existing onshore and offshore gas pipelines. Wärtsilä worked with the project partners during front-end engineering design to develop a propulsion arrangement tailored to the vessel's requirements.

"Being able to disconnect in case of a hurricane warning and sail to a safe location is essential for an FLNG Vessel off the coast of Louisiana. The chosen propulsion arrangement, including the ability to hoist the thrusters for inboard maintenance prior to the hurricane season, is part of the solution designed for reliable operations and to ensure the safety of crew and asset," said Björn Axfors, lead engineer, hull and marine, at Delfin.

Wärtsilä will supply three Wärtsilä 46DF dual-fuel engines with an exhaust gas treatment system featuring selective catalytic reduction with Oxicat technologies. The vessel will also have three custom-designed, inboard-mountable thrusters, which Wärtsilä said will be the largest it has ever produced. The patented design allows maintenance to be carried out from inside the vessel while operations continue.

"We are pleased to continue our collaboration with Wärtsilä on the Delfin LNG project," said Youngjin Jeong, vice president of the offshore procurement team at SHI.

The equipment is scheduled for delivery beginning in the third quarter of 2027, with the vessel expected to enter operation in early 2030.

text:
The same nutrients that help farmers grow food can become a pollutant when they wash off fields and into waterways.

MSU researchers are developing a new way to capture nitrogen and phosphorus from agricultural and urban runoff before those nutrients reach lakes and rivers. The goal is to recover these nutrients and turn a water pollution problem into a resource that can potentially be reused.

Shiqiang “Nick” Zou, assistant professor in the College of Engineering, and his Electrified Wastewater Treatment and Elemental Recovery, or E-WATER, Lab have received a three-year, $1 million award from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to develop and test a technology called Carbon-Loaded Electrochemical Artificial Retention, or CLEAR.

CLEAR is designed to address a growing challenge: What happens to nitrogen and phosphorus from agricultural and urban runoff and how do we prevent it from harming water quality and contributing to harmful algal blooms that impact fish and other aquatic life? The goal is to capture these nutrients before they reach waterways and create opportunities to recover and reuse them rather than letting them go to waste.

“It’s a double-edged sword,” Zou said. “Nitrogen and phosphorus are important, but they are also a pollutant if we use too much.”

For Zou, that creates a challenge at the intersection of two necessities: food and clean water. How can we protect water quality without compromising food production?

The CLEAR project is designed to address that challenge by intercepting runoff and removing a major portion of its nitrogen and phosphorus before the water reaches waterways.

“Phosphorus is predominantly from minerals and rocks, and it’s usually considered a nonrenewable resource,” said Zou. “We only have so much phosphorus available on Earth, so we really want to reuse and recycle it when we can.”

Using electricity to capture nutrients

The new approach grew out of Zou’s 15 years of research on nitrogen and phosphorus removal. His earlier work focused on biological systems that use bacteria to remove nutrients.

Wetlands already provide a natural way to retain nutrients from water. Other approaches use materials containing metals such as iron, aluminum, calcium or magnesium to capture nutrients.

Zou’s team is taking a different approach: Instead of relying only on natural processes, the researchers are creating an engineered system that mimics the nutrient-retaining functions of a wetland using carbon and a small amount of electricity to help pull nutrients out of water.

Carbon materials capture nitrogen and phosphorus, while electricity enhances the system’s performance. The electricity used in this process could eventually come from renewable sources such as solar power.

The researchers have already developed small, bench-scale laboratory systems that use carbon materials to remove nitrogen and phosphorus from water.

“Agriculture is critically important to our state and national economies,” said Peter Savolainen, chair of the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Dr. Zou is finding innovative ways to both address the underlying concerns about pollution and also to reuse these nutrients for other purposes. We are grateful for the EPA’s support of this critical research.”

From the lab bench to a farm

The next challenge is to determine whether the technology can perform under real-world conditions — and whether it can eventually be used on farms.

During the first stage of the project, the team plans to test water samples collected from local farmland. Later, researchers plan to deploy smaller systems at the edges of agricultural fields and divert a portion of farm drainage through them.

The project includes collaborators at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, Texas A&M University and the University of South Alabama. Testing in Michigan, Wisconsin, Texas and Alabama will allow the researchers to see how the technology performs under different agricultural and runoff conditions.

That field testing is important because it will help evaluate the system’s performance and help determine whether it could be practical for farmers to apply it to their agricultural operations.

Designing technology farmers can use

Zou’s team plans to work with farmers as the project progresses, seeking input on practical questions such as cost, installation, maintenance and how a nutrient-removal system could fit into existing farm operations. In early November, Zou will travel to Mobile, Alabama, to participate in an EPA Farmers to Farmers workshop and hear directly from farmers about their needs and concerns.

“Many times, we don’t see the concerns farmers have,” Zou said. “Those concerns could include cost, logistics and whether potential chemicals could be released that may affect their produce.”

That feedback could help researchers refine the technology while it is still being developed.

The broader goal is to create a system that can protect water quality while supporting agriculture — and potentially recover nitrogen and phosphorus that would otherwise be lost to the environment.

“We do need those infrastructures in place to help reduce pollution and help to curb the footprint,” Zou said.

Lessons from the project could also help address nutrient runoff throughout Michigan and the Great Lakes, while providing a model that could be adapted to other watersheds across the country.

text:
As world leaders gather in Türkiye, Oil Change International calls for concrete phaseout roadmaps, public finance, and international cooperation to deliver affordable energy, good jobs, and a safer future.

November 5, 2026 — As governments prepare to gather for the COP31 United Nations climate negotiations in Antalya, Türkiye, Oil Change International (OCI) calls on world leaders to turn their commitment to transition away from fossil fuels into concrete, publicly funded, government-led plans that protect people from worsening climate disasters, rising energy and food costs, and geopolitical instability.

COP31 comes at the end of the most seismic year for energy shocks, and amid wars, worsening climate disasters, and an escalating cost-of-living crisis. Fossil fuel dependence drives countries’ exposure to volatile prices, supply disruptions, and conflict, while communities living near fossil fuel extraction and infrastructure suffer from pollution, displacement, and threats to their health and livelihoods. As ordinary families struggle with rising bills, fossil fuel companies continue to profit from a system that puts people and the planet at risk.

Governments face a choice: continue deepening dependence on fossil fuels and leave people and economies exposed to recurring and escalating crises, or implement a fast, fair, full, and funded phaseout that delivers affordable renewable energy, good jobs, energy sovereignty, and shared prosperity.

What to Expect at COP31

Three years after governments agreed at COP28 to a fair and managed transition away from fossil fuels, COP31 offers an opportunity to turn that commitment into action. Governments must move beyond promises and develop credible national roadmaps with concrete, timebound policies to end fossil fuel expansion, phase out existing production and use, protect workers and communities, and build resilient economies beyond fossil fuels.

These roadmaps must be backed by public planning and investment. Leaving the transition to markets will not deliver the speed, scale, or fairness needed, particularly for Global South countries facing mounting debt, high borrowing costs, and unfair international financial rules.

Wealthy countries must move first and fastest, meet their climate finance obligations, and cooperate to remove the barriers preventing Global South countries from building renewable energy economies. A fair transition must also protect communities harmed by fossil fuel extraction and infrastructure and ensure that workers and frontline communities have a meaningful role in shaping their futures.

COP31 will also see discussions on accelerating electrification. Electrification powered by renewable energy can lower pollution, reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices, and expand energy access. But any new commitment must accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels, and be explicitly powered by renewable energy, not provide cover for further gas expansion, and must be backed by public finance and policies that protect communities.

Key COP31 Moments & New Research

Recent OCI research and data: Our latest Sky’s Limit analysis finds that existing fossil fuel projects threaten nearly seven times the remaining 1.5°C carbon budget, while Behind the Barrel exposes oil supply chains fueling Israel’s military operations. Our gas affordability analysis finds that wholesale gas prices are projected to average 80% higher between 2026 and 2040 than in the previous decade, with expanding U.S. LNG exports and surging data center demand adding pressure on prices. New polling shows major public support for transitioning away from fossil fuels, while our research on the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and G20 and multilateral development banks documents progress in shifting international public finance away from fossil fuels, alongside major gaps. Our Africa finance analysis shows how changing unfair financial rules could unlock $367 billion annually to support a publicly led renewable energy future.

New briefing on fossil fuel phaseout roadmaps: OCI’s Planning or Chaos: Roadmaps for Fair and Funded Fossil Fuel Phaseouts in Producing Countries will be published on November 10. The new analysis outlines how fossil fuel producing countries are far from immune to the disruptions driven by the inherent volatility of a global economy still running on fossil fuels, and makes the case for these countries to develop government-led roadmaps to plan for a world of declining demand for their products.

COP31 political developments: OCI will respond to national roadmap announcements, new public finance commitments, electrification proposals, and initiatives that advance or undermine a fair fossil fuel phaseout.

We’ll Be Paying Close Attention To:

Fossil fuel phaseout: Credible, equitable, and timebound national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels, end expansion, and support a just transition for workers and communities.

Climate finance: Wealthy countries delivering grant-based public finance, ending fossil fuel subsidies and public finance for fossil fuels, making polluters pay, and reforming unfair global financial rules.

Electrification and renewable energy: Commitments that expand renewable energy access, reduce fossil fuel dependence, and protect communities, rather than driving new gas expansion.

Fossil fuel industry accountability: Efforts to challenge LNG expansion, fossil fuel industry influence, war profiteering, and false solutions like carbon capture and offsets – including ongoing efforts to kick fossil fuel lobbyists out of the climate negotiations.

Global leadership: Governments advancing a fair, publicly funded transition and international cooperation despite Trump’s fossil fuel expansion agenda.

Statement

Shady Khalil, Global Policy Senior Strategist at Oil Change International, said:

“Fossil fuel dependence costs people their lives, livelihoods, and economic security. Families pay higher bills, communities are suffering from pollution and climate disasters, and countries are dragged into the next crisis every time oil and gas prices spike. Meanwhile, fossil fuel companies continue to reap massive profits, with the seven Oil Majors reporting over USD 60 billion in profits in the last quarter alone.

“At COP31, governments have a choice. They can continue leaving people at the mercy of volatile fossil fuel markets and powerful interests that exploit crises for profit and political gain, or they can take control of their energy future. A fast, fair, and funded phaseout of fossil fuels is how countries can build more secure economies, protect people from energy price shocks, create good jobs, and build a safer future.

“We already know what needs to happen. Governments must stop fossil fuel expansion, plan a fair phaseout of existing production, and invest public money in renewable energy and economic diversification. Wealthy countries must move first and fastest and provide the finance needed to make this transition possible everywhere.”

Media Interviews & Availability

Oil Change International spokespeople are available for interviews ahead of COP31, on-site in Antalya, and remotely throughout the negotiations, November 9–20, 2026.

OCI experts are available to speak about fossil fuel phaseout roadmaps, international climate finance, renewable energy and electrification, fossil fuel industry accountability, U.S. fossil fuel expansion, and the connections between fossil fuel dependence, affordability, security, and conflict.

text:
In a 110,000-sq.ft. manufacturing facility in Surrey, B.C., Moment Energy is giving electric vehicle (EV) batteries a new life.

The expansive facility with over 90 employees is a far cry from the tiny garage where the company, founded by four former schoolmates who studied together at nearby Simon Fraser University, got started.

"Now, our facility is capable of producing 200 megawatt-hours a year," said Moment Energy Co-Founder and CEO Edward Chiang. "That's enough to power 175,000 homes for a single hour."

The company, a TD Innovation Partners client, turns the EV batteries into power storage systems for businesses, utilities, airports, and other infrastructure.

Their business solves three problems.

“It delays the need to dispose of the battery, reduces the need for newly mined materials, and improves electrical grid reliability and resilience,” Chiang said.

The used batteries come to Moment Energy from electric vehicle manufacturers, who ship them to Moment's head office to help avoid having to pay costly recycling fees.

"Recently we've found EV batteries have 90 to 95% of their capacity left when they're taken out of vehicles, which would otherwise end up going to a landfill or being prematurely recycled," he said.

In September, TD unveiled a $150 billion commitment to drive new lending and accelerate investment, growth, and innovation in sectors critical to Canada’s economic future. One of those sectors is energy, which includes clean and conventional energy, grid and energy infrastructure, storage, and related services.

TD Innovation Partners (TDIP) will play a crucial role in helping more startups and growth-stage businesses access capital, banking solutions, and strategic advice as they scale, from early formation to post-IPO.

How EV batteries can help support the electricity grid

“Most electrical grids in North American cities are more than 100 years old,” Chiang said. “That makes them fragile and vulnerable to storms and outages.”

Some grids struggle to support an increase in home air conditioners and electric vehicle battery charging, on top of manufacturing and other industrial needs.

But the grids are costly for governments to update, he said. Placing stationary energy storage solutions throughout a city makes access to power more reliable and gives the grid much-needed support.

"People think it's about backup power, but it's more than that," Chiang said. "When connected to the grid, the energy storage solution can store power when demand is low and also discharge power when demand is higher."

Moment Energy has also provided energy storage solutions to off-grid homes and remote communities, reducing their reliance on diesel generators.

Moment supplied a solution to a hospital on the west side of Vancouver Island.

"Their electricity grid is very unreliable at end-of-line," Chiang said. "Imagine you're in the middle of surgery and the lights go off. They have generators, but they are slow to spool up. You need batteries to immediately provide power."

End-of-line communities are ones located at the terminus of electricity transmission lines, which leaves them particularly vulnerable to outages or voltage problems.

Supporting Canadian innovation

TD began working with Moment Energy in 2025 and has supported the company through several stages of growth, including its Series A financing, said Alida Kanani, Associate Director, TDIP.

After the Series A financing round, the Bank provided the company with a venture debt facility to complement the equity raised and give the company added flexibility as it scaled, she said.

"We have been consistently impressed by the quality and integrity of Moment Energy's founders, the pace at which they execute, and the growth of both the business and the broader team," Kanani said.

"Moment is a strong example of the kind of Canadian innovation company TD Innovation Partners wants to support over the long term, not only by providing capital, but by being a trusted banking advisor as the company moves from early commercialization toward large-scale manufacturing and global growth.”

"We choose banks based on that personal relationship, and we’re super excited that we’re building that foundation with TDIP in our corner," Chiang said.

TD continues to deepen its engagement with innovators on early-stage and emerging technologies, positioning the Bank and its clients to capture new opportunities.

“Moment Energy is a strong example of how innovation can create new opportunities for sustainable growth,” said Murat Basarir, Associate Vice President, Enterprise Sustainability at TD.

“Supporting innovators developing new clean technology solutions helps bring promising ideas to market and contributes to stronger, more resilient communities."

Paying it forward in Canada

Running Moment Energy in Canada has its challenges, but keeping headquarters in the country is important to Chiang.

He’s keen to contribute to a social safety net that supported him and his mother when he was growing up in the Lower Mainland.

"I was raised by a single mother who immigrated to Canada. We relied on social housing and assistance," he said. "As a CEO, I'm more than happy to pay taxes here."

title: Benin solar IPP reaches financial close as IFC and Proparco lend €30m for 62MWp
description:
AXIAN Energy has signed €30m of financing with IFC and Proparco for IPP50, four solar plants in Natitingou, Djougou, Parakou and Bohicon that make up Benin’s first solar project under an independent power producer model, four years after the concessions were signed, with commercial operation planned for the first quarter of 2028.
IFC and Proparco are lending €30m to IPP50, four solar plants with a combined 62MWp in Natitingou, Djougou, Parakou and Bohicon that their developers describe as Benin’s first solar IPP, under financing agreements with AXIAN Energy and CDC Bénin that AXIAN announced on 29 October.
Benin awarded the project to a consortium of GreenYellow and Egnon Consulting in July 2022, when the concession agreements were signed, and AXIAN Energy took it over in 2024, partnering with Sika Capital, an investment vehicle owned jointly by CDC Bénin and Egnon Consulting.
The plants will sell their power to the Société béninoise de production d’électricité (SBPE) under long-term power purchase agreements, within 20-year concessions from the government, and IFC is also mobilising concessional funds from the Clean Technology Fund for a project expected to cost about €45m in total.
Benjamin Memmi, chief executive of AXIAN Group’s energy division, described financial close as an important moment for the company and for Benin’s power sector, crediting its partnership with international lenders and local investors.

name: American Energy
title: A Green Electrification Target for All? - Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (SWP)
description:
“Electrify Now” … In June, in the run-up to COP31, the Euro­pean Commission proposed an initial roadmap for achieving the global electrification target with the help of “renewable and other clean energy” (“Electrify Now”).
The global electrification target – a foregone conclusion?
From the climate perspective, the global electrification target lacks binding com­mitments, and should ideally be limited to renewable electricity sources.
Energy price volatility, persistent fossil fuel supply bottlenecks, and rising global energy con­sumption have led the EU to pursue green electrification with greater vigour.
Com­bined with a global agreement of the kind envisaged for COP31, the electrification target could provide further impetus for international cooperation.
text:
Growing political interest and economic expectations

The Turkish initiative capitalises on grow­ing political interest in electrification. As the International Energy Agency (IEA) notes, the energy price shocks associated with the US-Iran war have accelerated a shift in thinking. The situation of persistently high and volatile oil and gas prices following the price shocks in 2022 and 2026 creates competitive disadvantages and social pressures in importing countries. For many, oil and gas imports are the Achilles’ heel of their economies. In the long term, importing nations in Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America can address that risk only by lowering the share of fossil fuels in their energy consumption.

Accelerating electrification is also expected to modernise economies and generate growth. Households and businesses will invest in new technologies, and infrastructure will need to be renewed and expanded. In Europe, weather-related fluctuations in renewable electricity supply must already be balanced with demand, making flexible electricity grids and large-scale battery storage increasingly important. Switching energy consumption in the transport and buildings sectors from oil and gas to electri­city requires electric drives, efficient battery technologies and heat pumps, as well as electrolysers to generate hydrogen. Rising demand for electrification technologies (clean tech) is also driving international competition to develop cost-effective solu­tions – as was the case with solar and wind energy technologies.

Global market share in clean technologies is a key benchmark for Germany and other EU member states when it comes to measuring innovative strength and geo-economic dominance, particularly in com­petition with China. Harnessing this com­petition to advance electrification and climate action at low cost while maintaining economic leadership is currently one of the major challenges facing European governments.

“Electrify Now” …

In June, in the run-up to COP31, the Euro­pean Commission proposed an initial roadmap for achieving the global electrification target with the help of “renewable and other clean energy” (“Electrify Now”). To that end, it is coordinating activities between the three current COP presidencies – Brazil, Turkey/Australia and Ethiopia. At the same time, the initiative is looking ahead to COP33, when the next Global Stocktake will assess progress in implementing the goals of the Paris Agreement. Other countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada, the Philippines and South Korea, are also participating in “Electrify Now”, and the two international energy agencies, the IEA and IRENA (International Renewable Energy Agency), are providing support, including through a special report commissioned at the request of Turkey and Australia.

In July the European Commission also proposed an Electrification Action Plan for its member states, as part of the reform of EU climate policy (see SWP Comment 42/2026). Electricity’s share of final energy consumption is to be doubled from the current 23 per cent to 46 per cent by 2040 (indicative target). In its proposal, the Commission links electrification to three key EU climate policy objectives: decarbonisation of industry, transport and buildings; security of supply; and strengthening Euro­pean competitiveness. European demand for electric vehicles, heat pumps, electrolysers and batteries is to be met primarily by European suppliers. In the meantime, fossil fuel price volatility is boosting efforts to gain greater control over energy price trends and to reduce energy costs for consumers in both the short and long term.

Denmark and the Netherlands, in particular, along with the 2021 to 2025 German government, have pursued an electrification strategy to achieve national emission reduction targets. Norway also stands out in Europe, as an early adopter of electrification. Norway is a prime example of a country with structural geographical advantages. Its abundant hydropower resources have kept electricity prices low, and the build­ings and transports sector both rely largely on electricity.

… but without China?

International cooperation on electrification is a balancing act for the EU. On the one hand, it wishes to advance global climate protection efforts. According to IRENA, meeting the global 1.5°C target would require 78 per cent of global electricity consumption to be supplied by renewables by 2035. Chinese products will be indispensable in scaling up the clean-tech sector internationally and reducing costs across the industry. European clean tech manufacturers require imported raw materials, chips and processors that can only partially be substituted by domestic production. On the other hand, the EU wants to protect European clean-tech companies from Chi­nese competition and curb China’s domi­nance. Its accompanying trade policy initiatives, such as the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), therefore take a different, non-cooperative approach.

China’s pace and dominance

China now accounts for around 80 per cent of the world’s most important clean-tech products. And the country is itself a front­runner in electrification, with an estimated 29 per cent share by 2025. In its latest Five-Year Plan, Beijing declares its intention to move even further ahead internationally. One component pursued under the heading of “green development” is “electric power substitution” to replace coal, oil and gas in end-use consumption. In other words: electrification, with a target of 35 per cent by 2030. The cornerstone of this policy is expansion of renewable energy, including green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol for industrial purposes and industrial parks planned in conjunction with large wind and solar farms.

From China’s perspective, electrification serves economic modernisation and inno­vation and contributes significantly to the national growth strategy. The initial focus is on the Chinese market, which – according to one of the benchmarks – is set to become the world’s largest market for electric cars. Electrifying industrial processes means increasing the production and use of heat pumps, electric heating systems and elec­trolysers. However, China’s growth strategy cannot succeed without exports, with sub­sidies and excess capacity being used to flood international markets with clean tech-nologies. Consequently, the competitive pressure on European companies will continue to increase, while Beijing’s eco­nomic expansion will drive the interna­tional trend towards electrification and, consequently, decarbonisation.

The United States remains a key player

The US market is equally important in the international context. Although Washington is no longer participating in climate negotiations, the US energy sector is devel­oping rapidly. The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) introduced by the Biden administration in 2021 included a comprehensive sup­port programme. Tax credits and investment incentives for green hydrogen, battery technology, electric vehicles and other clean technologies have expanded the manufacture of batteries, electric cars and solar instal­lations. Scientific calculations suggest that the IRA could have almost doubled US emissions reductions. The effects of the IRA are still being felt, with continuing invest­ment in renewable energy and battery tech­nology. Demand for electric vehicles is also growing in response to rising fuel prices. As the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) reports, investment in wind and solar power plants is rising, driven by record electricity demand from artificial intelligence applications. Although Trump scrapped the Biden administration’s fund­ing for two major projects – halting an offshore wind project on the east coast and a solar power plant – the energy demand for data centres cannot possibly be met without renewables. Rising oil and gas prices are doing their bit to boost growth and devel­opment in the clean-tech sectors.

The global electrification target – a foregone conclusion?

Although an electrification target would contribute to climate protection and provide a degree of insulation from volatile energy prices, agreement at Antalya is by no means guaranteed. This is evident from the efforts of the Turkish COP Presidency during New York Climate Week in September. Rather than prioritising a green target, the pledge is not specifically green. Environmentalists are particularly critical that this would encourage the expansion of nuclear power.

The Australian-Turkish COP Presidency is focused on diplomatic success and wishes to avoid restricting the scope for progress in individual countries. Instead, poorer nations need to be brought on board to agreeing to yet another target through financial com­mitments. To this end, it has also involved companies and other stakeholders in the Global Electrification Pledge, which aims to mobilise funding for the poorest countries, island states and developing nations. Power grids and storage top the list of necessary investments. Meanwhile, the number of countries wish­ing to participate in the “Elec­trify Now” campaign has been growing, with the new­comers including Germany, Uruguay, Jor­dan and Kenya. The Pacific Island Countries expressed their support for the global target in a communiqué at the beginning of Sep­tember, and coupled this with a clear call for technical and financial assistance.

The challenge remains to convince more developing countries to agree to an additi­onal global target and take on another obli­gation. While many developing countries point to past failures to provide promised support for their efforts, the growing crisis in international climate finance further eroded the credibility of any commitments. The COP Presidency will need to demonstrate particular diplomatic skill here, both before and during the conference, and organise concrete incentives.

From the climate perspective, the global electrification target lacks binding com­mitments, and should ideally be limited to renewable electricity sources. As with the other implementation targets – in particu­lar the global targets to double energy effi­ciency and triple renewable energy capacity by 2030 (COP28 in Dubai) – the targets should be formulated to enable monitoring and progress reporting. Codification will be required to ensure that progress is trace­able. The Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), which parties to the Paris Agreement are required to submit to the UNFCCC every five years, could serve this purpose, as they allow countries to choose which climate targets they intend to achieve and by what means. Ultimately, this would enable transparent tracking of progress on the global electrification tar­get, includ­ing its contribution to climate protection.

Beyond COP31

In Germany and the EU, pressure is mount­ing to rapidly transform the energy system to increase use of electricity from domestic sources and to protect value chains. There is therefore a strong self-interest in electri­fying on the basis of renewables, yet this is evidently not sufficient given the current energy supply risks and the anticipated costs of the system transition. For this rea­son, green electrification should be clearly named as a strategic goal. That will send an important signal to businesses across many sectors, charting a path towards greater stability of energy supply and safe­guarding the business environment. Energy price volatility, persistent fossil fuel supply bottlenecks, and rising global energy con­sumption have led the EU to pursue green electrification with greater vigour. Com­bined with a global agreement of the kind envisaged for COP31, the electrification target could provide further impetus for international cooperation.

Meanwhile, in competition with China the aim should be to support European pro­ducers of clean-tech products and secure markets in third countries. The international climate negotiations on electrification pro­vide an important signal in this regard and can help German clean-tech diplomacy to negotiate bilateral cooperation in more con­crete terms. Here, the ‘Electrify Now’ initi­ative can serve as a useful platform for engaging like-minded middle powers and other trading partners.

text:
Raman, who has a background in fighting homelessness and served as executive director of the anti-workplace sexual harassment group Time's Up before winning her City Council seat in 2020, was endorsed by climate action groups, the hospitality workers union UNITE Here Local 11, the public education advocacy group Eastside Padres Contra la Privatización, and the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Kurt Petersen, co-president of UNITE Here Local 11, told Politico that Raman's projected victory was "a monsoon, an earthquake, a leveling, a restructuring" that served as a rebuke by voters of the nation's second-largest city's political establishment, including the rest of the City Council members, all of who supported Bass.

"It was all of the above," Petersen said. “The political class of Los Angeles was absent at the Nithya Raman party because they were all with the incumbent... Even though every city councilperson said they were standing with Karen Bass, not very many of the people they represent followed them to the polls.”

Polls ahead of Election Day showed younger voters across the city leaning towards Raman, who has called for a streamlined process for approving housing projects and an end to "indefinite delays," an Office of Tenant Protections for the roughly 64% of Angelenos who are renters, and a reorganization of the city's homelessness interventions "to quickly shelter and house the largest number of people with the same dollars."

She has criticized Bass' Inside Safe anti-homelessness program as ineffective and expensive, with more than $300 million spent to house 6,000 people and 40% of those served by the program returning to the streets.

"Despite repeated efforts from the City Council to reduce costs in the program, Inside Safe costs an average of $85,000 a year for a motel room and services, and some rooms go as high as $100,000 per year," reads Raman's campaign website. "It is the most expensive temporary housing program in the city by far, and people are staying in the motel rooms for close to a year. For the same amount of money, we could rent three apartments using a short-term rental voucher and provide intensive services—housing more people in a program that has delivered much better outcomes."

Raman also highlighted a nearly 50% reduction in homelessness in her own district, even as rates have risen across the city, and pledged to reduce city-wide rates by 50% before the 2028 Olympics.

Ballot-tallying continued past Election Day, with officials counting late ballots that typically are cast by younger and more progressive voters.

“This city’s government has made solving problems look impossible for so long that I heard from people across this city who started to believe that it was impossible,” Raman told supporters who gathered at her election night party on Tuesday. “Hopelessness can be fatal for a city, but this campaign refused to accept that. You refused to accept that.”

Raman has centered efforts to make the heavily car-dependent Los Angeles safer for pedestrians and bikers, crack down on "disgraceful" delays in fixing 30,000 street lights across the city, and ramping up public transportation with "permanent, dedicated bus lanes and more buses running more often."

"Nithya Raman winning the mayor's office in the second largest city in the US is in my opinion the most important election of this season," said Matthew Lewis, communications director for California YIMBY. "Just the ground shifting on housing, transit, bicycles, and walkable urbanism."

Raman also denounced the mayor for what she called a "dysfunctional" and "indefensibly slow" recovery from the wildfires that devastated parts of Los Angeles nearly two years ago. She championed the creation of a "Recovery District" to "coordinate the recovery across jurisdictions, bring hundreds of millions of dollars into the Palisades, and ensure that local residents are at the table when decisions are made."

Bass received an endorsement from the Los Angeles Police Department's union, which poured more than $5 million into the push to defeat Raman. The union also donated $200,000 to the Republican Central Committee of Los Angeles County, which sent out anti-Raman mailers to voters.

Kenneth Meija, the progressive city controller who won his reelection bid in June, said on election night that he was “so damn proud to be the only one in City Hall who supported Mayor Raman."

“They were like, ‘Yo, the entire political establishment is supporting Mayor Bass,'" said Meija. "And I’m like, ‘So? She’s got Kenneth Mejia. She’s got the people.’”

According to the Sun, the document singles out some of "the biggest tech giants, artificial intelligence labs, natural gas firms, private prisons and nursing home operators, among dozens of others," including for their alleged roles in driving up prices for cash-strapped Americans in recent years.

Even on a night when Democrats clobbered the GOP up and down the map and won decisively in states as red as Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, and Iowa, very few analysts believed Mississippi—where President Donald Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024—would be competitive, let alone a nail-biter that dragged into the next day.

In a 5-4 decision that now looms large, the US Supreme Court shot down Republican efforts to stop the counting of mail-in ballots postmarked on or before Election Day that arrive afterward. Those ballots, which can continue arriving until November 10, may ultimately decide the election.

Even if Colom falls short, his strong showing was evidence of what the NAACP, the nation’s oldest civil rights organization, described as "historic voter turnout" in Black communities, in response to Republicans' attack on the Voting Rights Act.

Following the Supreme Court's Louisiana v. Callais decision earlier this year, several GOP-controlled states, including those in the Deep South, moved to redraw congressional and state legislative districts in ways that voting rights advocates warned would dilute Black voting power.

On the campaign trail, Colom described Callais as "a threat to our democracy" and said Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, who proposed legislative maps that would have drawn Black lawmakers out of their districts, was seeking to stop Black voters from "being able to pick leaders they want."

"Massive Black turnout helped Democrats coast to victory in Georgia and made the Senate races in Mississippi and Louisiana the tightest seen in decades."

Voter turnout in Mississippi is on pace to be about 40% higher than in the last midterm election in 2022. "The story of this election is not just about who won," said Dominik Whitehead, chief of field for the NAACP. "It's about the Black wave of voters who understood what was at stake and made their voices heard."

Democratic US Senate candidate Scott Colom of Mississippi stands outside the home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers in Jackson, Mississippi, in a video posted on November 1, 2026. (Screenshot from a video by Scott Colom)

In the nation’s poorest state, where nearly 1 in 5 residents rely on Medicaid or the Children’s Health Insurance Program, this message was potent. It was especially effective against Hyde-Smith, who has comfortably won her previous elections and was relentlessly criticized for dismissing voters’ concerns about high prices.

For example, in DeSoto County, which Trump carried by 24 points in 2024, Colom led Hyde-Smith by more than six points in early returns.

"[Colom] won many switchers, and the Republican vote collapsed," Hilder said. "Swing voters are more volatile than ever, especially when they’re economically hard-pressed. They respond to common sense, and they’ve decided Trump and the Republicans are not on their side."

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since Sen. John C. Stennis, a conservative segregationist, won his seventh term in 1982. And although it has the highest proportion of Black residents of any US state, Mississippi has not sent a Black senator to Washington since Reconstruction, when Republican Blanche K. Bruce, who was born into slavery, was elected by the state Legislature.

Colom told NPR last week he’s always believed change was possible and that it has failed to materialize only because of neglect by national Democrats, who have long written the state off as unwinnable.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause," he said. "We've been a betrayed cause."
