Environmental justice organizations and partners reject EPA’s attempt to repeal protections against climate pollution from power plants

WASHINGTON — This week, the public comment window closed on an effort by the Trump administration’s U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to abandon its duty to regulate greenhouse gases from power plants. Over 60 organizations have signed on to a joint public comment letter led by coalitions Clean Air for the Long Haul and Platform for a Just Climate urging the agency to end their proposal, and to instead fulfill their mission to protect the health and environments of people across the U.S., especially frontline communities most impacted.

In September, alongside finalizing the repeal of most of the 2024 carbon pollution standards, the EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, along with the findings that underpin them. Power plants are the second largest source of climate pollution, supercharging deadly impacts like extreme heat that are experienced most severely by environmental justice communities.

Due to discriminatory policies, these same communities are also more likely to live next door to coal and gas-fired power plants, causing greater exposure to toxic air pollution from these sources. Heightened exposure contributes to higher rates of severe health issues and even premature death. More than half of children and over 78 million people of color in this country breathe dirty air, linked in many cases to power sector pollution.

The over 60 organizations in opposition to these rollbacks emphasize that the EPA’s actions disregard the public health impacts and costs, and are unlawful as it is the Agency’s duty to regulate climate emissions.

See below for testimonials from the public comment letter.

“…the impact of this pollution is not only felt in our community via our health; greenhouse gas emissions from industries have continued to accelerate climate change and the associated environmental hazards and freak weather events. Pollution-burdened communities have already been—and will continue to be—impacted by climate change first and worst.” – Mia Ayala-Marshall, Duwamish River Community Coalition

“For Louisiana and Gulf Coast communities, this is about more than energy policy. It is about protecting our health, keeping families safe, reducing the risks that threaten our homes and livelihoods, and ensuring that communities can recover from disasters without facing additional environmental burdens. We urge EPA to withdraw its proposal and maintain strong greenhouse gas protections for fossil-fuel-fired power plants. Our communities deserve clean air, meaningful safeguards against climate pollution, and an energy future that prioritizes public health, environmental justice, and community resilience.” – Dr. Beverly Wright, Deep South Center for Environmental Justice

“Just as ‘Big Tech’ needs ‘Big Oil’ to power this expansion, the oil industry is relying on tech giants to justify further investment in fossil fuels. At a time when we should be accelerating our transition away from dirty energy, the EPA is proposing to remove the very safeguards intended to limit climate pollution from these facilities. Enough is enough. Communities like ours should not have to sacrifice their health, their environment, and their future so a handful of corporations can continue profiting from pollution.” – Yvonee Taylor, Seneca Lake Guardian

The power plant repeal sits inside Trump’s dangerous deregulatory agenda, including a concerted effort by EPA to target more than 30 environmental and health protections in the largest deregulatory action in U.S. history. Clean Air For The Long Haul and Platform for a Just Climate continue the work to engage with decision-makers and the EPA to defend clean air and climate protections including hosting a briefing this Clean Air Month in May, and will keep amplifying the stories of those most impacted. The CAFLH also recently released an IMPACT digital media partnership and an op-ed piece, both showcasing critical stories about effects of rollbacks to people on the frontlines of climate and health crises driven by power plant pollution.

###

About Clean Air For The Long Haul (CAFLH)

Clean Air For The Long Haul is a nationwide coalition of environmental justice groups that coordinates federal rulemaking campaigns to reduce air pollution from the U.S. power and transportation sectors. Coalition member organizations include: Duwamish River Community Coalition, Green Door Initiative, GreenLatinos, PODER Austin, RiSE4EJ, WE ACT for Environmental Justice, West End Revitalization Association and Wisconsin/Michigan Green Muslims.

Texas voters delivered a historic shift in statewide leadership on November 3, electing Democrats to several key offices responsible for environmental and energy policy. Gina Hinojosa defeated Governor Greg Abbott, Vikki Goodwin was elected lieutenant governor, Nathan Johnson was elected attorney general, and Jon Rosenthal won a seat on the Railroad Commission of Texas (RRC). Democrats also won all three seats on the Fifteenth Court of Appeals and all four Texas Supreme Court seats on the ballot.

The election will have significant implications for businesses operating in Texas. Changes in executive leadership, regulatory oversight, environmental enforcement, and the judiciary come as the state confronts growing pressure on water and electric infrastructure, increased scrutiny of data center development, and continued debate over industrial permitting, underground injection, and public participation.

Although existing environmental laws and permits remain in place, the election could substantially change how those laws are administered, enforced, and interpreted.

Who Won: A Historic Shift in Statewide Leadership

Governor Gina Hinojosa: Hinojosa will become Texas’s first Democratic governor since Ann Richards left office in January 1995. Hinojosa has called for greater oversight of data center development, stronger protections for water resources, and more local participation in decisions that affect communities.

Lieutenant Governor Vikki Goodwin: Goodwin will preside over the Texas Senate and exercise significant influence over legislative priorities and committee leadership. She has advocated for water infrastructure investments and proposed a constitutional amendment recognizing environmental rights.

Attorney General Nathan Johnson: Johnson has emphasized consumer protection, public safety, and a renewed focus on prosecuting environmental enforcement actions.

Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal: Rosenthal, a former oilfield engineer and state representative, will join the three-member RRC. He has called for additional technical resources, stronger environmental enforcement, and increased public participation in oil and gas oversight.

Fifteenth Court of Appeals: Jerry Zimmerer, Tom Baker, and Marc Meyer defeated incumbent Chief Justice Scott Brister and Justices Scott Field and April Farris, replacing the statewide court’s entire bench. See B&D’s earlier analysis.

Supreme Court of Texas: Maggie Ellis, Chari Kelly, Kristen Hawkins, and Gisela Triana won the four Supreme Court seats on the ballot. Four of the nine justices will be replaced, with five incumbent Republican justices remaining.

What the Election Means for Texas Agencies and Courts

TCEQ: Permitting and Enforcement

The new governor could influence the direction of the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), although changes to the Commission's membership are not automatic.

TCEQ’s three commissioners serve staggered six-year terms. The Senate confirmed Chairwoman Brooke Paup and Commissioner Catarina Gonzales in 2025, while Commissioner Tonya Miller, appointed in October 2025, has not yet been confirmed. Miller's pending confirmation presents an immediate opportunity for change, while other changes may occur through future appointments or vacancies. At the end of September 2026, former TCEQ Executive Director Kelly Keel vacated the position, now held by Interim Executive Director Steven Schar.

Changes to current Commission leadership could affect rulemaking, permitting, enforcement, affected person determinations, and contested case outcomes.

Attorney General: Environmental Enforcement and Consumer Protection

Johnson’s election could affect the State's environmental enforcement and litigation strategies, including defending agency decisions and challenging to federal regulations.

Johnson has emphasized consumer protection and public safety. One question is whether he will continue or expand his predecessor’s use of consumer protection authority to address environmental health and safety concerns. Attorney General Ken Paxton pursued investigations involving PFAS in consumer products, chemical safety representations, and pesticide use on organic produce, including an October 2026 settlement with Lululemon.

Texas’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act could provide additional avenues for scrutinizing manufacturers’ environmental claims, product safety representations, and disclosures of potential health risks.

Railroad Commission: Injection Wells and Environmental Oversight

Rosenthal has advocated for increased RRC funding, stronger enforcement, and greater oversight of underground injection, emissions, and oil and gas operations.

His election could lead to additional scrutiny of saltwater disposal wells and Class VI carbon sequestration projects, particularly concerning geologic confinement, groundwater protection, and induced seismicity.

Texas Appellate Courts: Judicial Review of Agency Decisions

The replacement of all three justices on the Fifteenth Court of Appeals could significantly affect environmental litigation. Established in 2024, the court has statewide jurisdiction over many appeals involving Texas agencies, including TCEQ and RRC. As discussed in B&D’s earlier analysis, its docket includes key disputes concerning affected person status, environmental permitting, and state enforcement actions.

Four new justices will also join the nine-member Supreme Court of Texas. One early case before the reconstituted Court is San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper v. TCEQ and Max Midstream, LLC, No. 25-0564, concerning affected-person status and judicial review of an air permit. Oral argument is scheduled for January 11, 2027.

These changes could shape Texas administrative law, including sovereign immunity, agency authority, and judicial review of permitting and enforcement decisions.

Industries and Regulatory Issues to Watch

Data Centers

Data center development was a central issue in the gubernatorial campaign and will remain a focus of the 2027 legislative session.

Governor Abbott initially promoted data centers as an economic development priority but shifted course amid public concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, infrastructure costs, and community impacts. On September 21, he directed TCEQ to pause data center permitting pending further review, as discussed in B&D’s September 2026 News Alert.

In her July 23, 2026, Texans First Data Center Priorities press release, Hinojosa called for a moratorium on new data center development until the Texas Legislature enacts protections. Her campaign commitments included comprehensive legislation on local siting authority, water protections, infrastructure costs, transparency, labor requirements, and public incentives.

The incoming administration must determine its proposed statutory modifications to pursue legislation addressing water use, grid interconnection, local siting authority, and public participation.

Water-Intensive Industries and Municipal Water Supplies

Texas’s ongoing water challenges, particularly the water supply crisis in Corpus Christi, have intensified questions about competing municipal and industrial demands. In March 2026, Governor Abbott directed state agencies to expedite emergency water projects and waived certain permitting requirements to protect the city’s water supply. Continued shortages could increase pressure to restrict industrial water use during drought conditions.

Hinojosa and Goodwin have emphasized water infrastructure investment and protection of water resources. Goodwin has also proposed a Stewardship Amendment recognizing a constitutional right to a clean and healthy environment.

Water-intensive industries should monitor potential changes to drought contingency requirements, emergency water allocation, industrial water rights, and funding for new infrastructure.

Oil and Gas Production, Underground Injection, and Carbon Storage

Rosenthal’s election could bring increased scrutiny of oil and gas operations, particularly saltwater disposal, carbon sequestration, methane emissions, and flaring.

Texas’s recent assumption of Class VI permitting authority places the RRC at the center of carbon storage development. Rosenthal has advocated for stronger technical oversight and enforcement, potentially increasing scrutiny of geologic confinement, groundwater protection, induced seismicity, and long-term monitoring.

Commissioner Wayne Christian’s September 2026 opposition to ExxonMobil's Rose carbon storage permit demonstrates that concerns about individual projects can cross party lines. Although their policy perspectives differ, Rosenthal and Christian could align on particular injection well applications or property rights issues, potentially affecting permitting outcomes.

title: New Analysis: Restarting Solar for All Could Cut Electric Bills 25% for a Million Households
description:
The new analysis examines how rising electricity prices, changes in federal solar tax credits, and delays caused by EPA’s termination have altered the program’s potential benefits and the urgency of restarting it.
Instead of keeping families in the dark, EPA should take this opportunity to help a million households cut their electricity bills.” “Groundswell stands at the ready to restart our Southeast Rural Power Solar for All program,” said Michelle Moore, CEO, Groundswell.
EPN’s modeling shows that if further delays prevent projects from qualifying for federal solar tax credits, the same $7 billion would reach about 40% fewer families.
Read EPN’s issue brief, Restore Solar for All: EPA Can Help a Million Families Cut Their Electric Bills by 25%.
ABOUT THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION NETWORK
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — As American families face record-high electricity bills, a new report released today by the Environmental Protection Network (EPN) finds that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) could still help 1 million households cut their electric bills by about 25 percent if the agency complies with two federal court rulings and promptly restarts the $7 billion Solar for All program instead of appealing.

The issue brief, Restore Solar for All, prepared by former EPA officials, comes as the agency weighs whether to appeal two separate federal court rulings in Rhode Island and Washington, D.C. that found its August 2025 termination of the program unlawful. The government’s 60-day window to appeal the rulings closes in mid-November.

The new analysis examines how rising electricity prices, changes in federal solar tax credits, and delays caused by EPA’s termination have altered the program’s potential benefits and the urgency of restarting it.

“Families are skipping groceries to keep their lights on, yet restarting Solar for All could ultimately deliver more than $450 million a year in electricity bill savings,” said Michelle Roos, Executive Director of the Environmental Protection Network. “Two federal courts have now said EPA broke the law when it terminated Solar for All grants. Instead of keeping families in the dark, EPA should take this opportunity to help a million households cut their electricity bills.”

“Groundswell stands at the ready to restart our Southeast Rural Power Solar for All program,” said Michelle Moore, CEO, Groundswell. “I’m confident we could reach thousands of families across the Rural South with deep bill savings by this time next year.”

Key findings from the report:

1 million households could cut their electric bills by roughly 25 percent if EPA restarts the program promptly.

$458 million in first-year savings, or about $456 per household, which could grow if electricity rates continue to rise.

An appeal could put Solar for All savings out of reach for about 410,000 households. EPN’s modeling shows that if further delays prevent projects from qualifying for federal solar tax credits, the same $7 billion would reach about 40% fewer families.

EPN is calling on EPA to forgo an appeal, immediately restart Solar for All and give grantees the flexibility they need to get their systems operating before the deadline.

Read EPN’s issue brief, Restore Solar for All: EPA Can Help a Million Families Cut Their Electric Bills by 25%.

Jet fuel production has undergone an even more pronounced shift.
U.S. refineries, meanwhile, increased crude processing by 500,000 bpd in the second quarter and another 500,000 bpd in the third, helping compensate for lost production elsewhere.

text:
U.S. refineries are producing a smaller share of gasoline from every barrel of crude oil they process and shifting production efforts toward diesel and jet fuel as soaring margins on those products reshape the economics of American refining.

Gasoline yields averaged below 45% during the first eight months of 2026, falling below the previous five-year low in every month, according to data published Thursday by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).

That's a significant departure for a refining industry that typically produces 45 to 50 barrels of gasoline for every 100 barrels of crude processed.

And even though gasoline prices are elevated, diesel and jet fuel are considerably more profitable to produce as global fuel shortages drive refining margins higher.

Distillate fuel oil yields, which include diesel and heating oil, exceeded their five-year average in every month through August. Jet fuel production has undergone an even more pronounced shift.

In March, jet fuel's share of U.S. refinery output exceeded 12% for the first time on record. It remained at or above that level through August, the latest month for which EIA data is available.

The changes reflect an increasingly strained global refining market.

The Iran war has disrupted Middle Eastern refining operations, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have further restricted supplies of diesel and other petroleum products.

Global refinery crude runs dropped by 4.8 million barrels per day in the second quarter, according to EIA data released earlier this week. Although throughput recovered by 1.8 million bpd in the third quarter, it remained approximately 5% below year-earlier levels.

U.S. refineries, meanwhile, increased crude processing by 500,000 bpd in the second quarter and another 500,000 bpd in the third, helping compensate for lost production elsewhere.

Diesel prices reached their highest nominal levels on record in September.

For U.S. refiners, the opportunity extends beyond processing more crude. The shortage has changed which fuels deliver the greatest returns, encouraging refiners to maximize middle distillates even at the expense of gasoline yields.

The result is a domestic refining system increasingly oriented toward supplying a global market short of diesel and jet fuel.

text:
Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari on Wednesday said that reducing pollution in the country will be the biggest challenge in the future.

Addressing 'EV Ecosystem Awards and the launch of Swiggy Instamart's EV Battery Swapping Network', Gadkari further said that India is trying to become self-reliant in the production of electric vehicles, as the cost of operating EVs is less than that of vehicles run on fossil fuels.

Advt

"Pollution is a major problem. You know how high the pollution level is in Delhi today...in the future, reducing pollution in the country will be the biggest challenge," he said.

Delhi's air quality was in the 'very poor' category again on Wednesday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) at 379, according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).

Gadkari also said there is a need to reduce fossil fuel imports and encourage EVs to cut the import bill of ₹22 lakh crore and reduce pollution.

"To create employment potential is the most important agenda of the government," the minister said.

Gadkari said state-owned NHAI has set a target to install 700 charging stations over the next two years and also claimed that by next year, at least 35-40 per cent of cars sold will be electric.

He said the government's aim is to make India's automobile industry number one in the world. "When I took charge as transport minister, the size of the Indian automobile industry was ₹14 lakh crore. The minister said green hydrogen is the future and India can become a net exporter of clean hydrogen.

Advt

E100 fuel allows vehicles to run on nearly pure ethanol. Flex-fuel vehicles are designed to run on higher ethanol blends such as E85 (85 per cent ethanol, 15 per cent petrol) and E100 (near 100 per cent ethanol), unlike conventional petrol vehicles currently approved for lower ethanol concentrations.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Europe's carbon credit purchases can raise global ambition, if the EU plays its hand realistically
description:
The final paper in EDF’s series on international carbon credits in the EU looks at the diplomacy behind Europe’s future credit purchases.
The last piece of the puzzle Our new paper, International Credits in the EU: Opportunities for Climate Diplomacy, takes on that question.
It is the final paper in EDF’s series, Importing international carbon credits to the EU: How to make it work?
Counting reductions across a whole sector or jurisdiction makes it harder to credit emissions cuts that would have happened anyway.
Built this way, EU credit purchases could pay for ambition as well as tons.
text:
The final paper in EDF’s series on international carbon credits in the EU looks at the diplomacy behind Europe’s future credit purchases. Its advice: be realistic about leverage, start simple and build deeper partnerships over time.

Europe is about to become one of the world’s biggest government buyers of carbon credits – and the rules for how it buys them are being written now.

The European Union has a 2040 target of cutting net emissions 90% and at least 85% of that must come from cuts at home. But starting in 2036, up to 5% can come from high-quality international credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, with a possible pilot from 2031. In July, the European Commission proposed a central facility to buy up to 260 million tons of these credits between 2036 and 2040.

The next few weeks will shape what that buying looks like. At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, governments will debate how carbon markets should work under Article 6. By mid-December, the Commission is expected to publish its proposal on how the EU will use international credits.

Most of the debate so far has been about how much to buy, how to pay and which credits qualify. Less attention has gone to a question that may matter just as much. Who will Europe buy from, and what can it ask of them in return?

That is a diplomatic question. Credit purchases mean signing agreements with other governments. Done well, they could help partner countries cut more emissions, set stronger climate targets and see the Paris Agreement as an economic generator. Done badly, Europe could end up with a long list of agreements and very few credits.

The last piece of the puzzle

Our new paper, International Credits in the EU: Opportunities for Climate Diplomacy, takes on that question. It is the final paper in EDF’s series, Importing international carbon credits to the EU: How to make it work?

The series began in October 2025 with Strategic Choices & Practical Implementation. That paper showed how importing credits, done right, could keep Europe’s compliance costs manageable, protect its climate ambition and increase its influence in international climate policy.

In May 2026, EDF and The Nature Conservancy released two more papers:

Buying the 5% looked at how purchases could be funded and governed, and what market design would send a credible signal to future suppliers.

Credit quality criteria and implications for the EU’s purchasing strategy looked at how the EU could define and protect credit quality. It recommended building on Article 6 and existing integrity frameworks rather than writing new rules from scratch.

Together, those papers made one point clear. If Europe uses international credits, it needs clear rules, credible governance and strong quality safeguards. This final paper asks what Europe can achieve abroad once those foundations are in place.

Be realistic about leverage

Europe’s credit budget will be significant, but its pull on large emitters will be limited. Take Indonesia, one of the largest potential sellers. Suppose the EU spends €20 billion on credits between 2036 and 2040, and Indonesia wins a fifth of it. That comes to about €0.8 billion a year, starting a decade from now. In 2024 alone, Indonesia received almost €8 billion in Chinese investment through the Belt and Road Initiative.

Selling credits also has real costs for the seller. Under Article 6, every credit sold abroad must be subtracted from the seller’s own climate accounts. Add stringent conditions for domestic policy on top – designed to meet the European Climate Law’s credit criteria of Paris Agreement compatibility, additionality and permanence – and many large economies will simply look elsewhere. Europe has more sway with smaller countries. But a deal with a small country on strengthened domestic policy does less to cut global emissions.

Don’t wait for the perfect partner

Few countries are large emitters with an ambitious climate plan, affordable credits to sell and a willingness to accept EU policy conditions. We call this the diplomatic trilemma.

An EU framework that insists on all of it at once could leave Europe with few partners, or none. The opposite extreme doesn’t work either. Switzerland has signed about 20 Article 6 agreements since 2020 and has received about 14,000 credits so far. Singapore has signed 12 and has yet to receive any. It’s early days, but signatures alone don’t guarantee supply.

Go wide first, then go deep

The paper proposes a two-stage approach.

Simple agreements with many countries. These set the accounting rules and confirm which credit types are eligible, with few extra conditions. They give Europe a broad supply base.

Deeper partnerships with the most promising countries. These combine climate policy commitments, development finance and large-scale crediting programs.

Europe can anchor these in partnerships it already has, such as the new Clean Trade and Investment Partnerships. A public roadmap of what the EU expects from partners’ national climate plans could help countries see how to move from the first stage to the second.

Think big on supply

Individual projects alone won’t deliver enough high-integrity credits at the scale Europe needs. The paper points to three larger-scale options:

buying allowances from emissions trading systems abroad that have binding caps

jurisdictional forest programs, such as those certified under ART-TREES

bilateral agreements on actual programs for decarbonization in countries that need financial support and capacity building to succeed with their clean energy transition.

Crediting at this scale also helps with integrity. Counting reductions across a whole sector or jurisdiction makes it harder to credit emissions cuts that would have happened anyway.

Set a clear test for host countries

The paper suggests three questions for deciding who Europe buys from:

Legal: Is the country eligible to trade under Article 6?

Policy: Is its national climate plan ambitious, and does selling credits help it meet that plan or make it harder?

Political: Is it a suitable partner for the EU?

Team up with other buyers and use the whole toolbox

Europe plans to buy credits for five years: 2036 to 2040. That is too short a window to finance most projects, which deliver credits over 10 to 15 years or more. Shared quality standards with other buyers would give suppliers a bigger, longer-lasting market. The Open Coalition on Compliance Carbon Markets, which the EU co-chairs, is a natural forum for that work.

Credit revenue is also only one of Europe’s tools. Its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), trade agreements, product rules and clean-industry partnerships may give it more influence over large emitters. Presented as one coherent offer, they can do far more together than credit purchases alone.

A new idea: pay for future ambition

The paper also puts forward a new idea. There is a cost that today’s carbon accounting ignores. When a country sells credits now, it uses up some of its cheapest emissions reductions. That makes its own future targets harder and more expensive to hit.

The paper proposes making part of a credit deal’s value depend on how ambitious each side’s next national climate plan is. These plans are known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). The idea borrows from sustainability-linked bonds, like those Chile and Uruguay issued in 2022. Their interest rates rise or fall depending on whether climate targets are met.

Applied to credits, it works both ways:

Host countries would be rewarded for raising targets in the sectors that generated the credits.

Buyers would pay more if credits start replacing their own domestic emissions cuts beyond an agreed limit.

The paper sets out five ways to do this, from simple to complex:

An escrow that holds 15–30% of the credit price until the host’s next NDC meets agreed criteria.

An ambition-linked sovereign bond issued by the host and backed by the buyer.

A buyer commitment to pay the host if the buyer overuses credits or misses its own domestic path.

A reserve of credits the host keeps only if it meets its ambition goals. Otherwise they are canceled.

A pooled facility run through a multilateral development bank, which spreads risk and acts as a neutral verifier.

The timing matters. Countries are due to submit their next NDCs in 2030. Deals struck in the next few years will fall right in that window.

Getting the design right, now

Europe’s credit purchases will be small next to its domestic climate effort. But the choices it makes in the coming months will shape markets far beyond its borders. They will signal what high-quality credits look like, who gets to sell them and what buyers owe in return.

Progress beats perfection here. Europe can start with a workable system and strengthen it over time. That means simple agreements to get started, deeper partnerships where they can deliver, supply at real scale and payments that reward rising ambition.

COP31 is a chance to test these ideas with partner countries. The Commission’s proposal in December is a chance to build them into law. Built this way, EU credit purchases could pay for ambition as well as tons.

title: Why Now Is the Moment for Electric Mobility in the Philippines - RMI
description:
In March 2026, the Philippines experienced a stark reminder of the risks of a fossil fuel-dependent energy and transportation system.
Transportation is at the center of the Philippines’ energy challenge Transportation is fundamental to everyday life and economic activity in this archipelago of more than 7,000 islands.
Electric mobility can address several Philippine priorities at once Transportation electrification offers one way to reduce that dependence.
For some vehicle use cases, electric vehicles (EVs) can also lower the cost of owning and operating a vehicle.
Electric mobility is emerging across a wide range of applications, from motorcycles and passenger cars to commercial fleets, jeepneys, and buses.
text:
In March 2026, the Philippines experienced a stark reminder of the risks of a fossil fuel-dependent energy and transportation system. As global energy markets were disrupted in March 2026 due to rising geopolitical tensions, fuel prices rose sharply across the country. By early April, regular gasoline prices in Metro Manila had risen nearly 80% compared to late February, reaching as high as ₱94.50 per liter (about US$5.6/gallon), while diesel rose by 150% to a high of ₱153.70 per liter (about US$9/gallon), according to the Department of Energy NCR price monitoring.

This increase affected all types of Philippine vehicle users. Public transport operators faced rapidly increasing fuel bills. The government provided emergency support to jeepney (the most popular form of public transportation) and tricycle drivers, among others, while bus operators warned that rising diesel costs were becoming increasingly difficult to absorb. Eventually, fare increases shifted some of those costs to commuters. Higher fuel prices also raised the cost of moving goods and food across the country. In the province of Benguet, the cost of transporting vegetables for farmers reportedly tripled during the height of the crisis.

The events of 2026 may be exceptional; however, the vulnerability they expose is not. Fortunately, electrifying transportation offers one solution to address this vulnerability.

Transportation is at the center of the Philippines’ energy challenge

Transportation is fundamental to everyday life and economic activity in this archipelago of more than 7,000 islands. Every day, millions of Filipinos rely on jeepneys, tricycles, buses, motorcycles, cars, ferries, and commercial vehicles to get to work, school, and other destinations, and to move goods between communities.

Keeping this system running depends mostly on petroleum. Transport accounts for approximately two-thirds of the Philippines’ oil consumption, which is overwhelmingly imported. This creates a direct connection between international energy markets and the cost of moving people and goods within the country. When global oil prices rise, the consequences therefore do not stop at the pump: they affect the economics of operating a jeepney or delivery fleet, the cost of commuting, and the price of food and other goods.

The government can (and during the 2026 crisis did) provide relief through fuel subsidies, price controls, and other measures, which are important to manage immediate impacts. But short-term solutions are not enough. Reducing the country’s exposure to fuel prices shocks long term requires reducing transportation’s dependence on petroleum itself.

Electric mobility can address several Philippine priorities at once

Transportation electrification offers one way to reduce that dependence. Replacing petroleum with electricity can reduce the transportation sector’s direct exposure to oil markets and allow vehicles to draw energy from a more diverse (and increasingly domestically generated) energy system.

However, energy security is only one part of the opportunity. For some vehicle use cases, electric vehicles (EVs) can also lower the cost of owning and operating a vehicle. Electricity can be cheaper and less volatile than gasoline or diesel, while electric drivetrains are generally more energy efficient and require less maintenance. These savings can be particularly important for vehicles that travel frequently, allowing operating cost savings to accumulate quickly.

Electrification can also improve local air quality by eliminating tailpipe emissions. This is particularly valuable in dense urban areas and along busy transportation corridors, where large populations are regularly exposed to traffic-related pollution. EVs alone will not solve all of the Philippines’ air quality challenges while fossil fuels remain part of the electricity mix, but transportation is a major source of pollution the country can directly address while continuing to increase renewable energy production.

Finally, the transition creates an economic opportunity. A growing EV market requires not just vehicles, but charging infrastructure, batteries and components, software, and a skilled workforce for maintenance and servicing. Developing more of these capabilities domestically could allow the Philippines to capture a greater share of the investment and jobs created by the transition.

Electrifying transport is therefore not just a climate strategy: it can simultaneously support energy security, lower operating costs, create healthier communities, and spur industrial development.

The foundations for deployment are taking shape

The Philippines is now at a decisive implementation phase — far ahead of where it was just a few years ago. Multiple national policy initiatives have set the direction:

The Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act (EVIDA) established a national framework for EV development

The Comprehensive Roadmap for the Electric Vehicle Industry (CREVI) has translated that framework into targets and actions across vehicle adoption, charging infrastructure, manufacturing, and other enabling conditions

The Electric Vehicle Incentive Strategy (EVIS) has strengthened incentives for investment and domestic manufacturing.

Industry is also responding: a larger number of EV models are being offered by the market, charging providers are growing and their networks are expanding, and domestic and international companies are investing across the EV value chain.

Consumer interest is growing as well, with EV registrations reaching 60,906 in 2025, a 2.5-fold increase from 2024. Electric mobility is emerging across a wide range of applications, from motorcycles and passenger cars to commercial fleets, jeepneys, and buses.

However, piecemeal growth in the EV ecosystem does not indicate that the market is yet capable of deploying EVs at scale. Though sales are growing, EVs still account for only about 0.4% of the overall Philippine vehicle fleet; charging infrastructure growth is concentrated in larger cities and dense locations; and financing remains difficult to access for many potential buyers. Additionally, vehicle availability, after-sales service, and technical capacity vary widely.

Lower lifetime costs can make EVs attractive to users, particularly where savings on fuel and maintenance can offset the higher up-front cost of the vehicle. However, favorable lifetime economics do not necessarily make EVs affordable today. For high-utilization vehicles, these operating savings can accumulate relatively quickly and strengthen the case for investing in an EV. In contrast, where utilization is lower or revenues are uncertain, savings may take longer to materialize and may not be sufficient to support higher financing payments. This is particularly relevant for public transport operators, where targeted government support and financing mechanisms can help bridge the gap between up-front costs and the operating savings that electrification can provide.

Sustained implementation of initiatives aimed at addressing these limitations requires coordination among national agencies, local governments, utilities, financial institutions, vehicle suppliers, charging providers, and transportation operators. While the Philippines has established many foundations for EV deployment at the national level, success will depend on making those pieces work together.

From building the market to scaling it

This does not, however, mean all vehicle types in the Philippines must be electrified at once. Different transportation use cases have very different economics and needs. A private motorcycle owner, delivery rider, jeepney cooperative, ride-hailing driver, and bus operator travel different distances, buy and finance vehicles differently, and have very different access to charging. Some applications are therefore much closer to being ready for electrification than others, in terms of operating and capital economics as well as operational feasibility.

The near-term opportunity is to identify where the economics, financing, charging, and operating conditions are already closest to alignment, and focus action on the specific barriers preventing those markets from growing. This could amount to converting successful pilots into repeatable fleet deployments and procurement models; developing financing approaches that allow buyers to benefit from EV operating savings; planning charging infrastructure around where vehicles are likely to be operated; and incorporating EV demand forecasts into electricity grid planning. In parallel, this will require translating national policy into clearer implementation pathways for agencies, local governments, businesses, and investors.

The 2026 energy crisis made the costs of petroleum dependence unusually visible, but it also comes at a time when the Philippines has more tools than ever to address that vulnerability. Transportation electrification has the policy support and national momentum it needs and is already proving its value to a wide range of consumers. The opportunity now is to translate that momentum into implementation.

text:
Announced strategic sale of the non-utility DTE Vantage business, advancing DTE's long-term strategy and continued focus on customer affordability

Google data center contracts approved, advancing responsible data center growth that delivers unprecedented affordability benefits to existing customers

Continued substantial investment to improve reliability, support cleaner generation; on track to invest $6.1 billion into its utilities in 2026

Filed Integrated Resource Plan for future power generation

Expanded Michigan-made renewable energy, completing Cold Creek Solar Park

Delivered progress toward a cleaner, more reliable and affordable energy future

DETROIT, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DTE Energy (NYSE: DTE) has entered into an agreement to sell its non-utility DTE Vantage business1 for approximately $3 billion to institutional investors advised by the Global Infrastructure group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, with the sale expected to close in the first half of 2027. The transaction advances DTE's long-term strategy and continued focus on customer affordability, while strengthening its ability to make significant utility investments that deliver affordable, clean and reliable energy for the customers and communities it serves. It supports a substantial increase in investment in the electric and gas utilities, which will total approximately $44 billion of customer-focused capital planned over the next five years. This includes investment to serve growing data center demand, which provides significant affordability benefits for existing customers.

The company has invested nearly $4.1 billion in its utilities through the third quarter of 2026 and remains on track to invest $6.1 billion this year as part of its long-term plan to meet Michigan's growing energy needs. The capital investments are strengthening and modernizing the company's electric and natural gas systems and supporting the transition to cleaner power generation, helping deliver safer, cleaner, more reliable and more affordable energy for customers today while preparing Michigan's energy infrastructure for continued growth.

The company also reported third quarter earnings of $470 million or $2.25 per diluted share, compared with $419 million, or $2.01 per diluted share in 2025. Operating earnings for the third quarter 2026 were $481 million, or $2.30 per diluted share, compared with 2025 operating earnings of $468 million, or $2.25 per diluted share. Operating earnings exclude non-recurring items, certain mark-to-market adjustments and discontinued operations. Reconciliations of reported earnings to operating earnings are included at the end of this news release.

"DTE Vantage has been a strong non-utility business and valued part of DTE Energy for more than 30 years," said Joi Harris, DTE president and CEO. "This transaction advances our strategy to focus our resources on our regulated electric and gas utilities, where we see significant opportunities to invest on behalf of customers and communities. The sale supports our plan to deliver meaningful affordability benefits for customers, strengthens our ability to execute a substantial utility investment plan and positions DTE as a high-growth, premium utility with a stronger long-term outlook."

Harris noted the following accomplishments:

Advanced responsible data center growth that delivers unprecedented affordability benefits to existing customers: Following the Michigan Public Service Commission's approval of DTE's energy contracts with Google for its planned data center in Van Buren Township, DTE is moving forward to serve two hyperscale data center customers in Michigan. These agreements are expected to deliver significant affordability benefits for DTE customers, with data centers covering the full cost of the energy and grid investments needed to serve them, while contributing billions of dollars to the electric system through 2045. These contributions will help reduce the amount needed from existing customers while supporting economic growth and cleaner energy. Michigan is uniquely positioned to lead the country in responsible data center development, supported by strong regulatory oversight, clear laws and additional safeguards in DTE's service contracts that protect customers.

Filed Integrated Resource Plan for future power generation: DTE Electric filed its 20-year plan with the Michigan Public Service Commission to deliver reliable and cleaner energy, while keeping customer bills as low as possible. Shaped by extensive customer input, the Integrated Resource Plan calls for a balanced mix of renewable energy, energy storage, nuclear and natural gas. It also maintains DTE's commitment to end coal use in 2032, reduces carbon dioxide emissions by 84% and is projected to cost $3.5 billion less than the company's previous IRP.

Partnered with Ford Motor Company to expand Michigan-made renewable energy: Through Ford's participation in DTE's MIGreenPower program, DTE completed the 100-megawatt Cold Creek Solar Park near Coldwater, advancing Ford's goal to assemble every vehicle made in Michigan with the equivalent of 100% carbon-free electricity by the end of 2027, while creating local jobs, generating tax revenue for the host community and bringing more Michigan-made renewable energy to the grid.

Delivered progress toward a cleaner, more reliable and affordable energy future: DTE's 2025 Sustainability Report details the company's work to strengthen the grid, expand renewable energy and support customers and communities. At year-end 2025, DTE operated 20 wind parks and 34 solar parks, generating enough energy to power more than 900,000 homes. The company also kept customer bills below regional and national averages and connected customers with nearly $125 million in energy assistance.

Outlook for 2026 and 2027

DTE Energy confirms 2026 operating EPS guidance of $7.59 to $7.73. DTE Energy also provided a 2027 operating EPS pro forma baseline2 range of $7.59 - $7.73, which reflects the DTE Vantage asset sale.

"Strong financial performance through the third quarter of 2026 positions us to continue investing in Michigan's energy infrastructure while delivering long-term value for our customers, communities and shareholders," said David Ruud, DTE vice chairman and CFO.

Advisors to DTE Vantage Transaction

Lazard is acting as exclusive financial advisor to DTE Energy, and Kirkland & Ellis LLP is acting as legal advisor to DTE Energy.

Footnote (1): Includes the sale of primarily all DTE Vantage assets, except EES Coke

Footnote (2): Reflective of closing the Vantage transaction by year-end 2026 and is subject to change based on impacts from discontinued operations, actual closing timing and the timing of deployment of sale proceeds

title: The Economics of Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels - EPIC - The University of Chicago
description:
First, fossil fuels are too cheap because prices do not reflect the damage they cause, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
These two market failures will need separate policy solutions: carbon pricing to accurately reflect the full cost of fossil fuels, and increased public investment and subsidies for clean innovation.
Carbon pricing is spreading, but it is not enough to meet climate goals on its own.
Lower clean technology costs are necessary but not sufficient to ensure diffusion of clean energy.
International development banks and trade organizations should provide preferential loans to encourage the adoption of clean energy and facilitate the lowering of trade barriers.
text:
At COP28 in Dubai, 198 countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) in energy systems “in a just, orderly and equitable manner” (UNFCCC 2024). The COP30 Presidency has developed a roadmap of concrete actions towards this goal, with contributions from UNFCCC Parties and non-Party stakeholders (UNFCCC 2026). This report contributes to the COP30 TAFF Roadmap by outlining the climate risks associated with fossil fuel use, the key market failures hindering the clean energy transition, and potential policy solutions to overcome them.

Our central message is simple. First, fossil fuels are too cheap because prices do not reflect the damage they cause, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Second, innovation in renewables is underfunded despite their role in lowering the price of clean energy. This is because innovators only consider their private gains from innovation, not the global returns. These two market failures will need separate policy solutions: carbon pricing to accurately reflect the full cost of fossil fuels, and increased public investment and subsidies for clean innovation.

Climate damages are large and unequal. Each additional tonne of carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted today causes an estimated $336 of damages worldwide over its lifetime (Carleton, Greenstone, et al. 2026). These damages are not shared equally, with the majority concentrated in hot lower-income regions that have contributed the least to historical emissions.

The world is on track for 3°C warming by end of century. Our modeling suggests the world is on track for roughly 3°C warming by 2100—far above the 1.5–2°C Paris target, and consistent with broader projections of 2.8–3.2°C, under current policies (IPCC 2023; UNEP 2025b; Larsen et al. 2023).

Carbon pricing is spreading, but it is not enough to meet climate goals on its own. Carbon taxes and emissions trading systems now cover approximately 29% of global greenhouse gas emissions, at an average price of roughly $21 per tonne (World Bank 2026b). Averaged across all emissions, priced and unpriced, this is only roughly $6.3 per tonne. Even under an ambitious and nearly politically unimaginable scenario of a global carbon tax of $50, rising 3% annually that covers all emissions, we find a 2100 temperature change of 2.2 °C. Carbon pricing on its own is unlikely to limit temperature increases to targeted levels.

Innovation policy is climate policy. The prices of green technologies are coming down, with the cost of solar PV panels falling 90% in the last 15 years (Figure 11). Falling renewable energy costs avoided approximately 1 Gt of GHG emissions in 2024. If clean energy prices continue to fall as they have over the last fifteen years, our model suggests 2100 warming of 2.5°C, without any carbon pricing. Local supply-side subsidies for renewables in China account for roughly half of the fall in solar PV prices; the Chinese experience illustrates how public support can enable private firms to innovate and cut costs (Banares-Sanchez et al. 2026).

Robust innovation policy and carbon pricing gets us to below 2°C. Neither feasible levels of carbon pricing nor innovation can deliver the Paris goals on their own. Our modeling suggests that if renewable costs keep falling at the recent pace, combined with a carbon price (starting at $50 per tonne and rising by 3% a year), warming would be approximately 1.9°C. If we take the final year of our data (2024), implemented carbon taxes and emissions trading systems deliver about 0.6 Gt CO2e of avoided emissions, while falling renewable costs, by contrast, have avoided 1 Gt in the same year, making it clear that both instruments are necessary to achieve climate goals.

What can countries do

Price carbon widely and at meaningful levels. A carbon price can be applied to high-emitting sectors, particularly energy, transport and polluting industries, before widening to land-use and other sectors of the global economy as measurement and verification methods mature. Whether applied as a tax or as a cap-and-trade market, it is important that the effective price of carbon is transparent and placed on a clear and increasing trajectory in and across as much of the global economy as is feasible. Given that 86% of GHG emissions over the remainder of the century will come from outside the OECD, it is necessary to design deals that incentivize the adoption of carbon pricing and markets in these countries.

Fund clean innovation, with a focus on the next wave of technologies. Public research and development subsidies should be directed towards leading-edge existing, as well as next-generation, clean energy technologies, including grids and storage that can speed diffusion and support future energy demands. The case for support is simple: if innovation makes clean energy cheap enough, the need for costly regulation diminishes—markets do the work instead.

Aid diffusion of clean energy. Lower clean technology costs are necessary but not sufficient to ensure diffusion of clean energy. Current fossil fuel subsidies, which act as a negative carbon tax, should be phased out. International development banks and trade organizations should provide preferential loans to encourage the adoption of clean energy and facilitate the lowering of trade barriers. This would allow greater investments in these technologies in emerging markets and developing countries (EMDEs), accelerating their diffusion and helping to reduce global emissions, thus benefiting all countries.

title: Opinion | Climate Action Collaborative: Training the clean energy workforce | VailDaily.com
description:
About one-third of Colorado’s clean energy jobs are in construction or manufacturing.
“While solar and wind often get the spotlight as the dominant clean energy sectors, cost-effective energy efficiency has been an anchor and continues to be a driving force behind Colorado’s clean energy growth,” said Patricia Rothwell, executive director of the Energy Efficiency Business Coalition, a statewide trade association.

“Energy Smart Colorado and our partners rely on our skilled clean energy workforce to offer home energy assessments, support households embarking on retrofit projects, and encourage electrification,” said Karlok.
By expanding career pathways, apprenticeships, and hands-on training, local colleges, businesses, governments and nonprofits help prepare workers for the clean energy transition.
text:
Did you know that the clean energy industry accounts for more than 70 percent of all energy and vehicle-related jobs in the state? According to E2’s Clean Jobs Colorado report, Colorado ranked 18th nationally for clean energy employment in 2024 with nearly 70,000 jobs, more than twice the number of fossil fuel jobs in the state. About one-third of Colorado’s clean energy jobs are in construction or manufacturing.

“While solar and wind often get the spotlight as the dominant clean energy sectors, cost-effective energy efficiency has been an anchor and continues to be a driving force behind Colorado’s clean energy growth,” said Patricia Rothwell, executive director of the Energy Efficiency Business Coalition, a statewide trade association.

In 2025, the State of Colorado released aClimate Workforce Analysis & Plan to forecast the workforce needed to achieve the state’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2050. The report identified 20 climate-critical occupations, ranging from automotive service technicians and mechanical and electrical engineers to firefighters, foresters, and heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration (HVACR) mechanics and installers. It also highlighted a challenge for rural communities: access to training can be limited when programs are concentrated along the Front Range.

Our region’s need for clean energy jobs

What does this mean for our region? To meet our local Climate Action Plan goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions 50% by 2030 and reaching 100% net zero by 2050, we need to significantly reduce the energy used by our buildings. Strategies include building to higher efficiency standards, reducing embodied carbon in construction materials, electrifying buildings where feasible, powering them with renewable energy, and retrofitting existing homes and businesses.

Achieving these goals requires a skilled workforce including construction workers, electricians, plumbers, and contractors. We need workers who can weatherize homes and businesses, install energy-efficient heating and cooling systems, and help make our buildings more comfortable and affordable to operate.

Fortunately, Colorado Mountain College (CMC) is helping meet this need by expanding training opportunities in the skilled trades.

Under the leadership of Jim Jones, CMC’s program director for skilled crafts and trades, the college has significantly expanded its skilled trades program in recent years. In 2025, voters approved a ballot measure supporting continued investment in skilled-trades training and other community-priority professions. This funding helps grow the workforce in high-demand fields while retaining local talent. Jones has also secured grants to purchase equipment and expand hands-on training.

CMC’s skilled trades program offers a range of training for careers in HVAC, automotive service technology, carpentry, welding, and ski area operations. Demand for these programs has been strong, prompting Jones to expand training capacity across additional CMC campuses.

Local apprenticeships provide options for students

Tim Braun, vice president of operations at R&H Mechanical, partnered with Jones to launch an HVAC apprenticeship program in the Valley. R&H offers CMC’s curriculum and hosts classes at its training facility in Eagle. More than 50 students are enrolled, with R&H staff serving as adjunct instructors.

“Students are gaining knowledge more quickly, which has allowed R&H to support clients and the community faster. Overall, it’s been a great fit,” Braun said.

Apprenticeships offer a practical pathway for people looking to develop technical skills while building a rewarding career. Braun and Jones regularly talk to high school students about the skilled trades program and apprenticeships. Several high schools offer core classes that are prerequisites for taking advanced trade courses. Jones hopes to strengthen school partnerships and welcomes opportunities to work with businesses that want to establish an apprenticeship.

The Vail Valley Partnership, Eagle County, and CMC also joined forces over the past year to convene a Talent Pipeline Management group for local HVAC and mechanical systems employers. The group met over several months to discuss job requirements, training curriculums, and how to recruit local residents interested in careers in the trades.

That collaboration helped the Vail Valley Partnership and Vail Valley Works secure state approval for an HVACR TechnicianRegistered Apprenticeship Program . Through the program, local businesses can apply for incentive funding to help offset the costs of establishing and delivering apprenticeship training.

“One of the best outcomes has been increased community awareness and discussion about the importance of the HVAC trades to our community,” said Erin McCuskey, economic resiliency manager at Eagle County.

Maren Cerimele, vice president of strategic initiatives at the Vail Valley Partnership, echoed that sentiment, adding that the initiative has also raised awareness of the workforce development resources already available in the community.

Other training collaborations

Earlier this month, Blue Sky Training brought amobile heat pump training lab to Eagle County, providing 10 local HVAC workers with hands-on training. The effort was made possible through a collaboration between Blue Sky, Energy Smart Colorado, Walking Mountains, the Community Office for Resource Efficiency (CORE) and Eagle County. Bringing specialized training directly to the region helps local professionals build new skills without having to travel elsewhere for instruction.

Energy auditing is another area of workforce need. Many incentives for high-efficiency equipment and systems require a home energy assessment before rebates can be awarded, making qualified energy auditors essential to helping residents access these programs.

To help build this workforce, Emma Karlok, workforce development manager at Energy Smart Colorado (ESC), developed acareer resource webpage outlining clean energy career pathways, including energy auditing, and the technical certifications required to conduct home energy assessments. Training is available online, and candidates can take proctored exams at the Northwest Colorado Council of Governments’ Building Performance Institute Test Center in Gypsum.

“Energy Smart Colorado and our partners rely on our skilled clean energy workforce to offer home energy assessments, support households embarking on retrofit projects, and encourage electrification,” said Karlok. “ESC invests in building up our local workforce through training, technical resources, and financial support to current and future contractors.”

Attracting the next generation of climate champions

A strong clean energy workforce supports local economic development while helping our region meet its climate goals. By expanding career pathways, apprenticeships, and hands-on training, local colleges, businesses, governments and nonprofits help prepare workers for the clean energy transition. With continued collaboration, our community can create rewarding career opportunities while building a more sustainable and resilient future.

Kim Burke is the Director of Climate Strategy for the Climate Action Collaborative with Walking Mountains. The Climate Action Collaborative is working to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Eagle County 50% by 2030 and 80% by 2050.

title: LSE Consulting report highlights need for EU/UK partnership to address global automotive race
description:
The report, Strategic Cooperation: UK–EU Automotive Value Chains Amid Global Challenges, finds that the global automotive industry’s focus is shifting towards China, while manufacturers in the UK and Europe face mounting pressures from the transition to electric vehicles, geopolitical competition and rising production costs.
The two markets are each other’s top automotive trading partners, and the UK is the EU’s largest parts export market, ahead of the US and China.
Deeper cooperation and coordination can turn this relationship into a strategic asset to help both sides secure future investment, jobs and industrial leadership in the transition to electric vehicles.
Providing stable, long-term investment frameworks, alongside better charging infrastructure, competitive energy costs and measures to support demand for electric vehicles.
The report was prepared by the Trade Policy Hub, part of LSE Consulting, for the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) and the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).
text:
The UK and European Union must strengthen cooperation on trade, batteries and critical raw materials to protect their automotive industries in the face of geopolitical challenges and reap the opportunity of deeper strategic cooperation, according to a new report from LSE Consulting.

The report, Strategic Cooperation: UK–EU Automotive Value Chains Amid Global Challenges, finds that the global automotive industry’s focus is shifting towards China, while manufacturers in the UK and Europe face mounting pressures from the transition to electric vehicles, geopolitical competition and rising production costs.

The research argues that, although these challenges are driven by global developments, the closely integrated EU-UK automotive relationship remains one of the most important levers available to policymakers to strengthen the industry's competitiveness and resilience. The two markets are each other’s top automotive trading partners, and the UK is the EU’s largest parts export market, ahead of the US and China. Deeper cooperation and coordination can turn this relationship into a strategic asset to help both sides secure future investment, jobs and industrial leadership in the transition to electric vehicles.

Professor Riccardo Crescenzi, Professor of Economic Geography at LSE and lead academic on the report, commented: “This report shows why decisions taken on either side of the Channel affect firms, workers and suppliers on the other, and why a more coordinated approach is in both sides’ interests. The policy debate is moving quickly, often faster than the evidence available to inform it.

“Our contribution is to use data to show more clearly the scale and structure of these interdependencies, and the risks of treating the two systems separately. At this point in the evolution of EU–UK relations, stronger evidence is essential to designing policies that support investment, resilience and competitiveness across the wider European automotive sector.”

The report identifies dependence on batteries and critical raw materials as one of the most significant shared vulnerabilities. Despite an estimated €72 billion invested in European battery and electric vehicle manufacturing facilities since 2017, the EU still imports around two-thirds of the lithium-ion batteries it uses, while the UK has a smaller domestic battery manufacturing base.

This poses an immediate challenge ahead of changes to the rules of origin under the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA), due to take full effect on 1 January 2027. The report warns that neither side can assume it will have sufficient battery supply that meets the requirements to avoid tariffs by 2027. With the UK the EU’s largest battery electric vehicle (BEV) market, the issue should be treated as a shared challenge for both the EU and UK, with firms warning of potentially substantial additional costs if no mitigation is agreed.

Drawing on firm-level data covering 62 automotive business groups between 2014 and 2024, a survey of businesses across the automotive value chain, and interviews with industry executives and policymakers, the report sets out recommendations for a more coordinated UK-EU response.

The report's recommendations include:

Addressing the 2027 rules of origin together, including considering appropriate flexibility while developing a joint roadmap to expand battery manufacturing and supply-chain capacity.

Recognising UK content in EU origin and include UK content and vehicles in “Made in Europe” local-content rules, helping to protect integrated supply chains and avoid displacing production to other countries.

Providing stable, long-term investment frameworks, alongside better charging infrastructure, competitive energy costs and measures to support demand for electric vehicles.

Strengthening cooperation on critical raw materials, research and innovation, including investment in processing, recycling and the development of more resilient supply chains.

The report was prepared by the Trade Policy Hub, part of LSE Consulting, for the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) and the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).

text:
DTE Energy in Detroit has agreed to sell its non-utility DTE Vantage business for approximately $3 billion to institutional investors advised by the Global Infrastructure group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, with the sale expected to close in the first half of 2027.

DTE Vantage manages and operates 59 energy projects in 14 states and one Canadian province. It employs 600 team members across three core groups: Renewable Energy, Custom Energy Solutions, and Emerging Ventures.

According to DTE, the transaction advances the utility’s long-term strategy and continued focus on customer affordability, while strengthening its ability to make significant utility investments that deliver affordable, clean, and reliable energy for the customers and communities it serves.

“DTE Vantage has been a strong non-utility business and valued part of DTE Energy for more than 30 years,” says Joi Harris, president and CEO of DTE. “This transaction advances our strategy to focus our resources on our regulated electric and gas utilities, where we see significant opportunities to invest on behalf of customers and communities.

“The sale supports our plan to deliver meaningful affordability benefits for customers, strengthens our ability to execute a substantial utility investment plan, and positions DTE as a high-growth, premium utility with a stronger long-term outlook.”

The company says it has invested nearly $4.1 billion in its utilities through the third quarter of 2026 and remains on track to invest $6.1 billion this year as part of its long-term plan to meet Michigan’s growing energy needs.

The capital investments are said to be strengthening and modernizing the company’s electric and natural gas systems and supporting the transition to cleaner power generation, helping deliver safer, cleaner, more reliable, and more affordable energy for customers today while preparing Michigan’s energy infrastructure for continued growth.

The company also reported third quarter earnings of $470 million or $2.25 per diluted share, compared with $419 million, or $2.01 per diluted share in 2025. Operating earnings for the third quarter 2026 were $481 million, or $2.30 per diluted share, compared with 2025 operating earnings of $468 million, or $2.25 per diluted share.

DTE Energy confirms 2026 operating EPS guidance of $7.59 to $7.73. DTE Energy also provided a 2027 operating EPS pro forma baseline range of $7.59-$7.73, which reflects the DTE Vantage asset sale.

“Strong financial performance through the third quarter of 2026 positions us to continue investing in Michigan’s energy infrastructure while delivering long-term value for our customers, communities and shareholders,” says David Ruud, vice chairman and CFO of DTE.

title: The US and the EU Bet on the Wrong Race in Zambia - German Marshall Fund
description:
From increasing domestic processing to extending bilateral critical mineral agreements, both are looking to de-risk.
The initial reflex in Washington and Brussels has been to read de-risking as a race against China for access.
Connecting Copper China, Zambia’s largest export market for refined copper, relies on mineral transport corridors.
While the EU signed a strategic partnership MoU with Zambia in 2023, its broader Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) targets 40% domestic processing by 2030.
President Hakainde Hichilema, re-elected in August after a first term that did little to ease the cost of living, campaigned on turning Zambia’s copper deposits into jobs and prosperity.
text:
Copper runs through everything the world's largest economies are racing to build over the coming decade, including electricity networks, electric vehicles, and data centers. The vulnerability of these inputs lies not in the mines but in the middle of the value chain. China absorbs around 60% of global unrefined copper and produces around 50% of its refined output, a share that is increasing. For the United States and the EU, this dependency risk has prompted protective measures. From increasing domestic processing to extending bilateral critical mineral agreements, both are looking to de-risk.

Zambia holds some of the world’s largest copper reserves, putting it at the center of the wider contest for access to African minerals to secure supply chains.

The initial reflex in Washington and Brussels has been to read de-risking as a race against China for access. Their strategies have therefore concentrated on the first link of the chain: extraction and the corridors that carry its output to the coast. Zambia shows why this misses the target. China’s leverage lies not in mining but in refining, the stage that turns concentrate into usable metal, and refining is precisely what Zambia lacks the capacity and power to expand. To reduce their dependence on Chinese refining, Western partners must recognize that their interests converge with Zambia’s. Lusaka wants to move beyond extraction and will favor partners that invest in refining and the stages beyond it. Those that fund only mines and railways risk financing supply chains that still run through China.

Connecting Copper

China, Zambia’s largest export market for refined copper, relies on mineral transport corridors. The main example is the TAZARA railway, which links landlocked Zambian mines to Tanzania’s Indian Ocean coast. China helped build the line in the 1970s after Western lenders refused to finance it. Chinese firms are now set to upgrade it for $1.4 billion, ensuring a steady flow of copper to Chinese refineries and manufacturing centers.

In reaction, Washington and Brussels placed their interests in the Lobito Corridor, a revived old colonial rail line linking the DRC to Angola, refurbished through a loan from the US government's development bank. A new 800km greenfield line to connect Zambia is planned, but unlikely to carry freight before 2030. Western leaders often brand the Lobito Corridor as a game-changing counterweight to China, but the facts on the ground tell a far less binary story of the corridor’s success in de-risking.

At the same time, the domestic policies of the United States and the EU focus on bringing mineral processing back within their borders or closer to home, which sidesteps the urgent need for deeper partnerships with African producers. While the EU signed a strategic partnership MoU with Zambia in 2023, its broader Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) targets 40% domestic processing by 2030. Most refined supply will thus come from non-European sources. Yet the Act suggests no public de-risking mechanism designed for refining in African countries. In the United States’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), clean energy incentives were scrapped, which ended the electric-vehicle tax credits that drove investment in the copper supply chain, weakening Washington’s own demand signal.

What Zambia Is Building

Zambia’s own priorities point to the stage the West is neglecting. President Hakainde Hichilema, re-elected in August after a first term that did little to ease the cost of living, campaigned on turning Zambia’s copper deposits into jobs and prosperity. Mining is central to the country’s economy, representing 72% of its total foreign export earnings and contributing 9% of GDP. Lusaka is therefore building policies to move beyond the raw-export model and capture more value from its resources at home. To keep processing in the country, it levies a 10% export duty on unrefined copper concentrate. However, in a sign of how thin refining capacity remains, the duty has been waived since August 2025 while domestic smelters undergo repairs.

Corridors fit into this strategy, but where most see a corridor as a route out for raw materials, Zambia sees the industrial base it can build along it. Lower transport costs ensure that mines with higher onsite processing demands are commercially competitive and connect regional initiatives. For example, Zambia and the DRC agreed to establish special economic zones for battery-precursor manufacturing along the Lobito railway, which could allow entry into a new section of the supply chain.

This logic is part of a continental wave of value-addition restrictions, including Zimbabwe’s pioneer raw mineral restrictions—which resulted in the country’s first domestic lithium sulphate exports this year. Washington and Brussels should recognize that this shift operates on a different layer from access. It decides where processing happens, not who reaches the mine. Zimbabwe’s lithium sulphate was produced domestically, but in a facility owned by China’s Huayou Cobalt. By aligning with domestic policy, Beijing kept its place in the chain, secured the partnership, and reinforced its dominance.

The Power in Processing

Rather than aligning with any single power, Lusaka is using intensifying great-power rivalry as leverage for its own growth. China holds a structural head start, built over decades of investment in Zambia’s mines, railways, and energy infrastructure, and through off-take agreements with non-Chinese mines. This is a strategy the EU and the United States cannot replicate due to time constraints and fundamentally different market models. They should instead differentiate their offer by backing the priorities of Zambia’s National Critical Minerals Strategy (NCMS) and the African Green Minerals Strategy (AGMS), which emphasize ownership, co-industrialization, and electrification.

Energy is the biggest operating cost in refining. Recent IEA findings state that it accounts for 44% percent of total production costs in Africa. While the NCMS sets out frameworks for Zambia to claim economic ownership of its resources, energy remains its main vulnerability. Recently, drought-induced load shedding forced domestic smelters to shut down, and industry estimates suggest that at least 2,000 megawatts of new generation are needed to meet the country’s output target. Zambia is thus looking for partners to end its energy deficits.

On top of energy partnerships, new partnerships should be built through market access clauses. To send clearer signals to private investors, both should extend friend-shoring through critical mineral agreements that define eligibility by stage of transformation rather than by mine of origin, so that African-processed materials, such as Zambian refined copper cathode or battery precursors from the planned special economic zones, count as eligible inputs. The US-Zambia minerals agreement now under negotiation is an immediate test. Granting this market access would connect Western de-risking with Zambia’s pursuit of autonomy and growth.

What Zambia Reveals

When Washington initially attempted to leverage a $1.5 billion health aid package to secure preferential access to critical minerals, Lusaka pushed back, insisting that humanitarian aid and mineral rights be decoupled. The ultimate signing of a standalone health deal with mineral negotiations moved to a separate economic track shows how critical minerals can be treated to capture economic growth. African producers are negotiating stage by stage, pricing each concession against their own industrial plans. Partners who invest in the stage a producer wants to reach next will gain supply security as a by-product. For Washington and Brussels, resource security and African value addition can meet not only at the mine, but further up the value chain.

The views expressed herein are those solely of the author(s). GMF as an institution does not take positions.
