Tesla has opened a new engineering hub in Berlin, putting the teams that design and test its European parts about 30 minutes from the factory that builds them.

The Berlin Tesla Engineering Center, or BTEC, opened Wednesday in the Köpenick district. Tesla Europe said on X that the project went from permit to operational in under a year and consolidates four engineering sites and 30 labs onto a single campus. It is the company’s third hub of this kind, after Fremont and Shanghai.

“We’re combining materials, powertrain, vehicle engineering & validation under one roof, enabling a short feedback loop between development & ramp,” Tesla Europe wrote.

Tesla converted the former production halls of a cable factory for the site. About 250 engineers and technicians are starting there, most of them relocated from existing Tesla facilities such as Tilburg in the Netherlands. Tesla has already applied for approval of a second phase that would take the headcount to roughly 500, and it put the total investment at €100 million.

Advertisement

-

The labs cover battery cells, motors, materials and complete vehicles, and a large hall is set aside for safety testing of components, including airbags. During the opening, staff demonstrated a pedestrian leg impact test on the front of a Tesla using a catapult rig, Tagesspiegel reported. The center’s logo is a cubist Berlin bear that employees call the “Cybaer.”

Tesla said its Berlin design and engineering teams already contributed to the Model Y, Semi and Roadster, and that the work continues at BTEC. The center will handle technical problem solving for Giga Berlin in Grünheide while also developing and validating parts for vehicles built in China and the United States.

“We came here to stay,” BTEC head Brückner told dpa. “We serve all of Europe via Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg.” He said a site close to the plant was a priority, and that the old industrial building allowed Tesla to move quickly.

That proximity matters more now that Giga Berlin is growing again. In June, Tesla said it would raise Model Y output at the plant to 7,500 vehicles per week and hire 1,000 more workers after a record first quarter of more than 61,000 units. The factory recently built 7,000 Model Ys in a single week for the first time. Tesla also more than doubled the planned 4680 cell capacity at the site to 18 GWh per year in May, and has talked about eventually taking Grünheide to one million vehicles annually.

Sales are giving Tesla reason to invest. KBA data released the same day showed Tesla’s German registrations nearly quadrupled year over year in October to 2,932 units, bringing the total for the first ten months of 2026 to 47,742.

Ferrari’s first electric vehicle, the Luce, is fully sold out for 2027, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna.

Presenting third-quarter results, he stated: “Everything we plan to sell next year is already fully allocated. Client test drives, scheduled for next year, will help further boost demand. We have no critical issues, neither on manufacturing nor on the demand side. Obviously, the car is more complex because it has many new parts and many new technologies.”

First customer deliveries are expected before the end of 2026, with the model already commanding waitlists despite a turbulent debut.

The Luce is a five-seat, four-door liftback saloon—the longest Ferrari ever produced—powered by four electric motors producing approximately 1,035 horsepower.

It features an 800-volt architecture, a 122-kWh battery, a claimed WLTP range of around 329 miles, 0-62 mph acceleration in 2.5 seconds, and a starting price near €550,000 in Europe (roughly $560,800–$615,000 in the U.S. depending on configuration).

Developed in collaboration with Jony Ive and Marc Newson’s LoveFrom studio alongside Ferrari’s own Centro Stile, it represents a deliberate departure from the brand’s traditional mid-engine sports cars toward a more spacious, grand-touring format.

Its exterior has proven deeply polarizing. Unveiled in Rome in May 2026, the design features smooth, sweeping surfaces, a large glass roof, and restrained detailing that critics described as bland, generic, or more reminiscent of an Apple product or mass-market EV than a Ferrari.

Ferrari unveils its Luce EV, and its reception has been a disaster

Online reactions included memes comparing it to a Nissan Leaf or Polestar, while former Ferrari chairman Luca di Montezemolo publicly warned of “the destruction of a myth” and suggested the prancing horse logo be removed. Italian politicians and longtime owners joined the chorus of disappointment, and Ferrari’s shares dropped roughly 8% in a single day, erasing billions in market value.

Design experts noted the absence of the brand’s signature tension, aggression, and emotional drama.

Yet the controversy has not translated into weak demand among the ultra-wealthy clientele who actually buy Ferraris. Production volumes remain tightly limited, as reports suggest fewer than 500 units in the current year and a longer-term pace of roughly 600 annually through 2030, preserving exclusivity.

One early chassis sold for $40 million at auction. Vigna has indicated that seeing the car in person, along with upcoming client test drives, is expected to strengthen rather than weaken interest. Ferrari aims for fully electric models to comprise 20 percent of its lineup by 2030, with a second EV now delayed to 2028.

For a brand defined by scarcity and desirability, the Luce’s sell-out status suggests that among those who can afford it, the polarizing design has not proven to be a commercial liability.

Tesla and SpaceX shares fell on Wednesday after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress. The decline stood out as broader market securities recovered and turned positive, while both of Musk’s publicly traded companies lagged.

CEO Elon Musk already joked about the unsuccessful campaigning for the Republicans, but now the new party will make pretty drastic changes to how it handles Tesla and SpaceX, and those companies will adjust their outlook.

Elon Musk hilariously comments on Midterm election results

Let’s take a deeper look.

Tesla ($TSLA)

Tesla shares traded lower during the regular session after Democrats secured both the House and Senate. The stock was down 2.32 percent at around 1:45 p.m. on the East Coast, trading at around $389.30.

The pressure is tied to more than the raw scale of Musk’s political spending, estimated at $450–474 million this cycle with roughly $224 million directed at Texas. In that state, Tesla now faces a Democratic governor and a Democratic senator after Gina Hinojosa unseated Greg Abbott and James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton.

The Austin Gigafactory, Robotaxi pilot programs in multiple Texas cities, and any related AI compute expansion sit under a new state executive who campaigned against certain corporate subsidies and floated a moratorium on new data-center construction.

Federally, Democratic control of key committees opens the door to deeper examination of Tesla’s autonomous-driving safety record, federal energy-storage and manufacturing incentives, and the national-security implications of any combination with SpaceX.

Investors are also weighing whether the company’s historically close alignment with the prior Republican leadership will invite slower permitting, additional hearings, or tighter rules on Full Self-Driving deployment.

For Tesla, the political shift adds near-term friction around state permitting and federal regulatory approvals for autonomy and energy storage. A potential merger with SpaceX may face slower review even if it proceeds.

Core growth drivers such as vehicle deliveries, energy deployments, and robotaxi rollout remain intact, yet the stock now carries a higher political-risk premium that could weigh on valuation until the company demonstrates workable relationships with the new Texas leadership and congressional majorities.

SpaceX ($SPCX)

SpaceX shares also declined in live trading on November 4 following the Democratic midterm sweep. The stock traded at $134.97, down 4.49 percent. The drop occurred even as broader indexes stabilized, highlighting a company-specific reaction to the election outcome.

Musk’s large contributions, concentrated in Texas races that both companies lost, place SpaceX’s Starbase launch facility and headquarters under a new Democratic governor.

At the federal level, Democratic control of Congress enables greater scrutiny of NASA, the Department of Defense, and other contracts that support a meaningful share of revenue, along with reviews of Starlink national-security uses and any Tesla merger. Analysts have noted that empowered committees can hold hearings and request documents on these relationships.

For SpaceX, the results raise the risk of delayed contract awards, higher compliance costs, and tighter constraints on AI and satellite infrastructure expansion, particularly in Texas where a data-center moratorium has been discussed.

A merger with Tesla could encounter political friction that slows integration of launch, connectivity, and autonomy capabilities.

While Starlink growth and launch cadence continue as primary drivers, the company faces a more contested path for federal funding and state-level operations, requiring management to rebuild ties with the new congressional majorities and Texas leadership to limit the overhang.

title: More Money, New Problems? What's Next For Hawaiʻi In A Blue Congress - Civil Beat
description:
For the last two years, Hawaiʻi and its congressional delegation have been playing defense against President Donald Trump and a Republican-controlled Congress.
While there will be checks on what the Hawaiʻi delegation can accomplish, it will gain clout in numerous ways.
More Power, More Money Historically, Hawaiʻi’s congressional delegation has placed a premium on bringing home the bacon.
“I try to make sure that I understand politics as building alliances that help Hawaiʻi,” Schatz said.
It remains to be seen whether the Hawaiʻi delegation’s new clout in Congress will restore those dollars.
text:
Sen. Brian Schatz is likely to take the No. 2 spot in the Senate as Democrats pick up seats. Is trouble with the Trump administration on the horizon?

For the last two years, Hawaiʻi and its congressional delegation have been playing defense against President Donald Trump and a Republican-controlled Congress. The administration and its allies have attacked Native Hawaiian rights, various DEI programs, science and health grants to the University of Hawaiʻi and earmarks that might help Hawaiʻi shore up its cultural institutions, such as ʻIolani Palace.

That all changed Tuesday night, as Democrats surged back into power in a rebuke of Trump and the GOP, retaking both the House and Senate by significant margins. While there will be checks on what the Hawaiʻi delegation can accomplish, it will gain clout in numerous ways.

Hawaiʻi voters once again elected Democrats to Congress, and now they’ll be watching to see whether the blue wave will make a difference in addressing some of their top priorities, such as the state’s high cost of living, limited housing supply and ambitious goals to address climate change.

With their new power, the congressional delegation can bring home more appropriations and earmarks. Sen. Brian Schatz is poised to become Senate majority whip, the second most powerful player in that chamber. And, instead of working to ward off threats to Hawaiʻi, lawmakers can play offense, even though Democrats are already engaged in a fierce debate about how aggressive they should be.

Here’s what it means for Hawaiʻi – in four key areas.

More Power, More Money

Historically, Hawaiʻi’s congressional delegation has placed a premium on bringing home the bacon. That’s why U.S. Sen. Dan Inouye — often dubbed the King of Pork — was able to amass such power and influence.

With Democrats firmly in control of Congress come 2027, Hawaiʻi’s representatives will have even more say over how federal dollars are spent. Schatz and U.S. Rep. Ed Case both sit on their chambers’ respective appropriations committees and will be moving up the ranks. The all-Democratic delegation will also be primed to pump more money into the islands through earmarks which tend to favor the party in power in terms of size and magnitude.

Already, Case has said he’s looking forward to securing funding for one of Hawaiʻi’s crown jewels, ʻIolani Palace, which has not been eligible for federal earmarks with Republicans at the helm.

Like voters everywhere, those in Hawaiʻi went to the polls with deep anxieties about life under Trump – from concerns about affordability and the cost of living to worries about self-dealing and corruption in government to the threat of immigration raids.

Prices aren’t just going to drop just because Democrats are back in control of Congress, said Carl Bonham, economics professor and executive director of the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization. Lawmakers still need to figure out a way to end the war in Iran and get rid of Trump’s tariffs before anyone in the islands can start to realize any relief in their pocketbooks.

“It’s not a silver bullet,” Bonham said. “You voted out the culprits, but the new people in power can’t just go in and change things.”

Many Democrats want to use their new majorities in Congress to launch oversight investigations of Trump’s actions, including accusations of self-dealing.

While oversight is important, U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda said Democrats need to move with urgency to address Americans’ economic woes. Among the first moves, she said, should be to suspend the federal gas tax even if that means moving a discharge petition before Democrats officially retake the majority in January.

“It’s time for us to get shit done,” Tokuda said. “Don’t wait another day. The next day may not be better than the today that we have.”

Who Does No. 2 Work For?

The new majority bodes well for Schatz, who’s currently in line to become the majority whip, which would make him the second highest-ranking Democrat in the Senate behind Chuck Schumer. (That of course presumes Schumer holds on as majority leader.)

Hawaiʻi’s senior senator watched the results roll in from his home in Washington, D.C., and pretty quickly realized that voters are looking to Democrats to ease some of the pain they’ve been feeling whether at the gas pump or after losing their healthcare — or seeing its costs skyrocket.

He said the party’s top priorities should be ending the conflict in Iran and restoring Republican cuts to food stamps and Medicaid. Democrats will have to balance that policy work, he said, with the need for accountability and oversight of the administration.

“We don’t feel cocky about this,” Schatz said. “We don’t feel like this is some permanent realignment of American politics. This was a flat-out rejection of Trump, and now people are going to give our party a chance.”

“Democrats should be happy, should be proud, should be thankful,” he added. ”But we should also be humble about what this means. It’s not that people love us. It’s that people have decisively decided to give us a chance on the national scene, and now it is our job to be worthy of that trust.”

Schatz described his bid for majority whip as a continuation of his work building relationships in Washington so that he can better represent the islands. At just 54, he has a long career ahead of him assuming he continues to win reelection in a state where so far he has drawn little competition and courted almost no controversy. One day he could find himself first in line to replace Schumer, especially if Schatz sticks to his pledge not to run for president.

“I try to make sure that I understand politics as building alliances that help Hawaiʻi,” Schatz said. “So obviously if I’m in the room where decisions are being made a little more frequently that benefits Hawaiʻi and that’s the way I try to think about it.”

Dealing With Trump’s Executive Power

Case warned it would be a mistake to assume that just because Democrats have regained some power it will mean the “sky is rosy again.”

A Democratic majority might make his work easier in terms of earmarking funds for Hawaiʻi, he said, but it doesn’t erase the Trump administration’s policies or immediately reverse Republican cuts to federal food assistance programs and healthcare.

Democrats are already preparing a robust oversight agenda that will include scrutiny of Trump’s tariffs and his family’s financial dealings, which have resulted in billions of dollars in additional income for the president since returning to office. Case said that means residents should be prepared for a contentious two years.

“It’s going to be very ugly, very angry, very divided, which it already is,” Case said. “But since Democrats will have the bully pulpit, they will be amplifying that voice a lot more.”

But Democrats will be limited in what they can do.

A lot of the chaos caused during Trump’s second term was the result of executive action rather than something Congress did, whether it was unleashing ICE agents into communities or targeting university grants, so much of what comes next, Bonham said, will depend on whether Democrats can use what leverage they have over the purse strings to get Republicans on their side and negotiate with the president.

One thing is for sure – the delegation won’t have to spend as much political capital when it comes to protecting places such as the East-West Center or “dancing around DEI.” While the Trump administration can continue to target programs that promote diversity, equity and inclusion, Case said it will be a harder sell to a Democratic majority.

Regardless, Trump will remain an obstacle as will the Senate’s filibuster rules, which still require a 60-vote majority to move major legislation.

Trump has already said he’s open to working with Democrats, but whether he follows through is another matter. The president is unpredictable, said Colin Moore, a political scientist at the University of Hawaiʻi. While he might be constrained, he may not be undeterred.

“The president still has awesome powers and can move very quickly,” Moore said. “Congress, in many cases, can only react.”

Making Progress On A Cleaner Planet

Local environmentalists will be watching closely to see whether Tuesday’s blue wave might also jolt Hawaiʻi’s fight against climate change after two years of assault on those efforts.

The island state’s ambitious goals to fully ditch oil, gas and other fossil fuels — replacing them with local sources of renewable clean energy by 2045 — are in alignment with a mandate on Democrats to bring down costs, they say, particularly in the form of cheaper utility bills.

But Trump has used much of his second White House term to stymie that clean energy transition in Hawaiʻi and other states. The so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” he signed into law in 2025 phases out key federal tax credits that have helped erect both utility-scale and home rooftop solar systems across the country.

Attorneys with the environmental legal advocacy nonprofit EarthJustice hope the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress will swiftly pass legislation to restore the tax credits – and dare Trump to veto it as energy costs linked to oil and gas continue to climb.

“If we can get back on script focusing on clean energy, led by now the federal government and Congress, where that leadership totally evaporated in the first two years of the Trump administration that would be a huge swing back,” Honolulu-based Earthjustice attorney Isaac Moriwake said. “That would be felt all the way down to Hawaii as well.

In Hawaiʻi, the state under Gov. Josh Green created a task force last year to make sure the dozen or so utility projects already in the pipeline stayed on schedule and got the tax credits needed to finance them before they expired. Still, Moriwake said, others that had been planned were cancelled after the tax credit was killed.

Further, many of the federal dollars used for climate research in the islands have dried up under Trump’s second term, forcing researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi and other institutions to seek alternative grants and funding to keep their research afloat. Some of the funding lost under Trump 2.0 helped maintain the islands’ specialized network of weather monitoring stations, bolstering local climate resiliency.

It remains to be seen whether the Hawaiʻi delegation’s new clout in Congress will restore those dollars.

text:
Why it Matters

Schwab is nominated to fill the Environmental Protection Agency's assistant administrator post, which oversees the agency's air and radiation programs. The seat opened in October when Aaron Szabo departed the agency; Justin Schwab, then a senior adviser to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, was nominated to replace him. The Senate's decision to move forward with a confirmation hearing puts Schwab's record and views on air policy directly before lawmakers at a moment when the EPA's regulatory direction is under scrutiny. The Senate hearing is titled "Hearings To Examine The Nomination Of Justin Schwab, Of The District Of Columbia, To Be An Assistant Administrator Of The Environmental Protection Agency" and is scheduled for November 10. The hearing record lists no committee chair or ranking member, and the committee field carries no entry. ​

Broader Context

Inside EPA reported on November 3 that the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee had scheduled the November 10 hearing, and the committee's own notice confirms the date and subject. Schwab's nomination was sent to the Senate on September 28, and Szabo's October 6 departure established the leadership vacancy the nomination is meant to fill.

The hearing arrives as Congress and the public have focused attention on how the EPA's air office exercises its authority over emissions rules that affect public health, energy costs, and industrial compliance. A confirmed assistant administrator would be positioned to shape rulemakings that touch every sector of the economy subject to Clean Air Act requirements.

Lobbying disclosure records from the past 12 months contain no filings directly tied to Schwab's nomination or to EPA air and radiation policy; the available filings cover gaming, sports betting, telecommunications, college athletics, and District of Columbia issues.

The Bottom Line

The November 10 hearing is the next formal step toward filling a vacancy at the top of the EPA office responsible for the nation's air quality and radiation standards. If the committee advances Schwab's nomination, the full Senate would then vote on confirmation. Advocates, regulated industries, and environmental groups tracking Clean Air Act rulemakings should watch the hearing record closely, senators' questions will signal which regulatory priorities are likely to face the most scrutiny in the 119th Congress.

text:
By Jamie Martin

Renewable fuel advocates are supporting a new proposal from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that would restore renewable fuel requirements reduced by recent small refinery exemptions.

The Renewable Fuels Association says the proposal is an important step toward protecting the goals of the Renewable Fuel Standard, a program designed to increase the use of renewable fuels and support American energy production.

The EPA proposal would reallocate renewable fuel volumes that were waived through additional refinery exemptions. Supporters believe this action would help ensure renewable fuel targets are fully maintained and continue delivering benefits to agriculture and rural communities.

According to the association, the original purpose of refinery exemptions was to provide temporary assistance to facilities facing exceptional economic challenges. However, industry representatives argue that exemptions have expanded over time and have reduced renewable fuel demand.

“Congress intended small refinery exemptions to provide temporary relief to refiners facing genuine disproportionate economic hardship—not to become a permanent entitlement. Yet, EPA continues granting exemptions under a flawed scoring matrix, despite its own findings that refiners generally recover RIN compliance costs through wholesale fuel prices,” said RFA President and CEO Geoff Cooper.

He added, “These unwarranted exemptions undermine the integrity of the RFS, reduce renewable fuel demand, and discourage investment by renewable fuel producers, farmers, and retailers who have invested billions to support this program.”

RFA says maintaining strong renewable fuel requirements is important for protecting investments made by fuel producers, retailers, and farmers. Many agricultural businesses rely on a stable renewable fuels market because crops such as corn are key ingredients in ethanol production.

Supporters of the proposal believe full reallocation can help prevent future declines in renewable fuel demand. Without reallocation, compliance credits linked to exempted volumes may be carried forward into future years, reducing the need for newly produced renewable fuels.

Industry leaders say restoring these volumes will strengthen confidence in renewable fuel markets and support long-term investment throughout the biofuels supply chain. They believe consistent policies encourage innovation and growth while providing economic opportunities in rural regions.

The Renewable Fuel Standard has played a major role in expanding renewable fuel use across the United States. Supporters argue that protecting the program's targets is essential for maintaining market stability and ensuring continued progress in renewable energy development.

During discussions surrounding the proposal, renewable fuel advocates also emphasized the potential consumer benefits of expanded renewable fuel usage. They noted that renewable fuels can improve fuel supply diversity and offer affordable energy options for drivers.

The organization further stated that full reallocation would help preserve the environmental and economic objectives established under the Renewable Fuel Standard. Maintaining those objectives, advocates say, is important for both agriculture and the broader renewable energy industry.

Agricultural groups continue to watch developments closely because renewable fuel policies can directly affect crop demand and farm income. Strong demand for biofuel feedstocks often contributes to economic activity throughout farming communities.

The EPA will consider public input before making a final decision. If adopted, the proposal could help restore renewable fuel demand, support rural economic development, and reinforce the role of renewable fuels in the nation's energy future.

Renewable fuel advocates say the proposal represents an important opportunity to strengthen the Renewable Fuel Standard while supporting farmers, renewable fuel producers, and consumers across the country.

text:
Exit polls from the US midterm elections highlighted a key concern shaping voters’ decisions: energy affordability. Nearly 90% of voters said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, with many pointing to gasoline and utility costs. Meanwhile, as the AI data centre boom strains power supply and infrastructure, 56% said the issue was a crucial or major factor in their vote.

With Democrats now set to control both the House and Senate, what does this mean for US energy and data centre policy?

Newly elected lawmakers will face pressure to address these concerns, requiring the Democratic Congress and Republican White House to find common ground on shielding consumers from data centre-related costs and accelerating new power supply, including through permitting reform. Onshoring and supply chain protections are also likely to continue. While they can raise near-term costs, they remain important to US energy security. Developments in all three areas could have significant implications for businesses.

That said, Congress needs to strike a balance when drafting legislation aimed at achieving these goals. More aggressive measures could face a veto from President Trump.

The data centre industry is facing heightened local opposition. Recent polls suggest that around one in seven Americans is concerned about or opposes data centre development in their neighbourhoods.

In response to this issue, there is likely to be tighter data centre regulation. State-level policy will be more important to watch, as action is politically and practically easier at this level. The most likely approach is targeted regulation, much of which is already emerging. This includes data centre-related taxes, reduced tax incentives, environmental standards, and requirements for developers to bear relevant cost increases. Outright moratoriums remain unlikely to become mainstream. Where they are introduced, they are more likely to be temporary, giving states time to develop a data centre policy framework.

At the federal level, the key unanswered question is how much authority should remain with the states and whether federal legislation should mandate state regulations or simply provide guidance. Republicans generally favour letting states lead, while Democrats tend to support a stronger federal role.

We think sweeping data centre legislation is unlikely because of President Trump’s veto power. Federal action is more likely to focus on affordability by protecting electricity customers from higher costs and formalising data centres' responsibility to help fund grid and energy infrastructure upgrades. Such measures could be added to broader legislation, such as must-pass spending bills needed to avoid a government shutdown, or a bipartisan package like permitting reform.

More broadly on AI, we expect the Democratic Party to increase scrutiny of technology companies, as discussed here, while utilising the next two years to prepare an AI governance framework for 2028 and beyond.

However, tighter AI and data centre regulation is unlikely to fundamentally alter the industry’s growth trajectory. AI’s importance to US economic growth and competition with China will remain powerful drivers of expansion.

Both parties support timely expansion of electricity supply to meet rising demand from AI and manufacturing reshoring. They also generally agree that energy abundance can help reduce cost pressures. While Democrats and Republicans differ on the preferred energy mix, there is still common ground. Technologies likely to retain bipartisan support include nuclear, geothermal, carbon capture, and biofuels.

However, the greatest potential for policy action may lie not in specific technologies, but in permitting reform.

Today, many energy projects can spend over five years navigating the federal permitting process. Around $240bn to $280bn of infrastructure investment across the eight sectors below enters the permitting pipeline each year. Lengthy delays can therefore leave substantial capital tied up and project benefits unrealised.

With both parties recognising the need for reform, the Senate introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) in September 2026. Key permitting proposals include:

Speeding up approvals for energy projects

Providing greater certainty and consistency across administrations

Making it easier to permit power transmission lines

Despite debate over its environmental impact, there is broad agreement that the BAAJA would meaningfully improve the permitting process. The key question is whether it can become law under the current Congress. The Senate is expected to vote on 9 November, after which the bill would still need approval from the House and President Trump. Democrats may want to delay the bill and seek changes once they regain control of Congress next year, but doing so could increase the risk of a presidential veto. This creates an incentive to reach a deal sooner rather than later.

Even if the BAAJA does not pass under the current Congress, permitting reform is likely to remain a bipartisan theme. The growing need to expand power supply and infrastructure more quickly will keep pressure on future Congresses to streamline permitting.

This creates two key risks. First, heavy reliance on China leaves US industries vulnerable to geopolitical tensions. We have already seen this with rare earths, where Chinese export restrictions contributed to disruptions for US auto manufacturers. Second, China’s supply chain dominance can put US manufacturers at a competitive disadvantage.

Building more secure energy and natural resource supply chains has long attracted bipartisan support in the US. The Trump administration has supported domestic rare earth production through funding, purchase agreements, and equity investments. In solar, China-focused trade and tax credit restrictions are also supporting the expansion of domestic manufacturing.

We expect this focus to continue. The executive branch could pursue further protective measures and is unlikely to face major opposition from Congress. Congress could also authorise additional funding to strengthen rare earth supply chains.

Furthermore, a Democratic-controlled Congress could push to extend clean manufacturing tax credits as part of broader negotiations with President Trump. Given the administration’s focus on countering China and expanding US manufacturing, an extension could emerge as a compromise in a broader legislative package under an optimistic scenario. All these efforts would also extend into future administrations.

As Democrats won race after race in Texas on Tuesday, the man who spent more than anyone else to stop them sat silently for hours.

Shortly after midnight, Elon Musk finally weighed in — on the future of data centers in the Lone Star State.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa made reining in data center development a central issue of her campaign, calling for strict regulation of water and power usage, as well as local control of development.

“The Greg Abbott corruption tax is why data centers have descended upon Texas,” she told a cheering crowd in Houston last Saturday. “I will freeze electricity rates and make sure the corporations, including the data centers, pay their fair share.”

A spokesperson for Gov. Abbott did not respond to a request for comment.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

So what does an unprecedented Democratic sweep mean for Texas data centers?

Hinojosa’s election makes it more likely that an existing moratorium on new data center development will extend well into 2027, and that the upcoming legislative session will be defined by fights to curtail data centers’ water and power use, according to interviews with a dozen industry officials, including developers, investors, energy analysts and consumer advocates.

Most predicted that some projects will be cancelled, and others could leave Texas for greener regulatory pastures. But in all likelihood, observers agreed, the state will continue to be a national leader in data center development in the years to come.

“I think the calculus has shifted drastically for developers,” said Gordon Johnson, the chief operating officer of GLJ Research, an industry research firm. “It’s not the end, but you're gonna have delays and potential cancellations of data centers in Texas.”

What will the Legislature do?

One of the biggest questions facing the industry is what regulations will be proposed when the state Legislature — with a Democratic House and a Republican Senate — reconvenes in January.

Lt. Governor-elect Vikki Goodwin, who will preside over the Senate, has called for a special legislative session to pass data center regulations.

Joshua Rhodes, an energy research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin, said he expects to see proposals that require data centers to supply their own power and cover the costs of any new transmission lines, restrictions on their use of water and the end of tax incentives for the largest projects.

He noted that most of the biggest data center developers had already begun agreeing to cover their own costs in recent months, in response to political pressure from Abbott.

“My hope is that it's just a harsher sorting of the wheat versus the chaff,” Rhodes said of potential new regulations. “Right now you have a bunch of fly-by-night charlatans out there, ruining it for anyone who was maybe trying to do it better. ”

For now, the technology giants behind the data center buildout — including Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft — say they are willing to negotiate.

In a statement Wednesday, Jess Heck, the Texas Director of Government Affairs for the Data Center Coalition, the industry’s leading trade association, said they were looking forward to working with state leaders on “responsible data center growth.”

“The data center industry is committed to advancing America’s digital infrastructure, including here in the Lone Star State, as well as supporting energy reliability and affordability and promoting long-term, responsible economic development,” Heck said.

Krysti Shallenberger, a researcher with the Energy and Policy Institute, which advocates for ratepayers, said the legislative session is likely to be a chaotic, uncertain affair.

But Tuesday’s “regime change” would push politicians to make data centers cover their own costs, she said.

“There is a bipartisan mandate to really uphold your end of the bargain to ensure ratepayers are protected from costs from utilities over data center development,” Shallenberger said.

Will data centers leave Texas?

As developers processed the election results on Wednesday, some said they were committed to staying in Texas, while others said they would potentially seek out more welcoming environments in other states.

Brent Whitehead, the president of Houston-based data center developer Giga Energy, said the company’s development philosophy aligned with Hinojosa’s regulatory goals, and that they wanted to assist in drafting “responsible” regulations.

But that didn’t mean he wasn’t exploring other options.

“Moratoriums may lead to delays or projects relocating to other markets,” Whitehead wrote in an email. “Giga Energy will continue to diversify our projects into states that have not introduced moratoriums.”

Balaji Tammabattula, the CEO of BaRupOn, a California-based company that develops infrastructure for data centers, said that Abbott's moratorium had shocked the industry.

One of Tammabattula’s AI clients was considering investing in a large data center campus in Texas, he said, but after Abbott paused permitting, they decided to wait until after the election. Now, they’re planning to commit to North Dakota, he said.

description:
Chinese EV makers are intensifying their push into Korea.
As BYD, China's leading EV seller, expands sales, Zeekr, owned by second-ranked Geely, has entered the market.
Although the figure includes Teslas manufactured in China, it signals an unprecedented threat to Korea's automotive industry.
The United States and European Union have imposed steep tariffs on Chinese EVs.
If Korea's automotive industry loses competitiveness, the consequences will extend beyond the 1.5 million jobs it supports directly and indirectly.
text:
Chinese EV makers are intensifying their push into Korea. As BYD, China's leading EV seller, expands sales, Zeekr, owned by second-ranked Geely, has entered the market. Third-ranked Leapmotor and fourth-ranked Changan Automobile are preparing to follow, while Chery and Xpeng are also considering entry. Chinese-made vehicles accounted for 38.1 percent of newly registered EVs in Korea from January through September. Although the figure includes Teslas manufactured in China, it signals an unprecedented threat to Korea's automotive industry.

The challenge is equally evident overseas. According to a report released Wednesday by the Federation of Korean Industries, Korea's revealed comparative advantage index for EV exports fell from 3.02 in 2019 to 1.48 last year. China's index, meanwhile, surged from 0.19 to 1.49, surpassing Korea's for the first time. China has repeatedly advanced in strategic industries through a strategy of leapfrogging established technologies. Its weak landline infrastructure facilitated rapid adoption of mobile communications and smartphones, while its disadvantages in combustion-engine vehicles became strengths in EVs.

Korea must mobilize resources to defend its automotive competitiveness. The United States and European Union have imposed steep tariffs on Chinese EVs. Korea tightened its evaluation of EV subsidy applicants in July, excluding BYD from eligibility, but the company responded with discounts. Meanwhile, the government's August tax reform proposal excluded finished EVs from tax credits for domestic production. With several amendments to the Act on Restriction on Special Cases Concerning Taxation pending in the National Assembly, lawmakers should act promptly. Supporting domestic manufacturing and employment can no longer be dismissed simply as preferential treatment for conglomerates.

If Korea's automotive industry loses competitiveness, the consequences will extend beyond the 1.5 million jobs it supports directly and indirectly. Parts suppliers and regional economies dependent on the industry would also suffer.

Yet amid this mounting threat, production at Line 1 of Hyundai Motor's Ulsan Plant 5 was suspended for two days, Monday and Tuesday, over disagreements concerning workloads for trial vehicle production. Even if working conditions were involved, blocking trial production and shutting down the assembly line was excessive.

How can workers repeatedly halt production through labor disputes while demanding massive taxpayer support for their industry? Confronting China's offensive requires government assistance, but public money alone cannot secure competitiveness. Management and labor must undertake painful reforms, improve productivity and cooperate to safeguard the industry's future. Without such efforts, tax incentives risk becoming temporary relief rather than a foundation for lasting industrial strength.

The stakes are especially high as Chinese manufacturers gain ground at home and increasingly challenge established Korean automakers abroad.

text:
Article Content

A delegation of students, faculty and staff from the University of California San Diego is heading to Antalya, Türkiye, to participate in international climate negotiations at the 31st United Nations (UN) Conference of the Parties, or COP31.

From Nov. 9-20, 2026, world leaders, policymakers, experts and other accredited observers will gather at the two-week conference to discuss the climate crisis and advance global cooperation on climate change. COP31 is focused on implementation of climate solutions and advancing the global energy transition that drives more economic growth, jobs, food security, better health and safety and affordable clean energy.

This year’s COP is also being called the “Blue COP” for its emphasis on placing the ocean at the center of global climate progress. As representatives of the University of California observer delegation at COP31, UC San Diego students and faculty will contribute their ocean and climate science expertise in the development of climate solutions through speaking engagements, panel discussions and other activities throughout the conference.

For the fifth consecutive year, UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution are bringing the Ocean Pavilion back to COP to serve as a voice for the ocean community and to highlight the convergence of climate, ocean, biodiversity and sustainability. The 2026 Ocean Pavilion will host more than 65 panel talks, keynote addresses, roundtables and multimedia art presentations in its official programming. The pavilion will also offer more informal opportunities for visitors to meet with scientists and learn more about their research.

“At COP31, we have an important opportunity to bring ocean science into global climate discussions and ensure that research informs the decisions shaping our future,” said Meenakshi Wadhwa, director of Scripps Oceanography and vice chancellor for marine sciences at UC San Diego. “Alongside our UC San Diego students and faculty, I look forward to engaging with delegates from around the world to turn knowledge into solutions that protect ocean ecosystems and advance climate action.”

In all, 24 representatives of the University of California system will travel to Türkiye for COP31. The contingent will include 17 representatives of UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

Travel for the Scripps Oceanography student delegation is generously supported by former Scripps Director Charles Kennel and his wife, Ellen Lehman; several individual donors; and Logitech, a global company that is committed to sustainable practices and designs technology for working, creating and gaming.

Scripps Oceanography will continue a pioneering program in which COP delegates pay the “equity-weighted” social cost of carbon (SCC) associated with delegates’ travel costs. The SCC is a science-based estimate of the true cost of economic damages created by each additional ton of carbon emissions incurred by the travel of UC travelers to international events. Round-trip international flights often incur costs between $400 and $1,000 per traveler using the UC estimate, depending on distance and routes taken.

Individual members of the delegation are encouraged to pay a portion of the cost, with Scripps Institution of Oceanography contributing to the remainder of the costs. The payment will be made in the form of donations to non-governmental organizations whose work focuses on helping societies and the environment deal with the impacts of climate change or reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

text:
Why It Matters

The 2023 U.S.-Japan critical minerals agreement took effect immediately upon signature without congressional approval and changed neither U.S. law nor existing tariffs, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. ​

The agreement covers cobalt, graphite, lithium, manganese and nickel, key inputs for electric vehicle (EV) batteries. Congress now faces questions about whether to authorize sectoral agreements of this kind, set negotiating objectives, and decide how to exercise oversight of the President's authority to negotiate with Japan on critical minerals.

Section 70502 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) terminated the EV tax credit from Sept. 30, 2025.

The Big Picture

The United States has 14 congressionally approved comprehensive free trade agreements with 20 countries, however Japan is not among them, and the Trade Promotion Authority expired in 2021. During the first Trump administration, the United States and Japan signed the 2020 U.S.-Japan Trade Agreement, which reduced tariffs on some goods but not in the automotive or critical minerals sectors.

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169) had provided consumers a tax credit of up to $7,500 for new EVs, with sourcing requirements tied to U.S. free trade agreement partners and restrictions on foreign entities of concern such as Russia and China.

In 2024, the U.S. Department of the Treasury designated the critical minerals agreement as a free trade agreement for purposes of that credit, drawing criticism from some members of Congress who said the designation overrode congressional trade authorities.

The U.S. ran a $48.5 billion deficit in vehicles and parts trade with Japan in 2025. Under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, the Trump administration imposed a 15% tariff on Japanese automotive products, and as of July a 12.5% tariff applies to most Japanese goods.

Three bills address congressional oversight of these agreements:

The Developing Overseas Mineral Investments and New Allied Networks for Critical Energies Act (H.R. 7037), sponsored by Rep. Young Kim (R-CA), would authorize the President to negotiate critical minerals agreements and set consultation requirements; it has passed the House.

The STRATEGIC Minerals Act (S. 429), sponsored by Sen. Todd Young (R-IN), was introduced and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on Feb. 5, 2025. Some members have asserted that Congress should authorize and approve sectoral agreements like those covering critical minerals, citing S. 429 as an example.

The Intergovernmental Critical Minerals Task Force Act (S. 823), sponsored by Sen. Gary C. Peters (D-MI), and its House companion H.R. 3198, sponsored by Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA), would involve allies including Japan in reducing U.S. reliance on Chinese critical minerals supply chains; both remain introduced.

The Bottom Line

H.R. 7037 passed the House on June 8 and awaits action by the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations; no floor vote has been scheduled.

text:
Volvo Cars announces a SEK 3.7 billion third-quarter loss for 2026, prompting a major turnaround plan with SEK 5 billion in cost cuts, 2 500 job reductions, and an accelerated EV rollout through 2030.

Volvo has announced that it will accelerate an intensive product offensive involving 13 new models scheduled for debut by 2030. Three new offerings will premiere in 2027, featuring one new vehicle targeted specifically at European buyers and two models developed for the Chinese market. The global lineup includes a lower-priced battery electric vehicle scheduled for introduction in Europe in 2027, targeting broader market adoption with customer deliveries commencing after mid-year.

Electrified models maintained commercial momentum despite wider market challenges, with fully electric variants capturing 32 per cent of total global sales during the third quarter. European markets recorded high battery electric adoption, representing 45% of regional deliveries. Customer demand for the new EX60 electric SUV surpassed 50 000 European orders, though industrial production ramps up gradually due to complex cell-to-body manufacturing integrations.

Regional adaptations extend directly to manufacturing and powertrain distribution. Volvo Cars is fast-tracking production of long-range plug-in hybrid variants of the XC60 and XC90 to meet interim market demand. Localised assembly of the XC60 in Charleston, South Carolina, will commence in early 2027, supported by plans for a second all-new vehicle platform in the United States later in the decade. For the Chinese market, Volvo Cars will leverage parent company Geely to co-develop six regional vehicles equipped with local digital software stacks, with the first two models set to enter production by mid-2027.

Also read: Volvo and Nvidia expand partnership to advance AI-powered vehicle safety

Financial losses trigger major turnaround plan

Swedish premium automaker Volvo Cars reported a steep operating loss of SEK 3.7 billion (approximately R6.2 billion) for the third quarter of 2026, excluding joint ventures and special items. This outcome represents a sharp reversal from the SEK 5.8 billion (R9.8 billion) operating profit recorded during the corresponding period in 2025. Group revenue dropped by 23% year-on-year to SEK 66.9 billion (R112.7 billion). The financial performance dropped the adjusted EBIT margin to negative 5.6%, while free cash flow contracted significantly to negative SEK 8.9 billion (R15 billion).

The sharp financial contraction follows deteriorating market conditions across key global territories. Revenue generated by Volvo Cars in China plummeted by nearly 50% year-on-year, driven by aggressive domestic pricing wars and hyper-competition from new local electric vehicle manufacturers. Meanwhile, operations within the United States suffered from trade tariffs, lower consumer demand, and the expiration of federal electric vehicle purchase incentives. Further financial headwinds included a write-down of SEK 1.1 billion (R1.9 billion) on American emissions credits and a negative impact of SEK 0.9 billion (R1.5 billion) linked to accounting losses at Polestar.

Structural cost reduction and restructuring programme

Volvo Cars announced a comprehensive restructuring plan designed to cut indirect spend and variable overheads by SEK 5 billion (R8.4 billion). This new cost-saving phase builds upon previous efficiency measures and seeks to lower overall indirect expenditure by 25% relative to 2024 levels by the end of 2027.

The structural overhaul requires reducing approximately 2 500 jobs across global operations. Sweden will bear the brunt of these reductions, with 2,000 positions slated for elimination via the non-renewal of consultant agreements, voluntary separation packages, and natural workforce attrition. Operational efficiency measures in China include consolidating twin office facilities in Shanghai by transferring commercial sales teams into the local Jiading corporate headquarters.

title: EPA Ends Biden's Costly Methane Mandates - American Energy Alliance
description:
The EPA is changing Biden-era rules that would have phased out some natural gas flaring–the burning off of excess gas during oil production.
They would much rather sell the natural gas, but pipelines may not exist.
Methane emissions come not only from producing and transporting fossil fuels, but also from livestock, other agriculture, and decaying waste in landfills.
EU Methane Regulations Several major oil companies have supported federal methane regulations, in part because they want to sell their fuels to countries implementing those rules.
The U.N.’s latest assessment shows methane emissions have not fallen in the five years since countries pledged to reduce them by 30% by 2030.
text:
President Trump announced in Texas his administration’s intention to scale back Biden-era federal requirements on methane emissions from oil and gas operations with goals of encouraging more domestic energy production and lower costs. The Environmental Protection Agency’s proposal would change leak-monitoring and flaring requirements, discontinue Biden’s “Methane Super Emitter Program,” and offer additional regulatory relief to low-output wells. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates the changes could save $45 billion and support production of an additional 210 million barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas between 2027 and 2050.

The EPA is changing Biden-era rules that would have phased out some natural gas flaring–the burning off of excess gas during oil production. U.S. oil and gas producers sometimes flare the excess gas because pipeline capacity is not available to move the fuel to demand centers. They would much rather sell the natural gas, but pipelines may not exist. Lifting pipeline construction constraints would help alleviate flaring, because companies could sell the gas instead, providing a win-win solution.

The Biden-era Super Emitter Program would have created a system for third-party groups to report methane leaks from natural gas production, which would have had to be detected by satellites or special thermal imaging cameras. The Trump administration paused implementation of the program last year and, after review, now plans to eliminate it.

The regulation changes would also affect marginal wells that produce no more than 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day (also called stripper wells), accounting for about 7% to 8% of U.S. natural gas production. Smaller, independent oil producers have said compliance costs can overwhelm the economics of operating older wells, effectively forcing them to shut down. According to the National Stripper Well Association, “the costs associated with complying with these regulations will make the wells uneconomical to operate.” While shutting down low-producing wells could reduce methane emissions, the resulting loss of supply would likely lead to more coal use to replace the natural gas.

Methane emissions come not only from producing and transporting fossil fuels, but also from livestock, other agriculture, and decaying waste in landfills.

According to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, “Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work. They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens.”

Before the changes can take effect, they must go through an EPA rulemaking process that includes a public comment period. If the EPA implements a final rule, it could face legal challenges from environmental groups.

EU Methane Regulations

Several major oil companies have supported federal methane regulations, in part because they want to sell their fuels to countries implementing those rules. The European Union, for example, had planned to require foreign oil and gas suppliers to monitor and report methane emissions or pay penalties, with the rule taking effect on January 1, 2027. The EU’s position came after John Kerry, who was President Biden’s “Climate Envoy,” was dispatched by Biden to craft agreements to regulate methane. About a month ago, the Commission proposed a one-year delay. More recently, the European Parliament voted to postpone the rules for three years, and some EU governments are pushing national capitals to adopt a similar delay because of the energy situation caused by the conflict in Iran and the Russian invasion of Ukraine. As energy affordability remains a central issue for governments and people worldwide, responsive governments are reducing regulatory burdens to aid consumers.

The EU responded to the United States and Qatar, both major LNG exporters, which have repeatedly said the methane regulation would hurt supply security and prices. The United States also warned that it will sell its oil and gas elsewhere if the bloc refuses to ease the regulations. According to Repsol SA, a Spanish energy and petrochemical company, about 90% of its crude oil supplies would breach EU law because suppliers would not agree to provide the information the regulation requires.

According to International Energy Agency analysis of updated Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement, as of early 2026, 141 countries had submitted NDC updates. Methane is included in the scope of essentially all of them, but only around 20 set out specific measures to cut emissions from fossil fuel operations, and just five include quantitative targets for those reductions. Separately, the Global Methane Pledge—a voluntary collective commitment launched at COP26 by the United States and the European Union to reduce global methane emissions at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030—now has 159 participating countries plus the European Commission. The U.N. Environment Program’s latest assessment shows that methane emissions have not fallen (and are still rising) since the Pledge launched, with current policies and commitments falling well short of the 30% target.

Conclusion

President Trump announced his intention to change Biden-era methane emission regulations. The Environmental Protection Agency’s proposal would relax leak-monitoring and flaring requirements, discontinue the Biden Methane Super Emitter Program, and offer additional regulatory relief to low-output wells. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates the changes could save $45 billion and support production of an additional 210 million barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas between 2027 and 2050. The U.N.’s latest assessment shows methane emissions have not fallen in the five years since countries pledged to reduce them by 30% by 2030. In fact, as energy affordability remains a central issue for governments and people worldwide, responsive governments are taking steps to reduce regulatory burdens.

title: EPA Proposes Significant Revisions To Oil And Natural Gas Methane Standards Under Clean Air Act

text:
Highlights

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published a proposed rule on October 29, 2026, that would, if finalized, substantially revise the 2024 New Source Performance Standards for new and existing oil and natural gas sources, commonly referred to as OOOOb and OOOOc.

EPA's most notable changes to OOOOb and OOOOc would include no longer treating routing gas to a sales line as the best system of emission reduction for associated gas from wells primarily producing oil; revising requirements for liquids unloading, process controllers, pumps, fugitives, storage vessels, covers and closed vent systems and control devices; and rescinding the Super Emitter Program not only for OOOOb and OOOOc but also for OOOO and OOOOa.

EPA also co-proposes two options for subcategorizing lower-emitting well sites: "marginal well sites" producing 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day or less, or "conventional" well sites producing from conventional formations, with the same reduced standards applying under either option.

EPA has asked for public comment on numerous aspects of these proposals, and industry should take advantage of the opportunity to provide input.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published a proposed rule on October 29, 2026, titled "Additional Reconsideration Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sources: Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review" (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0163) that would revise the agency's 2024 New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for new, modified and reconstructed oil and natural gas sources (40 C.F.R. Part 60, Subpart OOOOb) and existing sources (Subpart OOOOc) issued under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act (CAA), 42 U.S.C. § 7411 (collectively, the 2024 Rule). The proposal is EPA's second reconsideration package for the 2024 Rule.

This Holland & Knight alert summarizes the regulatory background, describes key components of the proposal and identifies considerations for regulated entities as the rulemaking proceeds.

Background

CAA Section 111 requires EPA to establish standards of performance for new, modified and reconstructed stationary sources based on the "best system of emission reduction" that has been "adequately demonstrated," taking into account cost, non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements. It also requires EPA to issue emission guidelines that states use to develop plans establishing standards for existing sources in the same source categories for which NSPS have been issued. For the oil and natural gas sector, EPA has implemented these provisions through a succession of rules, including Subparts OOOO (2012) and OOOOa (2016), which regulate emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and, with OOOOa, methane.

In the 2024 Rule finalized under the Biden Administration, EPA phased out routine flaring of associated gas from new oil wells, required zero-emitting process controllers in most scenarios, strengthened leak detection and repair (LDAR) requirements at well sites and established a Super Emitter Program under which EPA-certified third parties could use remote sensing to identify large emission events and notify operators. The 2024 Rule also established emission guidelines for methane from existing sources, which states must implement through state plans. (See Holland & Knight's previous alert, "EPA Issues Final Methane Regulations for New and Existing Sources," December 6, 2023.)

On March 12, 2025, EPA announced that it would reconsider the 2024 Rule as part of a broad set of deregulatory actions. (See Holland & Knight's previous alert, "EPA Announces Deregulatory Initiative to 'Power the Great American Comeback'," March 17, 2025.) Since then, EPA has taken several interim actions:

On July 31, 2025, the agency issued an interim final rule (IFR) extending several compliance deadlines in the 2024 Rule.

In December 2025, EPA finalized a rule reaffirming those extensions, providing an additional 180-day extension for compliance dates related to net heating value monitoring of flares and enclosed combustion devices and providing a 360-day extension for submission of initial annual reports.

On April 9, 2026, EPA finalized revisions to provisions governing net heating value and the time limits and justifying circumstances for temporary flaring of associated gas.

On May 1, 2026, EPA issued a clarification that existing federal regulations permit flaring of associated gas at new oil wells in limited circumstances after the May 7, 2026, phase-out deadline.

The Proposed Rule

In a press release announcing the proposal, EPA said the proposed changes to OOOOb and OOOOc would yield economic benefits of approximately $45 billion1 and allow production of an estimated 210 million additional barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion additional cubic feet of natural gas. In the proposed rule, EPA finds that the 2024 Rule delivered "more modest emissions reductions and more significant costs" than expected and significant parts of some of its best system of emission reduction (BSER) determinations are "inappropriate." EPA also notes that industry has raised concerns about compliance with the 2024 Rule.

Key changes proposed by EPA are summarized below.

Subcategorization of Well Sites

EPA co-proposes two alternative approaches to subcategorizing well sites in OOOOb and OOOOc and may finalize only one. Under the first option, wells would be subcategorized as "marginal" if their combined production is 15 barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) per day or less over the prior 12 months. Under the second option, wells would be subcategorized as "conventional" based on their well formation. EPA says subcategorization may be warranted for these wells based on the high cost of compliance for these types of sources.

EPA proposes the same reduced standards for "marginal" and "conventional" wells:

quarterly audio, visual and olfactory inspections for fugitive component emissions

low-bleed devices for continuous bleed natural gas-driven pneumatic controllers

routing VOC and methane emissions from natural gas-driven pumps to a control device that reduces emissions by at least 95 percent where such a device is already available onsite

routing associated gas emissions to control devices only if their potential to emit exceeds certain thresholds (20 tons per year (tpy) methane for associated gas and 20 tpy methane or six tpy VOCs for storage vessels)

"Marginal" status would be based on the site's average daily oil and gas production over the prior 12 months. Modifications and other actions that increase production would require a new determination within 45 days, based on the first 30 days of production. Triggering activities would include drilling, fracturing or refracturing, stimulation or workovers, shutting in one well to boost another, adding even one gas-driven controller or pump, and certain tank battery changes. Zero-emission controllers and pumps already installed would have to stay, and any new units would also have to be zero-emission. Sites below the 20 tpy associated gas threshold would still need to demonstrate it. If EPA splits the subcategory at six BOE per day, the lower tier will likely avoid the associated gas control requirement, while larger sites in the upper tier would likely face annual optical gas imaging (OGI) plus quarterly audio, visual and olfactory. EPA noted in the proposal that subcategorizing as "conventional" rather than "marginal" wells would provide more regulatory certainty over time because it would avoid the additional and ongoing requirement to determine BOE per day to justify a marginal well classification.

EPA further proposes what would constitute "modification" of an existing conventional well and trigger applicability of OOOOb – for example, if a new well is drilled at an existing conventional well site, an existing conventional well is hydraulically fractured, or there is an increase in natural gas-driven process controllers.

EPA estimates that this co-proposal could result in compliance cost savings of approximately $39 billion (present value 2027-2050, at a 3 percent discount rate) but may also result in an additional 88 million short tons of methane emissions and 25 million short tons of VOC emissions.

EPA seeks comment on numerous aspects of this subcategorization co-proposal, including whether marginal wells should be subcategorized further based on average production levels of six BOE and 15 BOE and with respect to EPA's proposed BSER for these sources and the costs and assumptions used to determine the BSER for these sources.

Rescission of the Super Emitter Program

EPA proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program for all NSPS Subpart OOOO programs (OOOO, OOOOa and OOOOb and OOOOc). EPA says the rescission is warranted because the program relies on "insufficient evidence of the nature and duration of super-emitter events";" adds little value on top of existing requirements; is overly broad and ineffective; and lacks adequate statutory authority, particularly for the role that third parties play. EPA notes that it can still use its CAA Section 114 information-collection authority to track compliance and that people may still submit methane data to the agency.

Storage Vessels and Centralized Production Facilities

EPA proposes to treat tank batteries at centralized production facilities the same as those at compressor stations and gas processing plants so that a reassessment of potential emissions would be triggered only if actual throughput exceeds the projected maximum average daily throughput or the throughput in a legally and practically enforceable (LPE) limit. EPA acknowledges that the 2024 modification provisions caused far more midstream storage vessels to be treated as modified than it had estimated and upstream changes unknown to the midstream operator could put sources out of compliance. EPA would also redefine "well site" and "centralized production facility" and base fugitive emissions modification triggers at centralized production facilities on actions within the operator's control. EPA solicits comments on whether the 2024 LPE criteria should be repealed and temporary shut-in sites could recalculate potential emissions for storage vessel control.

Covers and Closed Vent Systems

EPA proposes to divide the "no identifiable emissions" standard for covers and closed vent systems into separate design requirements and operational requirements. Under the proposal, the operational requirements would allow for repairs, rather than treating any identifiable emission as a potential deviation. That relief comes with new obligations that operators should plan for going forward. Routine leaks will have to be repaired within 24 hours, and sources not fixed on the spot would have to be tagged or otherwise documented and then resurveyed. Three or more events in a year would trigger an investigative analysis that EPA suggests could identify design flaws. The same approach would apply to self-contained process controllers. Because these provisions reach covers and closed vent systems at well sites, compressor stations and gas plants, they may significantly affect compliance and enforcement exposure across upstream and midstream operations. EPA has asked whether 24 hours is workable, making this a key comment issue.

Control Devices

Finally, EPA is proposing technical changes to provide flexibility, where appropriate, for continuous burning pilot flames, flame monitoring data deviations, control device alerts, visible emissions test conditions, control devices used on a temporary or backup basis and control device categories, and requests comment on whether automatic igniters perform comparably to continuously lit pilots. EPA would also allow temporary control devices during liquids unloading with streamlined compliance requirements and would let operators submit well closure notifications after closure is complete. The package also revises requirements for pumps and fugitives. These provisions have been a frequent source of operational difficulty and potential deviations under the 2024 Rule, and the proposed revisions could reduce the volume of reportable deviations associated with routine monitoring anomalies.

Associated Gas

EPA is proposing to drop "route to sales" as the BSER for associated gas from oil wells. In EPA's view, the 2024 approach depends on third-party midstream infrastructure that operators "cannot compel," making it "not an allowable form of BSER." For non-marginal wells, EPA would instead require routing associated gas to a control device or flare that achieves a 95 percent reduction, while associated gas at sites in the new subcategory would be subject to control only above the applicable threshold. EPA also requests comment on whether flaring during pipeline construction should be limited in duration (e.g., three years from when the well begins operation) and whether operators should report contractual arrangements and compliance schedules in annual reports. These are issues of direct interest to producers awaiting gathering capacity and midstream companies building it. The proposal would also remove the temporary flaring provisions addressed in EPA's April 2026 final rule.

Process Controllers at Transmission Compressor Stations

EPA is proposing to create a new subcategory for process controllers on high-pressure systems at transmission compressor stations, concluding that retrofitting to zero-emission controllers is not technically feasible or cost-effective. EPA's revised analysis estimates $2.4 million in capital costs and $33,100 per ton of methane reduced to convert these controllers to compressed air. Under the proposal, operators could either route controller emissions through a closed vent system to a control device achieving a 95 percent reduction or use low-bleed controllers in combination with intermittent vent controllers that are periodically monitored. Separately, temporary process controllers could use a low-bleed alternative for up to 60 additional operational days per site per year after the first 30 days, with recordkeeping.

Equipment Leaks at Gas Plants

For onshore natural gas processing plants, EPA proposes to allow a "first attempt at repair" of a leaking valve (such as tightening bolts or packing gland nuts) before requiring replacement or repacking with low-emission valves or packing. EPA also proposes to limit leak detection and repair applicability to equipment "in VOC service" (10 percent VOC by weight) or "in methane service" (1 percent methane by weight), restore "in wet gas service" to the equipment definition and allow OGI surveys under Appendix K.

Takeaways for Regulated Entities

The 2024 Rule Remains in Effect for Now. Companies' obligations under the 2024 Rule remain unchanged until this proposed rule is finalized.

Subcategorization Will Drive Applicability. Owners and operators should consider evaluating their well site portfolios under both co-proposed options, including the 15 BOE per day threshold and the potential six BOE per day split. The choice between a production-based and a formation-based approach and the specific thresholds and definitions EPA ultimately adopts may materially affect which sites qualify for the reduced standards. Stakeholders should also consider whether EPA's new profit-based cost reasonableness analysis is adequately supported.

Midstream Operators Should Review Modifications and Controller Provisions. Gathering, processing and transmission companies should evaluate the proposed throughput-based storage vessel modification triggers, high-pressure controller subcategory at transmission compressor stations, gas plant leak repair and applicability changes and 24-hour closed vent system repair timeline and consider submitting data supporting their positions.

State Plans. States developing plans to implement the Subpart OOOOc emission guidelines will need to assess how the proposal would affect their plan development and timelines.

Commenting Opportunity. Comments on the proposed rule are due December 16, 2026, and EPA will hold a virtual public hearing on November 13, 2026 (speaker preregistration closes November 10, 2026). Comments on information collection provisions are best submitted to the U.S. Office of Management and Budget by November 30, 2026. Given the short timeline and the dozens of specific comment questions posed, companies should consider preparing technical and economic data now to support their positions on the numerous issues for which EPA seeks input.

Footnote

1. Present value for 2027-50 at 3 percent discount rate. In EPA's regulatory analysis, this figure represents net surplus, consisting of $42 billion in compliance cost savings and $3 billion in savings from energy market impacts.
