text:
Capital-efficient financing supports domestic refining, 189 projected advanced manufacturing jobs and a $2.1 million workforce-training commitment

FISHERS, IN / ACCESS Newswire / November 5, 2026 / American Resources Corporation AREC ("American Resources") through its strategic minority holding in ReElement Technologies Corporation ("ReElement"), a leading U.S. developer and operator of advanced rare earth and critical-mineral refining capacity, today announced that its Marion, Indiana project is supported by an aggregate $46 million in non-dilutive federal New Markets Tax Credit (NMTC) allocation. The associated financing will support phase-one investment in refining equipment and working capital as ReElement expands domestic capacity to produce high-purity materials for U.S. and allied industrial supply chains.

The NMTC-supported transaction is part of ReElement's disciplined approach to capital formation. By accessing tax-credit-supported financing alongside other capital sources, the Company seeks to improve the cost and flexibility of funding for long-lived manufacturing infrastructure without issuing additional ReElement equity in connection with this financing. The structure is intended to complement ReElement's modular, demand-aligned expansion strategy while preserving financial flexibility as the business scales.

ReElement's Marion development builds on the city's industrial heritage and supports the domestic refining of rare earth elements and other critical minerals used in defense, aerospace, semiconductor, permanent-magnet, automotive and advanced manufacturing supply chains. The Company's refining-first platform uses advanced chromatography-based separation and purification technology to produce ultra-pure, specification-grade materials from diverse primary and recycled feedstocks. Its modular approach is designed to more efficiently align refining investments with secure feedstocks and verified downstream customer demand.

The first phase at Marion is expected to create 189 jobs, approximately 90% of which are expected to be accessible to individuals with a high school diploma. A $2.1 million funding commitment to workforce training and development will support career pathways that may include apprenticeships, two-year degree programs and advanced technical certifications. These initiatives are intended to expand access to skilled, higher-wage manufacturing careers and opportunities for long-term advancement in Marion.

"Building resilient U.S. critical-mineral supply chains requires disciplined investment in both advanced refining capacity and the people who will operate it," said Kirk Taylor, Chief Financial Officer of ReElement. "This NMTC-supported financing demonstrates how we are pursuing capital-efficient, non-dilutive funding to expand our domestic manufacturing platform while supporting meaningful job creation, competitive wages and accessible pathways to long-term careers in Marion."

The federal NMTC program is designed to attract private investment into eligible low-income communities by providing federal tax credits to investors in qualifying transactions. For manufacturers investing in facilities, equipment and workforce development, NMTC-supported structures can provide a complementary source of long-term capital while supporting local economic development.

About ReElement Technologies Corporation

ReElement Technologies Corporation, a portfolio holding of American Resources Corporation AREC, is a leading U.S. developer and operator of advanced rare earth and critical mineral refining capacity. The Company has developed a modular, refining-first platform that efficiently separates and purifies high-purity rare earth elements and critical minerals from a diverse range of primary mineral concentrates, recycled materials, industrial byproducts and other unconventional feedstocks.

Built around proprietary chromatography-based separation and purification technology, ReElement's commercial platform is designed to produce specification-grade materials while reducing chemical consumption, minimizing environmental impact and enabling flexible, capital-efficient deployment. Its modular architecture allows refining capacity to expand in alignment with customer demand, feedstock availability and evolving strategic priorities.

ReElement collaborates with commercial, industrial and government partners to strengthen secure, resilient and commercially sustainable domestic and allied critical mineral supply chains supporting defense, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, permanent magnets, energy and battery technologies. For more information visit reelementtech.com or connect with the Company on Facebook, X, and LinkedIn.

About American Resources Corporation AREC

American Resources Corporation is strategically developing an integrated critical materials ecosystem through its Platform Orchestration strategy, which brings together complementary capabilities across commercial feedstock origination, industrial processing, and advanced refining. Through this capital-efficient approach, the Company is building a flexible platform designed to adapt to evolving technologies, customer requirements, and national priorities while strengthening domestic and allied critical mineral supply chains.

The Company's operating platforms span conventional and unconventional resource sourcing, feedstock aggregation, recycling, processing, conditioning, and advanced refining through its strategic affiliation with, and former parent relationship to, ReElement Technologies Corporation, a leading provider of high-performance refining capacity for rare earth elements and critical minerals. Together, these complementary capabilities enable American Resources to efficiently align diverse feedstock sources with growing commercial, industrial, and defense-sector demand.

text:
KARAPINAR, Turkey (AP) — Row after row of solar panels stretches across a vast landscape in the central Turkish province of Konya, turning sunlight into electricity — and helping Turkey, the host of the upcoming U.N. climate summit, spotlight its efforts to expand renewable energy.

Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Turkey's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.

Campaigners also argue the country lacks concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, which when burned release greenhouse gases that heat the planet.

Turkey’s Energy Ministry says coal remained the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation. But it stressed that the share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Turkey has one of Europe's largest solar farms

The town of Karapinar in Konya is home to the Kalyon Karapınar YEKA-1 Solar Power Plant, which boasts more than 3 million solar panels perched on a terrain equivalent to the size of 2,600 soccer fields.

Operational since 2023, it generates enough electricity each year to meet about 0.7% of the country’s power demand, according to plant director Burak Dogru.

“We prevent approximately 1.75 million metric tons of carbon emissions every year,” Dogru told The Associated Press — evidence, he says, of how Turkey has been directing its economy and energy sector toward cleaner energy sources.

Turkey’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, the last year for which data is available, reached 584.5 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.

Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Turkey has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.

“But these plans contain neither a roadmap for a coal phase-out, nor any planning for a phase-out of other fossil fuels, including gas,” Kutluay cautioned, adding that this is "not compatible” with Turkey's pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2053.

Turkey is also looking to nuclear power to reduce its energy dependence. The country’s first plant is under construction on the Mediterranean coast, with plans for additional reactors still under consideration.

Concerns and criticism rise ahead of the summit

Some 265 kilometers (165 miles) away from Konya, the Nov. 9-20 summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya will bring together tens of thousands of delegates, world leaders, business and civil society representatives for discussions on implementing climate goals.

The summit — officially, the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes against a backdrop of deepening concerns over energy security and the Iran war, which has led to a rise in gas and oil prices and sent countries scrambling to meet energy needs.

Many experts have recently argued that a key mission — combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions — has been failing.

The United States, the world’s richest nation and second-biggest carbon polluter after China, will again be absent from the summit, after U.S. President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from global climate negotiations.

And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.

Turkey’s environment and climate change minister, Murat Kurum, who will preside over the summit, has said he wants COP31 to focus on turning climate commitments into action rather than new targets.

To that aim, Turkey will push a “climate implementation bridge,” an initiative to help countries turn climate pledges into action by connecting them with financing, technology and other support.

“Today, the world is not merely waiting for new decisions," Kurum said while presenting summit priorities earlier this year. "What the world wants is to see past decisions put into practice.”

Turkey has cast itself as an environment steward

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted his country is committed to environmental protection and combating climate change, and first lady Emine Erdogan has championed a “zero waste” campaign to encourage recycling and a more responsible use of resources.

COP31 will also prioritize electrification and reduction of waste and methane emissions, Kurum has said.

However, the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, has described Turkey’s climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to the early 1800s, directing countries to develop policies that would help meet that goal.

Meanwhile, human rights groups accuse Ankara of dismissing environmental concerns and frequently arresting activists.

Earlier this year, a court annulled an environmental impact assessment for a planned expansion of a coal-fired power plant at Afsin-Elbistan in southeastern Turkey. The ruling was hailed by environmentalists as a major victory.

But shortly afterward, plans emerged to expand another coal-fired power plant in Canakkale, in the country's northwest.

Like other Mediterranean nations, Turkey faces mounting risks from heat waves, drought, water scarcity, wildfires and flooding. Last month, rains described as the heaviest in more than 80 years caused severe floods in Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city, and left eight people dead.

Turkey was announced as the host of COP31 following a tug-of-war with Australia, which also wanted to host the summit. As a compromise, Australia has been leading consultations to help set the summit's agenda and will be in charge of summit discussions.

Climate advocates have slammed the summit for being awarded to coal-reliant Turkey; coal-exporter Australia has also come under criticism.

But U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell defended the choice, saying in February that a COP host country’s status on fossil fuels does not determine the success or failure of a summit.

With “Turkey and Australia leading this process, there is every opportunity to deliver a very strong outcome," he said.

___

Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey. Associated Press journalists Serra Yedikardes in Trabzon, Turkey, and Ayse Wieting in Istanbul contributed to this report.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 continues to deliver the breadth, efficiency, and capability that have made it a sales leader in the Toyota lineup, while adding thoughtful updates that enhance utility for the Woodland grade and charging convenience for PHEV customers. Updates for 2027 include:

Woodland receives new suspension components, including new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers – giving it 9.1 inches of ground clearance

Woodland also receives redesigned all-weather floor and cargo mats

All PHEV grades now have a NACS port and DC fast charging (Level 3) capability

Exterior

The 2027 RAV4 carries forward the all-new sixth-generation design with three distinct exterior themes: core, rugged, and sport. RAV4’s exterior proportions emphasize SUV strength and utility, with a high ride height, large tires, upright rear cargo area, and the unique Toyota hammerhead front-end treatment. Sculpted body surfaces, chiseled fenders, and distinctive LED lighting help create a modern and confident appearance across the lineup.

Distinct styling cues differentiate between each grade.

The functional LE, XLE Premium, and Limited core grades feature a clean and refined look. Woodland models add rugged visual elements and outdoor-ready details.

The sporty SE and XSE grades bring darker exterior accents, more aggressive trim elements, and performance-inspired character. Available two-tone paint combinations and unique wheel treatments further distinguish the grades.

The RAV4 GR SPORT incorporates sport style with functional components, like a front lip and rear wing spoiler for balanced downforce; air ducts in the front grille and bumper to help channel air and reduce drag; offset wheels with performance tires for maximum grip; and drive battery placement that lowers its center of gravity and stabilizes the chassis. It also has one additional inch of overall width due to wider fender flares.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 continues with a modern, functional cabin designed around comfort, flexibility, and technology. A clean center stack organizes major controls, while the center console maximizes usability with thoughtful storage and convenience features.

A 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster is standard across the lineup, providing a bright, customizable display with integrated multimedia information. Depending on grade, the cabin can also include Toyota’s shift-by-wire system, SofTex®-trimmed heated and ventilated seats, wireless charging, and a JBL® Premium Audio system.

Cargo versatility remains a priority, with a rear seatback that folds flat on all grades to expand utility and an available hands-free power liftgate that helps ease access. Grade-specific materials, stitching, trim accents, and color treatments give each RAV4 trim their own personality.

title: Is CEE Facing a Detroit Moment? - Visegrad Insight
description:
The latest Irish proposal cuts next EU budget’s competitiveness programmes by around 13 per cent and cohesion by about three.
When György Bacsa, Group Chief Strategic Officer of MOL Group, looks at Central Europe’s industrial belt, he sees two possible futures.
One is Bilbao or Antwerp, industrial cities that reinvented themselves as hubs for finance, energy and new business.
The European Competitiveness Fund (ECF), the instrument meant to carry Europe’s industrial ambitions, sits in the budget heading for a cut more than four times as deep as that of cohesion funds.
To be supported, to be settled in Europe’, Bacsa says.
text:
The latest Irish proposal cuts next EU budget’s competitiveness programmes by around 13 per cent and cohesion by about three. Music to CEE ears? Central Europe may be winning the wrong fight.

‘If there is somebody winning EU Commission contracts, they are primarily living abroad, not in Romania, not in Poland, not in Slovakia’, started off Janusz Lewandowski, former EU Commissioner and member of the EU Parliament.

Lewandowski opened a roundtable that Visegrad Insight convened in Brussels on 4 November around one claim. Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) needs a louder voice in the EU debate on growth, because the region’s economies are growing and its industries, heavy industry included, are needed for the further growth of the whole Union. Around the table sat Members of the European Parliament Lewandowski and Kinga Kollár, Nathalie Berger of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs (DG GROW), György Bacsa of MOL Group, leaders of Czech, Polish and Romanian industry and business organisations and Brussels think tank analysts.

The region is not one ‘that sits at Europe’s edge’ but ‘a region that beats right at the heart of the future of the continent’, as one participant put it. ‘We are part of the solution, not part of the problem,’ one of the industry leaders said.

When György Bacsa, Group Chief Strategic Officer of MOL Group, looks at Central Europe’s industrial belt, he sees two possible futures. One is Bilbao or Antwerp, industrial cities that reinvented themselves as hubs for finance, energy and new business. The other is Michigan, where car plants outlived their competitiveness and people moved away. The region’s manufacturing remains largely traditional, labour-intensive and energy-intensive, and if it cannot renew itself, Bacsa warned, ‘we can end up like Michigan in the United States’.

Which future the region gets will be shaped in part by the negotiations on the 2028–2034 EU budget, which negotiators aim to conclude by the end of this year.

The Irish presidency’s negotiating box, circulated on 10 October, trims the Commission’s proposal by eight per cent, or about 141 billion euros. It cuts competitiveness, prosperity and security programmes by around 13 per cent and cohesion and agriculture by about three per cent.

That reduction suits the region’s largest cohesion recipients, for whom the MFF has long been a matter of political survival. It suits their industries far less. The European Competitiveness Fund (ECF), the instrument meant to carry Europe’s industrial ambitions, sits in the budget heading for a cut more than four times as deep as that of cohesion funds. It is also designed to reward excellence, project pipelines and access to capital, all of which CEE has in shorter supply than the West.

‘We have a big challenge to transform this competitiveness from an economic policy issue into a European project owned by the society,’ one of the roundtable participants says.

The region’s growth model is wearing out

CEE countries have outperformed the rest of the EU for the last two decades thanks to lower labour costs, tax competition and lighter regulation. But all these three advantages may now be fading. Employment has risen to the point where there is ‘no more buffer, no more surplus’ of workers, demographics are as weak as elsewhere in Europe and there is little public appetite for labour migration. The region also spends less on innovation than the rest of the EU and receives less support from Brussels to tackle this. Direct innovation funding, as well as other things, therefore, demands some regional balance.

‘There is a very big anti-sentiment against a big number of guest workers or guest immigration for labour purposes. I don’t think that should be the solution. The solution should be to subsidise less labour-intensive industries. To be supported, to be settled in Europe’, Bacsa says. ‘The European champion should be a European pride’.

Bacsa also calls for abolishing the EU FDI screening rules introduced during the COVID-19 pandemic, which, in his view, governments in both Western and Eastern Europe use as discretionary bargaining tools against companies from other member states, attaching unrelated demands to approvals. ‘The single market is not working like that’.

Poland’s success has not reached Europe’s excellence funds

MEP and former EU Budget Commissioner Janusz Lewandowski believes that cohesion policy delivered ‘enormous, enormous progress with the help of Euro funds’ in Poland after 2004, because it offers ‘predictable money’, which infrastructure modernisation requires.

Centrally managed programmes, however, tell a different story. Apart from Erasmus, where Poland ranks sixth, Horizon Europe and the other competitiveness instruments bring the region ‘almost nothing’, and on the return from each euro contributed Poland ranks 26th in the EU, ahead only of Romania. ‘If there is somebody winning contracts, he is living abroad, not in Romania, not in Poland, not in Slovakia,’ Lewandowski says.

A competitiveness fund that does not do geography

‘If I want to scale up, if I want to grow, I escape to America’. The Polish MEP does not dispute that excellence should be the main criterion, since Europe competes globally, but wants the 2028–2034 Competitiveness Fund balanced geographically, with more privileges for SMEs and start-ups. This is necessary, in his view, because of fragmented capital markets in which ‘billions of euros are sleeping on bank accounts’ instead of funding innovation.

One could still argue, however, that the ECF merges 14 fragmented programmes into a single rulebook covering the path from research to industrial deployment, and its largest window, for industry, defence, security and space, matches CEE’s industrial profile. An 11-billion-euro horizontal envelope for the ECF InvestEU instrument, an advisory hub and SME-specific support are meant to make regional projects bankable. Measured against national GDP, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Bulgaria and Lithuania follow only Portugal among the largest users of InvestEU.

‘The ECF has an issue there because it’s only an excellent space. Then we have a structural deficit’.

Cohesion money alone may not sustain convergence, because Eastern Europe needs competitiveness funding as well. ‘If you look at Romania, for instance, we have high budget deficits, the high borrowing costs that induce capital cost growth,’ another participant points out, adding that there is little fiscal room to support project development. Those constraints weigh heavily on an instrument that is, by design, demand-driven and free of geographical earmarking.

Energy prices set the ceiling for industrial strategy

For industries and businesses, the energy bill comes before the budget. Energy ‘is basically at the foundation of any growth we have in Europe or elsewhere’, as the moderator noted. Bacsa cites estimates that the extra global energy bill since the Hormuz crisis already equalled Belgium’s annual output by the end of September and would match Poland’s by the end of the year. That spending buys no growth, he argues, only the ability to keep ‘running the business, running the society as it is now’. Counting non-fossil sources, Europe imports between 55 and 65 per cent of its energy by his figures, so the exposure is structural.

Bacsa is equally direct on climate policy. ‘The increasing carbon costs without protecting European industry is a dead end,’ he says, calling for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and the phasing-out of free allowances under the ETS to overlap rather than be switched on and off. He counts around 100 chemical and 35 oil- and gas-based assets closed in Europe, most of them relocated outside its borders, with their output now imported back.

EU rules also split the map. ‘Half of the EU has an exemption in energy. And if you see the map, it would be the left side, meaning the western part,’ an energy sector representative says of EU public procurement rules. ‘It is a discussion about technological neutrality. It is a discussion about trajectories. It is a discussion about flexibilities,’ another participant argues.

Unwanted simplification?

On regulation, the Commission counts 12 omnibus packages and other simplification measures proposed in a year and a half, with estimated net savings of 22 billion euros. ‘Omnibuses are a great way forward. But why do we have omnibuses? Because we overregulated before,’ one of the business leaders says, pointing to the digital rulebook from the Digital Services Act to the AI Act. The automotive sector alone is covered by around 180 regulations and directives, with about 100 more due in the next five years, while the automotive omnibus addresses only about six of them. ‘If we do not adapt ourselves, then long term there will be no money for the budget anymore,’ an automotive industry leader warns.

At the same time, some argue that the Commission’s impact assessments neither draw on data from business nor reflect differences in industrial structure between member states, although Czechia is among the most industrialised economies in Europe. Electric cars, which make up more than 30 per cent of new sales in some member states and single digits in parts of CEE, show how unevenly the same legislation lands. ‘Observing businesses coming from the Czech Republic to Brussels, they’re lost. They need to put the money into the growth of their business and not into compliance,’ one business representative says.

‘We are having a delivery gap between what we have diagnosed and what we then actually achieve,’ another participant concludes.

What the region should ask for

The region’s negotiators have until the end of the year to decide what kind of deal they want. Protecting cohesion is defensible, since it remains the most predictable investment money CEE receives. A deal that preserves national envelopes while cutting the ECF and leaving its design untouched would, however, buy another decade of little influence over the industries meant to replace today’s energy-intensive manufacturing.

The more useful requests should be specific. They should include advisory capacity and national promotional banks strong enough to make regional projects bankable, SME and defence windows open to frontline economies, technology neutrality in the IAA and the ECF, and relief on energy and carbon costs before the next wave of industrial legislation. Whether Central Europe ends up closer to Bilbao or to Michigan will depend on whether it wins a fair share of the money Europe spends on growth.

About the event

The roundtable ‘Translating Central Europe’s Growth Potential to the EU Competitiveness Agenda’ took place in Brussels on 4 November 2026 as a strategic foresight discussion within the EuropeFuture.Forum. It was organised by the Res Publica Foundation, powered by MOL Group and supported by the Czech Business Representation to the EU – CEBRE -. The roundtable brought together MEPs, European Commission officials, media, think tank analysts and business representatives from Central Europe.

title: Trump's veto could limit Democrats' energy policy changes | National News
description: (The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.
text:
(The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.

When the new Congress is seated in January, incoming Democratic majorities are expected to push efforts to increase oversight of methane emissions, limit drilling on federal lands and in offshore areas, and tighten environmental permitting requirements on new plants and equipment.

Trump declared an energy emergency during his first hours in office in January 2025, invoking the National Emergencies Act to accelerate fossil fuel development. In a flurry of executive orders since then, the president has made U.S. energy dominance one of his primary economic objectives, framing it as a matter of national security.

Tom Pyle, president of the Washington-based American Energy Alliance , told The Center Square that attempts by newly elected Democratic majorities to roll back those executive actions will be neutralized by Trump’s veto pen.

"They can do Congressional Review Act resolutions on his rulemakings," Pyle said — referring to the fast-track legislative tool Congress can use to overturn federal rules adopted since the president took office. "They can pass them, but they’ll be vetoed."

Pyle noted that while a Democratic majority can leverage committee leadership positions to launch investigations and issue subpoenas, the president’s veto will still leave the Trump administration's core deregulatory agenda – and the sweeping legislative victories won through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year – largely intact.

“It’s one thing to make a bunch of campaign promises. It’s another thing to deliver on them," Pyle said. "Democrats will have a very difficult challenge if they intend to try to undo the very policies that President Trump has enacted that make it easier to produce energy, easier to move it around this country."

Pyle said election results at the state level are a reason to worry. “The story of the night is Texas — it really was a wipeout,” said Pyle. “Texas Democrats will need to tread very carefully because oil and gas is their bread and butter. It will be interesting to see how the Democrats in Texas treat the industry there,” said Pyle.

Ed Hirs, an energy fellow and energy economist at the University of Houston, said the Democrats' control of Congress will have little effect on U.S. energy production. He said it is global markets and prices — not Washington politics — that really drive American energy production.

America had energy dominance under President Biden, too, and had approached it during the Obama years, Hirs said. Now, with energy prices high because of geopolitical events, the nation’s oil and gas production is at a new record level, said Hirs.

“Trump has ensured the energy dominance of the United States, perhaps inadvertently, by undertaking this war against Iran,” Hirs told The Center Square. “We are now facing several years of having higher oil and LNG prices, which will benefit the United States, for sure.”

While gross national product will be higher, gasoline prices will be, too, said Hirs. “But prices are higher because of the war, not because of market conditions,” he said.

Hirs added that high global crude oil prices have begun to depress consumption in the United States. "U.S. consumption of crude and refined products dropped by more than 2% last year because of those higher prices,” said Hirs.

text:
Expanded DER deployment could meaningfully reduce projected household electricity bill increases while helping the grid respond to uncertain demand

BOSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A new report prepared by The Brattle Group for The Pew Charitable Trusts finds that removing barriers and advancing policies that enable the use of more distributed energy resources (DERs) – including distributed solar, battery storage, and demand flexibility like managed electric vehicle (EV) charging – across residential, commercial, and industrial customers would avoid an estimated $614 billion in US power system costs through 2050. This would offset roughly half of projected household electricity bill increases, apart from those related to inflation.

The report, The National Case for a More Distributed Power Grid: New Evidence on Affordability and Demand Growth, pioneers an approach that examines how to leverage resources located close to electricity users in order to meet rising demand and support energy affordability. The authors conclude that removing key policy barriers to DER deployment would more than quadruple US DER capacity, adding over 400 gigawatts (GW) by 2050 – the equivalent of nearly one-third of the country's entire power generation fleet today. This new DER capacity would lower the risk and associated costs of overbuilding conventional energy infrastructure due to uncertain future electricity demands.

"Many homes and businesses already have technologies that could help the grid meet rising demand, and adoption of those technologies will continue to grow. The opportunity is to treat them as resources in utility planning rather than leave their capabilities untapped," said Ryan Hledik, a Brattle Principal and report coauthor. "At scale, DERs could avoid or defer a portion of US infrastructure investment needs, reduce pressure on household bills, and give utilities more flexibility in the face of uncertain demand."

In April, Pew released Distributed Energy Can Unleash the Resilient, Affordable Grid of the Future, which outlines six policy recommendations to accelerate the adoption of DERs. Brattle's report complements this DER policy playbook by estimating the scale and economic value of expanded DER implementation. The Brattle analysis finds that addressing three key policy recommendations – incorporating DERs into distribution system planning, reducing permitting costs, and reforming interconnection processes – could deliver $266 billion in avoided power system costs through 2050.

"At a time of historic demand from data centers, new manufacturing, and electrification, DERs can provide a significant new energy supply if barriers to their adoption are removed," said Maureen Quinlan, who leads Pew's work to decarbonize the grid. "This report underscores how pragmatic policy changes that enable DER technology can save billions, cut emissions, and help build a more affordable, reliable, and flexible grid that meets today's and tomorrow's energy needs."

Among its most notable findings, the study finds that expanded DER deployment could:

Soften future bill increases. DERs would enable a $122 per year reduction in average household electricity bills by 2050 (in current dollars). These savings would offset roughly half of the projected bill increase that is above the study's assumed rate of inflation.

Provide direct financial benefits. DERs allow customers – not large-scale power developers – to earn direct compensation for services they provide to the grid. The resulting net savings are large enough to benefit all customers through lower electricity rates.

Limit the cost of overbuilding for uncertain demand. In a scenario where anticipated load growth falls short, greater reliance on DERs would reduce overbuilding energy infrastructure costs by $33 billion between 2030 and 2040, a reduction of roughly 40%.

Increase grid-edge flexibility. Expanding DERs would shift approximately 105 GW of utility-scale storage capacity to distributed storage and other forms of flexibility at the grid edge.

Reduce natural gas additions. Expanding DER deployment could help avoid roughly 70 GW of projected net gas additions, a 22% reduction that is equivalent to 175 natural gas-fired plants nationally.

Decrease carbon emissions. DERs would also directly reduce cumulative power sector carbon dioxide emissions by an estimated 3% through 2050, relative to the status quo scenario, and could provide further reductions in other sectors through indirect impacts such as facilitating the deployment and integration of electric vehicles.

Make a decarbonized power system less costly. In a scenario requiring a carbon-free generation fleet by 2050, expanded DERs would offset approximately 175 GW of utility-scale capacity and lower annual generation costs in 2050 by $45 billion – nearly 20% of the incremental cost of decarbonizing the power supply.

The analysis combines long-term power system modeling with an assessment of opportunities to defer local distribution upgrades. It covers 25 US regions and examines impacts on both the bulk power and distribution systems. It also notes that benefits beyond its quantified estimates –including resilience and some potential transmission benefits – could provide additional value.

The report was authored by Principal Ryan Hledik, Energy Associate Kate Peters, Energy Specialist Sophie Edelman, Senior Energy Analyst Prisha Tiwari, Energy Analyst Carly McAdam, and Managing Energy Associate Akhilesh Ramakrishnan.

View the report on Brattle's website: https://www.brattle.com/the-distributed-grid/.

text:
Celebration broke out at Oakshire Public House on election night as early results showed Eugene voters backing Measure 20-388, which would establish the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.

Initial results showed more than 57% of voters supporting the measure.

It would charge roughly 70 large businesses in Eugene a 2% fee to help fund city climate and energy projects, including renewable energy programs, clean-energy job training, green infrastructure and future innovation.

“We are as a community taking steps to make the billion-dollar corporations that profit off of us contribute back to building those community benefits, and we’ve come together and made it happen,” said Alexi Miller, a newly elected at-large member of the Eugene Water & Electric Board.

The fee, which would be implemented in January of 2029, would apply to businesses with more than $1 billion in national gross profits and more than $500,000 in gross profits in Eugene.

The first funds from the fee must begin being allocated by 2030, but it could start in 2029.

"We actually looked really closely to make sure that none of our local big businesses would meet that threshold. So think about Nancy's, Yogi Tea, or Jerry's Hardware; none of those companies came even close to meeting the threshold," Deputy Director of the Sierra Club’s Clean Heat Campaign Dylan Plummer said.

A community commission will oversee the fund and allow for public input on what projects to prioritize with some funds dedicated to existing projects like EWEB's energy efficiency upgrades.

"EWEB already has extremely generous incentives for solar and for heat pumps and energy efficiency programs for homeowners. The fund allows for some of the money to go directly into these existing programs to help expand them. So that's one of the first things we want to see is that EWEB's programs become even more generous and be able to be adopted by more folks including homeowners and renters," Plummer said.

The final vote to approve projects belongs to the city council.

Job creation is also a big element of the fund.

"One of the things that I think hasn't been talked about enough is that this is going to be a huge jobs program that will create good paying union jobs in Eugene and help build clean energy infrastructure," Plummer said.

Plummer says that includes heat pump installers, solar installers, people to build renewable energy and transportation projects, and electrical and construction workers.

Opponents say they're concerned about the long term financial impact on the community as those businesses take on the new fee.

"The idea is there; it's wonderful, and I think the money will probably be spent as planned. It will be good for the community, " Eugene Resident Matt Bailey said. "But in the long term, these organizations have to make decisions. And it's going to come down to whether or not to do business here, whether or not to keep employees full time, whether to cut hours, whether to raise their prices here in Eugene."

The commission to oversee the fund will include one city council member, one EWEB representative, a representative from the Human Rights Commission, one Sustainability Commission representative, as well as five city appointed community members.

Some businesses, including health care providers and grocery stores, would be exempt from the fee.

The fund has a built in auditing process with an outside audit happening every four years.

The associated financing will support phase-one investment in refining equipment and working capital as ReElement expands domestic capacity to produce high-purity materials for U.S. and allied industrial supply chains.

The NMTC-supported transaction is part of ReElement's disciplined approach to capital formation. By accessing tax-credit-supported financing alongside other capital sources, the Company seeks to improve the cost and flexibility of funding for long-lived manufacturing infrastructure without issuing additional ReElement equity in connection with this financing. The structure is intended to complement ReElement's modular, demand-aligned expansion strategy while preserving financial flexibility as the business scales.

ReElement's Marion development builds on the city's industrial heritage and supports the domestic refining of rare earth elements and other critical minerals used in defense, aerospace, semiconductor, permanent-magnet, automotive and advanced manufacturing supply chains. The Company's refining-first platform uses advanced chromatography-based separation and purification technology to produce ultra-pure, specification-grade materials from diverse primary and recycled feedstocks. Its modular approach is designed to more efficiently align refining investments with secure feedstocks and verified downstream customer demand.

The first phase at Marion is expected to create 189 jobs, approximately 90% of which are expected to be accessible to individuals with a high school diploma. A $2.1 million funding commitment to workforce training and development will support career pathways that may include apprenticeships, two-year degree programs and advanced technical certifications. These initiatives are intended to expand access to skilled, higher-wage manufacturing careers and opportunities for long-term advancement in Marion.

"Building resilient U.S. critical-mineral supply chains requires disciplined investment in both advanced refining capacity and the people who will operate it," said Kirk Taylor, Chief Financial Officer of ReElement. "This NMTC-supported financing demonstrates how we are pursuing capital-efficient, non-dilutive funding to expand our domestic manufacturing platform while supporting meaningful job creation, competitive wages and accessible pathways to long-term careers in Marion."

text:
(CNN) —
Renewable sources of energy are on the rise around the world, from solar panels paired with battery storage to rapid electric vehicle adoption. Countries are expanding the share of energy coming from these cleaner sources when compared to fossil fuels, particularly outside of the US.
But there is a split screen between the speed and progress of the clean energy transition and the slow pace of climate diplomacy. When countries around the world gather in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9 for this year’s UN climate summit, known as COP31, they’re likely to find themselves in talks driven by longstanding tensions between industrialized nations (which are responsible for most global warming to date) and the developing world.
Experts say that balance between talks and action is less out-of-whack than it may initially appear, however. There’s progress being made, both at the negotiating table and in the real world. The talks lay some of the foundation for the growing reliance on renewables and provide a much-needed push to reduce carbon and methane emissions, they said.
The focus this year at COP is on implementing existing agreements, such as the Paris Climate Agreement, which is likely to put pressure on negotiators to make commitments on helping developing nations to finance their energy transition and compensate them for climate damages. These are two especially thorny issues at these meetings, with relatively scant progress made on them in previous years.
This doesn’t mean that COP meetings are unimportant. Experts say such summits are especially valuable for pushing countries to carve out their plans for cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
“The Paris Agreement operates on two tracks — negotiations and action — and it has delivered important progress on both,” said Rick Duke, who served as the deputy US special envoy for climate change during the Biden administration. “On the action front, for example, in 2021 over 100 countries joined the Global Methane Pledge and a declaration to end deforestation,” he said.
China and Brazil, in particular, have made progress, Duke said. China now includes methane in its national targets and newly-reelected Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is pushing forward on plans to end Amazon deforestation. “That said, the process needs to do a better job holding countries accountable for their national targets and focusing attention on the “emergency brake” solutions like methane and forests that can cut warming fastest,” he said.
Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth and climate research lead at Stripe, said the steep decline in the costs of clean energy sources has helped to lower the severity of expected warming during the coming decades compared to projections made just a few years ago.
But how much of this was an achievement of decades of COP meetings, as opposed to favorable economic factors and actions countries would have taken anyway, is not entirely clear, he said.
“It is difficult to separate out this progress from action countries may have taken in relation to the climate talks themselves, and simply the economics of renewables becoming far cheaper over time,” Hausfather said. “The COP process is sort of like the figurehead on top of all of the hard work that’s actually happening.”
The bottom line is that neither the policy discussions in Turkey nor global renewables deployment are happening fast enough to avert perilous amounts of further warming.
A
UN report released last month,
for example, warned that the world will soon overshoot the 1.5-degree Celsius warming target contained in the Paris Agreement, and that our best hope is to limit further warming, slash emissions and cool temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

text:
Gallium-containing feedstocks extend beyond China. Recovery plants, refining economics and customer approvals determine whether they become usable supply.

Gallium is present in industrial feedstocks outside China, but manufacturers cannot order a resource estimate. They need a supplier that can recover the metal, deliver the required purity and keep shipping when prices or operating conditions change. Research on U.S. recovery potential and a staged project in Canada show why diversifying gallium supply requires more than finding the element.

China accounted for approximately 99% of worldwide primary low-purity gallium production in 2025, according to the U.S. Geological Survey’s gallium summary. That concentration describes the first commercial recovery stage. It does not mean China contains 99% of the world’s gallium resources or produces every downstream gallium-containing material.

The Feedstock Exists Beyond the Dominant Producer

Most gallium is recovered as a byproduct of processing bauxite into alumina, with the remainder coming from zinc-processing residues. USGS estimates that world bauxite resources contain more than 1 million metric tons of gallium. The metal generally occurs in small concentrations, making the ability and incentive to recover it more consequential than its presence alone.

A Berkeley Lab study published in 2025 modeled U.S. material flows and North American production costs. It found sufficient domestic feedstocks to meet U.S. gallium demand under most scenarios through 2035. End-of-life recycling could supply up to 50% under a low-demand growth scenario, while primary recovery offered a cost advantage over recycling.

Those findings identify potential pathways, rather than committed production. The study’s modeled primary production costs of $422–$509 per kilogram are scenario estimates. They are not current offers for qualified semiconductor material, and the recycling result depends on the demand scenario and recovery assumptions.

For an industrial buyer, that leaves two separate questions: how much gallium a feedstock could yield, and what a supplier can deliver under a commercial agreement.

A Pilot Plant Is a Different Supply Commitment

Rio Tinto’s Quebec project illustrates the steps between those answers. In a March 2 announcement, the company said it would begin building a pilot plant to validate recovery technology in an industrial setting, with operation expected in 2027.

The company also described a planned demonstration plant with capacity of up to 4 metric tons annually. A subsequent commercial plant could reach 40 metric tons annually. These are distinct development stages. The eventual commercial volume cannot yet be treated as operating supply.

The U.S. Energy Department’s April TRACE-Ga announcement likewise describes a development pipeline. Approximately $5.4 million was announced for five selections involving different recovery technologies. DOE states that selection for award negotiations does not commit the department to issuing an award or providing funding.

Comparing those records requires keeping research, funded development, commissioning and commercial production separate. Adding every announced capacity figure would overstate the supply available to buyers.

Buyers Need Evidence at Each Production Stage

A manufacturer assessing a prospective supplier needs to establish who controls the feedstock, which facility will recover the gallium and who will perform any further purification. It also needs the product specification, demonstrated operating record and qualification requirements for its own manufacturing process.

Host-plant dependence belongs in that assessment. A recovery circuit attached to an alumina or zinc operation relies on that facility’s throughput and continued operation. A different country of recovery can diversify geographic exposure while leaving the buyer dependent on a single industrial site.

The commercial terms matter too. Buyers considering a long-term commitment need to know whether the project’s economics depend on temporary prices, anticipated coproduct revenue or future expansion. Producers need evidence that customers will accept and purchase the output once it is available.

text:
Federal energy-policy rollbacks could produce over 9 billion additional tons of heat-trapping pollution through 2040, according to an analysis by Energy Innovation.

Beyond the increased pollution, the analysis projects higher residential energy expenses and tens of thousands of additional early deaths because of poorer air quality.

Here's what to know

Dave Borlace, the creator behind Just Have a Think (@JustHaveaThink), examined the changes in a long-form YouTube video, citing research from Energy Innovation, Rhodium Group, and Wood Mackenzie.

Borlace asserted that renewable projects face new barriers as clean-energy incentives shrink. At the same time, the administration has also repealed power-plant carbon rules and weakened vehicle standards.

On February 12, 2026, President Donald Trump's administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency's endangerment finding, which was established in 2009. Borlace said the finding determined that six greenhouse gases endanger Americans' health and welfare, establishing the legal basis for federal rules governing greenhouse gas emissions from new vehicles.

The administration also eliminated those vehicle standards. According to the Trump administration, ending the rules would reduce Americans' vehicle-related expenses by over $1.3 trillion, though legal challenges could change the outcome.

The administration argues its approach will deliver stronger U.S. industry, a more reliable energy supply, and lower energy and vehicle prices. It disputes Energy Innovation's assessment.

More background

The Department of Transportation lowered its model-year 2031 fleetwide fuel-economy target for cars and light trucks to 34.9 miles per gallon, down from 50.4, as Borlace noted.

The administration's own analysis shows higher lifetime fuel expenses for vehicle owners, despite its claims of upfront savings. The administration says the change could cut roughly $1,300 from a new vehicle's average purchase price.

Reuters, as cited in the video, reported that the resulting increase in nationwide fuel use could reach approximately 4.6% by midcentury.

Wood Mackenzie estimated that heightened federal permitting scrutiny put proposed wind, solar, and battery projects totaling approximately 92 gigawatts in jeopardy, with about $121 billion in associated investment, per Borlace.

With federal support shrinking, proposed infrastructure must still navigate permitting hurdles. Those obstacles do not mean every project will be canceled.

What's being done?

The video noted that the U.S. Climate Alliance, whose membership includes Guam and 23 states accounting for about 55% of Americans, has pledged a collective pollution reduction of 50% to 52% by 2030 compared with 2005, alongside a net-zero goal for 2050.

Meanwhile, Rhodium Group reported that battery deployment at grid scale reached a U.S. record in 2025, while utility-scale solar recorded its second-biggest year. The group expects both technologies to set installation records in 2026 and 2027, partly as developers hurry to finish projects ahead of expiring tax credits.

"The federal government may have changed direction, but the underlying technology and fundamental economics remain essentially just as compelling now as they did before 2025," Borlace assessed.

Still, Rhodium's higher-pollution scenario projects that U.S. pollution reductions could lose momentum in the early 2030s before increasing again.

Commenters on YouTube hoped change could make its way through elections and the political process.

"I sincerely hope that the majority of U.S. citizens see sense and hobble this criminal administration," one wrote.

Where can I learn more?

These federal rollbacks reach across power generation, oil and gas production, and vehicle efficiency. Related developments include changes to pollution limits and fuel-economy standards, along with potential increases in household energy costs.

• The Trump EPA plans to erase climate pollution limits for coal and gas power plants.

• The U.S. EPA has scrapped most Biden-era power-plant climate rules and targets the remaining protections.

• Washington is considering a methane rollback for low-output wells responsible for half of oil-and-gas methane pollution.

• U.S. households could face higher energy costs by 2040 as clean-energy projects get axed.

New Jersey’s largest planned AI data center, DataOne, has stirred controversy since day one.

Persistent noise complaints, unpermitted construction and a contentious zoning process have plagued the project since it broke ground last year, but it wasn’t until the state fined the company more than $1 million last month over its fleet of unpermitted gas-powered generators that DataOne became international news.

A new short documentary from Floodlight shows how a thermal drone investigation in August first brought these generators to light, and how the Vineland community reacted to learning what was spewing into their air.

“What am I breathing in? What am I being exposed to?” said Tiffany Leone-Vespa, who lives about a mile from the generator fleet. “It's terrifying for me.”

Following New Jersey’s record fine against DataOne, Floodlight obtained public records showing the unpermitted generator fleet was capable of emitting staggering amounts of air pollution and had been operating for nearly a year before state regulators intervened. Floodlight also asked Ed Potosnak, commissioner for the state’s Department of Environmental Protection, why his agency was allowing the facility to continue running the generators despite the lack of permits.

As seen in the video, Potosnak refused to answer, instead suggesting to a Floodlight reporter that they set up a time for an interview. His office would later refuse that interview request.

Today, DataOne continues operating its fleet of generators as it works toward “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution,” according to its spokesperson.

Despite initially claiming they would apply for the necessary permits, the company has since requested a hearing to contest the state’s fine and argue the generators do not require permits.

Under the state’s enforcement order, DataOne has until November 6 to apply for the permits or stop operating them.

description:

However, demand for critical minerals from other sectors, such AI, is rising and amid heightened geopolitical rivalry and rearmament, demand from the defence sector has been growing fast.

Countries including China are contributing to those energy transition projects globally, but much more progress is required.

text:
Ahead of COP31 in Türkiye (9 – 20 November), IDS researchers call for critical minerals to be prioritised for clean electrification and a just energy transition, as the UN warns that a “massive global scale-up” of renewables is required to get global temperature targets back on track.

Critical minerals, like lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earths are vital components for solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicle technologies. However, demand for critical minerals from other sectors, such AI, is rising and amid heightened geopolitical rivalry and rearmament, demand from the defence sector has been growing fast.

Forthcoming research by Anabel Marin and Phil Johnstone for the Transition Security Project highlights concerning trends in this regard. Based on data from the International Energy Agency, they find that only 29% of copper and 17% of nickel and 20% of rare earths were used in energy technologies in 2024.

They also estimate that military applications account for around 10% of global copper consumption, while defence and aerospace account for 33% of chromium and 17% of beryllium. Of 36 rare minerals used in strategic technologies, drones require all of them, compared with around a dozen each for solar panels and wind turbines.

Prioritise critical minerals for renewables, not war

With this growing competition for these scarce critical minerals, IDS researchers warn that to achieve climate goals, critical minerals must be prioritised for renewable energies and not diverted for use in defence systems and weapons of war.

Anabel Marin, Senior Research Fellow, Institute of Development Studies, said:

“Despite being extracted in the name of the transition, critical minerals are increasingly used for other agendas, including data centres, and fossil fuel infrastructure and – most concerningly – in defence.

“At next week’s COP31, military use of minerals must be part of the climate change discussions. International leaders need to recognise that the scale of the energy transition required cannot be achieved without peace.”

In addition to discussing the military use of minerals at COP31, and prioritising them for uses that serve climate goals, IDS researchers recommend that countries report demand for critical minerals by use, including military, and support including destination and use in the global traceability framework proposed by the UN Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals. They also advocate for reciprocal transparency to be built into critical-minerals partnerships, along with support for mineral producing countries to develop traceability to final destination.

China’s role in renewables globally

One of COP31 priorities is to increase the global electrification rate to 35% by 2035. Progress on the renewable energies that rely on critical minerals has been made, with solar and wind power leading the way for increasing renewable electricity production. Countries including China are contributing to those energy transition projects globally, but much more progress is required. Only solar photovoltaics and electric vehicles are on track to meet 2050 Net Zero Emissions targets.

IDS, in partnership with the International Institute of Green Finance (IIGF), has been tracking China’s role in renewables globally. New analysis from the latest quarterly report from ‘The Landscape of Chinese Overseas Renewable Energy Projects’ research shows how China’s overseas renewable energy engagement is expanding across power supply, storage, and the industries that support their deployment.

Solar projects supported by China – via finance or technological capabilities – remained the largest generation category, with wind and storage project numbers increasing year on year. Geographically South-eastern Asia has the highest number of renewable energy projects supported by China, while several large developments are underway in Central Asia, Northern Africa and Western Asia.

For example, the Abydos II solar and battery storage project in Egypt combines Chinese engineering with international developers and development finance to deliver solar and storage infrastructure. In Malaysia, the Chinese company EVE Energy has its first overseas mass-production hub that will add 38 GWh of annual energy-storage battery capacity. The project illustrates a mode of Chinese overseas engagement that differs from mainstream project activities: manufacturing FDI (foreign direct investment) that builds a host-country industrial base, rather than the delivery of a generation asset.

text:
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. — A coalition of major environmental groups has formally urged the Environmental Protection Agency to abandon its proposal to stop regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, calling the plan “fundamentally unlawful,” the Union of Concerned Scientists said Nov. 4.

The comments, filed with the EPA late on Nov. 3, argue that the proposal conflicts with U.S. Supreme Court precedent and would gut key clean air protections, according to the science advocacy group, which signed the filing.

Other signers were Clean Air Task Force, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice, Environmental Defense Fund, Environmental Law & Policy Center, the Natural Resources Defense Council and the Sierra Club. Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin and Friends of the Earth also endorsed the comments, the group said.

Central to the EPA proposal, according to the groups, is the agency’s contention that limiting power plant emissions would be “futile” because the plants account for only part of the climate problem. Power plants are the nation’s second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions.

Editor’s note: The Trump administration is frequently dishonest, and has been known to lie about things great and small.

The groups said that futility analysis has no legal foundation or rational basis and is arbitrary and capricious. The filing says the EPA must withdraw the supplemental proposal “in its entirety,” according to the release.

The comments include new expert modeling that, the groups said, shows uncontrolled U.S. power plant greenhouse gases would cause $20.4 trillion in harm to human health and welfare by 2100, even using the EPA’s own emissions projections. By comparison, U.S. gross domestic product was $29.3 trillion in 2024, the release noted.

Under the EPA’s projections, the groups said, carbon pollution from power plants would also cause more than 100,000 childhood asthma cases, 22,000 hospital or emergency room visits and 1.8 million lost school days by 2100.

Scientists at the Union of Concerned Scientists contributed an appendix challenging the EPA’s reliance on global average surface temperature and global average sea level as the only measures of climate harm. The group said that approach runs counter to the scientific consensus that seemingly small increases in those measures bring compounding risks to Americans’ health and welfare.

Federal agencies are generally required to consider public comments before finalizing a rule.

This report is based on information from the Union of Concerned Scientists.

title: America got the anti-data-center wave it voted for. Here come the economic consequences
description:
And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted.
Unsustainable growth Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
text:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.

That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy.

Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.

That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.

But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.

Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.

But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.

Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.

What’s $1 trillion between friends?

AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.

The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.

Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.

But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).

State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.

Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.

The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.

If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.

“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.

Unsustainable growth

Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.

Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.

But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.

Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.

The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report, and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio, a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.

If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.

Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.

In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.

Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.

A path forward

“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.

Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.

“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.

It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.

The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.

A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.

There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.

“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

text:
Bridgepoint-owned Energy Capital Partners (ECP) has agreed to sell US low-carbon biofuels producer Harvestone Low Carbon Partners (HLCP) to Nasdaq-listed agribusiness The Andersons for an enterprise value of $915m (€815m).

HLCP operates three corn-based ethanol biorefineries across North Dakota and Indiana with a combined capacity of nearly 220m gallons per year.

Under ECP’s ownership, the platform was developed into one of the first commercial-scale ethanol carbon capture and sequestration platforms in the US.

Matt Delaney, partner at ECP, said: “HLCP demonstrates what active ownership can achieve in the energy transition. In less than four years, we partnered with an outstanding management team to bring one of the first US ethanol carbon capture and sequestration projects online and built a pipeline of attractive growth opportunities across the platform.

text:
Ozona CCS, a San Antonio-based carbon management company, announced a final investment decision (FID) on the Pawnee Carbon Sequestration Project, a 50/50 joint venture with Marubeni in Bee County in southern Texas.

The project is designed to capture carbon dioxide from a StarTex Field Services natural gas treating facility then compress, transport, and permanently store it underground. Ozona is set to build and operate the facilities, and investment company Marubeni is tapped to lead marketing and commercialization of carbon credits generated by the project. The companies are targeting first injection in the first quarter of 2027.

The project plans to use an existing well, O’Neal Gas Unit No. 4, to inject the gas. Ozona has said the well and associated storage area has a potential capacity of about 400,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide annually and reported that an injection test into the Sligo formation was successful.

“Pawnee moves our strategy from development into construction and ultimately operations,” Ozona CEO Rich Adams said. He said the project could expand as additional carbon dioxide sources are connected.

The companies said they also are evaluating other carbon capture and storage opportunities in Texas.

In 2024, the US Environmental Protection Agency approved a monitoring, reporting, and verification plan for the O’Neal No. 4 well. The plan calls for the well’s injection interval in the Sligo formation to be approximately 14,924 ft below the base of the underground source of drinking water. The plan states that the well will be used to inject a CO2 stream containing 98.2% CO2, 0.4% H2S, 1.03% hydrocarbons, and 0.37% nitrogen.
