title: Building an efficient European nuclear energy supply chain - Clean Air Task Force
description:
As Europe accelerates its clean energy transition and works to strengthen its energy security, nuclear energy has re-emerged as a vital pillar of the continent’s low-carbon future.
However, scaling up a fleet of conventional reactors and SMRs exposes a critical vulnerability in the clean energy supply chain: workforce.
If we are to build a European nuclear energy supply chain capable of delivering at scale, we must treat skilled human capital as a shared, flexible asset across the region.
Reviving a proven framework: The Nuclear Skills Passport Two decades ago, the UK’s National Skills Academy Nuclear (NSAN) introduced a groundbreaking concept: the Nuclear Skills Passport.
The Nuclear Skills Passport can function as a secure, standardised digital record of a worker’s training, safety credentials, security clearances, and technical competencies.
text:
As Europe accelerates its clean energy transition and works to strengthen its energy security, nuclear energy has re-emerged as a vital pillar of the continent’s low-carbon future. Meeting ambitious climate targets, ensuring energy security and competitiveness at the same time requires moving away from one-off, bespoke reactor builds and embracing a shift toward fleet deployment. Standardised, repeatable construction models lower capital costs, streamline regulatory oversight, and dramatically shorten build schedules.

This model is especially critical for small modular reactors (SMRs). Because SMRs are designed to be factory-manufactured and rapidly assembled on site, their economic viability relies heavily on swift, standardised, and overlapping deployment schedules across multiple locations.

However, scaling up a fleet of conventional reactors and SMRs exposes a critical vulnerability in the clean energy supply chain: workforce.

According to the European Commission’s Nuclear Illustrative Programme (PINC) report, the EU may see more than 60GW of new nuclear projects between now and 2025. To deliver multiple reactors across Member States within tight climate deadlines, Europe cannot afford localised labor shortages or fragmented qualification systems. Building a resilient nuclear energy supply chain requires a dynamic, mobile, and highly trained workforce that can seamlessly transition from one construction site to another across national borders.

The bottleneck: Workforce mobility across the fleet

Deploying nuclear energy at a fleet scale – particularly for SMR rollouts – creates a sequential, high-tempo demand for specialised labor. Specialised welders, quality assurance engineers, civil technicians, and radiation protection experts are needed in high concentrations during specific, condensed phases of construction.

Once an SMR unit’s site preparation or specialised module integration is complete, that skilled team must be ready to shift immediately to the next site – whether that is in Poland, France, the Czech Republic, or Sweden. Without efficient mobility mechanisms, the velocity advantage inherent to SMR fleet deployment is severely compromised.

Today, cross-border workforce mobility faces significant non-technological barriers. Redundant site-access vetting, varied national accreditation and safety standards, and fragmented vocational training requirements create administrative friction. Experienced professionals often spend weeks or months re-certifying skills they have already demonstrated elsewhere, stalling momentum and inflating project budgets.

If we are to build a European nuclear energy supply chain capable of delivering at scale, we must treat skilled human capital as a shared, flexible asset across the region.

Reviving a proven framework: The Nuclear Skills Passport

Two decades ago, the UK’s National Skills Academy Nuclear (NSAN) introduced a groundbreaking concept: the Nuclear Skills Passport. Recognised for its merit, the proposal was evaluated by the European Commission and considered across several nuclear energy-capable nations as a model for workforce standardisation.

At the time, some top industry players expressed concerns that such a tool would increase worker mobility after expensive and time-consuming vocational trainings and turn the labor market into a competitive “free-for-all,” potentially making worker retention harder for individual operators. However, today’s reality demands a shift in perspective. If Europe is to build a truly robust, resilient, and integrated supply chain, we must actively support workforce mobility rather than restrict it. A localised workforce model cannot sustain a multi-national fleet deployment strategy; cross-border fluidity is precisely what will allow both conventional builds and SMR fleets to remain on schedule and within budget.

It is time to formally reintroduce and elevate this framework into a recognised European vocational tool, endorsed and adopted by the European Nuclear Alliance and Member States.

The Nuclear Skills Passport can function as a secure, standardised digital record of a worker’s training, safety credentials, security clearances, and technical competencies. Implementing this tool across Europe would deliver key structural benefits:

Clear pathways for workers: It can provide vocational professionals with a transparent roadmap of their qualifications, career progression, and continuous professional development, making the nuclear energy sector more attractive to young talent and transitioning skilled labor from traditional industries.

Streamlined hiring for employers: Contractors and plant operators could gain verified, instant visibility into an applicant’s qualifications, dramatically accelerating onboarding times while reducing administrative costs across supply chains.

Uncompromising safety standards: A standardised passport can embed rigorous, European recognised safety and quality standards across all participating sites, reinforcing the nuclear energy sector’s core priority: safety above all.

Ready for execution: Built on EHRO-N research

Implementing a unified European vocational passport does not require starting from scratch. The groundwork has already been laid by the European Human Resources Observatory in Nuclear (EHRO-N).

Through extensive research and mapping, EHRO-N developed comprehensive job profiles and specified the exact skill sets, competencies, and learning outcomes required across the life cycle of nuclear energy facilities. By aligning the Nuclear Skills Passport directly with EHRO-N’s established job profiles, European institutions can bypass years of preliminary mapping and rapidly deploy a functional system.

Moving from ambition to deployment

Deploying a clean energy fleet – from gigawatt-scale plants to versatile SMRs – is an infrastructure challenge that requires proactive, highly coordinated planning. A supply chain is only as strong as the skilled people who build it.

To turn Europe’s nuclear ambitions into physical infrastructure, European policymakers, national regulators, and industry leaders must prioritize workforce logistics. Recognizing the Nuclear Skills Passport as an official European vocational tool will unlock cross-border mobility, protect worker safety, and build the resilient supply chain necessary to deliver clean energy at scale.

description:

text:
Greetings Agents of Impact!

In today’s Brief:

Economic and climate resilience in North Carolina

Fractal regenerative farming

A marketplace for ethical M&A

Builders Vision’s new CEO

Featured: Power in Place

In North Carolina, community investments in economic resilience paid it forward when disaster struck (video). The growing network of hiking and mountain biking trails in the Pisgah National Forest is making the small North Carolina town of Old Fort a mecca of outdoor recreation. At least two dozen new businesses have come in to revive its struggling downtown. That’s by design. “As soon as we opened the first six miles of trails, you saw six businesses open in town,” says Jason McDougald of Camp Grier, a summer camp for kids in Old Fort and one of the drivers of the economic development strategy built around outdoor recreation. With 21 miles of trails, 24 businesses have opened since 2022. McDougald describes the strategy in the first episode of “Power in Place,” ImpactAlpha’s series of short-form documentaries that illustrate the ability of local communities to invest in their own futures. Upcoming episodes will illuminate such “place-based” financial ecosystems in Philadelphia, Chicago, Minneapolis, New Jersey and other geographies.

Mutual aid. The 15-minute video shows how investments in community networks and leadership enabled the remarkable resilience and mutual aid in Western North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene, which hit the area in September 2024. “We forgot about anything else but serving each other,” says Stephanie Swepson-Twitty of Eagle Market Streets Development Corp., a local small business lender, in the new documentary. In Asheville, “the same people who you might assume needed support were offering support to the neighborhood,” says Alan Ramirez of PODER Emma, a cooperative social enterprise that became a hub of recovery efforts. In a reflective essay in Stanford Social Innovation Review, Andrew Crosson and Lauren Sowers of Invest Appalachia and Ryan Eller and Kalista Pepper of Appalachia Funders Network write, “The architecture of Appalachian recovery offers lessons for any region where post-extraction economies meet climate vulnerability.”

Community quarterbacks. Helping advance such efforts is Dogwood Health Trust, a $2 billion health conversion foundation that focuses on economic opportunity in Western North Carolina, and Invest Appalachia, a regional investment intermediary for the six states of central Appalachia. Dogwood helped mobilize commitments from national foundations. The MacArthur and Robert Wood Johnson foundations were among the investors in Invest Appalachia’s $35.5 million first fund. “They provide the capital, and we, because of our ecosystem and relationships on the ground, connect that capital,” Crosson says. In Old Fort, Invest Appalachia made a loan to Eagle Market Streets for the Catawba Vale Innovation Hub, a downtown commercial space that is incubating small businesses. “The reason you need hubs like Invest Appalachia to do this work is they’re deeply ingrained in community,” Dogwood’s Jerry Kenney says. “The role of Dogwood is we help unlock additional capital for them.”

Place-based. MacArthur Foundation provided support for the“Power in Place”series to illustrate what it means for national investors to support “place-based strategies that are locally conceived and deeply community-informed,” says MacArthur’s Allison Clark. Place-based investing is “having a moment,” Clark adds, because of the pullback in federal funding for community development and in recognition of the importance of “building a collective sense of community impact and purpose.” In Minneapolis, GroundBreak Coalition is looking to raise more than $5 billion over 10 years to close racial wealth gaps and shift the flow of capital into homeownership, small businesses and commercial real estate. “Minneapolis’ story was born out of the murder of George Floyd, but there’s something richer and deeper there: What this community is choosing to build,” says GroundBreak’s Adair Mosley. “We’re in a moment where we need to unleash the power of people and place.”

Keep reading, “In North Carolina, community investments in economic resilience paid it forward when disaster struck,” by Tiffani Hart.

Cash: The most overlooked asset class in the impact space. Today, more than $18 trillion in cash sits in US bank accounts, yet cash is typically viewed as a passive asset, held for spending, operations or emergencies. KEEP transforms otherwise idle cash into a catalyst for community impact. Through a network of more than 1,000 financial institutions (community banks, CDFIs, MDIs and low-income designated credit unions), KEEP helps direct deposits to the institutions that support local businesses, farms and municipalities nationwide.

KEEP is a cash solution designed exclusively for advisors and their clients. It combines high levels of federal insurance, a competitive yield and liquidity with meaningful impact; demonstrating that cash can do more than preserve wealth, it can generate real impact for real people. Request KEEP impact report.

Dealflow: Impact First

Social Finance invests in FARM Fund to support regenerative agriculture in the US. The Boston-based nonprofit impact investor committed $2.5 million to Fractal Agriculture Regenerative Management, or FARM, Fund, managed by Fractal Agriculture. FARM Fund makes equity investments in US-based row-crop farms, then allows farmers to buy back the share of their farms that they sell, getting a discount for each regenerative practice they implement. It made the investment from its Impact First Fund, a vehicle Social Finance launched in 2023 to invest in high-impact businesses and funds. Social Finance announced the investment along with its investment in Enable Ventures, a tech venture capital fund that has raised more than $50 million to invest in disability-focused solutions. Social Finance said both funds invest in enterprises that aren’t a fit for conventional financing. “Each fit what the Impact First Fund looks for: a first-time manager, a population others have overlooked, and a market solution that could benefit from greater access to capital,” the Social Finance team said in a statement. Check it out.

In other impact deal news:

Conservation finance. Fondation Valery provided a six-year, impact-linked loan to NatureRe to buy and restore degraded land in Colombia’s Antioquia region. NatureRe, a Swiss land regeneration company, has been working in the region since 2022 with a goal of restoring about 11,000 hectares of land that was wrecked by cattle grazing. It employs the former ranchers as forest rangers. The loan will support a roughly 1,700-acre plot. NatureRe will repay the loan’s interest in carbon credits. (Fondation Valery)

Circular economy. Aruwa Capital Management led a growth equity round for Polysmart Packaging, a plastic recycling company in Nigeria. The company helps divert plastic waste from landfills and the environment through direct collection and by working with Nigeria’s informal waste collectors. In addition to capital, Aruwa has supported the company in building its governance structures and practices and helped it appoint women to 40% of its board seats. (Aruwa Capital Management)

Private debt. Also in Nigeria, TLG Capital provided a line of credit to Koolboks, a company that makes solar-powered freezers and sells them on a pay-as-you-go basis to curb food, vaccine and pharmaceutical waste. TLG’s loan, under its guaranteed lending model, is backstopped by the Cascador entrepreneurship network and Morgan Stanley. (TLG Capital)

Energy transition. Two Point O Capital raised $10 million to help companies in India finance and install renewable energy and water management systems. The company primarily serves businesses in the automotive, pharmaceutical, manufacturing and healthcare sectors. It’s also looking at data centers. The round was backed by Transition Venture Capital, existing investor Omnivore and several individuals. (YourStory)

Signals: Impact Exits

Steward Market builds a marketplace for ethical mergers and acquisitions. Hannah Sandmeyer once sourced acquisitions for Thrasio, a $10 billion retail brand rollup that went bankrupt in 2024. She’s flipping the M&A playbook with Steward Market, a subscription-based marketplace that connects sellers of mission-driven businesses with values-aligned buyers. The goal is to enable more B Corps and social enterprises to navigate ownership transitions that preserve their mission and values. “Sellers deserve dignity in this process,” Sandmeyer tells ImpactAlpha. B Corps have shown their models work, but “we have not answered that they can survive an ownership change,” says Sandmeyer, who hosts the “Ethical Exits” podcast. Steward Market sorts listings by values and certifications, and lets buyers signal their ownership intentions, from converting to employee ownership to keeping teams together. “It’s not about just selling your business,” she says, “but finding your steward.”

Values-aligned. Sandmeyer pitches the marketplace as a way to enable more exits like Patagonia’s, which became steward-owned when the company’s founder Yvon Chouinard placed its voting shares in a perpetual purpose trust and directed its profits to fighting climate change (see, “Exit to stakeholders”). Buyers on Steward Market include a Michigan holding company acquiring small manufacturing businesses; a B corp seeking purpose-driven consulting firms, and a New England ESOP holding company. Capital providers on the platform include Regenerative Social Finance, Beneficial State Bank and AllHold Capital, a Philadelphia-based funder that helps transition local businesses and the real estate they occupy into employee-owned trusts. Legal and exit planning advisors include the Washington Center for Employee Ownership and Up & Over Advisors, a mission-driven M&A sourcing firm Sandmeyer founded in 2024.

Steward ownership. Steward Market is seeking $500,000 in patient capital, such as revenue-based financing or redeemable equity, as the company charts its own transition to steward ownership through a perpetual purpose trust (see, “‘Purpose trusts’ power a business movement toward broader ownership and stakeholder governance”). “Hannah’s quest is to turn M&A upside down, from a cutthroat world where price rules all, to a place where purpose joins with profits,” says John Abrams, founder of employee-owned South Mountain Co. and one of Steward Market’s early backers. Steward Market works with Impact Charitable on a donor-advised fund where sellers, buyers and advisors can allocate a small slice of a deal’s value, or the fees earned from it, for grants to finance steward and employee-owned companies.

Keep reading, “Steward Market builds a values-first marketplace for ethical mergers and acquisitions,” by Roodgally Senatus.

Agents of Impact: Follow the Talent

Builders Vision names Matt Knott as its CEO. Knott has served as interim head of the $20 billion investment and philanthropy platform for the past year… Village Capital adds George Sandilands to its board… Finnfund promotes Kristian Stenbacka to investment associate… Center for Sustainable Finance and Private Wealth adds Günther Dobrauz-Saldapenna, managing partner of Henley & Partners, to its global board.

British International Investment promotes Kate Perkins to debt investment director… The Nature Conservancy adds Simon Plested as global talent lead… Founders First Capital Partners is hiring a capital markets associate and a senior underwriting associate in San Diego… MCE Social Capital is on the hunt for a business development and operations analyst in Washington, DC… Closed Loop Partners has an opening for a project director for its Center for the Circular Economy in New York… CalSTRS is recruiting a chief operating officer in Sacramento, Calif.

View (or post) impact investing jobs on ImpactAlpha’s Career Hub.

Thank you for your impact!

– Nov. 5, 2026

text:
Few things could have soured last Friday's breakfast more than the news that dozens of large U.S. oil and gas companies were reporting combined profits of more than $130 billion from April through September, months in which the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran disrupted global energy markets.

That was nearly triple what the companies earned during the same period last year, according to a New York Times analysis.

Meanwhile, U.S. consumers have spent an estimated $150 billion more on gasoline and diesel since the war began, according to Al Jazeera, citing Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab. The estimate captures an added burden on consumers; it does not mean that all of that money went to oil companies as profit.

The companies did, however, benefit from the same market disruption that's squeezing consumers. Crude producers gained from higher oil prices, while refiners benefited from wider margins on gasoline, diesel and other products. When fuel supplies tighten, refined-product prices can rise faster than refiners’ crude input costs, widening the gap between the two. Al Jazeera reported that attacks and other disruptions damaged or sidelined refineries in the Middle East and Russia, while U.S. facilities were less exposed to the conflict.

Early in the war, oil executives warned that supply disruptions and falling inventories could keep prices high, even if the fighting stopped. Exxon CFO Neil Hansen acknowledged the pressure on families and businesses, while arguing that companies could not quickly add capacity: “The decisions that matter today were made years ago.” (According to Exxon's most recent filings, Mr. Hansen is eligible for long-term and bonus equity grants on top of his $1.02 million annual base salary.)

That may help explain why supply cannot quickly respond to a shock. But it offers little comfort to families paying more at the pump, and it does not erase the striking contrast between those costs and the industry’s profits.

For climate advocates, the contrast is hard to miss: Fossil-fuel companies are posting enormous profits as consumers face higher fuel bills, while a law President Donald J. Trump signed last year ended federal tax credits for clean vehicles and residential clean energy and accelerated the phaseout of wind and solar incentives. Yet tax preferences for fossil-fuel interests remain.

The Congressional Research Service puts the largest of those benefits at about $19 billion over five years. That figure covers a range of provisions, including carbon-capture support, as well as tax preferences that apply to oil and gas exploration and production.

This does not mean the tax code caused this price spike or that ending fossil-fuel preferences would lower pump prices. Oil trades globally, and refinery capacity takes time to restore. But policy choices shape the energy system consumers will rely on for years. Ending credits for electric vehicles, efficiency improvements and renewable power while preserving tax advantages for fossil-fuel production signals which investments Washington supports.

Policymakers should ask whether those choices will make households less exposed to the next global energy disruption, or keep them dependent on fuels whose prices can surge because of events far beyond their control.

If policymakers can change the tax code to withdraw support from electric vehicles and renewable energy, they can reconsider the preferences that remain for fossil fuels. When energy prices surge, they should ask whose interests those choices serve.

(The Center Square) - President Donald Trump’s energy dominance policies could face challenges after sweeping election victories by Democrats at both the state and national levels, energy market experts say.
When the new Congress is seated in January, incoming Democratic majorities are expected to push efforts to increase oversight of methane emissions, limit drilling on federal lands and in offshore areas, and tighten environmental permitting requirements on new plants and equipment.
Trump declared an energy emergency during his first hours in office in January 2025, invoking the National Emergencies Act to accelerate fossil fuel development. In a flurry of executive orders since then, the president has made U.S. energy dominance one of his primary economic objectives, framing it as a matter of national security.

, told The Center Square that attempts by newly elected Democratic majorities to roll back those executive actions will be neutralized by Trump’s veto pen.
"They can do Congressional Review Act resolutions on his rulemakings," Pyle said — referring to the fast-track legislative tool Congress can use to overturn federal rules adopted since the president took office. "They can pass them, but they’ll be vetoed."
Pyle noted that while a Democratic majority can leverage committee leadership positions to launch investigations and issue subpoenas, the president’s veto will still leave the Trump administration's core deregulatory agenda – and the sweeping legislative victories won through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed last year – largely intact.
“It’s one thing to make a bunch of campaign promises. It’s another thing to deliver on them," Pyle said. "Democrats will have a very difficult challenge if they intend to try to undo the very policies that President Trump has enacted that make it easier to produce energy, easier to move it around this country."
Pyle said election results at the state level are a reason to worry. “The story of the night is Texas — it really was a wipeout,” said Pyle. “Texas Democrats will need to tread very carefully because oil and gas is their bread and butter. It will be interesting to see how the Democrats in Texas treat the industry there,” said Pyle.
Ed Hirs, an energy fellow and energy economist at the University of Houston, said the Democrats' control of Congress will have little effect on U.S. energy production. He said it is global markets and prices — not Washington politics — that really drive American energy production.
America had energy dominance under President Biden, too, and had approached it during the Obama years, Hirs said. Now, with energy prices high because of geopolitical events, the nation’s oil and gas production is at a new record level, said Hirs.
“Trump has ensured the energy dominance of the United States, perhaps inadvertently, by undertaking this war against Iran,” Hirs told The Center Square. “We are now facing several years of having higher oil and LNG prices, which will benefit the United States, for sure.”
While gross national product will be higher, gasoline prices will be, too, said Hirs. “But prices are higher because of the war, not because of market conditions,” he said.
Hirs added that high global crude oil prices have begun to depress consumption in the United States. "U.S. consumption of crude and refined products dropped by more than 2% last year because of those higher prices,” said Hirs.

text:
The UK government has moved to ban any new exploration for oil and gas in the North Sea.

The Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority's ability to grant new oil and gas licences.

The legislation will not affect the decision on whether to allow drilling at Rosebank off Shetland - the UK's largest known untapped field - which was approved in 2022 before being subject to legal challenges.

The UK government said it was upholding Labour's 2024 manifesto vow not to issue licences for new oil and gas fields, as well as underpinning its commitment to reducing global warming.

The Conservatives described the bill as "dangerous" and accused Labour ministers of being "totally oblivious to the economic and energy threats this country faces".

SNP energy spokesman Graham Leadbitter said the legislation was "designed to exploit Scotland's energy" and reinforced the case for independence.

The Energy Independence Bill, if passed at Westminster, would introduce Transitional Energy Certificates, which would allow existing oil and gas fields to provide additional production from "areas bordering or in close proximity to already licensed fields" or in areas that are already part of an existing field.

The government said the move could produce about 60 million barrels of oil and support hundreds of jobs.

It vowed to sustain "growth and investment across North Sea communities as the energy sector transitions".

The wide-ranging bill would also formally scrap gas standing charges and introduce reforms designed to speed up grid connections.

The UK government has also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Together, these changes will bring bills down for good, give families greater security and put Britain back in control of its energy future."

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the bill would help to "build a clean energy future which people feel in their pockets, households and communities, ensuring support reaches those who need it most".

It comes two weeks after the UK government approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

Ministers said the site, off the coast of Aberdeen, would help heat millions of homes.

Environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank were approved by the previous Conservative government.

However, after being subject to legal challenges from environmental groups, Labour ministers have had to decide whether to continue with the projects.

Situated 80 miles north-west of Shetland, Rosebank is thought to contain between 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.

Backers say it would be a vital lifeline to the energy industry in the north east of Scotland, and improve energy security at a time when global supply chains are disrupted by conflict.

Opponents say it would accelerate the climate crisis, slow down the transition to greener energy sources and do little to improve energy security since its produce would largely be exported overseas to be refined.

Greenpeace UK called the bill a "positive step forward for the clean energy transition".

However, it called on the UK government to reject Rosebank.

Amy McCarthy, the campaign group's head of politics, said: "Saying a resounding no to this oil field - a project that would annihilate every single climate or cost-of-living benefit achieved through this bill - must be step one to securing our power and protecting lives."

Aberdeen and Grampian Chamber of Commerce chief executive Russell Borthwick argued that it made "no sense" to wind down North Sea oil and gas production.

"Britain will continue to need oil and gas for decades to come," he added.

"The question is whether we produce more of it here, supporting British jobs, investment and energy security, or pay other countries to produce it for us."

David Whitehouse, chief executive of industry body Offshore Energies UK, said the government was right to target energy affordability, but said it should also prioritise energy security.

"Today, Britain imports more than 40% of the energy it needs, leaving households and businesses exposed in an increasingly volatile world," he said.

title: October Auto Sales Slip Even as Incentives Rise - TheStreet Pro
description:

text:
In October, automakers cut prices and still sold less. U.S. light vehicle sales fell 0.8% from September on a selling day adjusted basis to a 15.5 million seasonally adjusted annual rate, down from 16.0 million in September and short of the 15.8 million consensus. At the same time, incentives went up.

Source: WardsAuto InfoBank, BofA Global Research. Chart: Sethi Associates.

A Decline Against an Easier Comparison

Bank of America Global Research analyst Alexander Perry noted the result undershot both the firm’s own 15.9 million mid-month estimate and the 15.8 million Bloomberg consensus.

He went on to say the drop reads worse than 0.8% suggests, because the bar was low. A year ago demand was light after having been pulled forward into September 2025 ahead of the expiration of electric vehicle tax credits. Perry said that makes the year-over-year decline “more notable.”

So October was the weakest selling month of 2026 other than January, even as it came against an easier comparison.

Blame Gas Prices

Perry understandably attributes the step down to “persistently elevated retail gas prices and a recent reacceleration in inflation against an already constrained affordability backdrop.” Gasoline was the single largest contributor to September’s retail sales gain, with pump prices near $4.50 a gallon, as I wrote in Gasoline Fuels Most of the Retail Sales Beat in September.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau. Chart: Sethi Associates.

The Increase in Incentives Was All Detroit

Industry average incentives rose to $3,493 a vehicle in October, up 0.6% from September, although year over year the average is still down 2.3%. But both of those headline numbers hide the same split. All of it was from the Detroit Three. Ford (F), GM (GM) and Stellantis (STLA) raised incentive spending 7.3% between them. The rest of the automakers cut it.

The Detroit Three raised incentive spending to $4,132 a vehicle. Everyone else cut it an estimated 3.9%, to roughly $3,122. Over the year the divide is even wider: Detroit up 13.4%, the rest of the industry down 11.6%. A year ago the two groups were spending within about $110 a vehicle of each other. They are now roughly $1,010 apart.

Getting more granular, Ford spent $4,598 a vehicle, up 16.5% from a year ago and 10.7% from September, putting it 31.6% above the industry average for the second straight month. General Motors spent $3,499, up 14.0% year over year and 15.3% from September, as it works down 2026 model year inventory. Stellantis remains the heaviest spender at $4,788, up 10.0% year over year though down 5.2% from September, and has moved closer to the pack at 37.1% above average from 50.3% the month before.

Source: BofA Global Research. Prior-period levels and the weighted and implied figures derived per Claude. Chart: Sethi Associates.

Now set that against sales. Detroit Three volumes fell 5.4% year over year and European brands fell 6.6%, while Japanese brands rose 4.2% and Korean brands rose 5.6%. So Detroit is discounting harder but still losing volume.

Source: WardsAuto InfoBank, BofA Global Research. Chart: Sethi Associates.

BofA Is Not Cutting Its Full-Year Estimate

Despite the soft month, Perry still sees 2026 finishing near 16.1 million, in line with where the firm started the year. The year-to-date pace stands at 16.0 million against 16.3 million in 2025.

Gas Prices Are Also Showing Up in Unit Mix

Elevated gas prices are also shifting the mix. Hybrid sales rose 20.3% year over year in October, lifting hybrid share 2.3 percentage points to 15.9%. Perry said that “may reflect consumers gravitating toward hybrids amid a prolonged period of elevated gasoline and diesel prices.”

Source: WardsAuto InfoBank, BofA Global Research. Chart: Sethi Associates.

After today’s data the two Q4 GDP trackers that updated are telling different stories, which is not unusual at this point in a quarter.

After this morning’s trade report, Goldman Sachs raised its Q4 GDP tracking estimate by 0.1 percentage point to 1.9%, citing a trade deficit that “narrowed by $0.7bn to $105.0bn in September, below expectations.”

Goldman doesn’t provide a component breakdown of their GDP tracker.

The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow, meanwhile, eased to 3.44% as of November 4, down from 3.74% on November 2 but still above its 3.22% initiation on October 29. It was driven mostly by a 0.17 percentage point pullback in the contribution from consumption (to 1.77 points from 1.94), with smaller declines in inventories (−0.05 point), net exports (−0.04) and residential investment (−0.03).

That leaves Goldman just below the Blue Chip consensus* of roughly 2.1% and GDPNow well above it, a gap of about 1.5 percentage points between the two.

History suggests the gap is more likely to close from the Atlanta Fed’s side. Its tracker started very strong in each of Q1, Q2 and Q3 before falling sharply as we approached the actual GDP reads: Q1 went from 3.13% to 1.99%, Q2 from 3.70% to 1.50%, and Q3 from 4.95% to 3.37% (more here: GDPNow Tracking Slowdown in Q4). Its first reading for a quarter has come in above the actual print in 34 of the last 57 quarters (excluding 2020). Goldman, for its part, was at 3.30% for Q3 the week before the release, within a tenth of the actual 3.37%, although its tracker has started the last two quarters below where it ended up.

Here’s GDPNow’s breakdown of the components as of November 4 and changes from my last update November 2:

Consumption = +1.77% (−0.17%)

Nonresidential fixed investment (business spending) = +1.34% (−0.02%)

Inventories = +0.55% (−0.05%)

Government = +0.21% (0.00%)

Residential investment = +0.02% (−0.03%)

Net exports = −0.46% (−0.04%)

GDPNow forecast: +3.44% (−0.30%)

*The top (bottom) 10 average forecast is an average of the highest (lowest) 10 forecasts in the Blue Chip survey.

Ahead of the election, there was much concern about the impact of a “Blue Wave” Democratic sweep on equities, particularly those related to the AI trade given the expressed desire from many Democratic candidates to slow the growth of data centers.

Predictably, as early returns showing just such a result came in Tech stocks fell with Nasdaq-100 futures down about 1.5% at midnight, but as of this morning, traders were rethinking things with those futures now higher and the S&P 500 indicated to open up around 1.2%. Meta Platforms (META), Amazon (AMZN), Nvidia (NVDA) and Alphabet (GOOGL) all trading higher before the open Bloomberg reported.

That may be because the first read from most analysts is that the Democratic sweep slows the AI data center buildout rather than stops it.

A Bigger Sweep Than Expected

Bloomberg reports that 54 Senate seats (a majority) are now in the hands of the Democrats with Alaska likely to follow (according to Goldman) and Mississippi a coin toss. In the House, Goldman sees a popular-vote margin of roughly 12 to 14 points, consistent with a majority of around 255 seats (Bloomberg has that currently at 232 Democrats). Its economists don’t think the Senate flip changes the federal outlook much, since the House was already expected to turn.

The bigger change perhaps is in the statehouses. Republicans lost governor’s races in Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Georgia and Michigan, and Democrats won full control in Pennsylvania and likely Arizona.

How Much of the Buildout Is Exposed

Goldman estimates the states likely to tighten data center rules hold about 45% of planned U.S. capacity, with Texas alone about 25%. It expects Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan to impose conditional moratoriums until new laws pass, which could end tax breaks and tighten water, power and environmental rules.

Texas is currently a key state for the buildout. Bloomberg cites SemiAnalysis putting Texas at nearly 30% of the U.S. capacity due online in 2028, and GLJ Research estimating about 13 gigawatts there is immediately exposed. GLJ expects fully permitted projects with power to keep going, while those with power but no state permits slip 12 to 18 months. Jefferies thinks new Texas rules are more likely to raise development costs than to materially shrink the pipeline, and PIMCO’s Libby Cantrill expects “a lot more sand in the gears” even without statewide moratoriums.

Similarly Goldman says Ohio was one state where Democrats didn’t run explicitly on tighter data center rules, but Bloomberg notes Governor-elect Amy Acton has called for a conditional moratorium, which matters for the cluster of projects around Columbus.

Jefferies: new Texas rules are more likely to raise development costs than to materially shrink the pipeline.

PIMCO’s Libby Cantrill expects “a lot more sand in the gears” even without statewide moratoriums.

Goldman: “In each of these states except Ohio, the Democratic side explicitly campaigned on stricter data center regulation, and we expect Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia, and Michigan to impose conditional moratoria pending new legislation restricting data centers. That legislation could end certain tax breaks (a priority for Hinojosa), tighten environmental, water, and electricity rules, and make it easier for localities to impose their own moratoria….since data centers are low on the list of priorities for voters this election, we expect that the issue will fade somewhat in importance in the ensuing months and that these moratoria will not be long-lived if they are enacted.”

So the thinking so far: slower permits and higher costs, not a shutdown.

The Positive Angle

Not everyone reads this as bad news. BofA economist Aditya Bhave notes real AI-related capital spending has grown at about a 26% annualized pace since the first quarter of 2025, a front-loaded wave he calls “symptomatic of over-investment.” Slowing it now, he argues, could lower the risk of a harder landing later.

Goldman’s head of European equities trading, Rich Privorotsky, told clients AI stocks had been “sold to death” into the vote, according to MarketWatch. He thinks companies may pull spending into 2027 to lock in today’s permitting, and that limits on new supply make capacity already running more valuable, which favors Amazon, Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet. For neocloud providers such as CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius (NBIS), he says it depends on how much of their compute is contracted versus already built. Privorotsky also expects volatility to fall quickly now that the election is over.

Beyond Data Centers

On fiscal policy, Goldman expects Democrats to reverse last year’s spending cuts, adding about 0.25% of gross domestic product to 2027 spending, per MarketWatch. The first test is December 11, when government funding runs out; Goldman sees a short-term extension to February or March as most likely. Corporate America is also bracing for a wave of congressional investigations once Democrats gain subpoena power, the Financial Times reports.

Treasury’s Quarterly Refunding announcement is out, setting auction sizes for the coming quarter. The sizes came in as expected, but the long end jumped on the release before settling back with several factors to blame for disappointment from bond bulls.

First, Treasury kept note and bond auction sizes unchanged at $125 billion for next week’s refunding auctions of 3-, 10- and 30-year securities. That means no cut to 20- and 30-year bonds, which some, including Citi, had expected this month. Treasury also repeated that it continues to see “strong demand” for bills.

Treasury also softened its guidance to holding auction sizes “for the next several quarters,” dropping “at least.” Starting in March 2027, the 7-year note will move to a new issue each quarter with two reopenings.

Second, the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee (TBAC), a panel of Wall Street bank and investor executives that advises Treasury on its debt sales, sounded less sure about that. In its report, the committee said money market fund assets “have leveled off” and that the bill market “has started to show some signs of price sensitivity.”

The committee also recommended larger coupon auctions in the second half of fiscal 2027 (April through September 2027), focused on 2- to 10-year notes, with “meaningful discussion” about future 20- and 30-year sizes. According to the meeting minutes, dealers see a $2.14 trillion funding shortfall in fiscal 2028 and 2029 at current auction sizes. Bills can cover fiscal 2027’s “modest” gap, but not that much.

The committee further advised that the mix of maturities should be managed through auction sizes, not buybacks. That came even as Treasury nearly doubled its planned liquidity buybacks this quarter, to as much as $70 billion from $38 billion in August’s plan.

As I noted in Monday’s post, bills could reach close to 24% of marketable debt by March, the highest since late 2020. The Fed has already hiked once, and markets price over two more increases over the coming year, according to the committee. If bill buyers also start demanding higher yields, it would be a double whammy for Treasury’s interest costs.

title: Natick's latest Net Zero Action Plan focuses on next 5 years
description:
Natick’s Sustainability Office has released a draft of its Net Zero Action Plan 2.0, a strategy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions over the next five years.
The plan details the town’s progress since 2021 and outlines actions residents and the municipality can take to reduce emissions.

text:
Natick’s Sustainability Office has released a draft of its Net Zero Action Plan 2.0, a strategy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions over the next five years.

The town published the draft of its 41-page plan on Oct. 9, and accepted public comments until Nov. 1. The plan details the town’s progress since 2021 and outlines actions residents and the municipality can take to reduce emissions.

“We’re really about activating our residents and doing what we can to lead by example as a town,” Director of Sustainability Jillian Wilson-Martin said.

Natick Town Meeting set a community-wide goal in 2018 to eliminate or offset greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. The appointed Natick Net Zero Action Committee was created to develop plans every five years with the Sustainability Office.

“Reaching this milestone requires making our buildings more energy-efficient, shifting to renewable power sources, and decarbonizing our transportation,” the plan says. “Together, these efforts offer a great opportunity to improve everyday life.”

The first step in creating the new plan was considering the progress Natick has made in the past five years.

“I was really proud of Natick when we completed our assessment of our ability to deliver on the initial plan because we really did do the plan and residents did it with us,” Wilson Martin said.

Of the 21 actions outlined in the 2021 plan, two have been completed, and 10 have made “meaningful” or “significant” progress. Three actions have had “minimal” progress: change zoning to make clean energy easier to install, require at least one climate-ready feature on new or replaced roofs, and partner with EV dealers to offer discounts and promote rebates.

Some actions like coaching residents on heat pumps and other clean energy will never truly be complete as Natick continues to make resident outreach programs more robust, Net Zero Action Committee Chair Kate Mora said.

Natick saw a 15% decrease in emissions since 2017, according to the most recent Greenhouse Gas Inventory completed in 2022. The drop was caused primarily by changes in how the town heats and powers homes.

“It’s hard to say that it exactly ties back exactly to this document, but I think it is part of a culture that has been building in Natick for a long time,” Mora said.

Waste was the only area where emissions increased during the five years—rising 13% because of new methods for measuring emissions, according to the plan.

In the last plan, waste disposal accounts for less than 1% of Natick’s emissions; however, the Sustainability Office and the committee chose to add a new waste category to the 2026 plan along with the previous sectors: energy, buildings and transportation.

The town will aim to reduce unnecessary waste, promote low-impact goods and packaging, and maximize reusing, repurposing, recycling and composting materials.

The new plan, featuring 25 actions, is adapted to the ever-evolving energy landscape, Wilson-Martin said.

“A lot has changed in the last five years,” she said. “Some things for good, some things for not.”

Many federal initiatives supporting climate action have been eliminated or challenged, including solar and electric vehicle tax credits and offshore wind development, the plan says.

On the state level, mandates for renewable energy currently outpace the clean electricity supply available on the grid, the plan says. As a result, the town will reevaluate the purchase of extra Renewable Energy Certificates, credits that represent clean power, that make the town’s electricity cleaner than the state requires since the certificates do not add any new renewable energy to the grid.

Instead, Natick plans to use its aggregation, or the program where the town negotiates a bulk energy deal for residents, for a low-income community shared solar program and to explore incentives that reward residents for shifting electricity use away from peak hours, according to the draft plan.

Peak demand management is a new energy focus for Natick in the 2.0 plan. The town hopes to connect residents with programs that reward them for using electricity during off-peak hours and enroll public infrastructure in demand response programs.

“We have to build our infrastructure for [peak demand], and if we actually modulate when we’re using energy, we could build less new infrastructure,” Wilson-Martin explained. “That’s the cheapest way to meet climate goals and keep things affordable.”

Amanda Elkin, a Natick resident and sustainability consultant, said the plan is a strong foundation for improvements throughout the town.

“While the plan is aspirational, it’s also well-grounded in the realities and challenges that accompany change on this level,” Elkin said.

Elkin said she hopes the town will address emissions from the closed town dump on West Street.

“Are landfill gases being captured and measured there? What are the emission-reduction impacts of the composting and waste diversion initiatives on-site?” Elkin asked.

Based on feedback the plan has received, the Sustainability Office will add more about how success will be measured in the future, Wilson Martin said.

An open house will be held to discuss the details of the plan and answer resident questions at the Morse Institute Library Wednesday, Nov. 18, from 7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m.

The sustainability office and the committee expect to publish the final plan by the end of the year, Mora said.

text:
ZF

High Revolution Drive

Thomas Meiser

ZF Unveils High Revolution Drive Operating At 30,000 RPM For Electric Vehicles

By MT Bureau

November 05, 2026

German tier-1 supplier ZF has developed the High Revolution Drive, a 3-in-1 electric drive system capable of reaching rotational speeds of up to 30,000 rpm. Designed as a variant of the company's modular SELECT platform, the unit integrates an electric motor, power electronics and a two-stage spur gear transmission with a reduction ratio of approximately 18:1. The system delivers a peak power output of 200 kW and peak wheel torque of 3,500 Nm.

Compared to a conventional SELECT drive operating at 18,000 rpm, the High Revolution Drive reduces overall installation space and weight by nearly 25 percent, while reducing required magnet mass by 50 percent. The architecture is scalable across power outputs ranging from 150 kW to 200 kW for 400-volt and 800-volt vehicle platforms, achieving a system efficiency of nearly 93 per cent. ZF is engaging with vehicle manufacturers regarding deployment, with volume production targeted for 2030.

Thomas Meiser, Head of the E-Mobility Business Unit, ZF, said, "The High Revolution Drive draws on ZF s full systems expertise. Rather than optimising individual components in isolation, we systematically coordinate the electric motor, power electronics and transmission. Robustness and low noise and vibration levels were stringent development targets from the outset. To achieve this, we considered the electric motor, gearing, bearings and tooth geometry as an integrated system. For the configuration presented, 30,000 rpm is the economic and technical sweet spot. With SELECT, we do not have to start from scratch for every new drive variant. We use our modular system to tailor new concepts to different customer requirements."

SMK Helmets is marking its international expansion at EICMA 2026, supported by distribution operations across more than 70 countries alongside dedicated regional headquarters in Europe and the United States.

The company highlighted its European division, SMK Europe, established in Reggio Emilia, Italy, in May 2026 under the leadership of Chief Executive Officer Matteo Schieppati, alongside its North American arm, Bikerz US, based in Fort Wayne, Indiana.

At the event, SMK unveiled two racing helmets, the Stratos and the Allterra Carbon, alongside Konnect, its first in-house Bluetooth communication system and Cygnus, its first flip-back helmet model.

Matteo Schieppati, CEO, SMK Helmets Europe, said, "The establishment of SMK HELMETS EUROPE is a significant move to strengthen our global presence. This strategic expansion is designed to provide dedicated commercial and logistical support to dealers and distributors across Europe, while establishing a permanent footprint in the region to optimise product and communication strategies. The new European division will serve as a hub for accelerating regional growth, ensuring streamlined supply chain operations, and delivering enhanced customer service to the company's growing network of partners. title: Fetterman, McCormick urged to back clean energy, lower costs | Opinion
description:
A new bipartisan bill aims to reduce emissions and lower energy costs for Americans.
Proponents say the bill will help connect more clean energy to the power grid, as 90% of projects in permitting queues are clean energy.
There’s a new bipartisan bill in Congress that will significantly reduce emissions, speed up clean energy, and lower energy costs for us here in Pennsylvania.
Reforming the process will help America build and connect clean energy much faster while preserving important environmental safeguards.
We need Congress to act, and passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the right next step.
text:
A new bipartisan bill aims to reduce emissions and lower energy costs for Americans.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act seeks to reform the permitting process for energy projects.

Proponents say the bill will help connect more clean energy to the power grid, as 90% of projects in permitting queues are clean energy.

Passing the bill could potentially reduce electricity bills for Americans by $19 billion, according to one analysis.

There’s a new bipartisan bill in Congress that will significantly reduce emissions, speed up clean energy, and lower energy costs for us here in Pennsylvania.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a comprehensive package of permitting reforms that was recently introduced in the Senate. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) were at the forefront of bipartisan negotiations, making sure the final product would advance climate goals and support clean energy while maintaining important environmental safeguards.

The Senate is set to take up the bill in early November, and I hope to see Sens. Fetterman and McCormick support it with a “yes” vote.

This bill is important to Pennsylvanians like me because it will lead to significant emissions reductions, which is absolutely necessary to address climate change. The bill contains strong transmission provisions that can help unlock the enormous amount of clean energy waiting to connect to the grid.

And there’s lots of clean energy waiting to come online. About 90% of projects stuck in permitting queues are clean energy projects. Reforming the process will help America build and connect clean energy much faster while preserving important environmental safeguards.

More abundant, affordable electricity will help lower energy costs for households and businesses. According to analysis by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, connecting more clean energy could reduce Americans' electricity bills by $19 billion.

Here in Pennsylvania, we need these changes. Affordability is an issue for all of us; and electricity rates have been skyrocketing even without the demand that AI data centers will add to the cost.

Simply put, the status quo isn’t working. It’s not working for the climate, which is changing rapidly. It’s not working for America’s transition to clean energy, which is going much too slowly. And it’s not working for American families, who are struggling with rising electricity costs.

We need Congress to act, and passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the right next step.

Bruce Cooper is group leader of the Slippery Rock chapter of Citizens’ Climate Lobby, a nonpartisan, grassroots advocacy organization that empowers everyday people to work together on climate policy. Find out more at cclusa.org.

name: American Energy
title: AI Data Centers Are Fueling a Nuclear Comeback
description:
It led to the closure of most of Germany’s nuclear plants, and nuclear power once again appeared to be in retreat.
As 2026 draws to a close, the question is whether this latest attempt to revive nuclear energy is gaining real traction.
According to Burt, the advantages of nuclear energy include operational reliability, zero emissions, and insulation from fuel price volatility.
IIR is tracking more than 100 nuclear energy projects across North America.
Google is working with NextEra Energy Resources to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which was shuttered in 2020.
text:
There was supposed to be a nuclear renaissance in the early 2000s. Then the Fukushima disaster in Japan halted that momentum. It led to the closure of most of Germany’s nuclear plants, and nuclear power once again appeared to be in retreat.

Today, the urgent need for more electricity to support AI data centers is giving the sector fresh impetus. Data Center Knowledge covered the trend in February. As 2026 draws to a close, the question is whether this latest attempt to revive nuclear energy is gaining real traction.

“Investment is rising for new and existing nuclear assets amid a sector revival,” said Britt Burt, an analyst at research firm Industrial Info Resource (IIR).

After years of almost no new construction investment, the nuclear spark reignited in 2024. IIR estimates that spending on new projects will total about $20 billion in 2026 and rise to nearly $50 billion by 2029. That growth is being driven not only by surging data center construction, but also by broader increases in electricity demand, the expansion of domestic manufacturing, and the need to replace aging power fleets.

Between late 2026 and 2029, IIR expects $68.3 billion in new nuclear plant spending and around $30 billion more for the expansion, maintenance, or revamp of existing facilities. A large share of that spending is expected to land in Canada, with Ontario and Alberta accounting for roughly $40 billion combined. Texas is next with $15 billion, followed by Tennessee at $10 billion.

According to Burt, the advantages of nuclear energy include operational reliability, zero emissions, and insulation from fuel price volatility. It also creates opportunities for behind-the-meter power. The challenges, however, remain formidable: massive capital costs, public opposition, potential fuel bottlenecks for advanced reactors, and a nuclear workforce that has largely aged out.

IIR is tracking more than 100 nuclear energy projects across North America. Sixty-one involve small modular reactors (SMRs), and 11 involve installing new conventional nuclear reactors. Additional projects include life extensions, modernizations, relicensing, and uprates to existing plants, as well as several efforts to restart retired nuclear assets to supply data centers.

“This signals a genuine nuclear energy revival after decades of stagnation,” Burt said.

Federal Support and Hyperscaler Deals Build Momentum

The US Department of Energy recently offered Constellation Energy a loan of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization at eight plants in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The work could add more than 1 GW to the grid. Earlier this year, the DOE also launched a program with funding support for 2.5 GW of additional nuclear capacity by 2027 and 5 GW by 2029.

Rather than waiting until the next decade for new nuclear assets to come online, the goal is to expand output from existing reactors, reopen dormant facilities, and extend the lives of older plants.

Meanwhile, hyperscalers are lending their financial muscle to a variety of nuclear projects. Amazon is working with American Electric Power and X-energy on a 1 GW SMR project in Indiana. Microsoft has a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy for power from the refurbished Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania, now known as the Crane Clean Energy Center. Google is working with NextEra Energy Resources to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center, which was shuttered in 2020.

SMRs, Restarts, and Fusion Expand Nuclear’s Role

Multiple types of nuclear initiatives are now underway. In addition to restarting or refurbishing older plants and developing new SMR designs, nuclear fusion is drawing greater attention.

Bellevue, Washington-based ExoFusion is among the companies focused on fusion design, simulation, and innovation. At the Data Center World Power conference in late September 2026, ExoFusion CEO Romi Mahajan outlined an energy stack built from multiple generation technologies. Rather than treating renewables, natural gas, and nuclear as competing alternatives, he argued that all of them will play a part in tomorrow’s energy mix and in providing reliable power for data centers and AI workloads. That view aligns with the approach many hyperscale developers are taking as they pursue every available avenue to secure the power they need.

Far from being purely theoretical, fusion is moving forward along the development timeline. Type One Energy, based in Knoxville, Tennessee, plans to start construction of a fusion power plant at the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run Energy Complex in Clinton, Tennessee, in 2027.

“The prototype’s purpose is to validate assumptions, advance open science, and [help] train a workforce rather than solve immediate data center power needs,” said Patrick Ellis, director of business development at Type One Energy.

Some of Type One Energy’s design elements are already operating at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and at Germany’s Wendelstein 7-X project.

Even so, it may still be years before fusion produces large-scale commercial plants.

Matthias Knolker, head technical solutions architect at General Atomics Magnetic Fusion Energy, said grid-connected commercial fusion demonstration plants and power purchase agreements may not emerge until the mid-2030s. GW-scale deployments, he said, may have to wait until the early 2040s.

While fusion research and development continues, SMRs and the rejuvenation of old nuclear plants are more likely to bear fruit on a timeline that matters to data center operators. The first operating SMRs may be only a couple of years away.

“US progress on SMRs is gaining momentum, but regulatory, financing, and workforce barriers remain,” Knolker said.

Cameron Hughes, an associate at law firm Orrick, said nuclear energy will need an all-of-the-above approach that advances traditional large reactors, SMRs, plant restarts, and power uprates. The market, she said, will decide which forms of nuclear energy prove most viable. On the regulatory front, she pointed to progress in reducing long delays, including long Nuclear Regulatory Commission review timelines.

“Recent reforms have cut key reviews to roughly 18 months,” Hughes said. “Additionally, modularization, factory fabrication, and supply chain improvements could compress deployment schedules once initial commercial projects are built.”

The Big Question: Can Nuclear Deliver Fast Enough?

Nuclear energy is clearly advancing on multiple fronts. It is drawing more funding, scientific support, and entrepreneurial interest than it has in decades. Whether that momentum will translate into enough timely capacity to serve the urgent power needs of AI data centers remains an open question.

“The nuclear renaissance is dependent on aligning many factors – science, engineering, capital, political will, and a skilled workforce,” Mahajan said.

text:
The Andersons Inc. today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Harvestone Low Carbon Partners (HLCP), an industry leader in low-carbon ethanol that owns and operates three ethanol production facilities in North Dakota and Indiana from Energy Capital Partners, for $915 million. Approximately half of the purchase price is attributed to expected 45Z and 45Q tax credit cash flows, with the remainder to the underlying base ethanol operations and additional low-carbon opportunities. Upon closing, The Andersons' (the Company) combined ethanol production platform will have approximately 730 million gallons of annual capacity. The purchase price includes a normalized level of working capital. The transaction is subject to customary adjustments and closing conditions.

HLCP has a demonstrated track record of innovation in renewable fuels, including the development and commercialization of vertically integrated carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) capabilities. Its facilities are strategically positioned to serve low-carbon fuel markets, supported by established customer relationships. Its operating CCS infrastructure reduces the carbon intensity of ethanol production and enables the business to capture value through low-carbon fuel markets and applicable tax incentives, with additional benefits anticipated from projects under development.

"Our Renewables strategy is centered on expanding our low-carbon production platform through disciplined investments and capturing the growing value of renewable fuels," said Bill Krueger, president and CEO of The Andersons. "We have been evaluating ethanol plant acquisition opportunities for several years, and HLCP is exactly what we have been looking for. Its production economics, established low-carbon ethanol capabilities, and strategically advantaged locations complement our existing network and together represent a combination that is difficult to replicate. We believe this acquisition strengthens our Renewables business and creates a differentiated platform for profitable growth and attractive long-term returns for our shareholders. We look forward to welcoming the HLCP team to The Andersons."

title: A new bill could change how the US builds energy infrastructure | MIT Technology Review
description:
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.
Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.
But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.
In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too.
text:
A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.

The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.

Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.

title: OEMs, Dealers Balance Stock as Hybrid Demand Dominates Mexico
description:
While North American industry roadmaps once anticipated an accelerated transition directly into battery electric vehicles (BEVs), distribution data from Mexican showrooms indicates a multi-tiered adoption curve.
Plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) expanded 207% to 15,464 units, while fully electric models totaled 13,768 units.
The Charging Deficit and Consumer Preference Tracking Consumer feedback tracked across dealership networks mirrors findings from major institutional automotive surveys.
Routine maintenance on pure battery electric vehicles generates an estimated 30% to 40% less revenue than equivalent ICE or hybrid services due to fewer mechanical moving parts, fluids, and wear items.
Franchised dealers, who rely heavily on service bays for gross profit, are using this data to push OEMs for broader hybrid allocations.
text:
Automotive original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and national dealership networks in Mexico are overhaul­ing commercial inventory forecasting, deploying granular dealer management analytics, regional allocation models, and multi-powertrain showroom strategies to navigate an uneven consumer shift away from pure internal combustion toward electrification.

While North American industry roadmaps once anticipated an accelerated transition directly into battery electric vehicles (BEVs), distribution data from Mexican showrooms indicates a multi-tiered adoption curve. According to domestic market data compiled by the Mexican Association of Automotive Distributors (AMDA) and the Mexican Automotive Industry Association (AMIA), and reported byMexico Business News, electrified vehicle sales reached 95,037 units during the first half of 2026, up 44% year-over-year.

However, standard internal combustion engine (ICE) models continue to represent the vast majority of mainstream automotive retail, while standard hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) dominate low-emission deliveries, claiming 65,805 units during the first six months of the year. Plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) expanded 207% to 15,464 units, while fully electric models totaled 13,768 units. This pronounced disparity has prompted OEM corporate planning offices and independent dealer groups to replace generalized nationwide sales projections with localized monitoring protocols.

Real-Time DMS Integration and Regional Turn Rates

Dealership groups in Mexico’s top metropolitan hubs—principally Mexico City, Guadalajara, and Monterrey—are leveraging modernized Dealer Management Systems (DMS) integrated directly with OEM supply chain portals. These systems track showroom "days-of-supply" metrics broken down strictly by propulsion architecture: ICE, HEV, PHEV, and BEV.

Showroom data indicates that traditional ICE passenger sedans, light commercial vans, and pickup trucks maintain standard inventory turns, cycling off dealership lots within 25 to 35 days. By comparison, high-ticket battery electric SUVs without dedicated fast-charging ecosystems often experience inventory holding cycles exceeding 70 days. Dealerships bear financing costs on floorplanned vehicles, making slow-moving EV stock an immediate threat to operational margins.

To mitigate this financial risk, automakers are utilizing geographic allocation strategies. As highlighted by MBN, 55.7% of all low-emission vehicle sales are concentrated in just four states: Mexico City (21,766 units), the State of Mexico (12,736 units), Nuevo Leon (9,947 units), and Jalisco (8,513 units).

In response, OEMs are concentrating their HEV and PHEV shipments into central metropolitan dealerships where environmental incentives—such as exemption from the capital’s Hoy No Circula driving restrictions and verification tax waivers—create genuine consumer pull. Conversely, distributors across northern industrial hubs and agricultural centers in the Bajio receive heavier allocations of traditional gasoline and diesel utility vehicles, where highway range and heavy payload capacities keep combustion demand resilient.

The Charging Deficit and Consumer Preference Tracking

Consumer feedback tracked across dealership networks mirrors findings from major institutional automotive surveys. According to findings from the EY Mobility Consumer Index, approximately 60% of Mexican consumers still intend to purchase conventional ICE vehicles, while only 23% intend to acquire a pure BEV.

Electric vehicles require specialized diagnostics, high-voltage handling, and new maintenance protocols, yet many independent and dealer workshops continue to rely on tools and expertise designed for combustion engines.

Beyond charging deficits, dealership associations monitor service absorption rates closely. Routine maintenance on pure battery electric vehicles generates an estimated 30% to 40% less revenue than equivalent ICE or hybrid services due to fewer mechanical moving parts, fluids, and wear items. Franchised dealers, who rely heavily on service bays for gross profit, are using this data to push OEMs for broader hybrid allocations.

This consumer and dealer preference for bridge powertrains is reinforced by the J.D. Power Mexico APEAL Study, which reported that hybrid powertrains score the highest levels of customer satisfaction and emotional appeal in Mexico, providing improved fuel economy without requiring access to non-existent public fast-chargers.

OEM Manufacturing Realignments

Automotive manufacturers are adjusting production schedules in Mexican assembly plants to reflect retail demand realities. High-profile strategic shifts, such as Honda's decision to halt production of the Ramos Arizpe-built Prologue EV in favor of expanding its hybrid vehicle lineup across North America, illustrate how assembly lines are reorienting around multi-energy platforms.

At the same time, commercial fleet monitoring through associations like AMAVe (Mexican Association of Vehicle Leasing Companies) indicates that corporate fleet managers are adopting hybrids for urban corporate pools and last-mile logistics to meet ESG targets, while keeping medium- and heavy-duty logistics reliant on diesel ICE until megawatt charging corridors are established along federal freight arteries like Highway 57.

Commercial and Regulatory Outlook

Over the next 18 months, OEMs and distributors will closely track potential tariff changes and trade reviews tied to the USMCA. In particular, potential regulatory revisions by the Ministry of Economy regarding tariff exemptions on imported electric models from Asia will impact competitive showroom pricing against locally built ICE and hybrid vehicles.

For both automaker executive suites and dealership dealer principals, maintaining flexible manufacturing allocations and managing showroom days-of-supply through granular DMS telemetry will remain the primary defense against vehicle inventory stagnation in Mexico’s bifurcated automotive market.

The 15,000-seat soccer stadium will be on the southern portion of the property. It will be available for community events, entertainment, and other sports. The city anticipates it will draw $5.5 million a year in tourism and visitor spending, along with $1.3 million annually in hotel rooms rented. EGLE funding will not be used for costs directly connected to stadium use, specific stadium utilities, or dedicated infrastructure.

One of the goals of this project is to make the stadium and team part of the southwest Detroit community, particularly the Corktown and Mexicantown neighborhoods. That’s why the city of Detroit and the soccer club have agreed on a $2 million community benefits package that will include:

Funding for local non-profits

A revolving loan fund for small businesses

Art and murals that highlight the area’s history

Complimentary tickets for neighborhood groups
