text:
Robinson Carbon plans to invest $16.3 million to establish a biochar manufacturing facility at England Airpark in Alexandria, creating 42 direct jobs and expanding the company’s operations into a new market for Louisiana’s timber industry.

Louisiana Economic Development announced the project, which is expected to generate an additional 60 indirect jobs, bringing the total potential employment impact to 102 jobs in Central Louisiana. The investment also will support the retention of 22 existing positions at Robinson Lumber Company, the fifth-generation family business behind Robinson Carbon.

Construction is scheduled to begin in November, with production expected to start in the second quarter of 2027. The company has begun hiring for its Alexandria operations.

The facility will convert wood manufacturing byproducts into biochar, a carbon-rich material used in agriculture, horticulture and environmental remediation. The project is expected to create a new market for wood residuals generated by Louisiana sawmills.

According to the company, the plant will operate two rotary drum pyrolysis reactors capable of processing approximately 100,000 metric tons of Southern yellow pine residuals annually into 16,500 metric tons of biochar.

The company plans to source raw materials from nearby mills and manufacture biochar to meet customer specifications for applications ranging from soil improvement to pollution remediation.

Robinson Carbon has relocated a pilot reactor from its manufacturing operation in New Albany, Indiana, to Alexandria, where it will be used to train employees before commercial production begins.

The company also expects the facility to generate approximately 40,000 carbon dioxide removal certificates annually once it receives certification under the Puro Standard. Each certificate represents one metric ton of carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere.

Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan B. Bourgeois said the investment demonstrates how the state’s established industries can expand into emerging markets.

“Louisiana has long been a leader in turning our natural resources into products used around the world. For more than 130 years, the Robinson family has been part of that history, and we are grateful for their continued commitment to Louisiana,” Bourgeois said in a statement.

Robinson Carbon is the carbon products division of Robinson Lumber Company, which was founded in New Orleans in 1893. The business has grown from selling Louisiana longleaf pine into an international wood products manufacturing and distribution operation serving customers in more than 70 countries.

“My great-great-grandfather founded our company in New Orleans in 1893 selling Louisiana longleaf pine. Since then, the products have changed many times over, but our passion for wood products hasn’t,” Robinson Carbon CEO Garner Robinson said in a statement. “Biochar is an exciting opportunity to make something truly new out of wood, and we look forward to planting new roots in Central Louisiana.”

The Alexandria project represents the company’s expansion into industrial-scale biochar manufacturing, combining its existing wood products supply network with technology designed to convert timber byproducts into commercial materials.

To secure the investment, Louisiana offered Robinson Carbon an incentives package that includes a $550,000 performance-based grant for site and infrastructure improvements.

The company also is expected to participate in the state’s High Impact Jobs and Industrial Tax Exemption programs, which provide incentives for qualifying business investments and job creation.

England Economic and Industrial Development District Executive Director Ralph Hennessy said the project strengthens England Airpark’s role as a location for industrial development and advanced manufacturing.

Chris Masingill, president and CEO of Louisiana Central, said the investment will connect the region’s established timber industry with new manufacturing opportunities.

“By connecting our region’s longstanding timber and wood products industry with innovative manufacturing technologies, this project strengthens our industrial base, creates high-quality jobs, and opens new markets for Louisiana’s natural resources,” Masingill said in a statement.

text:
By Staff Writer

Arab Finance: Egypt is stepping up efforts to localize automobile manufacturing and related industries, with plans to expand electric vehicle production and increase local content in vehicles, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said during a meeting to review the government's automotive localization plan.

In the meeting attended by Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem and Assistant Minister of Industry for Strategic Affairs Mohamed Sami, Madbouly noted that industrial growth is a key government priority, with a particular focus on the automotive sector.

The government is also prioritizing electric vehicle manufacturing and its inputs as part of its strategy to promote the green transition, reduce reliance on conventional fuels, and lower the import bill, Madbouly added.

For his part, Hashem outlined a partnership involving an unnamed international company, Egyptian industrial group El Araby Group, and the Arab Organization for Industrialization (AOI) to manufacture seven types of metal automotive components locally, targeting an annual output of 8 million units.

Efforts to develop the industry's technical workforce also include cooperation between the Brazilian Association of the Tool Industry (ABINFER) and Egypt's Productivity and Vocational Training Department to establish a vocational school specializing in molds and dies.

In EV battery manufacturing, Hashem highlighted a partnership between an international company and Egyptian bus manufacturer Manufacturing Commercial Vehicles (MCV) to supply batteries for buses, alongside an agreement under development with another international company to provide batteries for vehicles manufactured locally. The ministry is also exploring cooperation with a global manufacturer and AOI to establish domestic production of electric motors.

Hashem said a major international company planned to begin producing three electric vehicle models in 2027, with annual production targeted at 100,000 vehicles by 2032 and 222,000 vehicles by 2032. Local content is expected to start at 10% and rise to 27% by 2032.

The minister also highlighted the start of local EV production by Chinese automaker Dongfeng in partnership with Egypt-based SN Automotive and state-owned El Nasr Automotive Manufacturing Company, using El Nasr's production lines.

Beyond vehicle assembly, the government is working to expand domestic manufacturing of automotive components, including metal parts, batteries, and electric motors.

Alongside these manufacturing initiatives, the government is working to localize laboratory testing for automotive components and upgrade the Engineering Industries Technology Center in 10th of Ramadan City to strengthen technical support for local suppliers.

Hashem also reviewed cooperation with international companies to establish EV charging stations and develop the infrastructure and operating framework needed to support their expansion.

The meeting further addressed progress under the Automotive Industry Development Program (AIDP), which aims to increase local manufacturing within the automotive sector.

The minister discussed incentives and facilities currently under consideration to encourage automakers to establish EV production operations in Egypt, in line with the government's plans to expand the use of clean-energy vehicles.

title: Turkey's solar boom shines ahead of a UN climate summit but coal and other fossil fuels loom large
authors: Mehmet Guzel And Suzan Fraser, Associated Press

text:
KARAPINAR – Row after row of solar panels stretches across a vast landscape in the central Turkish province of Konya, turning sunlight into electricity — and helping Turkey, the host of the upcoming U.N. climate summit, spotlight its efforts to expand renewable energy.

Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Turkey's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.

Campaigners also argue the country lacks concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, which when burned release greenhouse gases that heat the planet.

Turkey’s Energy Ministry says coal remained the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33% of generation. But it stressed that the share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23%.

Turkey has one of Europe's largest solar farms

The town of Karapinar in Konya is home to the Kalyon Karapınar YEKA-1 Solar Power Plant, which boasts more than 3 million solar panels perched on a terrain equivalent to the size of 2,600 soccer fields.

Operational since 2023, it generates enough electricity each year to meet about 0.7% of the country’s power demand, according to plant director Burak Dogru.

“We prevent approximately 1.75 million metric tons of carbon emissions every year,” Dogru told The Associated Press — evidence, he says, of how Turkey has been directing its economy and energy sector toward cleaner energy sources.

Turkey’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, the last year for which data is available, reached 584.5 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.

Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Turkey has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.

“But these plans contain neither a roadmap for a coal phase-out, nor any planning for a phase-out of other fossil fuels, including gas,” Kutluay cautioned, adding that this is "not compatible” with Turkey's pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2053.

Turkey is also looking to nuclear power to reduce its energy dependence. The country’s first plant is under construction on the Mediterranean coast, with plans for additional reactors still under consideration.

Concerns and criticism rise ahead of the summit

Some 265 kilometers (165 miles) away from Konya, the Nov. 9-20 summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya will bring together tens of thousands of delegates, world leaders, business and civil society representatives for discussions on implementing climate goals.

The summit — officially, the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 — comes against a backdrop of deepening concerns over energy security and the Iran war, which has led to a rise in gas and oil prices and sent countries scrambling to meet energy needs.

Many experts have recently argued that a key mission — combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions — has been failing.

The United States, the world’s richest nation and second-biggest carbon polluter after China, will again be absent from the summit, after U.S. President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from global climate negotiations.

And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.

Turkey’s environment and climate change minister, Murat Kurum, who will preside over the summit, has said he wants COP31 to focus on turning climate commitments into action rather than new targets.

To that aim, Turkey will push a “climate implementation bridge,” an initiative to help countries turn climate pledges into action by connecting them with financing, technology and other support.

“Today, the world is not merely waiting for new decisions," Kurum said while presenting summit priorities earlier this year. "What the world wants is to see past decisions put into practice.”

Turkey has cast itself as an environment steward

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted his country is committed to environmental protection and combating climate change, and first lady Emine Erdogan has championed a “zero waste” campaign to encourage recycling and a more responsible use of resources.

COP31 will also prioritize electrification and reduction of waste and methane emissions, Kurum has said.

However, the Climate Action Tracker, which measures countries’ progress against goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement, has described Turkey’s climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient.”

The agreement set a target of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to the early 1800s, directing countries to develop policies that would help meet that goal.

Meanwhile, human rights groups accuse Ankara of dismissing environmental concerns and frequently arresting activists.

Earlier this year, a court annulled an environmental impact assessment for a planned expansion of a coal-fired power plant at Afsin-Elbistan in southeastern Turkey. The ruling was hailed by environmentalists as a major victory.

But shortly afterward, plans emerged to expand another coal-fired power plant in Canakkale, in the country's northwest.

Like other Mediterranean nations, Turkey faces mounting risks from heat waves, drought, water scarcity, wildfires and flooding. Last month, rains described as the heaviest in more than 80 years caused severe floods in Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city, and left eight people dead.

Turkey was announced as the host of COP31 following a tug-of-war with Australia, which also wanted to host the summit. As a compromise, Australia has been leading consultations to help set the summit's agenda and will be in charge of summit discussions.

Climate advocates have slammed the summit for being awarded to coal-reliant Turkey; coal-exporter Australia has also come under criticism.

But U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell defended the choice, saying in February that a COP host country’s status on fossil fuels does not determine the success or failure of a summit.

With “Turkey and Australia leading this process, there is every opportunity to deliver a very strong outcome," he said.

___

Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey. Associated Press journalists Serra Yedikardes in Trabzon, Turkey, and Ayse Wieting in Istanbul contributed to this report.
